en: Śrīḥ.
Salutation to the illustrious Rāmānuja.
Salutation to Śrī. Salutation to Śrīdhara.

By means of the two preceding chapters, the following meaning has been established: "The Vedāntas teach that Brahman—the sole cause of the entire universe, from whom even a trace of defect is removed, who is an ocean of immeasurable and sublime attributes, and who is distinct from everything else—is the object of worship for those seeking liberation. This conclusion is presented together with the purification of the essential nature of the subject matter—consisting of the removal of contradictions with Smṛti and logic, the refutation of opposing views, and the resolution of internal inconsistencies within the Vedāntic texts—as well as the reasons why that [Brahman] is invulnerable to attack.
Thus it has been established. Therefore, the true nature of Brahman has been expounded in these two chapters.
Now, following this, the manner of attainment together with the means for attaining it is intended to be considered.

In this regard, the third chapter contains an inquiry concerning meditation, which serves as the means [to liberation]. The means suitable for the commencement of meditation consists of detachment from objects other than the goal to be attained, and the cessation of craving; for the sake of establishing these, the defects of the individual soul (*jīva*)—as it wanders through other worlds, and in its states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and fainting—are examined.
Furthermore, the fact that the "Supreme" Brahman is free from such defects and possesses auspicious qualities are set forth in the first and second sections (*pādas*).

In this regard, there arises the inquiry: when this individual soul (jīva) goes from one body to another body, does it go enveloped by the subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣma), which are the causes for the commencement of the next body, or not?

The meaning of this [passage] is as follows: prior to the words "ityayamarthaḥ," the subject matter of the first chapter has been summarized. The meaning of the qualifiers beginning with "nikhila" (entire) is as explained previously. By the phrase "smṛtinyāya" (tradition and logic), the subject matter of the first and second quarters of the second chapter is summarized. By the phrase beginning with "vedāntavākya" (Vedāntic statements), the subject matter of the third and fourth quarters is summarized. Thus, the subject matter of the two chapters has been stated with some detail. With the word "ataḥ" (therefore), he states in brief the underlying meaning common to the first pair [of chapters].

"By the subsequent [section]" means a summary of the meaning of the latter two pairs. Now—meaning, the object being established; in the first pair, reflection on the nature of the already-established object was performed, whereas in the second, reflection on the nature of the object to be established is now performed.

Regarding the phrase "therein": the subject matter of the third chapter consists of the means (*sādhana*) and the fruit (*phala*), which follow a sequential order. "Preeminent" means internal (*antaraṅga*). Here, the intended meaning of the statement "he who is attached to the Supreme Self is detached from the non-Supreme Self" is what is meant. The defects of one wandering through other worlds are considered; therein, the defects of one in states such as waking have been brought to fruition.

Regarding this: Does the individual soul (*jīva*), when proceeding to another body, travel enveloped by the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*), or is it not so enveloped? Since it has been stated, "Do you know how, at the fifth libation, water comes to be called 'man'?", and since the subtle elements are easily available wherever the soul goes, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it travels unenveloped. Later, [the author] will set forth and refute the seeds of this prima facie view.

Having asked, "Do you know Prāvahaṇa of Pañcāla, the destination for those who perform ritual acts; the manner of their return; the divergence of the paths of the gods and the fathers; and that one who does not attain that world? he further asked this: "Do you know how, in the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called 'man'? Then, answering this final question, [the teacher] described the heavenly world as a fire: "In this very fire, the gods offer faith (*śraddhā*) as an oblation. From that oblation, King Soma comes into being."

By these and other passages, [it is shown that] the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) of the individual soul (*jīva*), known as the gods, cast the substance called faith (*śraddhā*) into the heavenly world, which is metaphorically represented as fire. That faith then transforms into a body consisting of nectar, known as King Soma. Those same vital breaths then cast that nectarian body into the rain-cloud, which is metaphorically represented as fire. That body, once cast there, becomes rain.

And they cast that year into the earth, which has been represented as fire; and that [year] thus cast there becomes food. And they cast that food into the person, who has been represented as fire; and that [food] thus cast there becomes semen. And they cast that semen into the woman, who has been represented as fire; and that [semen] thus cast there becomes an embryo—having said this, he says:
"But thus, at the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called 'man'"; the meaning is that when the fifth oblation has been offered, the waters become designated by the word "man."

By the passage beginning with "five fires" (*pañcāgni*), he shows that the context consists of a sequence of multiple questions and their respective answers, in order to dispel the suspicion that there might be an interruption by some other subject matter. One should not suspect that "an answer concerning the embrace by the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*) is not seen immediately following the question. The term "differentiation" (*vyāvartane*) refers to the two forms of that which differentiates. The phrase "by [the words] beginning with 'ityādinā'" connects with what follows later: "'uktavāha' (he said). By the word *śraddhā*, a particular state of the subtle elements is denoted.

The term "amṛtamaya-deha" (body consisting of nectar) is an explanation of the term "somarāja" (king of Soma). "Prāṇāḥ" refers to the vital breaths (mukhya-prāṇa) and the sense organs. Regarding the word "prakṣipanti" (they cast in): the intention is that the act of casting, which is dependent upon the vital breaths, is figuratively treated as a *homa* (oblation). In the compound "puru-cavacasaḥ," only a general relationship is understood through the *bahuvrīhi* formation. In this context, the word "puruṣa" refers to the essential nature (*svarūpa*), while the word "vacaḥ" refers to the expressive signifier (*vācaka*).
Therefore, in order to demonstrate that "the relationship established by the compound is a specific form known as the signifier-signified relation," it was stated: "denotable by the word *puruṣa*."

When this was said—it is stated that even in the preceding oblations, it is the subtle forms of the waters themselves that now assume the form of a person. Therefore, by means of these questions and answers, it is understood that [the soul] "goes along with the subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣma) which serve as the causes of the body, from place to place. || 1 ||

Now, an objection is raised: "When it is said, 'The waters take the form of a person,' since there is the perception of the transformation of the waters into the shape of a person, it follows that they alone are embraced by the departing soul. Therefore, how can it be that all the subtle elements of the gross bodies are embraced? To this, [the Sūtra] replies: **3.1.2. But because of their consisting of three elements, and because of their predominance.** The word "but" (*tu*) sets aside the objection. It is not the case that only the waters which initiate the body are meant. Why? Because they consist of the three elements. Since water is the most predominant among them, it is designated by its own name. Just as a mixture of curd and honey is called simply "curd," so too, because of the predominance of water, the entire aggregate is referred to as "waters. Furthermore, the presence of the other elements is established by the fact that the body possesses the qualities of all three elements—heat, moisture, and motility. Thus, it is all the subtle elements of the gross body that are embraced by the soul. This is the conclusion.

Thus: In both the question and the answer, when it is stated, "In the fifth oblation, the waters [become] man-like," since there is an expectancy for the substance to be offered (*hotavya-dravya*), the waters themselves—which are proximate as being situated within their own sentence—are naturally understood as the things to be offered. *Śraddhā* (faith), which resides in another sentence, is unfit to undergo transformation into the form of King Soma; therefore, that too is merely an indicator of the waters.

Regarding the phrase "consisting of *jyā*" (*jyātmaka*): the connection of the first word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamyanta*)—namely, "enveloped, it moves" (*saṃpariṣvakto raṃhati*)—is indicated by the word "envelopment" (*pariṣvaṅga*) found in the text of the objection. For the second word ending in the fifth case, the statement of the proposition (*pratijñāvākya*)—"the possibility of the commencement of the body"—is supplied by implication (*sāmarthyāt*). [This is because] when there is the commencement of the body and so forth, [the scripture says]: "Of those [elements], he made each one threefold. (*tāsāṃ trivṛtaṃ trivṛtamekaikāmakarot*) "Chandogyopaniṣad 6.3.3. And: "He made fire threefold. (*tejo 'mūm trivṛtamakarot*) "Chandogyopaniṣad 6.4.2. And: "He made water threefold. (*āpa imāṃ trivṛtamakurvan*) "Chandogyopaniṣad 6.4.3. And: "He made food threefold. (*annamimāṃ trivṛtamakarot*) "Chandogyopaniṣad 6.4.4. And: "He made speech threefold. (*vācaṃ trivṛtamakarot*) "Chandogyopaniṣad 6.5.1. And: "He made the breath threefold. (*prāṇaṃ trivṛtamakarot*) "Chandogyopaniṣad 6.7.1. And: "He made the eye threefold. (*cakṣustrivṛtamakarot*) "Chandogyopaniṣad 6.5.3. And: "He made the ear threefold. (*śrotraṃ trivṛtamakarot*) "Chandogyopaniṣad 6.7.2. And: "He made the mind threefold. (*manastrivṛtamakarot*) "Chandogyopaniṣad 6.5.4. And: "He made the skin threefold. (*tvacaṃ trivṛtamakarot*) "Chandogyopaniṣad 6.5.5. And: "He made the intellect threefold. (*dharmaṃ trivṛtamakarot*) "Chandogyopaniṣad

Thus ends the tripartition. As for the mention of water alone, it is because of its predominance; and since blood and so forth predominate in the body, the predominance of water among the constituent elements is thereby understood. || 2 ||

290. And because of the departure of the vital breaths. (Siddhānta) For this reason also, it is understood that "the soul must depart enveloped by the subtle elements. When the individual soul departs, the departure of the vital breaths following it is heard in scripture: [ŚBh 3.1.1] "When he departs, the vital breaths depart after him. [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.6] "When he departs, all the vital breaths depart after him. [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2] "When he departs, his speech follows. [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2] "When he departs, his mind follows. [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2] "When he departs, his sight follows. [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2] "When he departs, his hearing follows. [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2] "When he departs, his breath follows. Since the vital breaths follow the departing soul, they must necessarily be accompanied by their respective substrata, the subtle elements. Therefore, the soul departs enveloped by the subtle elements. Furthermore, the scripture states: [Praśna Upaniṣad 3.10] "When he departs from this body, he passes into the breath; the breath into fire; the fire into the sun; the sun into the supreme deity. Thus, the soul's departure is established as being enveloped by the subtle elements. Moreover, the scripture says: [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.1] "When he departs, he departs with the subtle essence of water. This shows that the soul departs enveloped by the subtle element of water. Since the other subtle elements are invariably associated with water, it is understood that the soul departs enveloped by all the subtle elements. Therefore, it is established that the soul departs enveloped by the subtle elements. End of section 1. Section 2: Whether the soul departs through an opening or through the entire body. Sūtra 1: [Sūtra 3.1.12] "And because of the scriptural statement regarding the smallness [of the heart]. (Pūrvapakṣa) It is not established that the soul departs enveloped by the subtle elements. Why? Because the scripture speaks of its smallness. [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.1] "This person consists of food, within the heart there is a space as small as a grain of rice or a grain of barley; within that is the person consisting of life-breath. [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.3.3] "Within the heart there is a space as small as a grain of rice or a grain of barley; within that is the person consisting of mind. [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.5] "Within the heart there is a space as small as a grain of rice or a grain of barley; within that is the person consisting of consciousness. [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.3] "Within the heart there is a space as small as a grain of rice or a grain of barley; within that is the person consisting of bliss. Since the soul is described as being of such minute size, it cannot possibly depart enveloped by the subtle elements. Therefore, it is not established that the soul departs enveloped by the subtle elements. Furthermore, the scripture says: [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.6] "When he departs, he departs upwards through this very artery. This indicates that the soul departs through a specific opening. Therefore, it is not established that the soul departs enveloped by the subtle elements. Sūtra 2: [Sūtra 3.1.13] "But [it departs] through the whole [body], because of the mention of the feet and so forth. (Siddhānta) The word "but" refutes the previous view. It is not the case that the soul departs through a specific opening. Rather, it departs through the entire body. Why? Because of the mention of the feet and so forth. [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.6] "When he departs, he departs either through the feet or through any other part of the body. [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2] "When he departs, his speech follows. Since the scripture mentions that the soul departs through the feet or any other part of the body, it is understood that it departs through the entire body. Therefore, it is established that the soul departs enveloped by the subtle elements. End of section 2. Section 3: Whether the soul departs with the subtle elements or without them. Sūtra 3: [Sūtra 3.1.14] "And because of the connection with the subtle elements. (Pūrvapakṣa) It is not established that the soul departs enveloped by the subtle elements. Why? Because the scripture speaks of its connection with the subtle elements. [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.5] "When he departs, he departs together with the subtle elements. Since the scripture speaks of the soul's connection with the subtle elements, it is understood that the soul departs without being enveloped by them. Therefore, it is not established that the soul departs enveloped by the subtle elements. Sūtra 4: [Sūtra 3.1.15] "But [it departs] with [them], because of the necessity of the connection. (Siddhānta) The word "but" refutes the previous view. It is not the case that the soul departs without being enveloped by the subtle elements. Rather, it departs with them. Why? Because of the necessity of the connection. Since the subtle elements are the substrata for the vital breaths, and the vital breaths follow the departing soul, the subtle elements must necessarily accompany them. Therefore, it is established that the soul departs enveloped by the subtle elements. End of section 3. Section 4: Whether the soul departs with the subtle elements alone or with the gross elements as well. Sūtra 5: [Sūtra 3.1.16] "And because of the mention of the gross elements. (Pūrvapakṣa) It is not established that the soul departs enveloped by the subtle elements. Why? Because the scripture mentions the gross elements. [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.5] "When he departs, he goes to the air; the air opens up a door for him; he goes to the sun; the sun opens up a door for him; he goes to the moon; the moon opens up a door for him; he goes to the world of Brahman. Since the scripture mentions the gross elements such as air and so forth, it is understood that the soul departs with these gross elements as well. Therefore, it is not established that the soul departs enveloped by the subtle elements alone. Sūtra 6: [Sūtra 3.1.17] "But [it departs] with the subtle [elements], because of the necessity of the connection. (Siddhānta) The word "but" refutes the previous view. It is not the case that the soul departs with the gross elements. Rather, it departs with the subtle elements. Why? Because of the necessity of the connection. Since the gross elements are composed of the subtle elements, and the subtle elements are the primary constituents, the soul departs enveloped by the subtle elements. Therefore, it is established that the soul departs enveloped by the subtle elements. End of section 4. Section 5: Whether the soul departs with the subtle elements alone or with the organs as well. Sūtra 7: [Sūtra 3.1.18] "And because of the mention of the organs. (Pūrvapakṣa) It is not established that the soul departs enveloped by the subtle elements alone. Why? Because the scripture mentions the organs. [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2] "When he departs, his speech follows. [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2] "When he departs, his mind follows. Since the scripture mentions the organs such as speech and so forth, it is understood that the soul departs with these organs
"As he departs, the vital breath (prāṇa) departs after him; as the vital breath departs, all the vital functions (prāṇas) depart after it.
And it is also recorded in the Smṛti:

"The Lord draws away the senses, of which the mind is the sixth, when they are situated in their source; whatever body he acquires and from whatever body he departs, taking these [senses] with him, he goes forth, as the wind carries fragrances from their receptacles. Since movement is not possible for things that lack a substratum, it must be admitted that the subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣma), which serve as the substratum for those [senses], also move. || 3 ||

Regarding the phrase "of the pure [elements]": in the sūtra beginning with "on account of their distinctness" (vaiśeṣyāt), it was stated that even among those elements that have been triplicated, the designation for each is based on the predominance of one [element]. However, this present sūtra is commenced in order to show that here, moreover, there is an excess of that [specific element]. || 2 ||
And [the word] "from here" (itaḥ) is for the purpose of excluding the connection with the intermediate probandum. || 3 ||

291. "If it be argued that [the soul] goes [to the deities] because of the scriptural mention of its going to Agni and others, we say no, because that is metaphorical. (Siddhānta-sūtra 3.1.4) "Where, when this person has died, speech enters into fire, breath into the wind, and the eye into the sun..."

If it is argued that, because of such passages as these which state that at the time of a living being's death the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) merge into fire and other elements, they do not travel together with the soul, and therefore the "scriptural statement of movement" must be interpreted otherwise—[we reply]:
no, because the statement regarding their merging into fire and so forth is figurative (*bhākta*).
How is it figurative?

"Herbs [are the dissolution] of the body hairs, and trees [are the dissolution] of the hair of the head," because this is heard in connection with the body hairs and so forth which do not merge [into the earth]. Therefore, the scriptural statement regarding the merging of the eye and other organs is intended to refer to the departure of the presiding deities. || 4 ||
292. "If it be argued that [the soul does not go enveloped by water] because it is not heard of in the first [offering], we say no, for it is those very [waters] that are appropriate.

(Sūtra 3.1.5, Siddhānta) As for what was stated—that from the question and the answer it is understood that "the individual soul (jīva) goes enveloped by subtle waters mixed with the other elements"—that is not tenable; because in the first oblation concerning the fire of the heavenly world, water is not heard of as being the substance to be offered (*homya*).

If it is argued: "In this very fire, the gods offer faith (*śraddhā*)," and since faith alone is heard as the object of the oblation, and faith is indeed heard as a particular mental modification of the individual soul (*jīva*), therefore water is not the object of the oblation there—if this is said, we reply:
No; because those waters themselves are designated by the word "faith" in that context. Why? Because of the consistency of the question and the answer.

Regarding the question, "Do you know how, in the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called 'man'?", at the beginning of the answer, faith (*śraddhā*) is heard as the substance to be offered into the fire of the heavenly world. In that context, if the word "faith" did not denote the waters, then the question would be one thing and the answer another, which would be inconsistent.
Thus it is said: "But in the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called 'man'."

Thus, both the response and the conclusion indicate the very path of faith (*śraddhā*). For the manner [of the process] contained in the question—"Do you know how?"—is concluded by the word "thus" (*iti*) in the response at the end of the fifth [section], as in the phrase "But thus in the fifth.

By saying "it is concluded," it means that because the manner contained in the question is concluded at the end of the response, even in the middle [of the passage], having described the transformation of the waters (*ap*) through the forms of faith, King Soma, rain, food, semen, and the embryo, it is concluded with the words: "In this way, the waters take on human speech."
Furthermore, the non-Vedic usage of the word *śraddhā* for "water" is observed:
"He brings forward the water; for water is indeed faith (*śraddhā*)."

"They offer faith as an oblation; from that oblation, King Soma arises"—thus, this transformation into the form of Soma is possible only for water itself. Therefore, it is logical that the individual soul (jīva) departs enveloped by waters mixed with other elements. || 5 ||

293. "If it be argued that [the soul does not go enveloped by water] because it is not mentioned [in the text], we say no, because those who perform sacrifices and other works are understood [from the context]. (Sūtra 3.1.6, Siddhānta) As for what was stated—that the meaning "the individual soul goes enveloped by water" is understood from this very passage—that is not tenable; for the soul is not heard of in this sentence. For here, it is faith (*śraddhā*) and the other elements in their specific states that are heard of as being the things to be offered in the oblation (*homya*), and not the soul enveloped by them—if this is the objection?

That is not so, because those who perform sacrifices and other rites (*iṣṭādikārin*) are clearly understood [from scripture]. For in this very passage, later on, it is stated: "Those who perform sacrifices, works of public utility (*apūrta*), and acts of charity, but are devoid of knowledge of Brahman, reach the heavenly world and become kings of Soma; and at the conclusion of their meritorious deeds, they return again and enter a womb. Starting from the words: "Now, those who in this village worship through sacrifices, works of public utility, and charity, they pass into smoke...
and so forth.

"From the world of the fathers to space, from space to the moon—this is King Soma, the food of the gods; the gods eat it. Having dwelt there as long as the [karmic] momentum lasts, they then return again by that very same path. For whoever eats the food and whoever sheds the semen, he becomes that very thing again. Here too, [the sequence is] from the heavenly world to fire.

"‘They offer faith as an oblation; from that oblation, King Soma arises’—since this has the same meaning [as the previous passage], it is understood that what is stated is that the soul, characterized by a body in the state of faith, becomes characterized by a body in the form of Soma. A word denoting a body, whose sole nature is to be a qualification of the living being (jīva), ultimately refers back to the qualified entity, the living being itself. Therefore, it is established that ‘the living being goes enveloped [by water]. || 6 ||

But is it not the case that in this very sentence—the meaning being "in this great sentence"—the state of being eaten by the gods is expressed in the phrase, "The gods eat him"? The meaning is that since the preceding sentence, in which the connection with the individual soul (*jīva*) is not explicit, has the same sense as the subsequent sentence, in which the connection with the individual soul is explicit, the stated meaning alone is correct. [The phrase] "of the body" [is explained as follows].

The Section Concerning the Passing Away of What Has Been Done (Kṛtātyayādhikaraṇa). || 3.1.2 ||
295. When the performed [karman] has been exhausted, one returns with a remainder (anuśaya), according to what is seen and what is remembered; both in the same manner as before and not so. (3.1.8)

It is taught that those who perform only sacrifices (iṣṭa), public works (pūrta), and acts of charity (datta) travel by the path of the fathers (pitṛyāṇa) via smoke and so forth, and upon the exhaustion of the fruits of their karma, they return again— as it is said: "Having dwelt there until the [exhaustion of their] merits, they then return again by this very same path."

In this regard, a doubt arises as to whether the soul descending [from heaven] descends with a remainder of its karma (*anuśaya*), or without it. What is the correct view? Since the entirety of the karma has been experienced, the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it does not descend with a remainder; for a "remainder" (*anuśaya*) is indeed karma left over after being experienced, and that is not left over when the fruit of the whole has been enjoyed. Furthermore, the statement "having dwelt there as long as the [karma] lasts" (*yāvat-sampātam uṣitvā*) makes known that there is complete enjoyment. "By means of this they go to the heavenly world" (*saṃpatanti anena svargaṃ lokam*); thus, *sampāta* refers to karma. And there is another scriptural passage:
"Whatever this person does here, he reaches the end of that karma;
from that world, he returns again to this world for the sake of karma.
Thus it is said.

This being the position reached, it is replied: "One who possesses residual karma (anuśaya) descends. Why? Because of both perception (dṛṣṭa) and scripture (smṛti)—that is to say, from Śruti and Smṛti. As for Śruti:

"Now, those here whose conduct has been pleasant, they quickly attain a pleasant womb—either the womb of a Brāhmaṇa, the womb of a Kṣatriya, or the womb of a Vaiśya. But those here whose conduct has been foul, they quickly attain a foul womb—the womb of a dog, the womb of a pig, or the womb of a Caṇḍāla."

Thus, with reference to those who have descended [to earth], there is the scriptural passage beginning, "Among those who have descended from that world, some perform pleasant deeds, some have pleasant conduct," and so forth. Does this sentence indicate that the words *saṃpāta* and the like refer to actions engaged in for the purpose of yielding results? Or does it not? Furthermore, in this context, does the word *caraṇa* refer to conduct (*ācāra*), or does it refer to good and evil deeds (*sukṛta-duṣkṛta*)?

When that [word *ācāra*] is understood as referring to conduct (*ācāra*), then, because the word "sampāta" and so forth in that statement would not be understood as referring to karma engaged in the bestowal of results, the statement "as far as the *sampāta*" and so forth would contradict the departure of one who possesses residual karma (*sānuśaya*); thus, it might be concluded that one departs without residual karma (*niranuśaya*). When, however, the word "conduct" (*ācaraṇa*) refers to good and evil deeds (*sukṛta-duṣkṛta*);

Then, because the words "saṃpāta" and so forth are understood—through their syntactical unity with such passages as "those who here have performed pleasant conduct"—to refer to karma that has begun to yield its fruit, and because the passage "as far as the saṃpāta" is not in conflict with the view that one returns with a remainder of karma (sānuśaya), it is established that "one returns with a remainder of karma."

"At the exhaustion of what has been done" (*kṛtātyaye*) means upon the destruction of performed action through its experience. Regarding the word "that" (*tat*): the pronoun *tat* refers to action in general. Regarding the phrase "they fall together" (*sampatanti*): the intention is that if the expression "as far as the falling" (*yāvatsampātam*) were taken to mean "until the falling," the sentence would be redundant. By the word "seen" (*dṛṣṭa*), direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*) is intended. The word *abhyāśaḥ* is in the nominative plural, like the word *diśaḥ*.

This form arises from the root *aś* (meaning "pervasion") preceded by the prefix *abhi*. Those who are "near" (*abhyāśa*) here—meaning those who are about to arrive—are "those of pleasant conduct" (*ramaṇīyacaraṇāḥ*), that is, those of good deeds;

they attain a pleasant womb, such as that of a Brāhmaṇa or others. Those of "evil conduct" (*kapūyacaraṇāḥ*), meaning those of despicable deeds, attain a despicable womb, such as that of a dog, a pig, or a Caṇḍāla. Thus, it demonstrates the connection with meritorious and sinful karma for those who have descended [from the world of Brahman].
Smṛti also states:

"The castes and stages of life, being devoted to their own duties, after experiencing the fruits of their actions in the hereafter, are then—by means of what remains—reborn with distinguished place, birth, family, form, lifespan, learning, wealth, conduct, happiness, and intelligence; whereas those who act otherwise, being contrary [to their duty], perish. Likewise, [it says]:

Then, upon returning, by the remainder of the fruits of their karma, they obtain birth, form, complexion, strength, intelligence, wisdom, wealth, and the performance of dharma; thus, like a wheel, it proceeds only toward happiness in both worlds.

Thus [it is said]: the phrase "as far as the completion" (*yāvat-sampātam*) refers specifically to those particular actions that have begun to yield their results. The statement "whatever he does here" (*yat kiñceha karoty ayam*) also refers to that same category. Furthermore, it is logically untenable for actions whose fruits have not yet been experienced, nor for those for which the prescribed expiation has already been performed, to be destroyed by the experience of the fruits of other actions. Therefore, having gone to this world, they return again with their residual karma (*sānuśayā eva*)—meaning they return both by the same manner of ascent and by a different manner.

The ascent is indeed by way of smoke, night, the waning fortnight, the southern solstice, the six months, the world of the ancestors (pitṛloka), and space, reaching the moon. The descent, however, is from the station of the moon by way of space, wind, smoke, mist, and cloud. Among these, [the descent] up to space is "as it came" (yathetam); because of the attainment of wind and so forth, and the non-attainment of the world of the ancestors and so forth, it is "not as it came" (an-evam). 8.

296. If it be argued that [the word *caraṇa*] refers to [karma], we say no; Kārṣṇājini holds that it is for the purpose of indicating [the agent]. (3.1.9) In the passages "those of pleasant conduct" (*ramaṇīyacaraṇāḥ*) and "those of foul conduct" (*kapūyacaraṇāḥ*), the word *caraṇa* does not denote action in the form of merit or demerit; for the word *caraṇa* is well-known in both common usage and the Veda as meaning "conduct" (*ācāra*).

Indeed, people in the world consider "conduct," "custom" (*ācāra*), "character" (*śīla*), and "behavior" (*vṛtta*) to be synonyms. And in the Veda: "Those actions which are blameless—those should be practiced."

"Those good deeds which are ours, those you must follow"—thus, conduct (*caraṇa*) and action (*karman*) are designated as distinct. Therefore, if it is argued that the attainment of a particular womb results from conduct—that is, from character (*śīla*)—and not from residual karma (*anuśaya*), that is not so. For the teacher Kārṣṇājini maintains that "the scriptural mention of conduct is intended to indicate action," because the attainment of pleasure and pain cannot result from mere behavior alone; for pleasure and pain are indeed the fruits of actions consisting of merit and demerit. (9)

297. "If it be argued that [the Smṛti] is useless, we say no, because it is dependent upon that. (Sūtra 3-1-10, Siddhānta) If it is thus argued: "Since the conduct prescribed by the Smṛti yields no fruit, it is indeed useless"—[we reply: No, because merit depends upon it. Only one who possesses right conduct (*ācāravat*) is entitled to perform meritorious acts. As the *Dakṣasmṛti* states: "One who neglects the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*) is eternally impure and unfit for all rites"; and as the *Vasiṣṭhasmṛti* says: "The Vedas do not purify one who is devoid of good conduct. Therefore, that [objection] is not valid.
From such statements as these, the intention of Kārṣṇājini is that the scriptural mention of "conduct" (caraṇa) is intended as an indicative mark for ritual action (karman). || 10 ||

298. "It is only good and evil deeds," so says Bādari (Sūtra 3.1.11). Because the verb *carati* is used in the sense of action in such expressions as "he performs a meritorious act" (*puṇyaṃ karma ācarati*) and "he performs a sinful act" (*pāpaṃ karma ācarati*), and because the separate mention [of *karma* and *caraṇa*] is justified by the maxim of the "cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*)—since it refers respectively to what is established by direct Vedic revelation and what is established by inference from observed conduct—it is not proper to resort to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) when the primary meaning is possible. Therefore, the teacher Bādari maintains that "only good and evil deeds are denoted by the word *caraṇa*."

"In this regard," it is accepted that Bādari’s own view is that the fruit of rites such as the twilight worship (sandhyāvandana), which are enjoined by scriptural texts inferred from traditional practice (ācāra), is the accomplishment of the qualification for other ritual acts. Therefore, those who depart [from this world] do so indeed with their residual karma (sānuśaya). 11.
The Section Concerning Those Who Perform Unrighteous Acts and the Like [3.1.3] (Sūtras 12–21).
299. And it is heard in scripture that even those who perform unrighteous acts and the like go there. [3.1.12] (Pūrva-pakṣa) What is the correct view? That they too go to the moon.
Why? Because their going there also is heard in scripture:
"Whoever departs from this world, they all go to the moon," since the departure of all without distinction is thus declared. (12)

If that is so, then the destination for both those who perform good deeds and those who perform evil deeds would be indistinguishable. (Objection: But [the destination] must be distinct, because it is observed that for others there is ascending and descending after they have experienced [their results] in Saṃyamana (the world of Yama). (Sūtra 3.1.13) This would be the case.

He says "no," because the word "all" has as its scope all *pretas* (departed spirits), since the statement beginning with "whosoever they may be" makes it known that everyone reaches the moon; thus, even those who perform undesirable acts, after experiencing torments, go to the moon and then return.

When the statement regarding the completion of the other world makes it understood that the third station—the formation of the body—does not depend on the fifth libation, then, because the attainment of manhood does not depend on the fifth libation, the introductory phrase "those who [do these]" is understood to refer specifically to those who perform sacrifices and the like (iṣṭādikārins) within the path of the fathers (pitṛyāṇa). Consequently, since that path is not accessible to those who do not perform sacrifices and the like, the word "all" refers only to those who perform sacrifices and the like; thus, by the sentence beginning with "whosoever they may be," [the text establishes] all [of them].
From the understanding of the passage concerning Candra-nāṭya, it is established that those who perform undesirable deeds do not go to the moon.

By the word "iṣṭādi," the acts of sacrifice (iṣṭa) and works of public utility (pūrta) are meant. Here, the scriptural implication regarding the necessity of the fifth libation for the commencement of a body is also intended. || 12 ||
"It would be indistinguishable" means that there would be a lack of fruitfulness for evil.
"But having experienced the ascent to and descent from the moon, [they undergo] torment under the command of Yama," because their destination is seen to be thus.

The word "but" (*tu*) sets aside a doubt. For "others"—namely those who perform undesirable acts and so forth—the ascent to and descent from the moon occurs only after experiencing the torments inflicted by him under the command of Yama in Saṃyamana, and not otherwise.

Why? Because their destination is seen. For indeed, the going there of those who have committed evil deeds is observed through their subjection to Yama; as in such passages as: "The man who thinks, 'This world exists, but the next does not,' falls again and again under my sway"; and "Vaivasvata, the gathering place of people, King Yama," and so forth. (13)
And they record this:
(Purvapakṣa 301) "And Parāśara and others record that all [beings] are subject to Yama."
"And all these, O Blessed One, indeed come under the power of Yama," and so forth. || 14 ||
"Even seven" (Pūrva-pakṣa).
They also remember seven hells, beginning with Raurava, as places to be traversed by those who perform evil deeds. 15.
"In Saṃyamana" is the locative case used in the sense of a cause; it means "by the command of Yama. "This world" means that there is no happiness here or in the hereafter. || 13 ||

Regarding the objection that the challenge remains as it was because no experience of the fruits of evil is heard of in the passage cited under the sūtra "Because their destination is seen" (3.1.12), the sūtra states: "And they [the Smṛtis] record this. (3.1.13).
"Even seven": this is not mentioned because the descriptions of the hells are already well known through their extreme renown. 15.

"O Blessed One, it is indeed traditionally remembered that all beings fall under the power of Yama; for by such traditional recollection (smṛti), their subjection to Yama is proclaimed. [The meaning of the Sūtra: Regarding others—those who perform undesirable acts—the sages remember that they must reach even the seven hells, numbering seven, beginning with Raurava.
"And it is understood that there are seven worlds for them, beginning with Raurava; having experienced the torments there, it is said that they proceed further."

[Objection: But how can those traveling through the seven worlds reach the abode of Yama? To this, he says: 303. "Even there, because of his activity, there is no contradiction" (Pūrva-pakṣa). Since they travel even to those seven [worlds] only by the command of Yama, there is no contradiction. || 16 ||

Therefore, when it is argued that even those who perform undesirable acts reach the world of Yama, undergo torments corresponding to their own deeds, and subsequently experience ascent to and descent from the moon, the following is stated:

**304. But [the path] is for knowledge and action, because they are the subjects under discussion.** (Siddhānta Sūtra 3.1.17) The word "but" (*tu*) serves to set aside the previous position. It is not tenable to say that "even those who perform undesirable acts reach the moon. Why? Because of the phrase "for knowledge and action. This is because the paths of the gods (*devayāna*) and the fathers (*pitṛyāṇa*) exist for the purpose of experiencing the fruits of knowledge and action.

This is what is meant: for those who perform undesirable deeds and so forth, because they are devoid of knowledge (vidyā), there are statements in the Purāṇas and other texts regarding their arrival at the abode of Yama by way of the path of the gods (devayāna) to various worlds and stations; this doubt is based on that. The phrase "by the command of Yama" refers to an activity in the form of a decree. The meaning is that there is no contradiction between the sequence of reaching the abode of Yama and [subsequently] reaching hell. || 16 ||

"Because it is for the sake of enjoyment" (bhogārthatvāt): this is a genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) denoting a general relationship. "For the sake of that" (*tādarthya*) means being for the purpose of enjoying its fruit.

Just as [going] is not possible [in that way], so too going to the moon by the path of the fathers (*pitṛyāṇa*) is not possible, because of the absence of sacrifices, works of public utility, and gifts.

If it is asked: "How is it understood that the path of the gods (*devayāna*) has knowledge as its object and the path of the fathers (*pitṛyāṇa*) has meritorious action as its object?"—it is because those two are the subjects under discussion. For knowledge is indeed the subject in the context of the path of the gods, and action is the subject in the context of the path of the fathers; for after stating, "Those who know thus, and those who in the forest worship with faith and austerity... [the text proceeds].
Because of the description of the path of the gods (devayāna) in the passage beginning with, "They attain the flame; from the flame, the day," and after stating, "Now,
those who in this world worship with the thought, 'Sacrifices and works of public utility are charity,'" [it continues:]

This is because of such statements as, "They pass into smoke," and so forth, which describe the path of the ancestors (pitṛyāna); and also because of this statement, "Whoever departs from this world, they all go to the moon," which must be understood to mean "all those who perform sacrifices and other rites. || 17 ||
Now, an objection is raised: if those who have performed evil deeds do not go to the moon, then—since the fifth libation would be impossible—the very commencement of a body would not be tenable.

For it is heard in scripture that the commencement of a body occurs at the fifth libation: "At the fifth libation, water becomes man-like. And it has been shown that this libation is preceded by the attainment of the moon.
Therefore, for the very purpose of initiating a new body, even for them, the ascent to and descent from the moon must necessarily be admitted; hence he says: 305.
*Na tṛtīye tathopalabdheḥ* || 3.1.18 || (Siddhānta) For the initiation of a body in the third place, there is no requirement for the "fifth oblation."

Why? Because it is perceived as such. By the term "third place," those who possess only evil karma are meant. In the response to the question, "Do you know how that world is not filled up? their independence from the five elements at the commencement of a body is perceived.
"Now, by neither of these two paths do those small creatures that repeatedly return come; they are born again and die again."

"This is the third place; therefore, that world is not filled"—since this statement regarding the non-filling of the heavenly world refers to the absence of ascent and descent for the third place, this third place does not require a fifth oblation for the commencement of a body. Furthermore, the phrase "in the fifth oblation" merely establishes that the connection with water five times is the cause for attaining the state of being called a "person" (puruṣa); it does not exclude anything else, because no restrictive particle (avadhāraṇa) is heard [in the text]. || 18 ||
And it is also recorded in worldly tradition: 3.1.19 (Siddhānta).

309. *Tatsvābhāvyāpattir upapatteḥ* || 3-1-22 || (Siddhānta) It has been stated that those who perform sacrifices and other rites, enveloped by subtle elements and accompanied by their residual karma (*sānuśaya*), descend from the moon. And as for the manner of this descent:
Then they return again by this very same path as they came: from here to space, from space to air;
having become air, they become smoke; having become smoke, they become mist; having become mist, they become a cloud.

Because of the statement, "Having become a cloud, he rains," it was said, "In this way and not in that way. Regarding the doubt as to whether, upon reaching the ether and so forth, he attains the state of ether etc. just as he attains the state of gods, humans, and so forth, or whether it is merely an attainment of similarity to them: [The answer follows: ... [as per the source text] ... [the conclusion follows]. The meaning is that the soul does not actually become ether etc., but rather attains a state of similarity to them. This is because of the scriptural statement, "He becomes like that" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.5). Furthermore, since the soul is atomic in size, it cannot occupy the entire extent of ether etc. Moreover, the soul's own nature is not subject to transformation; therefore, it is established that the soul merely attains a state of similarity to ether etc. during its journey. Thus ends the section on the soul's journey. Now begins the section concerning the soul's descent. The doubt here is whether the soul, while descending from the moon, proceeds by the same path as it ascended or by a different one. On this point, the prima facie view is as follows: the soul descends by the very same path by which it ascended. Why? Because of the scriptural passage, "Just as he came, and even other than that" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.5). The word "even" (api) implies "also" (ca); thus, the meaning is that the soul returns by the same path and also by a different one. Since the phrase "and also other than that" indicates a different path, it suggests that the soul may descend by a different route. However, the word "just as" (yathā) restricts the sense to the path of ascent alone. Therefore, the soul descends by the very same path by which it ascended. Furthermore, the scripture mentions the "path of the fathers" (pitṛyāna) as a distinct route for those who perform sacrifices and works of merit, leading to rebirth in this world. Since the descent of the soul under discussion occurs within the context of the "path of the gods" (devayāna), it must follow that the descent is by the same path as the ascent. Thus, the conclusion is that the soul descends by the very path by which it ascended. To this, we reply: the soul descends by a different path. Why? Because of the specific mention of the "path of the fathers" as a separate track for those who perform sacrifices and works of merit. If the descent were by the same path as the ascent, there would be no need to separately designate the "path of the fathers" for those who perform sacrifices and works of merit. Since the scripture mentions the "path of the fathers" as a distinct track, it follows that the descent of the soul under discussion is by a different path. Moreover, the scripture speaks of the "path of the fathers" as a route leading to rebirth in this world for those who perform sacrifices and works of merit. If the descent of the soul under discussion were by the same path as the ascent, then that very path would lead to rebirth in this world for those who perform sacrifices and works of merit, rendering the separate mention of the "path of the fathers" redundant. Therefore, the descent is by a different path. Furthermore, the scripture states that those who ascend by the path of the gods reach the world of Brahman and do not return again to this mortal realm. If the descent were by the same path as the ascent, then those who have reached the world of Brahman would also return to this world, contradicting the scriptural declaration that they do not return. Hence, the descent is by a different path. Additionally, the scripture describes the "path of the fathers" as a route consisting of smoke, night, the dark fortnight, the six months of the sun's southern course, and so forth. If the descent of the soul under discussion were by the same path as the ascent, then the ascent would also consist of smoke and the rest, which contradicts the description of the "path of the gods" as consisting of light, day, the bright fortnight, the six months of the sun's northern course, and so forth. Therefore, the descent is by a different path. Furthermore, the scripture mentions the "path of the fathers" as a track for those who perform sacrifices and works of merit, while the "path of the gods" is for those who possess knowledge. If the descent were by the same path as the ascent, then those who possess knowledge would also be subject to the "path of the fathers," which contradicts the distinction between the two paths. Therefore, the descent is by a different path. Consequently, it is established that the soul descends by a different path. Now begins the section concerning the soul's entry into a womb. The doubt here is whether the soul, having descended from the moon, enters a body immediately upon reaching the earth, or whether it remains in an intermediate state until it finds a suitable body. On this point, the prima facie view is as follows: the soul enters a body immediately upon reaching the earth. Why? Because the scripture says, "Having entered into these elements" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.9.3). The word "entered" (praviśya) implies immediate entry. Therefore, the soul enters a body immediately after descending from the moon. To this, we reply: the soul remains in an intermediate state until it finds a suitable body. Why? Because the scripture says, "Having entered into these elements" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.9.3). The word "entered" (praviśya) does not mean immediate entry, but rather refers to the soul's connection with the subtle elements that constitute the material cause of the body. It is only after the soul has entered into these subtle elements that it subsequently enters a gross body. Therefore, the soul remains in an intermediate state until it finds a suitable body. Furthermore, the scripture mentions the "intermediate state" (antarābhava) as a stage between death and rebirth. If the soul entered a body immediately upon descending from the moon, there would be no room for an intermediate state. Since the scripture acknowledges an intermediate state, it follows that the soul remains in that state until it finds a suitable body. Moreover, the scripture describes the process of conception as occurring when the soul, along with the semen and blood, enters the womb. If the soul entered a body immediately upon descending from the moon, it would not wait for the union of semen and blood. Therefore, the soul remains in an intermediate state until it finds a suitable body. Consequently, it is established that the soul remains in an intermediate state until it finds a suitable body. Thus ends the section on the soul's descent. Now begins the section concerning the soul's entry into a womb. The doubt here is whether the soul, having entered the womb, is conscious at the time of conception, or whether it is unconscious. On this point, the prima facie view is as follows: the soul is unconscious at the time of conception. Why? Because the scripture says, "Then he becomes united with the essence" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.6). The word "united" (saṃsṛṣṭa) implies a lack of consciousness. Therefore, the soul is unconscious at the time of conception. To this, we reply: the soul is conscious at the time of conception. Why? Because the scripture says, "Then he becomes united with the essence" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.6). The word "united" (saṃsṛṣṭa) does not imply a lack of consciousness, but rather refers to the soul's connection with the subtle elements that constitute the material cause of the body. It is only after the soul has entered into these subtle elements that it subsequently enters a gross body. Therefore, the soul is conscious at the time of conception. Furthermore, the scripture mentions the "intermediate state" as a stage between death and rebirth. If the soul were unconscious at the time of conception, there would be no need for an intermediate state. Since the scripture acknowledges an intermediate state, it follows that the soul is conscious at the time of conception. Moreover, the scripture describes the process of conception as occurring when the soul, along with the semen and blood, enters the womb. If the soul were unconscious at the time of conception, it would not be able to direct the formation of the body. Therefore, the soul is conscious at the time of conception. Consequently, it is established that the soul is conscious at the time of conception. Thus ends the section on the soul's entry into a womb. Now begins the section concerning the soul's experience of pleasure and pain. The doubt here is whether the soul experiences pleasure and pain while in the womb, or whether it experiences them only after birth. On this point, the prima facie view is as follows: the soul experiences pleasure and pain while in the womb. Why? Because the scripture says, "He experiences pleasure and pain" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.1). The word "experiences" (anubhavati) implies actual feeling. Therefore, the soul experiences pleasure

The Section on Being Presided Over by Another (Anyādhiṣṭhitādhikaraṇa) || 3.1.6 ||

311. "In the case of [the soul] presided over by another, as before, because of the verbal designation" (Sūtra 3.1.24). It is heard in scripture that souls descending are born in the form of rice and so forth: "Having become a cloud, he rains down; these are born here as rice, barley, herbs, trees, sesame, and beans."

What is the case here: do they cling to rice and other plants already presided over by other enjoyers whose bodies are those rice plants and so forth? Or are those enjoyers themselves born with rice and other plants as their bodies?

In this regard, [the conclusion is] that they are "born," because of the statement "they are born," just as in the expressions "he is born in a place" or "a human is born," [it refers to] having a body consisting of rice and so forth.

This being the position, it is replied: "In what is presided over by another. In a body such as rice and so forth, which is presided over by another living soul (*jīva*), there is for them [the souls descending from heaven] merely a state of conjunction.

Why? Because of the description being as before—that is, because there is only a description of their existence in that state, similar to the sequence beginning with space and ending with the clouds. For where the state of being an enjoyer is intended, there the action that serves as the means to that state is described:
"those of pleasant conduct... those of foul conduct."

Thus [it is said]. And here, karma is not denoted [by the term "becoming"], just as in the case of ether and so forth. This is because the karma such as sacrifices (*iṣṭādi*), which has set out to yield its fruit and whose fruit is to be experienced in heaven, is exhausted precisely through that experience of heaven. Furthermore, this is because it will be stated later that "those of pleasant conduct" and "those of foul conduct" refer to what has not yet begun [to bear fruit], and because there is no other intervening karma in the interim. Therefore, like the statement regarding the state of becoming ether and so forth, the statement regarding birth in the form of rice and so forth is merely figurative. 3.1.25. This is not so—that there is merely a physical attachment to the body of rice and other plants presided over by another, and that there is no birth in the form of rice and such because of the absence of a cause for being an enjoyer; for the cause of being an enjoyer does indeed exist. The very acts such as sacrifices (*iṣṭādi*) which yield fruits to be enjoyed in heaven are themselves impure, being mixed with evil because they involve violence such as the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice.

"Merely a conjunction" means because [the matter] is concluded by the statement, "Having dwelt there as long as the impulse lasts. "In the middle" means within the context of the section. For in such cases as these, because sacrifices and the like are taught as things to be performed by one who desires [a result], he understands that sacrifice and so forth are the means to heaven; then, solely out of attachment to the fruit, he engages in the sacrifice and other rites. That is not so. Why? Because of the scriptural word (*śabda*). For there is a scriptural statement regarding the immolation (*saṃjñapana*) of the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma that, as a cause for attaining the heavenly world, it lacks the nature of violence (*hiṃsātva*). Indeed, they recite a scriptural text concerning the animal stating that it attains the heavenly world by virtue of being immolated: "With a golden body, he goes upward to the heavenly world," and so forth. An action that is a means to an extraordinary prosperity (*abhyudaya*), even if it causes slight suffering, is not violence; on the contrary, it is indeed protection. And thus says a Vedic mantra:

"Or rather, O you who possess the triple power, you do not suffer; you go to the gods by easy paths, where the doers of good deeds go, and not the doers of evil—there may the divine Savitṛ place you. The passage beginning with "sarvavarṇānām" refers to the *Āpastamba-sūtra*. Furthermore, in the *Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa*, specific fruits for those who perform the duties (*dharma*) of their respective stages of life (*āśrama*) are described. Regarding the phrase "of these": the meaning is that even obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) and so forth are characterized by impurity due to such acts as the immolation of animals (*paśvālambhana*) performed annually. Regarding the term "excessive": the intention is that the slaughter of an animal, though a cause of suffering, is not indeed violence (*hiṃsā*). And regarding the phrase "likewise": the point is that non-violence is not merely inferred from the attainment of the heavenly world; rather, its status as non-violence is explicitly stated.

And as for the physician: for when there is injury (*hiṃsā*), indeed, the aforementioned fault arises; but because of the absence of injury, the fault is cast far away. This alone is the correct, unassailable resolution. Therefore, this is precisely the difference between the *Śyena* sacrifice and the *Āgneyīya* [animal sacrifice]: an action that, even if it causes slight suffering, accomplishes an extraordinary prosperity is "protection" (*rakṣaṇa*); an action resulting in misfortune is "injury" (*hiṃsā*)—this is the meaning. || 25 ||

In the third chapter on the Means of Attainment (Sādhanādhyāya), the second section concerning the two-fold characteristics (Ubhayaliṅgapāda).
1. The Section on the Twilight (Sandhyādhikaraṇa):
Objects that are to be experienced by the individual soul (jīva) are created by the Supreme Self (paramātman) alone.
2. The Section on the Absence of That:
For the individual soul (jīva) while asleep, there are three states of abode—namely, the various channels (nāḍīs), the pericardium (purītad), and the Supreme Self (paramātman).
3. The Section Concerning the Remembrance of Karma, Words, and Injunctions:
The individual soul (jīva) that has entered the state of deep sleep from the waking state is that very same one which awakens; it is not another.
4. The section on the bewildered state (mugdha-ādhikaraṇa):
The state of the individual soul known as fainting (mūrchā) is the attainment of the conditions for death.

5. The Section on the Two Attributes (Ubhayaliṅgādhikaraṇa): There is no contradiction whatsoever between Brahman’s pervasiveness everywhere and its being the antithesis of all that is to be discarded while simultaneously being the source of all auspicious qualities.

In the Śrī Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Bhagavad Rāmānuja, the second section of the third chapter, titled "The Section on the Two-fold Characteristics" (Ubhayaliṅgapāda), [is concluded]. || 3-2 ||
The Section on the Twilight Devotions (Sandhyādhikaraṇa) || 3-2-1 ||
315. "In the intermediate state there is creation, for so [the scripture] says! (Sūtra 3.2.1, Pūrvapakṣa).

Thus, the suffering of the individual soul (*jīva*) while awake—due to its connection with going and coming and birth in accordance with its past actions—has been explained. Now, its state of dreaming is examined. With reference to dreaming, it is heard in scripture: "There are no chariots there, no yoked horses, and no roads; yet he creates chariots, yoked horses, and roads. There are no joys, delights, or pleasures there; yet he creates joys, delights, and pleasures."
"In that state there are no pools, lotus-ponds, or rivers; yet he creates pools, lotus-ponds, and rivers—for he is the agent."
In this regard, there is a doubt: is this creation of chariots and so forth performed by the *jīva* alone, or rather by the Lord (*īśvara*)?

What is the correct view? That "in the intermediate state (sandhya), there is creation by means of the individual soul (jīva). Why? Because the term "intermediate" (sandhya) refers to the state of dream; for it is said, "The third, the intermediate, is the state of dream."

Because of this statement, that [creation] is performed by the *jīva* alone; for he says, "He creates," and "He is indeed the agent. Thus, the *jīva* himself is understood there as the subject. || 1 ||

316. "And some [scriptural texts] declare him to be the creator of sons and so forth. (Sūtra 3.2.2, Pūrvapakṣa) Furthermore, some followers of certain Vedic branches study this passage regarding this individual soul (*jīva*) as the creator of desires in the state of dream: "This person who remains awake while others sleep, creating each and every desire" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 4.3.11). Moreover, in that context, the word "desires" (*kāma*) refers to things such as sons which are desired, and not to mere volition. For in the preceding passage, it says:
"Ask for all desires according to your wish. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.2.1).
"Choose sons and grandsons with a lifespan of a hundred years"—
thus, it is sons and the like that are presented as the objects of desire (*kāma*).

Therefore, the individual soul (jīva) creates chariots and other objects in a dream. Furthermore, the soul's power of true resolve (satyasaṅkalpatva) is heard in the Prajāpati discourse; hence, even in the absence of external instruments and the like, creation is logically possible. || 2 ||
This being the position reached, it is replied:
"But [the world] is mere illusion, because its true nature is not manifested in its entirety" (3.2.3).

This sūtra is intended to address the objection that in another scriptural passage the term "creator" (nirmātāram) is heard as referring to the Supreme Self; furthermore, the mention of "sons and so forth" shows the characteristic marks of the individual soul (jīva).

"And of the individual soul" (jīvasya ca). Regarding the question, "How can there be creation for the individual soul when it is devoid of its equipment?"—the two sūtras beginning with "The creation in the intermediate state [is by the one who creates]" (sandhye sṛṣṭir nirmātāram) concern the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa). || 2 ||
"Merely an illusion"—meaning it is of a truly wondrous nature; the sense is that there is nothing whatsoever that is not of a wondrous nature.
And they recite in their own branch [of the Veda]: "The Person creating... [Some say:

"At the time of dreaming, the individual soul (jīva) alone would be the creator of desires; some followers of other branches state that sons and so forth are created by it under the designation of 'desires'. [The author replies:
"That which is recorded as being created in a dream was indeed made by Brahman; for the individual soul does not possess the power of true resolve (satya-saṅkalpatā) at that time."

It turns away [from reality] the collection of objects such as chariots and lotus-pools in a dream; for the word "māyā" indeed denotes something wonderful, as seen in such passages as, "Born in the lineage of Janaka, she was fashioned like the *māyā* of a god," and so forth. Likewise here:
"There are no chariots there, no yoke-horses, no paths."
The meaning is that [these things] do not exist because they are not experienced by all other persons.
Now, regarding the phrase "he creates chariots, yoked horses, and paths," the word "but" (*tu*) sets aside the previous position.

The meaning is that it was created by the Supreme Person (*parama-puruṣa*). He creates [these worlds] as things to be experienced by His own vision, which cease to exist at that very moment; thus, He establishes their very nature as a marvel. Such a marvelous creation is possible only for the Supreme Person, whose resolve is ever-true (*satya-saṅkalpa*); it is not possible for the individual soul (*jīva*). Even though the individual soul possesses qualities such as having a true resolve, because its essential nature is entirely unmanifest during the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), such a marvelous creation is not possible for the individual soul.
And the passage, "Fashioning desire after desire, the Person," speaks of the Supreme Person alone as the fashioner;
likewise, "He who wakes while these [others] sleep."
"That alone is the Bright, that is Brahman, that alone is called the Immortal;

upon it all worlds are supported, and no one transcends it"—since the nature common to the Supreme Person is perceived in both the opening and the conclusion [of this passage], and because of its agreement in meaning with the scriptural text, "He creates ponds, lotus-pools, and rivers; for He is the agent," it declares the Supreme Person alone to be the agent. (3)
If the soul's qualities such as being free from evil are innate, why are they not manifested?
To this he says:
"But [it is] concealed by the meditation on the Supreme; for from that [concealment], it [is so]. (3.2.5)
Bondage and its opposite [result] from that.

(Sūtra 3.1.4) The word "but" (*tu*) is for the purpose of removing doubt. From the contemplation of the Supreme—namely, from the volition of the Supreme Person—the natural form of this individual soul (*jīva*) becomes concealed. Indeed, because this soul has committed offenses through a beginningless succession of karma, the Supreme Person conceals its own natural, auspicious form. Consequently, it is from His volition alone that the bondage and liberation of this individual soul are heard of in the scriptures.
"When he finds fearless support in this invisible, incorporeal, inexpressible, and homeless [Brahman], then he has indeed gone beyond fear.
"For when he makes even a slight distinction within it, then fear comes upon him. "For He alone causes bliss.
"Out of fear of Him the wind blows..."

319. "Or that [concealment] also occurs through connection with a body" (sūtra 3.2.5). That too—meaning "concealment" as well—occurs either by way of connection with a body; or at the time of creation, by way of connection with the subtle power of consciousness (*acit-chakti*); or it occurs through conjunction with non-conscious matter (*acid-vastu*) existing in the state of a body. At the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), it occurs through connection with extremely subtle non-conscious matter that is unfit for the differentiation of name and form. Therefore, because its true nature is unmanifest, the individual soul (*jīva*) in a dream is not able to create chariots and other things by mere volition alone, [as stated]:
"In that [dream], all worlds are supported; no one ever goes beyond it."

Thus, qualities such as "remaining awake while all others sleep" and "being the refuge of all worlds" are possible only for the Supreme Person. Therefore, for the sake of the individual souls experiencing fruits corresponding to their respective small and limited actions, He brings forth objects that are perceivable by them alone and which last only for that specific duration of time. || 5 ||
320. For the scripture indicates [the existence of the subtle body], and those who know it declare this. (3.2.6)
Furthermore, dream objects are not preceded by the volitions of the individual soul (jīva),
because the dream is understood from scripture to be an indicator of prosperity and adversity.

"Or through yoga" (yogād vā): the meaning is that primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and so forth serve as the instruments for the Lord’s volition. Regarding "in creation" (*sṛṣṭau*): the word "or" (*vā*) does not denote an equal alternative; rather, the intention is that it denotes a regulated alternative (*vyavasthita-vikalpa*). By the word "power" (*śakti*) in "non-conscious power" (*acit-śakti*), what is intended is its status as a specific attribute non-different from the Lord. "Therefore" (*ataḥ*): the meaning is that there is the creation of various unstable objects for the sake of experiencing even small amounts of karma. || 5 ||

And as for the term "sūcaka" (indicative): it means that at that time there would be the manifestation of the individual soul's [powers] such as *satyasaṅkalpatva* (the power of true resolve), which are useful solely for the creation within dreams.

"The disappearance of the qualities (guṇas) occurs through yoga during the creation of the body; likewise, it occurs through yoga alone at the dissolution of nature (prakṛti). [This is the meaning of the Sūtra. For, a dream is an indicator of future events—both auspicious and inauspicious—pertaining to the individual soul (jīva); thus, the object of the dream is indeed created by the Lord. And its indicative power is understood from scriptural testimony (śruti), that is, from the words of the Veda. Those who know that—that is, those who know the treatises on dreams."

They report dreams and describe them as indicators of good and evil fortune; for it is seen in the Śruti that a dream is an indicator of auspiciousness and so forth. Furthermore, according to the testimony of those who know such things, there is no disappearance of the individual soul (jīva) during sleep. As for the objects of dreams: "When, in the course of optional rites, one sees a woman in dreams... [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.2.8].
"One should recognize prosperity in that vision of a dream";

and from such [scriptural] injunctions as, "Now, if in a dream one sees a black man with black teeth, he kills him. Furthermore, those who know the science of dreams declare a dream to be an indicator of both good and evil. And this quality of being an indicator would not be possible if [the dream] were dependent on one's own volition. Thus, because the inauspicious is undesirable, [the Lord] would create only that which indicates the auspicious and then show it; therefore, the creation in a dream is performed by the Lord alone. (6)
Thus ends the section on the twilight devotions (sandhyā). || 1 ||
The locus of that non-existence. 3-2-2.
321. "The absence [of that dream-experience] occurs in the channels and in the Self, because of scriptural statements regarding them.

(Sūtra 3.2.7, Siddhānta) Now, the locus of deep sleep is being examined. This is recorded in scripture: "Now, when one is thus asleep, composed, serene, and does not perceive any dreams; then he is asleep in these channels."
Thus it is said. Likewise:

"Now, when one is fast asleep and knows nothing of anything, there are the channels called *hitā*, seventy-two thousand in number, which extend from the heart to the pericardium; having descended through them, he sleeps in the pericardium."
Thus:

"When this person is said to be sleeping, then, my dear, he has become united with Being. In this way, the channels (nāḍīs), the pericardium (purītat), and Brahman are heard in scripture as the locations for deep sleep.

When there is a doubt as to whether these [states] are alternatives (*vikalpa*) or a combination (*samuccaya*), and this [doubt] having arisen, it is said: "The absence of that" (*tadabhāva*). "The absence of that" means the absence of dream, which is deep sleep (*suṣupti*); it occurs in the channels (*nāḍī*), in the pericardium (*purītat*), and in the Self (*ātman*). The meaning is that "this" is a combination of the states.

Why? Because of the scriptural statement (tacchruteḥ)—because scripture declares that these three are places (sthānatva). Furthermore, since a combination (samuccaya) is possible through a difference in function, an alternative (vikalpa) involving optional exclusion (pākṣikabādhagarbha) is not appropriate. And a difference in function among the channels (nāḍīs), the pericardium (purītat), and Brahman is indeed possible, like a palace, a bed, and a couch. In this context, the channels and the pericardium correspond to the palace and the bed, while "Brahman" corresponds to the couch. Therefore, Brahman alone is the direct place of deep sleep (suṣupti). || 7 ||

321. Therefore, awakening [occurs] from this. (Siddhānta) Since Brahman alone is the direct locus of deep sleep, therefore, the awakening of these individual souls (jīvas) from this Brahman, as it is heard in scripture, is logically consistent; for it is said:
"Having come from Being, they do not know; we have come from Being. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.9.2).
In such passages as these. || 8 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the non-existence of that [ether]. 2.
The section concerning the recollection of karma, words, injunctions, and established rules (3.2.3).

323. But he [the same person] indeed [arises], on account of the scriptural declarations concerning action, remembrance, and words. (Sūtra 3.2.9, Siddhānta) Is it the very same person who, having been in deep sleep, arises at the time of awakening? Or is it another? Regarding this doubt, [it is said]:
of him who is freed from all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and has become one with Brahman...
Since there is an absence of connection with a previous body, sense organs, and so forth, [the liberated soul] must be different—this being the initial position, we reply:
it is not so, because it is non-different from the state prior to liberation.
Furthermore, there is "recognition" (anusmṛti) in the form: "I who was asleep am now awake. Scripture also shows this, stating: "He who was awakened from deep sleep is that very same one."

"Therefore, whether they become a tiger here, or a lion, or a wolf, or a boar, or a worm, or a moth, or a gnat, or a mosquito—whatever they may be, they become that. Furthermore, the injunctions are for the sake of liberation; if deep sleep were itself liberation, those injunctions would be purposeless. Nor is this [state] one where all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) have been discarded and the true nature has manifested; for, with reference to deep sleep, it says, "Now, when he is thus in deep sleep... and so forth.
For it is said: "Indeed, he does not at this time know himself as 'I am this,' nor these beings; he has gone to utter destruction; I see no enjoyment here. And regarding the liberated one:
"Having attained the highest light, he manifests in his own form."
"There he moves about, laughing, playing, and rejoicing; he becomes his own ruler (svarāj). For him, there is freedom of movement in all worlds;
indeed, as a seer, he sees everything and attains everything in every way."
Thus, omniscience and other qualities are heard [in scripture].

Therefore, the individual soul (*subūta*), while transmigrating, being "exhausted" (*āyasta*) with all its faculties and incapable of knowledge, enjoyment, and so forth, reaches the Supreme Self—the place of rest—and having become refreshed (*āśvasta*), rises again for the sake of experience. || 9 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the injunction regarding the recollection of past actions (karmānusmṛti). 3.
324. "O charming one, fainting is a partial attainment [of death] by process of elimination" (Sūtra 3.2.10).

Because of the dissimilarity of causes and the dissimilarity of forms, [fainting] is neither deep sleep nor death. For the cause of fainting is injury and the like. By "process of elimination," fainting is a partial attainment leading to death. For death is the cessation of the connection between all the vital breaths and the body; whereas fainting is the persistence of the connection with the subtle vital breath and the body. 10.
Thus ends the section concerning the deluded. 4.
The Section Concerning the Possession of Both Characteristics (3.2.5).

325. "Not even from a different location does the Supreme possess both characteristics, for [He is] everywhere thus" (Sūtra 3.2.11). Having described the specific states of the individual soul (*jīva*) in order to generate detachment through the perception of defects, [the author] now begins [this section] to generate a longing for the attainment of Brahman, by establishing that the Brahman to be attained is free from defects and consists of auspicious qualities.
In that regard, those states of the individual soul (jīva) which are occasioned by the respective conditions during the stages of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, swoon, and departure [from the body]—

Regarding the word "doṣa" (defect): in this second quarter (*pāda*), which is intended to establish that the Supreme Self is free from defects and is a mine of auspicious qualities, two aspects of the Supreme Self are demonstrated through the examination of dream and deep sleep—namely, His being the creator of the diverse objects of dreams and His being the locus of deep sleep. Thus, since these qualities of the Supreme Self are established, their detailed exposition is undertaken in this quarter. As for the exposition of fainting (*mūrchā*) and so forth, it was not included here because it finds no place in the previous quarter and because it is dependent upon the examination of deep sleep; therefore, it is treated here. The phrase "He begins" implies that the author of the *Sūtras* [is the one who begins].

"States" (sthāneṣu) means conditions; that is, the question is considered whether the non-human goals (apuruṣārtha) belonging to the individual soul (jīva) necessarily follow for the Supreme Being who resides within the body of the individual soul while situated in states such as deep sleep and so forth—or not. Furthermore, is the fact that the connection with the body and so forth is the cause of non-human goals due to the inherent nature (vastusvabhāva) of that thing, or is it produced by specific karma?

And is the scripture concerning the Supreme Self, which possesses both characteristics (ubhayaliṅga-śruti), capable of setting aside the idea that non-human goals are due to the inherent nature of things and making it understood that they are dependent upon karma—or not?
