"No defect whatsoever exists in the Supreme Brahman even from the perspective of its location; for it possesses both characteristics, being free from defects and endowed with auspicious qualities."
It is now considered whether those defects belong even to that Supreme Brahman who dwells within them as their inner controller (antaryāmin). Are they present?
Or not? What is the correct conclusion? They are present. [Śrībhāṣya 3.2.5]
Why? Because it abides within the body in its various respective states.
But is it not said:
"If it be argued that there is the attainment of enjoyment, no, because of the distinction," and "And on account of abiding and eating"?

In such passages as these, it is stated that the Supreme has no defects because He is not subject to karma. How then can a defect be attributed to the Supreme Brahman—who is not subject to karma—on account of His connection with various locations?
It is explained thus: "Even karmas bring about a connection with a body and result in the production of what is not the goal of man."

This was stated in the passage beginning with "or from connection with a body" (*dehayogād vā*). And that [connection] occurs because the association with a body is not a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*). Otherwise, if actions alone were to produce suffering, what would be the purpose of the connection with a body? Therefore, even while one is not subject to karma, the connection with a body of various kinds of impurities is indeed a non-human goal.

Therefore, even if one enters [the body] by one's own will for the purpose of controlling it, a connection with that which is not the human goal (*apuruṣārtha*) is unavoidable. For immersion in pus, blood, and so forth is indeed nothing but a non-goal for a person, even if performed voluntarily.
Thus, although Brahman is the sole cause of the universe and a treasury of auspicious qualities such as omniscience, nevertheless, [He is] "that which dwells within the earth... [and so on].

"Abiding in the self"—this refers to "that" (tat) and so on. The word "that" refers to the waking state and the rest. The body's condition consists in being the cause of those states, such as waking. Regarding the phrase "that" and so forth: just as, although the king’s anger is the cause of execution and the like, the sword-stroke—which serves as the instrument—is the direct cause of the execution; likewise here too, the connection with the body, which serves as the instrument, is what constitutes the non-human goal (apuruṣārtha). This is the intended meaning.

Therefore, "that" [is said]. Even if one enters by one's own will without being subject to karma, connection with that which is not the goal of man (apuruṣārtha) is unavoidable because it depends on the very nature of things. Just as for one who is independent, the cutting off of one's own head by a sword—even by one's own desire—is indeed not the goal of man, so it is here; this is the intended meaning.

This is because of such scriptural statements as "He who dwells in the eye" and "He who dwells in the semen," which show that for Him who resides in various places, there exist non-final goals consisting of connection with those respective locations.

This being the case, we reply: "Not even on account of its location does the Supreme [possess such qualities]. Not even on account of its location—such as earth, self, and so forth—can even a trace of that which is not a human goal (apuruṣārtha) possibly belong to the Supreme Brahman.

Why? Because everywhere it possesses both characteristics; for everywhere in the Śrutis and Smṛtis, the Supreme Brahman is described as possessing both characteristics—that is, as endowed with the characteristic of being free from all defects and the characteristic of being a mine of auspicious qualities. This is the meaning.
"Free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true and whose resolves are true";

"He is the essence of all auspicious qualities, having brought forth the creation of beings by a mere fraction of His own power"; "A mass consisting solely of splendor, strength, great consciousness, and sovereignty"; "In Him, the Lord of the high and the low, there are no defects such as the *ku* [of *akuśala*] and so forth"; "The supreme state called Viyat (the ether), which is devoid of temporal limitations"—from such passages found in the Śruti and Smṛti, Brahman is indeed understood to possess both characteristics. 11.
326. If it be argued that [the Supreme Lord is subject to non-final goals] because of difference [of states], we say no, because it is not stated [to be so] with respect to each [individual].

(Siddhānta Sūtra 3.2.12) ...Just as the individual soul (*jīva*), although possessing both sets of characteristics such as freedom from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) as understood from the Prajāpati discourse, is nevertheless joined with what is not a human goal due to the difference in states consisting of connection with bodies such as those of gods; likewise, even for the Supreme Inner Ruler (*antaryāmī*), who by nature possesses both sets of characteristics such as freedom from sin, connection with what is not a human goal would be unavoidable due to the difference in states consisting of connection with the respective bodies of gods and others—if this is the objection!
Regarding that, [the Sūtra states]: "Because there is a statement concerning each [of them] individually"—
namely, "He who dwells in the earth" and "He who dwells in the self."

In each of these passages, by the statement that "the Self of the existent is the Inner Controller (antaryāmin), the Immortal," the immortality of the Inner Controller is declared; for while He exercises His governance over various things according to His own will, there is no prohibition of the human goals [of life] resulting from those respective relationships. However, in the case of the individual soul (jīva), that nature is concealed, as stated: "But through meditation on the Supreme, it is concealed."
Thus it has been stated here.
Now, an objection is raised: "Even for one who acts according to his own will, the connection with the human goal (puruṣārtha) dependent on the respective nature of each object is unavoidable.
This is not correct; for even insentient matter (acidvastu) does not, by its very nature, have the form of that which is not a human goal.

Regarding the word "yathā" (just as): the scriptural mention of possessing both genders applies to the individual soul (*jīva*) as well; in that case, it is established by means of different states (*avasthā*). The meaning is that the same applies to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Regarding the phrase "in each instance" (*pratiparyāyam*): if the word "immortal" (*amṛta*) were mentioned only once, it would refer to eternity; however, because it recurs in every instance, what is intended is simply the absence of connection with specific defects belonging to those respective liberated beings. As for the phrase "but of the individual soul": [the text continues].

Since concealment (*tirodhāna*) and so forth are established by scripture (*śruti*), the scriptural statement regarding the "twofold nature" (*ubhayaliṅgatva*) concerning the individual soul (*jīva*) is restricted [to that context]. However, since there is no scriptural statement regarding the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) being subject to concealment dependent on another, the scriptural statement regarding His twofold nature has an unrestricted application; this is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "for not": if [the connection with suffering] were dependent on the inherent nature of the thing itself, then indeed [there would be a problem]; for in that case, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of it not being a human goal (*apuruṣārthatva*). The meaning is that such a thing does not exist. Regarding the phrase "even though it is without marks" (*acihnastvapi*): it is not only for the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) that the connection with what is not a human goal is adventitious (*aupādhika*); it is so even for the insentient (*acetana*).

For those subject to karma, however, in accordance with the nature of their karma and by the volition of the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*), a single and the same object becomes a source of pleasure for one person and a source of pain for another, depending on differences in time and differences in persons. If, on the other hand, it were caused solely by the intrinsic nature of the object, then everything would always result in pleasure or in pain for everyone alike; yet this is not observed. Thus it has been said:
"O best of the twice-born, what are called hell and heaven are indeed demerit and merit."
A single object alone leads to suffering, to pleasure, and to the arising of envy.
Since it leads to anger, how can an object possess the nature of an object? That very same thing, having become a source of pleasure, arises again as a cause of suffering.
"Since that very same thing arises for both anger and for serenity, therefore nothing has the nature of suffering, nor does anything have the nature of happiness.
Furthermore, some maintain this as well: 3-2-13 (Siddhānta).

Moreover, some followers of a particular Vedic branch (śākhin) record—in their own words—that within a single conjunction with the body, while there is the absence of human purpose for the individual soul (jīva), for the other [the Lord], there is the absence of that [suffering] as well as sovereignty consisting of control and a connection with splendor: "Two birds, inseparable companions, cling to the same tree; of these two, one eats the sweet fruit, while the other looks on without eating. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.6) || 13 ||
Now, it might be argued:

"By entering with this living self (jīva), let me manifest names and forms"—thus, the manifestation of names and forms is preceded by the entry of the *jīva* whose essence is Brahman. Consequently, since Brahman itself has that as its nature, it possesses the form of gods, humans, and so forth, and shares in their names. Therefore, because it falls within the scope of scriptural injunctions and prohibitions such as "A Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice," its subjection to karma is unavoidable. To this, he says:

328. "For that [Brahman], even when associated with a form upon entering the bodies of gods and others, is indeed formless (arūpavat), because of its predominance. (Siddhānta Sūtra 3.1.14) Even when Brahman enters the bodies of gods and others, being joined with that form, it remains indeed formless—that is, Brahman is exactly like that which is devoid of form. The meaning is that, unlike the individual soul (*jīva*), it lacks subjection to karma, which is the cause of having a body. Why? Because of its predominance by virtue of being the sustainer (*nirvāhakatva*).

"Space, indeed, is the revealer of name and form; that which is within them is Brahman"—this [text] establishes Brahman as the very controller of name and form, even while it has entered into everything, by showing its lack of contact with the effects of name and form.
Now, an objection: if Brahman exists within [the world] as having that as its body, how can it be said to be "formless" (arūpavat), meaning equal to that which is devoid of connection with form?

Thus: just as the individual soul (*jīva*) has a connection with various forms by virtue of its experience of the pleasure and pain produced by those [forms], so too, due to the absence of that [experience], the Supreme has "formlessness" (*arūpavatvam*). Furthermore, the scriptures of injunction and prohibition apply only to one who is subject to *karma*.
This explains the meaning of the passage "that which is within" (*taṃ yad antarā*) by way of not touching upon the effects of name and form.

[Objection: "But surely..."—the meaning is this: the entry into those [effects] consists precisely in the culmination of those respective cognitions and words. And being an object of cognition and words necessarily entails being subject to *karma*. Therefore, how can there be no contact with effects? This is the sense of the objection.

Therefore, the Supreme Brahman is indeed identical to the "formless" (arūpa). Consequently, even though Brahman exists in the form of the Inner Controller (antaryāmin), it possesses both characteristics (ubhayaliṅga): being free from all defects and being a mine of auspicious qualities. || 14 ||

But is it not the case that Brahman is understood from such passages as "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite" to be of a nature consisting solely of non-dual, attributeless luminosity; whereas other qualities— such as omniscience, the power of true resolve, being the cause of the world, being the inner self of all, and having true desires— are [distinct]?

3. Since [the world] is negated by such statements as "not this, not this" (*neti neti*), it must be understood as being illusory (*mithyā*). How then can Brahman possess the nature of being a mine of auspicious qualities, being free from all defects, and having the characteristic of being devoid of fear? To this, he says: 329. *Prakāśavaccāvaiyarthyāt* (And like light, because [the scriptures] are not purposeless). (Siddhānta)

And just as the nature of Brahman is accepted as being of the essence of light on the grounds that scriptural passages such as "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1) are not to be rendered meaningless, so too, because scriptural passages declaring its possession of true volition, omniscience, being the cause of the entire universe, being the self of all, and having all defects such as ignorance entirely dispelled are not to be rendered meaningless, Brahman possesses both characteristics. 15.

330. And it says: "Only that" (tanmātram). (Siddhānta) Furthermore, the passage beginning with "Truth, Knowledge, Infinite" establishes only the fact that Brahman has the nature of light; it does not negate other attributes such as having true volitions, which are understood from other scriptural passages. Moreover, the object of the negation in the phrase "not this, not this" will be explained immediately hereafter. || 16 ||

331. "And it is shown, and moreover it is recorded" (Sūtra 3.2.17). Furthermore, the collection of Vedānta passages shows that [the Lord] is a mine of auspicious qualities and is free from all defects—not as a subordinate attribute, but primarily, because this is what is established by the Śruti. For that very reason, omniscience and other such qualities should also be accepted. Nor is there any contradiction with the rule of pervasion (vyāpti), since we observe that knowledge which exists as a subordinate attribute does not serve as the substratum for [qualities like] knowledge and so forth. Therefore, the sense is that everything is logically consistent. || 15 ||
"Not another" means that the word "only" (mātra) is intended to exclude other [entities] by way of negation. || 16 ||

The word *atha* (then/therefore) refers to the purpose [of the inquiry]. Regarding the phrase "the collection of Vedānta statements": "partless and actionless," for Brahman indeed possesses both characteristics, especially when one speaks of it.
...to avoid the meaninglessness of the sentence’s purport. [Regarding] the negation:

"Him, the supreme Maheśvara among lords, him, the supreme deity among deities"; "The cause of causes, the lord of the lords of organs, and there is no progenitor of Him, nor is there any ruler over Him"; "No effect or instrument is found for Him; neither anyone equal to Him nor anyone superior to Him is seen."

"His supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold, and His knowledge, strength, and action are inherent. "He who is all-knowing and all-perceiving, whose austerity consists of knowledge. "From fear of Him the wind blows; from fear of Him the sun rises. "That is the one bliss of Brahman.

"From which words turn back, together with the mind, not having attained It—knowing that bliss of Brahman, one fears nothing at all. "Partless, actionless, peaceful, blameless, and stainless," and so forth. And it is also recorded in the Smṛti:

"He who knows Me as unborn and beginningless, the Great Lord of the worlds... "Pervading this entire universe with but a single portion, I stand as the world... "Under My supervision, Nature brings forth the moving and the unmoving;
by this cause, O son of Kuntī, the world revolves.
"But the Supreme Person is another, declared to be the Supreme Self..."

"He is the imperishable Lord who, having entered the three worlds, sustains them; he is omniscient, the maker of all, endowed with all power, knowledge, strength, and prosperity; he is neither diminished nor increased, self-dependent, beginningless, and the controller. He is untouched by ignorance, sloth, fear, anger, desire, and the like; he is faultless, supreme, established in the highest, the unchanging, and beyond sequence. And so forth. Therefore, although Brahman is present everywhere, because it possesses both characteristics (ubhayaliṅgatva), the defects associated with various locations do not touch the Supreme Brahman. || 17 ||
332. And for this very reason, there is the analogy of the sun and so forth:

|| 3.2.18 || (Siddhānta) Since the Supreme Brahman, even though situated in various locations, does not partake in the defects caused by those locations; for this very reason, just as the sun reflected in water, mirrors, and so forth [remains unchanged], the scriptures employ the analogy that "the Supreme Self, though abiding here and there, is faultless"—just as the one space appears divided within jars and other vessels.
"Thus, indeed, though one, he is present in many places, like the sun in reservoirs of water. "For the Self of beings, though truly one, is established in every being;
it is seen as both single and manifold, like the moon reflected in water," and so forth. (18)
On this point, an objection is raised: 333.
"But because it is not perceived like [the reflection] in water, it is not so.

(Pūrva-pakṣa) The word "but" (*tu*) indicates the objection. The suffix *vati* is used after the locative form "in water" (*ambuvat*). Just as the sun, the face, and so forth are perceived in water, mirrors, and the like; the Supreme Self is not perceived in such locations as the earth and so on.

"But [in the case of] water and so forth, the sun and others are perceived as being situated there due to delusion; they are not actually situated there in the ultimate sense. But here [it says], 'He who dwells in the earth,' 'He who dwells in the waters.'"

By such passages as "He who dwells in the self," it is understood that, in the ultimate sense, the Supreme Self alone dwells within the earth and other elements. Therefore, the sun and other luminaries are not affected by defects caused by water, mirrors, and the like, precisely because they do not actually reside therein. Consequently, there is no such correspondence—the meaning is that the illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta) is not equal to the subject of the illustration (dārṣṭāntika). || 19 ||
He refutes [the objection]: "The participation in increase and decrease [is denied] because of being included [within the higher], because of the consistency of both, and because it is seen so.

(Sūtra 3.2.20, Siddhānta) Because the Supreme Brahman, the substratum, is included within the locations such as the earth and so forth, the mere possibility of its partaking in defects such as increase and decrease—pertaining to those locations—is negated by the examples of the sun and others, both in terms of its essential nature (*svarūpa*) and its attributes (*guṇa*). How is this understood?
It is determined to be thus precisely because of the consistency of both [illustrations]—that is, due to the consistency of the two examples cited:
"For space is one; yet it appears as distinct within jars and the like, just as the sun appears [different] in various vessels of water."

Thus, the employment of both examples—of space (*ākāśa*), which is in reality non-situated within many objects that possess defects, and of the sun (*aṃśumat*), which is in reality not situated [within them]—is indeed appropriate for the purpose of establishing the mere exclusion of the Supreme Self from partaking in the defects residing in earth and other elements. Just as space, even when joined individually with jars, water-pots, and the like that undergo increase and decrease, is not touched by the defects of increase, decrease, and so forth; [so too is the Self].

Just as the sun, though seen in various receptacles of water, is not affected by the increase, decrease, or other changes occurring therein; so too this Supreme Self, though abiding within the diverse forms of insentient things such as the earth, as well as within sentient beings, remains untouched by the defects of increase, decrease, and the like associated with those respective substrates. Although existing everywhere, it is one alone, untainted by even a scent of defect, and is the source of all auspicious qualities.

This is what is meant: just as the sun, which in reality does not abide in water and other such things, has no attachment to the defects of the water and so forth due to the absence of a cause [for such attachment], so too the Supreme Self, although abiding in earth and other elements, has no connection with defects because there is an absence of any cause for defects, owing to His nature being the very opposite of defects.

And because it is observed: even in the absence of complete similarity (*sādharmya*), the employment of an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) occurs on account of similarity in the intended aspect, as in "the boy is like a lion" and so forth. Therefore, for that [Brahman] which by its very nature is free from even a trace of defects such as ignorance and is a mine of all auspicious qualities, there is no possibility of defect even when residing in earth and other elements. || 20 ||

However, the perception of the sun in water at a distance does not [serve as a valid] illustration; therefore, the meaning is that one must accept a form that follows both illustrations and is free from defects such as increase and decrease.

Regarding the phrase "this [is] so": even for the sake of illustration, the absence of the triad of proximity—consisting of place, time, and intrinsic nature—is the underlying cause for the non-contact with defects. Conversely, the presence of the triad of proximity is the cause for contact with defects. The purpose of providing these examples is to demonstrate that, just like spatial distance (*deśaviprakarṣa*), temporal distance (*svabhāvaviprakarṣa*) is also a cause for the non-contact with defects. The example for spatial distance is the sun in water and the like; the example for temporal distance is space (*ākāśa*). || 20 ||
[The word] *svāpādanam* [is found in] Tha. 5. [The word] *nānāprakāreṣu* [is found in] Da.
Now, it might be argued:

having introduced [the topic] with "There are indeed two forms of Brahman, the formed and the formless," and having referred to the entire phenomenal world in its gross and subtle forms as being the form of Brahman, [it continues:]...
Having thus described the specific form of that very person with the words, "His form is like a garment dyed with turmeric," and so forth, [the text continues].

"Now, therefore, the instruction is: 'Not this, not this. For there is nothing else whatsoever beyond this 'not this. By referring with the word "this" (*iti*) to all the aforementioned modes of Brahman and negating them all, [the text] shows that Brahman is pure Being alone, the substratum of all distinctions, whereas distinctions are merely imagined by Brahman when it does not know its own true nature as being of such a kind. Therefore, how can Brahman possess both characteristics?—to this, he says: [The opponent] says here:
335. "For [the scripture] denies that the Brahman has only the nature previously stated; thereafter it speaks further.

(Sūtra 3.2.21, Siddhānta) This is not tenable—that the specific qualities of Brahman as previously stated are denied by the words "not this, not this" (*neti neti*). For if that were so, it would be like the prattle of a deluded person. Indeed, no sane person, having first taught everything unknown through other means of knowledge as a qualification of Brahman, would then subsequently deny those very qualifications.

Although some of the categories being pointed out are already established by other means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), nevertheless, their status as modes (*prakāratva*) of Brahman remains unknown. As for the others, both their essential nature and their status as modes of Brahman are unknown. Therefore, since it is impossible to merely restate them, they are taught right here. Consequently, their negation would not be appropriate. Because this is so—[the term] *mahārajana* refers to safflower (*kusumbha*). By the words ending with "therefore it is not appropriate," the word *hi* (for/indeed) found in the Sūtra... [is explained].
"Therefore, there is nothing else higher than this 'Not-So. Now, its name is 'the Truth of truth,' for it is indeed the truth of those [elements]."

"Life-breaths (prāṇāḥ) indeed are truth. This is the meaning: "That Brahman which has been established as 'Not this, not this'—there is no other entity higher than that. The meaning is that there is nothing else superior to Brahman, either in its essential nature (svarūpa) or in its attributes (guṇa). And the name of that Brahman is 'the Truth of truth' (satyasya satyam). Its etymological explanation is: 'The life-breaths are truth; of these, this [Brahman] is the truth. By the word 'life-breaths' (prāṇa), living beings (jīvāḥ) are referred to by association with the vital breaths. They are indeed truth;"

Because, unlike ether and the other elements, there is no modification consisting of a change in essential nature (*svarūpānyathābhāva*). "Of these, He is the Real"—of them too, this Supreme Person is the Real. For individual souls (*jīvas*), there exist contraction and expansion of knowledge in accordance with their karma; however, for the Supreme Person, who is free from all evil, those two do not exist. Therefore, even compared to them, He is the Real.

The meaning for the hungry ghosts (*preta*) has been stated. "Not at all, not so" means that the limitation (*iyattā*) of Brahman is established merely by being qualified by the aforementioned modes; since that [limitation] is also just a mode, it is referred to by the word "this" (*iti*). This is the sense.

The word "thereupon" (*tataḥ*) is explained by the word "immediately after" (*anantaram*). By the word "furthermore" (*bhūyaḥ*), abundance (*bhūyiṣṭhatvam*) is expressed. This is the beginning of the meaning. In the passage "for not from this," the intent is understood to be a negation; it is not intended to refer to qualities (*guṇa*), nor is it merely the truth of the essential nature (*svarūpa*). To dispel such doubts, [it is said] that by the phrase "superior both in its essential nature and in its qualities," the statement of the remainder of the sentence, "not this, not this" (*neti neti*), does not negate the fact that Brahman possesses distinctions (*saviśeṣatva*); rather, it negates only the limited extent (*iyattā*) previously mentioned.
Therefore, the Supreme Brahman indeed possesses both genders. || 21 ||

Since Brahman is not within the scope of other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it is impossible to negate its connection with the forms of the formed and the formless by way of restating them; therefore, the negation of its [intrinsic] magnitude has been stated in this context. That very fact—that it is beyond the scope of other means of knowledge—is confirmed by the following:

**336. "For the scripture says that it is unmanifest" (sūtra 3.2.22).** That Brahman is not manifested by any other means of knowledge. For the scripture declares: [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.19] "It is not manifest."
"His form does not stand within the range of vision; no one sees him with the eye," and "He is not grasped by the eye, nor even by speech," and so forth. || 22 ||
And he states another reason:
"337. Also, [the realization of Him] occurs during the act of propitiation, according to scripture and inference" (Sūtra 3.2.23).

Furthermore, it is understood from Śruti and Smṛti that His direct intuition (*sākṣātkāra*) occurs only during "propitiation"—that is, during perfect pleasing, which consists of meditative contemplation (*nididhyāsana*) characterized by devotion—and not elsewhere.
"This Self is not to be attained by instruction, nor by intellect, nor by much hearing.

Only he whom this [Self] chooses, by him is it attained; to him this Self reveals its own form. Thus says the Śruti. Smṛti also says: "But one whose being is purified by the clarity of knowledge, meditating upon it, then beholds that partless [Self]."

"Neither by the Vedas, nor by austerity, nor by charity, nor by sacrifice can I be seen in such a form, O Arjuna; but by exclusive devotion alone am I, who am thus, able to be known, seen in truth, and entered, O scorcher of foes. It has already been stated that "worship," "propitiation," and "pleasing Him" consist precisely in the form of devotion. Therefore, the scripture beginning with "Two indeed are the forms of Brahman," which teaches the nature of Brahman for the sake of *nididhyāsana* (meditative contemplation), is not capable of restating a previously unestablished qualification of Brahman as possessing two forms—the embodied and the unembodied. || 23 ||
338. And there is no difference [between the Lord and the individual soul] as between light and its source; moreover, the light [of knowledge] arises with respect to action through practice. 3.2.24.

For this reason as well, [the scripture] negates only the "limitedness of what has been previously described," and not the fact that [Brahman] is qualified by the formal and the formless; because, in the case of Vāmadeva and others who have directly realized the nature of the Supreme Brahman, just as with light and so forth—that is, just as the nature of knowledge, bliss, and so on [is perceived], the qualification of the world consisting of the formal and the formless is also perceived as being non-distinct from the qualities of Brahman, insofar as it takes the form of devotion (*bhakti*).

[Objection: Let there be direct realization through devotion; but what follows from that regarding the realization attained through *saṃrādhana* (intense contemplation)? [Response: To this, [the next sūtra is given]. 23.
"And in the practice of meditation, both proficiency and insight arise, due to the non-distinction between knowledge, bliss, and so forth, as well as certain supernatural powers. Thus he taught. No.

"Seeing this very [Self], the seer Vāmadeva realized: 'I became Manu and the Sun,'" and so forth. Furthermore, the light, bliss, and other qualities that constitute the nature of Brahman are perceived by those such as Vāmadeva through the practice of the rite consisting of *saṃrādhana* (intense contemplative devotion). Similarly, for those who have practiced *saṃrādhana*, their state as being characterized by both the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*) is also perceived without distinction; this is the meaning. ||24||

He concludes the statement regarding Brahman's possession of both characteristics: "Therefore, [Brahman is] with the infinite; for thus is the characteristic. (3-2-25) (Siddhānta) "Therefore"—that is, by the reasons already stated—it is established that Brahman is distinguished by infinite auspicious qualities. This being so, it follows that Brahman is logically endowed with both characteristics. 25.
Thus ends the section concerning the two-fold characteristics (ubhayaliṅgādhikaraṇa). || 5 ||

"—0— Regarding the phrase 'having become the very nature of Brahman': for it is precisely because [the attributes] such as light and bliss have been directly realized through meditation that they possess ultimate reality (*pāramārthya*), and not because they are established by delusion. Similarly, the meaning is that even the state of being qualified by the manifest and unmanifest universe (*mūrtāmūrta-prapañca*) possesses ultimate reality, since it too has been directly realized through meditation. || 24 ||

Regarding the word "ataḥ" (therefore): since there would be a confusion in the comprehension of the thesis (*sādhya*) due to the abundance of intermediate doubts and their refutations in this section, the intention of the Sūtra is to remove that [confusion] by summarizing the ultimate thesis. Thus, regarding the phrase "tathā hi sati" (for when it is so): the meaning is that when [the Sūtra] is intent upon negating a limited measure (*iyattā*), not only is the non-sublation of the dual characteristics (*ubhayaliṅgatva*) maintained, but rather, the dual characteristics themselves are established.

However, for those who take the position that [the Self] possesses both genders as the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), this Sūtra does not fit their system; for it concludes by establishing the possession of both genders. || 25 ||

10. On account of being of the same nature as that which has been described; 11. because that [Self] is unmanifest; 12. also because of the mention of "becoming one with" (saṃrādhana); 13. on account of light and so forth; 14. therefore it is infinite.
This concludes the section concerning the serpent and its coils (Ahikuṇḍalādhikaraṇa). 3.2.6.

340. But on account of the designation of both [aspects], like fire and its coils. (Pūrvapakṣa) The material world, consisting of both the formed and the formless, is the form of Brahman, as stated in the text: "Verily, there are two forms of Brahman."
Thus it is taught:
"Now, therefore, the instruction is 'not this, not this'";
by this, the limitation of Brahman as having the nature of the formed and the formless conscious entity is negated.
For it has been established by the statement, "There is indeed nothing else higher than this 'Not this'," that there is nothing superior to Brahman. To demonstrate this, it is said:

"Now follows its name: 'The Truth of truth. The vital breaths (prāṇas) are indeed truth, and He is the truth of them. This means that He is the truth even compared to the conscious beings designated by the term "vital breaths," because He never undergoes any contraction of knowledge and so forth. Thus...
"The Lord of Pradhāna and Kṣetrajña, the Master of the Guṇas"; "The Lord of the universe, the Sovereign of all"; "The Eternal among the eternal, the Conscious among the conscious."

From such scriptural passages as these, the following meaning is understood: the manner in which that insentient entity (acid-vastu) possesses the nature of Brahman is now considered for the purpose of establishing the faultlessness of Brahman—is this nature of Brahman belonging to the insentient entity according to the analogy of the serpent and its coils? Or is it through the connection with a single genus, like light and its source? Or is it by way of the relationship of part and whole (aṃśāṃśi-bhāva), as between the soul and its attributes (viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyatayā)? Thus [the inquiry].
In this context, having accepted the relationship of qualifier and qualified as being established, [the Sūtra states]:
"And the source-material [is Brahman], because the proposition and the illustrative example are not contradicted;
and because of such terms as 'originating' (ārambhaṇa), there is non-difference from that."

In this [passage], it is stated that there is the origination of Brahman qualified by gross sentient and insentient entities from Brahman qualified by subtle sentient and insentient entities, and that there is non-difference.
What is logical? That it is like a serpent and its coils.
Why? Because of the twofold designation:
"All this is indeed Brahman," and so forth.

Because of the designation of identity in such passages as "All this is indeed the Self," and because of the designation of difference in such passages as "Come, let me enter these three deities with this living self (jīva)," non-sentient objects are merely specific configurations of that very Brahman, like the coiled state or the straightened state of a snake. || 26 ||

342. *Pūrvavad vā* || 3-2-28 || (Siddhānta) The word "vā" (or) is for the purpose of excluding both [the preceding] positions. Even though a single substance possesses particular states, because the very nature of Brahman consists of non-conscious matter (*acit*), there is no liberation due to the aforementioned defect. Now, suppose it is argued that—just as between light and its substrate—there is merely a connection with the genus "Brahmanhood" (*brahmatvajāti*) for both non-conscious matter and Brahman. If that were so, then Brahman would be a universal (*sāmānya*) persisting in both conscious and non-conscious entities, just like "horseness" and "cowness" [persist in horses and cows respectively]; this would contradict all scriptural, traditional, and conventional usage. It is just as before.
"A part [of Brahman], because of the designation of difference," yet "the Supreme is not like this, being like light and so forth.
Just as in the case of the individual soul (*jīva*), non-sentient matter (*acidvastu*) is a part of Brahman by virtue of being an inseparable attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*).

The conventional usage of distinction is primary due to a difference in essential nature (*svabhāva-bheda*). Thus, the faultlessness of Brahman is preserved. Therefore, just as light, genus, quality, and body are parts of the gem, the individual, the possessor of the quality, and the self respectively—by way of being attributes characterized by inseparable existence (*apṛthaksiddhi-lakṣaṇa-viśeṣaṇatayā*)—so too here the individual soul and non-sentient matter are parts of Brahman. (28)
343. And because of the prohibition [of such qualities]. (Siddhānta-sūtra) "He is this great Ātman—undecaying and immortal; it does not decay through his decay."

By such statements as these, and because of the negation of non-intelligent attributes in Brahman, the relationship of part and whole exists solely through the relation of qualifier and qualified—this is the meaning.

Therefore, the following is all logically established: "Brahman as the cause is qualified by the subtle sentient and insentient reality; Brahman as the effect is qualified by the gross sentient and insentient reality"; "the non-difference of the effect from the cause"; and "the knowledge of the effect through the knowledge of Brahman, which is the cause. Furthermore, the faultlessness of Brahman is preserved. By virtue of Brahman’s faultlessness and its being a mine of auspicious qualities, its possession of both sets of characteristics (ubhayaliṅgatva) is also proven. || 29 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the serpent and its coils (Ahikuṇḍalādhikaraṇa).
The Śrībhāṣya 3.2.7: The Section on the Supreme (Parādhikaraṇa) || 3-2-7 ||
344. *Paramataḥ setūnmāna-sambandha-bheda-vyapadeśebhyaḥ* (Pūrva-pakṣa).

Now, having raised the doubt through certain fallacious arguments that there exists something even beyond this Supreme Brahman—the ultimate cause of the universe in the form of both efficient and material cause—this [doubt] is refuted, in order to establish that this object of meditation is faultless, uncontradicted, possessed of unsurpassed excellence, and a mine of innumerable auspicious qualities.
"In this regard, there is this doubt": that this Supreme Brahman possesses both characteristics; that there exists some reality even beyond this cause of the entire universe. How so?
"Now, that which is the Self is the bridge, the support."

Thus, because this Supreme is designated as a "bridge" (*setu*), and since the word "bridge" is well-known in common usage as the means for reaching the opposite bank, it is understood that there is something else to be reached by means of this [bridge]. Likewise, its state of being something to be crossed is expressed in the passage:
"Having crossed this bridge, even one who is blind becomes non-blind. Therefore, there exists another thing to be attained.

And because of the designation of measurement: this Supreme Brahman is measured and limited, as indicated by the designations "Brahman has four quarters" and "it has sixteen parts. This designation of measurement indicates the existence of that which is immeasurable and to be reached by means of that bridge.

Likewise, there is the designation of a relationship— characterized by the status of being an obtainer and that which is to be obtained between the bridge and the one possessing the bridge— as seen in such passages as "the supreme bridge of immortality, like fire whose fuel has been consumed" and "this is the bridge of immortality.
Therefore, there exists something higher than the highest.
And by way of distinction, it is designated as "higher than the high":
"He attains the Person who is higher than the high," and "that which is higher than the high, greater than the great."
And thus: "In this way,
all this is filled by that Puruṣa" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka).
"Then that which is higher than this is formless and free from suffering.
Therefore, for these reasons, it is understood that there is something even beyond the supreme Brahman—thus [ends the objection]. || 30 ||

Thus, because the scripture speaks of the prevention of the confusion of all worlds by virtue of its commonality as a *setu* (bridge), it is called a *setu* in the sense that "it binds (*sinoti*)"—that is, it holds together within itself the entire collection of sentient and insentient entities without confusion.
Furthermore, in the phrase "having crossed this *setu*," the verb *tarati* (to cross) signifies reaching [the goal], just as in the expression "he crosses the Vedānta. || 31 ||
346. That which has the sense of "intellect" (buddhi) [is derived] like the word "foot" (pāda). 3-2-32.

This designation of measurement— namely, "Brahman has four feet and sixteen parts," and "All beings are one foot of it"— is for the purpose of the intellect; that is, it is for the purpose of meditation.

Because Brahman, the cause of the world, is understood through such passages as "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite" to be unlimited, it is impossible for it to be measured by itself. Indeed, its status as the cause of the world is heard in scripture:
"From that very Self, indeed, space was produced," and "He desired: 'May I be many, may I procreate.'"

Thus, just as there is the designation of "feet" for Brahman (the mind) in such passages as "Speech is a foot, breath is a foot, sight is a foot, hearing is a foot," intended for the purpose of meditation, so too is this [designation]. || 32 ||; ||

As for what was stated—that because of the designation of a relationship between the attained and the attainer in the passage, "This is the bridge to immortality," there exists an object to be attained that is distinct from the attainer—that is not so;

for it is logically consistent that the Supreme Person, who is the object to be attained, is Himself the means for His own attainment. This is because scripture declares that there is no other means: "This Self is not to be attained by instruction, nor by intellect, nor by much hearing.
Only he whom this Self chooses, by him is He attained; to him this Self reveals His own form. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.3) Thus, it is heard that there is no other means. || 34 ||

349. Likewise, because of the negation of anything else. (Siddhānta) As for what was further stated: "That which is higher than that... [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.22]... [the following is established].
Because of designations of difference such as "the Person higher than the high" and "higher than the Imperishable," there exists that which is higher than the high.

That is not tenable; for in that very context, everything other than that is negated. [The texts state: "There is nothing else higher than which there is something else," and "There is nothing subtler or greater than which there is anything";
the meaning is that there is nothing higher in any manner whatsoever.

Thus, elsewhere as well, it is said: "For there is nothing else higher than this 'Not this'. The meaning is that there is indeed nothing else higher than this Brahman which has been indicated by the phrase "Not this."
Likewise:

"No one rules over him; his name is Great Glory. For that [Self] was just mentioned as the material cause of the world: "All moments of time were born from the luminous Person... he milked forth these two worlds and the waters."
By such passages as "Born from the waters, Hiraṇyagarbha," and "These eight," [the text] causes one to recognize this very Puruṣa as the cause of the world.

If it is asked, "Then what is meant by the phrase 'that which is higher than that'?"—[the answer is as follows]: In the preceding [passage], if the word *apara* were construed with the ablative form *yasmāt*, it would result in a negation of anything superior (*samādhika*). However, if it were construed with the word *para*, it would not result in a negation of equals (*sama*). And that is undesirable. For if that were the case, the previously stated fact—that the knowledge of the Supreme Person alone is the means to liberation—would not be established; there would be a contradiction with other scriptural passages that negate both equals and superiors; and the word *apara* would become redundant.
"I know this great Puruṣa, refulgent like the sun, beyond darkness;

only by knowing Him does one pass over death; there is no other path for going. Having thus taught that "the knowledge of the Supreme Brahman, the Great Puruṣa alone, is the means to immortality; there is no other path to immortality," [the text proceeds] to establish that through reasoning:

"Since there is nothing else higher than him, and nothing smaller or greater than him; standing alone like a tree in heaven, by that Puruṣa all this is pervaded"—having thus established the supremacy of the Puruṣa and the impossibility of anything else being supreme, [it continues]: "That which is higher than that is formless and free from suffering."

"Those who know this become immortal, while others enter only into suffering. Thus, he concludes the previously stated meaning by providing the reason: "That which is the higher reality of the Puruṣa is itself formless and free from affliction; therefore, those who know this reality of the Puruṣa—they alone become immortal. But others enter only into suffering. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the opening statement and a contradiction with what was said immediately prior: "He attains the divine Puruṣa, who is higher than the high. This was stated earlier.

Regarding the phrase "beyond the Imperishable" (*akṣarāt parataḥ paraḥ*): from the "Imperishable," which is the Undifferentiated (*avyākṛta*), there is one who is beyond—the Collective Person (*samaṣṭipuruṣa*). Beyond that is the Omniscient Supreme Person, whose qualities are invisibility and so forth; it is He alone who is here also designated as "beyond the High" (*parātparaḥ*), being spoken of as being beyond the Collective Person. [This is understood] from the word "and so forth" (*ādi*).
Passages such as "Brahman is all this" and "The Self alone is all this" are understood here. Therefore, this Supreme Brahman is indeed superior to everything. || 36 ||
Thus ends the section concerning another [agent]. 7.
The Topic on the Fruit (Phalādhikaraṇa) || 3.2.8 ||
[The fruit belongs] to the Supreme Self alone when pleased by worship; not to the worship alone.
"Because of the logical possibility of it being from Him" (Sūtra 3.2.37).
(Conclusion) 351.

—[The Section on the Fruit] From what [source does this follow]? From logical consistency (*upapatti*). For He alone is omniscient, omnipotent, and most magnanimous; when propitiated through sacrifices, gifts, oblations, and meditation, He is capable of bestowing the entire range of worldly and otherworldly enjoyments as well as liberation (*apavarga*), which consists in the attainment of His own essential nature. Indeed, insentient *karma*, which perishes in a moment, cannot possibly be the means for producing a fruit that arises at a later time. 3.7.17.
352. And because it is so stated in scripture.
(Sūtra 3-2-38) (Conclusion): "This indeed is that great Self, the eater of food, the giver of wealth; he indeed causes bliss."
—thus it is heard: "He alone bestows the fruit consisting of worldly enjoyment and liberation. || 38 ||
Now he states the prima facie view:
353. "Jaimini [holds that] dharma [is the purpose], for this very reason. (Pūrvapakṣa)

For this very reason—on account of logical reasoning (*upapatti*) and scripture (*śāstra*)—the teacher Jaimini maintains that only dharma in the form of sacrifice (*yāga*), gift-giving (*dāna*), oblation (*homa*), and meditative worship (*upāsana*) is the bestower of results. For in the world, actions such as agriculture or threshing are seen to be the means of attaining results either directly or indirectly by their own nature. Likewise, in the Veda as well, although sacrifices, gifts, oblations, and so forth lack direct efficacy as means to results, their status as means to results is established through an indirect process by way of the *apūrva* (unseen potency).

Likewise, a scriptural injunction such as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" (yajeta svargakāmaḥ), by prescribing sacrifice and other rites as a duty for the sake of the heaven one wishes to attain, makes known—through the principle of inexplicability otherwise—that these rites are the means to the result by way of the *apūrva*. || 39 ||

354. But Bādarāyaṇa [holds] the former [view], because of the designation of a cause. (Siddhānta) The word "but" (*tu*) is for the purpose of setting aside the previous position. The venerable Bādarāyaṇa maintains that the previously stated fact—that the Supreme Person alone is the bestower of the fruit—is correct.
Why? Because of the designation of a cause.
[The root] *yaj* [is used] in the sense of "worshiping a deity."

The same applies to the Veda as well. In the case of the injunction "One desiring heaven should sacrifice," it is to be understood that the sacrifice is the means to the result; thus, there is no contradiction. ||39||

"Bādarāyaṇa maintains that the previously mentioned capacity to bestow fruits belongs to Brahman alone, who possesses those respective bodies; this is understood from the scriptural word itself. And in common worldly experience, it is precisely this [point] that is conveyed—[the text reads] "massaging the body" (gātramardanādikaṃ) in the manuscripts *ca*, *cha*, *ta*, and *5*; while *vā*, *ga*, *gha*, *ṅa*, and *dā* read "giving and so forth" (*dānādikaṃ*); and *na* reads "it makes known precisely this" (*avagamayati*).

In passages such as, "One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu; Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity; he approaches Vāyu with his own share; he [Vāyu] leads him to prosperity," even the instruction regarding the manner in which the means for achieving the desired fruit is established for one who has a desire is precisely what is required by the injunction (*vidhi*); therefore, it is not reasonable to suspect that such passages are not *tatpara* (intended to convey that very meaning). Furthermore, when the manner in which the fruit is achieved is understood from the words themselves—despite its being required—those who accept authoritative scripture do not tolerate the abandonment of that [direct meaning] in favor of postulating an unmentioned *apūrva* (unseen potency) and so forth.
Thus, in the Antaryāmin Brāhmaṇa as well:

Or [it is that] which is heard in such scriptural passages as, "He who, dwelling in the wind, of whom the wind is the body," and "He who, dwelling in fire," "He who, dwelling in the sun," and so forth; and it is also recorded in the Smṛti:
"Whichever embodied being a devotee desires to worship with faith in whatever form, I make that very faith of his firm. Endowed with that faith, he strives for the propitiation of that [form],
and from that he obtains his desires, which are indeed ordained by Me alone."
Thus [it is said].
"For I am indeed the enjoyer and also the Lord of all sacrifices. Regarding the word "Lord" (prabhu): it means the bestower of the fruit [of action].
"Those who sacrifice to the gods go to the gods; My devotees go to Me as well"; "even those who sacrifice to Me come to Me."
And thus it is said.

"And in the world," having produced various kinds of specific goods through agriculture and other means, people honor the king either through his servants or directly. And the honored king, bestowing a reward corresponding to that honor, [rewards them].

"But as for the Vedāntas," they establish the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama)—who has transcended the sphere of all other possible means of knowledge, who is free from even a trace of defects such as ignorance, and who is an ocean of natural, limitless, unsurpassed, and sublime qualities; they describe His modes of worship consisting of sacrifice, charity, and fire-offerings, as well as praise, prostration, chanting, ritual service, and meditation;
and they declare that from that Supreme Person, when thus worshipped, there results the fruit in the form of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. Thus, everything is entirely consistent. || 40 ||
Thus concludes the section on the fruit (phalādhikaraṇa). || 8 ||
Thus ends the second quarter of the third chapter in the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Bhagavad Rāmānuja.
Śrīḥ!
In the third chapter on the Means of Realization, the third section: The Integration of Qualities (Guṇopasaṃhārapāda). || 3.3 ||

1. The Section on the Uniformity of All Vedāntic Cognitions: Since there is no distinction among the injunctions for knowledge, the Vaiśvānara and other such meditations, although found in various Vedāntic texts, are indeed non-different.
The Section on Difference:
The two Udgītha-vidyās found in the Chāndogya and the Vājasaneyaka are indeed distinct from one another due to the difference in their form.
3. The Section on the Non-Differentiation of All [Elements] – 2.2.
The Prāṇa-vidyās found in the Chāndogya and the Vājasaneyaka are non-different because there is no difference in their mode of presentation.

9. The Section on the Knowledge of the Person (Puruṣavidyā): There is a difference between the two Puruṣavidyās found in the Chāndogya and Taittirīya Upaniṣads, because of the difference in their form.
10. The Section on the Vedas and so forth:
Mantras such as "śukram pravidhya" (Pierce the semen) do not constitute an auxiliary part of knowledge (*vidyā*); rather, they are an auxiliary part of Vedic study (*adhyayana*).
11. The Section on Loss (Hāny-adhikaraṇa):
The consideration of the scriptural teachings regarding the loss and acquisition of good and evil deeds by the wise person departing [from the body] applies to all meditations (vidyās).
12. The Section on the Future World (Sāmparāyādhikaraṇa):
It is determined that at the very moment of departure from the body, the wise man’s merit and demerit are destroyed without remainder.
13. The Section on Non-Restriction [Sūtra 32]:
The path beginning with light belongs in common to all forms of knowledge for the one who possesses wisdom.

14. The Section on the Imperishable (Akṣaradhyadhikaraṇa): The inclusion of the qualities of Brahman—such as "not gross" and so forth—which are taught in the Akṣara-vidyā, in all other meditations on the Supreme.
15. The Section on Interiority: The knowledge established in the questions and answers of Uṣasta and the questions and answers of Kahola is one and the same.
16. Section on Desire, etc.:
There is no difference between the Dahara-vidyās of the Chāndogya and the Vājasaneyins, because there is no difference in their form.
17. The Section on the Non-Constraint of Selection:
There is no necessity of employing meditations such as that on the *udgītha*—which are based on auxiliary elements of ritual action—within the sacrifices.
18. The Section on Offering (Pradānādhikaraṇa):
Just as Indra and others [are contemplated] during the relinquishment of the sacrificial oblation, the mental state consists of contemplating the attributes of each [deity] as being the Supreme Self.
19. The Section on the Abundance of Indicative Marks (Liṅgabhūyastvādhikaraṇa):
The section concerning the determination that the *Sahasraśīrṣā* Anuvāka is devoted to identifying the specific object of worship for all higher knowledge (*paravidyā*).
20. Section on Previous Alternatives:
It is precisely the entrance of the "mind-altar" (manaścit) and the others mentioned in the *Agnirahasya* into the sacrifice consisting of knowledge (*vidyāmaya-kratu*).
21. The section on existence within the body: the meditation upon the inner self (pratyagātman) is to be performed precisely as possessing the eight manifest qualities.
Salutation to the illustrious Rāmānuja. Salutation to Śrī. Salutation to Śrīdhara.
In the Śrī Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Bhagavad Rāmānuja,
the third chapter (the Sādhanādhyāya),
the third section (the Guṇopasaṃhārapāda).

[Sūtras 1–54] First, it is considered whether the Vaiśvānara-vidyā and others, which are heard of in multiple recensions (śākhās), constitute a single vidyā or a plurality of vidyās. Since repetition without distinction and a difference in context are factors that differentiate [vidyās], and since both of these are unavoidable in different recensions, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that there is a difference between the vidyās. For this very reason:

"Let him teach this knowledge of Brahman to those by whom the head-vow has been performed according to rule"—this restriction regarding the instruction of the knowledge applies only to the Ātharvaṇikas who observe the head-vow. For if the knowledge were one and the same, the head-vow, being an auxiliary to that knowledge, would apply to followers of other Śākhās as well; thus, such a restriction would not be logical.

Regarding that which is heard as having a single designation and a single fruit despite being manifold... in the *Pūrvamīmāṃsā*, in the section on different recensions (*śākhāntarādhikaraṇa*), after stating the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) by means of the sūtra, "There is a difference of ritual acts in different recensions," it was established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) by the sūtra, "Or rather, it is one, because there is no difference in connection, form, injunction, or name. Here, however, having raised the doubt as to whether that same principle applies to the Vedāntic statements or not, it is determined that it does indeed apply.

Regarding the Vaiśvānara-vidyā and others mentioned in various recensions (*śākhā*s), is there a difference between each recension, or is there unity? Does recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) across different recensions lead one to understand their identity, or not? Does the restriction that the followers of the Atharva Veda must perform the "Head-vow" (*śirovrata*) when receiving instruction in this knowledge prevent the application of the principle of the "different recensions" (*śākhāntara-adhikaraṇa*) to the knowledges enjoined in the Vedāntas, or not? Is the Head-vow an auxiliary part of the knowledge (*vidyā-aṅga*), or an auxiliary part of the study (*adhyayana-aṅga*)?

If [the *śirovrata*] were an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the knowledge (*vidyā*), it would obstruct the application of the principle of "other recensions" (*śākhāntara-naya*); since recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) does not establish identity, there would be a difference between the knowledges. If, however, it were an auxiliary of the study (*adhyayana*), then because the *śirovrata* acts as an obstruction to the application of the principle of "other recensions" with respect to the knowledges, and because recognition establishes identity, there is oneness of the knowledge. Thus [it is concluded].

Regarding the term "aviśeṣa" (without distinction): although the word "juhoti" is heard again in such injunctions as "He offers the Agnihotra" and "He offers with curds," a specific qualification such as "with curds" is also heard. To exclude that case, the word "punaḥ" (again) was stated. For in cases such as "He sacrifices the iḍā," "He sacrifices the barhis," and "He sacrifices to Tanūnapāt," the repeated hearing of the word "yajati" and so forth is seen to be a differentiator even within a single Śākhā. Therefore, he states this as an additional argument for the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa).

The reasoning established in the *adhikaraṇa* concerning different recensions (*śākhāntara*) would apply here as well; that is to say, it is precisely because of the difference between the two knowledges (*vidyābheda*). Regarding the phrase "if there were identity of knowledge" (*vidyaikye*): if the knowledge of Brahman were one and the same, then the attainment of the head-vow (*śirovrata*), which is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to that knowledge, by followers of other recensions would be undesirable. Since the head-vow, as an auxiliary to that knowledge, would be attained by others as well if the knowledge were identical, the restriction [of the vow to a specific group] would not be tenable. Therefore, the meaning is that there is no identity of knowledge.
This being the case, it is said: meditation is one and the same, as recognized by all the Vedāntas.

Why? Because there is no difference in the injunctions and so forth. First, the injunction is of such a nature as "one should meditate" (upāsīta) or "one should know" (vidyāt), which is a prescription for the specific meaning of the verbal root. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), [the Sūtra refers to] the principle that "it is indeed one, because there is no difference in the connection, form, injunction, and name."

Thus, those [criteria] mentioned in the sūtras concerning other branches of the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*)—namely, connection (*saṃyoga*), form (*rūpa*), and name (*ākhyā*)—are here adopted. Because these [factors], such as the injunction (*codanā*) and so forth, are without distinction, this very same knowledge (*vidyā*) is recognized across different branches. For instance, in both the *Chāndogya* and the *Vājasaneyaka*, it is said:
"One meditates upon Vaiśvānara."

Thus, first of all, the injunction (*codanā*) is identical. Since the object to be known—the Vaiśvānara who is the referent of the term "Upāsīta," which is a synonym for "Vid" (to know)—is the same, the nature (*svarūpa*) [of the knowledge] is also undifferentiated. Furthermore, the name, "Vaiśvānara-vidyā," is the same. The connection with the fruit (*phala-saṃyoga*) is also identical in both cases, consisting in the attainment of Brahman. Therefore, because of this recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) through these factors, there is unity of the knowledge (*vidyaikya*) even in different recensional branches (*śākhāntara*). || 1 ||

356. "If it is argued that [the identity of the meditation] does not follow because of the difference [in details], even in the case of a single [meditation]," (Sūtra 3-3-2). If it is argued that there is no unity of the meditations (*vidyaikya*) because of the difference in what is enjoined (*vidheyabheda*), based on the repeated scriptural mention (*punaḥśruti*) without distinction and the difference in context (*prakaraṇāntara*); [we reply: even in the case of a single meditation, the repeated mention and the difference in context are justified by the difference among the practitioners (*pratipattṛbheda*). For where, with respect to a single practitioner, both a repeated mention and a difference in context exist, there a difference in the meditations arises from a difference in what is enjoined, due to the impossibility of any other explanation (*anyathānupapatti*).

But when there is a difference in the performers, since it is possible for [the text] to be a restatement (*punaḥśruti*) and so forth for the purpose of their performance, no other thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*) can exist therein. || 2 ||
As for what was said— that because a rule regarding the instruction of knowledge is observed specifically for the followers of the Atharva Veda who observe the head-vow (*śirovrata*),
a difference in the knowledge (*vidyā*) is perceived— to that he replies:
357. "Because of the same nature of the private recitation (*svādhyāya*), because of its application to the conduct (*samācāra*), and because of the rule regarding it being like the *Sava* sacrifice.

(Sūtra 3.3.3, Siddhānta) This is not so—that the observation of the rule concerning the instruction on the "Head-vow" (*śirovrata*) indicates a difference in the knowledge (*vidyā*). For the Head-vow...

"Because of the difference [of the perceivers]" (*bhedāt*). In the first sūtra, the reason establishing the conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the section concerning other recensions (*śākhāntara-adhikaraṇa*) was stated in brief. In the second [sūtra], the doubt regarding the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) was refuted. The general [subject] to be enjoined is [the Self]; the specific [aspect] to be enjoined is meditation (*upāsana*). "Because of the difference of the perceivers" (*pratipattṛ-bhedāt*) is the refutation [of the objection] when one accepts a difference in context (*prakaraṇa-bheda*). Furthermore, it must be refuted that there is no difference in context. "Otherwise" (*anyathā*): in the absence of a difference of perceivers, there would be the logical inconsistency (*anupapatti*) consisting in the futility of the repetition of what is not different and of the difference in context. || 2 ||

"If it be argued that the unity of the meditation is not established because of the repetition of the text without distinction, we say no; for even within a single meditation, there is a repetition of the text due to the difference among the listeners. [This is the meaning of the Sūtra. "Of one's own study"—that is, of the Veda being studied—for indeed, such a rule exists for the purpose of achieving the perfection of the impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the study.

Among the followers of the Atharvaveda, there is a restrictive rule (*niyama*) that the *śirovrata* (head-vow) is an auxiliary part of their study; this is known both from their traditional practice (*samācāra*) and from the extension (*atideśa*) of the *śirovrata* to the text bearing that name. And its restriction is like that of the *sava* offerings: just as there is a restriction that the *sava*-named oblations related to the single fire (*ekāgni*) do not apply to the three sacred fires (*tretāgni*), so it is in this case. As it is said: "The *śirovrata* is for the purpose of Vedic study; just as the *sava* oblation exists for them, it does not exist in the *tretā* fires and the others."

Because it is not an auxiliary part (*aṅga*) of knowledge. For [the rule] "But the restriction [of the head-vow] is for the sake of the Vedic study being such" means that the restrictive injunction regarding the instruction of the head-vow (*śirovrata*) is indeed for the purpose of establishing that the Vedic study is such—that is, for the purpose of establishing its possession of the refinement (*saṃskāra*) produced by that vow; it is not for the sake of knowledge. Why is this so? Because [the text says]:
"This has not been studied by one who has not performed this [vow]."

Thus, because of his connection with Vedic study— [as stated in the sūtra] "And because of the qualification in the *Samācāra*"— in the treatise called *Samācāra*, there is an extension [of the rule] stating: "This also has been explained by means of the Vedic vow."

"One should teach this knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā)—meaning the knowledge of the Veda—to them alone. And its restriction is like that of the *sava* sacrifices: for just as the *sava* offerings, beginning with the *Saptasūrya* and ending with the *Śataudanā*, which are connected to the *Atharvaśiras*, occur only there and not in the three sacrificial fires (*tretāgni*). || 3 ||
And scripture shows it. (Sūtra 3.3.4) (Conclusion) Scripture also shows that meditative worship has the same content across all Vedānta texts. For instance, in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad:

"Self-study... that is its rule. For if the *śirovrata* were an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to knowledge (*vidyā*), then, because of the unity of knowledge, the *śirovrata* would apply to followers of all recensional branches (*śākhā*). However, it is not an auxiliary to knowledge at all; rather, the meaning is that it is an auxiliary to Vedic study (*adhyayana*). By the phrase "by the Vedic vow," it is meant that this [the *śirovrata*] is explained by the same principle.

Having provided an extensive instruction on the *Śirovrata* and introduced another vow (*vratāntara*), the text, by means of a statement that extends the procedure prescribed for the *Śirovrata*, designated the *Śirovrata* by the term "Vedic Vow" (*vedavrata*). Regarding the phrase "of those very [people]": the rule is that the *Śirovrata* pertains only to them (the *Ātharvaṇikas* alone). How so? "Like the *Sava*. The meaning is that it is logical for a particular ritual act to be exclusive to those belonging to a specific recensional branch (*śākhā*), just as the *Saptasūrya* [is].

The ritual has as its deities the seven suns mentioned in the mantra: "Āroga, Bhrāja, Paṭara, Pataṅga, Svarṇara, Jyotiṣīmān, and Vibhāsa. There is also the ritual known as Śataudana (the Hundred-Rice). The meaning is that the oblations beginning with the seven suns and ending with the hundred-rice are performed by the followers of the Atharvaveda in a single fire alone; they are not performed in the three sacred fires (tretāgni), and such is the rule. || 3 ||

Regarding the phrase "he shows": because the Taittirīyaka requires [certain details] that are stated in the Chāndogya, it is established that it relies upon the subject matter taught there. And as for that, [the verse states]: "The eight qualities are heard of in the Chāndogya, while [others] are in another Yajurvedic text; the scripture itself declares the identity of the knowledge in both the Dahara and [the other] meditations. (Verse 2). In the commentary on this [verse]: "Thus... they become... (ta. tha.); "those who eat the hundred-fold rice-gruel" (śatodana—da); "in that which is within, that is what must be sought" (tasmin yadantastadanveṣṭavyam).

Having stated this, [the text] proceeds by means of the question, "What is there in this that ought to be sought? and establishes that the Supreme Self, characterized by the eightfold qualities such as freedom from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*), is to be meditated upon therein.
Thus it has been said.
However, in the Taittirīyaka, relying on the reference found in the Chāndogya, it says:
"In that case as well, one should meditate upon that which is within the space (ākāśa) which is free from sorrow."
Therefore, because the knowledge is one in both places, the meditation on the Supreme Self as qualified by the eight attributes is taught;
this is established precisely through the combination of those attributes. || 4 ||

Thus, having established the identity of the meditations (*vidyā*) as proven in the section concerning different recensions (*śākhāntarādhikaraṇa*), he states its purpose: **359. Upasaṃhāro ’rthābhedād vidhiśeṣavat samāne ca || 3.3.5** (Siddhānta) Since the meditation is the same across all Vedāntas, the qualities (*guṇa*) mentioned in one Vedāntic text must be combined (*upasaṃhāra*) with those in another Vedāntic text, just as in the case of supplementary ritual injunctions (*vidhiśeṣa*).

Why? "Because there is no difference in the meaning, as in the case of supplementary parts of an injunction. Just as a quality heard in one Vedānta text—which is a supplement to an injunction concerning Vaiśvānara, the *dahara*, and so forth—is practiced for the sake of accomplishing its purpose, namely by way of assisting that [primary] knowledge through its connection with that [injunction]; likewise, even a quality taught in another Vedānta text must be "collected" (incorporated) because of its connection with that same knowledge and because it provides a specific assistance to it. The word "ca" (and) is used in the sense of restriction. || 5 ||
Śrīmad-Bhāṣya 3.3.2: The Section on Change (Anyathātvādhikaraṇa) || 3.3.2 ||
Beginning with this, [the text says]:

"Those gods said, 'Come, let us overcome the Asuras in the sacrifice by means of the Udgītha. Having thus promised the destruction of the Asuras through the Udgītha, and having described their defeat by the Asuras when they perceived the deities beginning with Speech and ending with Mind within the Udgītha,"

Having explained the defeat of the Asuras through the meditation on the vital breath (prāṇa) within the *udgītha* by means of the passage beginning with "Then they spoke to this vital breath in the mouth," [the text continues]:
"He prospers in himself; his hateful enemy and rival is defeated, for one who knows thus."
Thus, for the sake of the fruit of defeating enemies, the meditation on the *udgītha* as the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is enjoined.
Similarly, among the Chandogas as well, it is said:
"The gods and the asuras, indeed, when they were contending..."
Starting from this point, [the text says]:

"The gods indeed took up the Udgītha, thinking, 'By means of this we shall strike them down. Having thus vowed the defeat of the Asuras by means of the Udgītha, and having likewise declared the defects in viewing speech and the other [organs] as the Udgītha, it continues: 'Then they meditated upon that which is this principal breath (mukhya prāṇa) as the Udgītha,' and so forth. Having described the defeat of the Asuras through the meditation on the breath as the Udgītha, it concludes:
'Just as a clod of earth striking a stone is shattered, even so he is shattered—anyone who desires evil against one who knows this.'"

Thus, for the sake of overcoming enemies, the meditation on the vital breath (*prāṇa*) within the *udgītha* is enjoined; even though no injunctive suffix (*vidhipratyaya*) regarding the object of knowledge is heard, an injunction concerning that knowledge is inferred because its status as a means to a result is heard. Although the *udgītha*-knowledge has the excellence of the sacrifice (*ṛtusādguṇya*) as its fruit by virtue of being "for the sake of the sacrifice" (*kratvarthatva*), it was established in the *Devatādhikaraṇa* that even a fruit mentioned in an explanatory passage (*ārthavādika*) must be accepted provided it is not contradictory to that [primary fruit].
In this regard, a doubt arises: is there identity of injunction here, or not?

What is the correct view? That there is oneness of the knowledge (vidyaikyam). Why? Because in both cases, we hear of the *udgītha* itself as the object of meditation when it has been superimposed with the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and because there is no difference in the injunctions (*codanā*) and other factors. First, the connection with the fruit—consisting in the overcoming of enemies—is not distinguished [in the two texts]. The form (*rūpa*) is also not distinguished, because the object of meditation called the *udgītha* is one and the same when superimposed with the nature of the *prāṇa*. Furthermore, the injunction, which consists in the meaning of the verbal root *vid* (to know), is not distinguished. And the name, "the *udgītha*-knowledge" (*udgīthavidyā*), is also not distinguished.

In this regard, the author of the Siddhānta raises an objection by way of a shadow [of an argument] and then refutes it: "If it be argued that there is a change of state because of the word, no, because there is no distinction."

As for what was said—that there is identity of the ritual procedure—that is not tenable, because of the difference in form. Indeed, a difference in form is understood from the Vedic text itself; for in the Vājasaneyaka...

The status of being a means to a fruit does not exist at all; for the fruit of the Udgītha-vidyā is merely the excellence (*sādguṇya*) of the ritual (*ṛtu*), since there is no intentionality regarding the defeat of enemies and so forth mentioned in the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*). This has been established. This has been established. For an *arthavāda* generates interest by way of praise. Since interest is not produced by a non-existent quality, there is indeed an intentionality even in that regard; this is the meaning of what was established in the sūtra, "Bādarāyaṇa [holds that] even above that" (*taduparyapi bādarāyaṇaḥ*). Thus, the purification of the subject matter (*viṣaya-śuddhi*) has been performed.

Regarding this: is there identity of knowledge in both cases, or is there a difference in knowledge? Is the same knowledge recognized in both places, or not? Is the *udgītha* alone the object of meditation in both cases, or is it that in one case the syllable *praṇava*, which is a part of the *udgītha*, is the object, while in the other the *udgātṛ* priest is the object?

Regarding the two statements, "One should meditate on this syllable 'Om' as the Udgītha" and "Of them, this Prāṇa sang the Udgītha": do they both convey that the meditation enjoined in each case has the Udgītha as its object and the Udgātṛ (the chanter) as its object, or not? If they do not convey this, then, because the same meditation is recognized through the identity of the Udgītha being the object of worship in both places, there would be a unity of the two meditations (vidyā).

But when two statements convey that the *praṇava*—which is a part of the *udgītha*—and the *udgātṛ* priest are both objects of meditation, then, due to the difference in form (*rūpabheda*), there would be a distinction between the two meditations (*vidyābheda*) because of the absence of recognition of a single meditation in the Chāndogya and the Vājasaneyaka.
Then they said to this breath in the mouth, "Do you sing the Udgītha for us. Saying "So be it," this breath sang the Udgītha for them;
thus, having described the defeat of the Asuras through the vision of the breath as the agent of the Udgītha-singing, [the text continues].
In the phrase "He who knows thus," it is understood from the word "thus" (*evam*) that the meditation on the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed upon the agent. In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad— "Now,

they meditated upon that which is this principal vital breath as the Udgītha"— it is stated that by means of the meditation on the vital breath within the Udgītha, the ritual act of chanting, there was the defeat of the Asuras.

If it is argued: "Because of the word 'thus' in the passage, 'He who desires evil for one who knows thus,' the meditation on the vital breath (prāṇa) is enjoined specifically upon the ritual action of the *udgītha*. Therefore, since there is a difference in form—clearly because of the mention of meditation on the vital breath as the agent in one case and as the object (the *udgītha*) in the other—and since a difference in the forms implies a difference in the things to be enjoined, the mere non-difference in the injunctions and so forth is irrelevant; thus, there is a difference between the two meditations. [Response: This is not so. Why? Because the context is the same. Just as in the case of the meditation on the *udgītha* as the sun, the moon, and lightning, the context is the same, and therefore there is no difference in the meditations despite the difference in forms, so too here.
