Furthermore, the word 'thus' (*evaṃ*) does not denote the ritual action (*karman*), but rather refers back to the previously mentioned meditation on the vital breath. For the word 'thus' is used to indicate that which has been previously stated, as in the examples: "Thus spoke Yājñavalkya" and "Thus said the teacher. Moreover, the word 'thus' is used in connection with the meditation on the vital breath in the passage: "One should meditate on the syllable Om as the vital breath; he who meditates thus... Therefore, the meaning is: "He who desires evil for one who knows the vital breath in this manner [as described before]. Consequently, there is no difference in the meditations. Furthermore, the fact that the fruit is mentioned in the third person is merely a commendation of the meditation, like the statement: "The earth is the sacrificial ladle; he who knows thus becomes the possessor of a world. Thus, there is no difference in the meditations. This is established.

That is not so; because there is no distinction. For, without distinction, in both cases, the "defeat of the enemies by means of the *udgītha*" is perceived at the outset. In the *Vājasaneyaka*, it is heard at the beginning: "Those gods said: 'Come, let us overcome the Asuras in the sacrifice by means of the *udgītha*. In the *Chāndogya* as well, it is stated:

"Then the gods took hold of the *udgītha*, [thinking]: 'By this we shall strike them down. Therefore, in order to avoid contradicting the initial context, [the *udgītha* must be understood as the means].

"Among them, this Prāṇa sang the Udgītha"—here, the Udgītha, which has the nature of Prāṇa superimposed upon it, is indeed the object of the act of singing (udgāna), just as rice and other items are in acts such as cooking; it is designated as the agent out of a desire to express an excellence of ease. Otherwise, the term occurring at the beginning [of the section] would be figurative. Therefore, there is identity of the knowledge (vidyaikyam). || 6 ||
Regarding the word *udgītha*, it might initially be understood as denoting the agent; however, we reply:
"Not so, because of the difference in context, as in the case of 'the higher than the high' (*parovarīyastva*) and so forth. (Sūtra 3.3.7, Siddhānta)
"Not indeed," he says, thereby setting aside the [opposing] position. This—that there is identity of knowledge—is not the case.
Why? Because of the difference in context:
"One should meditate on this syllable 'Om' as the Udgītha."
Thus, having introduced the *praṇava* as a constituent part of the *udgītha* under discussion, [the text proceeds] beginning with:
"This indeed is the further explanation of this very syllable: 'Once, indeed, the gods and the asuras contended.'"

"Now, they meditated upon that very Prāṇa which is principal as the Udgītha"— thus the Chandogas study a meditation concerning the *praṇava* (the syllable Om) which constitutes a part of the Udgītha. But the Vājasaneyins, due to the absence of such a preceding context, introduce the entire Udgītha with the words, "Come, let us overcome the Asuras at the sacrifice by means of the Udgītha."

Then they said to the breath in the mouth, "Do you sing for us," and so forth; thus, the entire section concerning the Udgītha is studied. Therefore, due to the difference in context, there is a difference in what is enjoined; and since there is a difference in what is enjoined, there is a difference in form, so there is no unity of the knowledge (vidyā).
Furthermore:
"Then, indeed, they meditated upon that which is this principal breath as the Udgītha."

Thus, while the *praṇava*— which was previously introduced as a constituent part of the *udgītha*— is superimposed with the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and is to be meditated upon by the Vājasaneyins as the performer of the entire *udgītha*, for the Chandogas it is the *udgātṛ* priest who is to be meditated upon through the vision of the vital breath.

"Do not chant the Udgītha. "So be it," [they said]. Then they spoke to this breath in the mouth, saying, "You chant the Udgītha. Thus, having designated the repetition of the term "breath" (prāṇa) with respect to the Udgātṛ priest, [the text continues].
"He who knows thus"— here, the Udgātṛ himself, with the nature of the vital breath superimposed upon him, is enjoined as the object of meditation. And for this reason, there is a difference in form.

Nor should it be suspected that there is a contradiction with the introductory narrative of the story—“Let us overcome [the enemy] by means of the *udgītha*”—when the worship of the *udgātṛ* (the chanter) is prescribed; for in the case of the worship of the *udgātṛ*, the *udgītha*, which is the object of the act of chanting (*udgāna*), is necessarily required, as it too serves as a cause for the fruit known as "overcoming others. Therefore, because of this difference in form, there is a difference between the two meditations (*vidyā*); thus, even though the injunctions and other factors are not different, there is no identity of the meditations.

—‘Like the case of the “higher than the high” (parovarīyastva) and so forth’: Just as, even though in a single branch there is the injunction of viewing the syllable *praṇava*—which is a constituent part of the *udgītha*—as the Supreme Self, the injunction of viewing it as characterized by qualities such as being “higher than the high” through the injunction of viewing it as the golden person (*hiraṇmayapuruṣa*) constitutes a different matter. || 7 ||

362. "If [it is argued that they are one] on account of the name, then that has already been stated; however, even that [name] exists [as a reason for difference]. (Siddhānta) If it is argued that because of the identity of the name "Udgītha-vidyā," there is an identity of the meditations (vidhā), then [the reply is: that identity of names does not [necessarily imply identity of meditations]. For it was stated in the *Upakrama-adhikaraṇa* that what is understood from the conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*) should not be discarded if it contradicts what is understood from the beginning (*upakrama*); rather, one must not cause the sublation of what is understood from the beginning. In this case, however, both what is understood from the beginning and more than that is accepted. The sense is that the statement "Let us overcome [difficulties] by means of the Udgītha" has its purport (*tātparya*) upon the Udgītha being sung by the Udgātṛ priest.

The sūtra states: "As in the case of being higher than the high (parovarīyastva) and so forth. Even though the object of meditation (*ugya*) is one and the qualification of the vision is also one, a distinction between the meditations is made there based solely on the difference in attributes—such as being golden (*hiraṇmaya*) and being higher than the high (*parovarīyastva*)—belonging to the Supreme Self who serves as the qualification of that vision. What then to say when there is a difference in the object of worship? This is the meaning. Like the term *parorajāḥ*, [the word] *parovarīyān* means "higher than the highest" (*varīyasām paraḥ*). Its state is *parovarīyastva*. Thus, the difference regarding the action and the agent has been stated. (7)

Regarding the term "by name": the *Agnihotra* performed as part of the *Kuṇḍapāyinām Ayana* sacrifice is completed in just one month. [Objection: "One should sacrifice with the *Jyotiṣṭoma*"; [Reply: "There is no meditation on the *Udgītha*. Thus, it might be argued that identity [of rites] follows from the identity of names. However, both the *Kuṇḍapāyinām Agnihotra* and the obligatory (*nitya*) *Agnihotra* indeed share the same name.

Regarding the section on "Difference of Injunction" (*anyathātvādhikaraṇa*), even when there is no difference in the injunction itself, there exists [a distinction] based on the difference in name, as in the case of the name "Agnihotra" applied both to the obligatory *Agnihotra* and to the *Agnihotra* performed during the *Kuṇṇḍapāyinām Ayana* sacrifice. And likewise, as in the case of the "Udgītha-vidyā," which refers to the many meditations taught in the first chapter of the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*. (8)
363. And because of pervasion, [the view] is consistent.

(Sūtra 3.3.9, Siddhānta) In the first chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, as well as in the subsequent meditations, there is a pervasive treatment of the *praṇava*—which is a part of the *udgītha*—as the primary object of meditation introduced at the outset. Consequently, that which occurs in the midst of it [is to be understood in the same way]. For it is said: "The gods, indeed, took hold of the *udgītha*."

Thus, it is most appropriate that the word ‘udgītha’ refers specifically to the *praṇava* (the syllable Om). Furthermore, a term for a whole is seen to be applied to a part, as in expressions such as “the cloth is burnt. Therefore, since the *praṇava*, which is a constituent part of the *udgītha*, is what is designated by the word ‘udgītha,’ it is that very [syllable] which is to be understood in the *Chāndogya* as the object of meditation through the vision of Prāṇa. In the *Vājasaneyaka*, however, the word ‘udgītha’ refers to the entire *udgītha*; thus, the *udgātṛ* priest who performs the entire *udgītha* is to be meditated upon through the vision of Prāṇa. Consequently, the difference between the two meditations is established. || 9 ||
Thus ends the section on "Alteration" (Anyathātvādhikaraṇa). [Śrībhāṣya 3.3.3] Now begins the section on "Non-difference of All" (Sarvābhedādhikaraṇa) 3-3-3.
Chāndogya Upaniṣad, Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.6.4: "On account of the non-difference of all [attributes], [the meditations] are different in these [two texts].
(Siddhānta) The knowledge of Prāṇa is recorded in both the Chāndogya and the Vājasaneyaka.
Verily, he who knows the eldest and the best becomes indeed the eldest and the best.
Breath, indeed, is the eldest and the best.

And so forth. In that passage, having first established the Prāṇa as the object of meditation, characterized by the qualities of being the eldest (*jyeṣṭha*) and the best (*śreṣṭha*), [the text] then attributes to speech, sight, hearing, and mind the qualities known as "being the most excellent" (*vasiṣṭhatva*), "being the foundation" (*pratiṣṭhātva*), "prosperity" (*sampatti*), and "abode" (*āyatanatva*). Having established the superiority of the Prāṇa by demonstrating that the stability and functions of speech and the rest, as well as the body itself, are dependent upon it and performed through its agency, [the text] finally attributes to the Prāṇa those very qualities—such as being the most excellent—that were previously heard as belonging to speech and the others.

Thus, in both the Chāndogya and the Vājasaneyaka, the Prāṇa is presented as the object of meditation, characterized by the qualities of being the "eldest" and the "best," as well as the qualities of being the "most excellent" (vasiṣṭha) and so forth.

In the Prāṇavidyā of the Kauṣītakins, however, the Prāṇa endowed with the quality of "eldest" (jyaiṣṭhya) alone is established as the object of meditation; the qualities such as "best" (vasiṣṭhatva) and so forth, which belong to speech and the other organs, are not, on the contrary, established here as belonging to the Prāṇa.
In this regard, there arises a doubt: is the knowledge (vidyā) different here, or not?
What is logical? That it is divided. Why? Because of the difference in form.

Although in both cases Prāṇa alone, characterized by the qualities of being the oldest (*jyeṣṭha*) and the best (*śreṣṭha*), is the object of meditation, nevertheless, in one instance Prāṇa is perceived as the object of meditation endowed with qualities such as being the most excellent (*vasiṣṭha*), whereas in the other it is devoid of them. Thus, due to this difference in the nature of the object of meditation, there is a difference between the two meditations (*vidyā*).

This being the position reached, we reply: "Because of the non-difference of all [qualities], these [qualities] exist elsewhere. There is no difference between the meditations here; for even in the Prāṇa-vidyā of the Kauṣītakins, these qualities such as being the most excellent (*vasiṣṭha*) and so forth are present as objects of meditation.

Why? Because of the non-difference of everything—the entire manner of establishing the pre-eminence (*jyaiṣṭhya*) and excellence (*śraiṣṭhya*) of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as promised is non-different even there [in the Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad]. To explain: in the knowledge of the vital breath (*prāṇavidyā*) of the Chandogas and Vājasaneyins, we find "They disputed over who was the best" (*ahaṃ śreyasi vyūdire*), and "Disputing over who was the best" (*ahaṃśreyase vivadamānāḥ*). Is this not absent in the Kauṣītakins? Furthermore, even in the absence of the specific restatement, "In that I am the most excellent (*vasiṣṭha*), you are that most excellent," does the description of speech and the other organs being dependent on the vital breath lead us to understand the attainment of qualities such as being the most excellent by the vital breath? Or not?

If [it is argued that they are different], because in the Kauṣītaki Prāṇavidyā there is no attainment of being Vasiṣṭha and so forth, and thus the meditation does not have those as its object—therefore, since the two meditations have different objects, there is a difference between them; or if [it is argued that they are the same], because even for the followers of the Kauṣītaki there is the attainment of being Vasiṣṭha and so forth, and thus the meditation has those as its object, there is no difference in form and hence identity.

"But in the other case," however—this means that there is no further expectancy because the requirement is satisfied by a quality residing within its own context. *Vyūdire* is the reading found in the Chāndogya; *vivadamānāḥ* is the reading of the Vājasaneyins. *Vyūdire* means "they engaged in dispute.
[The variants] *vaśitva* (tha), *vadvidhura* (ā, ta, tha).

Having begun with the words "SB IV-15," and having demonstrated— after the departure of each individual organ such as speech— that the other organs along with the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the body continue to exist and perform their respective functions, and having stated that upon the departure of the *prāṇa* all things fall apart and become incapable of performing their functions, the preeminence (*jyaiṣṭhya*) of the *prāṇa* is established through the fact that the existence and the functioning of all [organs] are dependent upon it.
Thus has been established the dependence of the functions of speech and the other organs upon the *prāṇa*.
Then speech said to him: "Insofar as I am the most excellent (*vasiṣṭha*), you are that most excellent one"—thus it is restated by such passages.

Furthermore, in the *Kauṣītakins'* science of breath (*prāṇavidyā*), qualities such as being the most excellent (*vasiṣṭha*) and so forth are attributed to speech and the other [organs] for the purpose of establishing the preeminence (*jyaiṣṭhya*) and excellence (*śraiṣṭhya*) of the breath.

Then, by the passage beginning with, "Then those deities, having approached Prajāpati their father, said: 'Who indeed among us is the best? and so forth, it is established that the qualities residing in speech and the other [senses], as well as speech and the rest themselves, and even the body, are dependent upon the vital breath (*prāṇa*); thus, the preeminence (*jyaiṣṭhya*) of the *prāṇa* is demonstrated. However, the qualities of speech and the others were not merely restated by speech and the rest themselves. It is not by this much—that is, merely by establishing that the functions of those endowed with distinct forms are dependent on the *prāṇa*—that the fact that the qualities such as being the "most excellent" (*vasiṣṭhatva*) belong to the *prāṇa*, and that the qualities such as being the "most excellent" belong to speech and the others because they are dependent on the *prāṇa*, is thereby established.

Because it is already established: "For that very thing!"—namely, the fact that the vital breath (prāṇa) possesses qualities such as being the most excellent (vasiṣṭhatva), which is the "cause" for speech and the other organs possessing excellence and so forth. Therefore, since here too the vital breath is recognized as the eldest due to its possession of qualities such as being the most excellent, there is no difference between the two meditations (vidyā). || 10 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the non-difference of all [meditations]. || 3 ||
The Section on Bliss and the Others (Ānandādyadhikaraṇa) || 3.3.4 ||

Another determination concerning the scope of the limbs of the science of the vital breath (*prāṇavidyā*) will be made immediately hereafter. For instance, since the contemplation of the pre-eminence and excellence of the *prāṇa* is impossible without the contemplation of its qualities such as being the "most excellent" (*vasiṣṭha*), those qualities—even if not explicitly mentioned—must be included in the Kauṣītaki *prāṇavidyā*. Likewise, whatever qualities cannot be logically established without the contemplation of the true nature of Brahman must be contemplated in all instances of the science of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). This is the point that is now demonstrated:
365. Bliss and the other [attributes] belong to the Principal [Brahman].
(Siddhānta) In this regard, it is deliberated whether there is a synthesis (*upasaṃhāra*) of the qualities of the essential nature of Brahman across all higher knowledges (*paravidyā*), or not.

[The prima facie view is: Since there is no authority for the synthesis of those qualities studied outside of a specific context (*aprakaraṇādhīta*), synthesis applies only to those qualities heard within a specific context (*prakaraṇaśruta*).

This being the case, we reply: "Bliss and so forth [belong] to the Principal. The term "because of non-difference" (abhedāt) carries over from the previous sūtra. Because of the non-difference of the Principal—the Brahman who possesses attributes—from all meditations, and because the attributes are not separate from that which possesses them, bliss and the other such qualities belonging to Him must be combined in every instance. 11.

If that were so, then because they are not distinct from the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*), attributes such as "having joy as its head" (*priyaśirastva*)—which are heard in passages like "Joy indeed is its head" as qualities of Brahman—would necessarily apply everywhere, just like bliss (*ānanda*) and other such qualities. "No," he says: **366. "The non-attainment of having joy as its head and so on, for increase and decrease [of qualities] occur only where there is difference. (Sūtra 3.3.12)** (Siddhānta)

When the attainment of the qualities that constitute the very nature of Brahman is being discussed, qualities such as "having joy as its head" (*priyaśirastva*) and so forth are not attained [as part of that nature], because they are not qualities of Brahman. This is because qualities such as having joy as its head are included merely within the metaphorical representation of Brahman as having the form of a person (*puruṣavidhatva*). Otherwise, if there were a distinction between limbs such as the head, wings, and tail, it would follow that Brahman itself undergoes increase and decrease. And if that were the case, it would contradict the scriptural definition: "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite" (*satyaṃ jñānamanantaṃ brahma*).
Thus, [this] and so forth is contradicted. || 12 ||

[Objection: But surely, in this very way, even if one were to include all the infinite qualities—such as sovereignty, profundity, magnanimity, and compassion—which belong only to Him who possesses them, merely on the grounds that they exist inseparably from the possessor of those qualities, then everything would follow everywhere, even for those qualities not mentioned in a particular context; furthermore, there would be an inability to include them all due to their infinity. To this, he says: **367. But the others [are to be included] because of the commonality of purpose.** (Sūtra 3.3.13) (Siddhānta)

The word "but" (*tu*) sets aside the objection. However, other qualities—namely bliss (*ānanda*) and so forth—recur everywhere because of the commonality of their referent (*artha-sāmānyāt*). Those qualities which are identical in referent—that is, those attributes which define the very nature of the referent and are inseparable from the cognition of that referent—recur everywhere just like the nature of the referent itself. These qualities are truth (*satya*), knowledge (*jñāna*), bliss (*ānanda*), purity (*amalatva*), and infinity (*anantatva*). [The phrase] "because they are not qualities of Brahman"—meaning because they lack the status of being qualities of Brahman—is used. With the words "otherwise," he explains the term "difference" (*bheda*).
Regarding the phrase "and so forth," by the word "etcetera" (ādi), sentences such as "neither gross, nor subtle, nor short" are included. || 12 ||

The particle *eva* in "evameva" (just so) is intended to show that the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) is unavoidable, as it connects with the subsequent phrase "evameva ... prasajyeran. The particle *eva* in "brahmasambandhināmeva" (only those connected to Brahman) serves to emphasize the firmness of the connection to Brahman; consequently, the intended meaning is the establishment of the reality (*vāstavatva*) of sovereignty and the other qualities. By the term "the nature of the object" (*arthasvarūpa*), the nature of the substratum (*dharmisvarūpa*) is expressed. This refers to the rule that [the quality] is necessarily perceived at the time of the cognition of the object, as indicated by the general term: "That meditative absorption (*samādhi*) is said to be when [the mind] shines as if possessing the nature of the object."
For such is the statement of Śaunaka;
the meaning is "equality. By the words "and these," he shows that they are included within the *śukriya* [section].
Because of their nature as *dharma*, due to equality, they follow everywhere.
Since the nature of Brahman is defined by qualities such as bliss and so forth, and because they share identity with the nature of Brahman,
it is established that these qualities persist [in the individual soul].
The profundity, as well as the joy and purity of the immeasurables— [these are] the infinitude and so forth.
"Brahman, characterized as the cause of the world by the passage beginning with 'from which indeed these...',
is Brahman that is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite."

"Brahman is bliss"—for by means of bliss and so forth, Brahman is indeed defined in its essential nature (*svarūpa*). Therefore, for the sake of understanding the essential nature of Brahman as the object of meditation, bliss and the other qualities recur in all meditations (*vidyā*).

As for those qualities such as compassion which are recognized as belonging to Brahman whose nature has been thus defined—even though these qualities exist separately from the possessor of the qualities (*guṇin*), because they lack an inseparable connection with the cognition [of the essence], those which are heard in a particular context are to be combined only there. Thus, the position is faultless. || 13 ||

If—due to the consequence of [the Brahman] undergoing increase and decrease—the qualities such as "having the beloved as its head" and so forth are intended merely for the purpose of representing Brahman in the form of a person, and are not actually attributes of Brahman, then for what purpose is this representation of Brahman, which is not of that nature, made as being of that nature? For when something that is not of a certain nature is represented as being of that nature, there must be some specific purpose for it. As, for example:

Regarding the phrase "as the cause of the world": in certain meditations prescribed by scriptural passages such as, "One should meditate on Him as 'born from that, dissolved in that, and breathing in that'; being tranquil," the state of being the cause of the world is to be contemplated; in others, it is not. This being the case, where it is to be contemplated, the state of being the cause of the world is a *viśeṣaṇa* (qualifier), because it is included within that which is to be made known (*jñāpya*). However, where it is not to be contemplated, it is an *upalakṣaṇa* (indirect indicator), because it is not included within that which is to be made known.

For this very reason, in the commentary on the *janmādi-sūtra*, both being a secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇatva*) and being a primary attribute (*viśe�ṣaṇatva*) are accepted regarding causality. The definition of [Brahman] as qualified by primordial matter (*prakṛti*), the person (*puruṣa*), and time is "being the cause of the world. Among these, the definition of the substantive (*viśeṣya*) consists of [qualities] such as bliss (*ānanda*). With the intention that in the contemplation of the qualified whole (*viśiṣṭa-anusandhāna*) causality is to be contemplated, but not in the contemplation of the substantive alone, it is stated that [Brahman] is "characterized" (*upalakṣita*). The scriptural texts concerning purity are those such as "partless" (*niṣkala*) and "free from evil" (*apahatapāpman*). "In its own nature" (*svarūpataḥ*) means in its unique, specific form. || 13 ||

Regarding the word "yadi" (if): the purpose for representing that which is not as it is has been observed elsewhere; however, since there is no such purpose here, the state of having "dear heads" and so forth is not a mere metaphorical representation (rūpaṇa), but rather an actual quality (guṇa) itself—this is the meaning.

It was stated that through passages such as "Know the Self as the rider," the soul and its instruments are metaphorically described as the rider, the chariot, and so forth, for the purpose of bringing under control the body, senses, and other means of meditation. However, no such purpose is seen here [in the case of the qualities of Brahman]. Therefore, one must necessarily accept that qualities such as having joy as the head belong to Brahman. To this, he says: 368. [The qualities are mentioned] for the sake of meditation, because there is no other purpose. (Sūtra 3.3.14, Siddhānta)

Since there is no other purpose, this instruction on the "forming" [of Brahman] is given for the sake of meditative reflection (*ādhyāna*). Meditative reflection—meaning constant contemplation—is what is called worship (*upāsana*). Indeed, it is for the sake of accomplishing the knowledge in the form of meditation taught in the passage, "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," in order to realize Brahman as consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*).

The Brahman consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is taught by being divided into the forms of joy, delight, and so forth, and then figuratively represented as having a head, wings, and other limbs. Just as this body is the person consisting of food (*annamaya*), with its head, wings, and so on, it is said:
"Of that, this indeed is the head."
By such statements as these, [the idea] is superimposed upon the intellect; and just as in the cases of the *prāṇamaya*, *manomaya*, and *vijñānamaya* [sheaths], it is said:
"Of that [self], *prāṇa* itself is the head."

By such means as these, the parts beginning with the vital breath (*prāṇa*) are superimposed upon the intellect (*buddhi*); likewise, the "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*), which is a distinct entity from these, is also superimposed upon the intellect for the sake of meditation by means of its constituent parts—namely, joy, delight, and so forth—which are figuratively represented as the head and other limbs. Thus, they persist in the cognition of the one consisting of bliss. || 14 ||

369. And because of the word "Self" [it is so]. (Siddhānta) Because of the designation by the word "Self" in the passage, "Another inner Self, consisting of bliss," and because a Self cannot possess a head, wings, and a tail, it is understood that the possession of a head made of pleasure and so forth is merely a figurative representation for the sake of easy comprehension. || 15 ||
Since the qualities such as "having joy as its head" serve merely as indicators for that which consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*), they do not necessarily apply at all times— just as it is said:
"Another inner self consisting of breath" (*prāṇamaya*) and "Another inner self consisting of mind" (*manomaya*).
Thus, since the word "ātman" has been used previously even for that which is not the Self— as in the passage,
"Another inner Self is the one consisting of bliss"— how is it determined that the word "ātman" here refers to the Supreme Self? To this, he says:
370. *Ātmagṛhītir itaravad uttarāt* (Siddhānta). The term "Self" (*ātman*) refers exclusively to the Supreme Self, as in other instances; for example, elsewhere:
"In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone. He thought: 'Let me now create the worlds. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1). Thus, here too, by the word "Self," the Supreme Self alone is understood.
In this regard,
In such passages as these, the word "Self" (ātman) refers exclusively to the Supreme Self; it is just like that. Why is this so? Because of what follows:
"He desired: 'May I be many, may I procreate.'"
—Thus, from the subsequent passage concerning that which consists of bliss (ānandamaya). || 16 ||

371. "If it be argued that [the Self is not meant] because of the recurrence [of the word 'Self']—[we reply]: It must be so, because of the definitive statement. (Sūtra 3.3.17) If it is argued that, because in the preceding sections concerning the sheaths consisting of breath (*prāṇamaya*) and so forth—which are non-Self—the word "Self" is seen to recur, it is therefore impossible to determine [that the Supreme Self is meant here]—[we reply]: "It must be so, because of the definitive statement. This means that there is indeed certainty.

Just as in other cases, such as the passage beginning with "Verily, this was the Self," even there, based on the subsequent sentence beginning with "He looked," the reference is to the Supreme Self alone. Thus is the meaning. 16.

"Regarding the phrase 'In the preceding [passage],' etc.: according to the principle of the section on the introductory statement (*upakramādhikaraṇa*), the subsequent must be interpreted in accordance with the preceding. Therefore, why [is it so]? From the subsequent sentence, because of the restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*). In the preceding [passage] as well:
'From this very Self (*ātman*), indeed, space (*ākāśa*) was produced.'"

Thus, because the Supreme Self alone has been determined by the intellect (*buddhi*), the notion of the Supreme Self first descends into the *prāṇamaya* (consisting of vital breath) which is within the *annamaya* (consisting of food); thereafter into the *manomaya* (consisting of mind) within the *prāṇamaya*; then into the *vijñānamaya* (consisting of consciousness); and finally, the notion of the Supreme Self proceeds into the *ānandamaya* (consisting of bliss), where it becomes firmly established because there is nothing further within it. This is confirmed by the subsequent statement, "He desired" (*sa īkṣata*). Therefore, even at the beginning, the application of the word "Self" (*ātman*) to that which is not the Supreme Self occurs through the notion of the Supreme Self; thus, the position is faultless. || 17 ||
Thus ends the section concerning Ānanda and others. 4.
The section concerning the manifestation of the effect (Kāryākhyānādhikaraṇa). 3.3.5.

372. *Kāryākhyānādapūrvam* (Siddhānta-sūtra). That which was previously introduced as supplementary to the Prāṇavidyā is now considered. In both the Chāndogya and Vājasaneyaka [Upaniṣads], after declaring the Prāṇa to be the most excellent (*jyeṣṭha*) and the best (*śreṣṭha*) object of meditation, water is designated as the "dwelling place" (*vāsa*) of the Prāṇa. First, in the Chāndogya: [The text continues with the specific scriptural passages.]

He said, "What shall be my garment? They replied, "Water. Therefore, those who are about to eat surround themselves with water both before and after; he indeed becomes a possessor of garments and does not go naked.
Thus it is stated in the Vājasaneyaka.
When questioned by Prāṇa with the words, "What is my garment?", Vāk and the others replied,
"Water is the garment."
Thus it is said:
"Knowing this, learned Vedic scholars sip water before eating and sip water after eating;

they do so thinking, 'We are thereby making this very [breath] not naked. Therefore, one who knows this should sip water before eating and should sip water after eating; he thereby makes this very [breath] not naked."
Thus [it is said]. In this regard, there is a doubt: Is the sipping of water (ācamana) enjoined here, or rather the contemplation of water as the garment of the vital breath (prāṇa)?

Because the injunctive suffix is heard in the rules for sipping water, namely, "one should sip water before eating" and "one should sip water after eating," whereas in the passage "he thereby makes this very [breath] not naked," there is no injunctive suffix regarding the knowledge [of the breath]; and because the mention of the state of being "not naked" can be logically understood as being for the purpose of praise; and because the sipping of water as an auxiliary to eating is already established by Smṛti and custom—another sipping of water is enjoined here as an auxiliary to the knowledge of the vital breath (prāṇavidyā) by the force of the injunctive suffix.

This being the position reached, we reply: here, the meditation on the water used for sipping as the clothing of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed enjoined as something new—something not previously established. This is because of the "mention of an action" (*kāryākhyānāt*), which means the mention of what was not previously established. For if it were not so, there would be an injunction for a different act of sipping; but since it is understood [as a meditation], it must be an injunction for the visualization of clothing within the water used for sipping.

"By way of being for the purpose of praise" means not by way of being for the purpose of meditative reflection (*anusandhāna*). "The word *aprāpta*" refers to the explanation of a previously unestablished term. Here, the word "here" (*iha*) refers to the context (*prakaraṇa*). What is intended is that it is endowed with another injunction regarding a meditative vision (*dṛṣṭi*).

The meaning is as follows: in the passage, "Whatever there is, from dogs down to insects and moths—that is your food," the intention is to enjoin the perception of all things edible by various living beings—which serve to nourish the vital breaths—as being the food of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). By association with that, it is appropriate to enjoin the perception of [the body] as clothing (*vāsa*). Regarding the phrase "in the case of stating what is not already established" (*aprāptākhyāne*), that which is not already established is enjoined; for if one were to say "because of stating what is not established," there would be the fault of non-distinction from the thing to be accomplished (*sādhya*). To avoid that, the term is used. For there is no purpose in making known what is already known.

This is what is meant: because the injunction "one who knows thus should sip water" and "having bathed, one should eat" applies only to that which has already been undertaken [as a duty], and because it is impossible to postulate a different meaning for something not so undertaken; and because these [texts] possess the indicative marks of the purport found in both the opening and the conclusion, and because they follow both recensional branches (śākhās), this is what is intended:
"What is my garment? Water is my garment."

Regarding the statement, "They surround [him] with water," since the beginning and conclusion of the passage— "He thereby makes this very [breath] non-naked"— indicate that the intent is to view the waters as the garment of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and since the act of sipping water (*ācamana*) is already established by Smṛti and custom, the text merely refers back to the sipping of water and enjoins the contemplation of those waters as being the garment of the vital breath. For this very reason, in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, it is said:
"Therefore, those who are about to eat surround this [food] with water both before and after"; thus, what is stated is the surrounding with water alone, not the sipping of water (ācamana). ||18||
Thus concludes the section concerning the description of the effect (kāryākhyānādhikaraṇa). || 5 ||
Co-referentiality. 3-3-6.
373. "And thus it is the same because there is no difference. (Sūtra 3-3-19) [This is the Siddhānta]. In the *Vājasaneyaka*, within the *Agnirahasya*, the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā is recorded:
"One should meditate on Brahman as Truth. Now, indeed, this person consists of will (*kratu*)."
Beginning with these words, it says:

"He should meditate upon the Self as consisting of mind, having the vital breath for its body, whose form is light, whose nature is space, ... whose resolve is true. Likewise, in that same Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā is again taught:

"This person consists of mind, is effulgence, and is truth. Within his heart, he is like a grain of rice or a grain of barley. He is the controller of all, the lord of all, the sovereign of all; he rules over all this, whatever exists.
Regarding this, a doubt arises: is there a difference in the meditation (vidyā) here, or not?

Even though there is no difference in the injunctions regarding conjunction for those [meditations] called "conjunction-injunctions," there is a distinction between the meditations (vidyā) because of the difference in form resulting from the difference in the qualities to be meditated upon, such as mastery (vaśitva).

This being the position reached, it is said: "It is the same in this way. Just as in the *Agnirahasya*, a collection of qualities such as consisting of mind (*manomaya*), having breath for a body (*prāṇaśarīra*), having light for a form (*bhārūpa*), and the state of having true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpatva*) is heard; so too in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*, when the qualities such as consisting of mind and the rest are the same, there is no difference in form because the additional qualities like mastery (*vaśitva*) and so forth are non-different from the quality of having true resolve. Therefore, the knowledge (*vidyā*) is one and the same. || 19 ||
Thus ends the section on grammatical coreferentiality (samānādhikaraṇa). || 6 ||
The Śrībhāṣya 3.3.7: The Section on Connection (Sambandhādhikaraṇa) || 3-3-7 ||
374. By the same principle of connection, it is so elsewhere as well. (3.3.20)
In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, it is heard: beginning with "Brahman is Truth," and so forth.

"That which is the Truth is that Āditya, who is this person in this orb; and he who is in the right eye"—having thus begun by stating that Brahman, the Truth, is to be meditated upon in the form of the *vyāhṛtis* both in the solar orb and in the eye, [the text continues]: "Its secret name (*upaniṣad*) is 'Ahar'."
With respect to the deities: "Its secret name (upaniṣad) is 'Aham'"; with respect to the self (adhyātma): "Its secret name is 'Aham'."

Thus, there are two secret names (*upaniṣad*), which are recorded as supplementary to the meditations (*upāsana*). When the doubt arises as to whether these are restricted to their specific positions as heard in the text or whether they are unrestricted: *Note: This is the opening of the discussion found in Śaṅkara’s commentary on the Brahma Sūtras (3.3.5–6).*

Furthermore, since both [meditations] relate to the same Brahman—which has the *vyāhṛtis* as its body—as the object of worship, and because of the identity of the object of worship, the non-difference of form, and the non-difference of connection and so forth, it follows that the two meditations are one and the same; thus, there would be no restriction [of place]. To this, it is replied: "On account of the connection, there is another [name] even elsewhere. This means: because of the specific connection [of the name *bhūḥ*] with the first meditation, the name is applied elsewhere [to the second meditation] as well. Thus, the rule of restriction remains valid.

Just as there is a combination of qualities because of the unity of the object of meditation—due to the identity of the one characterized by qualities such as "consisting of mind" (manomaya) and so on, and thus an absence of difference in form resulting in the unity of the knowledge (vidyā)—so too, in other cases, because of the unity of the True (satya) Brahman associated with the eye and the sun, and thus the unity of the knowledge, there is a combination of both [sets of qualities] in both places. || 20 ||

And this is not the case—that there is a combination [of meditations] because of the identity of the form (*vidhaikyāt*). Why? Because of a distinction—namely, a distinction in the nature of the object of meditation (*upāsyarūpa-viśeṣāt*). Even though Brahman is one, in one instance it is to be meditated upon as residing in the solar orb, while in the other it is to be meditated upon as having the eye as its locus; thus, due to the difference in form caused by the difference in connection with the location, there is a difference between the two meditations (*vidyābheda*). This is not so in the case of the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā, for the location of the object of meditation does not differ there; in both cases, it is to be meditated upon as having the heart as its locus. Therefore, they remain distinct. || 21 ||
377. "And for this reason, there is both the bringing together and the pervading.

(Siddhānta Sūtra 3.3.23) The singular form [of the compound] arises from a collective dvandva. Although the "bringing together" (*sambhṛti*) and so forth are taught as unconnected (*anārabhyādhīta*), they must nevertheless be established according to their specific locations; they are not to be combined in all cases.
How can those things taught as unconnected be restricted to specific locations?

We say: "By their own inherent power. First, there is the lack of pervasiveness; for in those meditations (*vidyās*) whose sphere is a small location, such as the heart and so forth, [qualities] cannot be combined. Furthermore, qualities such as the *sambhṛti* (the supporting powers) and others, being concomitants of those [meditations], belong to the same location; thus, they are not to be combined in meditations that have a small location as their object. This applies to the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā, the Dahara-vidyā, and other such meditations that have a small location as their object.

Statements such as "greater than the earth" and "as large as this space [of the sky] is, so large is this space within the heart," occurring here and there, cannot be combined [with other meditations], for they are intended to establish the majesty of the object of meditation characterized by qualities such as consisting of mind (*manomaya*) and being free from sin (*apahatapāpman*). || 23 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the materials for the sacrificial fire. 8.
The Section Concerning the Knowledge of the Person (Puruṣavidyā) || 3.3.9 ||
378. Also because in the Puruṣavidyā, the others are not mentioned.
(Siddhānta) In the Taittirīyaka, the Puruṣavidyā is taught:
"Of that sacrifice which is thus known, the self is the sacrificer, faith is the wife, the body is the fuel, the chest..."
"The altar is the hairs, the sacrificial grass is the body hair," and so forth.
Furthermore, the Puruṣa-vidyā is also handed down in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
"The person, indeed, is the sacrifice; those which are his twenty-four years," and so forth.
In this regard, there is a doubt: is the knowledge (vidyā) different here, or not?
Thus, having declared the knowledge of Brahman, it is stated that as its fruit one "attains the greatness of Brahman."

The Puruṣavidyā, which is recorded in the passage beginning with "Of him who knows thus," is understood to be the conceptualization of the sacrifice belonging to this very knower of Brahman. Therefore,
because it is an auxiliary part of the knowledge of Brahman, the attainment of Brahman alone is the fruit here.

According to the principle that "that which is without fruit in the proximity of something with fruit is a subordinate part (aṅga) of it," the Puruṣavidyā taught in the Taittirīyaka is understood to be a subordinate part of the Brahmavidyā. However, in the Chāndogya, it is stated that the Puruṣavidyā has the attainment of longevity as its fruit.

Therefore, because of the difference in form and connection [to fruits], there is a difference between the two knowledges; consequently, there is no inclusion of the qualities mentioned in one place within the other. || 24 ||
Thus concludes the section concerning the Knowledge of the Person (Puruṣavidyā). || 9 ||
The Śrībhāṣya 3.3.10: The Section on Piercing and Other [Rites] (Vedhādyadhikaraṇa).
"It is indeed a constituent part of the Madhu-vidyā, not a constituent part of [all] knowledge.
As for the Vājasaneyins, they have the *Pravargya* Brāhmaṇa:
"The gods, indeed, sat down for a sacrificial session (*satra*)."
And so forth.

In this regard, there is a doubt: Are the mantras studied at the beginning of the Upaniṣads—such as "Piercing the Bright" (*śukraṃ pravidhya*) and "May Mitra be auspicious to us" (*śaṃ no mitraḥ*)—as well as the *pravargya* rites and others, auxiliary parts of the knowledge (*vidyā*), or not?
What is reasonable? That they are auxiliary parts of the knowledge.
Why [is this so]? Because they are mentioned in close proximity, from which their status as auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) to the knowledge (*vidyā*) is perceived.

Although it is understood through the more powerful means of *śruti*, *liṅga*, and *vākya* that the application (*viniyoga*) of these mantras—such as "I pierce the bright" (*śukraṃ pravidhya*)—and of rituals such as the *pravargya*, belongs respectively to various ritual acts; nevertheless, [they are connected to the knowledge].

Since there is no application of the mantra beginning with "śaṃ no mitraḥ" and "sahanāvavatu" elsewhere, and because they fall within the scope of knowledge (vidyā), their status as auxiliary elements of knowledge is unavoidable; therefore, these mantras must be incorporated into all meditations (vidyās).
This being the case, we reply: on account of the difference in purpose, such as piercing and so forth—
as seen in "piercing the semen," "piercing the heart," and "I shall speak the Ṛta, I shall speak the Truth."

Because these mantras are understood to be employed in rites such as the study of malevolent spells (*abhicāra*) through indicative marks such as "I have spoken the *ṛta*, I have spoken the truth," and "May our study be brilliant; may we not hate each other," they do not constitute auxiliary parts of knowledge (*vidyā*).
The Topic of Diminution (Hāny-adhikaraṇa). 3.3.11.

380. But in the case of falling away [from a state], it is a matter of taking up [a new one], because the word "taking up" is the remainder [of the sense]; as in the cases of the *kuśa* grass, the meters, the hymns of praise, and the chanting. This has been stated [in the Sūtra]. (Siddhānta) 3-3-26. The Chandogas record:
"Shaking off evil as a horse shakes its hair, and freeing oneself from the mouth of Rāhu like the moon."
"Having shaken off the body, with a self perfected, may I attain the uncreated world of Brahman"—thus [it is said]. And the followers of the Atharva Veda:

"Then the knower, having shaken off merit and sin, stainless, attains supreme equality. But the Śāṭyāyanins: "His sons inherit his property; his friends his good deeds; his enemies his evil deeds," and so forth. And the Kauṣītakins:

Although both of these are mentioned in each individual *vidyā*, they must nevertheless be understood as auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) to all *vidyās*; for even one who is established in any *brahmavidyā* and attains Brahman necessarily undergoes the relinquishing of merit and demerit, and because this "taking up" (*upāyana*) has that relinquishment as its object. Furthermore, since the meditation upon this is enjoined, it ought to be an auxiliary element of all *vidyās*.

In this regard, the following is considered: Should the meditation on loss (*hāni-cintana*), the meditation on gain (*upāyana-cintana*), and the meditation on both be treated as optional alternatives (*vikalpyeran*) or as to be combined (*upasaṃhiyeran*)? What is the correct view? "They should be treated as optional alternatives. Why? Because of the force of their separate textual injunctions (*pṛthag-āmnāna*). For if there were a combination (*samuccaya*), there would have to be a pursuit of both in every instance; and since that is already established by the *Kauṣītaki* passage itself, a separate injunction elsewhere would be entirely redundant. Therefore, the purpose of their being enjoined in multiple places is precisely that they are optional alternatives.

Thus, the consideration of abandonment (*hāna*) and attainment (*upāyana*), which are mentioned in close proximity [in the text], follows immediately; this constitutes the connection (*saṅgati*). By the word "limb" (*aṅga*), that which is disregarded is expressed, as in the phrase "all... must be accepted. By the term "whose object has been abandoned" (*prahīṇaviṣaya*), the severance of connection is expressed. "Attainment" (*upāyana*) means entering elsewhere. It is called "attainment" in accordance with the scriptural text: "They attain their good deeds" (*sukṛtam upayanti*).

The meaning is that because meditation (*upāsana*) is connected with what has been abandoned, there must necessarily be an entry of the abandoned karma somewhere. And since that contemplation is being enjoined—by virtue of the principle of "the nature of one's resolve" (*tatkratu-nyāya*), and because of the hearing of the particle *iti* in the passage, "Having departed from here, I shall attain him," it is established by scripture that the mental coordination expressed as "I am attaining" (*abhisambhavāmi*) is what is being enjoined. Thus, it is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to all forms of knowledge (*vidyā*).

Since the contemplation of what is to be abandoned and what is to be attained is for the sake of accomplishing that [attainment], the meaning is that such contemplation is a limb of all vidyās. Thus, the subject matter has been clarified.

"By way of option"—that is, they might exist as alternatives. There is also a reading: "they would be optional. Regarding the meditations on abandonment (*hāni*), attainment (*upāyana*), and both: should they be optional, or should they be combined? Is the attainment [of the soul by the elements] a limb of knowledge (*vidyāṅga*) as a supplement to abandonment, or is it independent? Is the statement concerning attainment, even when studied in another recension (*śākhā*), a supplement to the statement concerning abandonment, or is it independent?

Is the twofold scriptural mention by the Kauṣītakins—namely, the statement regarding the "attaining" (upāyana) being a supplement to the statement regarding "leaving" (hāni)—contradictory? Or not? If there were a contradiction, then because the statement on attaining would be independent, attaining would be an independent limb of the meditation, and thus there would be an option (*vikalpa*) between the meditations upon those two. If, however, the twofold mention is not contradictory because it is a supplement [to the same meditation], then it cannot be established as restricted by a difference in meditations (*vidyābheda*), since it has been stated that "this contemplation is a supplement to all [meditations]."

"Because the word *upāyana* (attaining) is the remainder [of the context]. The word "but" (*tu*) is for the purpose of indicating the refutation of the position stated as "in the case of abandonment" (*hānau*). When abandonment alone or attaining alone is heard in the scripture, the mutual combination of those two is necessarily required.
To this, it is said: "[The text] sets aside [the idea of attaining] in the case of abandonment."

Why? Because it is supplementary to the word "appropriation" (*upāyana*); that is, because the word "appropriation" is supplementary to the statement regarding "abandonment" (*hāni*). For it is indeed appropriate that the statement concerning appropriation is supplementary to the statement concerning abandonment, since the statement concerning appropriation denotes the place of entry for the merit and demerit abandoned by the knower.

Examples are presented to show that a passage recited in one location may be supplementary to a passage recited in another location: "as in the case of the *kuśā* grass, the meters, the hymns of praise, and the singing. [The Kālāpinas say: "The *kuśā* grasses are of the nature of trees (*vānaspatyāḥ*). (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.3.1)

Thus they declare. For the Śāṭyāyanins, however, the sentence "The kuśa grasses are made of udumbara wood" functions as a supplementary statement (vākyaśeṣa) to that [other injunction], because it specifies—by means of the term "made of udumbara wood"—the kuśa grasses which are already understood in a general sense as being "of the nature of trees" (vānaspatya). Likewise, [so it is].
When there is the general mention of the meters of both gods and asuras in the passage beginning with "By the meters of the gods and asuras," the meters of the gods come first.

Thus, a statement that sets forth a specific sequence becomes a supplement (*vākyaśeṣa*) to that [general injunction]. Likewise, when it is obtained without qualification that "one begins the *ṣoḍaśin* hymn with gold," the statement specifying a particular case—"one begins the *ṣoḍaśin* hymn when the sun has half-set"—becomes a supplement to that [general injunction]. Similarly, [other cases follow].
Regarding the general rule that "the officiating priests (ṛtvij) sing along," there is the specific exception:
"The Adhvaryu priest shall not sing along."
This sentence, making it understood that its scope is not restricted to those other than the Adhvaryu, becomes a supplement (*vākyaśeṣa*) to that [other sentence].

Thus, for those who do not accept the status of being a supplement to that sentence—which is capable of establishing the meaning generally understood within a specific context—an option (*vikalpa*) between those two meanings must be resorted to; and that is not tenable when another way [of resolving the conflict] is possible.

This has been stated in the previous section: "But rather, because it would be improper for there to be an option [between two independent injunctions], it should be a part of the injunction [as a supplement to a sentence]. Thus, since the sentences concerning mere relinquishment and mere acquisition form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*), and since there is no such thing as mere relinquishment or mere acquisition [independently], an option is not tenable. As for the mention of both by the Kauṣītakins, it is not contradictory, because they are distinct recipients [of the teaching] due to the repetition of the text without any distinction [of purpose]. || 26 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the other [deities]. 11.
The Section Concerning the Future Life (Sāmparāyādhikaraṇa) || 3-3-12 ||
381. "Because there is nothing further to be crossed in the next world, so say others" (Sūtra 3.3.27). (This is the established conclusion.
It has been stated that the relinquishing and the taking up of good and evil deeds are to be considered in all meditations on the Self.

Regarding the doubt as to whether that abandonment [of the subtle body] occurs both at the time of separation from the body and on the path after having departed from the body, or only at the time of separation from the body—the reasonable conclusion is that it occurs in both cases; for it is heard in scripture in both ways. For thus do the Kauṣītakins record, beginning with:
"Having reached this path of the gods, he goes to the world of Agni."... [and so on].

"He comes to the river Virajā; he crosses it by means of the mind; there he shakes off his good and evil deeds. In this passage, the abandonment of good and evil deeds on the path is understood. But the Tāṇḍins [read]:
"Shaking off evil as a horse shakes its hair, and freeing himself from the mouth of Rāhu like the moon."

"Having shaken off the body, I, with a perfected self, attain the uncreated world of Brahman. Here, however, it is understood that this occurs "at the time of separation from the body. In the Śāṭyāyanaka as well, it is heard: "His sons inherit his property; his friends [inherit] his good deeds, and his enemies his evil deeds. Since the transfer of good and evil deeds is heard to occur simultaneously with the transfer of the inheritance to the sons, it is understood to take place "at the time of separation from the body. Therefore, one portion of the good and evil deeds is cast off at the time of separation from the body, while the remainder is cast off along the way.

This being the position, it is replied: "At the time of departure" (sāmparāye). At the very time of departure from the body, the good and evil deeds of the knower perish without remainder. Why? Because "there is nothing further to be crossed. For after the knower's separation from the body, there is no experience to be crossed over by means of good and evil deeds; indeed, apart from the attainment of Brahman which is the fruit of knowledge, there exists no pleasure or pain to be experienced through good and evil deeds.

For thus others teach that after the separation from the body, there is an absence of the experience of pleasure and pain distinct from the attainment of Brahman: "Pleasure and pain do not touch one who dwells bodiless," and "This serene being, having arisen from this body and having reached the highest light,
manifests in its own true form."
"For him there is delay only so long as he is not released; then he shall be united," thus [it is said]. || 27 ||

Regarding the syntactical connection of the phrase "He shakes off his good and evil deeds" (*sukṛtaḥ duṣkṛte dhūnute*), should it be construed prior to the passage "He [goes] along this path of the gods" (*sa etaṃ devayānam*)? Is it more reasonable to construe it earlier in order to conform to the scriptural teaching that a bodiless being experiences pleasure and pain, or is it more reasonable to construe it according to the reading of the text for the purpose of maintaining a subtle body for the journey along the path of the gods?

Does the persistence of the subtle body occur without action (*karman*), or not? If it does not, then—since the logical connection (*anvaya*) according to the reading is appropriate for the persistence of the subtle body—the connection must be exactly as [stated], because the loss [of merit and demerit] is heard of in both cases; thus, the loss would occur at the time of separation from the body and on the path [to the next world]. If the persistence of the subtle body does occur without action, then—since the description of the prior connection is logical—the connection must be exactly as [stated], because there is no mention of such loss in either case; thus, the loss of good and evil deeds would occur only at the time of separation from the body.

"Because there is nothing further to be done. Even though the scriptural statement exists, it is the very nature of the matter that is stated here as the reason; for this is what was declared in the Sūtra. ||27||

382. "According to one's wish, because there is no contradiction between both. (Siddhānta) Thus, when the time for the casting off of good and evil deeds has been determined by the very nature of things, the syntactical connection of the words should be described according to one's wish—that is, as desired—so as not to contradict either the scripture or the nature of things. In the Kauṣītaki passage, it says:
"He shakes off those good and evil deeds."
Thus, the latter part of the sentence, "having reached this path of the gods," is to be construed before the first-mentioned part; such is the meaning. || 28 ||
Here the opponent objects:
"The purposefulness of the movement [of the soul] is established in both ways; otherwise, there would be a contradiction. (Sūtra 3.3.29, Pūrvapakṣa)

The destruction of a portion of both good and evil deeds occurs at the time of separation from the body, while the remainder is destroyed later; thus, it is only when there is a destruction of karma in both ways that the journey has purpose—that is, the scriptural teaching regarding the path of the gods (devayāna-gati) possesses meaning. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction: if all karma were destroyed at the very moment of separation from the body, the subtle body (*sūkṣma-śarīra*) would also perish. That being the case, the departure of the soul alone would not be possible. Therefore, it is not tenable that the wise person's karma is destroyed without remainder at the time of departure. 29.
To this, the following reply is given:

384. "It is logical, because of the perception of objects characterized by that [state], as in the world" (Sūtra 3.3.30). It is indeed logical that there is a destruction of all karma at the time of departure.

How so? "Because of the perception of objects characterized by that"—namely, because even for one whose karma is exhausted and whose true nature has manifested, there is still perceived an object characterized by connection with a body.
"Having attained the highest light, he manifests in his own form.
"There he moves about, laughing, playing, and rejoicing. "He becomes his own ruler; for him there is freedom of movement in all worlds. "He becomes one-fold; he becomes three-fold."

In such passages as these, indeed, the meaning known as "connection with a body" is perceived. Therefore, even for one whose karma is exhausted, provided they are still joined with the subtle body, travel by the path of the gods is logically possible.

If it is asked: "How does the subtle body (sūkṣmaśarīra) persist even when the karma that initiated it has perished? We reply: "By the majesty of knowledge (vidyā). For although knowledge itself does not initiate the subtle body, it maintains the subtle body by means of the path of the gods (devayāna) in order to grant the attainment of Brahman—which is its own fruit—and to lead the soul along that path, even when all the karmas and the gross body (sthūlaśarīra), which is the instrument for the experience of natural pleasure and pain, have been exhausted without remainder.

"As in the world" (lokavat): Just as in the world, when a tank or similar work has been begun for the sake of the abundance of crops and so forth, even though the causes of that work—such as the desire for it and other factors—have perished, people continue to maintain that very tank and so forth without slackening, and therein perform activities such as drinking water; it is just like that. [The subtle state of the wise persists even after the fall of the body. 30. [The wise, even after the fall of the body...]

Now, it might be argued: "For the knowers who have directly realized the supreme reality, because their karma is exhausted without remainder at the time of the body's fall, only the subtle body persists after the fall of the body for the purpose of movement; there is no experience of pleasure or pain"—this is what was stated.

That is not tenable; for it is observed that Vasiṣṭha, Avāntaratapas, and others—who had directly realized the Supreme Reality—underwent the acquisition of another body after the fall of their previous bodies, and experienced pleasure and pain caused by the birth, death, and other events of their sons. To this, the author reads the following reply: 385.
*Yāvadadhikāram avasthitir ādhikārikāṇām* || 3.3.31 || (Siddhānta) [The souls of those entrusted with specific offices] remain [in their bodies] as long as their office lasts. (3.3.31) (Conclusion)

We have not stated that for all knowers (jñānins), there is the destruction of good and evil deeds at the time of the fall of the body. Rather, it is said that for those knowers who attain the path beginning with light (arcirādigati) immediately after the fall of the body, there is the abandonment of good and evil deeds at the time of that bodily fall. However, for those such as Vasiṣṭha who hold office (ādhikārikas), there is no attainment of the path beginning with light immediately after the fall of the body, because the office they have commenced has not yet been completed.

For those who have attained a specific office by virtue of a specific karma, that karma which initiated [the office] does not perish until the completion of that office. For indeed, the exhaustion of karma already begun occurs only through its fruition (bhoga). Therefore, for those holding office, the karma that initiated it persists as long as the office lasts. Consequently, for them, there is no attainment of the path beginning with light immediately after the fall of the body. Thus ends the section concerning the state after death (Sāmparāyādhikaraṇa). 12.
The Section on Non-Restriction (Aniyamādhikaraṇa) || 3-3-13 ||

386. There is no restriction for all; there is no contradiction, on account of scripture and inference. (Sūtra 3-3-32, Siddhānta) In meditations such as that of Upakośala, where the path of the rays (*arcir-ādi-gati*) is heard [to be the route], is the attainment of Brahman through that path restricted only to those established in those specific meditations? Or is it for all who are established in the meditation on Brahman? When this doubt arises, [the opponent argues] that because it is not mentioned in the case of other [meditations], [the path is restricted].

When the texts "And those who in the forest worship with faith and austerity" and "They worship truth as faith" are encountered, it is replied: "There is no restriction. This is because all those devoted to any form of worship must proceed by that very path; thus, there is no restriction that it applies "only to those devoted to that [specific one]. For when all proceed by that same path, there is no contradiction with scripture and inference—that is, with Śruti and Smṛti. Otherwise, there would indeed be a contradiction. This is the meaning.

Since the word "truth" (satya) is well-known to denote Brahman, and since the word "austerity" (tapas) has the same meaning as that, by the two words "truth-austerity" (satya-tapas), Brahman alone is designated.
Furthermore, the meditation on Brahman preceded by faith is heard elsewhere in scripture: "Truth indeed must be sought to be known."
Having begun thus, [the text continues]:
"Faith, indeed, is that which one should desire to understand."
The Smṛti also states: "Fire, light, day, the bright fortnight, and the six months of the northern solstice—
departing during these, the people who know Brahman go to Brahman."

Thus he states that all knowers of Brahman proceed by this very path; there are many such scriptural (śruti) and traditional (smṛti) texts of this kind. Therefore, this destination is common to all forms of knowledge (vidyā); it is already established and is merely restated in the Upakośala-vidyā and other instances. || 32 ||
Thus ends the section on the lack of fixed rule (Aniyamādhikaraṇa). || 13 ||
The Section Concerning the Imperishable (Akṣaradhyadhikaraṇa) || 3.3.14 ||

387. But there is a restriction of the cognitions of the letters on account of the commonality and their presence, as in the case of the *aupasad* [mantras]; so it has been stated. (Siddhānta Sūtra 3.3.33) In the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*, it is heard:

"O Gārgī, this indeed is that imperishable (*akṣara*) which the Brāhmaṇas declare—neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long, neither red nor oily, neither shadowy nor dark, neither air nor space, unattached, tasteless, odorless, without eyes, without ears, without speech, without mind..."
"Without heat, without breath, without mind, without bliss, without measure, without interior and without exterior— nothing whatsoever eats that.
By the command of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, the sun and the moon stand held apart."
Thus [it is said]. Likewise, in the Atharva [Veda]:
"Now, there is the higher [knowledge], by which that Imperishable is attained; that which is unseen, ungraspable, without lineage, without caste, without eyes or ears, and without hands or feet."

Are the attributes such as "not gross" (*asthūla*) and so forth—which are heard in connection with the Brahman designated by the word *akṣara* and which consist in being the very nature of the opposition to the phenomenal world (*prapañca*)—to be meditated upon in all knowledges of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), or only where they are actually heard?
In this regard, there is a doubt: which is correct? [The opponent argues: "Only where they are heard."

Why? (1) Because there is no evidence that the qualities which constitute the form of one knowledge can become the form of another knowledge; and because these [qualities], being of the nature of negations, cannot serve as means for the comprehension of the essential nature [of Brahman], unlike bliss (*ānanda*) and other such attributes. For it is only when the essential nature of Brahman has been comprehended through bliss and the like that the phenomenal attributes such as grossness (*sthūlatva*) are negated; for a negation cannot be established without a basis.

This being the case, we reply: "But there is an inclusion of the attributes of the Imperishable. The meaning is that the attributes of the Imperishable Brahman—such as "not gross" and so forth—are included, that is, gathered together, in all meditations on Brahman.

Why? Because of their commonality and because of their presence; for the Imperishable Brahman, which is the object of meditation, is the same in all meditations, and attributes such as "not gross" are present in the realization of its true nature.

This is what is meant: the apprehension of a thing indeed occurs through its unique (asādhāraṇa) form. And [the term] "mere bliss and so forth" does not present the unique form of Brahman, because bliss and so forth also exist in the inner self (pratyagātman). For bliss and so forth constitute the unique nature of Brahman, being the opposite of all that is to be discarded (heya). But in the case of the inner self, although it is by its very nature free from anything to be discarded, there still exists the capacity for connection with that which is to be discarded.

And its state of being the opposite of what is to be abandoned consists in having a form contrary to the grossness and other attributes belonging to the phenomenal world (prapañca), which is composed of the sentient and the insentient. Therefore, for one who contemplates Brahman through its unique, uncommon form, Brahman must be contemplated in the form of knowledge, bliss, and so forth, as qualified by "non-grossness" and the rest. Since non-grossness and the other qualities are included within the very perception of the nature of Brahman—just like bliss and the rest—Brahman must be contemplated in that very manner in all meditations on Brahman (brahmavidyās).

Regarding the subordination of subordinate elements (*guṇa*) to the principal element (*pradhāna*), he provides an illustration: "like the *aupasada*. Just as in the *Jāmadagnya-caturrātra* sacrifice, the mantra beginning with "agne ver hotra ver" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.2.2.1), which is recited in the Sāmaveda and serves as a subordinate element (*guṇa*) to the *puroḍāśa* offerings of the *upasads*, is employed according to the subordination to the principal by means of the *upāṃśu* (inaudible) intonation belonging to the Yajurveda. This has been stated in the first book (*Pūrvamīmāṃsāsūtra*): "In the case of a conflict between the subordinate and the principal, the connection with the Veda follows the principal, because [the subordinate] exists for the sake of that [principal]. (JS 1.3.9–10). || 33 ||

Indeed, since Brahman alone is the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*) in all Brahma-vidyās, and since qualities must conform to the principal entity, [it follows that] "He possesses all works... all odors, all tastes."
Even though this collection of qualities is established differently for each specific meditation (*vidyā*), there would be a lack of restriction [regarding their application]. To this, he says:
**388. iyadāmananāt || 3.3.34 || (Siddhānta)** Because [the scripture] declares "this much" [of the qualities]. (Sūtra 3.3.34) (The Established Conclusion)

"Āmananam" means thinking with direct orientation, that is, "contemplation. On account of this contemplation, this very collection of qualities—consisting of bliss and so forth, as qualified by the attributes of non-grossness and so on—is obtained as that which must be meditated upon everywhere. That collection of qualities without which the contemplation of the nature of Brahman, distinguished from all else, would not be possible—that alone is to be followed through all [the meditations]. And the meaning is that it is only this much. However, other qualities such as "possessing all works" and so forth, although they follow the primary subject, are established separately for each specific meditation as objects of contemplation. || 34 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the syllable *akṣara*. 14.
The Śrī Bhāṣya 3.3.15: The Section on Being Internal (Antaratvādhikaraṇa) || 3.3.15 ||
389. "If it be argued that, like the aggregate of living beings, there is no possibility of the Self being otherwise [than one], we say: No, because it is as in the case of instruction. (3-3-35)
In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, in the question of Upastha, it is thus recorded:
"Explain to me that Brahman which is immediate and direct, that Self which is within all."
To this, the reply is:
"He who breathes in by means of the out-breath (*prāṇa*), he is your Self, the innermost of all; he who breathes out by means of the in-breath (*apāna*), he is your Self."
And so forth. Being unsatisfied, he asked again, and [the Teacher] said:

"You cannot see the seer of seeing; you cannot hear the hearer of hearing; you cannot think the thinker of thinking; you cannot know the knower of knowing. This is your Self, which is within all. Anything other than this is perishable.
Likewise, immediately thereafter, in the question of Kahola, it is similarly recorded:
"Explain to me that which is Brahman, immediate and direct, that Self which is within all.
And the reply is:
"He who transcends hunger and thirst, grief and delusion, old age and death—having known this very Self, a Brāhmaṇa [renounces] the desire for sons and the desire for wealth..."
And so forth,
up to the words "from this, the goal is attained."
In this regard, a doubt arises: is there a difference between these two knowledges, or not?

What is appropriate? Difference. Why? Because of the difference in form. The form differs because of the difference in the answers. Even though the question is uniform, the manner of the answer is indeed perceived as distinct. In the former case, the agent of breathing and so forth is described as the innermost Self of all; in the latter, [the Self] is described as being devoid of hunger, thirst, and the like. Therefore, in the former passage, the inner Self (pratyagātman) is said to be distinct from the body, senses, intellect, mind, and vital breath.

But in the other [passage], there is the Supreme Self (paramātman), which is distinct from that and free from hunger, thirst, and so forth; therefore, the form [of the object] differs. Is the individual soul (jīva) the object of worship in the former case and the Supreme in the latter? Or is it the Supreme alone in both cases? In this regard, do "being within all" and "being the animator" refer to the states of waking and so forth relative to the body and the like? Or do they refer to the unconditioned [Self]? Is the statement "not the seer of seeing" a negation of anything distinct from the act of seeing? Or is it a negation of the status of being an object of thought for one who performs hearing and the other [means of knowledge]?

When there is a negation of [the Self] being distinct from the nature of the Seer (*dṛṣṭi*), then, because this [Seer] is possible in the individual soul (*jīva*), both its being the "innermost of all" (*sarvāntaratva*) and its being the "vitalizer" (*prāṇitṛtva*) are merely relative; thus, since the individual soul was the object of worship in the former [passage], the two meditations (*vidyā*) are different. When, however, there is a negation of the status of being the object of worship for the one who performs hearing and so forth, then, because both its being the innermost of all and its being the vitalizer are unlimited (*anavacchinna*), even in the former case the Supreme alone is the object of worship; thus, the two meditations are identical. Regarding the phrase "due to the difference in the answers": the sense is that the meaning of the question is understood precisely through the manner of the answer.

And for the inner self (pratyagātman) which possesses this aggregate of elements, its status as the "innermost of all" (sarvāntaratvam) is also logically established by virtue of being the inner self of that entire aggregate of elements. Although the inner self's status as the innermost of all is relative—being so only in relation to the aggregate of elements—nevertheless, that alone must be accepted. Otherwise, if one were to accept the supreme self (paramātman) out of a desire to grasp the primary inner self, the difference in the responses would not be justified.

For the first reply refers to the inner self (*pratyagātman*), because [attributes] such as being the animator and the non-animator are impossible for the Supreme Self (*paramātman*); and the subsequent [reply] refers to the Supreme Self, because it transcends hunger, thirst, and so forth. This is what the opponent objects to: "If it be argued that, like the aggregate of elements, the inner self is not different [from the Supreme Self], otherwise a distinction would be untenable. Here, "in between" means "as the innermost of all"; the first reply concerns the inner self, which possesses the aggregate of elements and stands within it—just as the aggregate of elements [is distinct from its possessor].

The meaning is that one's own self, the inner self (*pratyagātman*), is called "the innermost of all" (*sarvāntara*). If this were not so, there would be an inconsistency in the difference between the two answers: "He who breathes by means of breath" and "He who is beyond hunger, thirst, and so forth. If this objection is raised:
To this, the answer is: "No. This means there is no difference in the knowledge (vidyā). For in both cases, the question and the reply have the Supreme as their object. To explain:

The question, "That Brahman which is immediate and direct, that Self which is within all," refers exclusively to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Although the word "Brahman" is common to both the Supreme Self and the inner self (*pratyagātman*), since its usage is occasionally seen as a figurative application for the latter, the qualification "that which is immediate Brahman" is employed to distinguish it and establish the Supreme Self. Furthermore, "immediacy" (*aparokṣatva*) consists in being related to all places and all times, as in the definition:
"Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite."
