Thus, this [quality] is appropriate only for the Supreme Self, which is understood to be infinite. Its being the innermost of all is also established by the passage beginning:
"He who dwells in the earth, yet is within the earth," and so forth.
The statement, "He who, dwelling in the self, is within the self," is possible only with respect to the Supreme Self, the inner ruler of all;
the reply as well refers likewise to the Supreme Self.

The statement, "He who breathes with the vital breath (prāṇa)," establishes that the agency of breathing belongs exclusively to the Supreme Self (paramātman) without any limiting adjuncts (nirupādhika), because the individual self (pratyagātman) lacks such agency regarding breathing during deep sleep. Not understanding this, Upastha merely stated the agency in breathing by means of the mantra; however, dissatisfied—thinking the answer was common to the individual self as well—he asked again. In response to him, [the text] describes the agent of "breathing" as distinct from the individual self by virtue of being free from limiting adjuncts.

Do not think that the inner self (pratyagātman), which is the agent of seeing, hearing, thinking, and cognizing—functions dependent on the senses—is the one spoken of here as the agent of breathing; for it is not the agent of breathing and so forth during deep sleep, swoon, and the like.

Indeed, the status of being the cause of the breathing of all living beings belongs only to the Supreme Self, as heard elsewhere in scripture: "Who indeed would inhale, who would exhale, if this bliss in the ether did not exist?"

Therefore, the previous question and its answer concern the Supreme Self; the same applies to the subsequent ones as well, because the state of being beyond hunger and so forth is unique to the Supreme Self. In both cases, it is stated:
"Whatever is other than this is perishable."

And this conclusion is of a single form. However, the repetition of the question and the answer is for the purpose of establishing that the Supreme Brahman is the cause of the vitalization of all living beings and is beyond hunger and other such needs.
In this regard, he provides an illustration: "As in the case of instruction"—just as in the *Sadvijñāna* (Knowledge of Being) [Upaniṣad]: "Have you asked for that instruction? etc.
When this excellent instruction had thus begun, [Naciketas said]: "May the Blessed One indeed tell that to me;
may the Blessed One instruct me further."

Thus, the repeated recurrence of the question and the answer—“This is the subtle essence (aṇimā); this whole world has that as its self; that is the Truth”—is observed for the purpose of establishing the specific greatness of the existent Brahman. It is just like that. Therefore, because there is identity of form through the teaching of the single Brahman—which is the innermost of all—as the cause of the life-breath of all living beings and as being beyond hunger and so forth, there is identity of the knowledge (vidya). || 35 ||

This is what is intended. By this, the individual soul (*jīva*) is excluded; for it is sometimes the animator by virtue of being the presiding controller over the body, senses, and so forth, in accordance with its karma. With the word "thus" (*evam*), he dispels the suspicion that the subsequent question might have a different subject matter. Regarding the word "senses" (*indriya*):
the designation "the seer of seeing" (*dṛṣṭerdraṣṭāram*) is like the expression "he cooks the cooking of the rice" (*odanapākaṃ pacati*). This is the sense.
The meaning is that this also applies to the subsequent question and answer of Kahola. || 35 ||

3. [The opponent argues: "Because of the cause of breathing—now, let this be so—even though both the question and the answer concern the Supreme Brahman, nevertheless, a difference in the meditations (*vidyā*) is unavoidable. For in one case, [Brahman] is to be meditated upon as the cause of the breathing of all living beings; in the other, as that which transcends hunger and so forth. Thus, due to the difference in the qualities to be meditated upon, there is a difference in form, and because of the difference in the questioners: for in the former instance Upastya was the questioner, while in the latter it was Kahola. To this, he says: 390. *Vyatihāro viśiṣanti hītaravat* (Sūtra 3.3.36). (The Siddhāntin's position: There is an interchange [of attributes], for they distinguish [the object] just like the others. [Explanation: Although the two questions and answers differ in their specific qualities, the object of meditation is the same, namely the Supreme Brahman. Therefore, the attributes of one are to be combined with the other through an interchange (*vyatihāra*), just as in the case of other meditations where multiple qualities are taught. Furthermore, the distinction between the questioners does not establish a difference in the meditation, for both are inquiring about the very same Brahman. Thus, the meditation is one and the same.

There is no difference in the subject matter (vidyā) of the two sections, because they are understood to form a single syntactical unit (ekavākyatva) through the question and answer—which concern a single identical object—and by means of a single injunctive word. First, both questions have as their object Brahman characterized by being the innermost self of all.

In the second question, "That which is Brahman, immediate and direct, that which is the Self within all," the use of the restrictive particle *eva* confirms that Kahola’s question has as its object the same Brahman characterized by the qualities previously asked about by Upastha.

Thus, [the teaching] has as its single, uniform object Brahman characterized by being the inner Self of all. Furthermore, an injunctive suffix is seen later on: "Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa, having become indifferent to scholarship, should seek to abide in childhood. When it is thus determined that both [passages] have as their object the one Brahman characterized by being the inner Self of all, then, regarding that very same Brahman characterized by being the inner Self of all as the object of meditation, a mutual exchange of cognitions must be performed between Upastaka and Kahola.

Uṣasta should also form that understanding regarding the Brahman who is the innermost Self of all—which concerns its being the cause of the vitalization of all living beings—that was formed by Kahola; and Kahola, too, should form that understanding regarding that very same Brahman which transcends hunger and other such needs, that was formed by Uṣasta.

Thus, when the exchange has been made, the exclusion of the individual soul (jīva) from the Brahman that is within all is understood by both [Yājñavalkya and Maitreyī]. Indeed, Yājñavalkya’s replies qualify this innermost Self—which is distinguished from the individual self—by demonstrating its status as the cause of the vitalization of all living beings and its transcendence of hunger and other such needs, in order to lead one to understand it as distinct from the individual self. Therefore, the quality of being the innermost Self of all is the very attribute to be meditated upon (upāsya-guṇa) regarding Brahman;
whereas being the cause of vitalization and so forth are merely its supporting characteristics (upapādaka), not themselves the objects of meditation.

This is explained as follows: When Brahman, who is the inner self of all and is distinguished from the individual soul (jīva) by being the cause of the life-force (prāṇana) of all living beings, has been understood through the instruction of Uṣasta, Kahola—considering that the inner self of all must be further investigated by means of a specific nature of the jīva that is impossible for it to possess—put forward another question. Yājñavalkya, recognizing his intention, stated that the inner self possesses the quality of being the opposite of hunger and other such needs, which are impossible for it.
And for this reason, in order to establish the cognition of the exclusion of the object of meditation, a mutual exchange of cognitions must be performed by both.

[Explanation of the illustrative portion found in the Sūtra: "Like the other"—just as in the other case, namely the *Sadvidyā*, that very Brahman which is Being (*sat*) is determined through repeated questions and answers; and it is not the case that, on the basis of a quality already understood, a further meditation is taught by way of qualifying it with another quality—so it is here. || 36 ||
If it is asked: "Even there, since there is a distinction between question and answer, how is unity understood?
To this, he says:
391. "That very same [Self] is indeed [the subject of] 'truth' and so forth" (Sūtra 3.3.37).

(Siddhānta) The intention of the objection is: since the distinction [of the Self from the body] would be established by either one of the two—namely, being the cause of life or being beyond hunger and thirst—what is the purpose of mentioning the other?

Regarding the phrase "that is said": just as Uṣasta asked again for the sake of clarifying that [Brahman] is the cause of the vitalization of all living beings, so too, because no such exclusion of other possibilities had arisen in Kahola’s mind through his knowledge that [Brahman] is the cause of the vitalization of all living beings, a further question was possible. As for the word "all": when an exclusion of one or the other has occurred in the minds of both, there is a mutual exchange of their respective understandings.

The intention is that, for both [sections], the abundance of distinguishing attributes (*vyāvartaka-dharma*) serves as the cause for generating an excellence in the understanding of the distinction and the increase of the subject matter. Therefore—since it is observed that Kahola’s question is intended to clarify the distinction—the phrase "for the sake of the distinction" means: for the sake of producing an excellence in the cognition of the distinction by means of the abundance of distinguishing attributes. || 36 ||

For that very same one— designated by the word "Being," the supreme cause, the "lower deity" (aparā devatā)— is the subject under discussion in the passages: "That deity thought" and "Heat [was produced] in the higher deity."

This is established in all the sections beginning with, "Just as, my dear, the honey-makers collect honey. For the terms such as "Being" (satya) and so forth, which were declared in the first section—"All this has that as its self; that is Being; that is the Self"—are established and concluded in all the subsequent sections.

However, some maintain that the two sūtras—"There is an exchange, for they distinguish [each other] as in the other cases" and "For [the meditation on] Truth and the rest is the same"—constitute two distinct sections (*adhikaraṇa*). Regarding this, they say that by the former sūtra, it is taught that there is a mutual contemplation (*vyatihāra*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*para*) in the passage: "O venerable deity, I am indeed you; O venerable deity, you are indeed me," and "That which I am, that he is; that which he is, that I am."
Therefore: "All this, indeed, is Brahman"; "All this has that as its self."

Since this sentence has as its object the realization of the state of being the Self of all—expressed by "That thou art"—there is nothing new to be established here; thus, [the objection] is to be disregarded. That, however, will be explained later.
"But they acknowledge it as the Self and cause others to grasp it as such.

Furthermore, apart from the contemplation of the identity of all things, it is not possible for the contemplation of the individual soul (jīva) to truly exist within the supreme Brahman, nor for the contemplation of the supreme Brahman to truly exist within the individual soul.
And by the subsequent Sūtra,
[it refers to] the meditation on Truth (*satyopāsana*) as propounded in such passages as, "He who knows that great first-born Yakṣa, the Truth, as Brahman... and so forth.

[The opponent argues: "That which is the True is that Āditya—the Person who is in this orb, and also he who is here in the right eye"—thus, the identity of the meditation taught in such passages is being established.

This too is incorrect; for in the subsequent passage, there is a difference of meditation due to the difference in location (the eye and the sun), as was already stated [in Brahma-sūtra 3.3.57]: "Or rather [there is no difference], because of the distinction."
Because this has been established by the aforementioned [scriptural passage],
and because these two possess form, having the *vyāhṛtis* and so forth as their bodies,
[it is said]: "He who knows thus slays evil and abandons it."

And it is not possible [that this refers to the Self]—because the statement "on account of the teaching of what is well-known everywhere" (Brahma-sūtra 1.2.1) concerns those passages whose purport is the identity of the world [with Brahman], whereas the passage beginning with "the Self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.2) has the purport of the identity of the individual soul (jīva) [with Brahman]. Here, the state of being the Self of all is not being taught; rather, there is a superimposition of mutual identity between the individual soul and Brahman, which is a false attribution (asadāropaṇa), like the meditation on Garuḍa and so forth. That is not the means to liberation (apavarga). For the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna) alone is the means to liberation. This is the intended meaning.

The meaning of the passage beginning with "Thou art indeed I" (*tvaṃ vā ahamasmi*) is as follows: That which is the object of the word and the cognition "thou" (*tvam*) is the Supreme Self alone; that which is the object of the word and the cognition "I" (*aham*) is the same. That which is the object of the word and the cognition "I" is indeed the object of the word and the cognition "thou. The designations "I am" (*asmi*) and "thou art" (*asi*) employ the words "I" and "thou. These two words, "I" and "thou," terminate in Brahman because their respective grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) differ. The same is the meaning of the passage beginning with "He who is I" (*tadyo'ham*).
"And it abandons"—here the word "body" (*śarīram*) is to be supplied. The phrase "of the two first" refers to the two [preceding] sentences.

Thus, there can be no identity between the preceding single meditation and these two meditations which have separate injunctions for their conjunction, because they possess distinct results, forms, and other characteristics, and are independent [of one another], as shown by the passage: "He who knows this first-born Yakṣa as the True Brahman conquers these worlds."
The section concerning desire and so forth (Kāmādy-adhikaraṇa). 3.3.16.
392. "And [the mention of] desire and so forth [occurs] here and there, as well as [the mention of] the abodes and so forth.
(Siddhānta) Regarding this, there is a doubt: Is there a difference between these two meditations, or not? [The answer is: No, they do not differ, because both consist in the attainment of Brahman.

It has been determined in the section "The small [ether] on account of the subsequent [texts]" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.3.14) that the word "ether" (ākāśa) in the Chāndogya refers to the Supreme Self (paramātman). However, in the Vājasaneyaka, because qualities such as lordship (vaśitva) are heard in relation to one who lies within the ether, and since that one who lies there is the Supreme Self, the word "ether" which denotes its substratum— [...is also the Supreme Self.]

From the statement, "At its end is a subtle cavity," it is understood that the word "cavity" (suṣira) denotes the "ether" (ākāśa) situated within the heart. Therefore, there is identity of the vidyās. || 38 ||

Now, it might be argued: "What was stated—that in the Vājasaneyaka, the existence of the quality of having true desires (*satyakāmatva*) and so forth is understood along with the qualities of mastery (*vaśitva*) and the rest—is not tenable; for there, even those qualities such as mastery do not exist in an ultimate sense. And their non-existence is shown by the passage: 'It is to be perceived by the mind alone; there is no diversity whatsoever here.'"
"He who perceives here as if there were diversity goes from death to death. "This immeasurable, eternal reality is to be perceived as one alone"—
by that statement,
[it is shown that] this very Self is "not this, not this" (neti neti).

Furthermore, from the passage beginning with *hinduttareṇa*, it is understood that the Brahman to be meditated upon is perceived as being devoid of distinctions (*nirviśeṣa*). Therefore, qualities such as mastery (*vaśitva*) and so forth are also understood to be negatable, just like grossness and subtlety (*sthūlatvāṇutva*). For this very reason, even in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*, qualities such as having true desires (*satyakāmatva*) are not stated to be the ultimate attributes of Brahman. Thus, because such qualities are non-ultimate, they are omitted in meditations intended for liberation. To this, he replies:

"Regarding the word 'ether' (ākāśa), etc.: because the word 'ether' is most commonly known to refer to the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa), that [elemental ether] alone is naturally understood everywhere. In this context, the hearing of qualities unique to the Supreme Self (paramātman) serves as an exception to that common usage. Since such [qualities] exist in the Chāndogya, it has been stated there that the word 'ether' refers to the Supreme Self. However, in the Vājasaneyaka, because of the absence of those [qualities], the common usage itself is followed; this is the meaning. || 38 ||

Now, it might be argued as follows: In the Chāndogya, the "small" (dahara) meditation has as its object that which possesses qualities (saguṇa), because it is intent upon teaching qualities for the sake of a specific result; this [meditation], however, is a meditation on the qualityless (nirguṇa). Therefore, there is no identity of the two meditations—this is the meaning.

393. *Ādarād-alopaḥ* (Sūtra 3-3-39). (Commentary: Because these qualities, such as having true desires (*satyakāmatva*) and so forth, are qualities of Brahman not obtained through any other means of knowledge, they are not omitted [from the meditation on the small ether]. For it is said: "That which is within that [ether] is what must be sought; this is the Self, free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true, and whose resolves are true."
"He is the controller of all, the lord of all;
he is the sovereign of all, the ruler of beings, the protector of beings, the bridge for the separation of these worlds."

Because these two scriptural passages, as well as others, respectfully teach [these qualities] as attributes of Brahman for the purpose of meditation aimed at liberation, there is no omission of them; rather, they must indeed be combined. In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, for instance:
"Those who depart from here having understood the Self and these true desires—for them there is freedom of movement in all worlds."

Thus, having stated that there is a lack of knowledge regarding Brahman as qualified by attributes such as "having true desires" (*satyakāmatva*), the subsequent censure—"Now, those who depart after having known Him and these true desires, for them there is no freedom of movement in all the worlds"—demonstrates the importance of knowing Brahman as qualified by those attributes. Likewise, in the Vājasaneyaka: "The controller of all, the lord of all... He is the Lord of all, He is the sovereign of beings, He is the protector of beings."
Thus, from the repeated instruction regarding sovereignty, a regard for the qualities is perceived; so it is elsewhere as well.

Nor can it be said that the Śāstra— which is more affectionate than even thousands of parents— is capable of deceiving those seeking liberation (mumukṣus) by first instructing them with care on qualities that are non-ultimate, deceptive, and unestablished by any other means of knowledge, only to cause them to wander further through the cycle of saṃsāra after they have already been bound by it. For, by establishing the "single-fold vision" (ekadhā'nudarśanam) based on the fact that everything has Brahman as its essence because it is an effect of Brahman— through such statements as "There is no diversity here at all" and "It is to be viewed as one alone"— the Śāstra [prevents] that which does not have Brahman as its essence...

The word "again and again" (*bhūyo bhūyaḥ*) indicates repetition. Regarding the phrase "not perceiving" (*avedanā*): the meaning is that, having excluded the perception [of Brahman] as qualified by attributes, a censure is being made regarding the non-perception of that [Brahman] as its object.

The meaning is that reverence [for this knowledge] is observed through such factors as: the novelty (*apūrvatva*) of qualities like "desiring the truth" (*satyakāmatva*); the hearing of a fruit for its realization; the repetition [of the text] for the purpose of praising realization and censuring non-realization; the introduction and conclusion in the passage beginning with "He is the Lord of all" and ending with "That which is within Him is to be sought"; the status of being an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*); and the logical consistency (*upapatti*) consisting in the impossibility of negating what has been enjoined as something novel. The phrase "so too" (*tathā*) implies that one should likewise observe such signs of reverence in the Vājasaneyaka as well.

"And not," etc. The statement regarding qualities (*guṇa*) is not rooted in a desire to deceive; for if it were, the same consequence would apply even to the statement regarding the absence of qualities (*nairguṇya*). Nor is it intended for the purpose of meditating on a proximate fruit, because it occurs within the context of liberation and because of the scriptural testimony of "Truth" (*satya*). This is the sense. Regarding "not here": according to the maxim of the cow and the bull (*gobalīvardanyāya*), difference is enjoined as a mode of Brahman; therefore, since a general prohibition refers to things other than those specifically enjoined, the negation in passages such as "There is no diversity here" (*neha nānāsti*) has as its object a diversity that does not have Brahman as its self. (Śrutidīpikā)
"It should be viewed as one alone"—the meaning is that for some [beings] at any time, their state of being self-dependent or dependent on another should not be considered;

rather, they should be seen as having a single uniform nature solely through their dependence on the Supreme Self. The sense that this [text] negates the perception of pre-established plurality has already been explained in detail.

And in the passage, "This Self is 'not this, not this,'" the word "iti" refers back to the form of the phenomenal world as apprehended through other means of knowledge; thus, by stating "Brahman is not of such a nature," it is established that Brahman, who is the Self of all, is distinct from the phenomenal world. And immediately thereafter, the text provides the justification for this:
"It is ungraspable, for it is not grasped; it is indestructible, for it is not destroyed; it is unattached, for it is not attached."
"Unperturbed, he is not perturbed; he does not perish.

Because it is of a different nature from that which is graspable by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it is not grasped by another means of knowledge. Because it is of a different nature from that which is subject to dissolution, it does not dissolve. This same principle is to be understood in subsequent passages as well. In the *Chāndogya* Upaniṣad also, after establishing the absolute uniqueness of Brahman through the passage, "It does not age with his aging; it is not slain by his slaying; this is the true city of Brahman; in it all desires are contained," qualities such as having true desires are enjoined with respect to that [Brahman]. (39)
But even so—394. "Because of the statement regarding that [attainment] when [the Self] has arrived" (Sūtra 3.3.40).

"Arrival" (*upasthiti*) means approaching (*upasthāna*), namely, the attainment of Brahman (*brahmopasampatti*). When the inner Self has arrived—that is, when it has attained Brahman, is liberated from all bonds, and has manifested in its own true nature—it is stated that there is freedom to act according to one's desire in all worlds, precisely for the reason of that very attainment.
"Having attained union with the Supreme Light, he emerges in his own true form;

he is that Supreme Person. There he moves about, eating, playing, and rejoicing, whether with women, or vehicles, or kinsmen; not remembering this body, which is subject to rebirth. He becomes self-ruling; for him there is freedom of movement in all worlds. This very point will be demonstrated more thoroughly in the fourth [chapter].

Therefore, since the ability to move at will through all worlds is a fruit to be enjoyed by one who is liberated, the qualities such as "having true desires" and so forth must be combined for the seeker of liberation. || 40 ||
The section concerning the restriction of that determination. 3.3.17.
395. There is no rule regarding the restriction to that [particular part], because it is seen [in scripture]; for it is independent, and its fruit is liberation. (Sūtra 3.3.41) (Conclusion):
"One should meditate upon this syllable *oṃ* as the *udgītha*."

Thus, meditations based on the constituent parts of ritual action (*karmāṅga*)— such as those concerning the *udgītha* and so forth— are established as integral parts of the ritual through the medium of the *udgītha* etc., which are themselves constituent parts of the action, just as the quality of being made of *parṇa*-wood is an integral part of the ladle (*juhū*) and other implements. Because these meditations are connected to the *udgītha* and other such elements, and because it is impossible to conceive of them as having separate fruits— as in the case of hearing the "verse of no evil" (*apāpaśloka*) associated with the *parṇa*-wood— due to the present-tense indication in the text, "Whatever one performs with knowledge, with faith, and with the Upaniṣad, that alone becomes more powerful," they must be invariably combined within the rituals.

This being the position reached, we reply: "There is no rule regarding that determination. Determination (*nirdhāraṇa*) means the fixing of the mind through ascertainment; that is to say, meditation (*dhyāna*). "There is no rule regarding that determination" means there is no mandatory rule for the meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth among the ritual acts.
Why? Because that is observed. For indeed, the lack of a fixed rule for the performance of these meditations is perceived [in scripture].
"Both perform it— he who knows it thus and he who does not know it"—

since this statement regarding performance applies even to the ignorant, and because a fixed rule of performance would not be appropriate if meditation were merely an auxiliary (aṅga), it is certain that meditation is not an auxiliary. Once this is established, when the injunction for meditation seeks a fruit, it is understood— according to the principle of the *rāma* [passage]— that its fruit is indeed distinct from the fruit of ritual action, consisting in greater potency (*vīryavattaratva*).

What is this "state of being more powerful"? It is the non-obstruction of the fruit of action itself. For the fruit of an action is indeed obstructed by the fruit of another stronger action for a certain period of time. The absence of that [obstruction] is "non-obstruction. That non-obstruction is indeed a fruit distinct from the fruit characterized as heaven and so forth. This is what is meant by the statement: "For non-obstruction is a distinct fruit."

Therefore, since even those meditations based on the constituent parts of ritual acts possess separate fruits—just like the *godohana* vessel and so forth—there is no rule for the combination (*upasaṃhāra*) of meditations such as that on the *udgītha* within the rituals. || 41 ||
Thus concludes the section concerning the restrictive rule for the determination of that [single instance]. 17.
(The Section on Bestowal || 3.3.18 ||)
396. "That has been stated as being like the giving away [of the daughter]. (sūtra 3.3.42). In the Dahara-vidyā—me mine wame.

Regarding the passage, "Those here who depart having discovered the Self and these true desires," after teaching the meditation on the small ether (daharākāśa) as the Supreme Self, the separate meditation on the qualities is also enjoined by the words, "and these true desires.
In this regard, a doubt arises: when reflecting upon the qualities, must the small Self be meditated upon as qualified by each respective quality, and thus repeated? Or not?

Since qualities such as being free from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) belong to the small ether (*daharākāśa*) itself, and since that [ether] can be meditated upon as "Being" (*sat*), the meditation on it for the sake of those qualities need not be repeated. This being the position reached, it is said: "Just like the offering" (*pradānavadeva*). The meaning is that it must indeed be repeated, just like an offering. Although the small ether is one and the same—the substratum (*guṇin*) of qualities such as being free from sin—and although it was meditated upon initially, nevertheless, because the form qualified by attributes is distinct from the mere essential nature (*svarūpa*), [one must meditate on it again as] "free from sin, ageless," and so forth.

Because [the Self] has been prescribed as an object of meditation characterized by specific qualities through such passages, a repetition must be performed for the purpose of contemplating—as qualified by attributes such as being "free from sin" (apahatapāpmatva)—that which was previously contemplated in its essential nature alone. This is just as, in the injunctions "One should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra the King," "to Indra the Overlord," and "to Indra the Self-Ruler," although it is the same Indra who is qualified by the attributes of kingship and so forth, a repetition of the offering is made because the forms associated with each respective attribute are distinct. As it has been stated in the *Sāṅkarṣaṇa*:
(Saṅkarṣa) —
"Or rather, there are various deities, because of their distinctness," thus [it is said]. || 42 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the giving [of the sacrificial fee]. || 18 ||
The Section on the Abundance of Indicative Marks (Liṅgabhūyastvādhikaraṇa) || 3.3.19 ||
397. On account of the abundance of indicatory marks; for that indeed is more powerful, and that also [is stated].

(Siddhānta) In the *Taittirīyaka*, immediately after the *dahara-vidyā*, it is studied: "The thousand-headed God, the all-eyed, the source of all happiness, the all-encompassing Lord Nārāyaṇa, the imperishable, the supreme Master."
Starting from this point and ending with the words, "He is the Imperishable, the Supreme, the Self-ruling Lord."

In this regard, there arises a doubt: Is it intended by this [text] to determine the specific object of worship for that particular single vidyā which was previously introduced? Or is it intended to determine the specific object of worship for the supreme vidyā taught in all the Vedāntas?
What is appropriate? It is the determination of the specific object of meditation in the Dahara-vidyā.

Why? Because of the context. For in the preceding section, the Dahara-vidyā is indeed the subject under discussion: "The small, stainless lotus, the supreme abode, situated in the middle of the city; even there, the small ether is free from sorrow; that which is within it is to be meditated upon."
Thus, in this Anuvāka,

the description of the heart-lotus begins with the words, "The heart is like the interior of a lotus bud and is downward-facing," and so forth; this serves as an introductory support for establishing that the purpose of this Nārāyaṇa-anuvāka is to determine the object of worship in the Dahara-vidyā.

This being the case, we reply: "On account of the abundance of indicatory marks" (*liṅgabhūyastvāt*). There are seen many indicatory marks supporting the view that this [passage] serves to determine the specific identity of the object of worship in all higher knowledge (*paravidyā*). For instance, the object of worship in the higher knowledges is designated by such terms as "the Imperishable" (*akṣara*), "Śiva," "Śambhu," "Supreme Brahman" (*parabrahman*), "Supreme Light" (*parajyotis*), "Supreme Reality" (*paratattva*), and "Supreme Self" (*paramātman*); here, having referred to that very object by those same terms, its identity as Nārāyaṇa is enjoined.

Having restated what has been heard in numerous scriptures (*vidyās*), there is an abundance of injunctions regarding the nature of Nārāyaṇa; and in the determination of the specific [identity], there is a greater—i.e., more numerous—indicative mark (*liṅga*) that "Nārāyaṇa alone is the supreme Brahman, characterized by bliss and other qualities such as being non-material (*asthūla*), and the one to be meditated upon in all sciences.
Here, the word *liṅga* is a synonym for a sign (*cihna*). The meaning is that there are many sentences serving as such signs.
For that [context] is stronger than the topic. This has also been stated in the first book:
"In the case of a conflict between direct statement, indicative mark, syntactical connection, context, position, and name, each subsequent one is weaker because of its remoteness from the purpose."

As for the statement that the passage beginning with "resembling the interior of a lotus bud" serves to support the fact that [Nārāyaṇa] is the object of worship in the *dahara* (small) meditation—that is not so; for since it has been established by a more powerful means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that this [passage] serves to determine the object of worship in all meditations (*vidyā*), its mention is appropriate even in the *dahara* meditation because Nārāyaṇa himself is the object of worship there as well.

Nor should one suspect, on the basis of the accusative case in "thousand-headed" (*sahasraśīrṣam*) and so forth, that there is a connection with the object of worship mentioned in the preceding section;
for [the text states]: "That which is within it is to be worshipped."
Thus, because the suffix *kṛt* attached to *upāsin* expresses the object of worship (*upāsya*), the use of the accusative case for that object of worship is untenable.

Furthermore, from the initial designations such as "All this is indeed the Puruṣa" and "You are Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme," it should be understood that the accusative case is used in the sense of the nominative.
"Nārāyaṇa stands pervading all that is within and without;
in the center of that crest-lock (śikhā), the Supreme Self is established.
He is Brahmā, he is Śiva, he is Indra, he is the Imperishable, the supreme Svarāt."

Thus, by these explanations and because it is determined that "Nārāyaṇa alone is superior to all and is to be worshipped everywhere," it is concluded that the second case ending is used in the sense of the first. || 43 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the abundance of indicatory marks (liṅga). || 19 ||
The section concerning prior conceptual constructions. 3-3-20.

398. "The previous alternative [of figurative meditation] may apply here on account of the context, as the action is mental, like [the meditation on] the mind. (Pūrvapakṣa) In the *Vājasaneyaka*, in the *Agnirahasya*, fires such as the "mind-made" (*manaścit*) and others are heard:
"The mind-made, the speech-made, the breath-made, the eye-made, the ear-made, the action-made, and the fire-made."
Thus [the text says].

In this regard, there is a doubt: Are these fires, such as the mind-fire (*manas-cit*) and others, of the nature of knowledge (*vidyā-rūpa*) because they are produced through meditation (*sāmpādikatvena*), yet take the form of ritual action (*kriyā-rūpa*) by entering into a sacrifice consisting of action; or rather, do they take the form of knowledge alone by entering into a sacrifice consisting of knowledge? Regarding this point of uncertainty, [the author] first states that they take the form of ritual action with the words "The previous alternative" (*pūrva-vikalpaḥ*) and so forth. Since these fires—the mind-fire and others—produced as the *cityāgni* (altar-fire) require entry into a sacrifice, and since there is no injunction for a sacrifice in their own specific location in the preceding section, [they must enter the sacrifice previously mentioned].

Since the passage beginning with "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.19.1) refers to the fire-altar constructed of bricks—which is the subject under discussion—and since that altar is invariably connected to a ritual action (*kratu*) such that the ritual context is present there, the "mind-altars" (*manas-cit*) and so forth mentioned therein are included within that ritual context. Therefore, being optional alternatives to the fire-altar built of bricks, they must be of the nature of ritual action. Even those [meditations] whose form is knowledge (*vidyā*) possess the character of ritual action by way of entering into a ritual consisting of action; this is established just like the "mental cups" (*mānasa-graha*).

Just as in the *dvādaśāha* sacrifice, on the tenth day which is called *avivākya*, the *mānasa-graha*—though consisting of knowledge insofar as it involves the mental accomplishment of the taking up, placing, chanting, recitation, and consumption of the draught—is nevertheless of the nature of action because it is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the ritual action; so it is here as well. || 44 ||

399. And because of extension (*atideśa*). (Pūrvapakṣa) For this reason as well, there is an option (*vikalpa*) between the fire-altar built of bricks and those consisting of mind and so forth; furthermore, their nature as action (*kriyārūpatva*) is understood. By the statement, "Each one of these is as great as that former one," the power (*vīrya*) of the previously mentioned fire-altar built of bricks is extended (*atidiśyate*) to those consisting of mind and so forth. Therefore, because they perform an identical function, there is an option. Consequently, like the fire-altar built of bricks, since they fulfill that specific sacrifice (*kratu*), the "mind-built" and other altars—which are its constituent parts—participate in the sacrifice consisting of action and are thus indeed of the nature of action. || 45 ||
This being the case, we reply:
"But [they are] knowledge alone, because of the specific determination and because of scriptural vision" (3.3.46).

The word "but" sets aside the previous position. As for what was said—that the manas-cit and so forth, by entering into the ritual consisting of action, are indeed of the nature of action—this is not so. These are indeed of the nature of knowledge; the meaning is that they are connected with a ritual that is of the nature of knowledge.

Why? Because of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) and because of scriptural vision (*darśana*). First, as for the selection: "They are indeed built of knowledge alone; by knowledge alone these are built for one who knows thus. Since it is impossible for the operations of speech, mind, sight, and so forth to be "built" in the manner of bricks and the like, it is established that they consist of knowledge insofar as they are fires produced by the mind. Nevertheless, there is the restriction: "they are indeed built of knowledge" and "by knowledge alone these [are built]."
It is determined that this is for the purpose of making known the nature of knowledge (vidyā) through its connection with a sacrifice consisting of knowledge;
and it is seen right here [in the text]: "The sacrifice of these is of the nature of knowledge as their subordinate element;

they were studied by the mind alone, they were piled up by the mind alone, the cups were drawn by the mind, they praised by the mind, they recited by the mind. Whatever ritual act is performed in a sacrifice, whatever is a sacrificial act—that was performed by the mind alone upon those which consist of mind, which are piled by mind, and which are made of mind."

Thus: "In the case of fires built with bricks, whatever sacrificial rite consisting of action is performed, that very same [rite] is performed as consisting of mind alone in the fires consisting of mind, such as the fire of the mind and so forth. From this statement, it is understood that even the *ṛtu* sacrifice here consists of knowledge (*vidyā*). || 46 ||

[Objection: But surely—since no injunctive word (*vidhipada*) is heard here and no connection with a fruit is perceived, and because these [mantras] belong to the context (*prakaraṇa*) of a sacrifice consisting of actions performed with bricks, their nature as knowledge (*vidyārūpatā*) would be sublated by their association with a sacrifice consisting of knowledge (*vidyāmayakratu*)! [Reply: No, he says: "And because of the superior strength of direct statement (*śruti*) and so forth, there is no sublation" (Sūtra 3.3.47).

Since direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and syntactical connection (*vākya*) are stronger than context (*prakaraṇa*), their association cannot be sublated by the weaker context. Direct statement (*śruti*) is as follows: [text continues]
"Therefore, these [fires] are indeed built of knowledge.
He explains that "it" [the sacrifice] is the ritual known from the Śruti and other sources; of these...
"By knowledge alone do those who know thus become built up.

The meaning is: "By knowledge"—that is, by the *ṛtu* consisting of knowledge—they become "built up," such as the *manas-cit* and the others. "To them"—to those very ones who know thus—"all beings always build [them] up, even while they sleep."

This is the indicative mark (*liṅga*). There is also the sentence (*vākya*): "They pile [the fire-altar] for one who knows thus. A sentence consists of co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*). "For one who knows thus" means for one who possesses the mental resolve (*vidyā-makratu*); the meaning is that "all beings always pile it. Since the piling performed by all beings at all times is accomplished through the mind, and since it cannot possibly enter into a sacrifice consisting of limited agents, times, and actions involving bricks, it serves as an indicative mark for its entry into a sacrifice consisting of knowledge (*vidyāmaya-kratu*).
47 | 402. On account of the supplementary passages and so forth, [the meditations] are distinct, as in the case of other forms of wisdom; and this has been observed and stated. (Siddhānta)

This sacrifice consisting of knowledge is understood to be distinct from the sacrifice consisting of ritual action—which is connected with the piling of bricks—on account of its differences and other such reasons for distinction. The "connections" (anubandhas) are those elements connected to the sacrifice, such as the cups (grahas), hymns (stotras), and recitations (śastras).

[These meditations] are established by such passages as, "By the mind alone these [sacrificial] vessels are taken up; by the mind they were praised; by the mind they were recited," and so forth. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the previously mentioned *śruti* (scriptural testimony) and other means of knowledge are included. The meaning is that, through *śruti* and the rest, together with their attendant details (*sānubandhaiḥ*), a sacrifice consisting of knowledge (*vidyāmayaḥ kratuḥ*) is understood to be distinct [from the ritual sacrifice]. "Like the distinctness of another cognition" (*prajñāntara-pṛthaktvavat*): just as another cognition—such as the Dahara-vidyā and others—is understood through *śruti* and the rest to be separate from the sacrifice consisting of action (*kriyāmayāt kratoḥ*); so too is this [sacrifice of knowledge].

And thus, when it is understood that the sacrifice consisting of knowledge (vidyāmaya-yajña) is distinct [from ritual action] by virtue of its continuity and other such characteristics, an injunction (vidhi) is postulated. Furthermore, an injunction is postulated even when a restatement (anuvāda) is observed among similar forms. As it has been said:
"But the statements [are injunctions] because they convey what is not previously known" (Jaimini Sūtra 1.2.18). And there is a result [of this].

"Of these, each one indeed is as great as that former one"—from this rule of extension (*atideśa*), it is understood that whatever fruit belongs to the fire-altar built with bricks by way of its own sacrifice, that same fruit belongs to the *manaścit* and other altars as well, by way of their respective sacrifices. || 48 ||

"And it is seen" means that because the sacrifice consisting of knowledge (*vidyāmaya-kratu*) is understood through direct revelation (*śruti*) and other means along with their auxiliary elements, an injunction (*vidhi*) is postulated for the purpose of avoiding the contingency of [the rite] not being heard [in the context]. This is the sense. Regarding "whatever fruit": if it is performed out of desire for a fruit, there is the attainment of that fruit; otherwise, the fruit is liberation (*mukti*). This is the sense. || 48 ||

"Because of the scriptural statement that this [knowledge] is distinct from that which consists of action and distinct from praise and so forth, it is seen to be like the distinction between burning and other such acts; for indeed, even in a restatement (anuvāda), there is an injunction. Regarding the point that—because of the extension (atideśa) it is understood that they have the same function, and thus entry into the category of that which consists of action is understood—it says: "In their own natures... (*svarūpeṣu*); "of each one of those alone"—(variant readings: *teṣāmevaikaika*; *ṅa*); "as for what was further said"—that through extension, because of the understanding of equal functionality, entry into the nature of that which consists of action is understood—therein he says: *Note: The text provided contains Sanskrit fragments and commentary on the relationship between knowledge (*jñāna*) and ritual action (*kriyā*). The translation reflects the philosophical argument regarding the distinct status of knowledge as taught in the scriptures.*
403. "Not even on account of a mere similarity, for there is no attainment of the world [of ritual results], just as in the case of death.

(Siddhānta Sūtra 3.3.49) It is not necessarily the case that because of an extended application (*atideśa*), the intermediate operation must also be identical; whereby these [meditations] would enter into the sacrificial acts consisting of action (*kriyāmaya-kratu*). For an extended application is observed based on some mere similarity whatsoever. Indeed, it is so observed!

In passages such as, "This very person who is in this orb is death," the extension [of attributes] is based merely on the commonality of being the agent of withdrawal and so forth; for in that case, the person in the orb does not undergo rebirth in that world—nor even the reaching of that place—in the same manner as Death does.

In the same way here as well, although there is an extension of the nature of the mind-altar (manaścit) and so forth by means of the mere analogy to the brick-built fire-altar (iṣṭakacitāgni), it should not follow that they must also enter into the performance of the ritual acts consisting of form and action characteristic of the place of the brick-built fire-altar. Therefore, it is understood from the analogical extension (atideśa) that whatever fruit belongs to the brick-built fire-altar through its own sacrificial rite (kratu), that very same fruit belongs to the mind-altar and others through their sacrificial rites consisting of knowledge (vidyāmaya). || 49 ||

404. And by the subsequent Brāhmaṇa passage, the same nature of this word—which denotes the *manaścit* and so forth—is understood; that is, its "tādvidhya" (identity with that), namely, its being "consisting of knowledge. For by the subsequent Brāhmaṇa passage: "This world, indeed, is this piled fire-altar; its enclosing stones are the waters... [it is established].

By such statements as, "He who knows this thus [attains] the *lokampṛṇā*... he attains all this which is of such a nature," an injunction with a distinct fruit is indeed enjoined. Likewise, in the *Vaiśvānara-vidyā* and other instances, an injunction is indeed enjoined. Therefore, the *Agnirahasya* does not have ritual action (*kriyā*) alone as its subject matter.

If that is so, then why are the fire-altars consisting of knowledge (*vidyāmaya*), such as the *manascit* and others, which are to be connected in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*, connected here [in the *Chāndogya*] as well? To this it is replied: "Because of their abundance, there is a connection here" (*bhūyastvāt tv anubandhaḥ*). Because of the abundance of the constituent parts of the fires (*agnyaṅga*) to be accomplished in the *manascit* and other altars, the connection is made here in their proximity. || 50 ||
Thus ends the section on the prior conceptualization (pūrvavikalpādhikaraṇa). || 20 ||
The locus of existence is within the body. (3.3.21)
405. On account of the existence [of the soul] as one in the body, (Pūrvapakṣa) 3.3.51.

In all the higher knowledges (*paravidyā*), it has been stated that the nature of the worshipper (*upāsaka*) must also be known, just like the nature of the object of worship (*upāsya*) and the mode of worship (*upāsana*).
"And there is such an introduction and inquiry regarding these three alone.

Furthermore, he will state that this inner self (pratyagātman) is to be meditated upon as having the Supreme Self (paramātman) as its essence: "But they approach it as the Self, and they cause it to be grasped as the Self."
Thus [it is said].

Is this the inner self (pratyagātman)—the knower, the agent, and the enjoyer, capable of moving between this world and the next, who is to be sought after? Or is it the one whose nature consists of freedom from sin and other qualities as proclaimed by Prajāpati and Vāyu?
"What is correct? Is it merely the aspect of being a knower and so forth?"—thus some believe.

Why? Because this self of the worshipper exists within the body; for one who abides in the body, the form is exactly such [as it appears there], and because the attainment of that fruit is logically established through that much reflection alone.
This being the case, we reply:
"The distinction [of the Self] exists because [the liberated state] occurs when that [liberation] is present; but it is not like the perception [of the transmigrating state]. (Sūtra 3.3.52).

This is not so—that only the form consisting of the knower and so forth is to be meditated upon. Rather, that distinction of this Self which exists between the state of transmigratory existence and the state of liberation—consisting of freedom from sin and other such qualities—is what must be meditated upon. The meaning is that the Self must be meditated upon during the time of worship in exactly the same form that it possesses in the state of liberation.

Why? Because [the result] comes into being through the becoming of that [object of meditation], which is "due to attaining its form. As it is said: "In whatever way a person intends in this world, so does he become after departing from here"; and "in whatever way one meditates upon Him, so indeed does one become.
For it is heard in scripture that attainment occurs precisely according to the mode of meditation.

Nor can it be said that this [scriptural teaching] has as its object merely the form of "another's property" (parasva); for even the inner self (pratyagātman), by virtue of being the body of the Supreme Brahman which is the object of worship, is included within the category of the object of worship. Therefore, it is stated that for the meditation upon the Supreme Self—which has the inner self as its "body" and possesses qualities such as freedom from sin (apahatapāpmatva) as declared in the Prajāpati-vākya—the "attainment" is indeed of that very same nature.

For this very reason, it is said: "Thus, having departed, I shall indeed attain that world through my resolve (*kratu*). Therefore, the inner self (*pratyagātman*) alone, as the object to be attained, is what must be meditated upon.

"As in the case of the perception [of Brahman]—that is, as in the case of the perception of Brahman. The meaning is that just as the perception of Brahman, as enjoined, has for its object the true nature of Brahman as it actually exists, so too the perception of the Self has for its object the true nature of the Self as it actually exists.
This concludes the section on the "Subsidiary Parts" (Aṅgāvabaddha-adhikaraṇa). 3.3.22.
407. But those [meditations] connected with the limbs [of the sacrifice] are not [restricted] to the branches of each Veda.
(Siddhānta) "One should meditate on this syllable 'Om' as the Udgītha";
"One should meditate on the fivefold Sāman in the worlds. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.1; 2.2.1)
"Every hymn, every hymn," so indeed do people say. This very thing is the hymn; this earth itself is it.
"This world, indeed, is this built fire-altar"—such are the meditations based on the constituent parts of the sacrifice.

The inquiry is as follows: Are those [meditations] restricted only to those specific branches (*śākhā*) in which they are found, or are they connected to the *udgītha* and other elements across all branches?

Although it has been established that there is a single cognition across all Vedāntas, a doubt arises as to whether the *udgītha* and so forth are distinct in each Veda due to differences in accentuation, and consequently, whether the meditations should be restricted to their respective locations. This is a reasonable concern.
What is correct? That they should be restricted [to their respective branches].

Why? Because for that meditation which is heard in a general way as being connected with the *udgītha*—in the phrase "one should meditate on the *udgītha*"—its culmination in that very specific instance is logical, due to the proximity (*saṃnidhāna*) of a particular *udgītha* endowed with a specific tone within that same branch. Thus, these [meditations] and others like them should be restricted to those very branches.

This being the case, we reply: "But those connected with the members [of the sacrifice]. The word "but" (tu) sets aside the previous position. For meditations connected with members such as the *udgītha* do not remain restricted to those very branches [of the Veda] alone; rather, they should be connected with every branch within each Veda—this is the meaning. The word "for" (hi) indicates the reason: because by the scripture itself they are connected merely with the members such as the *udgītha*, therefore they should be connected wherever those members, such as the *udgītha*, occur.

Although individual instances of the *udgītha* differ according to variations in pitch, nevertheless, since all individual instances are brought into proximity by the general scriptural mention of the term "udgītha," there is no authority for any restrictive limitation (*vyavasthā*) in any particular case. If it is argued that there is a proximity of specific individuals based on the principle of "cognition across all branches" (*sarvaśākhā-pratyaya*), then because that very [specific] instance is what is denoted by the word "udgītha," the meditations would be restricted to those respective specific branches. If, however, it is argued that there is a proximity of all individuals, then because the word "udgītha" denotes the *udgītha* in its entirety, the meditations concerning it are not restricted.

Regarding the phrase *sarvavedānte*: just as ritual action (*karman*) and meditative worship (*upāsanā*) are one and the same across all Vedic branches (*śākhā*), so too, because the *udgītha* is one, the meditations would apply everywhere according to the *udgītha*. This constitutes the objection (*ākṣepa*) that initiates the present section (*adhikaraṇa*). The resolution of this objection is as follows: since there is a difference in individual instances (*vyakti*) of the *udgītha* and other such elements due to differences in accent (*svara*), should the meditations have as their object specific instances qualified by their respective particular accents, or should they have as their object every instance of the *udgītha*? Such a doubt might arise; this is the meaning of the resolution of the objection.

"In that very [context]" means that in common worldly usage, such as in "Bring the cow" (*gām ānaya*), it is observed that general terms terminate in the specific instance present at hand; this is the intended sense.

"Bound to the mere subsidiary" means they are understood as having the mere subsidiary as their object. "Nowhere" refers to cases such as "Bring the cow," where [the term] arises from the generality of the *go* (cow) [applied to] the *udgītha*.

And by logic as well: "In all branches (śākhās), the season (ṛtu) is one. Therefore, because a single season is present in all branches, the udgītha and other elements that are subordinate members of that season are also present; thus, there is no specific distinction of presence for any one [branch], and so there is no fixed restriction (vyavasthā). || 53 ||

408. Or, as in the case of mantras and so forth, there is no contradiction. (Siddhānta Sūtra 3.3.54). The word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of "and" (*ca*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), number (*saṅkhyā*), similarity (*sādṛśya*), order (*krama*), substance (*dravya*), and action (*karman*) are included. Just as in the case of mantras and the like, even though they are taught in individual recensions (*śākhā*), their application across all recensions—since the sacrifice (*kratu*) which is the beneficiary (*śeṣin*) is one and the same—is not contradicted by the respective direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and other means of proof; likewise, here too, there is no contradiction. 54.
Thus ends the section concerning that which is bound to the limbs. || 22 ||
The Section on the Superiority of the Bhūman (3.3.23).
409. The greater importance belongs to the whole, as in the case of a sacrifice; for scripture shows this to be so.

(Sūtra 3.3.55) The Vaiśvānara-vidyā is taught beginning with the words, "Prācīnaśāla Aupamanyava. In that context, Vaiśvānara is heard of as the Supreme Self, to be meditated upon as having the three worlds for His body, with heaven, sun, wind, ether, and earth as His constituent parts. Therein, heaven is the head, the sun is the eye, the wind is the breath, the ether is the trunk—the meaning being the middle part of the body—water is the bladder, and the earth is the feet; such are the specific limbs.
In this regard, there is a doubt: Should the meditation on this body of the three worlds be performed part by part? Or both part by part and as a whole? Or only as a whole?

Why? Because at the beginning, there is instruction regarding meditation on the parts individually. For instance, it is taught as follows: Aupamanyava and others, with Uddālaka as the sixth, having approached Aśvapati Kekaya, asked, "You indeed know this very Self, Vaiśvānara; tell us about that. And he, having told them each of the things they themselves meditated upon—beginning with the sky—taught them the meditation on these [limbs] individually in their respective heads and other parts, as well as the specific fruit for each.

"He sees what is exceedingly abundant; there arises in his family the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*), he who meditates upon this Self as Vaiśvānara—this, indeed, is the head of the Self;
this is the Vaiśvānara Self, possessed of excellent luster."

By such statements as these, he declares that Vaiśvānara is the object of worship in each of those various meditations. Therefore, it must be understood that the meditation is to be performed on the [Vaiśvānara] taken distributively (vyasta). Furthermore, in the passage, "But he who worships this Vaiśvānara Self, which is of the measure of a span and all-pervading," the summary of the meditation on the head and other parts—which was previously taught regarding Vaiśvānara as delimited by the regions beginning with the sky—is to be understood as a collective synthesis (samāsa).

Another says: "In this very way, the meditation on the whole [Vaiśvānara] must also be performed," because of the mention of separate fruits: "But he who meditates upon this Vaiśvānara Self as measured by a span, as the abode of all, eats food in all worlds, in all beings, and in all selves."
Thus, there is no split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) by this much; for example, in the introduction to the Bhūma-vidyā, after teaching the meditation on Name and so forth along with its fruit,
[the text] teaches the Bhūma-vidyā itself through the passage beginning, "But he indeed speaks transcendentally who speaks transcendentally by means of Truth."

"He becomes self-luminous; he has freedom of movement in all worlds"—thus it declares that fruit. In that case, even though the sentence refers primarily to the knowledge of Bhūman, the meditation on subordinate objects such as Name and so forth, as well as their respective fruits, are nevertheless admitted; so it is here as well.

Not having obtained the knowledge of the Vaiśvānara-Self, they approached Aśvapati Kekaya, who was a knower of the Vaiśvānara-Self, and asked him, "Teach us this very Self as Vaiśvānara; tell that to us. Having learned from him about the Supreme Self, Vaiśvānara—whose body extends from the heavenly world down to the earth—and having understood Him as the object of meditation, they attained the experience of Brahman, which is the fruit of that meditation, becoming the "Self of all worlds, all beings, and all selves. Thus, from the concluding summary, the unity of the text is understood.

Thus, once it is understood that they form a single coherent statement, it is determined that the mention of meditations on specific parts and the indication of results are merely restatements of portions of the meditation on the whole.

"Like a sacrifice"— for example, as in the case of the injunction, "One should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara when a son is born," [the rites in question] are merely parts of that very same sacrifice.

[The passages] beginning with "When it consists of eight potsherds" and so forth are merely reiterative; likewise, meditation on the whole alone is logical, not meditation on the parts. For this scripture demonstrates this by declaring that there is misfortune in meditating on the parts:
"Your head would have fallen off had you not come to me."
Thus,
[there are such thoughts] as, "I shall become blind, had I not come to you," and so forth.

Therefore, this [objection] is also refuted—that which was stated regarding the similarity between the meditation on Name and the others. For in that context, no harm is heard of in the meditations on Name and so forth; rather, the scripture declares that the meditation on the Plenum (Bhūman) possesses a superior fruit compared to the meditations on Name and the rest:
"But he indeed speaks with excellence who speaks with the Truth."

Thus, for that very reason, although the passage has the knowledge of the Infinite (bhūmavidyā) as its primary purport, the meditations on Name and so forth, along with their respective fruits, are intended to be taught. Otherwise, it would be impossible to justify the praise of the knowledge of the Infinite through hyperbolic language based on its superior fruit. Therefore, the meditation on the whole alone is logical. || 55 ||
Thus concludes the section on the preeminence of the "Much. (Sūtra 23)
The Section Concerning the Distinction of Sound and Other [Qualities]: 3.3.24.
410. [The difference between the individual souls is established] because of the diversity of sounds and other [sensory objects]. (3.3.56)

In this context, all the Brahma-vidyās—such as the Sad-vidyā, Bhūma-vidyā, Dahara-vidyā, Upakosala-vidyā, Śāṇḍilya-vidyā, Vaiśvānara-vidyā, Ānandamaya-vidyā, Akṣara-vidyā, and so forth, whether belonging to one's own Vedic branch (*śākhā*) or to another branch—are examples; these have liberation, characterized by the attainment of Brahman, as their sole fruit. Others, however, have fruits consisting of a single object such as the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
A doubt arises here as to whether there is identity of knowledge (*vidyaikyam*) or a difference between the two knowledges (*vidyābheda*).

In this very context, once mutual difference has been established, the principle of "recognition across all Vedāntas" (*sarvavedāntapratyaya*) applies to a single meditation, such as the Dahara-vidyā.
What is logical? The unity of the knowledge.
Why? Because of the oneness of Brahman, the object of knowledge. For the object of knowledge is indeed the form of the knowledge. Therefore—
Because the form is one, the knowledge is one.

[Śrībhāṣya 3.3.24] Although these [passages] have Brahman as their object, nevertheless, the meditations (vidyās)—which consist of the repetition of cognitions that bring about the realization of the mental modifications (pratyayavṛtti) characterized by attributes such as being the sole cause of the universe and being free from sin as taught in their respective contexts—distinguish themselves. It is determined that the sentences in each context, which declare specific forms of meditation connected to the fruit consisting of the attainment of Brahman and are complete in themselves, designate distinct meditations.

In this matter, although the point is already established by the sūtras propounded in the earlier section (Pūrvakāṇḍa), such as "There is a difference of action when there is a difference of words," its restatement here is for the purpose of refuting the false view that "Vedānta statements are intent upon knowledge which is not subject to injunction. Therefore, it is settled that there is a difference between the meditations (vidyās). || 56 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the distinction based on words and so forth. 24.

411. *Vikalpa* (optionality), because the fruit is not distinct. (Sūtra 3.3.57) (Siddhānta) It has been stated that there is a plurality among the various forms of knowledge, such as the Sadvidyā and the Daharavidyā, which have the attainment of Brahman as their fruit.

Now, a doubt arises: "Is it possible for these various knowledges to be combined (*samuccaya*) within a single person for the sake of some purpose, or, due to a lack of purpose, is there only an option (*vikalpa*) between them? Regarding this doubt:
Why? 1— “Because the fruit is non-distinct”— for it is heard in scripture that the fruit of all Brahma-vidyās is the experience of Brahman as infinite bliss, which is non-distinct and without limit.
"The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme"; "That is one bliss of Brahman; and of the learned Śrotriya who is untouched by desire";
"When the seer sees the golden-hued Maker, the Lord, the Person, the source of Brahman."
"Then the wise one, having shaken off merit and demerit, stainless, attains the supreme equality," and so forth.

For Brahman, being experienced as one's own self, is indeed infinite and unsurpassed bliss. If such an experience of Brahman is attained through one single knowledge (*vidyā*), what need is there for another? Thus, there is no possibility of their combination (*samuccaya*). For in the case of heaven and the like, because they are limited in terms of space, time, and essential nature, a greater abundance of them is possible depending on place and so forth; therefore, for one who desires those [results], a combination is possible.

But here, in the case of Brahman, whose nature is the opposite of that [world], such [sequential progression] is not possible. Furthermore, all forms of knowledge have as their fruit the attainment of Brahman by way of dispelling beginningless karma and ignorance—which are opposed to the experience of Brahman; therefore, because their fruit is indistinguishable, there is only an option (*vikalpa*) among them all. || 57 ||

However, those meditations (*vidyā*) whose fruits are distinct from the attainment of Brahman may be combined or optionally chosen according to one’s desire, like rituals that have heaven and other such results as their fruit; for since their fruits are limited, there is the possibility of a desire for more. Thus it is said: 412. "But those [meditations] pertaining to desires may be combined according to wish, or not, because of the absence of the previous reason. (Sūtra 3.3.58) (Conclusion) The meaning is: because they lack the quality of having unlimited fruits. 58.
Thus ends the section concerning conceptual construction (vikalpādhikaraṇa). || 25 ||
The substratum exists according to the nature of its basis. (3.3.26)

413. As with the limbs, there is the state of being a support [for the whole]. (Pūrva-pakṣa) But surely, it has been established that there is no fixed rule regarding these [meditations] because they exist for the sake of the Person (*puruṣārtha*); for it was stated: "There is no rule for their determination, because that [result] is seen; for they are separate, and the fruit is unobstructed."
Thus, in this case.

True; however, that very point is challenged by certain observations of indicative marks (*liṅga*) and by reasoning in order to strengthen it. For there, because of the observation of non-restriction in the statement, "By means of that, both perform [the sacrifice]," the fact of separate fruits has been stated. Furthermore, many reasons are found for the necessity of employing the meditations as subordinate members (*aṅga*), just like the *udgītha* and so forth which serve as the substrata for those meditations. Indeed, it is not the case here that—

Just as in the injunction, "One desiring cattle should fetch [water] with a milking vessel" (*godohanena paśukāmasya praṇayet*), a connection with a fruit is heard in the injunctive sentences concerning meditation (*upāsanā*). In the statement, "One should meditate upon the *udgītha*," meditation is understood precisely as being connected to the *udgītha* and so forth.

Therefore, just as the *udgītha* and other such elements, being the substrates of meditation, are invariably employed by the performance-injunction (*prayogavidhi*) as auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice, so too the meditations resting upon them become auxiliaries of the sacrifice through that medium; thus, they must indeed be invariably employed. 59.

414. And because it is taught [as such]. (Pūrva-pakṣa) "Teaching" (*śiṣṭi*) means instruction; that is to say, a prescription (*vidhāna*). Furthermore, because of the prescription of meditation as a subordinate part of the *udgītha* in the passage, "One should meditate upon the *udgītha*," there is a restriction of inclusion (*upādānaniyama*). Just as in the case of "One desiring cattle should fetch water with a cow-milking vessel" (*godohana*), it is understood from the injunctive statement that the very status of being a subordinate part of the *udgītha* and so forth is what is to be enjoined. (Sūtra 3.3.60)
Because no other office is heard of [in that context], and because of the combination; (Pūrvapakṣa-sūtra 3.3.61):
"Indeed, from the Hotṛ's station, he rectifies even a badly sung udgītha."

Thus, a rule for the combination of meditations is observed. Regarding the "bad udgītha"—that is, an udgītha performed without knowledge—the text, by stating that it is rectified by another [knowledge] when knowledge is lacking, demonstrates that its [the knowledge's] adoption is mandatory. || 61 ||

The *prayogavidhi* (injunction of performance) is an injunction that has reached the state of being an instigator (*anuṣṭhāpaka*), and not one in the state of being a mere indicator (*jñāpaka*). The reasoning (*yukti*) has been stated; for reasoning consists in the form of pervasion (*vyāpti*). There is an absence of subsidiary status (*aṅgatva*) regarding the connection with results found in injunctive sentences. And indeed, the presence of subsidiary status in the absence of a result mentioned in the injunctive sentence has been demonstrated. || 59 ||
By the words "In those remaining," etc., the signs are demonstrated. || 60 ||
Samāhāra is concentration (samādhāna). 61.

"One should meditate upon that *udgītha* there as well," according to this injunction; and because of the perception of its own constituent parts (*ṛk-aṅga*), there is the necessity of including it. Furthermore, the *Śruti* provides a remedy for the non-meditation on the *udgītha* by another means, and thus scripture is the authority for its mandatory inclusion.
(As stated in the *Daśopaniṣad-bhāṣya*: "udgīthāṅga-").

416. And because of the scriptural statement regarding the commonality of qualities. (Pūrvapakṣa) Regarding the *praṇava*—which is the locus of meditation and possesses the qualities of meditation—together with its meditation, by means of it this threefold knowledge proceeds: "With *oṃ* he causes [the Adhvaryu] to announce; with *oṃ* he recites the *śastra*; with *oṃ* he sings the *udgītha*."

Thus, because of the scriptural statement regarding commonality, the combination of meditations is understood. From the reference to the subject at hand by the word "by that" (*tena*), it follows that the *praṇava* accompanied by meditation alone moves everywhere. Therefore, because the rule of the coexistence of the *praṇava* with meditation is observed, the meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth must necessarily be adopted, just like the *udgītha* itself. || 62 ||

Why? Because there is no scriptural mention of its coexistence—that is to say, because there is no scriptural mention of its being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the *udgītha*. For indeed, a rule of coexistence exists only when there is the status of being an auxiliary.
Although no separate heading (*adhikāra*) is perceived within this collection of words, "One should meditate on the *udgītha*," nevertheless, immediately following that—

"Whatever one performs with knowledge, with faith, and with the secret doctrine (upaniṣad), that alone becomes more powerful"—by this, it is established that "knowledge" (vidyā) is a means toward the greater efficacy of the ritual. Therefore, knowledge—which is a means to a result distinct from the fruit of the ritual—is enjoined as something to be performed in the words, "One should meditate upon the Udgītha. It is not logical to apply meditation, which is understood to be a means to a result distinct from the fruit of the ritual, as a subordinate part of the Udgītha, which is itself a constituent part of the ritual.

Now, regarding the word "atha": when there is a requirement for a substratum (*āśraya*) for the meditation (*upāsana*), the *udgītha* mentioned in proximity serves merely as that substratum. Since the *udgītha* is an integral part of the sacrifice (*kratu*), this meditation—which has as its substratum the *udgītha* and so forth employed in the sacrifice—is a distinct qualification (*adhikārāntara*) based on the desire of the very person qualified for the sacrifice to make the sacrifice more efficacious (*vīryavattara*). Thus, there is no rule that it must be undertaken within the sacrifices themselves. Furthermore, "more efficacy" (*vīryavattaratva*) means the non-obstruction of the fruit of the sacrifice by the fruit of another powerful karma; this is what has been stated. It means that the fruit of the sacrifice is not delayed.

However, in the case of [the quality of] being made of *parṇa* wood and so forth, although it is heard that knowledge (*vidyā*) is a means for accomplishing a result—as in the passage, "Whatever one performs with knowledge... that alone becomes more powerful"—it is not heard that [the *parṇa* quality] is a direct means toward results such as hearing the "fame of the sinless" (*apāpaśloka*). Since there is no contradiction in its application as a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the ladle (*juhū*) and other implements which are themselves parts of the sacrifice (*kratu*), it is illogical to assume that those things which are subordinate parts [of the sacrifice] can be means for accomplishing a different result. Therefore, the mention of a result in that context must be merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). (Sūtra 6.2.35)
418. And because of scriptural evidence.
(Siddhānta) Scripture also shows that there is no fixed rule regarding the acquisition of knowledge for the purpose of officiating;

for it says, "The Brahman priest who knows thus indeed protects the sacrifice, the sacrificer, and all the priests," thereby stating that through the knowledge of the Brahman priest, everyone is protected. This is appropriate only if there is no fixed rule regarding the knowledge required by the Udgātṛ and other priests. By this indicative mark, it is understood that the previously mentioned marks—such as the combination of duties and so forth—are merely occasional. Therefore, it is established that there is indeed no fixed rule. 64.
Thus ends the section concerning the existence [of qualities] according to their substratum. 26.
Thus ends the third quarter of the third chapter in the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Bhagavad Rāmānuja.

0—“And because of the mention [in scripture]. In the previous sūtra, the argument for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) was refuted; here, the indicative marks (*liṅga*) will be addressed. Regarding the term “protection” (*rakṣaṇa*): it refers to the protection of the sacrificer by means of ensuring that the fruit of the sacrifice is not obstructed, and so forth. For the fruit of the knowledge of the Udgātṛ and others consists precisely in the non-obstruction of the fruit of the sacrifice and the like. Indeed, when the success of that [sacrifice] is established through the knowledge of Māruti Viśve, there follows the accomplishment of the duties of the Udgātṛ and others. Regarding the term “generality” (*prāyikatva*).

The meaning is that if the meditation on the *udgītha* has been resolved upon from the very beginning, then one must perform concentration (*samādhi*) upon the *udgītha* even when it is devoid of [specific] knowledge. || 64 ||
Thus concludes the section concerning the existence [of qualities] according to their substrata. 26.
The Third Section. || 3 ||
Even from the fact of comprehension, there is no fixed rule regarding meditation.
|| Śrīḥ ||
In the third chapter on the Means of Achievement (Sādhanādhyāya), this is the fourth section on the Limbs (Aṅgapāda).
Adhikaraṇas – 15. Sūtras – 51) 1. Puruṣārthādhikaraṇam:

The attainment of the supreme goal of human life is through knowledge alone, which has ritual action as its subordinate limb; it is not, however, from ritual action that has meditation (upāsanā) as its subordinate limb.
2. The Section Concerning Mere Praise (Stutimātrādhikaraṇa):
Passages such as "He is the essence of essences" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.3) are intended to establish the meditation on the *udgītha* and other elements as being the "highest essence.
9. The Section Concerning the Impaired (Vidhurādhikaraṇa).
Even for those of the three higher castes who do not belong to any specific stage of life (āśrama), there certainly exists the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman.
Salutation to the illustrious Rāmānuja. Salutation to Śrī. Salutation to Śrīdhara.
