In the *Śrī Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya* composed by the venerable Bhagavad Rāmānuja, this is the fourth section on the ancillaries (*aṅgapāda*) in the third chapter (*adhyāya*) concerning the means (*sādhana*).
The Section on the Purpose of Human Endeavor (Puruṣārthādhikaraṇa) || 3.4.1 ||
419. "Therefore, the human goal [arises] from knowledge; thus [says] Bādarāyaṇa" (3.4.1).

(Siddhānta) The investigation into unity and diversity was conducted with the result of determining whether there is a combination or non-combination of subordinate elements (*guṇa*). Now, it is considered whether the human goal arises "from knowledge" or "from ritual action that has knowledge as its auxiliary.
What is the correct view? "Therefore, the human goal arises from knowledge"—thus says the venerable Bādarāyaṇa.
It is so considered. Why? From scripture.
For the scriptural word of the Upaniṣads, speaking of the "human goal" (puruṣārtha) as arising from knowledge, [establishes this].

"The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme. "I know this great Puruṣa, resplendent like the sun, beyond darkness; knowing Him thus, one becomes immortal here in this world; there is no other path for the journey. "As rivers flowing along reach the ocean and vanish, losing their name and form..."
"Thus the wise one, liberated from name and form, attains the divine Person who is higher than the high," and so forth. || 1 ||

Does the human goal arise from knowledge (*vidyā*), or from ritual action that has knowledge as its constituent part? Is knowledge for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) by means of purifying the self who is the performer of the sacrifice, or is it for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*) by virtue of being a means to the fruit of non-return? Are such passages as "The knower of Brahman attains [the Supreme]" injunctions regarding the fruit, or are they merely explanatory statements (*arthavāda*)? In the higher knowledges (*paravidyā*), is the individual soul (*jīva*) the object of the action, or is it something other than that—the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)?

Does the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) of statements such as "That thou art," when supported by indicative marks (liṅga) such as the observation of [the Lord's] conduct, lead to the understanding that the object of meditation is in the state of a living being (jīva)? Or not? Is this indicative mark inconclusive (anaikāntika)? Or not?

In the absence of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*), since the state of being a living soul (*jīvatva*) of the object of meditation is understood through the coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) supported by that [inconclusiveness], the higher knowledges (*paravidyā*) serve as a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the living soul which is their own object. Because the scriptural mention of the fruit of self-knowledge is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), there is no separate means for attaining a distinct fruit; thus, knowledge is for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*). Consequently, the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) would result from the ritual action which is a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of that [knowledge].

If the inferential mark (*liṅga*) were inconclusive, then, due to the absence of its corroborative support, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) would not lead to the understanding that [the Self] is not distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*). Furthermore, since the higher knowledges (*paravidyā*) do not have the individual soul as their object, they cannot be mere purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) for it. Because the scriptural declarations regarding the fruit of the knowledge of the Self are not merely figurative (*arthavāda*), they constitute a means to a distinct result; thus, the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) is accomplished through knowledge itself.
And this is the commencement of the established doctrine (siddhānta); since knowledge was introduced in the preceding section (pūrva-pāda), it is referred to by the word "therefore" (ataḥ).

In the statement "the knower of Brahman," the attainment of what is to be reached through knowledge is expressed. In the passage "I have known [Him]," the meaning is that knowledge is the cause for attaining Brahman, while the removal of obstacles is the means; therein, the fact that Brahman possesses a form (*vigraha*) and so forth, as well as the practice of other means, are established. In the passage "as rivers [flow into the ocean]," both of these are stated. (1)
On this point, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) objects:
"420. Because it is a subordinate element (śeṣa), it is a statement of human purpose (puruṣārthavāda), as in other cases; thus [says] Jaimini. (3.4.2) (Prima Facie View)

This is not so—that the attainment of the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) results from knowledge, as is understood from the sacred word (*śabda*). For this scriptural passage beginning with "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" does not convey that the attainment of the human goal follows from mere knowledge; rather, its purpose is to establish the true nature of the Self as the agent in ritual actions. Therefore, since knowledge is subsidiary to the sacrifice by way of purifying the agent, the mention of a fruit in that context is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), just as in the case of other [subsidiaries] such as materials and the like—so the teacher Jaimini maintains. As it has been said:
"In the case of substances, purificatory acts, and ritual actions, because they exist for the sake of another, the mention of a fruit must be an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda).

Now, it has already been established that "in ritual actions, [the Self] other than the living individual soul (jīva) is taught in the Vedāntas as the object to be known, which is to be attained by those seeking liberation."
"Not the other, because of impossibility";
"and because of the designation of difference";
"but not the embodied soul, because of impossibility."

This is established by such sūtras as, "If it be argued that it is so because of the reference to the other, we say no, because of impossibility. Furthermore, the claim that "that very Brahman is non-different from the individual soul (jīva) through grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in passages such as 'That thou art'" is also refuted by sūtras such as, "But [Brahman is] greater, because of the mention of difference. And as for the mention of grammatical coordination, it is seen in such texts as, "All this has that as its self," and "All this, indeed, is Brahman."
Thus, this [existence] is common to both the conscious and the unconscious,
being based on the state of abiding as the Self of each respective entity, as understood from such passages as "He who dwells in the earth" and "He who dwells in the self."

This has been established by such [sūtras] as "Because of the abiding, so says Kāśakṛtsna" (BS 1.4.22). How then can it be maintained that "the words of the Vedānta are intent upon teaching the true nature of the self as the agent in ritual acts," thereby establishing that knowledge (vidyā) is merely an auxiliary to action?
[This is the demonstration of the indicative marks regarding the Vedāntas' focus on the true nature of the individual soul, according to the sūtras.]

Furthermore, what are those indicative marks (*liṅga*)? They are those by which, through the designation of a reinforced grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), it is determined that "the words of the Vedānta have the individual soul (*jīva*) as their primary referent. To this, he says: **421.

On account of the observation of conduct.** (Sūtra 3-4-3, Pūrvapakṣa) The conduct of those who know Brahman is observed to consist primarily of ritual actions. For instance, Aśvapati Kekaya—said to be the most eminent among those who know the Self—spoke to the sages who had approached him for the sake of that knowledge: [text continues]
"O venerable sirs, I am indeed about to perform a sacrifice.

Likewise, Janaka and others who were the foremost among the knowers of Brahman are seen in the *Smṛtis* as being established in the perfection of action: "For by action alone did Janaka and others attain perfection";
"He too, relying on knowledge, performed very many sacrifices."

Thus, since those who know Brahman are seen to prioritize ritual action, knowledge—being of the nature of knowing the identity of the agent—is merely a subsidiary part of that action; therefore, the human goal does not arise from knowledge alone. || 3 ||
"What is the indicative mark for this? Let the attainment be stated. To this, he says: "Because of the scriptural statement of that [attainment]. (Pūrva-pakṣa) 3.4.422.
For scripture itself declares that knowledge is an auxiliary to ritual action:

"Whatever one performs with knowledge, with faith, and with the Upaniṣad, that alone becomes more powerful. It cannot be established that this scriptural statement refers exclusively to the *udgītha* on the grounds of the context (*prakaraṇa*), because scripture is more authoritative than context. Indeed, this scriptural statement—"whatever one performs with knowledge"—refers to knowledge in general. || 4 ||
423. On account of the simultaneous commencement [of both] (samanvārambhaṇāt). (Pūrvapakṣa:
"Knowledge and action together take hold of him"—thus, the conjunction of knowledge and action is observed. And this conjunction, according to the reasoning already stated, belongs to knowledge.
It occurs only when there is the state of being a constituent part of the ritual action. || 5 ||
[The statement regarding the qualification of one possessing knowledge in the ritual injunctions also indicates the aforementioned meaning:
424. Because the injunction is for one who possesses that [knowledge]. (3.4.6)

From the injunction of ritual action for one who possesses knowledge (*vidyāvataḥ*), it is understood that knowledge is an auxiliary part (*aṅga*) of ritual action; [as stated in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad]:

"Having studied the Veda in the house of a teacher according to the rules, and having performed service to the teacher until the end, and having returned home, [one should dwell] in a pure place within the family."

In such passages as "Having studied the Veda," the injunction of ritual acts for one who has completed study implies that they are enjoined only for one whose study extends up to the comprehension of the meaning. For it has been established that "study indeed extends up to the comprehension of the meaning. Therefore, since even the knowledge of Brahman is employed within the context of ritual acts, it cannot be conceived as having a separate fruit [of its own]. || 6 || 425 On account of the restrictive rule (niyamāt). || 3.4.7 || (Pūrvapakṣa)

"Anvārambhaṇa" means touching; by that, a connection is intended to be expressed. By the word "nyāya," the intention is to express such things as the agent's self being subordinate to the action, the observation of custom, and so forth. || 5 ||
"By way of excess"—the meaning is "without remainder."
The meaning is that at the proper time, one should bring pleasant wealth to the teacher as the fee for the guru (*gurudakṣiṇā*) and so forth.
"Established"—this means that the Bhaṭṭas and Prābhākaras have established this in order to avoid defects such as the scripture (śruti) having an unintended meaning.

For if it were said, "Having bathed, one should sacrifice," then the sacrifice would become a subordinate part (aṅga) of the bathing; the implication is that this [knowledge] would be treated in the same way. Indeed, knowledge of the ritual is not a subordinate part of its performance; rather, knowledge of what is to be performed is a subordinate part of the performance.
Furthermore, for this reason also, the human goal does not arise from knowledge alone.

"Performing actions here alone, one should desire to live a hundred years"—since this indicates that for a knower of the Self, the entire lifespan is invariably employed in actions, it is understood that the fruit [of life] comes from action alone; knowledge, however, is merely an auxiliary to action. || 7 ||
This being the case, we reply:

"But because of the additional teaching, Bādarāyaṇa [holds] thus, for that is seen. (3.4.8) [Siddhānta] By the word "but" (tu), the previous position is set aside. The human goal arises from knowledge alone.

Why? Because of the teaching of a superior [entity]—because there is a teaching that the object of knowledge is the Supreme Brahman, who is distinct from the individual soul (jīva), the agent in ritual acts, and who is superior by virtue of being a mine of countless auspicious qualities and possessing ninefold excellence that is the opposite of all things to be abandoned; for the venerable Bādarāyaṇa’s view is precisely this: "The fruit [of liberation] arises from knowledge. Let the other indicative marks stand aside; at least, the teaching as the object of knowledge refers only to one who is superior to the agent, the inner self (pratyagātman).

How so? From the observation of that [in the scriptures]: for even though the inner self (*pratyagātman*) is impure, there is seen—in the scriptural passages teaching its knowledge—the Supreme Brahman, who is the Lord of the individual soul, the ruler of all, whose nature is both impure and pure, who is the source of infinite, inconceivable qualities, the object of knowledge, from whom every trace of what is to be discarded has been removed, whose play consists in the arising, sustenance, and dissolution of the universe by His own volition, who is omniscient, omnipotent, and whose bliss is beyond the reach of speech and mind.
As it is said: "He is free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true, and whose resolves are true."
"Then He thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate,' and He emitted heat";
"He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving";
"His supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold, as are His innate knowledge, strength, and action"; "That is one Brahman-bliss."

"From which words turn back, together with the mind, unable to reach it—having known that bliss of Brahman, one fears nothing from anywhere" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad, Ānanda Vallī 4.1). "He is the Lord of all, He is the sovereign of beings, He is the protector of beings; He is the bridge, the upholder. "He is the cause, the lord of the lords of the senses; there is no progenitor of Him, nor is there any lord over Him. "By the command of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, the sun and the moon stand held apart. "Out of fear of Him the wind blows; out of fear of Him the sun rises."

"From fear of Him, fire and the moon, as well as death, the fifth, run away," and so forth. Therefore, in those passages concerning the teaching of knowledge (*vidyopadeśa*), there is not even a scent of the individual self (*pratyagātman*) as the agent—an entity comparable to a firefly and subject to connection with things to be abandoned such as ignorance; rather, the immortality consisting of attaining Him, which is heard of here and there as the fruit of the knowledge whose object is the Supreme Person, is what is intended. Thus, it is well said that "the human goal [arises] from knowledge. || 8 ||

The indicative marks [of the opponent's view] are set aside: **"But the observation is equal. (3.4.9) (Siddhānta)** As for what was stated—that because the performance of ritual action is observed among those who know Brahman, knowledge is an auxiliary part of ritual action—that is not so. Even though knowledge is not an auxiliary part [of action], the observation is equal. The meaning is that the observation of the performance of ritual action by those who know Brahman is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because non-performance is also observed. Indeed, the abandonment of ritual action is seen among those who know Brahman; as it is said: "The seers of the Kavaṣeya clan [said]: 'For what purpose shall we study? For what purpose shall we sacrifice?'"
In such passages as these, since the abandonment of action is observed in those who know Brahman, knowledge is not an auxiliary part of action.
How is this possible: both the performance and the non-performance of ritual action by one who knows Brahman?

Because ritual actions such as sacrifice, when devoid of attachment to their fruits, constitute an auxiliary part of the knowledge of Brahman; and he will state later regarding such action: [the relevant verse].
"And there is dependence on all [works], because of the scriptural injunctions regarding sacrifice and so forth, as in the case of the horse.
This is because that very same work, such as sacrifice, when performed for the sake of [worldly] results, is opposed to the knowledge of Brahman, whose sole fruit is liberation.
In that case, the view of non-performance is more reasonable; for if knowledge were a subsidiary part of ritual action, the abandonment of action would not be possible in any way. (9)

Regarding what was stated—that by scripture itself it is understood that knowledge (*vidyā*) is a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of ritual action—he replies: "428. It is not universal. (Sūtra 3.4.10) [This is the Siddhānta.
By the word "anaikāntika," non-universality is expressed. What is the purpose? What is the intent? The sense is that if [knowledge] were a subsidiary part, its non-performance would be untenable.

"How so?"—the intention is that performance and non-performance are contradictory. "It is not tenable for knowledge" means: since liberation is the sole fruit [of knowledge], ritual action must be performed; whereas the three aims of life (trivarga) as fruits [of action] are not to be performed, because the fruits of the knowledge of Brahman are merely explanatory statements (arthavāda) and do not admit of a fruit called liberation. Thus, due to the impossibility of this distinction, the contradiction belongs to you alone. || 9 ||
But it concerns only the Udgītha-vidyā. [The verse:

"This scriptural statement, 'Whatever [one performs] with knowledge,' does not concern all vidyās; for since it concerns only the Udgītha, that vidyā would not be a subordinate member [of other rites].

This scriptural statement does not concern all vidyās, but rather concerns only the Udgītha-vidyā. This is because the word "whatever" (*yat*) in the phrase "Whatever one performs with knowledge" is unspecified.

Because the context is restricted to a specific *udgītha* introduced by the words, "One should meditate upon the *udgītha*. Indeed, it is not the case that the phrase "whatever one does" is connected with "by means of knowledge.

Rather, having pointed out by means of the word "whatever" that which is performed by knowledge in the statement, "Whatever one performs by means of knowledge, that alone becomes more powerful," it is the greater power of that very thing being performed by knowledge which is then stated. || 10 ||

As for what was stated—that because knowledge and action are seen to accompany one another in the passage, "Knowledge and action both take hold of him," knowledge is an auxiliary to action—regarding that, he says: **429. vibhāgaḥ śatavat || 3-4-13 ||** (Siddhānta) *Śrī Bhāṣya 3.4.1*: "Knowledge and action both take hold of him. [The meaning is: There is a distinction [between the two], as in the case of the hundred [cows]. [This refers to the passage:
"Knowledge and action both take hold of him."

Thus, because knowledge and action have distinct fruits as stated here, the distinction should be understood that knowledge leads to its own fruit and action leads to its own fruit. "Like a hundred"—just as when it is said, "A hundred follows the seller of a field and a jewel," the distinction is perceived that "one hundred is for the sake of the field and one hundred is for the sake of the jewel"; so it is here. || 11 ||

430. [The view] that it belongs to one who possesses merely the study [of the Veda]. (Siddhānta) As for what was stated—that because the injunction of ritual action applies to one who possesses knowledge, knowledge is an auxiliary part of the ritual—that is not correct; for the injunction is addressed to one who possesses merely the study [of the Veda], as expressed in the phrase "having studied the Veda."

Furthermore, the injunction for Vedic study (*adhyayana-vidhi*) does not itself impel one toward the comprehension of meaning; for, like the rite of consecrating the sacred fires (*ādhāna*), study culminates merely in the acquisition of the mass of syllables. And since it is observed that the self-studied Veda (*svādhyāya*), once acquired, leads to the knowledge of rituals that yield results, a person spontaneously engages in the inquiry into its meaning in order to determine it. Consequently, one seeking ritual action engages in the knowledge of ritual, while one seeking liberation engages in the knowledge of Brahman; thus, knowledge is not a subsidiary part of ritual action.

The scriptural passage concerning "taking hold" (*samanvārambhaṇa*), namely "One should know that... refers either to knowledge and action whose fruits belong to the cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*), or to knowledge of Brahman and the actions that are its auxiliaries. This is because of the principle stated in the verse, "In this [path], there is no loss of effort. Thus, it follows that [knowledge] grants liberation at the conclusion of *prārabdha* (commenced) karma; and the meaning is that action also contributes toward the production of knowledge even in another birth. || 11 ||

"Like the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) ritual. In the passage "one consecrates the fires" (*agnīnādadhīta*), it is merely stated that the fire is to be produced by the *ādhāna*; there is no mention of its application to subsequent rites. This is because the word "fire" (*agni*) naturally conveys only that much meaning; the point here is that it is the same in this case as well. Thus, the natural sense of the word has been established. Regarding the phrase "and of what has been grasped": now, the lack of purpose (*arthānupapatti*) is addressed. For the objection is that Mīmāṃsā should not be commenced because of the absence of a motivator—that is the "lack of purpose."

That [knowledge] is also obstructed by activity arising from passion (*rāga*). Furthermore, the objection that the meaning of the Veda is not intended to be expressed is thereby refuted. Moreover, it is established that the injunction for Vedic study culminates in its purpose through a traditional sequence—just as in the view that it culminates in the knowledge of the meaning. As for the phrase "because of the understanding of ritual action":
since rituals preceded by the ceremonial bath (*snāna*) are enjoined, knowledge is not a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of ritual action. Knowledge.

The Śruti passage, "Having studied the Veda," refers indeed to a person possessed of knowledge (*vidyāvat-puruṣa*), not merely to one who has memorized it; therefore, its status as a subordinate factor of ritual action (*karmāṅgatā*) is not accepted.

Even though the injunction to study (*adhyayanavidhi*) itself impels one toward the comprehension of meaning, nevertheless, knowledge (*vidyā*) is not an auxiliary part of ritual action (*karma*); for knowledge is a different thing from the mere understanding of the meaning. Just as the performance of a rite such as the Jyotiṣṭoma—which serves as the means to the result—is a different thing from the mere cognition of the nature of that rite, so too, knowledge—which is the means to the goal of man (*puruṣārtha*) and is denoted by terms such as "meditation" (*dhyāna*) and "worship" (*upāsana*)—is indeed a different thing from the cognition of the nature of Brahman, which consists of the understanding of the meaning. Thus, there is not even a scent of connection with ritual action for that knowledge. || 12 ||

431. *Nāviśeṣāt* (It is not so, because there is no distinction). (Siddhānta) As for what was stated—that the passage "only while performing actions here" enjoins the knower of the Self (*ātmavit*) to the lifelong performance of rites by turning him away from non-dual knowledge—that is not tenable; because "there is no distinction. For there is no specific reason to hold that this injunction refers only to independent rites which are means to a [separate] fruit, since it is equally logical that it refers to rites that are auxiliary members (*aṅga*) of knowledge. As it is said: "By action alone did Janaka and others attain perfection."
And thus: "But for the wise man, [the meditation continues] until the departure from the body," because the meditation persists until the final exit. (Sūtra 13)

Having thus resolved the objection by means of the absence of intrinsic nature (*svābhāvya*) in objects, [the author] states the meaning of the passage "Performing actions here indeed" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.23): "Or rather, it is a permission for the sake of praise. (Sūtra 3.4.14) (The established view)
The word "vā" has the sense of restriction. "All this is to be pervaded by the Lord.
All.

Thus, because this occurs in the section concerning knowledge (*vidyā*), this permission for the performance of ritual action at all times is intended as a praise of knowledge. For it is in this way that knowledge is praised: "By the greatness of knowledge, even while performing action at all times, one is not tainted by actions. And the remainder of the passage shows exactly this: "In this way, O man, action does not taint you; there is no other way. Therefore, knowledge is not a subsidiary part of ritual action.
433. And some [hold] that it is according to one's own will.

(Siddhānta) Moreover—thus some followers of other Vedic schools record that for one established in the knowledge of Brahman, the renunciation of the householder’s state may occur according to one's own will.

"What shall we do with offspring, for us who have this Self as this world?"—this statement, declaring the renunciation of the duties of the householder at will by one who is both learned and dispassionate, demonstrates that knowledge of Brahman is not an ancillary part of ritual action. For if knowledge were an ancillary part of rituals such as sacrifice, the renunciation of the householder's life at will by one established in knowledge would be impossible. Therefore, knowledge is not an ancillary part of ritual action. || 15 ||

434. And [there is] the destruction [of karma]. (Siddhānta) Furthermore, it is studied in every Vedānta text that there is the destruction by means of the knowledge of Brahman of karma—which consists of merit and demerit and is the root of all worldly suffering.
"The knot of the heart is severed, all doubts are cut asunder,
and his karmas are exhausted when that which is both high and low is seen"—
such passages as these would not be consistent if knowledge were merely an auxiliary part of ritual action (karma). (16)

Regarding the word *kāma*: the phrase "it is taught that there is the abandonment of the householder's life" (*gārhasthyatyāgamadhīyate*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis. Regarding the phrase *yajñādi*: for it is not possible to abandon the principal (*aṅgin*) by relying upon its subsidiary (*aṅga*). Therefore, the meaning is that the action to be abandoned does not possess the status of a subsidiary. || 15 ||

"Upamarda" (annihilation) is a designation where the primary meaning is intended; for it is not possible that a subordinate part should effect the annihilation of the whole. Therefore, knowledge, which is annihilating, cannot be a subordinate part of the action that is to be annihilated. || 16 ||

"What shall we do?"—thus [they ask] regarding the duties of the householder's life. However, some followers of the Vedic branches (śākhinaḥ) desire renunciation according to their own will, based on the vision that "when That, both the higher and the lower, is seen, all actions [cease]," and because of the teaching that the destruction of actions occurs through knowledge.

435. And [knowledge belongs] to those whose vital energy is drawn upward (*ūrdhvaretas*), for there is scriptural statement to that effect! (Sūtra 3.4.17, Siddhānta) Because Brahma-knowledge is seen to exist among those in the stages of life where the vital energy is drawn upward (*ūrdhvaretas*), and because rituals such as the *agnihotra* and the *darśapūrṇamāsa* are absent in those stages, knowledge is not an auxiliary part of ritual action.
[Objection]: But surely the stages of life in which the vital energy is drawn upward do not even exist; for it is said, "One performs the *agnihotra* as long as one lives."

Because of such scriptural injunctions as "as long as one lives" regarding the Agnihotra, Darśapūrṇamāsa, and other rites, and because Smṛtis that contradict Śruti lack authority, he says: "For in the Word (śabda)... Indeed, they are seen only in Vedic words: "There are three branches of dharma," and "Those who in the forest worship with faith and austerity."
In such passages as, "Desiring this very world, mendicants go forth," the scriptural injunction for lifelong [sacrificial performance] refers to those who are not yet dispassionate. || 17 ||
436. Jaimini [holds that there is] a reference [to the stages of life], because there is no injunction; for [the scripture] censures them.

(Siddhānta) This is not tenable, because in such passages as "There are three branches of dharma," there is merely a reference to those stages of life—the meaning being that it is a mere restatement (anuvāda). Why is this so? Because there is no injunction—that is, because there is no prescription. For no word of injunction is heard here. Indeed, by the passage beginning with "There are three branches of dharma," the meditation on Brahman by means of the *praṇava*, which is the subject under discussion, is being praised: "One who is firmly established in Brahman attains immortality."

This is because of the concluding summary. Therefore, what is done here is merely a restatement for another purpose regarding those stages of life (*āśrama*). Furthermore, in the passage, "And those who in the forest worship with faith and austerity," since the intent is to enjoin the path of the gods (*devayāna*), there is no possibility of an injunction for a different stage of life even there. Moreover, the Śruti indeed censures another stage of life: "He who lets the sacred fire go out is a slayer of the heroes of the gods."

Such is the [scriptural] passage. Therefore, the teacher Jaimini considers that there are no stages of life (*āśrama*) for those whose semen is drawn up (*ūrdhvaretas*). **3.4.19. Bādarāyaṇa [holds that they] are to be practiced, because of the scriptural statement of equality.** (Siddhānta) Furthermore, because of their equality with the householder’s stage of life (*gṛhasthāśrama*), other stages of life are also to be practiced here by the wise. For the Scripture declares another stage of life in such passages as: "There are three branches of duty (*dharmaskandha*)," and so forth. In these and similar texts, the venerable Bādarāyaṇa maintains that the other stages of life, like the householder’s stage, are indeed to be practiced.

Why? Because of the scriptural statement of equality. For indeed, the equality of those other stages of life with the householder’s stage—which is regarded as the one to be adopted—is heard in scripture. Beginning with "There are three branches of dharma," the mention [of the others] for the purpose of praising the one established in Brahman (*brahmasaṃstha*) is common to both the householder’s stage and the others.

Now, if it is argued that "the restatement (*anuvāda*) of the householder’s stage is only possible when it has already been established [by other means], and therefore its establishment must necessarily be accepted," that is equally true for the others as well, provided there is no specific insistence to the contrary.

Nor is it correct to argue that the term "sacrifice" (*yajña*), as well as the words "study," "giving," "austerity," and "celibacy," all denote only the duties of the householder— on the grounds that celibacy and austerity are possible only for a householder—
for [the text] groups them together as a triad under the statement, "There are three branches of duty."

Because a statement of division such as "the first, the second, the third" would be untenable; therefore, by the words "sacrifice, study, and charity," the householder's stage of life (*gṛhasthāśrama*) is denoted. The word "study" refers specifically to the practice of the Vedas. By the word "austerity" (*tapas*), both the forest-dweller (*vaikhānasa*) and the wandering mendicant (*pārivrājya*) are included, since austerity is the primary characteristic of both. Indeed, the word "austerity" is conventionally established in the sense of bodily mortification, and that is common to both. The duties of the religious student (*brahmacārin*) alone are designated by the word "celibacy" (*brahmacarya*).

Regarding the term "established in Brahman" (*brahmasaṃstha*) heard in the subsequent passage, "One established in Brahman attains immortality," it is etymological (*yaugika*) and common to all stages of life (*āśrama*), since it is possible for those in all stages to be established in Brahman. "Establishment in Brahman" (*brahmasaṃsthatva*) means abiding in or being firmly settled in Brahman; and that is indeed possible for everyone. Those who merely belong to the various stages of life without being devoted to Brahman partake of the worlds of merit; among them alone, he who is devoted to Brahman attains immortality. This very point has been clearly stated by the venerable Parāśara: "The stage of Prajāpati belongs to the Brāhmaṇas..."

Beginning with these words and ending with "is remembered as the [duty] of Brahmin renunciants," [the text] has described the fruit— culminating in the attainment of the world of Brahmā— for the various social classes (*varṇas*) and stages of life (*āśramas*) taken individually; [it now speaks of] those yogins who are single-mindedly devoted and always meditate upon Brahman.

"That is their supreme state, which indeed the wise behold"—thus [the scripture] declares the attainment of Brahman for those very [ascetics] who are established in Brahman. Therefore, since the stages of life (āśramas) involving the upward-directed vital energy (ūrdhvaretas) are seen to be equal to the householder's stage, they too are to be practiced.
"And those who, with faith, practice austerity in the forest... [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.23.1].

And because of the statement "in the forest," since the prescription of the Devayāna path depends primarily on the stage of life characterized by austerity (the vānaprastha), its attainment must also be admitted there. || 19 ||

Having established that, according to both the view that these [texts] are mere restatements (*parāmarśa*) and the view that they are injunctions (*vidhi*), their status as duties to be performed is equal to that of the householder stage (*gṛhasthāśrama*), he now says—[in order to establish] that this is indeed an injunction for all stages of life and not a mere restatement: **"Or rather, it is an injunction, like the wearing [of the sacred thread]."** (3.4.20) (Siddhānta) The word "or rather" (*vā*) is used for the purpose of emphasis. This is indeed an injunction regarding the stages of life, just like the wearing [of the sacred thread]—as in the case of the Agnihotra prescribed by fate.

Regarding the statement, "Holding the fuel-stick below, he should run after [the fire]; for he holds it above for the gods," an injunction is accepted here because holding it above is not already established, even though the sentence has the form of a restatement (anuvāda). As it is said in the section on the definition of subsidiary elements (śeṣalakṣaṇa): "But there is an injunction regarding holding, because it is something new (apūrva)"; likewise, here too, because it is not already established, an injunction alone must be accepted.

Regarding the phrase "And those who here" (*ye ceme*): the opponent has stated that because the passage beginning with "And those who here in the forest" (*ye ceme 'raṇye*) is intended as an injunction for the path of the gods (*devayāna*), it does not intend to enjoin the stages of life (*āśrama*). However, even though this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) made for the purpose of prescribing the path of the gods, it is dependent upon the attainment [of the stages] through other means of knowledge; thus, the meaning is that there is indeed an injunction (*vidhi*) regarding the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) and the wandering mendicant (*pārivrājya*) as well. || 19 ||

[Regarding the *diṣṭāgnihotra* and the *mṛtāgnihotra*: "The definition of the remainder" (*śeṣalakṣaṇa*). In the *diṣṭāgnihotra*, it is heard: "For he holds [the ladle] above for the gods. This is a restatement (*anuvāda*), because it is expressed in the present tense and because of the word "for" (*hi*). Furthermore, holding [the ladle] above is already established by customary practice (*ācāra*). Since the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) consists of a highly esteemed substance, it follows that it must be covered by something or other. Therefore, when another sentence—"Having grasped a fuel-stick (*samidh*) on the handle of the ladle (*srugdaṇḍa*), he runs after [the fire]"—is understood as a disposal (*pratipatti*), the fuel-stick is restricted [to that specific purpose].]

Therefore, when it is argued that this is a mere restatement (*anuvāda*), [we reply]: because the *samidh* (sacrificial fuel) is incapable of covering the oblation (*havir-ācchādana*), the meaning of the thread is that it serves as the handle of the ladle (*srug-daṇḍa*) for the oblation. Just like the act of holding—based on the statement "for above" (*upari hi*), which appears similar to a restatement—it is indeed an injunction (*vidhi*). Or rather, [it is an injunction] like the passage "There are three branches of dharma" (*trayo dharma-skandhāḥ*), which is an injunction for all the stages of life (*āśrama*s). "There is indeed an injunction regarding the celibate orders (*ūrdhvaretas*) in the words 'There are three branches of dharma'; just as in the case of the act of holding, based on the words 'for above the gods'."
"Having completed the student life (*brahmacarya*), one should become a householder; having been a householder, one should become a forest-dweller and then renounce.
Or else, in another way, one may renounce directly from the student life, or from the house, or from the forest.
On the very day one becomes dispassionate, on that very day one should renounce."

Having thus treated the rule for the stages of life (*āśrama*) of the Jābālas as if it were non-existent, it has been established that the attainment of the stages of life must necessarily be accepted even in those other scriptural passages.

Therefore, because of the injunctions for other stages of life, it should be understood that the scriptural texts concerning debts (*ṛṇa-śruti*), the texts concerning lifelong performance (*yāvaj-jīva-śruti*), and the texts concerning exceptions (*apavāda-śruti*) refer exclusively to those who are not yet dispassionate. Furthermore, other scriptural and traditional (*smṛti*) texts which enjoin the necessity of performing rituals until death for those who know Brahman pertain specifically to the duties of their respective stages of life.
Therefore, because the knowledge of Brahman is prescribed even for those who have sublimated their vital energy (ūrdhvaretas), it is established that the human goal arises from knowledge. || 20 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the purpose of human endeavor (Puruṣārthādhikaraṇa). || 1 ||

—0— Even though the eastern region has already been reached, since the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) has not yet been fully attained, it is established in the third book of the *Bhāṣyaprameya* that this is an injunction (*vidhi*). The scriptural text concerning debt (*ṛṇaśruti*) is: "A man is born with three debts," and so forth. The scriptural text as an exception (*apavādaśruti*) is: "He who [leaves home] is indeed a slayer of heroes among the gods; he causes the womb to perish. Regarding the phrase "not dispassionate" (*avirakta*): Since no fault is seen in a householder’s renunciation when it is preceded by the *utsarga-iṣṭi* sacrifice—which is prescribed for him—the scriptural text concerning the fault applies only to the case of abandoning [the world] without such prescription.

Furthermore, for one who desires to renounce and is dispassionate, since the rule for renunciation exists, the prescribed renunciation does not entail any fault. The sense is that the Vedic text stating "he is a slayer of heroes" (*bīrahā*) is applicable to one who, having entered the householder stage, proceeds to abandon it through negligence or ignorance, or to one who is not yet dispassionate. Regarding the phrase "and others," such Śruti passages as "He indeed, in this manner... and so forth, which are intent upon the non-performance of specific duties of the self, are likewise intent upon the performance of the respective duties of those belonging to each particular stage of life (*āśrama*).

But the duties of other stages of life (*āśrama*) do not contradict their being auxiliary to knowledge (*vidyā*). "Therefore" means: since for those of perpetual chastity (*ūrdhvaretas*) knowledge is enjoined independently, and because knowledge lacks the status of being an auxiliary to the duties of the householder stage—due to its being a means to a distinct fruit—the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) is accomplished through knowledge alone. This is the meaning of "the accomplishment of the human goal. Thus ends the section on the Human Goal (*puruṣārthādhikaraṇa*). 1.
The Section Concerning Merely Laudatory Passages (Stutimātrādhikaraṇa) || 3.4.2 ||
439. "If it be argued that it is merely a praise because of its being a subordinate element, we say no, because of its being something new. (Siddhānta Sūtra 3.4.21).
This is now considered:

Are such passages as "This Udgītha is the essence of essences, the highest, the supreme, the eighth"—do they aim merely at praising the Udgītha and other elements which are parts of the sacrifice? Or do they intend to enjoin the meditation upon the Udgītha and others as being the "essence of essences" and so forth?

Here, having accepted that these passages are devoted to meditation (*upāsana*), it was stated that because meditation serves as a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), there is no necessity of including them within the sacrificial rites (*kratu*).

What is correct? That they are intended merely as praise (*stuti*). Why? Because of the mention of the *udgītha* and other elements. For, having taken up the *udgītha* and so forth which have become constituent parts of the sacrifice, their status as "the most flavorful" (*rasatama*) and so on has been set forth. This is just as one who sets forth the earth-nature of the *juhū* ladle and other implements [does not thereby alter their ritual function].
Of the statement: "This very [ladle] is the *juhū*; the heavenly world is the *āhavanīya* fire."

Thus, passages such as these have the purpose of mere praise; so it is here as well. He raises this doubt: "If it be argued that it is mere praise because of the mention [of the Udgītha, etc.]"—that is, because of the mention of the Udgītha and other elements, if it be argued that the intention of these sentences is merely their praise!
To this, the reply is: "No, because of the novelty [of the teaching]. It is not tenable that they are mere praise.

Why? Because they are "unprecedented" (*apūrva*), that is, because they have not been established by any other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). For the *udgītha* and so forth have not been recognized through another authority as being "most savory" (*rasatama*) and so on, such that they would be restated (*anūdya*) as "most savory" for the purpose of generating a cognition of their excellence (*prāśastya*). Nor is there any injunction regarding the *udgītha* and so forth present here, by virtue of which one might resort to the view that this [passage] is intended as praise for them—forming a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with them—just as in the case of the passage, "This earth is indeed the *juhū* ladle, the heavenly world is the *āhavanīya* fire."

Regarding the phrase "kratvaṅga" (auxiliary to the sacrifice): praise consists precisely in the communication of a quality that cannot be accomplished by a person unless preceded by the employment of an auxiliary of the sacrifice; it is not the case that the communication of the *parṇatā* (being made of *parṇa*-wood) preceded by the employment of the *juhū* (ladle) as an auxiliary of the sacrifice constitutes praise. He states that this [latter] lacks the status of a sūtra because it possesses the nature of a doubt (*śaṅkā*).

"No," [it is argued]. For praise (stuti) is performed either by restating qualities already established by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), or by enjoining qualities not yet established, or—when qualities presented through the primary sense (*mukhyavṛtti*) are impossible—by connecting with qualities brought in through a secondary sense (*vṛttyantara*). Among these, the reason why praise is untenable as a restatement of qualities already established by another means of knowledge is explicitly stated in the Sūtra. However, it is not tenable to claim that the mention of "being the most flavorful" (*rasatamatva*) and so forth constitutes praise by way of enjoining qualities not yet established; [for those qualities are indeed established elsewhere].

The intended refutation in the Sūtra and the Bhāṣya is that because it is inappropriate for the *udgītha* and so forth to possess the quality of being "the most flavorful" (*rasatama*) and the like, and because it is impossible to enjoin something that is inherently inappropriate, the praise [of the *udgītha*] by means of [the word] "gift" (*dāna*) is untenable. Regarding the phrase "And not... and so on: by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the term "*udgīthādi*," the fivefold *sāman* and its injunctions are included. "By whatever method"—that is, by a non-primary (figurative) mode of application (*amukhyayā vṛttyā*). "Is resorted to" (*āśrīyate*)—Bhāṣya; "in the nature of the sentence" (*vākyatve*)—Da.

Or rather, because the seasons are more potent and so forth, it is logical that the injunction to view the *udgītha* and other elements as the "most flavorful" (*rasatama*) and so on is intended for the sake of accomplishing the fruit. 21.
440. And because of the word "bhāva" [in the sūtra], [the suffix *ṇvul* is applied]. (Siddhānta) 3.4.22.

Furthermore, because of verbal forms such as "one should meditate" (*upāsīta*), it is logical that they have the nature of injunctions (*vidhi*). For a word denoting action joined with an injunctive suffix conveys its own meaning only as something to be enjoined. Therefore, these scriptural passages have the purpose of enjoining meditation (*upāsanā*). || 22 ||
Thus concludes the section concerning mere praise (stutimātrādhikaraṇa). || 2 ||
The Section Concerning the Meaning of the Pāriplava. 3-4-3.
441. "If it be argued that [the texts] have diverse meanings, we say no, because they are specified. (Sūtra 3.4.23) [Examples:
"Pratardana, the son of Divodāsa, approached the beloved abode of Indra," and "Śvetaketu, the son of Aruṇi, existed [as a youth]."

Regarding the inquiry as to whether such narratives (*ākhyāna*) found in the Vedāntas are intended for the performance of the *pāriplava* rite, or rather for the purpose of elucidating specific forms of knowledge (*vidyā*):
if it is argued that they cannot properly have knowledge as their primary purpose because the injunction "they recite the narratives" assigns the narratives to the *pāriplava*, [we reply: no.
Not all narrative accounts are intended for application in the *pāriplava* recitation.
Why? Because the application is specified:
"They recite the narrative accounts."

Having said this, right there [the text] specifies the accounts of Manu and others with the words, "Manu Vaivasvata was the king," and so forth. Therefore, it is understood that their [accounts] alone are to be employed therein.

Therefore, not all scriptural passages concerning narration in the Vedānta texts are intended for the performance of the Pāriplava rite; rather, they are intended for the injunctions regarding knowledge (vidyā). || 23 ||

442. And likewise, because they are connected as part of a single sentence: (Siddhānta) "Because the narrative accounts (*ākhyāna*) are connected as forming a single syntactical unit with injunctions such as 'The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen,' those [accounts] have as their sole purpose the injunction of knowledge."—3.4.24. (Siddhānta)
Thus it is understood; as in the passage, "He wept.
Thus, passages such as these have the purpose of enjoining ritual actions, not the purpose of mere narrative recitation.
Thus ends the section concerning the meaning of the *pāriplava*. 3.
The section concerning fire, fuel, and so forth. (3.4.4)

443. For this very reason, these [ascetics] are independent of fuel and the like. (Siddhānta) Because those belonging to the stages of life in which the semen is drawn up (*ūrdhvaretas*) are embraced by the Śruti as being connected with knowledge, as in: "He who is established in Brahman attains immortality" and "And those who in the forest worship with faith and austerity."

This is shown by such passages as, "Desiring this world alone, mendicants go forth," and "Desiring which they lead the life of a student (brahmacarya). For this very reason, among those whose vital energy is drawn upward (ūrdhvaretas), knowledge does not depend on the kindling of fires and so forth. "Kindling of fires" means the installation of the sacred fires. Knowledge in their case is independent of rites such as the Agnihotra and Darśapūrṇamāsa, which are preceded by the installation of the fires. The meaning is that it depends solely on the duties prescribed for their own specific stage of life (āśrama). || 25 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the kindling of the fire and so forth. 4.
—Śrībhāṣya 3.4.5: The Section on the Dependence on All [Means] (Sarvāpekṣādhikaraṇa).
"And there is a requirement for all [works], because of the scriptural injunctions regarding sacrifice and so forth, as in the case of the horse. (Sūtra 3.4.26, Siddhānta) 444.

If knowledge were to accomplish immortality independently of sacrifice and other works, then it ought to accomplish it independently even among householders. Furthermore, the scriptural injunction regarding sacrifice and so forth—in the phrase "they desire to know" (*vividiṣanti*)—does not establish that ritual action is merely an auxiliary to knowledge. To this, he says: "There is a requirement for all"—meaning that knowledge requires all works, such as sacrifice, specifically among householders who possess those works.
Why? Because of the scriptural mention of sacrifice and so forth:
"Brahmins seek to know this very Self through the study of the Vedas, through sacrifice, through charity, through austerity, and through fasting."

By such statements as these, sacrifices and the like are indeed heard in scripture as being auxiliary to knowledge (*vidyā*). The phrase "they desire to know through sacrifice and so forth" (*yajñādinā vividiṣanti*) means they wish to know, that is, they wish to attain knowledge by means of sacrifice and the like. Only when sacrifice and the like are instruments for attaining knowledge is the designation "they wish to attain knowledge through sacrifice and the like" logically justified. Just as, when a sword is an instrument for killing, the designation "he wishes to kill with a sword" is appropriate;
therefore, it is understood that sacrifice and the like are instruments for attaining knowledge.

And we have already stated previously that knowledge—which is distinct from the knowledge of the meaning of a sentence, denoted by such terms as "meditation" (dhyāna) and "worship" (upāsanā), consisting of a most vivid form of direct perception in the nature of remembrance, supremely dear, possessing excellence acquired through daily practice, persisting until the moment of death, and being the means to liberation—will be described [later]. And he will say:

Like a horse: just as a horse, which is the means for locomotion, requires the preparation and equipment of its own trappings, so too does knowledge, which is the means for liberation, require the support of obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites. The Lord himself has said this: "Sacrifice, charity, and the act of austerity are not to be abandoned; they must indeed be performed.
Sacrifice, charity, and austerity are the purifiers of the wise."
"From whom the activity of beings proceeds, and by whom all this is pervaded—
by worshipping Him through one's own duty, a human being attains perfection.
Thus ends the section concerning the dependence on all [works]. || 5 ||
(Section on Tranquility, Self-Restraint, and so forth... Section on Tranquility, Self-Restraint, and so forth || 3.4.6 ||)

445. "But even so, he should be endowed with tranquility, self-control, and so forth; for since these are enjoined as auxiliary parts of that [sacrificial duty], they too must necessarily be performed.

(Siddhānta) In considering whether or not tranquility (*śama*), self-control (*dama*), and so forth are to be practiced by the householder—given that the performance of ritual action consists in the operation of the internal and external organs, whereas tranquility, self-control, and so forth are of a nature contrary to that—it might be argued that they are "not to be practiced. [The sūtra provides the conclusion: Nevertheless, he should be endowed with them, because they are enjoined as auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) of that [ritual duty], and therefore they too must necessarily be performed. Thus, even for the householder, tranquility, self-control, and so forth are indeed to be practiced.
Therefore, one who knows thus, having become calm, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, and concentrated, should perceive the Self in the very Self;
since these qualities— tranquility and the rest— are visible auxiliaries because they consist in the concentration of the mind necessary for the arising of knowledge,
and since tranquility, self-control, and so forth must necessarily be practiced, they too must be performed.

Furthermore, there is no mutual contradiction between the activities of the instruments [of action] for the sake of the attainment of knowledge and the actions such as tranquility (*śama*) and self-control (*dama*), which consist in the cessation of those very activities; this is because their objects are distinct. The activity of the instruments applies to what is enjoined, whereas their cessation applies to what is not enjoined and is devoid of purpose.

Furthermore, for one engaged in actions consisting of the operation of the instruments [of the body], it is not impossible for tranquility (*śama*) and the like to be adopted due to the force of latent impressions (*vāsanā*); for prescribed actions, being the means of propitiating the Supreme Person, serve as the cause for the eradication of all contrary latent impressions through His grace. Therefore, even tranquility, self-restraint (*dama*), and so forth, are to be practiced by the householder. || 27 ||
Thus concludes the section concerning tranquility, self-control, and the like. 6.
The Section on the Permission for All Food (Sarvānnānumati-adhikaraṇa) || 3.4.7 ||
446. And there is permission to eat all things in case of danger to life, because that is seen [in scripture].
(Sūtra 3.4.28, Siddhānta) — In the knowledge of the vital breath (*prāṇavidyā*) of both the Vājasaneyins and the Chandogas, it is said:
"Truly, for him no food becomes uneaten, nor does anything become unaccepted as food."
(Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 8.1.14:
"Indeed, for one who knows thus, nothing whatsoever becomes non-food"— thus, permission to eat all food is proclaimed for the knower of Prāṇa.)

Regarding the doubt as to whether this permission to eat all food at all times belongs to one who is established in the knowledge of the vital breath (*prāṇavidyā*), or only when one has reached the state of life-threatening danger— since no specific qualification is mentioned, the initial position is that it applies at all times.
The Śrībhāṣya (3.4.7) says: "In the case of the danger to life. The word "and" (*ca*) is used for emphasis; the meaning is: "only when there is the occurrence of a danger to life.

Why? Because it is observed (*taddarśanāt*); for elsewhere it is seen that even for those who know Brahman, the permission to eat all kinds of food is granted only when there is the occurrence of a danger to life—how much more so, then, for one who knows the Prāṇa?

It is said that Uṣasti Cākrāyaṇa, the foremost among the knowers of Brahman, while living in a village of wealthy men during a famine that had struck the Kuru country following a pestilence, reached a state where his life was in danger due to fasting. Desiring the exhaustion of his vital breaths for the sake of perfecting his knowledge of Brahman, he begged from a wealthy man some boiled beans (*kulmāṣa*) that the man was eating; however, being told by him, "These are leavings (*ucchiṣṭa*), there are no others," he replied once more, "Give me of these."

Having said this, he accepted the *kulmāṣa* beans that had been given to him by the *ibhya* after taking them from the leavings. When requested by the *ibhya* for a drink to accompany them, Cākrāyaṇa said, "This would indeed be a drink from leavings," and was then questioned by the *ibhya*: "Are these *kulmāṣa* beans not leavings?"

"I would not have lived had I not eaten these," he said, "for me, water was a desire. Because eating only those *kulmāṣa* beans would have placed his own life in jeopardy, drinking the leftover water—which would have been done out of mere desire—would have been forbidden for him whose life was sustained by eating only that much. Having said this, he gave the remainder of what he had eaten to his wife, who preserved them. On the following day, when he was about to depart with the intent of earning a livelihood among people, he again fell into a life-threatening crisis and ate those very same leftovers from the rich man's house, which had become his own leftovers and were now stale.

447. And because there is no contradiction [of scripture] (sūtra 3.4.29). (Siddhānta) From the statement, "When food is pure, the inner being becomes pure; when the inner being is pure, mindfulness becomes firm," it is understood that even because of the prescription of purity of food for the arising of knowledge (*vidyā*), the rule regarding the consumption of all kinds of food by those who know Brahman applies only to times of distress (*āpad-viṣaya*). Thus, since even for those who know Brahman—who possess extraordinary powers—the permission to eat all kinds of food is restricted to times of distress, the permission for one who knows the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and possesses limited power to eat all kinds of food must likewise apply only to times of distress. || 29 ||

448. "It is also recorded in Smṛti. (Sūtra 3-4-30) (Siddhānta) Furthermore, it is recorded in Smṛti that the practice of eating all kinds of food pertains only to times of distress, for both knowers of Brahman and others: "He who, having fallen into a life-threatening crisis, eats food from whatever source, is not tainted by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water."—Thus [it is said]. (30)
449. And on this account, there is a scriptural statement regarding the absence of acting according to one's desire.

(Siddhānta) Since for the knowers of Brahman as well as for others, the practice of eating all kinds of food is restricted solely to times of distress, for this very reason there exists a scriptural statement concerning the absence of acting according to one's desire—that is, a scriptural word which prohibits acting according to one's desire. For indeed, in the *Kaṭha Saṃhitā*, there is a scriptural statement prohibiting acting according to one's desire.

"Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa does not drink liquor, thinking, 'Lest I be released by evil,' that is, 'Lest I become contaminated by evil. This is the meaning: a Brāhmaṇa does not drink liquor. (31) Thus ends the section concerning the permission for all food. (7)
Section on Being Enjoined (Vihitatvādhikaraṇa) || 3.4.8 ||

[Even for those engaged in meditation (*upāsana*), although ritual actions (*karman*) serve as auxiliaries to knowledge (*vidyā*), they also serve as auxiliaries to the stage of life (*āśrama*) alone for those devoid of such knowledge.
450. "And because they are enjoined, the duties of the stages of life also [must be performed].
(Siddhānta) It has been stated that the knowledge of Brahman has rituals such as sacrifice as its auxiliaries.

Regarding the consideration of whether those rites, such as sacrifices and the like, are to be performed even by one who belongs solely to an *āśrama* (a stage of life) but does not seek liberation (*amumukṣu*), or whether they are not: since it would follow that there is a contradiction between the connection with what is eternal and what is non-eternal if these, being auxiliary parts of knowledge (*vidyā*), were merely subordinate to the *āśrama*, it is initially argued that it is impossible for sacrifices and the like to be duties belonging exclusively to the *āśrama*.
To this, the conclusion is reached that they are indeed to be performed even by one belonging solely to an *āśrama*. Why?

Because it is enjoined by such passages as "One performs the Agnihotra as long as one lives," the meaning is that it is prescribed as a compulsory (nitya) duty on account of being contingent upon life. || 32 ||

And likewise, because they are prescribed as "limbs of knowledge" (*vidyāṅga*) by such passages as, "This very [Self] one seeks to know through the recitation of the Vedas," etc., they must also be performed as subordinate to knowledge. Thus he says: **451. And as being auxiliary.** (Sūtra 3-4-33) They are to be performed also as auxiliaries to knowledge by way of bringing about its arising. Just as the Agnihotra and other rites have both a qualification based on life and a qualification for heaven, there is no contradiction in their serving a dual purpose through the distinctness of their application (*viniyoga-pṛthaktva*). This is the meaning. (33)

In the same way, he states that there is no difference in the nature of the action itself: **452. "In every respect, they are the very same, because of the dual indicative mark" (Sūtra 3.4.34). (Conclusion)** "In every respect"—whether for the purpose of knowledge (*vidyā*) or for the purpose of the stages of life (*āśrama*)—"they are the very same," namely, sacrifices (*yajña*) and so forth; this is how it should be understood. The meaning is that there is no difference in the essential nature of the action. Why? "Because of the dual indicative mark. This is because in both scriptural passages, the actions are enjoined after being recognized as the same through the use of words such as "sacrifice" (*yajña*), and because there is no evidence for a difference in the essential nature of the action. (34)
453. And it demonstrates non-overpowering. (3.4.35)

By stating "He removes evil through dharma" and so forth, [the text] points to those very same dharmas such as sacrifice, and shows that knowledge is not overcome by them—that is, there is no obstruction to its arising caused by sinful actions. For when the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is purified by sacrifices and other rites performed day after day, knowledge arises as it is further refined daily. Therefore, those same sacrifices and so forth apply in both cases. Thus ends the section on "Being Enjoined" (vihitatvādhikaraṇa). 8.
— Śrībhāṣya 3.4.9:
The Section on the Person Devoid of Rituals (vidhurādhikaraṇam) || 3.4.9 ||
454. And also because that [the intermediate state] is seen between [birth and death]. (Siddhānta) 3-4-36.
It has been stated that the four orders of life (āśramas) possess the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman, and that the duties of the orders are auxiliaries to that knowledge.
Now, regarding the doubt as to whether those who exist outside the orders— such as the widowers (*vidhura*) and others— possess the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman or not:

Why? Because it is observed: for it is indeed seen that Raikva, Bhīṣma, Saṃvarta, and others were devoted to the knowledge of Brahman even though they were not members of any [formal] stage of life (āśrama). Nor can it be said that "the favoring of knowledge occurs through the duties of the stages of life alone," as it is stated:
"By sacrifice, by charity, by austerity, and by fasting."

Thus, because it is observed that even those acts such as giving—which are not invariably restricted to a specific stage of life (*āśrama*) or path—are supportive [of knowledge]. For example: since it is observed that among those who have sublimated their vital energy (*ūrdhvaretas*), there is a dedication to knowledge, the support for knowledge is effected by means other than the *agnihotra* and other such rituals; likewise, since knowledge is observed even among those not belonging to any stage of life, the support for knowledge can be effected through practices not fixed to a stage of life, such as recitation (*japa*), fasting (*upavāsa*), and the propitiation of deities. || 36 ||

This matter is not to be established by logic (*nyāya*) and traditional law (*smṛti*) alone; it is also heard in scripture that the favoring of knowledge (*vidyānugraha*) occurs through specific duties not restricted to the stages of life (*anāśrama*), such as:
"One should seek the Self through austerity (*tapas*), celibacy (*brahmacarya*), faith (*śraddhā*), and knowledge (*vidyā*). (38)
457. "Therefore, however, the other is superior, and because of scriptural indication" (sūtra 3.4.39).

The word *tu* ("however") is used for emphasis. *Ataḥ* means "because of being without an order of life" (*anāśramitvāt*). *Itarat* means "the other," namely, the state of belonging to an order of life (*āśramitva*) alone is superior; the state of being without an order of life is restricted to times of distress (*āpad-viṣaya*). The meaning is that for one who is capable, the state of belonging to an order of life alone is to be adopted; for those possessing many duties and those possessing few duties do not have equal results. And "because of scriptural indication" (*liṅgāt*)—that is, from the Smṛti itself. It is recorded in the Smṛti that the adoption of an order of life is prescribed for the capable: "A twice-born man should not remain even for a single day without belonging to an order of life."

By such statements as these: "For one who has completed his period of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and whose wife has died, if detachment (*vairāgya*) has not arisen, the failure to obtain a wife is an *āpad* (calamity). [39]
Thus ends the section concerning the disjunction [of the soul from the body]. 9.
The Section on "That Being Present" (tadbhūtādhikaraṇa) || 3.4.10 ||

458. "But for one who has become that [ascetic], there is no returning to a non-ascetic state, according to Jaimini as well, because of the restrictive rule and because of the absence of those characteristics" (Sūtra 3.4.40). (This is the established conclusion.

In the inquiry as to whether there exists the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman even for those who have fallen away from the stages of life (*āśrama*) of the perpetual student (*naiṣṭhika*), the hermit (*baikhānasa*), or the wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*), [the opponent argues]: "There is such qualification, because, as in the case of the widower (*vidhura*) and others, the favor of knowledge can be attained through acts such as giving, even by those who do not exclusively belong to a stage of life."

This being the position reached, it is said: "But for one who has become that, there is no non-becoming of that" (tadbhūtasya tu nātadbhāvaḥ). The word "but" (tu) serves to exclude the previous view. For one who has become that—that is, for one established in a lifelong stage of life such as that of the *naiṣṭhika*—there is no "non-becoming of that," meaning no state of not being so; it is impossible for him to remain in a state of being without a stage of life (*anāśramitva*).

Why? Because of the restriction [imposed] by the absences of those forms. "Those forms" refers to the forms—meaning the dress and the duties—of those such as the *naiṣṭhika* (lifelong celibate); "the absences of those forms" means the non-existence of those. From these, there is a restriction by the scriptures.

For the scriptures indeed restrict those who have entered the *āśramas* of the *naiṣṭhika* and others from turning away from the duties of their own respective *āśramas*. As the scriptures state: "The third [type of student] is the lifelong celibate (*brahmacārī*) dwelling in the teacher's family; he should spend his entire life bringing himself to completion in the teacher's family."
"One should go to the forest and not return from there," and,
"Having renounced the sacred fire, one should not return."

And thus it is said. Therefore, since it is impossible for those such as the *naiṣṭhika* (lifelong celibates) to remain without belonging to an *āśrama*—just like the widower (*vidhura*) and others—the knowledge of Brahman does not qualify them [as candidates]. By stating "Jaimini’s also," [the author] demonstrates the absence of contradiction and thereby confirms his own intended view. || 40 ||

Now, it might be argued: for those such as lifelong celibates (*naiṣṭhika*) who have fallen from their vow of chastity, eligibility [for knowledge] is possible through expiation (*prāyaścitta*). And there exists an expiation, as established in the section defining eligibility: "And the animal sacrifice for one who has broken his vow of chastity is similar to that.

Therefore, since expiation is possible for one who has fallen from celibacy, one who has performed the expiation will be eligible for the knowledge of Brahman. To this, he replies: "And this is not inconsistent with the subsequent [stages of life]."

Thus, the meaning is that what has been stated regarding those dwelling in the house of the teacher (gurukula) applies without contradiction to the subsequent stages of life as well; likewise here too, since penance is possible even upon a lapse from the vow of studentship (brahmacarya), there exists fitness for the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā). || 42 ||

461. "But on both accounts they are excluded from outside [the community], according to Smṛti and custom. (Siddhānta) The word "but" (*tu*) serves to exclude other opinions. Whether they are guilty of minor offenses (*upapātaka*) or major sins (*mahāpātaka*), these persons remain excluded from those qualified for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). The meaning is that they are not entitled to the knowledge of Brahman. Why? Because of Smṛti—that is, because of the aforementioned Smṛti texts concerning their fall. Even though there exists an entitlement to perform expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*) for some through certain scriptural statements for the purpose of purification (*kalpa-nirharaṇa*), nevertheless—

The meaning is that an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) which serves as a cause for purification corresponding to the qualification for ritual action is not possible, according to the Smṛti: "I see no expiation by which he might be purified; he is a slayer of the self. This is also evident from established practice (*ācāra*): for the learned (*śiṣṭas*) avoid even those lifelong students (*naiṣṭhikas*) and others who have fallen from their vows, even after they have performed expiation. They do not instruct them in the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) and so forth. Therefore, they have no qualification for the knowledge of Brahman. || 43 ||
Thus ends the section concerning that which has become so (tadbhūtādhikaraṇa). || 10 ||
The Section on the Lord (Svāmyadhikaraṇa). 3.4.11.
462. Ātreya [maintains] that the fruit belongs to the master, because the scripture declares the fruit [for him]. (3.4.44)

Regarding the meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth, which depend upon the constituent parts of the ritual (*karmāṅga*), there arises the inquiry: "Are they to be performed by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) or by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*)?

In this deliberation, Ātreya maintains that they are to be performed by the sacrificer. Why? Because of the mention of the fruit (*phalaśruti*). This is because, in the meditations on the *dahara* (the small ether) and others ordained in the Vedāntas, one observes that the fruit and the meditation have a single locus; and here too, it is heard that the fruit of the *udgītha* meditation—which consists in the non-obstruction of the fruit of the sacrifice—has the sacrificer as its locus. This is the meaning.

Nor is it impossible for the sacrificer to be the agent by virtue of the meditation being subordinate (*aṅga*), as in the case of the *godohana* vessel and so forth. For in the case of the *godohana* etc., there is the employment of the *godohana* as the substratum for the act of carrying water (*praṇayana*) performed by the Adhvaryu priest; this cannot be done by anyone else. But here, even though the *udgītha* has the Udgātṛ priest as its agent, the contemplation of that *udgītha* and so forth as the "most excellent essence" (*rasatama*) can indeed be performed by the sacrificer himself. (44)

This being the position, it is replied: 463. *Ārtvijyam* [is the meditation], according to Auḍulomi; for he is hired for that purpose. (Siddhānta) The teacher Auḍulomi maintains that the *ārtvijyam*—the work of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), namely the meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth—is [the duty of the sacrificer]. Why? Because the priest is "hired" (*parikrīyate*) for that specific purpose; the meaning is that he is engaged for the sake of undertaking the sacrifice together with its constituent parts, which serves as the means to the fruit. This is evident from the injunctions regarding ritual acts: [Text continues: ...in the ritual injunctions—

From the scriptural injunctions, "He chooses the officiating priests" and "He gives the sacrificial fee to the officiating priests," it is understood that "the ritual action, together with its constituent parts, which serves as the means to the fruit, is to be performed by the officiating priests. Consequently, the physical and mental actions included therein are indeed performed by the officiating priests. Nor can capacity and incapacity be the basis for this [assignment].

Although meditation on the *udgītha* and so forth is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), nevertheless, because it pertains to one who is already qualified for the sacrifice (*kratvadhikṛtādhikāratvāt*), and because the sacrifice, along with its constituent parts, is to be performed by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), [it is said]:
"Whatever one performs with knowledge... that alone becomes more powerful."

Thus, because knowledge is heard to have a single agent [with the ritual] due to its utility for the action performed by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), these [meditations] are performed by the officiating priests. However, in the meditations on the "small one" (*dahara*) and so forth, since there is no scriptural statement regarding performance by officiating priests, and according to the maxim "the fruit of the scripture belongs to the performer," they must indeed be performed by the fruit-bearing agent [the sacrificer]. || 45 ||

Thus ends the section on ownership (Svāmyadhikaraṇa). 11.
