The Section Concerning the Injunction of Other Auxiliary Means (Sahakāryantara-vidhi-adhikaraṇa) || 3.4.12 ||

464. "The injunction of another auxiliary [is] by way of an alternative; it belongs to one who possesses that [knowledge], like the beginning of an injunction. (Siddhānta) "Therefore, having become learned, a Brāhmaṇa should remain in a state of childlike simplicity; he should possess both childlike simplicity and learning. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.5.1)
Having thus concluded, the sage [now addresses] the doubt: "Is silence (*mauna*) also enjoined like childhood and scholarship (*bālya-pāṇḍitya*), or is it merely restated (*anūdyate*)?"—
in this regard:

Since the two words "mauna" and "pāṇḍitya" have the meaning of knowledge, that very knowledge which was enjoined by the phrase "having become indifferent through scholarship" (pāṇḍityaṃ nirvidya) is here restated in the phrase "then he is a sage" (atha muniḥ). For no word of injunction is heard here.

Furthermore, by the passage beginning with "peaceful and self-controlled" (śānto dāntaḥ), the auxiliary means such as sacrifice and so forth, as well as tranquility, self-control, and the like, are enjoined; and just as...

Regarding the injunctions "it is to be heard" and "it is to be reflected upon," hearing and reflection are understood as being required for the sake of knowledge as its auxiliaries; likewise, by the passage beginning with "Therefore, a Brahmin, having renounced scholarship," the triad of "scholarship, childhood, and silence" is prescribed as another set of auxiliaries to knowledge.

And he says that "mauna" (sagehood) is something other than "pāṇḍitya" (scholarship), by means of the term "pakṣeṇa" (by way of an alternative). This is because we observe the use of the word "muni" in reference to Vyāsa and others who possess the habit of superior reflection; thus, mauna is the third [stage] following both pāṇḍitya and bālya.

Although no injunctive suffix is heard in the phrase "then [he becomes] a sage" (*atha muniḥ*), nevertheless, since the state of being a sage (*mauna*) has not been previously established, its status as something to be enjoined must be accepted—namely, "then he should become a sage. And this "munitude" (*mauna*) is distinct from reflection (*manana*), which is for the purpose of stabilizing what has been heard; it consists in the repeated cultivation of the object of meditation, taking the form of its deep contemplation (*bhāvanā*).
Having become disillusioned with mere scholarship—one should worship the reality of Brahman;

such is the meaning of the sentence. A "Brāhmaṇa" is one who possesses knowledge, having realized that which is pure and complete, meaning he has attained the realization obtained through hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and meditation (*nididhyāsana*). This is brought about by the increase of true goodness (*sattva*) assisted by devotion to the Blessed Lord, as it has been said:
And that [knowledge] begins with the passage:
"He knows destruction" (Bhagavad Gītā 11.53).
"But by unswerving devotion He can be known," and the Śruti also says:
"He who has supreme devotion for the Divine..."
"This Self is not to be attained by instruction," and so forth.

"One should remain in a state of childhood. The nature of childhood will be explained immediately hereafter. "Having become disillusioned with both childhood and scholarship, one should then be a sage"—that is, having properly adopted childhood and scholarship, one should become intent on contemplation (*manana*) regarding the pure and perfect Brahman, for the sake of attaining the knowledge consisting of deep reflection (*nididhyāsana*). He says that in this very way, by adopting the triad, one becomes one who has acquired knowledge:
"Having become disillusioned with both non-sagehood and sagehood, one is then a *brāhmaṇa*."

Thus: "Non-mauna" (amauna) refers to the entire collection of auxiliary factors other than mauna. The meaning is that by properly employing both that [non-mauna] and mauna, one shall attain the pinnacle of knowledge (*vidyākāṣṭhā*), which is produced solely by them.
When asked, "By what would he be a true Brāhmaṇa?"—that is, "Is there any means other than the one already mentioned?"—[the answer is:
"By whatever [means] he may be [so], it is precisely of this nature."

Thus, it has been refuted [by the opponent] with the argument: "By that very means—ending with *mauna* (silence)—whereby one becomes a *brāhmaṇa*, by that alone should he be such; not by any other means. Therefore, for the knower (*vidvan*) residing in any of the stages of life (*āśrama*), scholarship (*pāṇḍitya*) and so forth, along with *mauna* as the third, are enjoined as another auxiliary to knowledge (*vidyā-sahakāry-antara*), just like the duties of one's own stage of life such as sacrifice (*yajña*). || 46 ||

Now, it might be argued: if it is said that for the wise who abide in all the stages of life (*āśrama*), knowledge—accompanied by the duties of those respective stages and with silence as its third assistant—is the means for attaining Brahman; then how is it that in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*, beginning with "Having returned home, [dwelling] in a family in a pure place," and continuing until "he, indeed, conducting himself thus for the duration of his life, reaches the world of Brahman and does not return again"?

If it is asked: "Does this not imply that abiding by the duties of the householder (*gārhasthya-dharma*) is shown to be possible for as long as one lives? To this he says: **"But because it exists in its entirety, the conclusion is made with reference to the householder."** (3.4.47) [Siddhānta] The word "but" (*tu*) sets aside the objection. "Because it exists in its entirety"—that is, because it exists in all [stages of life]. Since knowledge (*vidyā*) is present in all stages of life (*āśrama*), it exists even in the householder; therefore, the conclusion is made with reference to him. In this regard, there arises a doubt: should the wise man adopt all the actions of a child, such as acting according to whim (*kāmacāra*) and so forth, or only that which is free from hypocrisy (*ḍambha*) and the like? For in the preceding section, the knowledge of Brahman has been introduced as the means for attaining immortality: "Verily, one who has a teacher knows [it]; through the knowledge of Brahman, one goes to immortality" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1). It is not possible for the mere actions of a child, such as acting according to whim, to be a qualification of the knowledge of Brahman. However, freedom from hypocrisy and the like is indeed a qualification of that knowledge. Hence, it is only freedom from hypocrisy and the like that is to be adopted by the wise man. Furthermore, the mention of "learning" (*pāṇḍitya*) here is intended to exclude the pride of learning (*śrotriya-māna*). Thus, the meaning is: "Having become free from the pride of learning, one should remain in a state of childlike simplicity. There must be repetition [of meditation], because of the instruction given more than once. (4.1.1)

In the third chapter, knowledge (*vidyā*) was considered along with its means (*sādhana*). Now, however, the fruit of knowledge is considered, preceded by a clarification of the nature of knowledge itself. In this regard: "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme";
"Having known Him alone, one goes beyond death"; "One who knows Brahman becomes Brahman indeed."

Regarding Vedic statements such as "When the seer sees the Golden-hued One," there arises a doubt: is the knowledge enjoined as the means for attaining Brahman something to be performed only once, or is it to be repeated?
What is logical? That it is accomplished once.
Why? Because [the scripture says]: "One who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself."
This is because only the act of knowing is enjoined, and there is no evidence for its repeated performance.

Nor can it be argued that, like the act of threshing, knowledge must be repeated until the effect is achieved—namely, the direct realization (*aparokṣya*) of Brahman—since knowledge lacks the nature of a visible means (*dṛṣṭopāya*). For it has been established in the sūtra *Phalamata Upapatteh* ("The fruit [comes] from Him, because that is logical") that rites such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and the knowledge prescribed in the Vedāntas are both forms of propitiation of the Supreme Person; and from the Supreme Person thus propitiated, the attainment of the human goals known as virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation occurs.

Therefore—[the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) being]: "Just as in the case of the Jyotiṣṭoma and other rites, the purpose of the scripture is fulfilled by performing it only once according to the word [of the text]," so it is obtained; [we reply] by explaining the meaning of the Sūtra: "Repetition is not once" (*āvṛttirasakṛt*). Knowledge that has been repeated more than once is indeed the purpose of the scripture. "Why? Because of the teaching" (*upadeśāt*)—because of the teaching by means of the words "knowledge" (*vedana*), used interchangeably with "meditation" (*dhyāna*) and "worship" (*upāsana*). And that these terms are interchangeable is understood from their usage in sentences teaching knowledge regarding a single object. For instance: [The text continues with scriptural citations. Thus it is. Therefore, the purpose of the scripture is knowledge that has been repeated more than once. Furthermore, since the result of knowledge is the attainment of the nature of Brahman, and since that attainment occurs through the removal of ignorance, which is of the nature of a beginningless non-existence, it follows that this removal requires a long time. Consequently, the repetition of knowledge is established by the very nature of the result. Moreover, we observe in the world that the comprehension of subtle objects, such as the meaning of the Vedas or the art of archery, results from repeated practice. Similarly, here too, the realization of the Self, which is extremely subtle, must arise from the repetition of knowledge. Furthermore, there are scriptural texts indicating the repetition of knowledge, such as: "One should meditate on the Self as 'I am He'" (*ātmānam eva lokam upāsīta*); "He who knows it as such becomes one who breathes with the breath" (*sa ya etam evaṃ vidvān ātmānaṃ vaiśvānaram upāste*); and "The Self, my dear, is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon" (*ātmā vā are draṣṭavyaḥ śrotavyo mantavyo nididhyāsitavyaḥ*). Also, there is the text: "Let him repeat [it] until he is freed from doubt" (*tāvad evaṃ vicared yāvad vimokṣye'tha saṃpatsye*). Thus, because of the teaching, the nature of the result, the observation of the world, and the indicative marks of scripture, the repetition of knowledge is established. This is the conclusion. As for the argument that the scripture's purpose is fulfilled by a single performance, like the Jyotiṣṭoma, that is not so; for in the case of the Jyotiṣṭoma and similar rites, the result is heaven, which is something to be produced (*bhāvya*). Since heaven is a state of pleasure, it is logical that it should be accomplished by a single performance. However, in the present case, the result is the attainment of the nature of Brahman, which is already existent and merely concealed by ignorance. Therefore, its attainment depends on the removal of that ignorance, and since that removal requires time, it is logical that the means—the knowledge of Brahman—should be repeated. Furthermore, the scripture teaches that the fruit of knowledge is the cessation of transmigration, which is the very nature of the Self. Since the nature of the Self is eternal, it cannot be produced by action; rather, it is attained through the removal of ignorance. Hence, the scripture does not intend a single performance of knowledge. Moreover, the scripture teaches that the fruit of knowledge is the cessation of all karma, both past and future, as in: "His actions are destroyed when he sees the Self" (*kṣīyante cāsya karmāṇi tasmin dṛṣṭe parāvare*). Since the destruction of karma is a result that must be accomplished, it is logical that the means—knowledge—should be repeated. Also, the scripture shows that knowledge is the cause of the cessation of karma through the example of the arrow: "Just as the impulse of an arrow shot by an archer is spent gradually, so the karma of one who sees the Self is spent" (*tad yathārdraidhāgner abhyāhitasya pṛthagdhūmā viniścaranty evaṃ vā are'sya mahato bhūtasya niḥśvasitam etad yad ṛgvedo yajurvedaḥ...* etc., and *tasyaiva syāt padavittaṃ viditvā na lipyate karmaṇā pāpakena*). Therefore, the repetition of knowledge is established. This is the conclusion. The sense is as follows: regarding the passage "One should meditate [upon] the mind as Brahman," the subject matter introduced by the meditator is treated according to the principle of "the performance [of a rite].

Having established the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that "there may be an abundance of fruit through repetition, as in the case of a seasonal sacrifice (*ṛtu*) by means of inference," the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) was established with the statement, "Or rather, it is done once, because it has a single cause," on the grounds that the purpose is accomplished by performing it just once, and because there is no evidence for an increase in fruit when there is merely a repetition of the subordinate parts (*aṅga*). Thus, there is no need for repetition.

For this very reason—since there is no gradation in the fruit consisting of liberation, and according to the maxim, "Because it is to be brought about by an undertaking, the fruits [of actions] would be distinct with each undertaking, like agriculture," as well as the principle that "Just as there is repetition of optional rites for the sake of a greater abundance of results, there must likewise be repetition of the knowledge"—it is concluded with the verb *vid* (to know) in the passage:
"He who knows thus shines and glows with fame, glory, and Vedic splendor.
Likewise, [the text continues:]

In the opening statement, "He who knows what he knows—that has been told by me," the knowledge of Raikva is spoken of by means of the verb *vid* (to know); then, in the conclusion, "O Venerable Sir, instruct me further in that deity which you worship," it is concluded by means of the verb *upās* (to worship). Likewise, [it begins with] "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme."

In sentences such as these, which have the same meaning as the aforementioned passage—namely, "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5), and "Then, meditating on the partless [Self], one sees Him" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.8)—the act of knowing (*vedana*) is expressed by the term "meditation" (*dhyāyati*). And meditation is reflection (*cintana*). Furthermore, that [reflection] consists of a continuous flow of memory (*smṛti-santati*).
It is not mere mindfulness.

Meditation (*upāsti*) also has that same single meaning; for we observe the use of the term in the sense of the uninterrupted continuity of one-pointed mental states. Because both [meditation and knowledge] have this same single purpose, it is determined that here the continuous flow of memory (*smṛti-santati*), when repeated more than once, is designated by words such as "knowing" (*vedana*) in passages like: "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself," and "Having known God, one is released from all fetters. || 1 ||

"And when there is a cognition of that [object], the continuity [of consciousness] becomes one-pointed and indifferent to anything else;

"But they [the followers of the Upanishads] understand it as 'Self' and cause others to grasp it as such. (Siddhānta Sūtra 4.1.3)
This is now considered: is the Brahman to be meditated upon as something other than the meditator, or rather as the very self of the meditator?
What is correct? [That it is] by way of being other.

Why? Because Brahman is an entity distinct from the individual self (pratyagātman) who is the worshiper. And this distinction [is established] by the sūtras: "But [Brahman is] greater, because of the designation of difference" and "because of the teaching of its superiority."

This has been established in such passages as "Not the other, because of impossibility. Furthermore, Brahman must be meditated upon exactly as it exists; for if one meditates on it incorrectly, even the attainment of Brahman would be incorrect.
"According to the principle that 'in whatever manner a person intends in this world, so does he become after departing from here,' it must therefore be meditated upon as something distinct."

Six. This being the position reached, it is replied: "But [it is] the Self" (ātmeti tu). The word "but" (tu) is used for emphasis. That which is to be meditated upon is indeed the Self of the meditator. The meditator is the inner self (pratyagātman); just as one's own body has oneself as its Self, so too should one meditate that the Supreme Brahman is the Self of one's own Self.
Why? Because the ancient meditators approach [the goal] in this very way.

"O Blessed One, O Divinity! You indeed am I; I indeed am you. How can they accept that the Brahman, who is an entity distinct from the worshipper, is the "I" of the worshipper? To this he says: "And they cause [the worshippers] to grasp"—meaning that the scriptures cause those worshippers to grasp this truth, they establish it for them. "He who, dwelling in the self, is within the self, whom the self does not know, whose body is the self, who controls the self from within—he is your self, the inner controller, the immortal."
Thus it is said; likewise:
"O gentle one, all these creatures have Being as their root, Being as their abode, and Being as their support. All this has that as its essence.
And: "All this, indeed, is Brahman, because it originates from it, dissolves into it, and breathes in it."

And thus, because all things—both sentient and insentient—are born from Him, dissolve into Him, consist of Him, are governed by Him, and have Him as their body, He is the Self of all. Therefore, He is your Self. Consequently, just as one identifies with one's own body because it is one's own self, thinking "I am a god" or "I am a human," so too, since the Supreme Self is the Self even of the individual self (pratyagātman), it is logical that He should also be identified as "I" alone.

Thus, accepting that all words have Brahman as their ultimate ground—just as all cognitions have Brahman as their ultimate ground—as established by the scriptures, they spoke with mutual interchange [of identities], saying: "I am indeed you, O venerable deity! You are indeed me, O venerable deity!
And so it is.
"But he who worships another deity, thinking, 'He is one and I am another,' does not know" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.4.10).
"One should worship [the Self] as the Self alone."
"He who knows all this as other than the Self is abandoned by it all"—this is a prohibition against failing to contemplate [everything] as being the Self. [This is supported by such texts as:
"Having conceived of oneself and the Impeller as distinct," and "For he is incomplete."

Thus, the injunction for the contemplation of distinctness (*pṛthaktvānusandhāna*) is not contradictory. Because one contemplates [the Self] as "I" by way of its own nature (*svātmatayā*), the prohibition against contemplating it as something else is preserved. And because one contemplates the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) as superior even to one's own self—just as one contemplates one's own self as superior to one's own body—the injunction for the contemplation of distinctness is likewise preserved.

Since the inner self (*pratyagātman*) is the self of the superior Brahman, and since that [inner self] is the body (*śarīra*) of Brahman, the prohibitory statement "for this [self] is incomplete" (*akṛtsno hy eṣaḥ*) applies.
Thus it has been said. Therefore, it is established that Brahman is to be worshipped as the very Self of the worshipper. || 3 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the meditation on the Self (ātmatva). || 2 ||
The Section on Counter-Services (Pratīkādhikaraṇa) || 4.1.3 ||

473. "Not in a symbol, for he [is not that]. (Siddhānta-sūtra 4-1-4) In the case of meditations on symbols (*pratīkopāsana*), such as "One should meditate on the mind as Brahman" and "He who meditates on Name as Brahman," should one perform the contemplation of [the object] as being the Self (*ātmatva-anusandhāna*)? Or not? This is the inquiry.

Because of the commonality of being meditations on Brahman— as in "One should meditate on the mind as Brahman"— and because Brahman is the Self of the meditator, one should meditate [on it] simply as the Self.

This being the position reached, it is replied: "Not in the symbol" (*na pratīke*). One should not perform the contemplation of the Self in the symbol; for indeed, the symbol is not the Self of the worshiper. In the meditations on symbols, the symbol itself is the object of worship, not Brahman; Brahman is merely a qualifying attribute of the vision there. For what is called meditation on a symbol is the contemplation of the vision of Brahman upon that which is not Brahman. Since the symbol, which is the object of worship there, lacks the nature of being the Self of the worshiper, it should not be contemplated in that manner [as the Self].

[Objection: But even here, Brahman alone must be the object of meditation; for since it is improper to resort to the mind and other such non-conscious, limited powers as the objects of meditation when Brahman is available as the object of meditation, Brahman alone should be meditated upon through the vision of the mind and so forth. To this, he says: **4.1.5. The vision of Brahman [is to be applied to the mind, etc. because of its superiority.**

It is proper that the vision of Brahman alone be applied to the mind and other [instruments], and not the vision of the mind and others to Brahman; for Brahman is superior to the mind and others, and there is a reversal in their case. For indeed, viewing a superior king as a servant brings about demerit, whereas viewing a servant as a king leads to prosperity. || 5 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the Pratīkas. 3.
—0— Section 4.1.4:
The Topic Concerning the Notion that [the Sun] and Others Are [Brahman].

475. *Ādityādimatayaścāṅge upapatteḥ* (Siddhānta). Regarding meditations based on the constituent parts of ritual acts, such as "One should meditate on him who shines yonder as the Udgītha," a doubt arises: Is the perception of Āditya and so forth to be applied to the Udgītha and other parts of the rite, or is the perception of the Udgītha and so forth to be applied to Āditya and so forth?

According to the maxim that "one should apply the perception of the inferior to the superior," and because the *udgītha* and so forth—being constituent parts (*aṅga*) of rituals that are means to attaining results—are superior to the fruitless sun and other objects, one should apply the perception of the *udgītha* and so forth to the sun and others.

Regarding the word "Āditya": because of the exaltation (*utkarṣa*) of the deity, it was stated that [the deity] serves as a qualification for the visualization (*dṛṣṭi*). By raising an objection to that exaltation, there arises an intermediate connection (*avāntara-saṅgati*) based on the doubt as to whether the exaltation belongs to the ritual action itself. In the case of meditations (*upāsana*) based upon the constituent parts of the sacrifice (*kratvaṅga*): is the visualization of the *udgītha*, etc., to be applied to the Sun (*āditya*), etc.? Is the exaltation due to being a means to the fruit (*phala-sādhanatā*) attributed to the Sun, etc., or to the *udgītha*, etc.? If it belongs to the *udgītha*, etc., then the visualization of the *udgītha*, etc., should be applied to the Sun, etc.; if it belongs to the Sun, etc., then the visualization of the Sun, etc., should be applied to the *udgītha*, etc.

Since the primary ritual action is enjoined as the means for accomplishing the fruit, the propitiation of the deity is merely an intermediate operation (avāntaravyāpāra), like the flame produced by pieces of wood; thus, its lack of primacy is suspected. [Objection: Since the deity’s status as the means for accomplishing the fruit has already been established, how can this prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) arise? [Response: It is like the meditation on Brahman. The meaning of the word "and" (ca) is that there are also meditations on Āditya and so forth. In the passage "Mind is Brahman," that which is to be meditated upon is first indicated, and the qualifying attribute is mentioned last.

Likewise, in the passage "That which shines yonder is the Udgītha," because the Udgītha is mentioned last, it is the object qualified by the vision (*dṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, the reasoning for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) intended here is that the deity is the subject (*uddeśya*) because of its connection with the word "that" (*saḥ*) and because of its priority. "From those that are fruitless" means from those that are not means to a fruit.

This being the position, it is replied: "And the meditations on the Sun and so forth [are to be applied] to the subsidiary parts. The word "and" (*ca*) is used in the sense of restriction. Meditations on the Sun and so forth are to be performed specifically upon the subsidiary parts of the sacrifice, such as the *udgītha* and others.

Why? Because of logical consistency (*upapatti*); for it is logically consistent that the Sun and so forth alone are superior. Indeed, it is by means of propitiating deities such as the Sun that even ritual actions become instruments for attaining results. Therefore, the meditation on those [deities] is to be applied to the subsidiary parts like the *udgītha*. (Sūtra 6)
Thus concludes the section concerning the meditation on the Āditya and others. 4.
—0— The Topic Concerning Sitting. 4.1.5.
476. "Because it arises [only] when seated" (Sūtra 4.1.7).

It has been stated that the knowledge enjoined by the Vedānta scriptures as the means to liberation—expressed by such terms as "knowledge," "meditation" (*dhyāna*), and "worship" (*upāsanā*)—is of the nature of continuous recollection (*smṛti*) that occurs through repeated practice.
While performing that, one should practice it without restriction— whether sitting, lying down, standing, or walking— since there is no distinction between these states.

This being the case, it is replied: "Seated. One should perform meditation while seated. Why? Because of its possibility. For it is only for one who is seated that the possibility of one-pointedness of mind exists; because standing and walking require effort, and because sleep might occur when lying down. To avoid the effort required for supporting the lower half of the body, one should perform it while seated with support. (Sūtra 7)

"Regarding 'mokṣa' and so forth: since the two preceding sections were incidental, the connection is stated with the meditation on Brahman, which is the primary subject at hand. Alternatively, although meditations involving visualization (*dṛṣṭy-upāsanā*) may require a posture (*āsana*), the connection is stated here because one-pointedness (*aikāgrya*), the reason for establishing the posture, was established in the first section. Should one contemplate while sitting? Or rather, while sitting, lying down, standing, or walking?"
Is meditation possible during activities such as walking, or not? If it is possible, there is no restriction regarding posture; if it is not possible, then there is such a restriction.

[The phrase] "because of possibility" means because of the possibility of meditation (*upāsana*), and by extension, because of the possibility of one-pointedness (*ekāgratā*), this is appropriate. Even when it is said "because of the possibility of meditation," since the doubt as to how that might be must be resolved with reference to one-pointedness, [the reason is established]. ||7||
477. And because of meditation [it must be so].

(Siddhānta) Since meditation (*dhyāna*) constitutes the nature of worship (*upāsana*), as indicated by the scriptural injunction "he is to be meditated upon" (*nididhyāsitavyaḥ*), one-pointedness of mind is necessarily required. For meditation has been defined as the contemplation of a single object uninterrupted by other heterogeneous cognitions. || 8 ||
Thus, like the earth, mountains, and so forth, the immobility of the practitioner through one-pointedness of mind would be possible only while sitting. || 9 ||
479. And they record [it]: "And they record that meditation belongs to one who is indeed seated":
"Having established a firm seat for oneself in a clean place... (YS 2.46).

"Neither too high nor too low, covered with cloth, a deerskin, and kusha grass— one should sit upon that seat, making the mind one-pointed, with the activities of the mind and senses restrained, and practice yoga for the purification of the self. (10)

480. "Where there is one-pointedness, [there it occurs], because there is no distinction" (Sūtra 4.1.11). What is intended is similarity in its own nature alone. Immobility arises from one-pointedness. And that belongs only to one who is seated; for in walking and so forth, movement is possible due to heterogeneous mental impressions (pratyaya). This is the meaning. (9)

"And they remember" means that its establishment is not only through the force of the context, but also from a direct scriptural statement. Regarding the phrase "where there is one-pointedness": the meaning is that there is no restriction regarding lunar days, constellations, and so forth. In that regard, one-pointedness is indeed enjoined for meditation by the Smṛti as well: "Having made the mind one-pointed therein, with the activities of the mind and senses restrained."

"Wherever one-pointedness (ekāgrya) occurs, that indeed is declared here to be *upāsana* (meditative worship). Specifically from the scriptural statement, 'favorable to the mind,' [it follows that] since no specific place or time other than one-pointedness is heard of, whatever place and time are favorable to one-pointedness,
those alone are the place and time for *upāsana*."

The statement, "level, clean, free from pebbles, fire, and sand," describes a solitary place for one-pointedness; it does not restrict the location [to a specific type], because of the supplementary phrase, "conducive to the mind. || 11 ||
Thus ends the section concerning one who is seated. 5.
— Śrībhāṣya 4.1.6 —
The Section Concerning Until Departure (Āprayāṇādhikaraṇa) || 4-1-6 ||

481. "Because it is seen even there, until the departure" (Sūtra 4.1.12). Regarding this doubt—whether this meditation, which has been described as the means to liberation, is to be accomplished in a single day alone, or whether it is to be continued every day until death—the conclusion is that it should be completed by that much alone, since the purpose of the scripture is fulfilled in a single day.

This being the position, it is replied: "Until death" (Āprayāṇāt). It must be continued until the moment of death. Why? Because it is seen even there; for it is observed that throughout the entire period from the commencement of the effort at meditation until death, meditation is to be practiced, as stated: "Practicing himself in this manner, he reaches the world of Brahman for the duration of his life. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.7) || 12 ||
Thus concludes the section concerning [the meditation] up to the time of departure. 6.
1. The Section on the Realization of That [Brahman]. 4.1.7.
*Tadadhigame uttarapūrvāghayor aśleṣavināśau tadvyapadeśāt* || 4.1.13 || (Siddhānta) "He alone knows the path; having known Him, one is not smeared by evil action. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.3)
Thus ends the connection with the subsequent [passage].

"Just as a tuft of reed-wool thrown into a fire is utterly consumed, even so are his evils burnt away; and his actions perish when He, who is both the high and the low, is seen"—this refers to the destruction of prior karma.

Is it possible that these two—non-clinging (*aśleṣa*) and destruction (*vināśa*)—are effects produced by knowledge? Or not? Such is the doubt. What is the correct position? That they are not possible. Why?

Because it would contradict scriptural injunctions such as: "Karma that has not been experienced does not perish even in hundreds of millions of aeons. However, the designation of non-clinging and destruction is possible as a mere eulogy of knowledge, occurring within the context of the passages enjoining the knowledge that serves as the means to liberation.

Nor is knowledge enjoined as an expiation for prior and subsequent sins, such that by means of that expiation one would be called "one whose sins have been destroyed. For knowledge [is taught thus]: "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme."

"By knowing Brahman, one becomes Brahman itself"—thus [the knowledge of Brahman] is enjoined as the means for attaining Brahman. Therefore, this mention of the destruction of evil and its non-clinging is merely an explanatory praise (arthavāda) of that knowledge.

This being the case, it is replied: "Upon the attainment of that"—that is, upon the acquisition of knowledge by the person—due to the majesty of knowledge (*vidyā-māhātmya*), the non-clinging and destruction of subsequent and prior sins are established. Why? Because such is the majesty of a person's knowledge understood from scripture: "In one who knows thus, evil action does not cling."
Because of such scriptural declarations as, "In this way, all his evils are burnt away."

And there is no contradiction with the scriptural text stating, "Karma that has not been experienced does not perish," because their subject matters are different. That [text] concerns the firmness of the capacity of karmas to produce results; this [text], however, concerns the power to destroy the capacity of sins committed prior to the arising of knowledge to produce results, and whether or not they will arise. Furthermore, even in the absence of experiencing the results, the destruction of karmas through expiation (prāyaścitta) is observed.
Karma is not exhausted without being experienced—Atha. Da. SB IV-40.

And since it establishes both the capacity to produce the fruit of cognitions and the capacity to obstruct the production of that capacity, the objects of these two [cognitions] are distinct. Just as fire and water possess the capacities for heat and its removal respectively, and thus both are valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) due to the difference in their objects, so it is here as well; therefore, there is no contradiction whatsoever.

The non-clinging of sin (*aghasyā’śleṣakaraṇam*) means the prevention of the production of the capacity that causes unfitness for Vedic rites, latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and transgression (*pratyavāya*). For sins, once committed, produce in a person unfitness for Vedic rites, a tendency toward the commencement of other similar actions, and transgression. The destruction of sin (*aghasya vināśakaraṇam*) means the destruction of that produced capacity. Furthermore, this capacity is nothing other than displeasure toward the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*).

Thus, knowledge—being itself supremely dear because the object of knowledge is exceedingly dear to the knower—and having as its very nature the propitiation of the Supreme Person who is the object of knowledge, destroys the displeasure of the Supreme Person produced by the accumulation of previously committed sins. That same knowledge also prevents the arising of displeasure toward the Supreme Person caused by poverty occurring at any time subsequent to its own origination.
This statement regarding non-attachment should be understood as referring to cases of negligence;

for, through scriptural injunctions such as "not one who has not desisted from evil conduct," it is understood that knowledge—which arises day by day until death and partakes in an ever-increasing excellence—is to be accomplished by the cessation of evil conduct. || 13 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the attainment of that [state]. || 7 ||
The Section on the Other [Deity]. 4.1.8.

483. *Itarasyāpyevamasaṃśleṣaḥ pāte tu* || 4-1-14 || (Siddhānta) It has been stated that for both future and past sins, there is non-clinging (*asaṃśleṣa*) and destruction (*vināśa*) through knowledge (*vidyā*). By the same reasoning, for the "other"—that is, merit (*puṇya*) as well—there would likewise be non-clinging and destruction through knowledge, because of the commonality of being opposed to the fruit of knowledge. [Merit also is denoted by the word "sin" (*pāpa*); for there is indeed such a designation, as both good and evil deeds are pointed out together in the passage: "All evils (*pāpmānaḥ*) turn back from him."]
Thus [it is said];
and also: "He shakes off both good and evil deeds. Because even good deeds have undesirable results for one seeking liberation, they are designated by the word "evil" (pāpman).

Because even "well-performed action" (sukṛta) is scriptural, and because its fruit is seen to be desired by some, this extension [of the previous argument] is made to dispel the doubt that it might not be in conflict with knowledge (vidyā).

Now, an objection is raised: even for the knower, fruits such as rain and food are indeed desired for the sake of completing the meditation along with its constituent rites (*itikartavyatā*). How then can their destruction be asserted on the grounds of contradiction? To this, he says: "But at the fall [of the body]. At the fall of the body, however, there is the destruction of those [fruits]. The meaning is that after the fall of the body, the well-performed deeds (*sukṛta*) which yield visible fruits in accordance with knowledge perish. || 14 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the other [the subordinate]. || 8 ||
The Section Concerning Those Whose Karma Has Not Yet Begun to Bear Fruit (Anārabdhakāryādhikaraṇa). 4.1.9.
"But only those whose effects have not yet begun [are destroyed], because that is the limit" (4.1.15).
(Siddhānta) 484. Regarding the good and evil deeds existing prior to the arising of the knowledge of Brahman, their non-clinging and destruction have been stated.
Then, regarding the doubt as to whether there is a destruction of all previously existing good and evil deeds without distinction, or only of those whose effects have not yet begun—
given that "all evils are consumed" and that the persistence of the body occurs subsequent to the arising of knowledge; [the answer follows].
Thus, because the scripture declares that there is "no difference" in the fruit of knowledge,

it is logically consistent— even on account of residual impressions (*saṃskāra*), as in the case of the continued spinning of a potter's wheel— that [the state of liberation] occurs without distinction.

This being the position, it is said: "But only those previous [deeds] whose effects have not yet begun. The good and evil deeds prior to the arising of knowledge perish through that knowledge only if they are *anārabdhakārye*—that is, if their results have not yet commenced.
Why? Because of that limit:
"For him, there is delay only so long as he is not released; then he shall be merged [in the Absolute]. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.14.2).
For it is heard that the limit for the falling of the body is [the time] until then.
The section concerning the Agnihotra and other rites. 4.1.10.

"But the Agnihotra and so forth are for that very purpose [of the knowledge], because it is seen [in scripture]. (Sūtra 4.1.16, Siddhānta) By the statement, "In the same way, there is no connection for the other as well," it was stated that by the power of knowledge (*vidyā*), even good deeds (*sukṛta*) are not connected [to the self]. Now, since the Agnihotra and other obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites—which are the duties of one's own stage of life (*āśrama-dharma*)—are also common instances of "good deeds," their fruits would likewise not be connected; thus, the contingency arises that one might fail to perform them without desiring to do so. [The sūtra addresses this.]

It is said: "But the Agnihotra and so forth. The word "but" (*tu*) is for the purpose of distinguishing these from other good deeds. The duties of the stages of life (*āśramadharma*), such as the Agnihotra, must indeed be performed because it is impossible for their fruits to adhere [to the knower]. And that impossibility exists because those [duties] exist for the sake of their result; for the performance of the Agnihotra and so forth by the knower is solely for the sake of the result known as knowledge (*vidyā*). How is this understood? From scriptural observation (*darśana*); for it is observed: "Brahmins seek to know this very [Self] through the study of the Vedas, through sacrifice, through giving, through austerity, and through fasting."
By such statements as these, the status of the Agnihotra and other rites as means to knowledge is established.

Furthermore, since knowledge—which is to be perfected through practice until death—must be produced day after day, the duties of the stages of life (*āśramakarma*) must also be performed daily for the sake of its production. Otherwise, if the duties of the stages of life are neglected, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) would become defiled, and the arising of knowledge itself would not occur. || 16 ||

If good deeds such as the Agnihotra and other rites are for the purpose of producing knowledge, and if the merit prior to the arising of knowledge is [exhausted] by the phrase "having dwelt [in the world of the fathers] as long as the residue of their works lasts" (yāvatsampātam uṣitvā),...

"Having reached the end of his karma"—this [refers to what] has been destroyed by experience; and "the remainder of what was done" refers to that which has begun to bear fruit. "Friends [take over] his good deeds" (Śāṭyāyanaka).
What is the scope of this [statement]? To that he says:

486. *ato 'nyāpi hy eṣām ubhayoḥ* || 4.1.17 || (siddhānta) "From this"—that is, from the meritorious deeds (*sādhukṛtyā*) such as the Agnihotra and so forth, which serve for the arising of knowledge—there exists indeed another [kind of] meritorious deed, distinct from those, whose fruit is obstructed by a more powerful karma, belonging to both the prior and subsequent [periods] relative to the attainment of knowledge; such endless [deeds] are certainly possible. This statement of certain followers of a Vedic school refers to that [other kind of merit].

"His sons inherit his estate, and his friends his good deeds" (Śāṭyāyanaka). And the scriptural texts concerning the non-clinging and destruction [of karma] through knowledge refer to that same subject. || 17 ||

He recalls the previously mentioned possibility of an obstruction to the fruit of even a performed action: "For it is said: 'Whatever one performs with knowledge... that alone is more powerful'" (4.1.18). By this statement—that the Udgītha-knowledge has as its fruit the non-obstruction of the ritual result—it is indeed indicated that there can be an obstruction to the fruit of even a performed action. Therefore, for the knower, the [passage concerning] "the good deeds of friends" refers to actions whose fruits have been obstructed despite being performed.
Thus says the Śākhyāyana school. 18.
Thus ends the section concerning the Agnihotra and other rites. 10.
The Section on the Destruction of Other [Obstacles] (Itarakṣapaṇādhikaraṇa) || 4.1.11 ||

488. "But having exhausted the others by experience, he then attains [Brahman]. (Sūtra 4.1.19). Regarding the merit and demerit whose non-clinging and destruction were previously mentioned, there arises a doubt: are the other two—the merit and demerit that have already begun to bear fruit—exhausted at the end of the body born of knowledge (*vidyā*), or at the end of that specific body, or at the end of some other body? There being this uncertainty, the conclusion is that they are exhausted at the end of that [very] body, because of the scriptural statement: "For him there is delay only so long as he is not released; then he shall be united" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.14.2), which indicates that the exhaustion occurs upon the release from that body.

This being the position, it is replied: "But by experience" (*bhogena tu*). The word "but" (*tu*) serves to set aside the previous view. As for the others—the merit and demerit whose effects have already begun (*ārabdhakārya*)—one attains Brahman after exhausting them through the experience of their own commenced fruits, immediately following the completion of that experience of those fruits. And as for those merits and demerits, if their fruits are to be experienced in a single body, one attains [Brahman] at the end of that body; if their fruits are to be experienced in multiple bodies, one attains [Brahman] at the end of those. This is because the two types of karma whose fruits have begun must be exhausted precisely through experience.

And as for the statement, "For him there is delay only so long as he is not released," it is said that the release from those two types of karma occurs through experience; for there is no scriptural injunction limiting [the duration] to the end of the body.

Thus, in this manner, the merit and demerit in the form of actions whose fruits have not yet been experienced and whose fruits have not yet begun—which were performed prior to the knowledge of Brahman, accumulated since beginningless time, and are infinite—is destroyed by the majesty of that knowledge. Furthermore, that which is performed after the commencement of knowledge does not adhere to the soul. In that regard, all merit is taken up by the friends of the knower, and the demerit is taken up by those who hate him; thus, there is no fault. 19.
Thus ends the section on the destruction of other [defilements]. 11.
Thus ends the first section, "The Section on Repetition," of the fourth chapter, "The Chapter on the Fruit," in the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Bhagavad Rāmānuja.
To whom?
Śrī!
In the fourth chapter on the fruits [of knowledge], the second section, the Section on Departure (Utkrāntipāda), 1. The Topic of Speech (Vāg-adhikaraṇa):
Regarding the statement "Speech is merged in the mind," this merging of speech in the mind refers to the very nature of speech itself, and not to the function of speech.
8. The Section on the Abode (tadoko’dhikaraṇa):

The departure of the knower through the cranial aperture, as described in the passage beginning with “And a hundred and one,” is easily accomplished through the grace of the compassionate Supreme Self.
Śrīḥ!
Salutation to the illustrious Rāmānuja. Salutation to Śrī. Salutation to Śrīdhara.
In the *Śrī Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya* composed by the venerable Bhagavad Rāmānuja,
this is the second section, "Departure," in the fourth chapter, "Fruit."
Sūtras 20: The Topic of Speech (vāg-adhikaraṇam) || 4.2.1 ||

489. *vāṅmanasi darśanācchabdācca* || 4.2.1 || (siddhānta) Now he begins to consider the manner of departure for the knower. First, the process of departure (*utkrānti*) is considered. In this regard, it is declared in scripture:
"O dear one, when this person departs, speech merges into the mind; the mind into breath; the breath into fire; and the fire into the supreme deity."
Thus [it is said].

Here, regarding the scriptural statement "Speech is merged in the mind" (*vāṅ manasi saṃpadyate*), there arises a doubt: does this scriptural teaching of the merging of speech in the mind refer merely to the function of speech, or to speech itself? Thus [ends the section]. Regarding the scriptural statement "Speech is merged in the mind," there is a point of doubt: does it concern only the function of speech, or speech itself?
It is logical that [the text] refers only to the functions (*vṛtti*);

why? Because the mind does not have speech as its material cause (*prakṛti*), and therefore the perfection of the nature of speech is impossible therein. When this [objection] has been reached, it is replied: "Speech [merges] into the mind. It is the very nature of speech that merges into the mind. Why? Because of observation. For it is observed that even when the organ of speech has ceased its activity, the mind continues to function. If it is argued that this is possible even through the merging of the mere *vṛtti* (function), to that he says: "And because of the scriptural statement. The statement, "Speech merges into the mind," refers specifically to the merging of the nature of speech itself, not merely to the merging of its function.

Regarding the term "attainment" (*sampatti*): is it of the nature of dissolution (*laya*), or is it of the nature of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) preceded by the cessation of activity? Does the mention of the "attainment of another sense-organ" hold true even if it refers to dissolution, or only if it refers to conjunction? When it holds true even if it refers to dissolution, then, because attainment would be of the nature of dissolution, it would be impossible to accept the primary meaning of the word "speech" (*vāk*); thus, "attainment" would have to refer to the functioning [of the senses].

Since the justification lies precisely in the sense of conjunction, and since conjunction constitutes the nature of "attainment" (sampatti), the word "speech" (vāk) retains its primary meaning; thus, attainment would have as its object the essential form [of speech].

"From what [reason]? and so forth. For dissolution occurs into the cause; however, the mind is not the cause of speech, since the mind is the cause only for the activity (*pravṛtti*) of that [speech]. Thus, the meaning is that there is no attainment of the object of the function [of speech]. For speech is the substratum of the function of speech, not the mind. Therefore, the phrase "in some way" is used with the intention of pointing out the lack of natural consistency in the claim that there is a dissolution of the mind into the function whose nature is being the cause of the emergence [of speech].
For at that time, when the function has ceased, the organ of speech is not perceived by any other means of knowledge such that one could say it "merges" (*sampadyate*) as mere activity.

As for what was said—that because the mind does not have speech as its material cause (*prakṛti*), the merging of speech into the mind is not tenable—that must be refuted on the grounds that, according to the statement "speech merges into the mind," speech is merely joined with the mind; it does not dissolve (*līyate*) therein. || 1 ||

495. "And because the departure and the undertaking of the journey are common [to both], and immortality is attained without having burned [the body].

(Sūtra 4.2.7, Siddhānta) In considering whether this departure is common to both the knower and the non-knower, or belongs to the non-knower alone, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it belongs to the non-knower alone.
Why? Because immortality is declared for the knower right here, and because there is no departure [of the soul] for the knower. Indeed, immortality is heard of for the knower right here:

this being the position reached, it is replied—"And [the departure] is the same up to the beginning of the path. "There are a hundred and one channels of the heart; of these, one extends to the crown of the head. Thus, because of the identity of purpose with this scriptural passage, "A hundred and one [channels] of the heart," the departure through the crown of the head pertains to the knower, while the other pertains to the non-knower.

As for what was said—that immortality is declared for the wise person right here—it is replied: "And immortality without having burned [the body]. The word "and" (*ca*) is used in the sense of emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*). "Without having burned" (*anupoṣya*) means without having burnt away the connection with the body, senses, and so forth; that immortality which is attained in the form of the non-clinging and destruction of subsequent and prior sins is what is referred to by the scripture beginning with, "When all are liberated," etc. And as for the statement, "He attains Brahman right here," the intention is that this refers to the experience of Brahman that occurs at the time of meditation. || 7 ||

500. "If it be said [there is no departure] because of a prohibition, we say no; [the prohibition refers] not to the embodied soul, for it is explicit in the case of some.

"By that light this self departs; as it departs, the vital breath (prāṇa) follows after it"—having thus described the manner of departure for the ignorant person, [the text continues]: "It fashions another, newer, more beautiful form" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.4).
Thus, having described the assumption of another body,

[the text] concludes the section concerning the ignorant person with the passage: "Whatever he does here, at the end of his life, from that world he returns again to this world for the sake of action" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.6), provided he is one who desires.

Now, [the text] "But for one who does not desire—[he] who is without desire, free from desire, whose desire is attained, whose desire is the Self—for him the vital breaths do not depart; being Brahman, he merges into Brahman"—thus the departure of the knower is prohibited. Likewise, in the earlier question of Ārtabhāga as well, the prohibition of the knower's departure is seen:
Having introduced the knower with the words, "He indeed overcomes repeated death," [the text continues]:
"O Yājñavalkya," he said, "when this person dies, do his vital breaths (prāṇas) depart from him, or do they not?"
Thus questioned, Yājñavalkya said, "No; right here they dissolve. It swells up and becomes bloated; bloated, it lies dead.
If it be argued that, therefore, the knower attains immortality even here in this world—
That is not so; for here what is denied is the departure of the vital breaths from the embodied self, the inner Self (pratyagātman), and not from the body.
In the passage, "His vital breaths do not depart," the word "his" (tasya) refers to the embodied self alone, which is the subject under discussion in the phrase, "Now, he who is without desire."
It is that which is being referred to; it is not the unmentioned body.

The genitive case in the word *tasya* ("of him") indicates that the embodied self (*śārīra*) is mentioned as being related to the vital breaths (*prāṇas*), but not as the point of departure for their exit. If it is argued that the body itself is the point of departure for the exit, we say no; for when there is a requirement for a point of departure, since the self—mentioned as being related [to the breaths]—is more proximate than the body which is not explicitly mentioned, the self alone must be understood as the point of departure.

Furthermore, since the vital breaths (prāṇas) are already known as being related to the individual soul (jīva), there is no purpose in stating that relationship again; therefore, it is determined that the genitive case, which expresses mere relation, specifically denotes the "ablative" (apādāna) sense—as in the expression, "he hears from the actor" (naṭasya śṛṇoti).
And there should be no dispute on this point; for it is clear from the recension of some—the Mādhyandinas—that the embodied soul itself is the point of departure, as stated:
"He who is without desire, free from desire, whose desire is fulfilled, whose desire is the Self—from him the vital breaths do not depart."
If it is argued that the denial of departure is not tenable because there is no possibility of the vital breaths departing from the embodied soul, we say:
no;
for [the scripture says], "For him, the delay is only so long."

Thus, by the statement regarding the wise person's attainment of Brahman at the time of separation from the body, it would follow that even the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) of the wise person must separate from the body at that time. Consequently, attainment of Brahman via the path of the gods (*devayāna*) would not be possible.
To this [the text] replies: "His vital breaths do not depart"; that is, prior to reaching Brahman via the path of the gods, the vital breaths do not become disjoined even from the living wise person.

505. "Following the rays" (sūtra 4.2.17). For the knower who has departed from the heart through the hundred-and-first artery at the crown of the head, it is heard in scripture that he proceeds to the solar orb by following the rays of the sun: "Now, when he departs from this body, he ascends upwards by these very rays."
Thus [it is said].
In this regard, when the question arises as to whether this restriction regarding the path—namely, "only by following the rays"—is possible or not, the established view is reached:
it is said, "following the rays. The knower goes upward only by following the rays. Why? Because [the scripture says]: "Then, by these very rays..."

Because of this restrictive emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*). For if [the departure] were merely occasional, the particle *eva* would be purposeless. As for what was said—that because rays are impossible at night, departing by following the rays is not tenable—that is not so; for even at night, following the sun's rays is possible. Indeed, it is observed that even at night during the summer season, the existence of rays is established through the perception of heat. However, in the winter and similar seasons, heat is not perceived due to the overpowering of frost, or on cloudy days. Moreover, scripture declares the constant mutual connection between the channels (*nāḍī*) and the rays.

"Just as a great highway, being extended, goes to both villages—this one and that one—even so these rays of the sun go to both worlds—this one and that one. They extend from yonder sun and enter into these channels; they extend from these channels and enter into yonder sun. Thus ends the section concerning the following of the rays (Raśmyanusārādhikaraṇa).

— 0 — 506. [Objection: "Not at night. [Reply: No, because the connection [to the path] exists as long as the body lasts; and the scripture also shows this. 4.2.18. (Siddhānta) This is now being considered: Is there attainment of Brahman for the knower who dies at night, or not?

Although movement by following the rays is possible at night because the sun's rays exist during the night, nevertheless, since dying at night is censured in the scriptures, the attainment of Brahman—which is characterized as the supreme human goal—is not possible for one who dies at night. In the scriptures, dying during the day is praised, whereas dying at night is the opposite; "Dying during the day, in the bright fortnight, and during the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa) are praised for those wishing to die, while the opposite is censured."

Thus [it is said]. Regarding the fact that dying by day and dying at night are respectively commendable and contrary [to that], the *Śrībhāṣya* (4.2.10) states that they are the causes for attaining the highest and lowest destinies.
Therefore, "dying at night" is not a cause for attaining Brahman, because it is a cause for an inferior destiny.
If it be argued that [the two] may exist [simultaneously], we say:
"That is not so," because for the knower, the connection with karma persists as long as the body exists.

This is what is meant: because actions whose effects have not yet begun—which serve as causes for rebirth in lower states—are destroyed precisely through their connection with knowledge (*vidyā*), and because future actions do not adhere [to the knower], and because the body that has already begun its effect lasts only until the final physical death, there is an absence of any cause for bondage; thus, the attainment of Brahman by the knower is established even if they die at night. 509. *Arcirādinā tatprathiteḥ* || 4.3.1 || (Siddhānta) The commencement of the journey for the knower who has departed, by means of a specific channel due to the grace of the one within the heart, has been described. Now, the path of that departing soul is being determined.

In that regard, various modes of the path are recorded "in many ways" in the Śrutis. In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, for instance, after beginning with, "Just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, even so evil action does not cling to one who knows thus," and having taught the knowledge of Brahman, it is further recorded:

Now, whether they perform the funeral rites for him here or not, they depart from this world by means of the light (*arcis*). From the light, they go to the day; from the day, to the waxing half of the month; from the waxing half of the month, to those months during which the sun moves northward; from the months, to the year; from the year, to the sun; from the sun, to the moon; from the moon, to the lightning. There, a person who is not human (*amānava*) dwells. He leads them to Brahman. This is the path of the gods, the path of Brahman. Those who proceed by this path do not return to this human whirlpool. Thus it is stated in that very [Upaniṣad], in the eighth [chapter].
"Now, by these very rays, he ascends upwards.
And the Kauṣītakins describe the path of the gods differently:

"Having entered this path of the gods, he comes to the world of Agni; he [comes] to the world of Vāyu, he to the world of Varuṇa, he to the world of Āditya, he to the world of Indra, he to the world of Prajāpati, and he to the world of Brahman."

Thus it is said. Likewise, in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*: "Those who know this thus, and those who, in the forest, worship truth with faith—they pass into the light; from the light into the day; from the day into the waxing fortnight; from the waxing fortnight into the six months when the sun moves northward; from those months into the world of the gods; from the world of the gods into the sun; from the sun into lightning. A person consisting of mind comes from the lightning and leads them to the worlds of Brahman. In that very same context, however, it is stated otherwise:

"When a person departs from this world, he goes to Vāyu. There, Vāyu makes way for him, as the hole of a chariot wheel does. By that, he ascends upward. He goes to Āditya. There, Āditya makes way for him, as the hole of a drum does. By that, he ascends upward. He goes to Candramas. There, Candramas makes way for him, as the hole of a kettle-drum does," and so forth.

In this regard, there is a doubt: Is it that the single path beginning with light (*arcirādi*) is taught by all these scriptural passages, such that the knower goes to Brahman by that very path alone? Or are there other paths elsewhere, such that there is no fixed rule as to whether one goes by those or by this one? [What is the prima facie view? The prima facie view is as follows: Since the texts mention different sequences of stations—some omitting certain elements while including others—and since they do not state that one must traverse all of them, it appears that each passage teaches a distinct path. Furthermore, because the texts speak of "going" (*gacchati*) and "reaching" (*prāpnoti*), which imply a transition from one place to another, and because the stations are mentioned in the locative case, it follows that these are different paths. Moreover, the mention of various means of conveyance, such as "lightning-bolts" (*vidyutaḥ stanayitnavaś ca*), suggests a plurality of paths. Therefore, the conclusion is that there is no fixed rule; rather, there are multiple paths, and the knower may proceed by whichever one he chooses. This is the prima facie position.

What is correct? Why is there no fixed rule? Because of the manifold nature [of the paths] and because of independence—this being the position reached, it is replied: "By the path beginning with light" (*arcirādinā*). The single path beginning with light is taught everywhere; therefore, one goes by means of that very path beginning with light.

Why? Because of its manifestation; that is, because it alone is manifested everywhere. "Manifestation" means well-knownness (*prasiddhi*). The meaning is: because of the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of that very same [entity] everywhere.

Because of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), that very same path is taught everywhere, though with variations of deficiency or excess; just as there is a combination of knowledge and qualities (*vidyā-guṇopasaṃhāra*), what is stated in one place is combined with what is stated elsewhere. In the *Chāndogya*, for instance, it is recorded in an identical form both in the Upakośala-vidyā and the Pañcāgni-vidyā. And in the *Vājasaneyaka*, in the Pañcāgni-vidyā, the path beginning with light (*arcirādi*) is recorded in exactly the same way, with only slight differences. Therefore, it is understood that it is the very same [path] even there. Furthermore, in all other instances as well, fire, the sun, and so forth are recognized. 1.1.26. *Pratyabhijñānāt* (Because of recognition).
Thus ends the section concerning "not long" (*acirāt*), the first.
— 0— [Śrībhāṣya 4.3.2] The Section on Air (Vāyvadhikaraṇa) || 4.3.2 ||

510. *Vāyum abdād aviśeṣa-viśeṣābhyām* || 4.3.2 || (Siddhānta) Although the scriptural sequence denoted by the fifth [case-ending] is equal for both the year and the world of the gods mentioned in the two [passages], [the soul goes] from the light to the day, from the day to the waxing fortnight, from the waxing fortnight to those months during which the sun moves northward.

Thus, since it is observed that longer durations are positioned successively after shorter ones, and because the year alone naturally occurs to the mind immediately after the month, it is determined that the year itself must be placed after the month; and after that, the world of the gods (*devaloka*). Elsewhere, the Vājasaneyins state: "When a person departs from this world, he goes to Vāyu; for him, Vāyu makes way there, as [the hub] of a chariot wheel, and by that he ascends upwards and reaches the Sun."
Thus, the Kauṣītakins study Vāyu before Āditya:
"Having entered upon this path of the gods, he comes to the world of Agni; he comes to the world of Vāyu.

Thus, they study Vāyu as being after the *arciḥ* (flame) designated by the term "world of Agni. In that regard, according to the order of recitation of the Kauṣītakins, Vāyu—which is obtained as being after the *arciḥ*—[is placed] for the Vājasaneyins...

By the statement, "Thereby he ascends upwards; he reaches the sun," the word "upwards" (ūrdhva), as indicated by the Vedic sequence which is stronger than the order of the text, establishes that his entry occurs prior to the sun. Therefore, before reaching the sun, he attains the year and, alternatively, the world of the gods and Vāyu.

Does he go to Vāyu? Or, being non-different [from the preceding], does he go to Vāyu, who is already present in the world of the gods after a year? What is reasonable? That they have different meanings, because that is well-known. And since they have different meanings, both [Vāyu and the world of the gods] are established by the sequence of the text as being in the interval between the year and the sun, due to the use of the word "above" (ūrdhva) and the ablative case; and since there is no specific distinction [between them], one may choose as desired. This being the position, it is said: "Vāyu [is reached] after the year. He goes to Vāyu above the year.

Why? Because it is specifically the wind (*vāyu*) that is indicated by both the general and the specific. For the word "world of the gods" (*devaloka*) denotes the wind in a general or universal sense as "the world of the gods.

The word "wind" (*vāyu*), in the passages "he goes to the wind" and "to him there," denotes the wind specifically. Therefore, since the wind alone is denoted by the words "world of the gods" and "wind" through the general and the specific, one should go to the wind itself after the year.

Furthermore, the term ‘vāyuloka’ in the Kauṣītakins, like the term ‘agniloka’, denotes vāyu itself through the etymological derivation ‘vāyuścā’sau lokaśca’ (it is both vāyu and a world). And it is heard elsewhere that vāyu is the dwelling place of the gods: “He who blows here—he indeed is the ‘houses’ of the gods. || 2 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the air (vāyvadhikaraṇa). || 2 ||
511. Varuṇa is higher than lightning, because of their connection. (Siddhānta) In the Kauṣītaki [Upaniṣad]:

"Having reached this path of the gods, he comes to the world of Agni; he comes to the world of Vāyu; he comes to the world of Varuṇa; he comes to the world of Āditya; he comes to the world of Indra; he comes to the world of Prajāpati; he comes to the world of Brahman. In this passage, the primacy of the word "world of Agni" as a synonym for "flame" (*arcis*) is undisputed. Furthermore, the placement of Vāyu after the year has already been stated. As for Āditya, here [his position] must override the order established by the sequence of the text.

According to the sequence of the Vājasaneyaka text, "from the world of the gods to the sun; from the sun to lightning," it is established that [the soul] is situated above the wind, which is designated by the term "world of the gods. Now, consideration must be made regarding Varuṇa, Indra, and the others.
In this matter of doubt: are these Varuṇa and the others to be placed within Vāyu according to the order of the text, or rather above Vidyut?
In all cases beginning with "light" (arcis), because of the non-obstruction of the sequence of the Śruti text starting with "from light to the sun" (arciṣo'haḥ), and after lightning, [the text says]:
"His person, who is not human; he leads them to Brahman."

Furthermore, because the scripture declares that the person of lightning (*vidyut-puruṣa*) leads one to Brahman, and because there is no room for him anywhere else as he would otherwise remain unplaced, it is necessary to sublate someone in order to avoid rendering the instruction purposeless. Consequently, in accordance with the order of the text, Varuṇa must be inserted immediately after Vāyu. Since the sequence between Vāyu and Āditya is thus sublated, Indra and Prajāpati must also be inserted in this very same place.

This being the position, it is replied: "Varuṇa is above lightning" (Taṭito'dhi Varuṇaḥ). He is to be placed higher [than lightning]. Why is Varuṇa placed above lightning? Because of their connection; for lightning resides within the interior of clouds, and the connection between lightning and Varuṇa is well-known in both common worldly experience and the Vedas.

This is what is meant: since Varuṇa and the others must be placed somewhere so that their instruction is not rendered meaningless, and given that the order of meaning (arthakrama) is stronger than the order of the text (pāṭhakrama), Varuṇa must be placed after lightning. From this, it is understood that the role of the non-human conductor is capable of tolerating an interval [in the sequence].

And because that [position] is capable of accommodating an interval, and because Indra—who has been taught [in the text] and must necessarily be inserted—is taught after Varuṇa, and because adventitious elements are to be inserted at the end, Indra and the others must be inserted after Varuṇa. Thus [is the conclusion]. || 3 ||
Thus concludes the section concerning Varuṇa. 3.
The Section on the Conveying Body (Ātivāhika) || 4.3.4 ||
512. "They are conducting [souls], because of the indicative mark.

(Siddhānta) Alternatively, these may be places of enjoyment; for it is untenable that well-known divisions of time such as days and so forth should serve as landmarks on a path, since there is no mention of anything else serving as a landmark for them. Furthermore, their status as places of enjoyment is established by the statement that days and so forth are "worlds": "These indeed are the worlds: namely, the days and nights, the half-months, the months, the seasons, and the years. For this very reason, the Kauṣītakins state: "He goes to the world of Agni."
By such statements, they recite the *arcis* and others in conformity with worldly terminology—thus [it is said].

This being the case, we reply: "They are the conductors. These [beings], beginning with Light (arcis) and so forth, are specific deities designated as "conductors" (ātivāhika), appointed by the Supreme Person for the purpose of conducting the knower.

Why? Because of the indicative mark (liṅga) of that—namely, the indicative mark of conducting. For "conducting" (ativahana) means causing those who go to reach their destination. And "causing to reach" is—

The concluding statement, "That person who is not human leads them to Brahman," indicates that he alone is the one connected with all the preceding stages as well, since they are heard without distinction. Furthermore, words such as "light" (arcis) and so on denote specific presiding deities who have light and the rest as their own bodies, just as in the passage, "The earth spoke to him.
(Sūtra 4)
If this is so, then since the scripture states,

"That person who is not human leads them to Brahman," and thus only the person belonging to lightning is heard to be the one who leads to Brahman, how can Varuṇa and the others who are beyond the lightning be connected as conducting deities (ātivāhika)? To this, he says:
513. "From there, by means of the one belonging to lightning, because of that scriptural statement" (Sūtra 4.3.5). [Commentary:
From there—above the lightning—by means of the one belonging to lightning, namely, by the non-human *ātivāhika* (conductor) alone, there is the journey of the knowers until the attainment of Brahman.
Why?

Because of the scriptural statement to that effect—namely, "He leads them to Brahman"—which declares Him alone to be the leader. As for Varuṇa and the others, they are merely assistants; thus, their connection as conducting deities (ātivāhika) certainly exists as well. || 5 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the subtle body (the *ātivāhika*). 4.
The Section on the Effect (Kāryādhikaraṇa) || 4.3.5 ||

514. The [group] leads to the effected [Brahman], because the attainment of that state is logical. (Pūrva-pakṣa) It has been stated that the knower proceeds by way of the path beginning with light (*arcirādi*); that group starting with light and ending with the non-human (*amānava*) is the escort (*ātivāhika*) which leads the knower to Brahman.

Now, this is being considered: Does this group beginning with light lead those who meditate upon the *kārya-brahman* (the effected Brahman, Hiraṇyagarbha)? Or those who meditate upon the supreme Brahman? Or those who meditate upon the supreme Brahman, as well as those who meditate upon the inner self (*pratyagātman*) as having Brahman as its essence? Such is the doubt.
"The teacher Bādari maintains that [the scripture] leads only those who meditate upon the effected [Brahman].
Why? Because for one who meditates upon Hiraṇyagarbha—the effected Brahman alone—going [to that world] is logically possible;
for it is not [possible] for one who [meditates upon] the Perfect [Brahman].
For one who meditates upon the Supreme Brahman—which is omniscient, all-pervading, and the self of all—travel to another place for the sake of attaining it is not possible;
precisely because it has already been attained.

For the effect of the higher knowledge (paravidyā) consists solely in the cessation of ignorance regarding the Supreme Brahman, which is eternally attained. However, for one who meditates on Brahman in the form of Hiraṇyagarbha—which is limited to a specific location—the journey for the sake of attaining that which is to be reached is appropriate. Therefore, the group of conducting deities beginning with "light" (arcirādi) leads him [to that very place]. 6.
515. And because of being specified [as such] (sūtra 4.3.7). (Pūrva-pakṣa:

Because of the word "world" (*loka*) and the plural number in the passage, "The non-human person, having approached, leads the mental person to the worlds of Brahman," it is specified that the non-human person leads only one who meditates upon Hiraṇyagarbha as residing in those specific worlds. Furthermore, [it says], "I enter the assembly hall and the abode of Prajāpati."
Thus, having gone by way of the path beginning with light, he "reconnects" with the effect, namely Hiraṇyagarbha. || 7 ||

But if this were so, the designation, "That person who is non-human leads them to Brahman," would not be appropriate; for if Hiraṇyagarbha were being led, the designation ought to have been, "He leads them to Brahmā. To this, he says:
516. "But that designation [of Hiraṇyagarbha as Brahman] is due to proximity" (Sūtra 4.3.8).

[Pūrvapakṣa: Regarding the statement, "He who creates Brahmā," because Hiraṇyagarbha is the first-born, he is designated by the word "Brahman" due to his proximity to Brahman; this is determined by the reasons already stated, such as the impossibility of the path and specific qualifiers. This is the meaning. || 8 ||

Now, it might be argued: upon reaching Hiraṇyagarbha by way of the path beginning with light (arcir-ādi), [the texts state], "This is the path of the gods, the path of Brahman; those who proceed by this do not return to this human whirlpool," and, "Going upwards by that, one attains immortality."

Thus, the designation of the attainment of immortality and non-return is not tenable; for there is a scriptural teaching that Hiraṇyagarbha, being a product of action (*kārya*), undergoes destruction at the conclusion of the period of two *parārdhas*.

Furthermore, because of the statement, "All worlds up to the realm of Brahmā, O Arjuna, are subject to return," it follows that for one who has attained Hiraṇyagarbha, return is unavoidable. To this, he says: "Upon the dissolution of the effect, [he goes] together with its presiding overseer, for this reason... (Sūtra 4.3.7)
"But from here [they go] beyond, because of the mention [of it].

(Pūrva-pakṣa) Upon the passing away of the effected world— the world of Brahmā— they, having attained knowledge there, proceed from that effected world with its presiding deity, Hiraṇyagarbha, who holds office.

Having completed his task, he himself, together with the wise one, attains the Supreme Brahman from the world of Brahman; for it is stated that for one who has gone by the path beginning with light, there is the attainment of immortality and non-return. This is also understood from the scriptural statement: "But at the time of their final departure, they all, through the supreme immortality, are completely liberated in the world of Brahman. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.6) || 9 ||
518. And on account of Smṛti. (Pūrvapakṣa: From Smṛti also this meaning is understood:
"When the time of universal dissolution has arrived, all those [attainers] together with Brahmā..."

"Those who have perfected themselves enter the supreme state at the end of their journey. Therefore, it is the opinion of Bādari that the group beginning with light (arcis) leads only those who meditate upon the effected (kārya) Brahman. || 10 ||
On this point, Jaimini objects by adopting an alternative position:

519. *Paraṃ jaiminirmukhyatvāt* (4.3.11). (Pūrva-pakṣa: The teacher Jaimini maintains that it is only one who meditates upon the *paraṃ brahma* (the higher Brahman) that the path beginning with light (*arcirādi*) leads. Why? Because of its primary significance (*mukhyatvāt*).

"A superhuman person [comes] there; he leads them to Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15.5).
