Since the word "Brahman" has its primary meaning only in reference to the Supreme Brahman, it is only when the status of being an effect is established by another means of knowledge that a figurative sense would be appropriate.
(6) "At the end of the Supreme" means at the end of the lifespan of Brahmā. (10)

By "adopting another position"—that is, by means of an alternative position rather than the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), but not by the entire established conclusion (*siddhānta*)—it is known from this scriptural indicator (*smṛti*): "And from the traditional teaching (*smṛti*): 'When the time of reabsorption arrives, they lead all those who meditate upon the Creator (Dhātṛ) along with Brahmā. ||1||

"The conductors lead those who meditate on the Supreme [Brahman] to that very place, because the word *brahman* has its primary meaning there; thus says Jaimini. (2) Nor is there any logical inconsistency regarding the journey, for although the supreme Brahman is omnipresent, scripture teaches that the cessation of ignorance occurs only when the knower reaches a specific location. For just as the arising of knowledge depends upon the duties of one's caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama-dharma*), purity, conduct, place, time, and so forth?

This is understood from scriptural passages such as, "Him by the recitation of the Vedas... and so forth; likewise, that the accomplishment of knowledge—which consists in the removal of ignorance without remainder—is dependent upon reaching a specific place, is understood from the scriptures concerning the journey (gati). As for the prohibition of the departure of the soul (utkrānti) for the knower, that has already been resolved previously.

As for the argument that—on account of the qualification by both the word "world" (*loka*) and the plural number in the phrase "the worlds of Brahman" (*brahmalokān*)—there is the cognition of Hiraṇyagarbha as an effect (of Brahman)—that is incorrect; for, according to the *niṣādasthapati* maxim, the interpretation as a *karmadhāraya* compound—"Brahman itself is the world, the world of Brahman"—is more appropriate. Furthermore, once the unity of the referent is established, the use of the plural number is justified, as in the case of "Aditi [released] the bonds" (*aditiḥ pāśān*).

The worlds fashioned by the will of the Supreme Brahman—who is perfect, omnipresent, and of true resolve—being unique to Himself and non-material, do not absolutely cease to exist, according to the authority of the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, and Purāṇas. || 11 ||
520. And because of scriptural evidence. (Pūrva-pakṣa:

Scripture also demonstrates that for one who has departed through the cranial artery and traveled by the path of the gods, there is the attainment of the Supreme Brahman: "This serene being, having risen up from this body and having reached the highest light, appears in its own true form" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.3).
Thus [ends the section]. 12.
As for what was stated—

that in the passage, "I enter the hall and the abode of Prajāpati," a realization of the effect (kārya) is seen in one who has traveled by way of the path beginning with light— the answer to that is as follows:
521. "And there is no intention toward the effect" (Sūtra 4.3.13).

[Pūrvapakṣa: This intention is not directed toward the effect, Hiraṇyagarbha; rather, it is directed toward the Supreme Brahman itself. For in the remainder of the passage, it says: "I become the glory of the Brāhmaṇas."

Thus, because that aspirant intends [to attain] all states of self-existence preceded by liberation from all ignorance; and because it is heard that the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*) to be attained is "uncreated" (*akṛta*)—as in the passage: "Shaking off evil like a horse its hair, and freeing myself like the moon from the mouth of Rāhu, having shaken off the body, being perfected in soul, may I attain the uncreated world of Brahman"—and because the liberation from all bonds is directly heard [in scripture], therefore the view of Jaimini is that the group of conducting deities beginning with Light (*arcis*) leads the one who meditates upon the Supreme Brahman itself. (Sūtra 4.3.13)
Now the venerable Bādarāyaṇa states his own conclusion according to his own view:
522. "Bādarāyaṇa [holds that the path] leads those who do not rely on symbols; and because there would be a fault in both cases, it is also according to their resolve" (4.3.14).
(Siddhānta) "Bādarāyaṇa holds that the path beginning with light leads those who do not rely on symbols"—that is, those other than those who rely on symbols. It leads them... [to Brahman].

"13. Regarding the passage beginning with *apratīka* (not the symbol): For one who meditates on the Supreme Brahman is indeed distinct from those who take recourse to symbols (*pratīka*). Since there is the scriptural observation that [the guides] lead him [to Brahman], one might ask: what is the distinction between the view of Jaimini and that of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*)? [The answer is: In this position, there is both meditation on the effect (*kārya*) and the principle of "according to one's resolve" (*tatkratu*), as in the text, "As is a person’s resolve in this world... Furthermore: "The guides (*ātivāhika*s) lead those who are distinct from those relying on symbols; Bādarāyaṇa considers that [the former case] because of the fault in the previous [view], and because of the principle of 'according to one's resolve'."*1* *1 This verse summarizes the argument: while Jaimini holds that the guides lead all meditators, Bādarāyaṇa maintains they lead only those who meditate on the Supreme Brahman, not those who rely on symbols, due to the flaw in the latter's path and the necessity of the *tatkratu* principle.*
2. I am born—ta, tha; 5. the conceivable Brahman—tha; 1.
the effect, Hiraṇyagarbha—ta; I am born—pā; 3.
the self made—ta, tha; of the liberator—ta, tha.

"The group of those who perform the transport" (vāhika-gaṇa)—thus the venerable Bādarāyaṇa opines. What is meant by this is as follows: the position that "he leads those who meditate upon the effect" is not tenable; nor is there a restrictive rule that he leads only those who meditate upon the Supreme [Brahman]. Nor does he lead even those who take hold of mere symbols (pratīka). Rather, he leads both kinds of people: those who meditate upon the Supreme Brahman, and those who meditate upon the Self, which is distinct from primordial matter (prakṛti) and identical with Brahman.

However, those who meditate upon objects such as names and so forth—which are included within the effects of Brahman—either by viewing them as Brahman (just as one might view Devadatta and others as lions) or as merely those respective objects themselves, He does not lead them. Rather, He leads those who meditate upon the Supreme Brahman, and those who meditate upon the Self as being free from primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and having Brahman as its essence. Thus [it is said].

Why? Because there are faults in both cases. If one holds the position that [the path] "leads those who meditate on the effect," then scriptural passages such as "having risen from this body and having reached the highest light" would be contradicted. Alternatively, if one maintains the restrictive rule that [it leads] only "those who meditate on the supreme Brahman," then the scriptural passage—"Those who know thus, and those who in the forest meditate with faith and austerity, they attain the light"—and the teaching that the group beginning with light leads the "knowers of the five fires," would be contradicted. Therefore, there would be a fault in either alternative.

Nor is one who takes a symbol as a support (pratīkālambana) included; likewise, one who meditates by superimposing the vision of Brahman upon names and so forth is not included. Furthermore, the term "pratīkālambana" does not refer exclusively to meditation through such a superimposition (dṛṣṭyupāsanā), according to the maxim of "the cow and the bull" (gobalīvardanyāya). There is a distinction: Jaimini has stated that for some who are distinct from those taking symbols as supports, there is the path beginning with light (arcirādigati); whereas the view of the Siddhāntin is that [Brahman] leads all those in whom the condition of being distinct from those taking symbols as supports is present. Thus, there is a specific difference.

"This is not the case," [it is argued]. For those who meditate upon Hiraṇyagarbha, the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi-gati*) is untenable, because one who has traveled by way of light reaches Brahman. Indeed, there is no attainment of Brahman for a meditator on Hiraṇyagarbha; for the fruit corresponds to the meditation. Therefore, only a meditator on the Supreme Brahman proceeds by way of light and so forth, not a meditator on the effected [Brahman] (*kārya*); such is the meaning.

"bhūtanāmā" (gha. ḍa. vā. 5) — "iti" (ā.). Therefore, [the text] says: "He leads both kinds"—meaning he leads those who possess both types of knowledge. This very point is stated in the words: "And [he is] of the same resolve as that" (*tatkratuśca*). "Of the same resolve as that" means that one attains exactly what one meditates upon; as it is said: "In whatever way a person is in this world, so does he become after departing from here," and "In whatever way they meditate upon him..."

This is according to the stated principle; for even in the case of one who knows the five fires, there is scriptural mention of the journey by way of the light (*arcis*) and so forth, and because it is heard that one who has gone by way of the light and so forth attains Brahman and does not return. Therefore, by the principle of "as was his resolve, so was his destination" (*tatkratu-nyāya*), the meditative realization of the Self as identical with Brahman, liberated from primordial nature (*prakṛti*), is established.

However, for those who take as their support meditative objects (*pratīka*) beginning with Name and ending with the Vital Breath (*prāṇa*), there is no journey by way of the path of light (*arcirādi*) nor attainment of Brahman; this is because they lack the two kinds of meditation established by scripture, and because, in the case of meditation on that which is mixed with the non-sentient, the principle of "as is one's resolve, so is one's destination" (*tatkratu-nyāya*) applies. ||14||
Thus ends the section concerning the effect (kāryādhikaraṇa). || 5 ||
Thus ends the third section, "The Way," of the fourth chapter, "The Chapter on the Fruit," in the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Bhagavad Rāmānuja.
In the fourth chapter on the fruits [of knowledge], the fourth section concerning liberation (*muktipāda*):
1. The Topic of Manifestation upon Attainment (*sampadyāvirbhāvādhikaraṇam*).

The specific state attained by the liberated self after reaching and uniting with the supreme light (*paraṃ jyotiḥ*) is precisely the manifestation of its own true nature (*svasvarūpāvirbhāva*); it is not, however, the production of a previously non-existent form.

2. The Section on Perception Without Distinction regarding the Liberated One: The experience of the Supreme Self, who has become one's own self, is as one's own self without distinction, namely, simply as "I"; it is not with distinction. Salutations to the illustrious Rāmānuja. Salutations to Śrī. Salutations to Śrīdhara.
The fourth quarter, on liberation, of the fourth chapter in the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Bhagavad Rāmānuja. || 4.4 ||
The Section on the Manifestation upon Attainment (Sampadyāvirbhāvādhikaraṇa) || 4.4.1 ||
[The ninth prior section: 524. *sampadyāvirbhāvaḥ svena śabdāt* (Sūtra 4.4.1).

For those who meditate upon the Supreme Brahman, and for those who meditate upon the Self as being of the nature of Brahman when separated from Prakṛti, the "attainment" (*gati*) characterized by non-return has been described via the path beginning with light (*arcis*). Now, he begins to consider the manner of the sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) of the liberated ones.
The following is recorded in scripture:
"In this very way, this serene being (samprasāda), having risen up from this body and having reached the highest light, manifests in its own true form.

Does this statement teach that for one who has risen from the body and reached the highest light, there is a connection with an acquired form—such as the form of a god or similar being—or rather, does it teach the manifestation of one's own natural essential nature?

In this state of doubt, it is logical that there is a connection with the nature of the goal to be attained (*sādhya*). Otherwise, the scripture concerning liberation would fail to communicate what is beneficial for man (*apuruṣārtha*); for we observe that the essential nature (*svarūpa*) by itself does not constitute a human goal. Indeed, when the activities of the body and senses have ceased in deep sleep, no connection with a human goal is observed for the mere essential nature of the Self.

Moreover, the mere cessation of suffering is not the supreme human goal for one who has attained the highest light; otherwise, it would have been stated that "liberation is simply the manifestation of one's own nature. This is because of such scriptural passages as, "That is one bliss of Brahman; and of the learned man who is free from desire," and "For having obtained this very essence, he becomes blissful," from which we learn that the liberated soul possesses infinite happiness.

Is it not so? Does the nature of the Self inherently possess unlimited bliss? Is it not so? Is the concealment of the nature of bliss possible? Is it not so? And does such concealment serve any purpose, or is it not?

When there is futility because the scripture does not culminate in a human goal due to the absence of *nanda* (bliss), then the relationship [of the self] with its state as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) would be what is to be taught. When, however, there is no futility of the term "manifestation" (*abhiniṣpatti*), and when—due to the possibility of the removal of concealment—the fact that bliss is inherently undivided is established, such that the scripture on liberation culminates in a human goal, then the manifestation of one's natural form (*svābhāvikarūpa*) would be what is to be taught. "By form" (*rūpeṇa*) means by way of appearance (*ākāreṇa*).

"And it is not merely the cessation of suffering. If liberation were merely the cessation of suffering, it would be no different from cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), because it would be mixed with what is not a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*). Both the cessation of suffering and the attainment of happiness are desired; the cessation of happiness and the attainment of suffering are undesired. In that case, since the cessation of suffering is desired and the cessation of happiness is undesired, liberation—being mixed with the desired and the undesired—would be equal to cyclic existence.

Is it possible to claim that the word "attainment" (*abhiniṣpatti*) refers to manifestation, such that one could say: "Since concealment is impossible, His very nature is consciousness whose bliss is inherently unlimited; and that [nature], which was concealed by *avidyā* during the state of transmigratory existence, becomes manifest for one who has attained the supreme light"? This cannot be maintained, because concealment of that which is of the nature of knowledge is impossible; for it has already been stated previously that the concealment of knowledge—which is synonymous with illumination—is nothing other than its destruction.

Furthermore, mere luminosity cannot constitute bliss. For the nature of bliss is the nature of happiness, and the nature of happiness consists in being favorable to the self. For one who maintains that the self is mere luminosity, whose luminosity would it be that could be experienced as favorable? Thus, for a proponent of the doctrine of mere luminosity as the self, the nature of bliss is difficult to establish in any way whatsoever.

If the goal were merely the attainment of one's own nature (*svarūpa*), then since that nature is eternally established, the statement "he is manifested in his own form" (*svena rūpeṇābhiniṣpadyate*) would be purposeless for one who has already attained it. Therefore, he is connected with a previously non-existent form that is to be accomplished. In this way, the expression "is manifested" (*abhiniṣpadyate*) retains its primary meaning, as does the phrase "in his own form" (*svena rūpeṇa*).
Thus it is consistent that [the self] is accomplished through bliss alone, which is its own unique [attribute].

This being the position reached, we reply: "The manifestation of its own nature upon reaching [the Supreme]. This inner self, having reached the highest light by way of the path beginning with light (*arcis*), attains a particular state which consists in the manifestation of its own essential nature; it does not consist in the production of a previously non-existent form. Why? Because of the word "by itself" (*svena*); that is to say, because of the inclusion of the qualification "in its own nature" (*svena rūpeṇa*). For if it were to assume some adventitious attribute, the qualification "in its own nature" would be purposeless, since even without such a qualification, its status as its own nature would already be established. || 1 ||
As for what was said— that because one's own nature is eternally attained,
one "attains" (*abhiniṣpadyate*) by "reaching" (*upasampadya*)— it refers to this.
The statement [that the soul is liberated] is purposeful; to this, the reply is: 525. "He is liberated because it is so declared" (Sūtra 4.4.2).
[This means that he is] freed from the connection with karma and the body etc. produced by it, and abides in his own natural form; herein [it is said]: "he manifests himself in his own form."

Thus it is said. Therefore, although its own nature is eternally attained, the cessation of the concealment of that nature—which, being of the form of action, was hidden by ignorance—is here called "manifestation" (*abhiniṣpatti*).
Why? Because of the initial proposition; for that [nature] was indeed proposed as the subject to be established.
How is this understood?

In order to demonstrate that the Self under discussion— the inner Self (pratyagātman)— is indeed free from the three states beginning with waking and is also free from the body initiated by karma which serves as the cause of pleasure and pain,
[the text says]: "In this very way, I shall explain it further to you."
Because this has been stated repeatedly,
and because it is declared: "In this very way, this serene being, having risen up from this body and having attained the highest light, manifests in its own true form."

Therefore, for one who is bound by karma, having attained the supreme light, it is said that he "emerges in his own nature," which is liberation in the form of the cessation of bondage. Even in the case of the manifestation of one's true nature, the word "niṣpatti" (emergence/accomplishment) is seen, as in such expressions as "this matter is accomplished through reasoning. || 2 ||

As for what was said—that because the nature of the Self is seen not to be a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) during deep sleep, if liberation were merely the manifestation of that nature, the scripture on liberation would teach something that is not a human goal—and therefore, "manifestation" (*abhiniṣpatti*) must be the attainment of another state connected with happiness, similar to the states of gods and so forth; to that, the reply is:

**526. The Self [is the one who manifests], because of the context.** (Siddhānta Sūtra 4.4.3) It is understood from the context that "this very Self, by its own nature, possesses attributes beginning with freedom from sin and ending with the power of true resolve."

"For that Self which is free from evil, free from old age, free from death, free from sorrow, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true and whose resolves are true"—such indeed is the introductory statement of Prajāpati.
Therefore, qualities such as freedom from evil and the rest are the natural attributes of the inner self; they become manifest upon reaching the supreme light, rather than being newly produced.
As it was said by the Blessed One, and also by Śaunaka:
"Just as the moonlight of a gem is not created by the washing away of its impurities,
so too knowledge of the Self is not created by the abandonment of defects."
Just as by the making of a well, "water-space" is not created [but rather] that which already exists is brought to manifestation;
for how could there be the arising of what is non-existent?
"Likewise, qualities such as consciousness and the rest are manifested through the destruction of [limiting] qualities; they are not produced, for they are indeed eternal attributes of the Self.

Therefore, it is not untenable that there is a manifestation in the form of expansion—upon reaching the Supreme Light and the destruction of the bondage consisting of karma—of those qualities such as knowledge and bliss which were contracted within the Self by karma. Thus, it is well said: "Upon attaining [the Self], there is manifestation" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.2). ||3||
Thus concludes the section concerning the manifestation [of the soul] upon reaching [the state of union]. || 1 ||

—0— In this context, the quality of being free from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) and so forth, as well as the essential nature (*svarūpa*) qualified by those qualities, are not adventitious. During the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), because the attribute-consciousness (*dharmabhūtajñāna*) is obstructed by karma, it lacks the capacity to take as its object the essential nature of the Self as qualified by the eightfold qualities such as freedom from sin. However, upon the cessation of that concealment (*tirodhāna*), that [nature] becomes an object; consequently, a supreme knowledge having that as its object arises.

It is not taught that [the liberated soul] possesses the nature of being "freed from evil" (*apahatapāpmatva*) and so forth, nor its specific form qualified by those attributes; however, the arising of even the attribute of knowledge (*dharmabhūtajñāna*) in liberation is not denied. This much, however, is the distinction: in the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), knowledge regarding objects such as jars depends upon the operation of the sense organs, such as the eyes; whereas in liberation, upon the removal of concealment (*tirodhāna*), all-encompassing knowledge does not require any adventitious cause. It is with this intention that there is the traditional teaching regarding the absence of any adventitious form. (3)
Moreover:
1. Having attained [Brahman], 2. liberated, 3. the Self (pra) [is one] through non-distinction (pra), because it is seen as such—this is the section concerning the basis of vision. 4.4.2.
527. Because it is seen as non-differentiated. (Siddhānta) || 4.4.4 ||

Regarding the doubt as to whether this inner self, having attained the supreme light and being liberated from all bonds, experiences itself as distinct from the Supreme Self, or rather as non-different from it by virtue of being a mode (*prakāra*) of that [Self]—[the scriptures declare]: "He enjoys all desires together with the wise Brahman"; "When the seer beholds the golden-hued one, the maker, the Lord, the Person, the source of Brahman;
then the knower, shaking off merit and demerit, stainless, attains the highest equality"; and "Having taken refuge in this knowledge, they have attained a state of similarity to me."

"Even at creation they are not born, and at dissolution they are not distressed," and so forth; from these Śruti and Smṛti passages, since it is understood that the liberated one possesses association, equality, and similarity with the Supreme, he experiences [the Self] as distinct [from the body].

This being the position, it is replied: "In non-separation. The liberated one experiences his own self as non-separate from the supreme Brahman. Why? Because it is so seen. For one who has attained union with the supreme Brahman and whose concealment by ignorance has ceased, his own self is seen in its true nature. Indeed, the very nature of one's own self is this: [text continues]
By such designations of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) as "That thou art," "This Self is Brahman," "All this has this as its essence," and "All this, indeed, is Brahman."

"He who, dwelling in the self, is within the self, whom the self does not know, whose body is the self, who controls the self from within—he is your self, the inner controller, the immortal"; and by such passages as "He has entered within, the ruler of people, the Self of all," it is established that [the individual self] is the body of the Supreme Self and is of the nature of being "modeled" (*tatprakāra*) after Him—as stated in the *Brahma-sūtra*: "Because of its abiding [in the Supreme], [it is one with it], according to Kāśakṛtsna. Therefore, without distinction, one experiences: "I am Brahman."

The designation of "equality" (*sāmya*) and "commonality of nature" (*sādharmya*) means that the essential nature of the inner self (*pratyagātman*), which is itself a mode of Brahman, is equal to That; it thus establishes that through the abandonment of the natural forms such as those of gods and so forth, one attains a purity identical to that of Brahman. As for the scriptural mention of "together" (*saha*), it establishes that such an inner self experiences the qualities of Brahman, the possessor of those modes; therefore, there is no contradiction whatsoever.

For, since that division is stated as being of the nature of Brahman, [the Sūtra] "Because of the scriptural statement of [creation] from mere volition alone" (Brahmasūtra 4.4.8) and so forth is not contradicted.
Furthermore, [the Sūtra] states, "Because of the specific mention of distinctions," and so forth. || 4 ||
The Section on Brahma. 4.43.

What, then, is the established conclusion? The teacher Jaimini considers that [the term] "Brāhmaṇa" [refers to the individual soul]. The meaning is: because of qualities such as having evil destroyed (*apahatapāpmatva*). For qualities such as having evil destroyed are heard in the *Dahara* passage as belonging to Brahman. How is it understood that [the term] "Brāhmaṇa" refers to this? From the introductory statement (*upanyāsa*) and so forth. For qualities of Brahman, such as having evil destroyed, are introduced in the *Prajāpati* passage with respect to the inner self (*pratyagātman*) as well, in the section beginning with "The Self which has evil destroyed...
and ending with "...whose resolve is true" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.1).

By the word "etcetera" (ādi), activities such as eating (*jakṣaṇa*) and so forth—which depend on qualities like the power of true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpatva*) and are mentioned in passages such as "eating, playing, and rejoicing"—are included. Therefore, it is the opinion of Jaimini that the nature of the inner self (*pratyagātman*) as consisting of pure consciousness alone is not possible based on these [scriptural] presentations and other [evidences]. || 5 ||

529. "Because it consists of that [consciousness] alone by means of consciousness alone," says Auḍulomi (Pūrva-pakṣa). The teacher Auḍulomi maintains that "pure consciousness" alone is the "essential nature" of this Self, and that it manifests in that very form.

Why? Because it consists of that—because this inner self (pratyagātman) consists of nothing but that. "Just as a lump of salt has no interior or exterior but is entirely a mass of flavor, even so, my dear, this self has no interior or exterior but is entirely a mass of consciousness (prajñānaghana), a mass of cognition (vijñānaghana)."

Because of this restriction, it is understood that its very nature is consciousness alone. Therefore, since there is an absence of other qualities in it, words such as "free from evil" (*apahatapāpmā*) are intended to exclude attributes consisting of ignorance, such as modification, pleasure, and pain; thus, according to the view of Auḍulomi, its manifestation is in the form of pure consciousness alone. || 6 ||
Now the venerable Bādarāyaṇa states the final conclusion according to his own view:

530. *Evamapyupanyāsāt pūrvabhāvādavirodhaṃ bādarāyaṇaḥ* || 4.4.7 || (Siddhānta) "Even so"—that is, even when there is the presentation of the nature of [Brahman] as consisting of pure consciousness (*vijñānamātra*), there is no contradiction, and indeed no sublation, of the previously mentioned qualities such as having true desires (*satyakāmatva*) and so forth; this is what the teacher Bādarāyaṇa maintains.

Why? Because of the introductory statement and because of the prior existence. From the introductory statement found in the Upaniṣads—namely, the authoritative text beginning with "That Self which is free from evil" (Chāndogya Up. 8.7.1)—and because of the prior existence—that is, the presence—of qualities such as being free from evil, having true desires, and so forth in the preceding [sections], it is not logical for there to be mutual sublation among those things established by equal authority; this is the meaning.

Nor is it logical that qualities such as being free from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) are merely imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*), because that would contradict the nature of reality; for, since there is no distinction [between the two views], one could equally ask why the opposite is not the case—according to the principle that when two positions are of equal strength, it is more reasonable to interpret the [scriptural] passage as having another purpose than to establish what is impossible to determine. Indeed, when the strength is equal, it is only reasonable that the [text] has another intent.

Even so, there is no contradiction—saying this while accepting [the opponent's position], [the text] states: "The meaning is that his essential nature is knowledge alone, and nothing else exists at all; thus, 'he is a mass of consciousness alone. (PFI) *Vijñānaghana eva*.
One might think that [the Self] is not established by such statements as these. What, then, is the meaning of the restriction "a mass of consciousness alone" (*vijñānaghana eva*)?

It means that the entire Self is non-inert, self-luminous, and does not have its manifestation dependent on anything else; there is not even the slightest portion (*pradeśa*) that is otherwise. This meaning is very clearly evident from the sentence itself.
"Just as a lump of salt has no interior and no exterior, but is entirely a mass of taste, even so, my dear, this Self has no interior and no exterior, but is entirely a mass of consciousness."

Nor is there any contradiction here with other scriptural passages that establish the connection of the inner self—which, as its very nature, is a mass of pure consciousness—with attributes such as being free from sin and having true resolve; for even though the entire mass of salt is perceived by the sense of taste as a mass of flavor, its color, hardness, and other qualities perceived by the eyes and other senses are not thereby contradicted.

The intended meaning of this statement is as follows: just as in juicy mangoes and the like, although there are differences in taste according to the distinction between parts such as the skin and so forth, rock salt possesses a single uniform taste throughout; likewise, the Self also has the nature of consciousness everywhere—that is to say, its nature is self-luminous. || 7 ||
Thus ends the section concerning Brahmā. 3.

If it is asked: "Since there is no difference [between the individual soul and Brahman], and since the suspicion that [the soul] might be insentient in one part does not even arise, for what purpose is this statement?"—the meaning is as follows: For the proponent of the view that liberated souls consist of pure consciousness alone (Auḍulomi), who maintains their omnipresence, the possibility of insentiency arises through the theory that they are subject to transformation into the insentient phenomenal world due to spatial distinctions. Therefore, the intent of the author of the Sūtras, as the purport of the Bhāṣya, is that this [statement] is intended precisely to refute that [possibility], and thus the position of Auḍulomi is perfectly acceptable. || 7 ||
Thus ends the section concerning Brahmā. 4.
Section 4.4.4: The Topic of Volitional Resolve (Saṅkalpa-adhikaraṇa)

531. *Saṅkalpādeva tacchruteḥ* || 4–4–8 || (Siddhānta) It has been stated that the liberated one, having attained the Supreme Brahman, manifests as the very nature of knowledge (*jñānasvarūpa*), possessing attributes beginning with freedom from sin and ending with the power of true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpatva*). With reference to such a person, various activities resulting from his power of true resolve are recorded in scripture: "There he moves about, eating, playing, and rejoicing, with women, or with carriages, or with kinsmen."
(Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.3).
Regarding the doubt as to whether his attainment of kinsmen and so forth depends on other efforts, or whether it occurs through the mere volition of the Supreme Person alone:

since in the world, even those such as kings who are conventionally described as possessing "true resolve" (satya-saṅkalpa) are seen to depend on other efforts for the accomplishment of their tasks, [it might be thought that] this [attainment] also depends on such effort.
This being the position, it is replied: "By mere volition alone. Why? Because of that very teaching:
"If he becomes desirous of the world of the fathers, by his mere volition the fathers arise for him."

For thus, it is heard in scripture that the emergence of the fathers and others occurs from mere volition (*saṅkalpa*) alone. Nor is another scriptural passage seen which speaks of a dependence on some other effort, by which the restriction "from mere volition" might be limited, as is done in the case of the phrase "consisting of a mass of consciousness" (*vijñānaghana eva*). || 8 ||

532. And for this very reason, he has no other lord (ananyādhipatiḥ). (Sūtra 4.4.9, Siddhānta) Since the liberated one possesses true volition (satyasaṅkalpa), for that very reason he has no other lord. For if there were another lord, that would constitute bondage! This is because his volition could be subject to obstruction dependent upon karma; because, unlike the Lord (Īśvara), his volition would lack infallibility; and because, being unable to set aside the limitation of being equal to a king or similar beings, the liberated one’s attainment of kinsmen and so forth would have to depend on further effort.

When there are no longer any bonds, then for the liberated soul, since there can be no obstruction to its will dependent upon karma, and because its will can become unfailing like that of the Lord, the attainment of kinsmen and so forth by the liberated one—being capable of setting aside the restriction [of the body]—would be rooted in mere volition (*saṃkalpa-mātra*). The phrase "dependent on that" (*tatsāpekṣā*) means dependent on another effort.

However, the particle "only" (*eva*) in the expression "by volition alone" (*saṃkalpād eva*) is intended to exclude non-connection (*ayoga-vyavaccheda*), as in the case of the expression "a mass of consciousness alone" (*vijñānaghana eva*); it is not intended to exclude connection with something else (*anyayoga-vyavaccheda*). This is the intended meaning.
By the phrase "consisting of nothing but consciousness" (vijñānaghana eva), a specific connection is intended. || 8 ||

"And for this very reason" (ata eva ca): this sūtra establishes the possession of true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpatva*). Since activities such as eating and so forth consist of merit and demerit, and since the liberated one has attained the supreme state, he is no longer subject to prohibitions or injunctions.

It is the fitness for injunction and prohibition. For if there were fitness for injunction and prohibition, there would be the state of having frustrated intentions. Therefore, by the very scriptural statement of "truthfulness of intention" (*satya-saṅkalpatva*), "lordship over others" (*ananya-adhipatitva*) is established. For this very reason, it is said:
"He becomes self-ruling" (*sa svarāḍ bhavati*).
Thus ends the section concerning the resolve (saṅkalpa). 4.
The Topic of Non-existence (Abhāvādhikaraṇa) || 4.4.5 ||
533. "Bādari says there is non-existence, for so [the scripture] states.

(Pūrva-pakṣa) Regarding the doubt as to whether the body and senses of the liberated one do not exist, or whether they do exist, or whether they exist according to his will—Master Bādari maintains that there is an absence of body and senses.
Why? Because it has been said thus:
"For one who possesses a body, there is no removal of pleasure and pain; but for one who is indeed bodiless, pleasure and pain do not touch."

Thus, having stated that suffering is unavoidable when there is a connection with a body, the Śruti declares that the liberated one is indeed bodiless: "Rising up from this body, attaining the supreme light, he manifests in his own true form. || 10 ||

It is understood that [pleasure and pain] are bound to the body; however, the statement regarding "bodilessness" (aśarīratva) refers to the absence of a body caused by karma. For it is precisely that body which is the cause of pleasure and pain. || 11 ||
[The intention of Bādarāyaṇa, representing the established conclusion:
But the venerable Bādarāyaṇa states the established conclusion according to his own view:
"535. Like the twelve-day sacrifice, it is of both kinds, so says Bādarāyaṇa; therefore. (Sūtra 4.4.12, Siddhānta)

The phrase "from mere volition" (*saṃkalpād eva*) is referred to by the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*). Therefore, from such a volition, the liberated one becomes both—embodied and disembodied; this is what the venerable Bādarāyaṇa maintains. And in this way, both types of scriptural testimony are justified. It is like the case of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*): as it is said, "Those desiring prosperity should undertake the twelve-day sacrifice," and "One should cause him who desires progeny to sacrifice with the twelve-day sacrifice."
Thus, through the distinction in intention arising from the injunctions to "undertake" and "sacrifice," it becomes both a *sattra* and an *ahīna*.

This is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "for that very [body]": because the body is denied on the grounds of being a cause of what is dear (*priya*), and because both the dear and the undear are the fruits of karma, the denial refers to a body produced by karma—this is the meaning. Therefore, since there is no subverter of the scriptural statement regarding embodiment, and since no occasional alternative cause has been stated, the conclusion is that there is always embodiment; such is the intention of the Sūtra. || 11 ||

Regarding the phrase "by mere volition" (*saṃkalpādeva*): when there arises an expectation for a cause for his becoming threefold and so forth, the scriptural statement regarding his "truthful volition" (*satyasaṅkalpatva*) itself fulfills that requirement; the sense is that this is appropriate because scripture declares that very volition to be the cause even in other activities. Regarding the phrase "both kinds," etc.: the meaning of the commentary is that once it is accepted—on the basis of the scriptural texts concerning the possession of a body which are supported by statements such as those on "truthful volition"—that he can assume a body at will, then the scriptural text concerning his bodilessness becomes meaningful, and the scriptural text concerning his possession of a body remains uncontradicted.

The meaning is that since both the status of a *satra* (sacrificial session) and an *ahīna* (non-session) are established by scriptural authority through the distinction of intention (*saṅkalpa*), it is the specific difference in intention that serves as the determining factor for each particular performance. A *satra* arises from the intention of many sacrificers; an *ahīna*, from the intention of one. || 12 ||
The teacher Bādarāyaṇa considers that which is liberated to be both "embodied" and "disembodied," in two ways, like the twelve-day sacrifice.

1. *Apriya*—likewise. ... The Blessed One—likewise. When there is a need for instruments such as a body, there is no rule that those instruments, such as the body, must be created by oneself; thus he says: **4.4.13. "Because [experience] is possible even in the absence of a body, as in the case of the intermediate state" (sūtra).** In the absence of instruments such as a body created by oneself, experience is possible through instruments created by the Supreme Person; therefore, even one whose will is true does not create them himself. As in a dream, so it is here.
Starting with, "Then he creates chariots, draft animals, and roads," and continuing,
"Then he creates ponds, lotus-pools, and rivers; for he is the agent."
Thus,
that Person who remains awake while these [senses] sleep, fashioning desire after desire—
that alone is the radiant, that is Brahman, that alone is called the immortal.

"All worlds are supported in Him; no one transcends Him. And thus, the individual soul (jīva) enjoys [the world] by means of instruments such as chariots created by the Lord; likewise, even the liberated soul enjoys the essence of divine play (līlā-rasa) through the worlds of the ancestors and so forth, created by the Lord who engages in play. || 13 ||

537. *Bhāve jāgradvat* || 4.4.14 || (Siddhānta) — [The meaning is: "by those created by the Supreme Person"—that is, by those created directly (*advāraka-sṛṣṭaiḥ*). Regarding the phrase "because experience is possible": even if it is admitted that the creation of the body and so forth is not included within the experience of Brahman, and that consequently His will and other factors are impossible therein, the sense is that a resolution is appropriate by postulating a mode consistent with that [creation], on the strength of scriptural texts such as "becoming manifold" (*ekadhā-bhavanādi*). || 13 ||

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: "In the absence of a body"—that is, when the liberated soul lacks a body and so forth created by itself—"as in the state between [waking and sleep]"—meaning as in a dream—"because of the possibility," that is, because experience is possible through bodies and other instruments created by the Supreme Person. "When one is devoid of the instruments such as the body created by oneself, then, like in a dream, one possesses the instruments created by Brahman."

Regarding the existence [of these objects]: just as one who is liberated experiences the flavor of divine play (*līlā-rasa*), so too does the liberated one experience the flavor of divine play, even though he has created his own body and other instruments such as the world of the ancestors (*pitṛ-loka*) by his own volition alone, like a waking person. Just as the Supreme Person, for the sake of divine play, creates the world of the ancestors and so forth—including Daśaratha, Vasudeva, and others—for Himself and experiences the flavor of divine play characterized by human attributes through them; likewise, He sometimes creates the world of the ancestors and so forth Himself for the sake of His own divine play with respect to the liberated souls as well.

And sometimes, being liberated, they themselves create their own worlds, such as the world of their fathers, which are included within the divine play (līlā) of the Supreme Person (paramapuruṣa) by virtue of their true resolve (satyasaṅkalpa); thus everything is logically consistent. || 14 ||

Now, an objection is raised: "It was stated that the self (*ātman*) is of atomic dimension (*aṇuparimāṇa*). How, then, is the conceit of a single atom-sized self possible with respect to multiple bodies? To this, [the Sūtra] says: **538.

*Pradīpavadāveśastathāhi darśayati* || 4.4.15 ||** (Pūrva-pakṣa) Just as a single lamp, while remaining in one place, enters other places by means of its own light; so too, the self, while residing in only one body, enters all bodies by means of consciousness (*caitanya*), which is of the nature of its own light.

It is not untenable; for just as in a single body, although consciousness resides in one specific location such as the heart, there is a sense of self-identification (ātmābhimāna) throughout the entire body due to the pervasion of that consciousness, so it is in this case as well.

This is the distinction: for one whose knowledge is contracted due to [past] karma, an expansion of pervasion corresponding to self-identification with other bodies is not possible; however, for the liberated one, whose knowledge is uncontracted, an expansion of pervasion corresponding to self-identification as he wills, as well as one corresponding to the apprehension of "this," is not untenable. For thus the scripture shows: "Of the hundredth part of the tip of a hair, divided a hundredfold..."

"That part is to be known as the individual soul (jīva), and it is capable of attaining infinity. This is the distinction: for one who is not liberated, karma is the regulator; but for one who is liberated, it is his own will. || 15 ||

Objection: But does not the Śruti show the cessation of both internal and external knowledge for one who has attained the Supreme Brahman? [It says]: "Embraced by the conscious Self (prājña), he knows nothing without, nor anything within. How then can the omniscience of the liberated one be asserted? To this, the reply is: 539. "With reference to either deep sleep (svāpyaya) or union (sampatti), for it is so revealed. (Sūtra 4.4.16) (Conclusion) This means that the cessation of knowledge mentioned in the scripture refers to either the state of deep sleep or the state of union with Brahman, as is clearly indicated by the context. It does not apply to the state of liberation. Therefore, there is no contradiction in asserting the omniscience of the liberated soul.
This statement does not refer to liberation, but rather depends on either deep sleep (*svāpyaya*) or death (*sampatti*). Deep sleep is "suṣupti," and death is "sampatti."
Starting from "he becomes unified with speech," up to "heat [is merged] in the highest deity."

Because of this statement, both of these states—the attainment of the conscious self (*prājña*) and the state of being devoid of consciousness (*niḥsaṃbodhatva*)—are found to exist. Therefore, this statement refers to one or the other of those two. Indeed, the state of being devoid of consciousness is revealed by the Śruti in the cases of deep sleep and death, while the omniscience of the liberated one is also revealed:
"Verily, in this state he does not know himself as 'this I am,' nor indeed these beings; he has gone to utter annihilation. I see no enjoyments here."
Having thus stated the state of non-cognition during the period of deep sleep, the same text, referring to the liberated one, says:
"He, indeed, with his divine eye—the mind—beholds these desires and rejoices; those which are in the world of Brahman."
Thus, omniscience is stated.

Likewise, in the passage, "The seer sees all; he attains all in every way," omniscience is indeed clearly stated. Similarly, there is also the state of being devoid of consciousness at the time of death.
It has been stated: "Having arisen from these elements, it perishes after them. To perish means that one does not see.
Therefore, the expression "by the conscious self" (prājñenātmanā) must refer to either deep sleep (svāpyaya) or union with the Supreme (sampatti). || 16 ||
The section concerning the exclusion of the world's activity [from Brahman]. (4.4.6)
540. "Except for the activity of governing the world, because of the context and because of non-proximity.

(Sūtra 4.4.17, Siddhānta) The doubt is as follows: Does the sovereignty of the liberated one include the creation of the world and so forth—the state of being the Lord of All which is unique to the Supreme Person—or is it devoid of that and consists solely of the experience of the Supreme Person?
[Śrīmadbhāṣya 4.4.6] What is logical? That He is also the Lord of the universe.
Why?

"Being stainless, he attains supreme equality," because of this scriptural statement regarding the attainment of supreme equality with the Supreme Person, and because of the scriptural statement regarding [the soul's] possession of true resolve.

For indeed, both supreme equality and the state of having true resolve (*satya-saṃkalpatva*) are not possible without the governance of the world, which is unique to all the Lords (*sarveśvara*). Therefore, for the sake of establishing true resolve and supreme equality, the liberated one’s sovereignty consists in the governance of the entire world; this is the "sovereignty of the liberated one."

Is the scriptural statement regarding non-return (*anāvṛtti*)—like the scriptural statement that the fruit of the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices is inexhaustible—to be understood as intending a long duration, or does it have its primary meaning? Is it impossible for the Lord’s resolve to concern the non-return of the liberated soul, or is it possible?

When [the soul] does not return, bliss is delimited because of the scriptural statement regarding non-return (*anāvṛtti*), which implies that a return is possible after a long duration; because independence (*svātantrya*) consists in the nature of sovereignty, if it were of the nature of happiness, then from its deficiency would follow a deficiency of bliss. Furthermore, if the worlds of transformation are objects of enjoyment by virtue of their being of the nature of modification, then due to their impermanence, there is an impermanence of bliss.

Therefore, since the wandering through the worlds of transformation is not for the sake of mere enjoyment but for the purpose of self-restraint (*niyamana*), it is improper to rely on the world-activity as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of Brahman. Because that [world-activity] lacks the status of a defining characteristic, there is no contradiction with the scriptural declarations of "supreme equality" and so forth; for these declare that the liberated one's sovereignty includes the world-activity within its scope. Thus, the sovereignty over the world-activity would indeed be possible for the liberated one.

When the Lord’s volition regarding non-return becomes possible for those who are liberated, then, because non-return is possible in its primary sense according to the scriptural texts on non-return, there is no impermanence of bliss. And when sovereignty—which is of the nature of bliss—is in accordance with one's self-conception, then, since sovereignty among the liberated is in accordance with their self-conception, there is no deficiency in bliss due to any deficiency in that sovereignty.

And when the worlds of transformation possess the status of objects of enjoyment for the liberated as manifestations of Brahman's glory (*brahmavibhūti*), then, even though that which consists of transformations is impermanent, there is no interruption of bliss because the state of the world being a manifestation of Brahman's glory persists in all conditions without loss.

Thus, even though there is no necessity for the Lord to govern the world in order to wander through the worlds of transformation, since this does not contradict His being of unlimited bliss, it is logical to maintain that the activity of the world constitutes a characteristic of Brahman—provided it is not for the sake of mere enjoyment. Furthermore, because scriptural texts concerning supreme equality and so forth indicate that the sovereignty of the liberated includes the governance of the world, the sovereignty of the liberated must indeed exclude the activity of the world.

If "non-return based on the word" constitutes a separate section (adhikaraṇa), then the series of investigations connected with non-return must be pursued separately; however, the possibility of that purpose should be regarded as serving merely for the sake of establishing a formal connection (saṅgati).

This being the case, we reply: "With the exception of the activity of governing the world. The "activity of governing the world" consists in the regulation of the existence, maintenance, and specific functions of all sentient and insentient beings. With that excluded, the sovereignty of the liberated one consists in the unimpeded experience of Brahman, for whom all concealment has been dispelled.

Why? Because of the context; for the regulation of the entire world is taught in reference to the Supreme Brahman: "From which indeed these beings are born; by which, once born, they live... (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1).

"That which they enter upon departing—that you should desire to know; that is Brahman. If this [characteristic of] governing the entire universe were common even to those who are liberated, then this definition of Brahman as consisting in lordship over the world would not be consistent. For a definition must be unique (asādhāraṇa). Likewise:

"In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second. It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate. It emitted heat. Or: "In the beginning, this was Brahman alone. Being one, it did not flourish."
He created the Kṣatra as a form superior to that [the Brahman].
These are the Kṣatras among the gods: Indra, Varuṇa, Soma, Rudra, Parjanya, Yama, Mṛtyu, and Īśāna.
In the beginning, this universe was indeed the Self alone; there was nothing else whatsoever, not even a blinking thing.

He thought, "Shall I create the worlds? He created these worlds. Indeed, in the beginning, Nārāyaṇa alone existed—neither Brahmā, nor Īśāna, nor these two, heaven and earth, nor the stars; neither water, nor fire, nor Soma, nor the sun. Being alone, he did not find delight. As he remained absorbed in meditation, a maiden appeared from within his thought—the maiden who is the ten sense organs.
In such passages as these.

Beginning with "He who, dwelling in the earth, is within the earth," and continuing in passages such as "He who, dwelling in the self," the Supreme Person who governs the entire universe is indeed heard of as the subject. Furthermore, because He is not proximate, the liberated soul has no presence in these contexts concerning the governance of the entire universe, whereby the activity of the world would belong to him as well. (17)

541. "If it be argued that [the liberated soul] possesses the activity of the world because of the direct scriptural teaching, we say no; for [the scripture] speaks of one who occupies the sphere of authority. (Sūtra 4.4.18) "He becomes a self-ruler; he moves at will in all worlds," and "moving through these worlds, assuming forms at will according to his desires"—by this direct scriptural statement (*pratyakṣa-śruti*), the activity of governing the world is taught for the liberated soul. Therefore, [if you argue] that [the liberated soul] does not exclude the activity of the world! [The sūtra refutes this: No, because the scripture speaks of one who occupies the sphere of authority (*adhikārika-maṇḍala-stha*). This refers to those who, having attained liberation while still in their bodies, reside in the realm of the Lord and exercise authority over the world. It does not refer to those who have attained disembodied liberation (*videhamukti*). Thus, the activity of governing the world is restricted to those in the state of qualified liberation (*sālokyamukti*) or those in the sphere of authority, and does not apply to the fully liberated soul who has transcended all distinctions.

That is not so; for there is mention of the spheres of those invested with office (*ādhikārika*). Those invested with office are Hiraṇyagarbha and others who are appointed to specific offices. Their spheres are their respective worlds. The meaning is that the enjoyments residing therein belong to the liberated one who is no longer subject to karma, as expressed in the passage:
"For him, there is freedom of movement in all worlds."

This and more is stated [in the following]. The meaning is that one who is liberated, whose knowledge is unimpeded by karma, having experienced the "transformations" (vikāra)—the worlds that constitute the manifestations of Brahman—rejoices according to his desire. By this statement, it is said that such a person experiences all enjoyments existing within those transformations and situated in the spheres of authority (ādhikārika), which are themselves manifestations of Brahman;
it does not refer to the "activity of the world" (jagadvyāpāra). || 18 ||
[The refutation of the doubt that liberation entails finitude:

1. If the liberated one, like the transmigrating soul, were to experience enjoyments that exist within the realm of transformation (*vikāra*), then, just as for the bound soul, the collection of objects of enjoyment for the liberated one would also be finite and limited! To this, he says: 542. "And [the liberated state] does not abide in the realm of transformation, for thus the scripture declares its condition" (Sūtra 4.4.1). (Siddhānta)

The term *vikārāvarti* means that [the Supreme Brahman] does not abide within modifications such as birth and so forth. [Śrī Bhāṣya 4.4.6] The liberated soul experiences the Supreme Brahman—which has shaken off all modifications (*nirdhūta-nikhila-vikāram*), which is the opposite of everything to be abandoned (*heya-pratyanīka*), which is solely composed of auspicious qualities (*kalyāṇa-ekatānam*), and which is unsurpassed bliss (*niratiśayānandam*)—together with its manifestations (*savibhūtikam*), meaning endowed with all auspicious attributes. Because the worlds that abide within modifications are included within those manifestations, they too are objects of enjoyment for the liberated. For it is thus that the Śruti declares the state of the liberated one abiding as an experiencer within the Supreme Brahman, which is changeless and possesses limitless, unsurpassed bliss.
"And when he finds fearless support in that which is invisible, bodiless, indefinable, and without abode, then he becomes free from fear. And:
"He is indeed the essence (rasa); for having obtained the essence, he becomes blissful," and so forth. Furthermore, the world, which is His manifestation, exists in Him alone.
"In that all worlds are supported; no one transcends it"—
so says the Śruti.

Therefore, it is stated that "experiencing Brahman together with its manifestations, he enjoys even those enjoyments situated within the spheres of authority," and "he moves at will in all worlds," and so forth; however, there is no activity regarding the governance of the world for the liberated one. || 19 ||
543. And thus [the scriptures] demonstrate perception and inference.

(Sūtra 4.4.2) It has been stated that for this inner self (*pratyagātman*), who is liberated and subject to control, governance in the form of the world-activity—which is unique to the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*) as the controller—is not possible. [The Sūtra] states that the activity consisting of the governance of the entire universe is unique to the Supreme Person; thus do the Śruti and Smṛti demonstrate.
"Out of fear of Him the wind blows; out of fear the sun rises; out of fear of Him Indra, Agni, and Death as the fifth run on.
(Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.8) Who is He?
What is He like?
"Under the command of this very syllable, O Mārgī, the sun and the moon stand held apart," and so forth; likewise, [it says]:
He is the Lord of all, he is the Sovereign of beings;
he is the bridge, the upholder.
And the Śruti says: "This is the guardian of the worlds for the sake of their non-confusion" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.8). Smṛti also [confirms this].
"Under my supervision, O Kaunteya, Nature gives birth to the moving and the unmoving; by this cause, the world revolves."
"Śaṅkara said:
'Having transcended these [states] characterized by qualities, one is fit for becoming Brahman; for I am the foundation of the immortal and immutable Brahman.'"
"And of the eternal Dharma, and of absolute bliss.
Thus [it is said].

Although the multitude of qualities beginning with freedom from sin and ending with the power of true resolve is indeed the innate nature of the individual self (pratyagātman) when it becomes manifest, nevertheless, its being of such a nature depends entirely upon the Supreme Person (paramapuruṣa). Its eternal persistence is also dependent upon Him, because the Supreme Person eternally desires this constancy of his; thus, there is no contradiction in saying that it exists eternally.

In the very same way, it is understood from the scriptures that the implements for the enjoyment and the sportive pastimes (*līlā*) of the Supreme Person exist in such a state because they are eternal and because the Supreme Person eternally desires them. Therefore, the liberated soul possesses the power of true resolve (*satya-saṃkalpatva*) and equality with the Supreme Person, with the exception of the activity of creating the world (*jagad-vyāpāra*). || 20 ||
544. And because of the indicative mark of equality in respect of enjoyment alone.

(Siddhānta) From the indicative mark of the teaching that the liberated one attains equality with Brahman solely through the enjoyment whose nature is conformable to the true essence of Brahman, it is understood that [the liberated soul] is "devoid of the activity of governing the world";
for [the scripture says]: "He enjoys all desires together with the wise Brahman."

Thus, the equality of the liberated soul with the Supreme Person and its possession of the power of true resolve (satyasaṅkalpatva) must be described in accordance with the scriptural texts concerning the governance of the entire universe, which are unique to the Supreme Person; therefore, the sovereignty of the liberated consists exclusively in the exclusion of the activity of governing the world. || 21 ||

If the liberated one possesses sovereignty equal to that of the Supreme Person, then, because He is independent, there might be a suspicion that the liberated one could return again by virtue of His will; to this, he says: 545.
"No return, on account of the scriptural word; no return, on account of the scriptural word" (Sūtra 4.4.22). (Siddhānta)

For instance, it is understood from the word "is" that there exists the Supreme Person, designated as the "Supreme Brahman," who is the eternal stream of auspiciousness opposed to all that is to be discarded, the cause of the birth and so forth of the world, distinct from all other entities, omniscient, whose will is infallible, an ocean of affection for those dependent on Him, supremely compassionate, and one in whom the possibility of any equal or superior is utterly excluded.

Thus, pleased by that worship in the form of meditation (*upāsanā*) supported by the duties of caste and stage of life (*varṇāśramadharma*) performed day after day, [the Lord] removes the ignorance consisting of the beginningless and endless accumulation of difficult-to-cross karmas from those who meditate, and grants them nothing other than the experience of His own true nature. Regarding "the true nature of Brahman": the sense is that the similarity understood in a general way—according to the maxim "it is a goat, because of the wording of the mantra"—when seen in the context of equality of enjoyment, culminates in such a specific kind of similarity. || 21 ||

Regarding the term "non-return" (*anāvṛtti*): the opponent’s position is that the scriptural statement concerning non-return refers only to a partial case, because it is possible for some to return due to the sovereign independence of the Lord (*īśvara*). The qualities such as being the adversary of all that is to be discarded (*nikhila-heya-pratyanīkatva*) and so forth are mentioned for three purposes: to establish that the liberated soul cannot be abandoned by the Blessed Lord; to demonstrate that no desire to relinquish the experience of Brahman arises in him; and to provide an established example for the sake of validating the authority [of the scripture]. The phrase beginning with "dispelled" (*nirasta*) and so on is intended to exclude any suspicion of cessation [of those qualities] by another means.
The non-return of the liberated one is understood from scripture; for even regarding the existence of Brahman, scripture alone is indeed the authority.
That he does not return again after having attained the unsurpassed bliss consisting of the nature of existence is also understood from the scripture itself.
And the scripture says: "He who conducts himself thus, until the end of his life, attains the world of Brahman."

"Nor does he return again, nor does he return again," and so forth. And likewise, the Blessed One himself has said: "Having come to Me, the high-souled ones, having attained the supreme perfection, do not undergo rebirth, which is an impermanent abode of suffering. O Arjuna, all worlds, up to the realm of Brahmā, are subject to return."
"But having come to Me, O Kaunteya, rebirth does not exist.
Thus [it is said].

Furthermore, for one whose bonds of karma are severed, whose knowledge is uncontracted, whose sole nature is the experience of the Supreme Brahman, who finds delight solely in that, and who experiences the Brahman as infinite and unsurpassed bliss—there can be no suspicion of return, because it is impossible for such a person to have any dependence on other things or to undertake actions for their sake. Nor will the Supreme Person, whose resolve is ever true, ever cause the knower—who is exceedingly dear to Him—to return once He has attained him.
Thus says [the scripture]:...

The passage beginning with "rebirth" (*punarjanma*) and so forth—including the statement "if he is desirous of the world of the fathers," etc.—is cited for the purpose of excluding the notion that the Lord assumes a physical form (*vigraha*) for the sake of attending to [devotees]. The citation of the statement "rebirth does not exist" and so forth is intended to show that even in the absence of specific qualifiers such as "being an abode of suffering," there would be consistency with this same meaning. By this, it is established that "return is not caused by karma," because of the "wandering at will through these worlds" mentioned in the text.

And he does not fear... because action, along with its latent impressions (*savāsanā*), has perished, and since it is impossible for another action to begin, action is not the cause of returning [to worldly existence]. For one who is single-mindedly devoted to the experience of the Lord, whose bliss is unsurpassed and infinite, there is no dependence on anything else; thus, his own will (*svayam*) is not the cause of his own return—this is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "of true resolve" (*satya-saṅkalpa*): this was said with the intention that the resolve, "I shall not cause the liberated ones to return," should not be otherwise. And because the Knower (*jñānin*) is exceedingly dear [to Him], such a resolve exists. "He who speaks thus"—exceedingly...
It is understood—da.

'For I am exceedingly dear to the knower, and he is dear to Me.
All these [others] are indeed noble, but the knower, in My opinion, is My very Self; for he, being disciplined in mind, is established in Me alone as the unsurpassed goal.'"

The proof for [the Lord’s] being dear is as follows: by the words "and not," the reasoning that supports the scriptural statement regarding non-return (*apunarāvṛtti*) has been stated. Thus, "everything is consistent. By the word "everything" (*sarva*), one intends the scriptural texts concerning difference, those concerning non-difference, those enjoining or prohibiting attributes and so forth, the supreme statements regarding the Lord’s grace, sovereignty, and the like, as well as perception and other means of knowledge; the consistency of these is thus declared. The word "iti" refers to the entirety of the meaning expressed in the commentary beginning with "akhila-bhuvana... and so on.

By the word "all" (sarva), the statements of the Śrutis, Smṛtis, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas that have not been specifically cited, as well as the collection of reasonings (tarka) that support them, are intended. Their consistency should be understood by way of this direction. There is indeed here a refutation of all those proofs and reasonings employed by opponents as contradictors of the stated meaning. There is no matter not included within this. Therefore, the intention is that the refutation of the contradicting proofs and reasonings should be investigated in the manner already described.
