Salutation to the lineage of gurus. Salutation to the venerable Rāmānuja. Salutation to Śrī. Salutation to Śrīdhara. The first quarter of the third chapter.

The Section on the Attainment of the Intermediate State (Tadantarapratipattyadhikaraṇa) || 3.1.1 || Composed by the venerable Seneśvarārya: A Compendium of the Logical Principles of the Śārīraka [Mīmāṃsā].

The embodied soul does not go along with the subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣma), for it is easy to obtain them right there; nor does it go with the waters, because of the Vedic revelation that "waters do not become persons. Thus, [the soul] departs together with those [subtle parts].

The embodied soul (*dehī*), being joined with the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣmaiḥ*)—the subtle portions of the elements such as ether (*ākāśa*) and so forth—which are useful for the construction of the body and other functions, does not go [to another place] at the time of attaining another body from the current one; rather, it goes to that very place where it proceeds for the sake of obtaining another body. This is because those subtle elements useful for that purpose are easily available there, since they exist everywhere due to their pervasiveness in the region below the eternal manifestation (*nityavibhūti*). Thus, it is "with ease" (*sukhena*).

[Objection: Because [the soul] is capable of obtaining [a new body], such is the prima facie view. [Reply: It is not so; the aforementioned method is certainly not appropriate, because it is stated in the Śruti: "The waters become the person. Since it is clearly stated in the Śruti that "the elements characterized by water become what is denoted by the word 'body'," the individual soul (jīva) goes together with those subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣma); it does not go alone. || 1 ||
The *Adhikaraṇasārāvali*, composed by the illustrious Vedāntācāryas.

If liberation were not something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), then the formulation of the means for its attainment would be rendered fruitless; yet if it were something to be accomplished, it would be transitory. How then could final release (*apavarga*) be devoid of rebirth? Do not say so; for the realization of Brahman by one devoted to the Supreme is indeed something previously unestablished that must be accomplished, and this [realization], being the destruction of the contraction of the intellect, transcends all limits of time. || 1 ||

Regarding liberation (*mukti*): if the state of the individual soul (*jīva*) as propounded in the scriptures under the term "liberation" were not something to be accomplished—that is, if it were not something to be produced through effort, nor something that arises [as an effect]—then the formulation of the third chapter of the *Śārīraka*, known as the "Chapter on Means" (*Sādhanādhyāya*), would result in being fruitless; it would become purposeless (for the contemplation of means toward a liberation that is not to be accomplished would be equivalent to contemplating the horn of a hare). However, if liberation is indeed something to be accomplished—the state of the soul in the form of liberation—[then the aforementioned formulation is meaningful].

If it were something to be produced through effort, then it would be perishable—it would possess the very nature of passing away (since being a produced entity is the cause for subjecting itself to destruction). This being the case, here—in the Vedāntas—the prescribed *apavarga*—the specific state of the Self known as liberation (here, *apavarga* refers to the particular condition called liberation arising within the Self)—[is not such].

[Or rather: How is it established that [the liberated soul] is "devoid of return"—that is, how is it established that it is not co-located with rebirth within itself? [If this were unestablished,] there would be a contradiction with the scriptural statement, "And he does not return. Do not say so; let such a doubt not arise. Liberation is the experience of Brahman—that liberation described in the scriptures as consisting in the experience of the perfect Supreme Brahman is indeed, prior to the meditation on the Supreme Self, unestablished, meaning its essential nature is unaccomplished in the individual soul (*jīva*).

This liberation—which is to be accomplished by a specific conscious being endowed with the particular means taught in the Vedānta, namely the worship of the Supreme Person—is of a nature that must be brought about. This liberation, which is to be achieved through the worship of the Supreme Person, consists in the destruction of the contraction of the intellect; for while the intellect (the attribute-knowledge) is established as non-contracted by its very nature, its contraction is caused by beginningless karma.

[This refers to] the non-apprehension of the objects consisting of the nature, qualities, and manifestations of the Lord’s own form; and because its nature is that of cessation—for this very reason, it transcends any subsequent limit. Being devoid of temporal limitation thereafter, and possessing an unchanging intrinsic nature, it remains awake. (Therefore, there is not even a trace of any defect [in this view]; that is to say, because there is no destruction of destruction. || 1 ||
In this [Purāṇa], the first two quarters (pādas) generate in living beings the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman;

thereafter, with both [quarters] and all their constituent parts, it declares that [knowledge] in its many varieties. Furthermore, by means of the quarters in sequence, it teaches detachment from sovereignty and the like, as well as longing for the Person of infinite glory, and also the various divisions of knowledge along with their auxiliary means. || 2 ||

In this third chapter, titled "The Means" (*sādhana*), by means of the first two quarters—the first two feet known as "Detachment" (*vairāgya*) and "The Two Marks" (*ubhayaliṅga*)—the author first generates, at the outset of the chapter, the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā-adhikāra*) among sentient beings who are bound to *saṃsāra* due to their transgression of the beginningless teachings of the Lord; that is, he first produces in them the fitness for the knowledge of Brahman, which consists in the perfection of tranquility (*śama*) and so forth, by way of generating detachment from the enjoyment of fruits pertaining to this world and the next.

Having first accomplished [the purpose] through the initial task, he subsequently—by means of both the following two feet known as the "Inclusion of Qualities" (*guṇopasaṃhāra*) and the "Limbs" (*aṅga*)—speaks later (as the subsequent task of this chapter) regarding those transmigrating conscious beings who have attained the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman; addressing those conscious beings, he speaks of that manifold, variously categorized knowledge of Brahman, together with all its limbs without exception, along with everything that assists in the completion of that knowledge. Subsequently...

It makes this clear through its four quarters, following the sequence of their appropriate mutual relationship: (1) detachment from sovereignty and the like—meaning a state of thirstlessness regarding sovereignty and such (by the first quarter); (2) longing for the Person of boundless glory—meaning the living soul’s state of possessing desire solely for the Supreme Person, whose nature is unlimited, infinite, and wondrous majesty (by the second quarter); and (3) reliance on the distinctions of knowledge—

For the sake of liberation, [Bādarāyaṇa]—who desires to favor conscious beings—has correctly expounded: (1) the reliance upon a specific branch of knowledge (suitable for one's own practice) [by means of the third quarter]; (2) its auxiliary means—the entire collection of supportive factors that bring about the perfection of that knowledge and also enhance its excellence [by means of the fourth quarter]. || 2 ||

It is true that for embodied beings whose minds are weary of *saṃsāra*, this first section concerning the body (*śārīraka*) serves the purpose of generating detachment (*vairāgya*); but why was this [section] composed by the authors of the Sūtras? [The answer is: It is for the purpose of placing other attainments on a scale equal to hell, as a means to liberation.
At the beginning, that which is most worthy of honor should be placed; indeed, hasten here, for your own fault is clearly seen. || 3 ||

"Saṃsārodvignacetāḥ" means one whose internal organ (mind) is filled with agitation (or intense fear) due to reflecting upon the continuation of the stream of birth, old age, and death—which has been extending from beginningless time—even after this present life. "Tanubhṛt" means an embodied being (a conscious soul endowed with a specific body and so forth suitable for reflecting on the meaning of the scriptures). "Atra" refers to this portion of the *Śārīraka*—which is included within the *Mīmāṃsā* system consisting of the treatise on the investigation of Dharma—specifically that part which consists of the investigation into the Supreme Brahman, who is the supreme Dharma.

He is qualified for—and thus engages in—the study of the Uttara-mīmāṃsā. (This being the case,) this first section of the third book, titled "Dispassion" (*vairāgya*), which has the purpose of producing detachment from everything other than the Supreme Self—why was it composed by the authors of the *Śārīraka-sūtras*, namely Bādarāyaṇa?

—Or why has it been applied again in the *Śārīraka*? (For, due to the absence of anything yet to be accomplished, it would result in futility. To this objection, the answer is: True—it must indeed be admitted that there is futility in engaging in an activity for the sake of producing detachment (*vairāgya*) when that detachment is already established, and that detachment is established prior to the commencement of the *Śārīraka*. Nevertheless, regarding all other objects of attainment—those other than the Supreme Brahman—which are merely conceivable as things to be acquired...

The weighing against the multitude of hells—the realization of one's equality with the mass of human beings—is something to be utterly avoided; it generates supreme dispassion (*paramavairāgya*). At the commencement of the means to liberation—that is, at the time of beginning the contemplation of the knowledge that serves as the instrument for *apavarga*—this would be most worthy; it would indeed be absolutely necessary, there is no doubt about this. Indeed, the conscious being (*cetana*) who has clearly perceived his own faults is precisely one who has distinctly realized his own nature, both with and without limiting adjuncts (*sopādhika-nirupādhika*). Here—

Regarding the reliance on the means for the attainment of knowledge, he hastens—that is, he proceeds without delay. (Therefore, the intention is that reflection on dispassion at the beginning of the chapter on the means is indeed fruitful. || 3 ||

Furthermore, when the soul’s transition from one body to another occurs—whether in heaven (*divi*) or on earth (*bhuvi*), that is, in the celestial realm or the terrestrial world—the body, senses, and so forth, which serve as the limiting adjuncts for experience and are the very instruments of enjoyment, are like objects fit for enjoyment; they are obtainable and easily acquired precisely where the soul goes by the power of destiny, in whichever place it may go. (This being the case,) [to claim that these are obtained] "in vain" (*mudhā*) from the previous body—that is, from the former body being abandoned—is [unreasonable].

It is indeed fruitless: by what has been taken up—at the time of departure, the vital breaths and senses (prāṇa, indriya, etc.), the means for life, knowledge, and so forth; and even by the subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣma), the subtle portions of the five elements which serve as the means for producing another body—what is the gain here for the individual soul (jīva) who is subject to coming and going? For the atomic (aṇu) soul, whose dimension is limited and who is conscious, there is movement—that is, the transition from one body to another—and likewise the course of the vital breath (prāṇanīti).

In whatever manner—that is, in exactly that way—the Lord, the Supreme Self who is the controller of all, would Himself bring about [the departure] even without relying on the assistance of the subtle elements and so forth; He would certainly accomplish it, for He is not incapable in this regard. Therefore, one should not accept that at the time of death, the individual soul departs together with the subtle elements and the rest.

Regarding the objection that "this is due to [scriptural] authority" (*gauravāt*) in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*): let it not be so. One should not contemplate a meaning contrary to the Veda by means of such a reasoning fabricated from one's own imagination. For, in the case of an independent action—where the effect depends solely upon the Lord’s own volition—and provided that the rule is determined by the Veda alone and is well-established through the Veda, any consideration of parsimony (*lāghava*) or complexity (*gaurava*) applied to a postulated object (*kalpye 'rthe*) is improper, because such a practice would be illogical and irrelevant. || 4 ||
People designate a collection of various kinds by the name of its predominant part; for this very reason of abundance, the group of elements is said to be "water-like" (āpaḥ puruṣavacasaḥ).
Indeed, that all-pervading Lord creates through those [elements] which have been individually and collectively quintuplicated (pañcīkṛta).
Furthermore, the word "faith" (śraddhā) here denotes water, because it is spoken of in the Veda with that specific designation. || 5 ||

The word "śraddhā," when used in its primary sense, denotes water—that is, it expresses the subtle elements characterized by that [water]; it does not, however, denote a particular modification of the mind associated with the Self. This is because in the Vedic statement, "śraddhā indeed is water," it is spoken of as having that same designation—since we observe the use of the word "śraddhā" as being equivalent to a term denoting water. || 5 ||
Having thus conceived these five fires— namely, heaven, Parjanya, earth, man, and woman— the Pañcāgnividyā, together with its ancillaries, [is established].
Through a gradual transformation, the subtle element called *śraddhā* (faith) becomes the moon, rain, food, and semen.
He declares that the winds offer up the very form of living beings, which possesses a body, as an oblation.

Dyu is the world named after the sky, attainable by those conscious of their good deeds, serving as the locus for the experience of happiness; Parjanya is a specific region attainable at the time of descent immediately following the cessation of merit.

(The synonym for *megha*), then—immediately after reaching—the *pṛthvī*, the specific location denoted by the term "earth"; and following that, immediately thereafter, the *puruṣa*, the conscious embodied being who is the enjoyer of the grain and other produce arising from the crops grown on the earth; the *yoṣit* (the object in the form of a woman, who is reached in the form of semen immediately after its presence in the man); and [the womb], the specific location that holds the descending soul within the embryo—thus, these five objects of the aforementioned forms.

Having conceived five fires—endowed with their respective retinues, namely the five groups consisting of five each, associated respectively with the Ādityas and others, the winds and others, the years and others, the speech and others, and the generative organ and others, which are superimposed as the retinues of the fires—one should establish those fires; that is, having superimposed upon them the nature of fire by virtue of their similarity to the attributes of fire, one should meditate upon them as being fivefold, having attained the state of fire.

The subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*), which constitute the oblation (*havya*) and are accompanied by the descending living soul (*jīva*), assume the form of the body-bearing winds—the vital breaths (*prāṇa*)—within the rain-cloud, the earth, the male, and the female; these winds, worthy of being called "Faith" (*śraddhā*) at the outset, attain through a gradual process of transformation (*kramapariṇati*) specific forms consisting of Soma, rain, food, and semen—that is, they attain the particular states known as King Soma, rain, food, and semen.

The *pañcāgnividyā*—a specific portion of the Upaniṣads belonging to the *Chāndogya*—declares, that is, establishes, this meaning: "They offer," meaning "they cast," the subtle form consisting of the five elements into the fire, which is similar [to themselves]. || 6 ||
In the two subsequent chapters known as the *Viṣayādhikaraṇa*, the manner of attaining Brahman is considered along with the means for that attainment.

Therein, in the third chapter on meditation (*Upāsanādhyāya*), meditation—which serves as the means—is considered. Among those, in the first [pāda], the *Jīvadoṣapāda*, the defects of the individual soul (*jīva*) in its states such as waking are treated. In the second [pāda], the *Ubhayaliṅgapāda*, the faultlessness of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) and its nature as a mine of auspicious qualities are established; this is done both to generate a longing for the object to be attained and to produce a state of detachment from everything other than that which is to be attained, for the purpose of commencing meditation.

In that regard, in the section concerning the transition to another body (tadantarapratipattyadhikaraṇa), having raised the doubt that the individual soul (jīva) moving from one body to another goes there unenveloped by subtle elements because such subtle elements are easily available everywhere, it was stated—by means of the question "Do you know how... and its subsequent answer—that the soul goes indeed enveloped by subtle elements.

But the fruit is bound to action: the fruit consisting of birth in a high or low family immediately following the descent is caused solely by the action that motivates it (and is not without cause, as that would lead to the fallacy of spontaneity); and because of the scriptural statement, "those of foul conduct [enter] a foul [womb], those of beautiful conduct [enter] a beautiful womb" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.7), which clarifies this—it must be accepted that the soul descends while still possessing a remainder of its karma. || 2 ||

—0— The performer of ritual action (*karmī*): having performed rites such as those prescribed by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti* with a desire for their fruits, if that conscious being, upon death—that is, having attained separation from the body—[proceeds] in due order to smoke, to night—that is, to the specific stations known as smoke and night; to the dark fortnight—that is, the fortnight called "black" which is obscured by darkness; to the six months of the sun's southern course—that is, the six months caused by the sun's transition during its southern solstice (the station known as the Southern Course); and thereafter, immediately following that, to the world of the ancestors (*pitṛloka*).

He goes to—the place called the world of the ancestors (*pitṛloka*), then the sky (*gagana*) which is subsequently designated by the term "space" (*ākāśa*), and then the specific station designated by the term "moon" (*candra*)—that is, having reached each of these in succession at the time of ascent, he proceeds.

But upon returning—that is, at the time of descending back to earth after having experienced the fruits of meritorious deeds—one [obtains] from the Moon (from the station called Candra) the two specific stations named Sky and Wind (gagana-satataga); then smoke and cloud (dhūmam abbhram ca megham)—the station called Smoke, the station called Water-bearer, and the station denoted by the word "Cloud" which is in the state of raining water; and then the plants and so forth (hyādīn), beginning with the herbs, together with sentient beings.

Then [the soul] reaches those worthy of being devoured and so forth; then it reaches the *retassica*—that particular man who will become its father by discharging semen into a woman—and thereafter, the mother—that woman who will attain the state of its mother. Thus the living being (*jīva*), wandering as a sovereign of torments through unstable, specific locations whose nature is to revolve incessantly like a wheel amidst suffering, goes from one place to another. || 8 ||

The term *caraṇapada* (the word "foot") is applied even to ritual acts such as sacrifice; it is primary (*mukhya*) by way of its function (*vṛtti*), precisely because of the abundant grounds for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*) established through the power of linguistic usage—just as in the case of conduct (*ācāra*)—and not because of secondary figurative usage (*gauṇavṛtti*). Therefore, it does not apply merely to a single part or a subordinate element alone.

It is not to be suppressed—it cannot be described as having its functions ceased—birth (*jāti*), and so forth: birth, lifespan, and experience, which arise from the differentiation of karma and are accomplished by distinct karmic causes, being thus established as objects of valid cognition through the words of the Seers (*ārṣavacana*); [furthermore, it is] to be accomplished through conduct—that is, to be brought about by practices such as the *saṃdhyā* rites—and to be reflected upon—to be determined by carefully contemplating with a mind refined by the ascertainment of the meaning of the scriptures; it is not to be determined as being fruitless. || 9 ||

Regarding the transgression of established conduct, the sages remembered the specific prohibitions for each step, as well as the destruction of ancient sins and the fitness for meritorious deeds resulting from following them.
One should not harbor the doubt that conduct may be abandoned under the notion that heaven is attained through mere virtuous acts alone;
for when conduct is discarded, even the entire collection of the Vedas is no purifier than water trodden upon by a dog.

When there is a transgression—that is, the non-performance and thus the violation—of established customs such as the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*) that have come down through tradition, the great sages (*maharṣis*), who know the nature of dharma and adharma, repeatedly and at every step recalled in their own *smṛtis* the faults consisting of sin, such as falling from one's status; and by following those [recollections], there occurs the destruction of ancient sins through the performance of the established customs.

The Smṛtis have declared that there is the destruction of previously accumulated sins, as well as the fitness for performing virtuous deeds that bestow heaven and other rewards upon those deserving of meritorious actions. Therefore, since there is the incurrence of sin from transgressing established conduct (*ācāra*) and the attainment of results such as the destruction of evil through its performance, one should not entertain the doubt of abandoning it—meaning one should not harbor the suspicion of neglecting the *saṃdhyā* and other rites—based on the notion that "heaven comes from mere virtuous action alone," or the thought that "heaven is attained simply by performing the rituals prescribed for the day. Thus, no doubt regarding their abandonment should be entertained.

The Veda Section: Even the collection of the Vedas, which serves as the purifier of the world, does not act as a cleanser—that is, it does not produce purity—for a person who has abandoned right conduct and forsaken practices such as the *saṃdhyā* prayers; rather, it is like water placed upon a dog's hide. || 10 ||

Now, by the principle of "one who has only one more birth" (*ekabhavika*), when the remainder of karma is eliminated, the connection of what remains after being experienced is declared according to the principle of "the passing away of what was done" (*kṛtātyayanyāya*). (113)
Thus ends the section concerning the passing away [of those who have performed works]. || 2 ||

"For all"—meaning for all embodied beings alike, both those who perform sacrifices and other meritorious deeds (*iṣṭādikārin*) and those who perform the opposite (*aniṣṭādikārin*)—when the fall of the body occurs, that is, when death has arrived, the attainment of the moon—the arrival at the station in the form of the moon—is "regulated," meaning it is necessarily occurring and unavoidable. This is stated [in the scripture]: "All of them go to the moon alone. Therefore, because it is so declared by the Śruti, even for those whose conduct is dominated by sin—[those who perform] only...

If it is argued that for evildoers, that conjunction with the moon is one that precedes their arrival in hell—that is, it occurs immediately prior to reaching hell—such a suspicion is not tenable. This is because of the scriptural statement, "That world is not filled by them," which means "The other world (the moon) is not filled by those who perform only evil deeds. Thus, the word "all" [in the context of the Vedic text] refers to this.

The word "all" (*sarva*) found in the sentence, "They all go to the moon itself," would be restricted—that is, limited to referring only to those who have performed sacrifices and the like—and thus would not, without such restriction, convey the sense of everyone. Therefore, because that "all" in the sentence refers only to all those who have performed meritorious acts such as sacrifices, they [the others] are those who have committed only evil deeds.

At the end of that torment—that is, at the conclusion of the hellish experience of suffering—they suddenly and forcibly, without even requiring a fifth oblation, enter and take birth in a contemptible womb here in this world—a sinful womb conducive to experiencing the remaining fruits of their own associated sins.

(11) For living beings, the attainment of birth in the various wombs such as the amniotic sac and so forth is diverse due to the ripening of their karma; it is characterized by many merits and sins, and, like a slanderer, it requires a fifth oblation.

In the same way, by means of various auspicious and intense [deeds], many have become well-known as having departed immediately upon the fall of the body after attaining divine forms, celestial chariots, and the like, via the path of smoke and so forth. For living beings (*jīva*) engaged in the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), the attainment of birth—the acquisition of a physical body within the skin-sack of the womb or within eggs and so on—due to the ripening of karma (*karmapāka*), that is, through specific transformations of those actions, occurs in a manifold, indescribable, and most wonderful manner; this depends upon the "fifth oblation" (*pañcamāhuti*), which is established by the Vedas regarding the attainment of birth.
Necessity also arises from the majority of merits and demerits, as well as from a preponderant mass of merit or a corresponding mass of demerit; thus, it is generally characterized by exception.

It is not universally true that [birth] is free from exception; for just as birth itself ought to be distinguished by specific merit and demerit, so too—in the attainment of birth—just as there are exceptions regarding the fifth oblation, the path of smoke and so forth—the departure via the path of smoke and the rest—is likewise subject to exceptions. How many, indeed—how many countless sentient beings—by means of intense and preeminent merits serving as the instruments, at the fall of the body—the time of the falling away of the attained body—[attain] a divine form?

Even the celestial chariots (*vimāna*) and other such extraordinary forms of specialized appearance attainable by those in heaven—as well as the divine chariots and so forth that serve as the means for traveling toward the destination to be reached—they immediately, at that very moment, having obtained them through the grace of fate, went to the world of heaven and other realms; they are well-known, having been heard of in the *Itihāsas*, *Purāṇas*, and other such texts. || 12 ||
A summary of the meaning of the topic.

In the section concerning those who perform undesirable actions and so forth: having raised the doubt that even evildoers go to the moon, because the scripture states without distinction that "all who depart from this world go to the moon," [the following is addressed].

Having stated, "Now, those here in the village who worship with the thought, 'Sacrifices and meritorious works are gifts,'" and so on, the text continues with "they pass into smoke," etc., thereby teaching that the path of the fathers (pitṛyāṇa) belongs exclusively to those who perform sacrifices and the like. Furthermore, since the statement "all of them go to the moon" must be interpreted as referring specifically to those who perform sacrifices and the like, it is concluded that evildoers do not go to the moon.
In the *Adhikaraṇasārāvali*, it is stated:

"That the two oblations possess a body is indisputable in the first and last [stages]; likewise, birth occurs in ether, air, and so forth, because of the application of the root *bhū*—this is not the essence. According to the principle of 'the semen and blood' (*retaḥ-siṃbhāvanī*), there is no separate mention; this is merely the mantra."

The fruit to be accomplished through merit in the two worlds of heaven (*dyubhuvau*) is taught here [in the Veda], yet there is no mention of enjoyment in the interval. Regarding the first and last oblations: in the first oblation—which was stated as "The gods offer faith; from that oblation, King Soma arises"—which brings about the state of being Soma, [and likewise] in the case of [the statement]: "A man pours forth semen..."

When it is stated, "In the fifth oblation, the waters come to possess human speech," regarding this final oblation which brings about the state of being a person, the possession of a body is beyond dispute—that is, the state of having a body consisting of a physical form is uncontested. Just as that is the case, so too in the instances of becoming ether, air, and so forth—in the states of ether, air, and the rest—there must be birth alone; that is, the assumption of a body must constitute that respective state, because of the etymological derivation of the root *bhū* (to become) at both the beginning and the end.

The claim that the root *bhū* is connected here as well (and that there is no reason for its meaning to be inconsistent) is unsubstantial; such a reflection is weak (far removed from supporting logic).

According to the principle of the "semen-discharger" (*retaḥ-sic*)—"he who discharges semen becomes that very thing"—by the logic of attaining the state of the semen-discharging person, what is intended here regarding the ether and so forth is not a separate [substance], but rather a specific relation unfit for distinct cognition or conventional usage, which is expressed by the term "becoming ether" (*ākāśādi-bhāva*).

In this context, that [result] does not consist in having those various bodies as its form. "Here"—in this section—wherever it may be, "in heaven or on earth," the "fruit" to be accomplished through merit—the purpose consisting of enjoyment—is declared in the Śruti as occurring at the beginning and the end of the oblation. Furthermore, "in between"—that is, after attaining the state of a deity and prior to attaining the state of a mortal (within these two intervals)—there is no enjoyment; there is no possibility of experiencing the fruit of merit. It is merely a state of abiding in those respective places.

For those who perform sacrifices and other rites, as they descend here [to earth], there occurs a refinement of their state into water and so forth, according to the principle of attaining the nature of that [element]. (115)
Space: the state of abiding in space and so forth, as described in the Śruti, for the individual soul (jīva) descending [from Brahman].

(Regarding the state: "Condition" (*avasthā*) means stage; because there is no rule for delay in the stage of union with the semen (*retaḥ-saṅgata-avasthā*), there is "non-determination" (*aniyati*). This is because it is devoid of any fixed limit of time regarding the forms of speed or delay, such as "for a long time" or "not for a long time," since there is an absence of explicit mention in the Veda by words like "long" (*cira*) which denote delay, or by words like "not long" (*acira*) which denote the meaning of speed. (Thus, in the prima facie argument. This is not so—such a doubt is not appropriate.

Because the spontaneous activity—that is, the operation directed toward making known the meaning residing in the Vedic sentence established by its own nature—determines one of the two alternatives; for (hi), from the grains and so forth—that is, from the objects existing in the form of rice and other such things which serve as the locus for the soul's abiding.

Regarding those [beings] who have become limiting conditions (*avadhibhūta*), the scripture states: "it is more difficult to emerge" (*durniṣprapataram*). This word *durniṣprapatataram*—which indicates that the accomplishment of emergence is more painful—is recited in the Śruti with its final vowel elided (*luptaitakāra*). Therefore, by virtue of this scriptural word acting as a restrictive factor (*niyāmaka*) which indicates a delay in emergence from the state of being rice and so forth, [the soul] previously—in the prior time consisting of the state of being ether and so forth—emerges "quickly," that is, without any delay at all.

"Of those respective states"—that is, of the conditions such as space, air, mist, clouds, and so forth—"the relinquishing," meaning the abandonment, "is understood"—that is, determined without doubt—by the power of the sentence, namely by the power residing in the scriptural statement to convey its necessary meaning. || 14 ||
The Section Concerning the Presiding of Another (Anyādhiṣṭhitādhikaraṇa) || 3.1.6 ||
A Compendium of the Collection of Aphorisms on the Embodied Soul.

"From the specific term 'are born,' living beings indeed come to possess bodies such as those of rice and other grains. However, this designation of 'birth' is not figurative, because there is no cause for it [to be so understood] and because [the state of being a body] occurs subsequently. (6)

Because of the specific term "are born"—that is, because there exists this very specific word "are born" which denotes birth consisting of a connection with a body—the individual souls (jīvas), while descending from specific locations such as heaven, become possessors of birth, existing indeed as bodies of rice, barley, and so forth.

[The opponent] objects: "But [the souls] do not possess mere contact with that [rice]. This objection is not at all sound. The designation "birth" (*janana*), expressed by the word "they are born" (*jāyante*), is a description of origination; however, it is merely figurative—being metaphorical simply because of the attainment of another state—and not primary (in the sense of establishing a specific state called "birth"), because the cause for that [primary birth] is absent: since the karma that brings about experience in the form of rice has not been exhausted, and because [the soul] exists thereafter.

This is because, immediately following the attainment of the five oblations just explained, there is the presentation of the cessation [of the subtle body] due to the existence of karma—whether pleasant or foul—which brings about the body and, through that, brings about experience. || 6 ||

If it is argued that trees and other immobile beings such as herbs lack selfhood—that is, they are not presided over by a Self—and thus do not establish or maintain [themselves] (since there is a necessity for the fourfold body to be presided over by a Self), and therefore [one might suspect] that the descending soul enters into a body consisting of rice and the like—[the author replies: this is not correct. For when the process has begun to be described, specifically in the enumeration of the fruits of merit alone, and in the calculation of the sequence of results arising from merit alone...

Because it would be improper to speak of "stationariness"—that is, because it would result in the inappropriateness of describing the fruit of karmic defects in the form of stationariness—therefore, [the soul's connection] is like that in the case of the "semen-discharging" (retaḥ-sig) [ancestors], i.e., like the connection in the father's body consisting of mere contact [of the conscious being destined to become a future son], as in the case of the body of the father who emits the semen.

In the case of the stationary (sthāvare)—that is, the immobile—and even in another body (anyadehe)—a body presided over by a different self—the Śruti employs the verbal root *jan*, which denotes birth (*janim*), in a figurative sense (*gauṇyavṛttyā*). Alternatively, the meaning is that the Śruti uses the term "birth" figuratively to refer merely to conjunction (*saṃśleṣamātram*). || 15 ||
It is argued that even sacrifices such as the *iṣṭi*, though enjoined by the Vedas, are improper because they involve violence;
furthermore, it is incorrect to say that a virtuous person experiences a portion of that sin in the form of rice and other grains.
For it has been stated through mantras and explanatory passages (*arthavādas*) that the sacrifice is for the benefit of the animal, and thus this [violence] is like medical treatment.
Manu declares that this killing in a sacrifice is not killing; another [teacher], skilled in censure, praises the opposite.

Sacrificial rites (*iṣṭādi*)—actions such as sacrifices—which are enjoined by the scripture known as the Veda, taught with great affection for sentient beings, and which are indeed righteous because they are prescribed by that very scripture acting for their welfare; even though they do not deviate from reason, they are nevertheless impure because they involve injury to living beings (*hiṃsāyogāt*), namely, the slaughter of animals performed in animal sacrifices and the like. Consequently, due to being permeated by sin, the conscious person who performs such meritorious acts as sacrifices is a "doer of good deeds" (*sukṛtī*).

The claim that "the sinful portion" refers to a part of the sin connected to a ritual act prescribed by scripture which yields heavenly bliss, and that [the soul] "experiences" this in its state as a stationary being such as rice or barley—attained through its own [past actions]—by way of experiencing their fruits, is also untenable. For, on this view, the state of being a stationary being for the descending soul would merely be the experience of the fruit of sin occurring immediately after the experience of the fruit of merit; thus, even mentioning it in the interim would not be improper. Therefore, this too is incorrect.

Even the suspicion [of sin] is not appropriate; for this act of killing—which consists of an operation conducive to the separation of a beast's life-force—is considered beneficial, being declared by mantras such as "na vā u vetan triyase" and by explanatory passages (arthavādas) such as "hiraṇyaśarīraḥ" to be for the welfare of the beast, that is, to be of a nature that serves as a cause for its future happiness. Therefore, because it is of a beneficial nature, this act of slaughtering a beast, though suspected of being violence, is like medical treatment.

It is similar to the physician’s activity of administering medicine, not to the activity of a killer. *Manu* refers either to a specific Vedic mantra or to the sage named Manu. In the *yajña*, that is, the *śrauta* sacrifice dedicated to the gods, "this killing"—the specific activity consisting of the ritual slaughter of animals (*paśusaṃjñapana*) and so forth, which might be suspected of being "killing"—is called "non-killing" (*avadha*). He says—that is, he declares—that because it does not produce sin, it is not in reality denotable by the word "killing. As for the censure found here regarding sacrificial acts and the like, it is a censure arising from the statement that they involve violence; there is no other [intention] regarding the act itself.

It praises and extols the other knowledge; that is, it makes one understand: "One should not strive for the impermanent happiness of heaven and so forth; one should strive only for the eternal liberation. || 16 ||
"The slaughter of an animal here would assign blame to the agent and benefit the sacrifice;
therefore, the followers of Sāṃkhya say that this [scripture] prohibits [slaughter] and does not enjoin it. [Reply:
When the harm to the animal has been refuted, such a claim is certainly not appropriate, for there is the alternative of using a flour-animal and so forth.
Since it is restricted to specific qualified persons at that particular time, there can be no contradiction anywhere. || 17 ||

In this context—namely, in Vedic rituals such as the animal sacrifice (*paśuyāga*)—the act of immolating the animal, which consists of the procedure of slaughtering the animal, might indeed produce a fault for the agent—the person performing the sacrifice by means of the animal—by generating sin caused by the injury to a living being; and yet, it may also serve the purpose of the ritual (*ṛtu*) by imparting an excellence to it. What contradiction is there between these two?

Therefore—the Sāṃkhya followers (Sāṃkhyabhaktāḥ), those who follow the Sāṃkhya system, have stated that since there is no contradiction between causing harm to a person and being an auxiliary to a sacrifice, this injunction "one should immolate an animal" (paśumālabheta)—which is the injunction for animal immolation—does not set aside, but rather sublates by way of exception, this general prohibition of injury established in the Upaniṣads (śrutyantasiddha), namely, "one should not injure" (na hiṃsyāt). Thus, the objection regarding the animal's lack of benefit—that the sacrifice consists in the injury of an animal—is shaken off.

When [the objection] has been refuted by Vedic statements that indicate [the attainment of] cattle and heaven, it is certainly not proper—not indeed reasonable—to strive for an equalization by separating the two objects of concern, namely, the production of defects in the performer and the contribution to the ritual (*kratu*), without resorting to the relationship between a general rule and its exception (*utsarga-apavāda*). As for the "method of performing the sacrifice based on a flour-made animal" (*piṣṭapaśvādi-kalpa*)—that is, the manner of completing the sacrifice by means of an animal made of flour—that [is intended for] those respective occasions...

"Fixed" means that which conforms to the specific rules established according to particular times and particular qualifications; thus, in any given matter, there shall be no contradiction—no inconsistency whatsoever will arise (and so, according to the established order, everything is entirely consistent). || 17 ||
Furthermore, for one who abandons here the sequence of general rules and exceptions (*utsarga-apavāda*), what kind of "constant non-violence" could there be?

Indeed, for you, no pure [action] would ever be established, since every injunctive term (*vidhi-pada*) is touched by its respective prohibition. Where untruth and so forth are enjoined, and subsequently an expiation (*niṣkṛti*) is prescribed on account of that, it may happen thus only as a last resort (*agatyā*), like other cases; or else, it is merely caused by that [untruth]. (18)

Furthermore—and moreover—in this context, regarding the locus of general and particular injunctions, they abandon the principle of the general rule and the exception (*utsargāpavādanyāya*), which consists in the form: "The scope of a general injunction is that which is distinct from the scope of a particular injunction."

For one who does not accept [the authority of the Veda], such as a Sāṃkhya and others—who wish to avoid the sin incurred by non-performance [of obligatory rites] yet have no desire for fruits such as heaven—the violence produced by the immolation of animals and so forth, which is inseparable from the performance of obligatory rites like the Jyotiṣṭoma: how can it be determined what kind of violence this is—is it produced by passion, or is it obtained through scriptural injunction? For you, who abandon the principle of general rule and exception (*utsargāpavādanyāya*), where could there be anything "pure"—that is, free from being mixed with sin—[even in the case of that which is the object of an injunction]?

Nowhere would it be established—that is, its true nature would never be attained—for indeed, everything that has become the object of a positive injunction (*vidhi*) is seen everywhere to have its very essence permeated by the respective specific prohibitions (*niṣedha*) pertaining to each particular context; thus, in specific instances such as marriage and the like, even that which is "untrue" (*asatya*)—namely, speaking falsehoods and so forth—is *vaidha*, meaning it becomes the locus of scriptural authorization (*abhyanujñā*).

Following that—and immediately thereafter—the expiation (*niṣkṛti*), which is the means of removing the fault arising from such causes as speaking untruths, has been ordained and made known by the scripture itself in those specific instances. This occurs out of necessity—that is, because there is no other way (*agati*) due to the distinction between the scope of injunctions and prohibitions, characterized by the relationship of general rule and exception (*utsarga-apavāda*). Thus, both the injunction and its corresponding expiation are established solely on the basis of the scripture.

Let it be established as such, or rather, like other cases—just as in the case of an injunction for speaking falsehood—it is merely on account of that cause; that is, relying solely upon the fact of speaking falsehood as the occasion (and not by considering it a fault), the eating of food free from pungent and salty substances and so forth is enjoined. || 18 ||
The conclusion of the verse.

Embracing by means of subtle elements, being assisted by the remainder of karma, the non-ascension of the unmeritorious, and similarity with ether and the other elements. (7)
In that regard, the non-durable state of rice and other grains, as well as their coagulation—these six meanings have been correctly considered by means of this [eighth] quarter-verse. (8)

*Bhūta-vangaḥ*—(In the first section: At the time of attaining another body, the soul departs only when it is joined with the five subtle elements (*bhūtas*) that serve as the means for the commencement of the new body; as it is said—(In the second section: At the time of descending after the experience of heaven and so forth, its state is maintained precisely through the accompaniment of the remainder of its own experienced karma; (In the third section: Only sinners ascend to the moon.

...as if wounded—(in the fourth [verse]) the state of the self becoming ether and so forth during the descent consists in its having a resemblance to ether and so forth; therein... the station—(in the fifth) the absence of delay in remaining in those stations such as ether and so forth; ... the lack of hindrance... likewise—(in the sixth) the state of the self, as described in the Śruti, becoming rice and so forth consists merely in its being in close contact with them. These are the six meanings—thus these sixfold meanings are properly considered—that is, skillfully investigated—by this quarter [of the verse] beginning with the third quarter. || 7, 8 ||

They say that even liberation—known as the departure from the bonds of *saṃsāra*—belongs only to the unmanifest (*avyakta*), which is a modification (*vikāra*) of *prakṛti* denoted by the term "unmanifest"; and they say that even the living being (*jīva*), though regarded as existing through the state of *saṃsāra*, is beginningless (*anādi*).

They [the Sāṃkhyas] assert that the entity (*bhāva*) is liberated by its very nature from beginningless time (and not through the practice of means). Regarding these aforementioned two types of conventionalists, he [the author], by means of these logical arguments (*nayaiḥ* = *adhikaraṇaiḥ*), has set aside—meaning he has rejected—the view (*manīṣām*) of such a kind, namely, a cognition that fails to grasp the true state of things concerning the nature of the Self, its actions, their fruits, and liberation. This third chapter, titled the "Chapter on Detachment" (*vairāgyapāda*), has thus excluded what is not intended by the Śruti. || 19 ||

In this context, there are six meanings for the word *pāda*. Here, one who has abandoned the body along with the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*) may ascend to heaven; then, descending with the residual karma (*anuśaya*), his path is divided according to the measure [of that residue].
There would be no such thing as dwelling in the moon or similar states for one who has taken the path to hell.
Therefore, the descent from the celestial realms is swift, whereas the connection with the bodies of others—beginning with rice—is long-lasting. || 20 ||

In this quarter—specifically in the first part of the third chapter, titled "Detachment" (vairāgya)—the following points are determined and concluded: six in number, 1) here in this mortal world, the living being (jīva), while abandoning the body (vapuḥ)—the physical form previously assumed—goes to another world (iyāt) accompanied by the subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣmaiḥ)—that is, together with the five subtle elements that serve as the material cause for the commencement of a new body; 2) [and] having experienced the group of objects...

One whose merit is exhausted through the attainment of the experience of heaven, which is the fruit of merit, yet who remains possessed of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*)—that is, still joined with the remnants of karma already experienced—and whose path is divided by the *mātrās* (the lunar digits), having deviated slightly from the upward path, would descend—that is, he would undergo a descent from the celestial realm back toward the earth. For those who resort to the path of hell—those who rely solely on the path of hell by performing exclusively sinful deeds—there would be no such thing as dwelling in the moon or similar states; it simply would not exist for them.

4) Regarding "in space and so forth" (*ambarādau*): at the time of reaching the state of space and so on, "concomitance" (*sahatvam*) means precisely equality with space and the like; it does not mean having space and so forth as a body. 5) Therefore—due to the location of space and so forth—the descent is "swift," meaning the process of returning occurs without delay. 6) Regarding "in rice and so forth" (*trīhipū*): in a supreme body consisting of rice, barley, and the like—that is, in the body of another living being—for a long time, meaning for a delayed duration; however, "union" (*yoga*) during the time of descent is merely a contact of the soul; it is not the state of having that as a body. — Thus [ends verse] 20.

A Compendium of the Collection of Logical Principles Concerning the Body (Śārīraka).
The desire to undertake [the path] is established by the investigation into the modes of going and coming;
however, if one does not perceive some fault residing within oneself, then one falls into error regarding others. || 1 ||

Reflection on the manner of going and coming: the inquiry—conducted in the preceding section—into the manner in which the individual soul (*jīvātman*) departs from the body, proceeds to another body, travels to another world for that purpose, and returns from that other world to this earth; [this was done] for the sake of accomplishing the intense desire (*utkaṭecchā*) regarding the meditation (*upāsana*) enjoined by the Vedāntas with the attainment of Brahman as its goal, so that any given living being may [realize] that which resides in the Self.

If one does not perceive the defect existing within the individual self—that is, the portion consisting of that which is not the goal of human life—then, provided that such a portion never exists at all, [only then would it be so]; however, when [the transmigrating self's state of being composed of what is not the goal of human life] becomes inlaid through constant contemplation of its own nature throughout the states of waking and so forth, then indeed one worships only the Supreme Self (which is far removed from even the scent of such non-goal-oriented human aims)—that is, the faultless and unconditioned Self.
For the sake of attaining the manifestation of one's own true nature, he worships by means of the practice of meditation. || 1 ||

By means of its own unique attributes, Bādarāyaṇa described—in many ways—that very same Supreme Brahman already defined; here, within the second quarter (pāda) of the present third chapter—which is devoted to propounding the means that serve as the instruments for attaining Brahman—he has drawn back that subject for further reflection, a re-examination like chewing what has already been chewed, preceded by this drawing back: "for what purpose? (i.e., for what fruit?).

Is it being done? (The meaning is: no new fruit whatsoever is accomplished. Not so—it is not appropriate to raise such a doubt; for the sciences (*vidyās*), consisting of the knowledge of Brahman, the knowledge of the one made of bliss (*ānandamaya-vidyā*), and so forth, are the means for attaining Brahman.

The author of the Sūtras clarifies—that is, explains in detail by means of analytical exposition—the Supreme Brahman, which is the perfected means [to liberation]. He defines it clearly through its two characteristics: freedom from all defects and being the source of all auspicious qualities. For that clear definition of the Supreme Brahman is established precisely through the specific nature of its forms—namely, the attributes, glories, and so forth related to Brahman—for the sake of extinguishing the thirst for objects of attainment in all individual souls.

In this [work], He extensively expounds—that is, elucidates—the state of being a perfected means (*siddhopāyatva*) of the all-pervading Supreme Self, which possesses both the nature of being the goal to be attained (*prāpyatva*) and the nature of being the means that attains it; a state distinct from the "means-to-be-accomplished" (*sādhyopāyatva*) found in [ordinary] knowledge, and characterized by perfection (*siddhatva*). Likewise, He explains the state of being the goal (*upeyatva*)—which is co-located with the state of being the means—as well as the state of being the goal to be attained (*prāpyatva*), for the purpose of generating a specific, intense longing preceded by a lack of thirst for other objects toward the Supreme Brahman, which inherently possesses the quality of being the goal to be attained.

In the section on the "Two-fold Characteristics" (*ubhayaliṅga-pāda*): (Therefore, even though the established Brahman is described here in this chapter on the means of proof (*sādhana-adhyāya*), it does not give rise to any such issues as irrelevance or tautology; this is the intended meaning. || 1 ||

If Brahman is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), then the division of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) according to qualities here is false; if you say that this [division] exists through these imagined qualities, then there is a contradiction with the scriptures (*śruti*), nor is there even a sequence of perception here.
Furthermore, if you claim its qualitylessness is eternal, then effort for the sake of pacifying defects is in vain.
And if ugliness were the very nature [of the body], this quarter-verse is for the purpose of refuting the opponent's position. || 2 ||

If the Supreme Brahman—the object of worship and the goal to be attained—is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇya*), meaning if the absolute absence of all qualities is its ultimate nature, then here—in the *Sādhanādhyāya* (the third chapter) of the *Śārīraka*—the classification of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) based on qualities, that is, the distinct designation of those meditations taught as means for attaining Brahman which are grounded in the qualities of the Supreme Self serving as attributes of the object of worship, would be useless (*vitatha*). That is to say, this classification of the knowledge of Brahman based on qualities would be purposeless.

If you suspect, "Let it be by means of these imagined [qualities]," meaning "let it be through qualities merely superimposed," then there is a violation of the scriptural view; for this would result in a contradiction of the purport of the scripture (which states: "Knowledge, power, and action are His very nature"). Furthermore, in this context—namely, the sphere of meditation for the sake of liberation—even the method seen in passages such as "The mind is Brahman," which consists of the superimposition of the attributes of one thing upon another for the sake of a specific result (the sequence of visualization), cannot at all be asserted if you maintain that [Brahman] is eternally faultless.

If you accept that Brahman is eternally free from defects, then every effort for the pacification of defects—such as the hearing of Vedānta, tranquility (*śama*), self-control (*dama*), and so forth, which belong to the individual soul (*jīva*) who is distinct from Brahman—is also conducive to the removal of defects.

If it were argued that "effort would be in vain—meaning useless—if [Brahman's faultlessness] were merely to be postulated; for if it were so, Brahman's faultlessness would not be eternal, but rather something merely to be assumed," then [the consequence would be] that "defilement would be its very nature"—that is, Brahman's state of possessing faults would be inherent. This second section of the second chapter, beginning with the sūtra *ubhayaliṅgāt*, is intended precisely to refute those who hold such views, namely the proponents of Māyā. || 2 ||

Furthermore, how could there be, in that which is devoid of distinctions, the state of being an object of thought at the outset, the status of being an object of valid cognition, the nature of bliss arising from itself, and the consciousness of becoming manifold as its presiding controller?
There would be the abandonment of the meaning of all the scriptures, the contradiction of one's own words, and subversion by all means of valid knowledge.
Thus, for those possessed of deceit and insolence, the section on the meditation upon the qualified state is also untenable. (3)

Furthermore, at the outset—that is, at the commencement of the treatise—there are the following attributes of Brahman: its state as an object of inquiry (*jijñāsya*); its being the objective domain of valid cognition (*pramiti-viṣayatā*); its self-evident nature (*svapramātva*), which is its self-luminous essence (*svayaṃprakāśa-svarūpatva*); its nature as bliss (*sukhatva*), consisting in its exclusive concentration on bliss; its being the substratum of the universe (*viśvādhiṣṭhānatā*), that is, its being the locus for the superimposition of the world; and its resolve to become manifold (*svabahubhavana-dhīḥ*), which is the volition to attain a state of multiplicity within itself. (Thus ends this section on the attributes.)

How could that [distinction] exist in Brahman, which is without distinction and whose nature consists solely of a subject devoid of attributes? (If one accepts the unreality of these very qualities—such as being the object of inquiry—that were stated for the sake of preserving its lack of distinction,) it would entail the abandonment of every single meaning established by the Śruti, or the consequence that all the Śrutis are devoid of purpose, or the contradiction of one's own words—the occurrence of a mutual conflict between the "lack of distinction" and "being the object of inquiry" asserted by oneself—and [the abandonment of] everything...

Furthermore, there is sublation by all means of valid cognition—namely perception, inference, and scripture—and their own stated thesis is contradicted by those who resort to the doctrine of *māyā*. This consequence applies to the Advaitins, who are false-speakers characterized by such audacity as to claim: "By relying on a single entity called *māyā*, we can account for everything. When considered in this manner, the section concerning the meditation on Brahman with attributes (*saguṇa-dśopāsanā-pāda*) is intended solely to establish the practice of meditation upon Brahman during the state of having attributes.

The third quarter, which is the section on the "Combination of Attributes" (*Guṇopasaṃhāra-pāda*), is also difficult to maintain—its singular position is hard to establish. (Therefore, the implication is that the entire *Śārīraka* [Brahma-sūtra] consists of nothing but such difficulties for them. (3) (292) If it is argued: "If that Brahman, which is free from defects and rich in attributes, were to be contemplated here again, then how could the reflection upon the states of the individual soul (*jīva*) such as dreaming and so forth be consistent? We reply: No; for the purpose of establishing the manifold greatness of Brahman, beginning with its being the creator of the objects of dreams.
This is presented here in order to demonstrate that this living being is as utterly dependent [on another] as a pearl is to its own setting.

In this quarter—namely, in this commenced "Quarter on the Two Characteristics"—if that Brahman, which is free from defects (having a nature consisting solely of faultlessness) and rich in qualities (having a nature completely filled with infinite auspicious attributes), and which is the goal to be attained and the perfected means, [is indeed such]...

If it is argued: "If [the soul] were to be reflected upon—that is, if there were an investigation—then how could the 'reflection on the soul' (jīva-manana), which is the rational contemplation of the states of the individual self such as dreaming and deep sleep, be consistent? In what manner would it be appropriate? (Because the description of the attributes of the individual soul is irrelevant in a section devoted to describing the attributes of the Lord)," we say: No—this is not correct. For here, in this chapter (*pāda*) devoted to the subsumption of the attributes of the Supreme Self, this reflection on the states of the individual soul, such as dreaming and so forth, [is relevant].

For the sake of clearly realizing the manifold majesty of the Supreme Brahman—consisting of its being the creator of objects pertaining to the dream state, which are inconceivable and of an exceedingly wonderful nature—and likewise for the purpose of making known the extreme dependence upon the Supreme Self of this transmigrating individual soul (*jīvātman*) in its own state of liberation, there is no inconsistency whatsoever. || 4 ||
some have studied the first half-verse of this quarter, and the remainder of the preceding quarter.
"But the latter half [of the verse] is not directly connected [to the preceding], because it mentions various qualities for the purpose of meditation (*upāsti*).

This is not very pleasing, due to the reversal of skill in the manner of narration; for while in the description of Brahman there is the attribution of the defects of the individual soul (*jīva*), here, however, that very [attribution] serves as the face for establishing its opposite. (Verse 5)

Some—certain individuals engaged in investigating the meaning of the *Śārīraka* [Brahma-sūtra]—regard the first half of this third chapter on "The Two-fold Characteristics" (*ubhayaliṅga-pāda*), which consists of the first four sections (*adhikaraṇa*), as supplementary to the preceding section on "Detachment" (*vairāgya-pāda*). They hold that the remainder of this chapter is beneficial to it, insofar as it establishes the defects pertaining to the states of dreaming and deep sleep belonging to the individual soul (*jīva*) as defined therein. (And likewise...)
The latter half, however, follows immediately after that—the latter half of this chapter, consisting of four sections beginning with "Upāsya... which proceeds immediately thereafter.

Because of the statement "not so stated"—that is, for the reason that the specific attributes of the Lord which are conducive to the meditation on the Supreme Self are expounded therein—they have understood and declared it to be "directly connected," meaning it is related to the primary subject matter of this [chapter] directly, without being mediated through a traditional succession. They said: "Such a description is not *atīva hṛdya*—it is not exceedingly beautiful. This is because, when a single foot (quarter-verse) is made to describe two distinct, combined meanings in a variegated manner (*śabalita-kathane*), it results in a lack of harmony.

Because of the reversal of skill—since it would result in a lack of skill on the part of the author of the Sūtras [if he intended such a thing]. (If this were his intention, he would have applied the remainder of the first section (*pāda*) to that very first section, and the latter half to the section on the "Combination of Attributes" (*guṇopasaṃhāra*). The author of the Sūtras would not compose a single section devoid of a consistent, unified meaning. Regarding the statement about Brahman: while the exposition of Brahman—who is eternally faultless and the source of all auspicious qualities—is being carried out, here—in this section (*pāda*)—there is the "taking up of the defects of the individual soul" (*jīvadoṣagraha*), namely, the defects pertaining to the *jīva*.

The apprehension [of the fault] is indeed the "mouth"—that is, it is merely the door—because of the establishment of its opposite; for there is the establishment of the cognition of the presence of faults, which is the adversary to the absence of faults (since the cognition of the counter-positive is the cause for the cognition of an absence). || 5 ||
A Compendium of the Multitude of Principles of the Śārīraka [Mīmāṃsā]

It should not be suspected that the individual soul (jīva) is the agent of its own purpose merely because of its possession of qualities (guṇitva) and its proximity (saṃnidhi); for the performance of harmful actions is impossible [for it], and its quality is obscured (tirohita). || 2 ||

The individual soul (*jīva*)—the transmigrating being who experiences the objects of dreams and so forth—is the creator of the objects experienced during its own state, because it possesses qualities such as the power of true resolve (*satya-saṅkalpatva*) suitable for creating the objects to be experienced by itself, and because of its constant proximity to those objects being experienced by itself; thus, in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), it is the maker of the objects of its own [dream] state. This is not to be doubted—the aforementioned capacity to create the objects of one's own state is beyond doubt, for there is no obstacle to such an action.

Because the activity of creating suffering for oneself—which would entail transforming one's own happiness into suffering—is impossible; because it cannot be conceived even by oneself as being preceded by conscious intent (*buddhipūrva*); and because this quality—namely, the quality of having true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpatva*) and so forth, which belongs to Him and is indeed natural—is obscured, that is, unmanifest, the stated point is established. || 2 ||

Since it is impossible to abandon what has been heard when an object is determined to be real by means such as its existence [in experience]—that is, because it is improper to discard the portion that was heard—one accepts the mere creation, namely, the objective world in the form of a dream-creation as having a real nature; yet, regarding only a certain other portion, due to sublation—that is, due to a valid cognition apprehending the absence of that [object]—one recognizes even the state of error, just as one does with respect to cognitions regarding objects experienced in the waking state.

And just as there is a corresponding conjunction of both [error and latent impression] in the case of delusion, so too in the dream state there exists a corresponding meeting of both; we do not deny this, nor shall we ever reject it. || 6 ||
Some, by the power of yoga, having exited their own body according to the method of a thief moving between his own and another's house, enters another’s body and subsequently regains his former one;

such is the state of affairs even in dreams. Some say this occurs through the activity of the vital breath (*śvāsa*), while others say otherwise, because the acquisition of another body—beginning with the arising of the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth—is established by the logic of the submarine fire (*sāmarinyāya*).

By his own method—just as the activity of coming and going proceeds at will for embodied beings in this world through the operation of their own hands, feet, and so forth, performed in cooperation with their own volitions in their own homes or in the homes of others—so too, O Great God among Men, by the power of yoga—that is, by a specific capacity residing in the mind and other faculties produced by a particular yoga—a certain yogi who has attained such power [can depart] from his former body, his previous physical frame.

Having departed—having risen—he enters another body—the body of another—and again, once more, he regains his former own body through that entry (this is understood from the Yoga Śāstra, as well as from the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, to be accomplished through Haṭha-yoga and other means). In this very manner—even in such a specific case—the state of affairs is the persistence of the narrative; thus do the thinkers (carry out the operation of dreaming), while others [do not].

Others, observing the bodily functions such as inhalation and exhalation to be present, explain the dream-experience in another way: through the expansion of the intellect arising from the mind—that is, by the activity consisting of the spreading forth of that intellect known as *dharmabhūtajñāna* which arises and attains manifestation through the cooperation of the mind (meaning that the performance of activity occurs both in the body while lying down and in the body created in the dream)—thus [they explain] the other body.

Regarding "bhajane"—when the assumption of another body is being performed, as established by the principle of Saubhari: just as in the case of the sage named Saubhari, at the time of assuming various bodies, it was observed that while consciousness remained in one body, the maintenance of worldly activity was carried out through the mental faculty directed toward the remaining bodies; likewise, when the individual soul (*jīva*) has entered the state of dream, the functioning of breath and so forth occurs in the body where it lies, while functions such as going and coming occur elsewhere, thereby establishing the consistency of all worldly activities. || 7 ||

Even in the state called "dream"—that is, during certain phases of the individual soul's life—some [beings] perform the activities of living through their own power, as was previously stated regarding the subjects in the former body. Just like the one dwelling in the heart (*dahara*), this very agent under discussion here creates the dream-object, characterized by the possession of true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpatā*) and so forth, as well as sons and other such things. For in the case of liberation, it is impossible for there to be the production of undesired things, given the description of such qualities;
furthermore, because dreams are indicative [of future events], this creation belongs to the Creator of the entire universe. (8)

By the Lord of Creatures—by Prajāpati, the four-faced one—the collection of qualities such as "having true resolves" (*satya-saṅkalpatva*), "having true desires" (*satya-kāmatva*), and so forth, was stated with respect to the Supreme Self denoted by the term "small ether" (*dahara-ākāśa*), and also with respect to the individual self (*jīvātman*) which participates in transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). This was established by the scriptural passage beginning with, "This Self is free from evil" (*eṣa ātmāpahatapāpmā*). Therefore, this individual self is the agent of [the desire for] sons and the like. [The word] *putra* [refers to] son...

Even though he is the creator of all desired objects in the form of wife and so forth, he is the subject here—introduced in this context (in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad passage beginning, "Fashioning every desire at will, choose sons and grandsons"). And he would indeed be capable of creating objects for his own dream—that is, he would have the power to fashion specific objects to be experienced by himself during the state of dreaming.

(Thus one might object): "Not so—such an objection is not appropriate, because such qualities are stated [to exist] in liberation; for in the *Prajāpati-vākya*, the manifestation of the collection of qualities such as 'having true resolves' (*satya-saṅkalpatva*) is established as occurring precisely at the time of the individual soul's liberation, and thus the production of what is undesired and so forth is impossible. Furthermore, since in a dream one perceives even disagreeable objects just like agreeable ones, if [the soul] were itself the creator, the activity consisting in the creation of disagreeable objects would be untenable; for no one [creates such things for themselves]."

[The Lord] Himself desires or strives to create that which is indeed disagreeable to Himself; for it is established by the Śrutis and other authorities that dream-objects—those things experienced during the state of dreaming—are indicative, in that they generate knowledge regarding desired or undesired objects pertaining to the waking state. Furthermore, this creation—the creative act concerning dream-objects—belongs solely to the Blessed One (Bhagavat), the creator of the entire universe, and not to the individual soul (jīva). || 8 ||
The suffix *ṇamul* is prescribed even when the verb *vidhātā* (the ordainer) is repeated for each desire (*kāmaṃ kāmaṃ*), and thus the Lord is described as such;

He remains awake while others sleep, as is clearly stated in the *Sampariṣvaṅga* dialogue. It has been declared by the authoritative sages that there are many fixed distinctions of purpose during His wakefulness, ending at their respective times, and that He bestows fruits in accordance with those specific actions. || 9 ||

Regarding the phrase "vidhātā" in the statement from the Kaṭha Upaniṣad, "kāmaṃ kāmaṃ puruṣo nirmimāṇaḥ": the word "vidhātā" is a restatement of the meaning of the Vedic term "nirmimāṇaḥ. Furthermore, the suffix "ṇamul" is appropriate; the word "kāmam," repeated twice, ends in the "ṇamul" suffix which conveys the sense of the "ktvā" suffix, and this alone is the correct interpretation—not as a word ending in the accusative case. Therefore, from the root "kam" (in the sense of "desire") with the "ṇamul" suffix, the meaning is "having willed" (saṅkalpya).

"But not the various objects of desire, such as sons, friends, wives, and the like"—in this manner, by way of being the agent of various volitions in accordance with the karma of individual souls, the Lord—the Supreme Self, the Sovereign of All—is restated; that is, He who has been taught in other Vedic texts is made known once again. This very Supreme Self, having been made known as being characterized by the possession of various volitions, remains awake even while living beings are asleep, because His external activities have ceased.

While the beings remain [in their respective states], he remains indeed vigilant, not forgetting his own duty. This is clear—that even during the waking state, within the visible world, how many, indeed how many countless [beings] exist—[this is evident] from the statement regarding the soul's state of deep sleep being the waking state of the Supreme Self, based on the scriptural passage containing the word "Prājña" which teaches the embrace of the soul by the Supreme Self in deep sleep: "He is embraced by the conscious Self" (*prājñenātmanā sampariṣvaktaḥ*). This is made clear by the sentence concerning the complete embrace (*sampariṣvaṅga*). Even in the waking state, while the world is being perceived, how many, that is, how many innumerable [beings] [exist].

The distinctions of objects—meaning specific objects—are restricted, in that they are subject to the rule of being experienced by particular individuals alone; they terminate at their respective times, meaning their essential nature ceases (is destroyed) as soon as the specific time suitable for their experience has passed. This is experienced [in the case of lightning, rain, and so forth, because they are momentary] even by authoritative persons such as astrologers and great yogis, who are knowers of reality, according to those respective karmas—that is, in accordance with the karma of the individual soul.

This "bestowal of fruits" is said to be the essential nature of the Supreme Self: the granting of the experience of long-lasting or quickly perishing pleasure, pain, and so forth. This has been clearly elucidated in the scriptures.
(9) Because they have obtained the designation of being "mere illusion" (*māyāmātra*), those who are well-versed in the Vedas and the Sugata [Buddha] declare that the entire universe is false.

Since this was stated by them at the beginning of their respective treatises, it is here rendered untenable due to its internal inconsistency and other flaws. The word *māyā* does not denote falsity; rather, it is used here figuratively. What follows from that?
Because weapons and the like are employed within the truth, yet are properly restrained, this is the sense of being wonderful.

Because of the attainment of the designation "mere illusion"—in the *Śārīraka-sūtra* (Brahma-sūtra), specifically in the sūtra "But it is mere illusion" (*māyāmātraṃ tu*)—the proponents of non-duality (Advaitins), who are followers of Sugata through the mouth of the Vedas (*śrutimukhasugatāḥ*), proclaim their own Vedic orthodoxy; yet, having ultimately set their minds upon the Buddhist emptiness (*śūnyatva*), they describe that falsity of the entire universe (*viśvamithyātva*) at the very commencement of the treatise, namely, in the commentary on the first sūtra of the *Śārīraka*. (Note: The phrase "like a 'cow-faced tiger'" [*gomukhavyāghraḥ*] is an idiom used to describe someone who adopts the outward appearance of one thing while internally adhering to another.)

By these—those belonging to the school of Advaita—it has been stated—that is, described as the intended meaning of the Sūtra; therefore—for that reason—here, in this section of the *Sādhanādhyāya*, the establishment of the state of being "mere illusion" (*māyāmātratva*) would be problematic, being fraught with defects such as inconsistency and redundancy. The word "māyā"—this very term "māyā"—is not a synonym for "unreal," nor does it signify a lack of ultimate reality (*apāramārthya*).

Since it is understood from the statement of the Naighaṇṭukas—"*māyā* is *vayuna*, [which is] knowledge"—that the term denotes a specific kind of knowledge synonymous with volition (*saṅkalpa*), let us here grant for the sake of argument that the word "*māyā*" in the Sūtra "the world is merely *māyā*" might be used figuratively (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*)—by abandoning its primary denotative sense—to convey the falsity of the universe, as received from Bādarāyaṇa, the author of the Sūtras.
