Even so, what would follow? What purpose would be gained by that?

Nothing at all, O Truthful One—for when the word *māyā* is employed in its primary sense (*paramārthabhūta*) as a weapon or the like (*astrādirūpe'rthe*), as seen in Puranic usage such as "by that [he created] a thousand *māyās*" (*tena māyā sahasram*), and when the learned are establishing the etymological power (*śakti*) of the word *māyā* in its appropriate meaning through a proper regulation (distinguishing between figurative and non-figurative uses)—then this very word *māyā* found in the Sūtra, which was introduced as having a disputed meaning, signifies "wonder" (*āścaryatā*).
It is determined that [the dream] is the indicator of a specific object within the dream, by relying on its wondrous nature as the basis for its occurrence. || 10 ||
Summary of the Meaning of the Section.

Now, regarding the section on the twilight state (*sandhyādhikaraṇa*), having raised the doubt—based on the scriptural hearing of the agency of the individual soul (*jīva*) under discussion in the passage beginning with "There are no chariots there, no paths" and ending with "For he is the agent"—that "the creation of objects for his own sake belongs to that [jīva] itself," [the Sūtra] states: "The creation of his own [dream] is indeed caused by the Supreme Self. This is because the individual soul lacks the power to create diverse objects during the state of transmigratory existence due to the non-manifestation of its true resolve (*satya-saṃkalpa*) and other attributes; and because in passages such as "He who wakes among these sleeping ones," the agency of the Supreme Self in the creation of dreams is determined.
Thus, it is said that "the creation of one's own [dream] has the Supreme Self alone as its agent."

"Ground" (*bhūmi*) means the foundational location; "channels" (*nāḍyaḥ*) refers to the channels called *hitā*; "pericardium" (*purītat*) is either a specific channel of that name, or else "the Supreme" (*paramaḥ*)—meaning the Supreme Self itself (any one of these being possible by way of alternative)—"might be" (*syāt*), i.e., it ought to be. Thus he raises this doubt: "This [doubt] is not [correct]; such a doubt is not sound because of the defect of conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Since there are eight defects in a case involving imagined conceptualization, it would be like a palace. (*prāsāda vat syāt*): as in the case of a palace.
Therefore, it follows that the three—the cross-legged posture, the specific manner of sitting, and the particular ground—must necessarily exist in combination.
A summary of the meaning of the section.

In the section concerning the absence of that [dreaming], with regard to the passages beginning with "Now, when this person is asleep," since it is heard that the channels (nāḍīs), the pericardium (purītat), and Brahman are the places of deep sleep—stating respectively, "He sleeps in the channels," "He lies in the pericardium," and "Then, my dear, he has become united with Being"—and because it is impossible for the individual soul (jīva) to be active in multiple locations simultaneously, one might suspect that these [three] are places of deep sleep by way of option (vikalpa). Having raised this doubt:

Because the three are heard of as being the locus of deep sleep—just as a palace, a couch, and a bed [are all loci for a king]—and because there is a difference in function among the channels and so forth, and since a combination is possible, a disjunctive alternative (vikalpa) involving occasional sublation is impossible; therefore, it has been stated that their status as the locus is through combination alone.
The Garland of Logical Connections (Nayasaṅgatimālikā) — 0—

Let the living being (jīva) in the dream state be defective, and that in the state of deep sleep be free from defects; however, this [objection] is raised against the theory of their non-existence (tadabhāvanaya). || 120 ||
Thus concludes the section concerning the non-existence of that [self].
The Adhikaraṇasārāvalī.
"That deep sleep is such that the multitude of pleasures from the delights of union with the Brahman is absent;

therefore, the embodied soul awakening thereafter must be different from it"—do not say so. Because of the persistence of karma, because of the rule of memory, because of the scriptural statement "it is the very same," and because the teacher of the means to liberation taught it as his own state, the one who was previously asleep is indeed the one who has awakened.

Liberation (*mukti*) is the state designated by the term "liberation," which abandons the multitude of pleasures and consists in the cessation of the mass of sufferings. It is absorption in Brahman—the merging of the individual soul (*jīvātman*) into the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), an absolute union. This very state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*)—the state of the individual soul known as deep sleep, which is synonymous with slumber—is of such a nature that it consists of a firm embrace within Brahman; it is called "dissolution in sleep" (*svāpyaya*) and is capable of bringing about the absolute cessation of suffering. Thus, it can be said that this is indeed liberation itself, as stated by the Scripture: "He has gone to his own (*svam apītaḥ*)."

This is declared by scripture itself in such passages as, "He becomes united with the intelligent Self," and "O dear one, he is then merged with Being"; thus, the state of the individual soul (*jīva*) being absorbed into Brahman during deep sleep is made manifest. Therefore, because there is no difference between liberation and deep sleep, [one might object]: "After that—that is, following sleep—the embodied one—the *jīva*—who is awakening, attaining consciousness, must be distinct from the sleeping *jīva*. To this, [the author] says: "Not so."

Let there be no doubt in this manner, because of the persistence of karma: since the previously acquired *prārabdha* karma that exists in the living being (*jīva*) persists even during the state of dreaming, and it persists even upon waking from sleep; because of the rule of recollection—that "I am that very same person"—there is the recognition of non-difference between the states of deep sleep and waking; and because we observe the rule that objects experienced at a time prior to sleep are remembered only by the one who has woken up, and not by another.

"From the word 'precisely the same' (pūrva eva): this one who has arisen from sleep is precisely the same as he existed previously in the form of a tiger, a boar, and so forth; it is not someone else. This is the meaning [of the passage]: "Whether a tiger or a boar... and so on.

This is because of the scriptural statement, "Whatever they become, that they then become," and because it would follow that the scriptures—which enjoin the performance of the means to liberation and their constituent parts—would be rendered purposeless if the state of deep sleep were the very nature of the individual soul (*jīva*). Since liberation is established as being natural (*nisargasiddha*) to the soul's own nature, its identity with that state cannot be accepted; for, since a state characterized by non-return would be impossible [if it were merely a temporary state], that very state must necessarily be one of awakening, as indicated by the repetition of the word "own" (*sva-pada*).

In the dialogue between Indra and Prajāpati, beginning with "Indeed, this [person] does not [exist]," the sleeping person is referred to, and his state being unsuitable for enjoyment is stated by the sentence, "I do not see anything here to enjoy. Since that state cannot be of the nature of liberation, the awakened one—the person who has passed from deep sleep to the waking state—is indeed the same as the former one; that is, he is the very same person who previously attained deep sleep in various bodies, and no other. || 12 ||
The plurality of souls has been declared; the imitation of a stone will be refuted at the time of liberation;

the engagement in activities for the sake of heaven and so forth is known through the method of the Śruti; and the Buddhists and others have been defeated. The statement of oneness even at the end of a kalpa is restricted in its scope due to the abandonment of name and form; furthermore, reflection upon deep sleep is for the sake of establishing the desire to abandon [the world] and so forth, which is equal to the state of dissolution.

The beginninglessness of souls (*jīvānāditvam*)—the state of being without beginning due to the absence of origination for conscious beings—was stated by Bādarāyaṇa himself as having been established previously in the sūtra beginning with "not so, because of the non-distinction of karma" (*na karmāvibhāgāt*). Furthermore, in the state of liberation (*apavarga*), [the soul] becomes like a stone (*dṛṣadanukaraṇam*).

By relying on this, the doctrine of the annihilation of consciousness (*caitanyocchedavāda*) will be cast aside; indeed, it is refuted by the Sūtra beginning with "In the equality of mere experience" (*bhogamātrasāmye*). Furthermore, the engagement for the sake of heaven and so forth—the effort of a conscious embodied being directed toward sacrifices and the like—is established in its true nature by the Śruti-method, that is, by the Śruti connected to the *Karmakāṇḍa* and by the Pūrva-mīmāṃsā-śāstra consisting of the inquiry into its meaning [which establishes the stable status of the individual soul (*jīva*) regarding the arrangement of actions conducive to both this world and the next].

Because [the self] is established solely on the basis of its own admission, even the Buddhists and others—namely the Buddhist and Cārvāka non-Buddhist philosophers who maintain the final conclusion that the self is eternal—are shattered; they have indeed been refuted in the second chapter, which is devoted to the rejection of opposing views. Furthermore, the statement regarding "oneness" at the time of the great dissolution at the end of a kalpa—the scriptural teaching of the soul's becoming one with the Supreme Deity—is restricted in its scope to the abandonment of name and form, referring only to the cessation of distinct cognition and worldly transaction.

This [scriptural statement] intends merely the absolute disappearance of the distinction between name and form; it is not concerned with identity of essential nature. (Thus, when all these matters have been established from other sources,) there arises further reflection: the investigation conducted in this section regarding deep sleep—that state called "sleep" belonging to the conscious embodied being—is for the purpose of establishing the state of liberation by demonstrating its similarity to the state of cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*), thereby proving that the state of liberation is distinct from it, and to ensure the realization that even the state of deep sleep, like the waking state, must be transcended. || 13 ||
The section concerning the deluded [soul] (mugdhādhikaraṇa). ||3-2-4||
A Compendium of the Multitude of Principles of the Śārīraka [Upaniṣads]
Fainting is indeed death due to the withdrawal of all the senses from the vital breath (prāṇa) and the cessation of its activity;
however, that state of "death" would be [distinguished] by the loss of consciousness and the emergence of a distortion of physical form. (13)

Fainting (mūrchā) is a state observed at times in an embodied being, termed "fainting"; death, however, is the state designated by the word "death," which is simply the cessation of the vital breath's activity.

(At that state,) because the specific functions of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) have ceased in the body, and because all the sense organs are withdrawn—as seen by the cessation of the activity of all internal and external organs—it might be suspected that this is not so; for the state existing in a person who is fainted (*mugdha*) or swooning (*mūrcchita*) would be a partial attainment of death—a state consisting of reaching half-way through the condition of death—due to both the alteration of physical form and the lack of recovery.

Because the state of having entered a swoon is distinct from the states of other conditions, and because one observes "arising" in the form of regaining the waking state after the swoon has passed. || 13 ||

In the contemplation of the ultimate reality, within this state of swoon (mūrcchā) experienced by the embodied being, there exists the nature of the "half of the fourth" (turyārdha). Among the four states—waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and death—it is logical that the fourth state, which consists of death, should itself possess the nature of a half-state. || 14 ||

—0— Even when there is a connection with the respective locations (the *nāḍīs*), that is, even when there is a relation with the bodies of those various individual souls (*jīvātman*) that have entered the states of waking and so forth, the "sinless and auspicious quality"—meaning the state of being entirely pure and free from the touch of defects—is purified; that is, it is clearly demonstrated through both authoritative means (*pramāṇa*) and reasoning (*yukti*). This is because the remainder of the book, consisting of the four subsequent chapters (*adhikaraṇas*), is devoted to establishing the faultless Supreme Brahman; for [Brahman] indeed possesses both characteristics (*ubhayaliṅga*).

By means of the two sections concerning the earrings (*kuṇḍalādhikaraṇa*), [the author] removes—meaning he dispels—the defects that might be suspected as being rooted in the identity with the body in its various states or in the non-difference from the world, which would contradict the determination of his faultlessness; [the author of the Sūtras] makes known [the Self] as being untouched by Brahman.

Furthermore, by means of the subsequent pair of arguments—namely, the two sections consisting of the establishment of the supreme fruit—he removes both the Lord of the World’s inferiority (in the form of being surpassed) and His loss of magnanimity (in the form of the absence of bestowing fruits upon His own worshippers). || 15 ||
What is the section concerning that which possesses both characteristics? (3.2.5)
A Compendium of the Collection of Aphorisms on the Embodied Soul.

Or, even if it were by one's own will, since there is no possibility of its being abandoned, the contact with pus and so forth would be the fault of another; [one might argue] that this is due to its connection with that location, but this is not so, because the word "possessor of qualities" (guṇin) implies that it is entirely free from defects in every respect. || 14 ||

By virtue of being connected to those locations—that is, by reason of abiding in various places such as the body and the senses, which are not the locus of the goals of human life—or even by the will of the Self, despite the fact that [the Supreme] is dependent upon its own volition, there is contact with pus and the like, meaning contact with pus, blood, and so forth. Because this is an utterly contemptible state—because it is absolutely to be shunned—it constitutes a defect for the Supreme, the Paramātman; that aforementioned connection with impurity is a fault.
"Only that which does not establish the goal of human life"—thus is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). To this, [the author replies]: "This is not so; this is indeed not logical. Why?

Because in all cases—namely, in all means of valid knowledge such as Śruti, Smṛti, and so forth—there is the word "possessing faultless qualities" (*nirdoṣa-guṇitva-śabda*); that is, from the word and the indicator which establishes that the Supreme Self possesses the quality of being the source of auspicious attributes. || 14 ||

In the Upaniṣads—the concluding portions of the Vedas—which dispel all defects, which are devoted to Janārdana, which bestow liberation upon those who seek it from Janārdana, and which are intent upon the glorious Nārāyaṇa; and in which the comprehension of meaning proceeds by relying on the principles of general and specific application (the restriction of the meaning of a general term to a specific one denoted by the word, for the sake of resolving doubt); and which consist of both prohibitions of qualities and injunctions of qualities regarding Brahman.

Certain individuals who employ the terminology of Vedānta—namely, some Advaitins—under the pretext of the *apaccheda* principle (the logic of the section on the "simultaneous occurrence of two disabilities"), namely by following the reasoning of the *apacchedādhikaraṇa*, have introduced the discussion of relative strength and weakness; that is, they have asserted that among the statements concerning the absence of qualities (*nirguṇa-vākya*) there is superior strength, while among the statements concerning the possession of qualities (*saguṇa-vākya*) there is weakness, on the grounds that the negation of qualities refers to qualities in general, whereas the injunction of qualities refers to specific ones, and thus no qualities exist apart from those specifically enjoined.

Regarding the phrase "they have reflected": such reflection is *mīmāṃsā*... [this] *karma-mīmāṃsā* shines forth—that is, it appears—attractive only to those who are far removed from the practice of the path and possess dull intellects; it does not, however, [shine] among those who are true *mīmāṃsakas*, because they have understood through correct reflection that the logic of the "severance" (*apaccheda-nyāya*) is not of that nature. || 68 ||
Regarding Brahman, whose body consists of the transformation of qualities (*guṇavikāra*),
the words of injunctions and prohibitions concerning distinctions such as birth and action have mutually distinct objects and do not possess even a scent of contradiction.
Those [injunctions] do not apply; they are sublated by prohibitions. 69.

Is the scriptural injunction "Do not harm any living beings"—which is intent upon a general prohibition of violence—rendered nullified by having its scope obstructed [by a specific rule]? No, indeed. For the subject matter of that injunction regarding animals refers specifically to the animal designated as a *chāga* (goat)—a particular species of animal—and not to animals in general. This was established through logical analysis in the *Pūrvamīmāṃsā* by the Jaiminiya Sūtra, "Or rather, the goat [is the victim], because of the wording of the mantra" (*chāgo vā mantravarṇāt*). Furthermore, the meaning of the word "animal" contained within that injunction is restricted to the goat alone. Thus, it has been determined through the principles of the *Nyāya* system.

This has been determined by two principles: by the principle of the general rule and its exception (*utsargāpavādanyāya*) as already stated, and by the principle of the goat and the sacrificial animal (*chāgapaśunyāya*). Thus, in Brahman—the Supreme Self—who is stainless (*nirmale*), meaning free from all defects, and who possesses a multitude of auspicious qualities established by the Vedas (*śrutaśubhaguṇake*), the statement of "being devoid of qualities" (*nirguṇoktiḥ*)—that is, the verbal expression negating qualities (to be understood as occurring in the Śruti and other scriptures)—is intended for the purpose of excluding qualities that are not goals of human endeavor (*apuruṣārthabhūta*) and for the purpose of removing those attributes that are to be abandoned (*heyadharmakṣepārtha*). || 70 ||

An object that exists here as inherently causing suffering must be abandoned by one's own will; otherwise, its status as something to be discarded would not exist, for there can be no abandonment of an object of rejection that lacks such a nature. Nor is there any fault in this, just as for a living being who possesses eternal sovereignty, there are different states according to the distinction of conditions;
for within a single body, both purity and impurity are observed in relation to oneself and others respectively. (17)

Whatever object—whatever nature of a thing—is inherently [to be] abandoned (*heya*) by virtue of its own form and essential nature, and is not to be accepted; in such an object, "abiding"—its presence—even if attained through one's own will, that is, even if reached by one's own resolve alone without the prompting of another, would indeed become a cause of suffering, producing opposition.

(Since there is no dispute that contact with impurity—whether self-inflicted or caused by another—is a cause of defilement,) otherwise—that is, in the absence of such a state—the quality of being rejectable would not exist; the very fact of that object being something to be abandoned would not be established (for nothing can be both un-rejectable for someone and acceptable for another, as that would entail the loss of the necessity of inherent nature). This objection is not sound, because it refers to the Supreme Self, which is beyond all determination and untouched by any general adjunct (*upādhi*).

Since there is no possibility whatsoever of the abandonment—meaning the rejection—of anything on account of its being disagreeable to Him, the Supreme Person, who possesses eternal sovereignty and whose natural activities and so forth are independent and not imposed [by others], does not incur any blemish—that is, the state of being subject to defects—even by way of a difference in condition (*daśābheda*), that is, even depending upon a difference in state, unlike the bound soul (*baddhajīva*). For indeed, even within a single body, in one and the same physical frame, [He remains untainted].

Regarding the two—the Supreme Self and the individual self (jīvātman)—there is the absence of defects caused by the state of being embodied in the case of the pure one, and the presence of such defects in the other; this is established by the Śruti itself in the verse "Two birds... (*dvā suparṇā*), specifically in the section read as: "Of these two, one eats the sweet pippala fruit, while the other looks on without eating. || 17 || [The Lord], though all-pervading, dwells within the bodies of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and others in the form of the Self, like an atom.

Because no [other] exists, he is not made known, nor is he one who is to be made known; (therefore, in the case of God, there is an absence of the purpose of an injunction consisting in making known what was previously unknown). Because he is the ruler—due to his inherent nature as the controller of all—he is not one who is to be ruled; (therefore, in the case of God, there is an absence of the purpose of an injunction consisting in impelling one to engage in what has not yet been engaged in). In the world—that is, in common life—by a person who knows what is beneficial and understands the means to security, for [such a person] is indeed one who knows only a little...

For a person who possesses knowledge of only a single portion of what is to be known is informed—that is, made aware—concerning an object not yet known, and is impelled—that is, incited to act—toward an object that was previously not the scope of his activity. || 18 ||
Those who know the principles of logic certainly do not tolerate the subversion of a general rule by an exception;
therefore, regarding the qualities and so forth of Brahman, a prohibition must remain restricted to its specific scope without overstepping the domain of the injunction.
Thus, when the contradiction is resolved, there is no justification for establishing a principle based on the partiality of equal domains.
A permanent prohibition is desired here for others, and from that, the principle of "introductory speech" (upakrānti) would follow. || 19 ||

Those who know the method—those skilled in Mīmāṃsā—are well known to not tolerate, indeed to never accept, the doctrine that an exception (apavāda)—which is synonymous with a specific scripture—is sublated by a general rule (utsarga), which is to say, a general scripture. Therefore, since it is established that a specific scripture is not sublated by a general scripture, the prohibition found in passages concerning the absence of qualities (nirguṇa-vākya) regarding the attributes such as the qualities and the form belonging to the Supreme Brahman (brāhme guṇādau)—is [not applicable].

The absence of qualities (*guṇābhāva*), or the negation such as "devoid of qualities" (*nirguṇam*) which makes that absence known; or [the positive injunction], the object of an injunction—the domain of the scripture that makes qualities known, such as "having true resolve" (*satyakāmatva*) and so forth—having transcended these, that is, having abandoned them, one should remain: one should abide in one's own essential nature. (One should not, however, act by transgressing the scope of the injunction. In this way, through the consideration of the distinction between objects, when the conflict—that is, when one of the two, the injunction or the prohibition, has its scope subsumed by the other—is stilled, meaning it has been resolved, [one attains] equanimity...

The attainment of the scope of the *apacchedādhikaraṇa* maxim—which concerns only those matters that share a common subject—is the acquisition of the status of being the subject matter for both saguṇa and nirguṇa passages. Indeed, a negation is not a doctrine of negation unless it is possible [for the thing to exist]; rather, it is invariably observed as being subsequent to an injunction, established by experience; it does not, however, concern those whose sequence is indefinite. (The *avaccheda* maxim, on the other hand, concerns only that which has an indefinite sequence.)

Because, in the case of the interruption (*apaccheda*) of the *udgātṛ*, *pratihartr̥*, and others, a fixed sequence of priority (*paurvāparya-naiyatyā-siddheḥ*) is not established; therefore—since there is a rule that a prohibition follows immediately after a mandatory injunction (*vidhyānantarya-niyamāt*)—here, regarding the subject matter of the passages concerning the qualified (*saguṇa*) and the unqualified (*nirguṇa*) [Brahman] (which depend on the necessity of establishing the qualities), the principle of the beginning (*upakrama-nītiḥ*), namely the logic of the section concerning the beginning where no contradiction has yet arisen (*asañjātavirodhopakramādhikaraṇa-nyāyaḥ*), applies; it is capable of proceeding, but the logic of interruption (*apaccheda-nyāyaḥ*) does not. || 10 ||

The word "all" protects the effect [from being non-existent], for it removes the notion of difference from the effect by means of the study [of the Upanishads]— thinking, "How could the existent arise from the non-existent?"— while the word "only clay" indicates the supreme [cause].
Because the world is included within the distinguished Blessed Lord, the statement "not here, not manifold" is appropriate.

"How could there be an intellect from non-existence?"—this scriptural reading, which proceeds after beginning with "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," asks: "How could Being be born from non-existence? Here, "Being" refers to the existence of an entity that is being born as an effect.

It conceals—that is, it renders uncontradicted—the state of being real (sadrūpatām). Since there must necessarily be a correspondence between cause and effect, when the effect called the "world" is produced from that which is real, its cause must also necessarily be real, and not of the nature of the unreal. This is what the word "clay" implies, immediately following the statement: "The modification is a mere verbal handle, a name."

The Vedic statement, "It is truly just clay," serves to eliminate only the difference in form regarding an object being produced; for it indeed excludes only absolute difference from the perspective of the causal substance.

(But it does not teach the unreality or non-existence of the effect), because the world—the phenomenal universe—is included within the qualified Supreme Lord, the Supreme Self who is qualified by the entire world consisting of both sentient and insentient beings; since the world exists as a part (*aṃśa*) in the form of being a single constituent portion of that qualified whole, the Vedic statement "not here, not manifold"—namely, "there is nothing whatsoever manifold here," which is intended to negate everything other than Brahman—is logical—that is, its meaning is uncontradicted (but not [the negation of the effect]).

It is appropriate that [the scripture] is intent upon negating what is other than Brahman; for even the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka* Śruti statement, "Now, the instruction regarding this is 'not this, not this'," removes—meaning it dispels—the doubt and the delusion that the previously mentioned endowment with qualities belongs only to the lower [Brahman], rather than the higher Brahman. It does not, however, negate the possession of qualities [in the higher Brahman], because qualities even greater than those are subsequently stated. Therefore, there is no contradiction in Brahman possessing both sets of characteristics. || 20 ||
Indeed,

it is said that the Supreme Self— the sun— is fully visible in every object and location due to its possession of all attributes, and is devoid of distinctions such as increase or decrease; this is the teaching regarding the sun reflected in reservoirs of water.
If it is argued that there is no mention of being intangible, we say no; for the logic of the analogies of the space within a jar and the space within a water-pot applies here.
Therefore, the position of the Vedānta is that Brahman possesses two characteristics and a twofold manifestation. || 21 ||

The Supreme Self—the Supreme Person—is to be perceived by yogis as complete in every respect—being filled with all auspicious qualities—in each respective location of those various objects, such as the earth and so forth; He is to be seen as unlimited and is indeed devoid of distinctions such as increase or decrease—that is, He is not the locus of the particularities of growth or decay that belong to limited things. With this intention, there is the statement of His being like the sun reflected in a reservoir of water.

If it is argued that the justification for the description of the sun being visible [in the Paramātman] is the citation of its lack of touch—that is, the analogy of the sun reflected in water serves as an illustration of the Paramātman’s unfitness for touch—such a doubt is not tenable; for [the case of] a jar...

The reasoning—that the analogy of the real space situated within a water-receptacle such as a jar or a bowl is not consistent—is refuted by the aforementioned collection of reasons; therefore, Brahman is the Supreme Brahman, possessing both genders (ubhayaliṅga), having a twofold manifestation known as the two types of glory called the Tripād-vibhūti and the Līlā-vibhūti—such indeed is the Vedānta position, the intention of the Upaniṣads. || 21 ||
The Garland of Logical Connections.

In the section concerning the "two-fold characteristics" (ubhayaliṅgādhikaraṇa), the following doubt was raised: since the individual soul (jīva) resides in states such as waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, whatever defects are associated with those respective states would also apply to the Supreme Self (paramātman) because of its presence therein.

Having raised this objection, it was stated that because the scriptures declare both sets of characteristics—such as "free from evil," "blameless," and "stainless"—there is no defect in the Supreme Self even when it abides in those various states.

In the world—that is, in any worldly transaction whatsoever—a specific type of hornless cow known as *muṇḍa* (shorn) is certainly never denoted by the word *khaṇḍa*, which signifies a half-horned cow of that same species; indeed, it is never so employed. This is because such usage would be inappropriate for both of the aforementioned positions. Furthermore, regarding the world—the insentient phenomenal universe—and Brahman—the Supreme Self—the state of being a part (*aṃśatva*) or the state of possessing parts (*aṃśitva*) consists in having the nature of a specific portion.

Both [the individual soul and Brahman], being characterized by the nature of being a part (*aṃśa*), would be like the Self—that is, the relationship of part and whole between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman would be logical. || 15 ||

Some—certain philosophers—assert that within Brahman, the Supreme Self, there exists a certain, singular, and eternal portion consisting of non-consciousness (acid-aṃśa), which, while being established from the beginningless past, undergoes various transformations—that is, it assumes manifold modifications of form.

Thus they describe their own established doctrine; others—certain others intent on describing the ultimate reality—maintain that within the Supreme Brahman, which is denoted by the term "Being" (sat), there are three portions consisting of the conscious, the unconscious, and the omniscient Lord, due to a specific internal modification, according to the analogy of foam and the like in the ocean, such as foam, bubbles, and waves.

— Some say, and others as well; here, in this investigation of reality, being engaged [in inquiry], they declare that there is a unity of genus (*aikajātyam*)—a continuity of the same class identical with the nature of Brahman—between the world and Brahman, between the phenomenal universe and the Supreme Self, according to the analogy of the moon and its moonlight, like light and its radiance. All of them, those three types alike, in this matter, because of the consequence of violating the natural intent of all the Vedas—the reason being the occurrence of a breach in the inherent consistency of the entirety of the Śruti—[do not accept this].
Those who are to be terrified—(those who are to be removed by punishment)—are to be rendered speechless by refutation. || 23 ||
A summary of the meaning of the section.

In the section concerning the serpent and its coils (*ahikuṇḍalādhikaraṇa*), having raised the doubt as to whether the non-sentient entity possesses the nature of Brahman either through a difference of states— like a serpent and its coils—
or through the connection with a single genus— like light and its possessor— [The sūtra refutes this.]
Because both positions are untenable, it has been stated that [the relationship] is like that between the individual soul (jīva) and its parts, by way of the relation of part and whole.
The Garland of Logical Connections.
For it has been stated that the coiling [of the breath] is for the sake of the purification and complete cleansing of the unmanifested;
therefore, the nature of Brahman belongs to the unmanifested, and thus there is a connection by way of introduction (upoddhāta).
Thus ends the section concerning the serpent and its coils (Ahikuṇḍalādhikaraṇa).
The Section on the Refutation of Others (Parādhikaraṇa) || 3-2-7 || A Compendium of the Essential Principles of the Śārīraka [Mīmāṃsā].

Because of the designation as a "bridge," because of being designated by one of limited intellect, because of the scriptural statement regarding that which leads [to it], and because of the apprehension of difference in the passage "that which is higher than the high" (*tato yad uttarataram*), it might be thought that there is some other entity to be reached even beyond that. This is not so, because there is no merging of essential natures; because it is the object of meditation; because it is the means for attaining liberation; and because it is designated as the cause [of that attainment]. (Verse 16)

On account of the designation "bridge"—from the scriptural usage of this Supreme Self, who is the cause of the world, as a bridge in the passage, "Now, that which is the Self is the bridge," and because of the mention of "crossing over" in the phrase, "having crossed this bridge"; and on account of the designation by those of limited intellect through the notion of being delimited by parts and digits—as in "Brahman has four quarters" and "Brahman has sixteen digits"; and also from the scriptural statement of its being the means of attainment: "This is the bridge to immortality."

Because the existence of another [entity] to be attained is understood through the cause that is the "attainer," there is a grasp of difference from that [cause] by means of the scriptural designation, "That which is higher than that" (*tato yad uttarataram*), which indicates that the object to be attained possesses a transcendence relative to the object that is the cause of the world; thus, from this certainty of difference regarding the Supreme Object, it follows that there might be yet another entity beyond even that—namely, some other entity distinct from the Supreme Being who is the cause of the world, [which would be] "higher than the high" (*parātpara*).

As for the doubt that "it exists," this is not correct, because all things are non-distinct, since [the Self] protects its own essential nature and intrinsic being; because it is to be meditated upon as the means to liberation (*apavarga*); because it is to be worshipped as the Supreme Self who is the cause of the world and the reason for attaining liberation; and because it is designated as a "bridge" (*setu*) in the Śruti, being spoken of as a bridge.

Therefore, with respect to the Supreme Brahman, it is not tenable to raise a doubt regarding its being merely a means of crossing over, its being that which is to be crossed over, its being merely the agent that causes attainment toward the goal to be reached, or its being merely that which limits the transcendence inherent in the object to be attained. || 16 ||

5) How so?—In the Śruti and other scriptures, since deities such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Indra, and others are described in various places as the objects of worship and their excellence is proclaimed, how can one reach the certainty that "Viṣṇu alone is the supreme reality"?

6) Regarding the reality... [the answer is: Those Vedāntic texts such as the Taittirīya Śruti, which possess the primary purport of determining the Supreme Self after having perceived and worshipped the truth—as in "Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Brahman; Nārāyaṇa is the supreme reality"—[the certainty arises] from the thorough study and comprehension of them. (Thus are the question and answer.)

7) [Question: "In that case, how are other statements to be understood? Once it has been determined that Viṣṇu is the Supreme, by what means can the words found in the Śrutis and other scriptures—which teach that Śiva and others possess supremacy, being the object of meditation, and so forth—be explained as having a consistent meaning?

8) [Answer: "By virtue of their qualities (guṇavaśāt)—that is, because words such as 'Śiva,' 'Śambhu,' and so on are applied to Viṣṇu alone by taking into account qualities residing in Viṣṇu, such as His being the source of unconditioned bliss and His being the unsurpassed auspiciousness; thus, there is consistency without contradiction."

9) Here, how does Rudra speak? Since the stated meaning is beyond doubt, when Rudra says, "I alone existed in the beginning, I exist now, and I shall exist in the future" (by thus establishing his own existence prior to and subsequent to creation), how can that be uncontradicted?

10) [The answer is: By means of contemplating non-difference—according to his own perspective—between Viṣṇu within his own inner self and himself, who is governed by Him. (Thus are the question and the answer.)

11) How does he arise?—Viṣṇu, who is the cause of the world, is the locus of birth as established by the Veda, wherein it is said: "Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra—all these are produced. How can this be possible, given that the one who is the cause of all cannot himself be subject to origination? (This is the question. 12) It is answered: Viṣṇu possesses incarnations known as *āvirbhāva* (manifestations); he is not, however, subject to birth produced by karma, such as that described in the Yājñika Upaniṣad regarding his boundless majesty.

He is declared to be the Supreme Person as the cause in the Puṃsūkta; furthermore, in the Saucālīkya Upaniṣad and the Mahopaniṣad, the path is likewise described; understand it to be so in the Kaṭhavallī and other such texts as well. || 72 ||

In the *Yājñikī Upaniṣad*—namely, the *Taittirīya Ānandavallī* and *Nārāyaṇa Upaniṣad*, beginning with the words "In the waters" (*ambhasi*) and so forth—that Supreme Person who is described as possessing boundless majesty and infinite greatness through such statements as, "The sages weave Him within the ocean; in that Imperishable, the highest, are all creatures," and who is thus established as the Puruṣa, He alone is the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*), the most excellent Being, as the causal source in the *Puruṣasūkta*—the portion of the Veda which is the essence of all the Vedas.

It has been stated—in the passage beginning with "From him the meters were born" and ending with "so they fashioned the worlds"—that he is established as the creator of the entire universe (since he alone is established [in the verse] "I know this great Puruṣa"). Furthermore, the very same point already established there is stated again here in the Saubāli Upaniṣad: "He who moves within the earth, whose body is the earth... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.6.6).

"The divine god is one, Nārāyaṇa"; likewise, even prior to that, in the *Mahopaniṣad*, he is described as having all forms: "In the middle is the divine Person, the thousand-headed Person... from his heart all this is born. Furthermore, the method of describing the causal reality related to the *Mahopaniṣad* is also thus: passages such as "Verily, in the beginning, there was only Nārāyaṇa" are seen to be intent upon the fact that the Supreme Person named Nārāyaṇa alone is the cause of all. Just so—

Just like the Upaniṣads such as the Yājñikya that have been mentioned, consider the Kaṭhavallīs—the verses contained within the Kaṭhopaniṣad—such as "That supreme abode of Viṣṇu," "The one controller, the inner self of all beings, who makes the single seed manifold," and so forth; likewise, determine that all other various words found in other Upaniṣads are also devoted to Viṣṇu, the Great Person of boundless majesty, as the ultimate cause.

(Therefore, all Vedic utterances are intended solely to establish that Viṣṇu alone is the cause of the world accompanied by His supreme excellence; there is no room here for contradiction or any other misconception. || 72 || Nārāyaṇa proclaimed Himself as the sole cause of the universe with intentional meaning through the declaration of the *Mahopaniṣad*, which begins with "Eko ha vai...
[He who, at the time of the destruction of the entire world, including Brahmā, Śiva, the Earth, the Ocean, the Lord of Waters, the Moon, and the Sun, manifests forth]. || 73 ||

Nārāyaṇa—the Blessed Mahāviṣṇu—with intent—that is, accompanied by a specific underlying purpose—by means of the proclamation of the *Mahopaniṣad*, which begins with "Eko ha vā" (Indeed, there was one alone), namely the passage starting with "Eko ha vai nārāyaṇa āsīt" (Indeed, Nārāyaṇa alone existed), and through its unambiguous and lucid arrangement of words, has designated himself as the sole cause of the universe; that is, he exists as the locus of a second-order causality consisting of both the efficient cause (*nimitta*) and the non-distinct material cause (*upādāna*) of the entire world.

Likewise, he who is the sole cause of the universe—that very Nārāyaṇa who, at the time when Brahmā, Śiva, and Viṣṇu perish, and when the entire world including the earth, stars, water, fire, moon, and so forth is utterly destroyed, emerges unimpaired and remains awake—he alone is the singular cause of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the world, the Supreme Person beyond all. || 73 ||

...Because [the cause] has not been previously established in this great Upaniṣad, there could be no restatement (anuvāda) of the world-cause in the passage "One indeed... according to the principle seen in passages such as "For above the gods... and so forth; for, by the natural sense of the sentence, the Lord's causality was disregarded by others.
And its being an effect is not contradictory; furthermore, there is nothing else here that remains to be enjoined.

In the *Mahopaniṣad*, the passage beginning with "Eko ha vā" (Indeed, there was one) is the scriptural portion stating, "Indeed, Nārāyaṇa alone existed. This would not be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*)—that is, it would not be a sentence whose purpose is to make known an already enjoined matter; rather, it is indeed an injunction (*vidhi*) intended to make known what was previously unknown. This is because the cause of the world has not been established by other means of knowledge—the fact that the entity called Nārāyaṇa is the cause of the world is not proven by any other authority. (One should not think that it is logical for this to be a restatement simply because of the presence of the particles *ha* and *vai*, which indicate the nature of a restatement.)

Just as in the case of the statement "He holds [the fuel] above the gods" (*upari hi devebhyo dhārayati*), where—despite the presence of the particle *hi*—the status of this sentence as an injunction (*vidhitva*) is determined by its capacity to convey a meaning not established by any other means of knowledge (*mānāntara*), as concluded in the sūtra "But it is an injunction regarding holding, because of novelty" (*vidhistu dhāraṇe 'pūrvatvāt*); likewise, in the sentence "That which is the cake on eight potsherds for Agni" (*yad āgneyo 'ṣṭākapālo bhavati*), despite the presence of the word *yat*, which is a mark of a restatement (*anuvāda*).

Since the Āgneya sacrifice is not established by any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), its status as a restatement (*anuvāda*) is set aside and its nature as an injunction (*vidhi*) is determined, just as it was concluded in the sūtra "But [these] statements are [injunctions] because they convey something not previously known" (*vacanāni tvapūrvatvāt*); and it is the same in this case.

(Alternatively), for—since—the causality of the Blessed One, Nārāyaṇa, who is full of the sixfold attributes such as knowledge and sovereignty, namely His being the creator of the entire universe, and the effect-nature of others, such as Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, and so forth—that is, their being created by the Blessed One—is established through the natural sense of the statement; that is, by reflecting on the complete form of the sentence beginning with "Eko ha vai," in such a way that the syntactical connection remains effortless, [the author] deliberated and determined this. Therefore, all of this has been concluded.

"Uncontradicted" means unobstructed. Furthermore, whether these two words "ha vai" are accepted as being injunctive or as restating an established fact, there is nothing else that is superior to the Blessed One—that is, anything other than the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa which could serve as a basis for superiority. Nor is there any thing to be enjoined—something that, because it exists during both creation and dissolution, would be fit to be prescribed; such a thing does not exist, nor is it found at all within this collection of passages from the Mahopaniṣad.

(For even though it restates what is established by another Śruti passage—"In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second"—the status of being a restatement (*anuvāda*) indicated by the word "vai" still finds its purpose; furthermore, because it is mentioned in proximity to explicit negations such as "neither Brahmā nor Īśāna," there is not even a scent of doubt regarding any contradiction with [the fact that] Nārāyaṇa is the source. || 74 || [That which belongs to the Supreme Person, the creator of names and forms, who is designated by the name "Space"...]

In the heart-lotus, that which is to be worshipped—the "Supreme" (Para) sung by the chanters of the Sāmaveda—is to be meditated upon, as declared in the Upanishads. There, through a series of questions and answers, the learned ones proclaim His eight qualities—beginning with the removal of sin and ending with the power of true resolve—which arise from Him and are distinct from this [empirical] world. || 75 ||

From the one known as Ākāśa—the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) who is designated by the term "Ākāśa" in that very [text] of the Sāma-veda students (Sāmagānas), namely the Chāndogas, who study the Sāma-veda; and who, at the "head of the Śruti"—that is, within the concluding portion of the Vedic branch to be studied (the Upaniṣad)—is the "designator" (saṃjñā), meaning the bringer-about of name and form belonging to all created objects, and who is the "creator of forms" (mūrtikartṛ). Superior to him...

Something else—namely, that whose specific nature has not been specified therein should be worshipped within the heart-lotus; it should be the object of worship as delimited by the lotus of the heart. That which was sung [in the scripture]—the reality enjoined by the scriptural fragment, "What is within that [space] is to be sought"—that very reality, which serves as the object of worship, consists of those qualities beginning with freedom from evil and ending with the power of true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpatā*), such as being free from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) and so forth, up to the power of true resolve. These are its [qualities].

They are the objects denoted by the term "space," which are unrelated to this world and do not arise with it; at the time of liberation, they are natural and distinct from the qualities of the individual soul (jīva) that are fit for manifestation for the first time.

The "remaining" [qualities]—those taught in that very same context—refer to the eight qualities consisting of freedom from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*), freedom from old age (*vijaratva*), freedom from death (*vimṛtyutva*), freedom from sorrow (*viśokatva*), freedom from hunger (*vijighatsatva*), freedom from thirst (*apipāsatva*), having true desires (*satyakāmatva*), and having true resolves (*satyasaṅkalpatva*). These eight numbered qualities are [established] therein through a question and answer—the inquiry and the rejoinder concerning that subject within the section on the Dahara-vidyā in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "What is there found? Are desires contained within this?"

Thus, by means of these two forms [which determine the intended meaning], those skilled in contemplating its significance recite—that is, they state with certainty—that "the object of worship residing within the category of space is indeed its own eightfold set of qualities, and nothing else. || 75 ||
Having introduced the Primordial Being as the cause of death and having disparaged another path, [the author] describes this all-encompassing [wisdom] of his for the sake of attaining that wealth.

In that context, the statement "that which is higher than that bestows liberation" refers to the Primordial Person—Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person who is the cause of the universe and the source of immortality—having introduced Him [with the words] "he goes to death. By setting aside—that is, by disparaging or teaching as non-existent—another path, namely another means for crossing over death [with the words] "there is no other path," this is intended to establish the fact that the Primordial Person is the means for transcending death, and to reinforce the stated meaning that such a means does not exist elsewhere; [this refers to] that aforementioned Primordial Person.

Unrivaled by any other, she is the Mistress of All—having proclaimed her unimpeded state as the Sovereign of All with the resonant proclamation of the Śruti: "Than whom there is nothing higher... everything is by means of the Person," and having made this clear, regarding that very context, there is the statement: "That which is higher than that bestows liberation"—"That which is higher than that is formless and free from ailment."

The statement seen as "Those who know this become immortal"—that sentence is a conclusion (*nigamana*), meaning a final summary, which establishes the nature of each successive reality as being changeless, formless, and the object of the knowledge that serves as the means to liberation; it is endowed with a statement of reason (*hetūktimat*)—meaning it includes the expression of a reason such as "therefore" or "for that reason"—regarding the specific subject matter described throughout the entire *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* as proclaimed in the *Śvetāśvatara Āgama*.

But it is not a description for the first time, as something entirely new, of an object that is already the highest of the high. (Therefore, Brahman alone is the cause of the world, the highest of the high; there is no other distinct reality apart from it. || 76 ||
Furthermore, the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* provides another clear application [of the term] regarding the Blessed One:

"The Person" (*puruṣaḥ*)—meaning *Puruṣottama*, or one who possesses the state of being the Person without limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika-puruṣatva*). This is again made explicit by the *Śvetāśvatara Śruti* itself: "The Great Lord, indeed, is the Person, the impeller of *sattva*. (Therefore, this word *śiva* is not merely conventional; because it denotes Nārāyaṇa through the instrumental cause of being the bestower of auspiciousness without limiting adjuncts. || 77 ||

Since the *aitareya* Śruti speaks of the state of Śiva as being employed before Hara, it is indeed appropriate that it refers to the Supreme Cause of the universe; for those portions of the Upaniṣads desiring that [state] declare Him to be the Cause, while Viṣṇu, Bhagavān, Nārāyaṇa, and others are mentioned only in a general sense. (78) Those portions desiring that [state]... (78)
The Śvetāśvatara Śruti—the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad—applies [these names] to Hari: "O Blessed Viṣṇu, You are the eternal, auspicious, and infallible"; "Sarva, Śarva, Śiva, Sthāṇu, Īśāna."

In such usage as this, the term *śivapada*—which expresses the word "Śiva" in the manner of the verse, "When there is darkness, that is neither day... nor being, nor non-being, Śiva alone exists"—is employed because that term *śivapada* has as its intended meaning the Supreme Cause of the Universe (*viśvakaraṇaparam*), namely the principle that constitutes the cause of the world. Therefore, even prior [to creation], at the time of waking—that is, during the period preceding creation—and even in the state of dissolution (*pralaya*), it remains established with an unswerving essential nature and character, having abandoned its state of being withdrawn; in that very state—

It is proper—that is, it is right—to employ [these terms] for Hari alone, the Supreme Cause. The "Upaniṣadic portions" are specific sections related to the Upaniṣads; being intent on making this Person known as the Cause, distinguished by those specific attributes suitable for causality that they require, they call upon Him—the ascertained Cause of the universe—by means of names such as "Sādhāraṇya... and so forth, which are the Lord's unique designations: "Viṣṇu," "Bhagavān," "Nārāyaṇa," and "Puruṣa."

By such names as these, they speak and enlighten [beings] here and there. [Terms like] Śiva and so forth are general terms, because they apply to objects possessing both qualified (*sopādhika*) and unqualified (*nirupādhika*) forms of Śiva-nature. Terms such as Nārāyaṇa, however, are specific. Indeed, there is no contradiction in the application of either type of term to those respective objects. (78)

That Supreme Brahman, the cause of the universe, whose auspicious state is known through sacred learning, awakens at the beginning; that Blessed Lord is employed in the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* at its conclusion,
wherein the word "Śiva" is used in that *Yajus* [verse] as the crest-jewel of the Vedas.
The commonality between "sva" (self) and "tat" (that) was not reckoned as equal to the words of Nārāyaṇa. || 79 ||

The term *śrutaśivapada* refers to that supreme reality which is the Supreme Brahman, determined by the Vedas (*śruti*) to be denoted by the word "Śiva. At the conclusion of the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad*, this subject is clearly set forth in the subsequent passage: "What is the cause? Brahman... the Supreme Brahman. This very object, which is the referent of the word "Śiva" and is of the nature of Brahman—the Lord who is the cause of the universe—is [the subject] in such passages as, "In the beginning, indeed, Nārāyaṇa alone existed," regarding the world.

Nārāyaṇa alone, as established by the Śruti through His existence from primordial time, is [the subject], and no other; regarding that Nārāyaṇa who is the cause of the universe, the word "Śiva"—this term "Śiva"—is employed in the Yajus, specifically in the *Taittirīya-Nārāyaṇopaniṣad* which is included within the Yajurveda, for the purpose of denoting Him, as in such passages as "the eternal, auspicious, and infallible."

Therefore, the fact that the word "Nārāyaṇa"—the term *nārāyaṇa*—is unique to Him, meaning it is not capable of denoting both Nārāyaṇa and anyone other than Him, has not been equated [with other terms] by the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) nor accepted by authoritative scholars (*prāmāṇika*). (The term *Śiva*, taking its capacity to bestow auspiciousness as the basis for its application, may appropriately be used for Nārāyaṇa as well as for others such as Rudra who possess a mere fraction of those qualities; however, the term *Nārāyaṇa* cannot be applied elsewhere in any manner whatsoever, because the primary function of the word is unique and not shared by any other. || 79 ||
When questioned by the gods, Rudra, desiring a reply, withdrew from his own form and assumed the great office of the Supreme Lord upon the head of Atharvan;
he, the abundance of the Blessed One who had manifested within as the inner self, spoke thus: "Oṃ."
"Danta entered" [is explained] by way of a grammatical rule of dependency, like the case of Vāmadeva and others. || 80 ||

In the *Atharvaṇa-mūrdhan*—that is, in the portion of the Upaniṣads known as the *Atharvaśiras*—Rudra, the deity presiding over dissolution, being questioned by the gods (*suraiḥ*) with the inquiry "Who are you?", and desiring to give them an answer (having set about to provide that answer), revealed within his own self (*ātmani*), in his true nature, the great and uncontracted office of the Supreme Lord (*adhīśvara-dhurām*), the pinnacle of all sovereignty, beginning with "I alone existed in the beginning," and so forth, up to "by Dharma..."

Having spoken at length up to the words, "I satisfy Dharma with my own splendor," he then spoke—that is, he gave a reply. When that giving of a reply is reflected upon and considered, it is determined as follows: Rudra, who had set out to give the answer, manifested... [as] the *bhūman*—one who has attained the state of being directly perceived, possessing the majesty of the Lord who is the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of all beings; he [appeared] within...

"Viśa" (enter) is according to the method studied [in scripture]: in that very *Atharvaśiras*, it says, "He entered from within to the innermost. The individual soul (*jīva*) named Rudra entered the Supreme Self, which is subtler than the subtle soul in relation to the body and so forth; that is, he attained a subtle state consisting of the realization of his own inner-selfhood within Him. In the manner recited by the Śruti, like Vāmadeva and others, he spoke—just as Vāmadeva and others, having perceived their non-separate existence from the Blessed Lord, [spoke] of themselves.

They abandoned [the sense of duality] through non-difference from the Supreme Self; likewise, by means of the contemplation of non-difference between the Lord below (Aghośvara) and the Blessed One, he described his own essential nature. || 80 ||

"Anuyuktaḥ" means: as before, following the subsequent statement, [he is addressed] by way of such formulations as "Am I eternal or non-eternal? etc. "Nānyaḥ kaścinmattaḥ" means: from the statement found in the *Atharvaśiras* beginning with "There is nothing other than me," which is of that nature; "from the ugra-statement" means from the statement uttered by Rudra, who is denoted by the word "ugra"; "above" means heard subsequently.

The word *iti*—the term *iti* (referring to the sequence of the sentence: "There is nothing whatsoever other than Me")—does not express, nor does it convey, its own conclusion—the end of Rudra’s statement. Just as before this sentence, there was the existence of Rudra’s statement "I am one," so too after this sentence is concluded by the word *iti*, there is the persistence of Rudra’s statement; for [the knowledge] follows from Rudra’s statement because [the word *iti*] functions as a marker indicating that Rudra’s statement continues.

Because it contradicts the cognition at the conclusion of that statement, [he speaks] in such a manner as "I am both eternal and non-eternal," and so forth. (If it is asked, "How is it determined that Rudra's speech continues in what follows?", the answer is: by means of a style of expression composed of the word "I" (*aham*), consisting of such statements as "I am eternal and non-eternal; I am manifest and unmanifest. (This refers to the sentence composed of the word "I": "I alone was first.")

Indeed, this sentence composed of words was uttered by Him alone and not by anyone else. This scriptural statement situated within it—"He entered into the space within the space"—reveals the meaning of the subject matter under discussion; it is not part of Rudra's own speech. "He" refers to the Supreme Self, Nārāyaṇa. From the "space within"—that is, from even the vital breaths and other elements residing within the body—He "entered the space within," meaning He entered into the individual soul (jīva) residing therein.
Therefore, because the Supreme Self has entered into the interior of the individual soul known as Rudra, [the latter is designated as such].

The statement of Rudra, "I am one," and so forth—which proceeds from the recognition of non-difference from Him—is not due to a delusion regarding himself as the Supreme Self; thus the scriptural declaration intervenes. Furthermore, the words of Rudra continue [as follows]. (81)
Regarding this, the *Neti* [Upanishad] states the reason: "No. Prahlāda stated the manner [of entry]: "the entry into the Infinite.
Prahlāda’s statement—that it is because of the Infinite's omnipresence—is clearly set forth in the *Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa*. (82)

Therefore, since the word *iti* heard in the phrase "there is nothing else whatsoever distinct from Me" cannot have the sense of completion (*samāptyartha*), this word *iti* situated in that sentence expresses the reason—namely, that because the Supreme Self has entered within and without everywhere ("He entered into what is innermost, and He entered into the space between the quarters"), it conveys this intention and not a mode of completion, just as it does not express a conclusion.

Likewise, [the statement] "He said that there is no one else distinct from the Mind" does not state the manner or the object; rather, "entry within" means the entry of the Supreme Self into the interior of all things, and "cause" means the factor that motivates the cognition and the conventional usage of non-difference between the individual self and the Supreme Self—this has indeed been made manifest by Prahlāda in his own words. Prahlāda’s speech—that is, the well-spoken words of Prahlāda expressing his intended meaning—is as follows: "Because He is infinite and omnipresent... — "Because He is infinite and omnipresent, He... that."

The form "I am thus situated" is clearly perceived in the Purāṇa known as Vaiṣṇava—that specific Purāṇa renowned among the eighteen Purāṇas as belonging to Viṣṇu. (And the Śruti passage "from within" is not in the form of Rudra’s words; rather, it is in the form of a Vedic statement. Its meaning was stated in the previous verse. || 82 ||
By the word "or" (athavā), the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is stated here as the reason, and not any other; thus it is avīta.
The positive concomitance (anvaya) expressed by "I am one" is a mode that is easy for the cognizer to apprehend. || 83 ||

Alternatively—even if one abandons the relocation of the word *iti*, which occurs in the text, from its original position and instead inserts it in its own place—the phrase "there is no other" (*atra nānyaḥ*) as studied here refers to what is established by the scripture in the *Atharvaśiras*: "There is no other whatsoever distinct from me. This "distinction" (*vyatirekaḥ*) is the absence of any other entity residing in itself (as a separate, independent reality) apart from the referent of the word "I" contained in the sentence "I am one alone" (*ahamekaḥ*). Regarding the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) expressed as "I am one alone," [it means]: "I alone am the creation..."

Regarding the relationship with existence (*bhāvasambandha*) expressed as "I exist in all three times—past, the time of creation, and the time of dissolution—in the form of a reality established in My own self," the cause [of this relationship] was stated by the word "from the Śruti" (*śrutigatāt*), which establishes it as the instrumental motivator (*prayojaka*). [The meaning is: "Since I alone remain non-dual, possessing a nature whose essence is never lost throughout the three times; therefore, there is no other object whatsoever established in its own right apart from Me. This is the "aspectual interpretation" (*prakārapakṣa*), wherein the word *iti* carries the sense of "in such a manner" (*prakāra*).
(Thus— likewise, the position [pakṣa], meaning the manner of perceiving— that is, of accepting)— || 83 ||

It is easy to accept—that is, it becomes readily established—[that] since there is necessarily an absence of smoke where there is an absence of fire, there must necessarily be fire where there is smoke; thus, once the positive concomitance (*anvaya-vyāpti*) between smoke and fire is proven, just as the non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) of the two negative instances—the absence of fire and the absence of smoke—is a proof [of the pervasion], so too, because nothing other than the Supreme Self exists anywhere throughout the three periods of time, it is logically consistent that the one Supreme Self alone persists in all places, at all times, and in all states.

Rudra’s statement, "He who is within," implies that he is someone other than that [individual soul], his inner self; and it is said that he is the inner self of others as well— this is the meaning of "the one within and so forth."
Thus addressed by Raudrī, he too became the celebrated Viṣṇu. || 84 ||

Therefore—since the word *iti* is accepted as having the sense of "manner" (*prakāra*), the statement "He entered from within" refers to this very utterance found in the Śruti: "He entered from the innermost interior, He entered the interior of the quarters"—this [is] the statement concerning Rudra, that is, Śiva alone.

Not from scripture; therefore—since the passage "He who is within" is a statement by Rudra, and because it is spoken by Rudra through the words "He who is within"—by this speech uttered by Rudra, it is established that there is no other [self] distinct from Rudra or from other individual souls (jīvātman), namely some particular deity of unspecified name who is called the "inner self" (antarātman)—one who, having entered within, is the sustainer and controller—and he too is of the nature of the inner self.

Furthermore, Viṣṇu is well known as a specific deity, as understood from such Śruti passages as, "This is the inner Self of all beings, free from evil, the divine, the one God, Nārāyaṇa," and from Smṛti passages such as, "He is the inner Self of you and of me. Thus, it is known that [the deity] is indeed Viṣṇu. (84) Or rather, let this statement conclude with the words of Hara: "May he [the Lord] be within the sun; let there not be a mention of Rudra. This being the case, there is no contradiction whatsoever with our own doctrine. For Rudra, desiring to enter fully into Hari—who is his own self—with a mind free from impurity—
The Vedic word clearly reveals that the nurse is certainly another man. || 85 ||

The word "iti" occurring in the sentence "There is no other whatsoever distinct from me"—this is the statement. Or let the word "iti" signify the conclusion of the speech of Hara—that is, let it indicate the end of the declaration by Śiva that began with "I am one. For this reason—because the word "iti" indicates the completion of Rudra's utterance and because [the subsequent passage] does not follow after Rudra's speech—the phrase "He is from within" (so'ntarād), namely the statement "He is from within, more within," may not be considered the speech of Śiva.

Let it not be so; even if this were accepted, there would be no possibility—even the slightest—of any contradiction or weakening of our own position, namely the Vaiṣṇava doctrine which accepts Nārāyaṇa as the inner self of all. Rudra, that is Paramaśiva, [worships] Hari, the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa, who is his very own self, who sustains him by being the controller of even his own essential nature, and who is the supreme object of service.

With *apaladhiyā*—that is, with a stainless intellect (*manīṣayā*), desiring to bring [the Lord] under his own control—that is, wishing to make His inner being gracious toward himself—he entered [into Him]; with a pure understanding (*śuddhabuddhyā*), he grasped the true nature of the Blessed One, or rather, through an intellect consisting of surrender (*prapadanātmakayā śemuṣyā*), he performed the total self-offering to the Blessed One (and the subduing of Him is nothing other than taking refuge in Him).

(When one asks, "How did he enter?": Desiring to make another person—another individual—his own subordinate, wishing to make him inclined to act in accordance with his own will, like a wise man—a particular person skilled in means—who has set out to cause another person to adopt behavior favorable to himself (just as, having entered that other person, he becomes solely intent on discerning that person's gestures and so forth;).

And by that [wind], it is conventionally designated as "the one who has entered into that person"; likewise, the meaning is that Supreme Śiva also became fully entered into the Supreme Self—this is what the Śruti declares with the words "He [entered] within" (so 'ntarā). This meaning is manifested by the voice of the Veda; this very point is illuminated by the words of the *Atharvaśiras*. 85.
Having heard those words of Rudra, the immortals exerted themselves to offer hymns of praise to Him; yet, even though they sought to attain all-encompassing sovereignty through the *Atharva-śiras*,
those very utterances of Rudra are indeed manifested here as the means for attaining the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) upon the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*).
Those who are joined with that, those who have not been told that, those who dwell in heaven, or those who share a single intention with him—[all these are included]. (86)

In the *Atharvamūrdhan*— that is, in the Upaniṣad named *Atharvaśiras*— the immortals, the gods, having heard the words of Rudra beginning with "I alone was the first," and having listened to that speech uttered by Śiva, [approached] for the sake of praising his majesty— that is, to speak aloud of the glory resulting from the realization of Rudra’s status as being internally presided over (antaryāmin) by the Blessed Lord.

Since they have clearly declared—through such statements as "He who is Rudra, he is the Blessed Lord"—that even the universal sovereignty of Rudra, which consists in being the controller of all and is a supremacy exceeding all others, is established as having the Blessed Lord as his inner controller (*antaryāmin*); these declarations by the immortals are caused solely by the continuous meditation upon the nature of the Blessed Lord as residing within that very form called Rudra, [and thus] constitute his universal sovereignty.

That [teaching] is indeed centered on the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin); for even in the case of Rudra, because of the contemplation of duality, what was intended was the meditative absorption on the Inner Controller (antaryāmi-samādhi), owing to its inherent nature. For this reason, here—in this section contained within this Upaniṣad—the utterances of Rudra, such as "I am alone" and so forth, which are the words of Śiva, are clearly evident as being endowed with that [meditation]. Furthermore, the speech of the gods (diviṣadvākāḥ)—the utterances of the deities—also possess that same intent, having that [Absorption on the Inner Controller] as their primary purport.

The subsequent utterances, however, consist precisely of the form of reasoning based on inference (*anumā-yukti*). It should be understood that while the speech of the gods, such as hymns of praise, proceeds through the continuous cultivation of the inner controller (*antaryāmī*), the same occurs for others as well through the uninterrupted cultivation of the inner controller. (86)
O virtuous ones,
therefore,
are not these other names, preceded by the syllable *oṃ* and thus established, indeed synonymous with the city of Rudra?

In the *Atharvaśiras*, however, those [names] are not capable of establishing the status of being the well-known presiding Lord (*prasiddha-deśitṛtva*). In the *Atharvaśiras*—that is, in the Upaniṣad called the *Atharvaśiras*—other names, such as Rudra, Īśāna, and so forth, are indeed presented preceded by the syllable *Oṃ*; that is, they are certainly stated with the presentation of the *praṇava* (the sacred syllable) at the outset. However, those names do not establish the status of being the well-known presiding Lord (*prasiddha-rudreśitṛtva*) over the Trimūrti.

In order to establish Rudra’s status as the Lord of All—he who is renowned in the Śrutis and other scriptures as the sole agent of dissolution even while remaining neutral—it is not possible, nor are they capable, to provide a logical understanding [of this]. || 87 ||
Although the etymological explanations (niruktas) for Rudra and others— which concern the *praṇava* introduced at the beginning— are stated word by word on the head of Mahādeva,
this very majesty of the *tāra* [Oṃ] resides upon the head of the *Atharvaṇī Śruti*.
The manifest form (vyakti) shall be the syllable Om, which serves as the surrounding ornament for the higher Vidyā. || 88 ||

In the *Atharvaśiras Upaniṣad* (the fifth section) of the *Ātharvaṇī Śruti*, there are names pertaining to the *praṇava* under discussion—names related to the syllable *kaṃ* introduced in the preceding section because it represents the Blessed Lord—which are the designations beginning with "Rudra" and ending with "Mahādeva. These names, being verbal appellations, are etymologically explained at every step by demonstrating the derivation of each individual word.

As for that which exists [in the form of] "those whose etymologies have been established," this very thing—the demonstration of these etymologies found in the Śruti—manifests the glory of the syllable *oṃ*; it clarifies the majesty of *oṃ* (since the glory of the expressive word culminates in the glory residing in its expressed meaning), such that *oṃ* is the most glorious.

The *praṇava* being manifested here would certainly be necessary as a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the *vidyā* taught in the sixth section—which consists of the worship of the Lord clothed in the form of the deity named Rudra—and would thus serve as its preparatory framework (*parikara*). (88) "The path to bondage and to peace"—here, in this *Atharva* [Upaniṣad], the worship of Paśupati is proclaimed at the very head; by that statement, Hari, whose essence is that [Paśupati], shines forth as the one to be worshipped here. Just as in the *Madhu-vidyā* and others, there exists the relationship of creator and created between the bodies of other deities.
But here too, the Vedic method is equal; what has been heard here is supplementary to the meditation under discussion. (89)

In this *Atharvamūrdhan*—in this Upaniṣad known as the *Atharvaśiras*—the worship of Paśupati, that is, the meditation upon Rudra named Paśupati, is declared to be the path for the cessation of bondage, specifically for the removal of the bondage called *pāśa* from those living beings designated as *paśus*. This being the case, how can your endeavor to prove that this Upaniṣad, which is devoted to the worship of Rudra, is instead devoted to the worship of the Lord (Viṣṇu), appear at all appropriate?

If this is argued, the reply is as follows: By the ancient speech residing in the eastern region, in the form of "He entered from the interior into the interior," and by the Upaniṣadic statement beginning with "This is His supreme conduct," Hari—the Lord Nārāyaṇa who is the inner controller (*antaryāmī*) of Rudra—is to be worshipped here; that is, He is prescribed as the object of worship in the *Atharvaśiras*. (If it is asked: "For what purpose is the Supreme Self, whose body is Rudra, to be worshipped? [The answer is: In the *Mādhvī* and other *vidyās*...

In the Madhuvidyā, the Indraprāṇavidyā, and others, just as the Supreme Self is to be meditated upon as having the bodies of other deities—such as the Vasus and Ādityas—and as having the body of Indra; so too [is He to be meditated upon here].

In the same way, here the Supreme Self, having Rudra as its body, is to be worshipped—this is the answer. The scriptural state of being the creator and the created, that is, the nature of cause and effect, is equal—that is, common to both the Lord Vasu-Indra and the Lord Rudra (according to the Śruti: "From the forehead was born Rudra, born of wrath"). Here, "heard" means prescribed by the Śruti within this context (as that which is to be worn); "bhasita" means ash; it is a supplement to the worship under discussion.

This is a subsidiary part of the worship of the Supreme Self within the body of Rudra as previously introduced; it is not, however, this wearing of ashes established by the Pāśupata scriptures. || 89 ||

Having introduced the knowledge of Puruṣottama in his form as Rudra, which has the *Atharvaśiras* as its limb, there is no application of ashes elsewhere, just as there is no application of the cup of wine mentioned in the context of the Sautrāmaṇi sacrifice outside that specific rite.

Of the Supreme Person—the Lord Mahāviṣṇu, whose body is Rudra, a specific deity presiding over the function of dissolution—having introduced the *vidyā* (the means of knowledge, i.e., worship) in the *Atharvaśiras*, that is, having begun to enjoin it in the *Atharvaśira Upaniṣad*, the *aṅga* (subsidiary element) of this—that is, the ritual action consisting of the bathing with ashes (*bhasmasnāna*), the wearing of ashes (*bhasmadhāraṇa*), and so forth, which serves to assist the aforementioned *vidyā* known as the worship of the Lord whose body is Rudra—is declared [in the passage]:
"Ashes are fire" (*abhir iti bhasma*) and "ashes... (*bhasma*).

There is a possibility [of application] based on the injunction beginning with, "Having taken [the ashes], he should wipe them and touch his limbs"; however, such an application of wearing those ashes does not arise, nor is there even a possibility of it occurring, in other cases—namely, in other forms of meditation (*upāsanā*).
