Just as, in the context of the *Sautrāmaṇī* sacrifice—the taking of the *surā-graha* (a specific vessel for liquor) as prescribed by the Vedic text, "He takes the *surā-grahas*," does not have application in other sacrifices, and just as the possibility of such a taking is not at all conceivable;
so it is here. || 90 ||

In the *Atharvaṇīya-śikhā*, that birth of the Blessed One was enumerated as an "incarnation by will" (*icchāvatāra*), which is solely intent upon making Him the sole object of meditation for the cause [of liberation] and for the benefit of the world. For Viṣṇu, there is the clear teaching of His causality through aphorisms exclusively devoted to that cause;
likewise, the word *Śambhu* is clearly applied to Him because He produces happiness. (91)

In the *Atharvaśikhā*—an Upaniṣad of the Atharvaveda which proceeds with the primary intent of establishing that the one Cause alone is the object of meditation, as stated in the text "But the Cause is to be meditated upon"—there is described the birth of the Blessed One, Mahāviṣṇu, which is otherwise impossible for him: "Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra—all these are born from Him. This very portion, established by the Śruti in the form of His birth, [manifests] for the benefit of the world... [to subdue] the wicked... (Note: The provided fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available text.)

The descent [of the Lord] is for the purpose of benefiting the world through acts such as the punishment of the wicked and the protection of the virtuous; it is an appearance brought about by His will, dependent on [past] karma, and preceded by His resolve (*saṅkalpa*). For which reason—by which cause—the teaching of the causality of Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self Nārāyaṇa, occurs: namely, the instruction regarding the unknown causality of the universe through the utterances of the *Śruti* (Vedas)—utterances whose primary intent is to establish the reality that is the cause of the birth and so forth of the world (or: whose intent concerns the one Reality alone who is the cause)—such as: "In the beginning, indeed, there was only Nārāyaṇa," and "Then, indeed, there was the Person, Nārāyaṇa."

"May I create progeny," [he] desired; "The world has arisen from Viṣṇu and remains in him alone"—by such words of Śruti, Smṛti, and other sources, the teaching of Viṣṇu’s causality—that is, the injunction that Viṣṇu alone is the cause of the world—is clear and beyond doubt. In that Viṣṇu, who is thus determined to be the cause of the world, even the word *Śambhu*—this term *Śambhu*—is seen to be used elsewhere in its familiar application based on the reason of being a producer of happiness (*sukhajanakatayā*). || 91 ||
The two forms of worship taught in the *Atharvaśiras* and the *Śikhā* Upaniṣads have been clearly explained for the sake of non-rebirth by one whose body is as dark as the enemy of cities (Śiva).

For the wise one with lotus-like eyes, who dwells within the cavity of the heart, there are in certain places, for specific reasons, two meditations prescribed by his own and other scriptural traditions. In the *Atharvaśiras Upaniṣad* and the *Atharvaśikha Upaniṣad*, these two meditations—namely, "This very one should be meditated upon" and "Śambhu is to be meditated upon in the midst of space"—are enjoined as the means for the sake of liberation (*apunarbhava*). Thus, it becomes clearly and well-known that these two meditations possess distinct natures.

And in one place—in the *Atharvaśiras Upaniṣad*, which is among those whose secret doctrine has been stated—there is the worship of the lotus-eyed Lord, the embodied one named Rudra, by the enemy of the cities (Śiva). In another place—in the immediately following *Atharvaśikhā Upaniṣad*—[the worship] of the Cause...

The meaning is that the worship of the lotus-eyed one (Viṣṇu)—who is taught in the Śrutis engaged in propounding the Supreme Reality which is the cause of the universe, and who dwells within the cavity of the heart of the knower—is easily understood. (Therefore, although the worship prescribed by the two Upaniṣads is distinct as being "with a medium" and "without a medium," it is indeed the worship of the Lord; thus, there is nothing difficult to comprehend here. || 92 ||

It has been stated by some that "Īśvara" is a synonym for Puruṣa; however, the terms Śiva and Śrīśa are frequently found in the Mahatparā and Vāmya scriptures even when [the context] is distinct [from Puruṣa]. Thus, between these two terms—which are explained through words falling within the spheres of excellence and inferiority—it is appropriate to declare the superiority of Giriśa over Puruṣa, just as [one declares the superiority] of Pradhāna [over Puruṣa].

When [the word] is qualified by the two secondary terms (*upapada*) "great" (*mahat*) and "supreme" (*parama*) at the beginning—whether joined with them or even when separated from those two secondary terms and used alone—the words *īśvara* and *puruṣa* are thus expressed as *maheśvara*, *parameśvara*, and *īśvara*; likewise, [the words] *mahāpuruṣa*, *paramapuruṣa*, and *puruṣa* are used in many ways.

Generally speaking, Śiva and Śrīśa exist as the two who provide awakening—namely, Śambhu and the Lord of Lakṣmī. Thus, between these two, Śiva and Viṣṇu, whose natures are manifested by the term ‘Īśvara’ which denotes excellence and by the term ‘Puruṣa’ (which functions commonly for servants and others) denoting inferiority relative to that [excellence], [the former is superior] just as the Puruṣa is superior to the Pradhāna, the principle of primordial nature.

It has been stated by someone—one engaged in proclaiming the supremacy of Śiva—that "the excellence of Giriśa—Śiva—is fit to be spoken and proper for worldly discourse; for between the two mentioned as 'Pradhāna and Puruṣa,' Puruṣa is superior while Pradhāna is inferior; likewise, between the two mentioned as 'Śiva and Viṣṇu,' Śiva is superior while Viṣṇu is inferior. (93)

This is not correct; for it is not fitting for anyone to assert the superiority of Giriśa on the basis of a name that is powerful yet has a different meaning, as in the case of Devendra. Otherwise, Indra would be the Supreme Lord due to those various names; however, a name is indeed sublated by stronger means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) in his case, like the term "great tree" (mahāvṛkṣa).

This—both the assumption of inferiority regarding Śrīśa based on the application of the word *puruṣa*, and the assumption of superiority regarding Śambhu based on the application of the word *īśvara*—is neither good nor correct; for [the latter] is obstructed by stronger means of knowledge consisting of syntactic connection (*vākya*), indicative power (*liṅga*), and direct statement (*śruti*), which possess the comprehension of their own denotative meanings, by means of *samākhyā* (name/designation)—which, though falling among the group beginning with *śruti* and *liṅga*, is a derivative word functioning as a valid means of knowledge.

The superiority (*utkarṣa*) of Giriśa—that is, Śiva’s preeminence over Viṣṇu—is not fit to be asserted or declared by anyone, even by one skilled in deliberating upon the strength or weakness of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). [Words such as] *Īśvara*, *Puruṣa*, and so forth, possessing specific etymologies as they are conceived, attain the status of conventional designations (*samākhyā*). And in accordance with that, they acquire the status of authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in the comprehension of their specific meanings.

The meaning is that since sentence (*vākya*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and direct statement (*śruti*) have already been established as means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) prior to this, they obstruct the determination of the intended meaning [that would otherwise be derived] from the name (*samākhyā*). This is like the case of Devendra: when the inquiry arose, "Between Mahādeva and Devendra, which one is superior?", through reflection on the etymology of the words, it was determined that Śakra—who possesses supreme sovereignty—is superior to Śiva, who is a deity by virtue of his greatness (*mahattva*). Just so [is the superiority of *śruti* over *samākhyā*].

It is not appropriate otherwise—that is, if, setting aside the consideration of the relative strength or weakness of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), a determination of meaning were valid even by the mere grasping of a single part [of a word]. In that case, by virtue of various designations (*samākhyā*) based on the specific etymological derivation of the components—as in the words *indra* and *mahendra* (where *ind* signifies supreme sovereignty)—one would have to accept that *Indra*, the king of the gods, namely Śakra, is the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), possessing sovereignty that is unsurpassed and unrestricted, rather than Giriśa.

Nor is he the Lord of Śrī (Viṣṇu); for—since—the "name" is the denotative word, and with respect to that [name], in the case of Śakra, it is like the word "great tree" (*mahāvṛkṣa*) applied to a small species of tree; just as in that case the literal meaning of the parts [of the compound] is sublated by direct perception, so too here the meaning is sublated by a stronger means of knowledge—by such authorities as *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, which possess greater force than the denotative word itself.

In the same way, even terms such as "Maheśvara" (Great Lord) and so forth, having fulfilled their purpose by conveying relative sovereignty, greatness, and the like, are not at all capable of contradicting the absolute, unconditioned, and unrestricted sovereignty of the Blessed One established by the Vedas and other authoritative sources. || 04 ||

By mere designation, does it follow that the individual soul (jīva) is the object of the term "Person" (puruṣa)? Then the Lord of Śrī would also be the individual soul as the object of that term; and would Viṣṇu and Dhruva not both be designated by the name "Stump" (sthāṇu)?
O Teacher, why should one strive to carve out faces from the earth?
Does a lion become a frog by touching the feet of Hari? (95)

The individual soul (*jīva*)—that is, the individual self—is the object of the term "person" (*puruṣa*); that is, for the reason that it is understood by the word "person," it is the referent of that term, being denoted by the word "person. [One might ask: could even the Blessed Lord (*śrīśa*), Nārāyaṇa, be the individual soul? Or rather, would he be fit to be the individual soul?

Is it not the case that both of them—the specific piece of wood in the form of a stake and Śambhu—are designated by the term *sthāṇu*? That is to say, since they are both denotable by the word *sthāṇu*, does it follow that Giriśa—Śambhu—is also fixed (*dhruva*)? Is he perhaps a piece of wood in the form of a stake? Or rather, would it be possible for him to bring about the state of a carpenter (*takṣatva*)—that is, to reduce even the Brahmins (*mukhabhuvām*, those born from the mouth) to the status of craftsmen (*vardhakibhāva*)? Would he be capable of such a thing? No, indeed not. Furthermore, regarding the designation of "Teacher" (*ācāryasaṃśabdana*) applied to the Brahmins, would he be able to achieve that as well? No, he could not.

What? Indeed, O wicked one, would even a *kaṇṭhīrava*—a lion—attain the state of a frog merely by contact with the word *hari*—that is, by the mere connection with the word *hari* as its denotation? Would it attain identity with it? Certainly not! The meaning is that the mere identity of words does not sublate the distinction between two different objects. || 95 ||

Is the Supreme Brahman not celebrated in the Upaniṣadic sections through such terms as "Prāṇa," "Ākāśa," and "Mukha"? Does its status as the "Supreme" (para) cease to exist merely because of that? If that supremacy is attributed to Rudra and others—who are themselves created by the Blessed Lord as established by various causal statements regarding Prāṇa and the rest—then from where does that [supremacy] derive? 96.

Is that Supreme Brahman—which is universally acknowledged as the cause of the creation and so forth of the universe—not indeed celebrated in the Upanishadic portions, the final parts of the Vedas, by such words as "Prāṇa" and "Ākāśa," for instance in passages such as: "All these beings, verily, enter into Prāṇa alone and from Prāṇa they emerge," and "All these beings, verily, arise from Ākāśa alone and into Ākāśa they dissolve"? Thus it is stated here and there.

Has it not been heard many times being proclaimed? Indeed, it has certainly been heard. Yet, by that much alone, regarding the objects such as the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the ether (*ākāśa*), does the reckoning of supremacy—the conventional usage of being the most excellent—awaken or proceed? It certainly does not proceed. If that Supreme Brahman is designated by words such as Śiva—that is, if it is taught and made known by terms such as Śiva, Rudra, and so forth—then merely by that much, [it is] one among those various causes... in the things to be created by each of them.

By such causal statements as "Verily, Nārāyaṇa alone existed" and "Then the Person, Nārāyaṇa, desired: 'May I create progeny,'" the Blessed One is established as the cause. How, then, could supremacy—meaning being higher than all else—be established for those conscious beings such as Brahmā and Rudra, who are objects of worship for Rudra and others? By what reason could their state of being superior be proven? || 96 ||
That the supreme majesty of the lotus-eyed one was proclaimed by the Upanishads, which have attained refinement through pure reasoning,
leads others to conclude that their own words can only strive to conform to this very [truth].
Even the sages, headed by Manu, clearly corroborate this. || 97 ||

By those who have acquired the refinements obtained through the pure method—refinements which are free from obstruction by means such as valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and logic (*tarka*), which are attained within the body [of the *Śārīraka*], and which are capable of determining the meaning of the Vedānta.

By means of the Upaniṣads—the words of the Vedānta—which have attained refinement in the form of resolving doubts such as mutual contradictions, the supreme majesty (*parivṛḍhimā*), that is, the highest excellence beyond which nothing else is superior, was fully manifested for the lotus-eyed Lord Nārāyaṇa, whose eyes are as pure as the petals of a white lotus. That this very thing—the state of the Lord possessing an excellence surpassing all others—is what has been revealed by the Upaniṣads; [whereas] other words—that is, those studied...

Not even all the Vedic words found within the various branches of the Vedas that have been studied are capable of—meaning, able to—follow or conform to this [teaching]; for even the sages headed by Manu, such as Manu, Parāśara, and others, though intent upon the Smṛtis concerning the meaning of the Vedas, clearly and without doubt exalt it—that is, having fully nourished that very same meaning—they describe with their own words: "The Supreme Brahman is indeed Viṣṇu, the one higher than the highest. (97)

The term "bridge" (setu) is appropriately applied here because it is similar to a bridge, either by virtue of its function as a support or a restraint, or because of its binding nature; thus, even though this [Brahman] is all-pervading, the description of it as having limited dimensions through limiting adjuncts (upādhi) is meaningful, as was previously established in the Sūtra. Furthermore, the fourfold division [of the Self] is postulated for the sake of the infinite Being in accordance with the scriptural texts; thus it is said, "of the immortal" (amṛtasya), or else liberation itself may be the immortal. || 25 ||

In this context—"in the Supreme Brahman which is to be attained"—the nature of being a "bridge" refers first to that bridge-hood established by the scripture: "This is the bridge, the upholder. This is because it shares common attributes with a bridge as perceived in the world, namely the quality of "upholding" (vidharaṇa) and "regulating" (niyama). This is indicated by the word "of immortality" (amṛtasya) in the scriptural passage: "This is the bridge of immortality."

It has been stated [in the scripture]: "This is the Supreme Self; He is the bridge, the means of attainment, for His own immortality—that is, for that which is of the nature of immortality. It is not said, however, that He is the bridge for an immortality other than Himself (and thus the statement regarding His being the means of attainment does not contradict His being the object of attainment). Alternatively, if another meaning were considered, "immortality" (amṛta)—the referent denoted by the word "immortality"—would be liberation itself; it would be the very release from the bondage of saṃsāra. "This is the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa, for immortality..."

Because it is the bridge for liberation from saṃsāra, the means of attainment, and the giver of release—by implication—the inconsistency of identity between the goal and the means does not apply. (Therefore, Brahman is the cause, higher than the high. || 25 ||
In a statement regarding the superiority of one thing over another, that which is observed as the ultimate limit is the cause;
where the *vyākṛta* (the differentiated) and so forth serve as such a limit in relation to others, it is both "that" (*param*) and "beyond" (*para*).
This is because, with respect to the subject matter thus described, there is nothing further beyond it—this is the reasoning behind the term *tatpara*.
Or rather, let it be that what was stated [previously] refers to the pervader, following the statement "the Sun shines" (Revatī-aditya-anūktyā). || 26 ||

In whatever place—wherein a cause is established by scripture as the cause of a particular entity—the object denoted by the word "supreme" (*para*) is seen as the substratum; that is, it is the defining factor (*nirūpaka*) for the state of supremacy residing in a particular object (by way of possessing inferiority).

Regarding the phrase "the sixfold learning" (*sat-śruta*) [in such a context], when there is a statement asserting the superiority of one thing over another—such as the statement establishing the excellence of a different entity, for example, "Higher than the Imperishable is the Supreme"—in such a case, that which serves as the limit (*tad-avadhi*), namely the inferior object that defines the second "higher-ness," must be understood according to the context as being either the unmanifest principle (*avyakta-tattva*), the individual soul (*jīva*), or the collective person (*samaṣṭi-puruṣa*), Hiraṇyagarbha; this aforementioned object, such as the unmanifest and so forth, is [to be understood] in relation to the other.

With respect to its own effects (*svakārya*), with respect to non-conscious things (*acetana*), and with respect to its own individual manifestations (*svavyaṣṭi*), another indeed exists as something superior; there is no dispute on this point. However, regarding the subject matter of the other [text], namely the meaning conveyed by the word *yat* ending in the ablative case in the phrase "than which nothing higher exists" (*yasmānnāparamasti kiṃcit*)—which aims to establish the absence of any other superior beyond itself—the statement of something superior to that is inappropriate. This is because, since the preceding sentence has declared it to be superior to everything, stating that there is something even superior to that in the subsequent sentence would be contradictory.

Regarding the word "tataḥ" from the phrase "tato yaduttarataraṃ tadarūpam," its restatement as "evantvāt" means "because of being beyond all that has been mentioned"; thus, it is indeed merely a restatement of what was previously stated.

But it does not serve as a point of reference (*avadhi*) for "otherness" (which might lead to the confusion that there is another "other"), whether it be one way or another; rather, that [point of reference] is to be understood by the word "from that" (*tataḥ*), which is in the ablative case. Let the pervaded (*vyāpya*) mentioned be this: "All this is filled by that Puruṣa"—let all that which was declared to be pervaded by the Puruṣa be [the point of reference]. (The meaning of *tataḥ* is: from all that which is pervaded by itself. || 26 ||
— 0— Section on the Fruit (Phalādhikaraṇa) ||3-2-8||
A Compendium of the Collection of Aphorisms on the Embodied Soul.
Since it is observed that [an action] yields fruit either directly or through a sequence, let karma itself grant the fruit here as well;
for it is not [assumed] to have another purpose, and according to both Śruti and Smṛti, that very [karma] bestows it.

"Directly"—either without an intermediary (as in the case of *mardana*) or gradually (as in agriculture and so forth)—or "indirectly through a succession," because it is observed that [action] yields fruit (*phaladatvadṛṣṭeḥ*), meaning because it is seen that action (*karmaṇaḥ*) produces results; even in this context—namely, in the sphere of sacrifices, meditations, and the like, which are established by the Vedas and other authorities as the means for attaining the three aims of life (*trivarga*) and liberation (*apavarga*)—it is action alone—whether it be sacrifice and so forth, or meditation and so forth—that "should grant" or bestow the fruit, namely the fruit known as the three aims and the fruit known as liberation (and not anything else).

(An objection is raised that there must be a necessity for a bestower of the fruit: "This [Paramātman] is not to be propitiated by ritual action; that the fruit is bestowed by the action alone is not at all correct. This is because, according to the Śrutis and Smṛtis—that is, from the Vedas, their supplements such as the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, and so forth—it is observed that practices such as the meditation on the Cow (gopāsanā) are prescribed specifically for the purpose of producing the gratification of a particular deity other than Himself. Therefore, He alone—the Paramātman who is to be propitiated through both ritual action and meditation—is the one who grants the fruits, such as heaven and liberation. || 27 ||

In this section as well, by these many [verses]—starting from the first ten verses—the Supreme Person alone is the objective (*lakṣya*), characterized by the fear of worldly existence (*bhava-bhaya*). For sentient beings whose inner faculties are bewildered by the directions due to having no other refuge and being terrified by the forest-fire of *saṃsāra*, He is determined to be the individual objective; thus, He alone is the sole objective for worship, according to the respective requirements of the meaning of the scriptures: namely, the meaning of the scriptures prescribing rituals such as sacrifices, and the meaning of the scriptures prescribing the means to liberation such as meditation.

Having established that [the Lord] "bestows grace" by granting the desired fruits—the three aims of life (*trivarga*) and liberation (*apavarga*)—which are His purpose and are sought after by each individual, He is now declared to be "supremely generous. In this section, it is further confirmed that He is endowed with a great magnanimity that excludes any equal or superior, consisting in the bestowal of everything from His own divine manifestations down to His very self. || 27 ||
The fruit of agriculture and even of massage and such acts arises either through an intermediate step or otherwise;
the fact that dharmas are means to an end is understood from the scriptures, which are free from the sublation of defects.
Therefore, if it is argued that the statement "the fruit comes from the grace of the Lord" is merely for the sake of praising Him—that is not so.
Because it is impossible for there to be a novel creation resulting from the abandonment of the grace of the one to be worshipped according to the Śruti. || 28 ||

Just as from agriculture and even from massage—through activities such as plowing the earth after sowing seeds, or through activities such as massaging the limbs after applying oil—and whether by way of a medium—that is, by making something an intermediate step—or otherwise, without making anything an intermediate step, a result arises—namely, results such as health, prosperity, and abundant harvests—in the same way, [the results] of dharmas, such as sacrifice and giving...

The fact that actions denoted by the term *dharma*—such as *homa*, worship, and so forth—serve as the means for bestowing the fruits of the three aims of life (*traivargika*) and liberation (*apavargika*), is clearly known through the *śrutis* (the words of the Veda), which are free from defects, devoid of contradiction, eternally faultless in nature, and uncontradicted by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, since it is established that only those actions denoted by the term *dharma* yield results, the statement that "the result comes from the grace of the Lord" is [not the primary view].

If it is argued that the statements in the Purāṇas and other texts—meaning that the attainment of results occurs through the grace of the Blessed Lord—are merely for the purpose of praising Him, being in the form of *arthavāda* intended as a hymn to the Lord, we say: no; such a doubt is not correct, because [the Lord is] the object of worship according to the Śruti...

From the standpoint of logical consistency (*kadanataḥ*): there would arise the defect of abandoning the status of being the bestower of the fruit—which is established by such scriptural passages as "He alone leads him to prosperity"—for the grace of the deity worshipped through ritual action; and because it is improper (*ayogāt*), that is, impossible on the grounds of reason (*aucityāsambhavāt*), to postulate the bestowing of the fruit upon some previously unheard-of entity called *apūrva*, which would intervene between the rituals and meditations (such as karma and upāsanā) and the results (such as heaven and liberation). || 28 ||

Although it has been established in the *Devatādhikaraṇa* that "the fruit results from propitiating the root [deity]," and thus dependence on ritual action (*karman*) was stated regarding the primary impulsion toward the production of the fruit, nevertheless—
having observed the supreme qualities such as witnesshood and indifference— one [proceeds] toward propitiating that [deity].
Now, such noble speech is intended to hasten that doubt which has been suppressed.

Even though—in reality, when properly considered—the result (*phala*) is that which is intended as the goal of the action (*karman*) performed with a view toward that result; and "the root to be propitiated" means that [result] has as its very cause that which is to be pleased by the ritual act; and in the *Devatādhikaraṇa* (the section on deities) in the first chapter, it is established as the very fruit of the inquiry into the nature of the deity, their form, their presence, and their fitness for worship; likewise, in the same manner, regarding the production of the result—

Regarding the impelling of others and so forth—in the granting of fruits by the Lord (who has become the presiding deity), in the instigation toward actions designated as prescribed or prohibited, and even in the entry of speech and other faculties into the sense-organs such as the eyes—there is dependence on karma, that is, reliance upon the cooperation of the prior karma belonging to each respective individual soul. This has been stated and established in the *Parāyattādhikaraṇa* and other sections; nevertheless, although these specific points are obtained from other sections, [the Lord remains] the witness...

"Having observed the qualities"—namely, those specific attributes residing in the Supreme Self which, while appearing as obstacles to accessibility, consist of being a witness characterized by activitylessness despite possessing the state of being a pure seer; and being indifferent, characterized by remaining silent after treating the entire world as a blade of grass due to having attained all desires—and "having perceived" them—that is, having understood them through the scriptures—one [should engage] in the activity of pleasing Him and so forth, that is, in the operation of generating delight in the Supreme Self who possesses such specific qualities.

To urge on those people whose activities are obstructed by the distress of doubt—by fears, uncertainties, and the like—and to make them intent upon pleasing Him with urgency rather than indifference, [the author] now, in this section of the Sādhanādhyāya, offers such noble speech: a description of the Lord’s supreme magnanimity, which consists in His being devoted to bestowing the fruits of all actions out of an excess of parental affection. || 29 ||

Sons obtain from their father— who is a sovereign, compassionate, knowledgeable in what is appropriate, impartial, and generous— each respective object according to his fixed inclinations and constraints;
therein they find that which is to be attained by themselves, that from which there is no obstruction here, and that from which comes peace.
It should be given without distinction; likewise, subduing [the senses] and even the worldly mantras should be employed accordingly. || 30 ||

From his father—the sovereign of the realm, who was compassionate, merciful, a knower of what is appropriate (discerning the proper from the improper), impartial toward his sons (behaving without partiality), generous (of noble disposition), and a universal monarch—his sons, those very children, were destined...

Being constrained—having their desires regulated by their respective particular inclinations which possess a natural disposition toward each individual—they obtain—that is, they acquire—at the proper time—the various objects they have sought; in that case, namely in the relationship between sovereign and subject or father and son, whatever such thing as a house, field, or garden is naturally obtainable *svataḥ*—that is, acquired by its very nature—from such a cause as the transgression of an order or the performance of an undesirable act.

In this context, "removal" (vihatih) refers to the fact that an obstacle arises regarding an object to be attained by oneself; because of patience and supplication, there occurs the cessation of that obstacle which had arisen,
and thus the obstacle ceases.

Because there is no distinction—due to its being common to all sons—or else, whatever object is to be given, which is indeed to be bestowed by the king upon his sons, and even punishment—that which consists of chastisement when an offense has been committed and pardon is not sought—all that, just as in the world (*yathāloka*), would likewise apply here—in this case of the individual soul and the Supreme Self, which constitute the subject of the analogy—it would follow as a consistent conclusion. ||30||

—0— Awakening (*bodhana*) is the state of the functioning of all the sense organs, termed "waking" (*jāgrat*); likewise, there is the state of activity (*kārya*), which takes the form of specific diseases; these are the states pertaining to the individual soul (*jīva*). Furthermore, there is fainting (*mūrchā*), which is the removal of pleasure and pain.

Even for the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), there is the state of being free from defects—being untouched by any defect whatsoever, consisting of being the adversary of all that is to be abandoned (*akhilaha-ya-pratyanīkatva*) together with being a mine of all auspicious qualities (*samastakalyāṇaguṇākaratva*). There is the state of being the whole (*jagadaṃśibhāva*)—the state of being the substratum of the world in both its embodied and unembodied forms according to the analogy of the earring and gold. There is universal sovereignty (*sarveśvaratva*)—the state of being the controller of all, endowed with being higher than the highest, and the bestowing of fruits; and the fact that He alone is the giver of all fruits, whether pertaining to the three aims of life (*traivargika*) or the ultimate goal (*apavargika*), through both mediated and immediate means.
(No necessity for the postulation of apūrva) These are the matters established by these eight topical sections. || 18 ||
The first quarter has already been considered through the four principles beginning with the spokes;
therefore, in this [second] quarter, [the analysis] starting from the fifth [letter] is well-connected. (19)

By means of the first four principles belonging to this [first] chapter—namely, the four initial sections (*adhikaraṇas*) characterized by *sandhyabhāva*, *karma-anusmṛti*, *śabda*, and *vidhi*—the remainder of the preceding chapter has been reflected upon; that is, it has been deliberated and determined as being merely a portion supplementary to the first chapter, which was devoted to demonstrating the defects of the individual soul (*jīva*).

Therefore—for the reason stated—here in this second quarter (pāda), starting from the fifth [sūtra] onwards, namely the four sections beginning with the "Section on the Possession of Both Characteristics" (known as Ubhayaliṅga, Adhikuṇḍala, Para, and Phala), there is a perfect coherence; that is, they possess a sound connection through their relation to the subject matter of the primary quarter. || 19 ||

"Because it is the locus, because of its identity with the non-conscious, because it is inferior, and because it does not bestow fruit"—it was this doubt that [the Lord] shattered here with the four subsequent verses. (20)
The Adhikaraṇasārāvalī.

Thus, let the Veda be ever-watchful toward Hari—the source of heaven and liberation, an ocean of auspicious qualities, whose own body is pure bliss, eternal, and truly real; who excels through the ornaments, weapons, and other attributes of the Goddess; who shines with the splendor of manifold, enduring relationships such as being the Residual Lord (śeṣitva) and the substratum; and who manifests the play of radiant enjoyments. // 31 //

That—by means of establishing that the Supreme Self is the bestower of all fruits—in this manner, according to the method to be explained hereafter: in Him who is Pure Bliss, whose essential nature consists solely of bliss untouched even by a trace of suffering; in Him who is an ocean of auspicious qualities, a repository of infinite, auspicious attributes that are favorable to Himself and others and are inseparable from the goals of human life; in Him who possesses a true, eternal body, endowed with a supreme, ever-present, divine, and auspicious form.

He who is preeminent in excellence, being distinct from all others, by virtue of His divine consorts such as Lakṣmī and others, His divine ornaments such as the Śrīvatsa and Kaustubha, and His divine weapons such as the Sudarśana; He who shines with His two manifestations—the manifest glory of enjoyment (*bhoga-vibhūti*), which is eternally resplendent, and the manifestation of sport (*līlā-vibhūti*), known as the Supreme Abode (*paramapada*), which persists incessantly in the form of a continuous flow; and He who is radiant as the Sovereign (*śeṣitva*), possessing the natural state of being the unconditional Lord of all.

[He is] possessed of manifold, diverse, and eternally inherent relations—such as being the support of the entire universe, the controller of all, the source of all, non-different from all, the body of all, and the cause of all—which bestow a unique splendor upon both the world and Himself; He is the progenitor of heaven and liberation, possessing inconceivable and infinite majesty within His own self, and is the one who, by encompassing within Himself the collection of fruits pertaining to the three aims of life and liberation, bestows grace at the appropriate time according to the fitness [of beings].

May our "hearing"—the very crest-jewel of the eternal and faultless Vedas, which is like an eye free from even a trace of negligence and the foremost among all means of valid knowledge—be fixed upon the glorious Lord Mukunda as its object. (This is the meaning intended primarily for the first quarter of the verse. || 31 ||

In the *Pāda* [section], He is described as the cause of His own manifestation, the sustainer of the sleeping world, the protector of those who sleep, the awakener of the deluded, and the possessor of faultless, auspicious qualities; He is the partaker of portions through His own bodies with non-conscious matter,
the sole limit of supremacy, and the bestower of all fruits— thus He is spoken of when the ground of devotion has been reached.

But in the case of Truth, when there is such [a distinction] as the primary quality (guṇa) and so forth, or in the worship of the Supreme, one should contemplate the differences in form and other such attributes. || 32 ||

That—because the subject matter of this section is primarily concerned with the feet—in this foot, namely in the second quarter of the third chapter (in all eight topical sections), this [subject] is Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Self who is the Supreme Brahman, endowed with divine qualities, a form, opulences, and so forth.

The cause of dream-objects: the creator of those objects experienced by the individual soul (*jīvātman*) during the state of dreaming; the support of deep sleep: the place of rest for the soul whose aggregate of organs is suspended in the state known as deep sleep; the protector of the sleeping: the guardian who, having granted the peace of sleep until the end of the slumber, protects by bestowing awakening; and the awakener of the fainting and so forth: the one who brings about the recovery of consciousness or death for those who have fallen into a swoon, according to their karma.

"Anaghaśubhaguṇaḥ" means one whose divine, auspicious qualities have cast out all that is to be abandoned; "sāṃśaḥ" means possessing parts through non-sentient bodies of His own, as well as through sentient bodies consisting of the world of both the manifest and the unmanifest; "pāramyasya ekasīmā" means the ultimate limit of supremacy, having reached the highest pinnacle of transcendence;

and "sakalaphaladaḥ" means the bestower of all fruits, both of this world and the next. In this manner—by being the locus of qualities that constitute the goals of human life—it is described for the sake of the abundance of devotion—that is, for the increase of worship—that the Supreme Self alone is described through various distinctions of context.

Thus—in the manner described above—when the Truth alone exists—that is, when that which constitutes the ultimate reality exists—even though qualities, form, and so forth (guṇavigrahādi) exist; then, in the subsequent third chapter, regarding the worship of the Supreme (parabhajana), i.e., the meditation upon the Supreme Self, the various distinct forms and so forth—which serve as specific attributes of the object of worship—are to be contemplated, meaning they are fit to become the objects of such meditation. || 32 ||
Thus ends the second quarter of the third chapter. || 2 ||
