Salutation to the illustrious Rāmānuja. Salutation to Śrī. Salutation to Śrīdhara.
The third quarter of the third chapter.
The Section Concerning the Uniformity of Knowledge in All Vedānta Texts. (3.3.1)
A Compendium of the Collection of Logical Principles Concerning the Body (the Self).

Knowledge is distinct because it is heard without qualification and because there is a difference in context; however, the means of attainment (pratipatti) is not distinct in this way, because there is no difference in the injunction and so forth. || 21 ||

Because it is heard without distinction—just as it is heard in one particular branch (śākhā), so too is it heard again without difference in another branch—and because of the difference in context (prakaraṇa)—for even within a single branch, the context of the meditation (vidyāprakaraṇa) in the form of its introduction is different—one might suspect that the meditations, such as those on the "small" (dahara) and the "universal fire" (vaiśvānara), are entirely distinct, being different from those found in the Chāndogya and others than those found in the Vājasaneyi and others. But this is not so.

Such an approach is not appropriate because the practitioners are distinct—since the students of the various recensions (*śākhā*) are different—and because there is no difference in the injunctions (*codanā*) and so forth; for even though the injunction itself, its nature, its name, and its connection with the fruit are identical, the distinction between the meditations (*vidyā*) based on differences in recension or context (*prakaraṇa*) does not arise through mere repetition without qualification.

In order to state the means called *upāsanā*—which, as the most esteemed method for attaining the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*), is established by the Vedānta—and to determine it through reasoning regarding the reality (*tattva*) consisting of the three principles known as the sentient, the insentient, and the Lord; [he addresses] those delirious ravings born from the great fever of speculative logic (*tarka-jvara*) concerning that reality—those unstable arguments which, failing to culminate in the determination of ultimate truth, are designated by the term "fever" solely because they cause affliction—and the [delusion] produced by their continuous persistence...

Addressing those non-dualist philosophers who proclaim that "nothing whatsoever remains to be accomplished"—meaning nothing at all exists—that must be performed for the sake of liberation by a wise person who has attained the realization of reality once the awakening to truth is perfected, having shaken off (distantiated) the specific conventional usages of that time, which are denoted by the term "conjunction" (*saṃnipāta*) and constitute a particular state of disequilibrium; [this is said] for the sake of attaining liberation when the realization of the Supreme, known as the undifferentiated pure consciousness (*nirviśeṣacinmātra*), has been established.

For the sake of attaining liberation, Bādarāyaṇa—instructs and makes known through the remainder of this chapter that the worship of the Enemy of Mura (Viṣṇu) must be practiced throughout one's life—that is, the adoration of the Blessed Lord should be performed until the end of one's bodily existence and until death, as it is the most beneficial means. || 1 ||
Fearing the terrible torments of the Brahman of inward reality, and fearing the journey upon the path of the ancestors and the failure to return;
Thirst leads one to the supreme ocean of black nectar; as far as that extends, so much has been said.

Having thus obtained authority, it exercises supreme control over the practice wherein the two feet are complete with all their limbs; therefore, it here declares this excellent [path] in its many divisions. || 2 ||

From the terrible torments—that is, from the most fearsome hellish agonies—and from the ascent and descent on the path of the ancestors: namely, from the ascent dependent upon one's merit while on the road known as *pitṛyāṇa*, and from the descent caused by the exhaustion of that merit, [there occurs] repeated entry into the womb.

Furthermore, the conscious being, fearing—that is, experiencing dread—of even that which continues to arise from its own nature, should, by means of knowledge of the faults of the individual soul (*jīva-doṣa*) and the qualities of the Lord (*bhagavad-guṇa*), direct his supreme thirst—meaning an intense desire (reaching the highest pitch, culminating in the attainment of self-sustenance without [the Lord])—toward the nectar-ocean of Kṛṣṇa, the great ocean consisting of nectar known as Śrī Kṛṣṇa; he should indeed constantly embrace it as inseparable from himself. This much is to be known.

Thus far, the range of objects has been described, as set forth by the preceding two quarters [of the verse]. In this manner—by way of the fulfillment of one's desire—the conscious being, having obtained authority—that is, having attained the fitness for engaging in the practice of the means (*sādhana*)—is indeed qualified for that supreme means known as the worship of the Lord (*bhagavad-upāsana*). This means consists of either *bhakti* or *prapatti*, known as the eight-fold or six-fold limbs, which is the resolve to restrain the Supreme Person, and in which all auxiliary factors (*parikara*) are complete.

The Lord Bādarāyaṇa presides over [the section] beginning with "nivarta ke" and proceeds to attain that—namely, such worship of the Supreme Person (paramapuruṣopāsana) as is found here in this chapter. In the latter pair of quarters—the subsequent two quarters known as the third and fourth—he explains, by first providing a detailed exposition of all matters to be stated, that which is "barbarous" with many divisions—that is, endowed with the many diverse distinctions mentioned in various Vedānta texts. || 2 ||

In this single section alone, there is no deliberation based on two [contradictory] methods; for here, identity and difference cannot be a single subject, as that would entail the loss of the other. Therefore, when this work is scrutinized, it is seen that the various methods are scattered throughout; thus, its capacity for purposefulness (*aidamarthya*) lies in its being the regulator of knowledge as delimited by the objects of cognition. || 3 ||

"Composed by a skillful logician"—by an adept author of Nyāya treatises, "in a single quarter"—that is, within one undivided *caraṇa* included in a Nyāya work—"there would not be a deliberation upon two"—that is, reflection on both meanings—would not be at all appropriate; for here, in this quarter, "difference and non-difference" would not constitute a single subject—that is, it would be impossible for either difference or non-difference of the sciences to be the form of the object to be investigated, because of the consequence of the loss of the other—in the case of deliberating upon difference.

Because, if one were to investigate non-difference, it would follow that difference is abandoned, which would result in the impossibility of this [work] being an inquiry into both difference and non-difference; therefore—due to the reason consisting of the aforementioned logical inconsistency—in this third chapter (*adhyāya*), the expansion of *nayās* (the application of groups of topical sections) is scattered, mixed, and indeed possesses many meanings;

it is not, however, of a single meaning following all the chapters (*pādas*)—such being the nature of the perceived text, when a doubt arises in a person who has not grasped the meaning from the mouth of the Teacher but merely observes the commentary text; [This is the context in which the following objection is raised:]

This is the third quarter: "the object of knowledge is the Brahman characterized by various specific qualities, which establishes the arrangement of specific forms of knowledge (*vidyā*) associated with those objects of knowledge. *Aidamarthyam* means having the aforementioned purpose; *sāmarthyam* means that which is to be clearly established. || 3 ||
Having declared that this [section] is a single Vidyā by way of summarizing the qualities, they stated that the consideration of difference arises here because of the mention of disparagement; thus,
the Commentator spoke as follows to dispel the doubt of one desiring to hear:
The investigation into their difference and non-difference is the subject matter here, and it is stated [in the verse] as "the object here" (viṣayas tv atra), which persists [throughout]. || 4 ||

"This third section"—that is, the third section of the third chapter—[is so called] because of the "compilation of qualities" (*guṇopasaṃhāra*); that is, for the reason that in those meditations which have a single name, the qualities of Brahman understood from all the Vedānta texts are collected together for the purpose of meditation. [The elders who contemplate this meaning] "taught" it—that is, they designated it by the name "the section on the compilation of qualities. Therefore, for that reason, in this [section], which is intent upon determining the non-difference of the meditations (*vidyā*) for the sake of uniformity...

In the third chapter (*caraṇa*), there is an inquiry into distinctions—the investigation of the differences among the various forms of knowledge (*vidyās*). This has arisen merely by way of reference for the purpose of demonstrating the aspect of aesthetic relish (*rasa*) in those [knowledge-forms] that were introduced as primary subjects of the chapters, having been occasioned by the context of refutation; it does not depend on the inherent nature of the chapter itself. In this manner, the commentators—the venerable Rāmānujas—have undertaken an examination of both the difference and non-difference of these knowledges, in order to dispel—that is, to remove—the doubt residing in the hearts of students concerning the subject matter of this chapter.

This very reasoning has been stated here at the beginning of the chapter; it was clearly declared as something to be performed. Here—in this chapter—the subject matter that continues is the single underlying theme already stated in the previous verse: that the nature of knowledge is to be the regulator of the objects of cognition.
[This occurs] within the mass of infinite qualities and boundless bliss, which is free from all limitations.
If it were argued that, by dividing knowledge according to its different types, there might be an attainment here even in part through such resolve;

let it not be so, for for one whose desire is fulfilled by those very same dharmas combined with their opposites, Brahman alone is the full attainment and no other fruit whatsoever exists—thus is established the principle of "the nature of the sacrifice" (*tad-kratu-nyāya*). || 5 ||

*Nissīma* ... *duṇauve*: If, at the time of practicing the means, there is focused attention (*praṇidhi*) here—having distinguished, in a non-confused manner, the specific meditations (*vidyābheda*) upon the Supreme Self who is the Supreme Brahman, who bestows an infinite excess of great bliss, and who is filled with a multitude of auspicious qualities consisting of future, limited, and abundant prosperity; [thinking], "In this particular meditation (*vidyā*), the worship of the Lord is characterized by such and such qualities. *(Note: The term *nissīma* appears to be a scribal or typographical error for *niḥsīmā* (boundless/limitless). The phrase *duṇauve* is interpreted here as a corruption of *dhyāne* or *dhyānaviṣaye*, meaning "in meditation" or "regarding meditation," which fits the context of the surrounding text on *upāsanā* and *praṇidhi*.)*

If worship is performed in the form of an uninterrupted continuity of meditation, then the attainment—the realization of the object of pursuit—would also be only partial; that is, it would pertain only to that portion of the Lord which consists of a limited set of qualities (since the Lord possesses an infinite multitude of attributes). This is because the attainment takes the form of experiencing the Lord according to the specific mode of the worship, in accordance with the principle of "as is one's resolve, so is one's attainment" (*tatkratu-nyāya*).

If one should raise such an objection, it is not so; for such an objection is improper in the case of one whose desires are fulfilled—the meditator who desires the experience of the perfect Brahman. By those very attributes—those qualities contemplated as the attributes of Brahman at the time of meditation—conjoined with others—that is, having attained co-referentiality with attributes other than those meditated upon at the time of realization—the perfect Brahman itself is eternally enjoyed; the Supreme Brahman alone is the goal to be attained, as that which is to be experienced in the state of liberation.

There is no other fruit whatsoever—there is no fruit for the practitioner other than the experience of the perfect Supreme Brahman; therefore, by this reason, the principle of *tatkratu* is established—the application of the *tatkratu* principle (through the identity between the nature of the meditation and the nature of the experience at the time of dissolution). || 5 ||

In the *vidhis*—that is, in those words containing the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, which are synonymous with *codanā*, such as "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) and the like—there is a distinction, namely a difference in essential nature, established in the second chapter of the Karma-kāṇḍa (the second book of the Pūrva-mīmāṃsā) by means of six [criteria]: distinctness of word (*śabdāntara*), repetition (*abhyāsa*), number (*saṃkhyā*), name (*saṃjñā*), accessory quality (*guṇa*), and context (*prakaraṇa*).

It is established as the authoritative means of determination; it is regulated and fixed as being distinct from others—that is, its nature is non-different [from the whole]. It is regulated and fixed by the necessity of the aggregate, which arises from mutual cooperation and combination; and because there is no distinction between conjunction (*saṃyoga*), form (*rūpa*), injunction (*codanā*), and designation (*ākhyā*), that same principle applies even to those subjects of knowledge such as the *dahara* and *vaiśvānara* meditations.

In the determination of difference and non-difference, it is precisely the reliance upon the means of knowledge (pramāṇas) declared in the *Karmakāṇḍa* that serves as the instrument for the effect [of knowledge]; no other branch of knowledge (*vidyā*) is to be resorted to. For, by relying on that very method, there is no difference in the injunctions (*codanā*) and so forth—due to the fact that the injunctions and the rest are characterized by non-distinctness. This was stated at the outset by the author of the Sūtras, namely, the principle regarding different recensions (*śākhāntara-naya*) concerning the uniformity of all Vedāntic cognitions (*sarvavedāntapratyayatva*) of the various knowledges (*vidyās*), having been raised by the Śruti itself in the words: "Of these very [rites], this... (*teṣāmevaitām*).

Having addressed the suspicion of impropriety by relying precisely on the *Muṇḍaka* Upaniṣad, he—by describing the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of that Vedic passage which was the object of doubt regarding its being a differentiator, through the statement that it has another purpose as a differentiator—re-established his own position, namely that there is a single uniform cognition (*pratyaya*) across all Vedāntas; he made it once again firmly established. || 6 ||
In the various recensional branches (*śākhā*), there is a different method of treatment, and moreover, the scriptural hearing (*śravaṇa*) is defective in its specific details;
therefore, one might think that there is a difference in the knowledge (*vidyā*). However, both of these [objections] are untenable because of the difference among the students.
Since the statement "of those very [students]" exists, any suspicion of difference arising in some instances is improper.

For in this context, the term "knowledge of Brahman" (brahmavidyā) occurs in the section on private Vedic study (svādhyāya), because it is stated that [the seeker] is connected with that [study]. || 7 ||

In different branches—that is, in distinct Vedic recensions—a difference in procedure (*prakriyā*) or a separate context (*prakaraṇāntara*) is observed; likewise, repetition (*punaḥśravaṇa*), which is synonymous with "reiteration" (*abhyāsa*) and devoid of any other specific distinction, is also observed. Therefore, because one perceives such factors as a change of context and reiteration, which differentiate the objects to be enjoined, there must be a difference in the knowledge (*vidyābheda*) even in the case of meditations on the Imperishable, the Small Space (*dahara*), Vaiśvānara, and so forth, which are found in different branches.

It is indeed possible that there is a difference in knowledge; therefore, such a doubt is not appropriate. Both of these—namely, a different context (*prakaraṇāntara*) and repetition (*abhyāsa*)—are justified due to the difference among students, [pertaining] to their respective branches (*śākhā*).

It is appropriate [to conclude that the Upanishads are distinct], because the persons produced by the successive lineages of specialized students are distinct (and thus [the distinction between texts] is not otherwise established). Even in the absence of a difference in the knowledge itself, [the distinction] remains fruitful in certain cases—specifically regarding the particular subject known as the "Akṣara-vidyā" of the *Muṇḍaka*. This is due to the restrictive emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*) found in the final statement, "One should impart this Brahma-vidyā only to those who have duly performed the head-vow" (*muṇḍakīyākṣaravidyākhya-viṣaya-viśeṣe*, *teṣāmevaitāṃ brahmavidyāṃ vadeta śirovrataṃ vidhivadyastu cīrṇam*). It is from such a statement that [the distinction is established].

The understanding arises from the fact that [the knowledge] rests solely upon those who perform the *śirovrata*; however, the suspicion of difference—the possibility of being distinct from the science of syllables belonging to the *Udaniṣad*—is neither logical nor appropriate, because here, in the statement "of them alone" (*teṣām eva*), the term "brahmavidyā"—that is, the word *brahmavidyā*—[refers to this very knowledge] by means of that vow, namely the vow consisting of the Vedic observance to be performed by the followers of the Atharvaṇa, which consists in carrying a vessel of coals on the head.

Because of the statement of the positive concomitance, "One who has not observed the vow does not study this," since such a connection is heard [in the text] as an indicator (*jñāpaka*), [the word *svādhyāya*] must apply to the Vedic recitation—that is, to the subject matter consisting of the Vedic branches (*vedaśākhā*)—as its denotation; it cannot, however, apply to the specific form of meditation known as the "knowledge of the syllable" (*akṣaravidyā*) which is taught in the *Muṇḍaka-śākhā*. Thus, there is no fault whatsoever. || 7 ||
If the identity [of the attributes] is established through the identity of form, what other quality remains to be integrated?

If there were no difference [between them], then why should anything be conceptualized here? Is that reflection not fruitless? If you say this, we reply: O Vaidya, the identity that effects the action indicates that something further is drawn in;
likewise, in the case of the ritual act as well, the object of the mental impression (*prahṛti*) is something beyond the aspect of difference.

Because of the identity of form—that is, because the Vaiśvānara and other objects of meditation are non-different, and thus their unity is established—when there is certainty regarding the non-difference of the knowledge (vidyā) consisting of that meditation, what else is to be combined? That is, what remains to be meditated upon by collecting and uniting elements from other recensions (śākhās) beyond the nature of the object of meditation itself? What, in other words, is left over?

If there were another quality—one distinct from the form of the object of knowledge, residing in the object, and restricted to a specific knowledge—then that specific quality alone would be subject to integration; in that case, there would be no distinction, and the very fact of the difference between knowledges would not be established (because everything would be integrated everywhere, leaving no specific attribute restricted to any particular knowledge). Therefore, for that reason, "here"—in a specific knowledge—it must be considered as something to be chosen, meaning it should be employed only in its respective place without being integrated from other knowledges.

What is this specific form that must be determined? It follows that there is none at all; for by that very reason—that is, by the consequence already established (since it is unavoidable that the unique, specific forms particular to each respective meditation cannot be combined)—the inquiry consisting of deliberation (*cintā*) performed for the sake of determining the combination or the optionality of qualities (*guṇopasaṃhāra-vikalpa-nirṇaya*) would be fruitless. If this is the objection, we reply: no, it is not correct to suspect that it is without purpose. (This is the meaning of the established conclusion.)

—) Identity of the form of the object of knowledge (*vedyākāraikya*): the identity of the form of the object of knowledge, which consists of the qualities and so forth that serve as attributes of the object of meditation (*upāsya*). It "indicates unity" means it determines the unity of the meditative knowledge (*vidyaikya*)—(it does not indicate the unity of the object of meditation alone as the unity of knowledge). "Beyond that"—something additional to the form of the object of knowledge which brings about the determination of the unity of knowledge; some "limb"—an auxiliary element useful for the meditation (which is not heard in its own context but is heard elsewhere)—is "attracted"—that is, it is brought together—even in the case of ritual action (*karman*), such as the *agnihotra* and other rites.

In this context, it should be understood as a universal principle that even for a collection of auxiliary elements (*aṅga-kalāpa*) not explicitly mentioned in one's own recensional branch (*sva-śākhā*), there is a firm practice of bringing them in from another branch; therefore, the "object of inclusion" (*upahṛti-viṣaya*)—the portion that serves as the basis for the synthesis—is precisely the constituent part distinct from the "differentiating portion," that is, the part belonging to the auxiliaries, which is different from the portion that constitutes the essential difference between knowledge (*vidyā*) and action (*karman*). || 8 ||

In that regard, concerning the section on the "Cognitions based on all Vedāntas," when there arises a doubt as to whether the Vaiśvānara and other meditations heard in various recensional branches (śākhās) constitute a single meditation or not—given that repetition without distinction and a change of context are factors that differentiate [meditations]—one might suspect that a difference in meditation is unavoidable in different branches. To this, [the author] replies: "And because... [of the following reasons].

It has been stated that there is no difference between the two meditations (vidyā-bheda), because the injunction "one meditates on Vaiśvānara" is identical, because the object of meditation is one and the same, because the name and form are not distinct, and because the repetition of the teaching without qualification is based on the difference among the practitioners.

If one objects thus, this is not so; for it has been stated that it is not appropriate for the two sciences called Udgītha to have an identical nature, since the Chāndogyas direct the vision of Prāṇa toward the syllable *praṇava*, which is a constituent part of the Udgītha.

In the Vājasaneyins, the meditation on the vital breath (*prāṇadṛṣṭi*) is directed toward the *udgītha* as a whole; thus, because of this difference between the two cases as an indicator, it is so. Likewise, due to the distinction that among the Chandogas the meditation on the vital breath is upon the act of singing (*udgānakarma*), whereas among the Vājasaneyins it is upon the singer (*udgātṛ*) who performs the act of singing—because of this difference, and because of the non-identity of form, meaning the perception of a difference between the forms of the respective objects to be enjoined.

The word *udgītha* in the Chāndogya refers to the whole *udgītha*, because it is well-known from the beginning of the context; however, for the Vājasaneyins, it might refer to a part of it due to the absence of such a restrictive context. Furthermore, their mention of the *pluta* [protracted] vowel in the term *udgītha* does not apply to the singer (*gātṛ*), as it is found in the introductory passage.
Because there is no contradiction in stating that the pacification of enemies is the fruit [of the action] to be accomplished by its agent. || 10 ||

The word *udgītha* in the Chāndogya [Upaniṣad]—this term "udgītha" heard in the section on the Udgītha-knowledge contained within the Chāndogya—is, due to its established usage at the beginning and end of the context, understood as referring to the syllable *oṃ*. This is because, at the commencement and conclusion of the Upaniṣad, it is understood to refer to the syllable in the form of *oṃ*, as in the passages: "One should meditate on this syllable *oṃ* as the Udgītha" and "He meditates on the syllable as the Udgītha. Therefore, it refers to that part which constitutes a portion of the *praṇava*, which is itself a specific division (*bhakti*) of the Sāman known as the Udgītha.

It is determined that [the term *udgītha*] has that as its purport for the Vājasaneyins; however, the word *udgītha* in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka—due to the absence of a restrictive context, meaning that because the restricting factor known as "context" (*prakaraṇa*) is absent as it is in the Chāndogya, and thus no such restriction is established (due to the absence of limitation)—must denote the entire *udgītha*. It ought to be the designator of the whole *udgītha*, which consists of the single part called the *praṇava*, and not merely of a single part; this is the position of these Vājasaneyins at the outset.

The term "udgītha" is heard at the beginning [of the section], as in the statement, "Let us overcome [the enemy] by means of the udgītha. Furthermore, the word "udgītha" occurring in this sentence is not used figuratively for the singer—that is, it is not figurative when applied to the udgātṛ, who is the actual performer of the udgītha.

There is no suspicion that [the term] "application" (*prayoga*) is secondary; for, regarding the result to be accomplished by its agent—the result consisting in the pacification of enemies, namely the defeat of the foes called *asuras*, which is to be brought about by the person who is the singer (*udgātṛ*) of the *sāman* portion known as the *udgītha*—there is no sublation of the statement that it has that [result] as its fruit. Since the status of being the fruit of the operation is uncontradicted in the case of a result to be accomplished by the agent through an operation, the non-figurative nature of the statement that the *udgītha* is the instrument (*karaṇa*) is established. || 10 ||

Although non-Vedic knowledge (abrahmavidyā) prompted by harmful purposes such as the humiliation of others is not to be accepted in the scripture of liberation (mokṣaśāstra), some maintain that it is nevertheless examined therein for the sake of equanimity.
Even desired knowledge (kāmyā vidyā), when employed in service to the knowledge of Brahman through means such as the removal of undesirable things, [is likewise considered].
Others say that the eye is appropriately [classified] according to the various distinctions of its objects of cognition. || 11 ||

Even though, when considered in reality, this knowledge called *udgītha*—which consists of the meditation on Brahman—is directed toward worldly purposes such as the humiliation of enemies by others, and is thus not to be accepted—that is, it is not to be adopted or subject to inquiry—in the *Śārīraka-śāstra*, which is the science of liberation consisting of an investigation into matters that serve solely as the means to the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*); nevertheless, because it is equally a form of meditation enjoined by the Śruti, [it is to be included].

Since this [Udgītha-vidyā] is not distinct from the other Brahma-vidyās, some maintain that its examination—the inquiry into the Udgītha-vidyā—is likewise appropriate; thus ends this section of the Upaniṣads.

Some, having entered [the path], indeed intend [to attain specific results]; others likewise hold that this Udgītha-vidyā—even though it is a "desirable" knowledge (*kāmyā vidyā*)—is for the purpose of performance by those attached to fruits, through the desire for particular results. These results consist of the removal of undesirable things, such as the destruction of the enemy known as sin which opposes the attainment of knowledge; they are conducive to the knowledge of Brahman, useful for the meditation on Brahman, and are specific fruits required by various practitioners according to their respective goals.

Because it is to be undertaken even by those who have desisted from fruits pertaining to this world, there arises a "proper discernment"—that is, it becomes endowed with the fitness for investigation—as they say: they declare. || 11 ||
One who has not realized the true nature of Brahman—how indeed could such a person contemplate the vision of Brahman anywhere?

Therefore, for those of such a disposition, there should be an investigation here into the appropriate course of action. Furthermore, they should apply themselves to rituals so that, through their superior potency in bestowing their own fruits, those acts may generate an excellence in the meditation on Brahman; that is what is required in the present context. || 12 ||

A person who is ignorant of the reality of Brahman—one devoid of knowledge regarding the supreme reality whose nature is Brahman—how indeed could he contemplate the vision of Brahman (*brahmadṛṣṭi*), that is, the meditative cultivation of Brahman, upon something other than Brahman, such as the *praṇava* which is a constituent part of the *udgītha*, or anywhere else? By what means could he possibly resort to it? (For just as superimposition is not established when the substratum is unknown, it is likewise not established when the object of superimposition is unknown.)

(For indeed, without the knowledge that it is a rope, the cognition of a snake would not arise regarding the rope! Therefore—because meditations involving visualization (*dṛṣṭy-upāsanā*) are unestablished without the knowledge of Brahman, and because there is no other way (*agateḥ*)—that is, due to the absence of any alternative—the investigation (*mīmāṃsana*) or deliberation of such *vidyās*—consisting of the visualization of Brahman upon what is not Brahman—is appropriate and fitting (*samucitaṃ syāt*) precisely here in the *Śārīraka*, which is engaged in the inquiry for the sake of liberation. (These are the *vidyās* of the *udgītha* and so forth.)

Of ritual actions—namely, those actions that constitute auxiliary members (*aṅga*) of meditative worship—they would bestow an excellence of potency (*vīryavattvātiśaya*) in the granting of their own fruits; that is, in the performance of the task of producing results such as the removal of obstacles to the attainment of knowledge (*vidyāsiddhi*) and the full realization of knowledge (*vidyāsamṛddhi*), they would bring about an excess of potency in the form of unimpeded power. For that reason [stated above], Brahman...

Regarding its origin: because it produces the excellence of those rituals that are the means for the worship of the Supreme Self, this investigation into the perspectives within the *Śārīraka* is indeed suitable for achieving the objective of the present *Śārīraka* scripture under discussion. || 12 ||

Having raised the objection that the two Udgītha-vidyās mentioned in the scriptures constitute a single vidyā— because they both have as their object the Udgītha upon which the nature of Prāṇa is superimposed, and because there is no difference in their form and other characteristics— [the author proceeds].

In the Chāndogya, because the very same *praṇava* introduced as "One should meditate on this syllable 'Om' as the Udgītha" is to be meditated upon through the vision of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), whereas in the Vājasaneyaka, because its scope is the entire Udgītha, there is a difference in form; thus, it is stated that there is a difference between the two meditations (*vidyā*).
—0— *Adhikaraṇasārāvali*:

Even when seniority, excellence, and so forth are equal, in some cases [the teaching] appears more extensive, as in the case of Vasiṣṭha and others; thus, due to such differences in form, the Prāṇavidyā found in many Vedas must be distinguished.

Not so; for there is no difference in the description of their being subject to their respective qualities such as speech, and therefore, even though speech and the others did not perform the service of their own specific functions, there would be no distinction [between them] on that account. || 24 ||

Although there is no difference in the fact that qualities such as being the "eldest" (*jyeṣṭha*) and "best" (*śreṣṭha*)— which belong to the principal vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*)— are presented as attributes for meditation in the *Chāndogya*, *Kauṣītaki*, and *Vājasaneyaka* (i.e., *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*) Upaniṣads, nevertheless, in the two Upaniṣads other than the *Chāndogya*, the group of qualities beginning with "being the most excellent" (*vasiṣṭhatva*) is mentioned prior [to the others].

That which is "additional" (*samadhikam*) shines forth as something perceived in excess of the qualities established by the *Kauṣītaki* Śruti; by that—namely, by the disparity caused by the non-perception of every worshipful quality in every [text]—in this manner, through the aforementioned method, because of the difference in form—that is, because of the existence of distinctness in the form consisting of the worshipful qualities—the knowledge of the vital breath (*prāṇavidyā*), which resides in many *Nigamas* (various Vedic branches), may indeed differ—that is, it may attain mutual distinction.

Regarding the prima facie argument that "this is because there is an additional [text] determining [the superiority of the chief vital air]," we say: do not think so; such a doubt is not appropriate. For the description of speech and the other [organs]—namely, the demonstration that all qualities residing in those respective vital airs, beginning with speech, are dependent upon the chief vital air—is without distinction, being the same in all scriptural passages. This includes the performance of their respective functions by speech and the other organs, as well as their respective attributes, such as being the most excellent (*vasiṣṭhatva*) or the foundation (*pratiṣṭhātva*).

The figurative treatment consisting in the description of connection with the chief vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*), which is observed in both the *Chāndogya* and the *Vājasaneyaka*, is absent—i.e., not performed—in the *Kauṣītaki*; yet by that much alone, there would be no difference—that is, a mutual distinction between the two forms of the science of breath (*prāṇavidyā*) is not possible. || 24 ||
The Garland of Logical Connections.

In the section concerning the non-difference of all [vidyās], the doubt regarding a difference in the Prāṇavidyā is set aside by the prescription of a difference in form, because it is included therein. (131)
Thus concludes the section on the non-difference of all.

The venerable Bādarāyaṇa will explain that what is read in one context is distinct from what is recited in the context of a particular meditation—that is, the form consisting of the qualities of Brahman belonging to one meditation is not to be applied elsewhere; it does not admit of being joined to another meditation, because it is improper to apply what resides in the context of one meditation to another. Thus, qualities of Brahman such as truthfulness, knowledge, infinity, bliss, and so forth—beginning with truthfulness—are [to be understood in their respective contexts].

One might object: "Should not those other qualities, which are recognized as being restricted to their respective specific meditations (*vidyās*), be established as such—like various distinct attributes—and be contemplated as resting solely within the *ānandamaya* meditation? They should not, however, be understood as following all meditations indiscriminately through a lack of restriction. To this we reply: "It is not right to raise such an objection; for here—in the context of the Brahma-vidyā—by whatever collection of attributes the realization of the nature of Brahman occurs, there is an understanding of the very nature of the Brahman that is to be meditated upon."

(There is no finality in the mere connection with Brahman. That collection of attributes belonging to Brahman, being of such a nature, is to be required without distinction in all general Brahma-vidyās—it is to be resorted to as the qualities of Brahman that serve to delimit the object of meditation (*upāsya*). || 14 ||
The quality of reality (satyatva) belongs to the Cause of the Universe because it is free from the multitude of various transformations of the conscious and the unconscious;

the quality of knowledge (jñānatva) because of its nature as a knower and because of its self-luminosity due to the abundance of its own light. That which is other than Brahman is measured here by all three [qualities] through the delimitations of cognition;
however, for that Abode of Pure Bliss, there is eternally an infinity even with respect to those three, owing to its state of non-attachment. || 15 ||

In the Supreme Brahman, who is the universal cause—possessing the twofold causality known as efficient and material causality with respect to the world—the absence of contact with the multitude of defects called "modifications" (*vikāra*), which are observed in various forms among both sentient and insentient things that possess causality; [this constitutes] its "reality" (*satyatva*), meaning it is denoted by the word "real" (*satya*) found in the Śruti; its "cognition-ness" (*jñānatva*), meaning it is expressible by the term "knowledge" (*jñāna*); and because of its state as a knower—that is, because it is the substratum (*āśraya*) for knowledge—it is knowledge itself.

The term *jñāna* [applies to Brahman] because it possesses knowledge (*asyāstīti jñānam*), formed with the suffix *ac* according to the rule for words beginning with *arśas*; and because of its self-luminosity—that is, due to being self-manifesting (*svayaṃprakāśatvāt*), Brahman is denotable by the word *jñāna*. Both of these [grounds] are established through the abundance of the *svarita* accent, on the basis of the fact that the final *udātta* accent in the word *jñāna* is optional. [Thus,] by means of the word *jñāna* possessing a final *udātta* accent, the property of having eternal, uncontracted knowledge is established.

And by that [Brahman] being devoid of those [limitations], its self-luminosity (*svayaṃprakāśatva*) is established. Everything other than Brahman—indeed, everything consisting of both sentient and insentient entities apart from Brahman—is excluded here in this statement by means of three, two, or one delimitations (*pariccheda*): namely, by the three delimitations consisting of space, time, and substance; by the two delimitations dependent on space and substance; and by the single delimitation of time. It is excluded through the communication of its delimited nature in this sentence.

"Measured to the utmost" (*pramita*) refers to that Supreme Brahman, who is the abode of eternally stainless bliss and whose nature is exclusively auspicious, being the opposite of all that is to be abandoned even throughout the three periods of time. Because He is devoid of the three types of limitations—that is, because He is free from the three kinds of circumscriptions—He possesses infinity, which is the state of being denoted by the word "infinite" (*ananta*) found in the Vedas. This is established by the purificatory statement (*śodhakavākya*), "Truth, Knowledge, Infinite," which removes the defects suspected in Him due to His being the cause [of the universe]. || 15 ||

[Objection: Was it not stated in the *Janmādyadhikaraṇa* Sūtra that the definition of Brahman consists in being the cause of the entire world? Therefore, the comprehension of its essential nature (*svarūpa*) here through [qualities] such as truthfulness (*satyatva*) and so forth is redundant. [Reply: This is not so, because it would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the Lord, who is the cause, being subject to various defects inherent in other causes.

For when [the doubt] has ascended upon the Śaṅka, its fruitfulness is established by the subsequent differentiation of the other [alternatives]. In the Sūtra on Birth and so forth (*janmādi-sūtra*), namely in this sūtra—"From which the birth and so forth of this [world proceed"—it was indeed stated that being the cause of the world, that is, being the source of the universe, is the characteristic (*lakṣma*) of Brahman, meaning the definition of Brahman. Indeed, it was described by that very [sūtra]—on the basis of the scriptural passage beginning with "From which, verily, these..."—that the nature of Brahman is to be understood precisely through this characteristic consisting in being the cause of the birth and so forth of the world; [for it is] the object of meditation...

If it is argued that knowledge of the nature of Brahman already exists [in everyone], and therefore the description here—in the section on Bliss (*Ānandādhikaraṇa*)—of the characteristics such as truthfulness, consciousness, and infinity (taking up the Śruti: "Brahman is Truth, Consciousness, Infinite") for the sake of realizing Brahman is useless—that is, merely in vain—this doubt is not appropriate. Why? Because of the Lord, the Supreme Self who is the cause of the universe, there is another reason...

In the context of *prasaṅga*—that is, when there arises a ground for suspicion based on the occurrence of various types of defects inherent in other causes observed in the world—the [text] proceeds "gradually" (*krameṇa*), meaning in successive order, by means of distinguishing [the Self] from others: namely, from non-conscious things associated with the transmigratory state, from conscious beings bound [to it], from conscious beings liberated from contact with *prakṛti*, and from eternal beings untouched by the connection to *prakṛti*. This is done by way of making known the distinctness of that [Self]—the one cited here—from those [others].

Because the collection of qualities such as truthfulness (*satyatva*), which are understood from the statements in the *Ānandavallī* and which define its essential nature (*svarūpa-nirūpaka*), attains fulfillment—that is, it achieves meaningfulness. || 16 ||

[Objection: But surely meditation (*ādhyāna*) can also occur by means of "beloved ones" (*priya*) and so forth, taking the forms of the head, wings, tail, and so on. [Reply: Certainly; in that case, however, the realization of That occurs through those [qualities] such as being "beloved," for they are common to all [beings]. The status of being a "tail" and so forth does not apply to the partless [Brahman], nor is there a perception of it in a superior reality.
Therefore, just as in the case of the preliminary ritual involving the fire-altar (cityāgni), the metaphorical representation (rūpaṇa) performed here should apply to Brahman. || 17 ||

"Meditation" (*ādhyānam*) means the contemplation of Brahman through forms consisting of a head, wings, a tail, and so forth—being represented by imagined shapes such as "headness," "wingness," and "tailness. It is indeed accomplished even by means of "the dear" (*priya*) and so on—that is, by "the dear," "joy" (*moda*), "exultation" (*pramoda*), and "bliss" (*ānanda*), which are constituent parts of bliss. Indeed, it certainly becomes complete. (And this being so, just as reality (*satyatva*) and the other qualities are connected to all meditations, what contradiction is there in the fact that "the dear" and the rest are also connected to all meditations?)

To this objection, [the reply is]: "Certainly"—the stated meaning must indeed be accepted. In that regard, by means of "the beloved and so forth"—namely, *priya*, *moda*, *pramoda*, and *ānanda*—which exist as constituent parts within Bliss (*ānanda*), there arises the realization of that, which is the ascertainment of the nature of the Supreme Brahman consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*). For this very reason, those objects—the beloved and so forth—are indeed "all-pervasive," meaning they follow along in all meditations (*vidyās*). Nevertheless, in Brahman, which is partless and without divisions, there can be no distinct, limited portion such as a "tail" or the like.
It does not come into being, nor indeed would it remain stationary;

likewise, with respect to Brahman—the supreme reality, the most excellent, which is of the nature of dependent origination—there is that vision [of it] as having a tail, wings, and so forth, based on inferiority.

Furthermore, even worship [based on the reverse view] is not at all appropriate for the sake of attaining a specific result; for it is observed that in meditative practices involving the viewing of one thing as another, it is only when one views a lower object as something superior that the goal is reached, whereas viewing a superior object as something inferior is nowhere seen in the scriptures. Therefore, for the reason stated above, "here"—that is, at the occasion of defining Brahman as consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) in the *Ānandavallī*—the description applied to Brahman—the imaginative portrayal of the Supreme Self characterized by having joy as its head and so forth—is like the introductory metaphor of the fire-altar (*citvagni*).

(In the section concerning prior conceptualization: When the mind-altar, speech-altar, and so forth—which consist of knowledge—have entered into the sacrifice, one should follow that very sequence by which the form of the fire-pile suitable for the ritual altar is fashioned as it enters into the action-based sacrifice; thus it would be "accomplished" (sampanna). || 17 ||
Some here understand the word "bliss" (*ānanda*) in the Sūtra as primarily referring to the bliss of the Self;
others see it as denoting the bliss of [worldly] qualities (*dharma-ānanda*); and some perceive it as expressing both.
Regarding this, [the author] says: "This is just as it was stated in the case of knowledge (*jñāna*). To the extent that there is equality with the other [cases], there should be no doubt.
In this world, the practice of Dharma is established among many inhabited lands for that long. || 18 ||

In this section beginning with "Ānandādyadhikaraṇa," some scholars—certain commentators—understand the word "ānanda" found in the aphorism *ānandādayaḥ pradhānasya* as the nominal stem *ānanda*, meaning that it primarily denotes the state of being bliss (*ānandatva*), which is the essential nature of Brahman; while others say that it designates the bliss that constitutes an attribute of the Lord’s own nature (*svarūpa-dharma*).

Regarding the phrase "or the expression of both": according to the *tantra* (system), some perceive that this [word] denotes two types of meaning—the blissfulness inherent in the essential nature (*svarūpa-gata*) and the bliss that exists as an attribute (*dharma-bhūta*). Furthermore, certain other commentators recognize this diversity of intention, namely that it may refer to the quality of knowledge inherent in the essential nature, to the knowledge that exists as an attribute, or to both. And regarding the mention of "knowledge," even in the word "knowledge" from the scriptural passage "Truth, Knowledge... (*satyaṃ jñānam*), which is cited from the Sūtras and other texts, [this same principle applies].

Thus, it proceeds just like the word "Ānanda" (bliss): by as many qualities as define the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of Brahman that are predicated of it, there should be no suspicion of its equality with anything other than itself—that is, no apprehension of Brahman being equal to any sentient or insentient entity distinct from it; such a contingency should not arise regarding Brahman. This persistence of those qualities—their connection as defining attributes (*upāsyatāvacchedaka*)—occurs within the Supreme Brahman, which is the object of manifold worship (*bahubhajanapada*), the sphere of diverse meditations.
It is said: it is established here—it is confirmed in this section. || 18 ||

Since Brahman is one in all vidyās, and since qualities are not separate from the possessor of qualities, and since bliss and the other [attributes] define its very nature, it has been stated that bliss and the others follow after all vidyās.

"One should sip water"—this act, which is enjoined by the sentence, "Therefore, one who knows this should sip water before eating and should sip water after eating," is here [the subject] of the injunction; for in this sentence, because of the hearing of the optative suffix (*liṅ*), which is a marker of injunction, it pertains to one who possesses the knowledge of *prāṇa*.

(An objection is raised: "For the person appointed as the guardian, there should be a previously unestablished sipping of water (*apūrvācamana*); that is, there would be a brand-new rite called 'sipping' distinct from the sipping established by the Smṛti texts. (The author replies: "Not so—such an objection is not sound. It is merely a restatement (*anuvihita*) established by the Smṛti and other sources; that is, it is brought to the status of an injunction by following the rite of sipping already obtained through Smṛti and custom. Furthermore, the contemplation of the waters used for sipping as being the 'garment of the vital breath' (*prāṇavāsastvadṛṣṭi*) is the primary element."

The very view (*dṛṣṭi*) [is] unattained; that which rests upon the meaning of the verbal root already attained—that is, even an injunction (*vidhi*), namely the injunctive suffix, appearing as a correlate when the meaning of the root has been obtained from another scriptural source—is consistent—that is, it becomes non-contradictory and coherent—just as in the case of "one should eat after bathing" (*snātvā bhuñjīta*), where, by way of restating eating already prompted by desire, the injunction results solely in the restriction (*niyamavidhi*) of performing the bath first. This is how it fits together.

In the preceding section, prior to the *Ānandādi* (Anandādi) section, the *prāṇavidyā*—the knowledge consisting of the meditation on the pre-eminence (*jyaiṣṭhya*) and excellence (*śraiṣṭhya*) of the vital breath (*prāṇa*)—was stated and considered. However, its subsidiary element—the specific reflection on the wearing of the garment accompanied by sipping water (*ācamana*), which constitutes a limb of that *prāṇavidyā*—was already introduced previously; it was now considered at the appropriate time when an occasion arose, since no resolution had been obtained for this strong doubt until the conclusion of the *Ānandādi* section. Thus, having reached the proper moment, it has been deliberated upon. || 19 ||
The wearing [of the garment] at the beginning and at the end is declared to be a protective enclosure (*paridhi*); here, the act of thinking is observed as its purpose.

Furthermore, this praise for the sake of pleasing [the deity] would not be possible were there no other recourse; it is to be welcomed because it brings about a state not previously attained. It is fitting that they clothe themselves with speech, for such is the intention of the injunction;
and the vital breath (*prāṇa*), being worthy of worship, is properly joined by the virtuous with water once the garment has been donned. (20)

In the beginning and at the end—that is, in the introduction and the conclusion—the act of girding is expressed by the word *vāsaḥ* ("garment") in the phrase "What is my garment? (*kiṃ me vāsaḥ*), and by the verb *paridadhati* ("they gird") in the phrase "They gird with waters" (*adbhiḥ paridadhati*). Furthermore, the root *man* is used here in this science of breath (*prāṇavidyā*) in the sense of mental reflection, as in "those who perform this non-eating [vow] reflect upon it" (*etad anamananaṃ kurvanto manyante*); for it is observed that even while indicating meditation in the form of mental reflection, it also indicates its nature as a direct perception (*dṛṣṭi*).

It exists, and that view is one which, being "pleasing to the one to be propitiated"—meaning it has as its fruit the production of affection for the life-deity who is to be worshipped—is "to be welcomed due to the absence of any other course," meaning it must be resorted to precisely when there is no other alternative. Furthermore, even praise—which here would not rest in mere eulogy of the contemplation of her garment—should not be what is resorted to here; [this is expressed] by the words "they clothe her with speech," namely, by the statement "they clothe her with waters."

The intention regarding that procedure—the determination of the rule for the mental application of wearing—is indeed appropriate because it concerns something not previously established; it is logical precisely because it was not attained before. It is to be propitiated—that is, to be pleased—and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as well, which is a specific deity, being "clothed with waters"—that is, having attained the state of being clothed in water—becomes joined with the virtuous, meaning it becomes the object of yoga performed by holy men. || 20 ||

Thus he raises the doubt: "Is it not so? But this is not tenable, because—for what reason—the quality called *vaśitva* (mastery) in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*, which is the expansion of the truthfulness of resolve (*saṅkalpasatyatā*), is indeed just the extension (*vitati*) in the form of an effect of the truthfulness of resolve mentioned in the *Agnirahasya*; therefore, since there is no difference in form, there is no difference in the knowledge (*vidyā*).

Nor is there any other quality to be made known—indeed, no further specific quality exists (by the knowledge of which the second recension would become meaningful). Therefore, since there is no difference between the students nor any difference in the injunctions, why should the hearing of what was already stated without distinction—not being a differentiator in this context—fail to differentiate the *vidyā*, namely the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā? Or rather, from what [could it differ]?

"One should not make known a nature that is redundant! (regarding the aforementioned suspicion)—it is not so; this suspicion is not appropriate. Although in reality this is a *anuvāda*—a restatement in another place of this very same Vidyā already mentioned—and thus it does not suffice for the injunction of qualities—that is, it is not capable of enjoining a specific quality—even so, by the logic of "the dispersion and collection" (*vyasanasaṃsana*), even in the absence of a purpose consisting in the instruction of an unknown specific quality, [it is accepted], for it is desired...

According to the maxim that "in the world of the learned, there is the retention [of a teaching] both in its summarized and detailed forms," the detailed statement (*vibhajyokti*) is for the sake of clarity and ease of understanding; the concise statement (*saṅkṣipyokti*) is for the sake of the lucidity of manifestation; and the restatement (*anūkti*) is for the sake of ease of grasping and retention. Thus, the repetition is fruitful because the identity [of the knowledge] is established—since it is determined to be non-different even though this same knowledge is recited in two places within one and the same branch (*śākhā*). || 22 ||

The Śāṇḍilya-vidyā clearly appears to have been recited by both the Chandogas and the Vājasaneyins; why, then, has the Commentator not demonstrated here the distinction or non-distinction [between them]? To this we reply: wherever there is an additional recitation, there [the additional elements]— Please note that the provided text fragment ends abruptly.
