"Or rather, it is more or less than that, being joined with inclusion and so forth"—this is stated as a general rule. || 23 ||

By the Chandogas and the Vajins—that is, by the followers of the Sāma Veda and the White Yajur Veda—the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā (the knowledge named after Śāṇḍilya), being clearly and unobscuredly studied, shines forth as it is recited in both the Chāndogya and the Vājasaneyaka. Here, regarding the two instances of the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā found in these respective branches, for what reason—that is, based on what motive—did the commentators, the venerable authors of the Śrībhāṣya such as Rāmānuja and others, engage in an investigation into difference and non-difference, that is, a deliberation on whether they are distinct or not?

It has not been shown—that is, it has not been made manifest as something requiring investigation; therefore we say this: we shall describe the appropriate resolution in that regard. In whichever specific branch (*śākhā*) there exists an additional recitation—an authoritative teaching of an additional portion such as "mastery" (*vaśitva*) and so forth—in those respective places, there is the inclusion and so forth of those additional qualities—namely, mastery and the rest—which are not recited elsewhere, within [the already recited qualities] such as "truthful resolve" (*satya-saṅkalpatva*), by way of being subordinate effects or constituent parts.

Since the application of "having entered" and so forth is possible, the statement regarding the commonality—"whether it is non-excessive or excessive"—is intended to introduce an investigation as to whether the recited form is redundant or not redundant; for this is stated as a formulation applicable to all instances, and even therein, the definitive conclusion is obtained through this very investigation. || 23 ||
A summary of the meaning of the legal case.

In the *Vājasaneyaka*, both in the *Agnirahasya* and the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*, the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā is recorded. In the *Agnirahasya*, the object of meditation is characterized by qualities such as "having true resolve" (*satyasaṃkalpatva*), whereas in the other [the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*], it possesses qualities such as "mastery" (*vaśitva*). Raising the objection that there is a difference in the meditation due to this difference in form (*rūpa-bheda*), it is stated that since the qualities such as "consisting of mind" (*manomayatva*) are identical in both places, and since qualities like mastery are non-different from the quality of "having true resolve," there is no difference in form; therefore, there is no difference in the meditation (*vidyā-bheda*).
— 0— Adhikaraṇasārāvaliḥ ||

The worship of the Blessed One, who is indicated by the eye and the sun, would be one because there is no difference between the injunctions and so forth; therefore, there is no restriction regarding the two names. This is not so, because of the difference in form due to the difference in location. Location is taught for the sake of the cognition that [the deity] resides therein; if it were not so, there would be no extension of the form.
Therefore, the two names, "Day" (Ahar) and "Sun" (Arka), should be established through their connection with the eye and the sun. 24.

In the case of "the eye and the sun" (*akṣyāditya*), which are to be characterized—that is, made known—by way of their forms and locations (just as the moon is [known] by its branches), with respect to the Blessed One—the Supreme Self—there should be a single worship (*bhajana*, i.e., meditation). Because of the non-difference of the injunctions and so forth—that is, because the injunction, the connection with the fruit, the form, and the name are indistinguishable—it must be one; that is, it must indeed be non-different. By that reason—namely, the oneness of the worship—of the two names, "day" (*ahaḥ*) and "I" (*aham*).

It is precisely because of this lack of fixed determination that such a doubt should not be entertained; for there is a difference in form based on location—that is, due to the difference in the locations of meditation, the form associated with the knowledge is distinct. "Location" refers to the eye as a form of the Lord and the solar orb as another form. Indeed, it is for the sake of the realization of His abiding in those places—to establish the cognition that He resides in the forms of the eye and the sun—that the Śruti teaches and makes known. Otherwise, the distinction between the two knowledges would not be the intended meaning of the scripture.

If there were no transfer of form—that is, if the transfer of form had not been stated in the scripture as "The form of this [latter] is the very same as the form of that [former]"—then it would not be so. Therefore, because of the distinction between the two meditations according to the method already described, and because of their connection with the sun and the eye—namely, their connection with the solar form and the ocular form—their names, "Day" (*ahaḥ*) and "I" (*aham*), are to be applied respectively to the two meditations in a fixed order: "Day" is one name for the first meditation, and "I" is another name for the second meditation. || 24 ||
The Garland of Logical Connections (Nayasaṅgatimālikā) — 0—

Now, in the section concerning connection (Sambandhādhikaraṇa), [the notion] based on the conceit of a difference in form is set aside by the knowledge of the eye and the sun, due to the difference in location.
Thus ends the seventh section, the Sambandhādhikaraṇa.

If it is argued that, because of the absence of explicit recitation—and since no specific meaning is found to be the primary subject introduced in the subsequent passages—it should be connected with all branches of knowledge; that is, it should be integrated as a quality of Brahman in all Brahma-vidyās, [we reply: such a doubt is not tenable. This is because, in the *Pūrva-mīmāṃsā* itself, it has been established without doubt by relying on the principle of "resort to indicative marks when there is no other way" (*agatikataḥ*), that connection occurs only in certain instances based on indicative marks (*liṅga*) that are otherwise established.

In the case of the "small" meditations (*vidyās*)—namely, those meditations on the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) such as the "Cave" meditation (*dahara-vidyā*), which consist in the worship of that which exists within extremely limited spaces like the human heart—the presence of an all-pervading nature (*dhruvavyāpti*) whose essence is not restricted [to a small space] is unavoidable; for it is necessarily understood that its natural state consists in a connection with all locations, from the earth through the intermediate region (*antarikṣa*) up to the heavenly world (*dyuloka*), residing in its own appropriate places. This is due to the fact that they are recited together in a single mantra, within one and the same [text].

From the scriptural declaration in the mantra "brahmajyeṣṭha" (with Brahman as the eldest), which indicates the grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇya*) between the accumulation of power (*vīryasambhṛti*) and the pervasion of the heavenly world (*dyulokavyāpti*), it is made known that all other qualities, such as the accumulation of power and so forth—which are distinct from the pervasion of the heavenly world—are co-located with that [pervasion]; that is, they are indeed connected to the meditations (*vidyā*) that teach qualities residing in the Brahman understood as the substratum possessing qualities such as the form of the heavenly world. || 25 ||
-o- Section on the Knowledge of the Person (Puruṣavidyādhikaraṇa) || 3.3.9 || A Compendium of the Collection of Principles from the Śārīraka [Bhāṣya].
There is a distinction between the two sciences despite the identity of their names, namely that of the Puruṣavidyā.
Because there is a difference in form produced by the distinctions in the conceptualization of sacrifices, such as the *savana* and others. || 29 ||

Even though there is identity of name in the term "Puruṣavidyā"—that is, even while the designation of the knowledge (*vidyā*) exists in the same form as "Puruṣavidyā"—there is nonetheless a difference between the two Puruṣavidyās found in the Taittirīyaka and the Chāndogya; they are distinct and not one, because of differences such as the *savana* (pressings of the Soma). In the Chāndogya, there is a conceptualization of the *savana*s and so forth within the threefold division of the human lifespan and other elements.

In the *Taittirīya* [Upaniṣad], there is the conceptualization of that [knowledge] at the beginning of the morning and evening rites, and the conceptualization of the sacrifice and so forth starting from the sacrificer and his wife; thus, because there exists a difference in form caused by differences in such conceptualizations, [the objection stands]. If it is argued: "Since the difference in form and other characteristics is clear, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the identity of the person based on mere similarity of name and so forth is weak; therefore, this application [of the same ritual details] is fruitless"—we say no. For the knowledge of renunciation (*nyāsavidyā*) recited in its own context is primarily concerned with the injunction for that [renunciation];
thus, the division between these two [texts] is highly meaningful for the sake of establishing their independence and so forth. || 27 || || 29 ||

When the difference in form and other characteristics—which establishes the mutual distinction between both the Puruṣavidyās found in the Taittirīya and Chāndogya Upaniṣads—is clearly and distinctly perceived, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the Puruṣavidyā has arrived merely through the superficial appearance of a common name, relying solely on the similarity of their designations.

This prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*), which constitutes a subordinate part of the section concerning the *Puruṣavidyā*, is "mild"—that is, it is not capable of withstanding rigorous scrutiny. Therefore, this objection—that this section on *Puruṣavidyā* within the *Śārīraka-mīmāṃsā* is fruitless and thus useless—is not correct. For the knowledge called *Nyāsa* (the renunciation of all actions), which is the primary form of *Brahmavidyā*, is recited following its introduction within the context of the *Nyāsa-vidyā*. It is taught as being primarily concerned with that injunction.

The *puruṣavidyā* engaged in for the purpose of teaching the science of ritual placement (*nyāsavidyā*) is entirely different—indeed, it is in every respect distinct—from that found in the *Taittirīya*. This is for the sake of establishing [the latter’s] independence and so forth (such as the attainment of a full lifespan and other separate fruits in the case of the *Chāndogya* *puruṣavidyā*). Likewise, for the sake of obtaining specific meanings in the *Taittirīya* version—such as its being subordinate to the supreme knowledge (*paravidyā*), its having a single essential nature, and the absence of separate fruits for these two.
Because it serves to demonstrate the distinctness of the two Puruṣa-vidyās, and because it is exceedingly meaningful—thus this section is in every way purposeful. || 27 ||

If this view of sacrifice is enjoined regarding the person who knows the Supreme (paravid), then how is it that various elements not belonging to the constituent parts of the sacrifice are imagined here and there in connection with that [person]?
Therefore, some say that this is appropriately a glorification (stuti) of the knowledge under discussion; others, however, say otherwise.
Let this [objection] stand aside for now; however, the well-established tradition under discussion must be considered. || 28 ||

In a person who is conscious (the substratum), who possesses accompaniments known as internal and external, who is endowed with the knowledge of the Supreme (the realization of the Supreme Self), and in whom the practice of meditation has reached perfection—if the perception of sacrifice (the conceptualization of sacrifice) is enjoined—that is, if it is prescribed by the Śruti;

In that case, how is it conceived—by what manner or by relying upon what fitness—that various types of ritual acts (*karmajāta*), which are not auxiliary members (*anaṅga*) of the sacrifice as a whole (having themselves become primary acts such as the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and others, rather than having attained the status of auxiliaries toward some specific sacrifice), are superimposed and become objects of reflection here—in the midst of the sacrifice—in this or that particular scriptural passage, such as: "Those [are] the *cāturmāsya*s, those [are] the seasonal sacrifices (*ṛtu*), those [are] the animal sacrifices (*paśubandha*)" and so forth?
Therefore, from what has been stated...

"Because of the lack of consistency, this series of conceptual constructions beginning with 'of that one who knows thus' is appropriate—that is, conducive to inspiring interest in knowledge—and constitutes a praise of the knowledge already introduced—a mere glorification of the science of renunciation (*nyāsa*) that has been commenced. Thus say some; in this manner, certain commentators explain [the text]. Others, however, describe the independence of the scripture in defining its subject matter as not requiring any other form of appropriateness, [claiming it is] well-integrated with the present context.

Let this [method], which is free from non-conformity with the subject matter at hand, remain for now; let both types of style mentioned previously also remain as they are. However, the tradition must be reflected upon—the specific traditional method concerning the subject matter of the section on Nyāsa-vidyā, which is here to be thoroughly considered. (This is that which has been well-determined through the scriptures, the Āgamas, and the experiences of yogins as being skilled in the liberation of the self for the Śrīvaiṣṇavas, the followers of Viśiṣṭādvaita. || 28 ||

—0— Just like the mantras beginning with "pravidhya," these mantras are auxiliary to the study (adhyayanāṅga), being merely subordinate to the act of study; for the same reason, because of the indicative power (liṅga) residing in the mantras, which exists here as well as in those [other cases]. || 30 ||
— 0— Adhikaraṇasārāvalī — 0—

The mantras beginning with "śaṃ naḥ" (may there be peace for us), which are recited in the vicinity of the Brahmavidyā, would be applicable to all vidyās because they serve that purpose; however, this is not so, due to the indicative mark (*liṅga*) that they are subordinate to the specific instruction mentioned therein. If it is argued that other mantras such as "śukraṃ pravidhya" (pierce the bright one) should also be [applicable] in the same way because of their proximity in the text, we reply:
no, for they do not serve that purpose, as this [argument from proximity] is weaker than the indicative mark (*liṅga*). || 29 ||

And as for the claim that the mantras recited in the vicinity of the *brahmavidyā*—namely, those mantras such as "May Mitra be auspicious to us" (*śaṃ no mitraḥ*) and "I pierce the bright [disc]" (*śukraṃ pravidhya*), which are recorded in proximity to the Upaniṣads that teach meditations (*upāsanā*)—should be employed in all meditations because they serve that same purpose (that is, because they equally constitute supplements to the knowledge), and thus ought to be connected as auxiliary parts to every single meditation; such a doubt is not correct, for...

On account of the *liṅga*—that is, from the indicative power (*sāmarthya*) residing in the mantra which establishes its status as a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*) for the study undertaken through that specific mantra; for otherwise, if one were to abandon its subsidiarity toward the study expressed by the mantra and instead accept its status as subordinate to the *vidyā* based solely on proximity (*saṃnidhi*), then other mantras of this kind, such as "śaṃ no mitraḥ" and so forth, as well as others like "śukraṃ pravidhya," would likewise [be subordinate to the *vidyā*]. [The mantra "śukraṃ pravidhya" refers to] piercing the heart...

Mantras such as "pravidhya" and others may, by virtue of being recited in proximity—that is, solely by the force of their placement in close vicinity—be considered as having that [Vidyā] as their purpose; let it be accepted that they are indeed subsidiary parts of the Vidyā. However, this acceptance is not tenable; such an assumption does not at all cohere because proximity is weaker than *liṅga* (indicative power). Since the placement in proximity is of lesser strength compared to *liṅga* (because it is incapable of performing its own function when faced with a stronger proximity, and thus lacks the capacity to indicate subsidiariness to the Vidyā), the hypothesis that they are subsidiary to all Vidyās remains unestablished. || 29 ||
The Section on Decrease (Hānyadhikaraṇa) || 3-3-11 ||
A Compendium of the Essential Principles of the Śārīraka [Upaniṣads]
"Between the loss of merit and so forth, and the acquisition [of merit], one [of these two] should be considered appropriate here;
it is not both, because they are taught as separate fruits, and because they are mutually dependent. (31)

Regarding the two meanings mentioned in the scriptures—namely, the abandonment of merit and demerit and their transference elsewhere—which relate to the person attaining Brahman: only one of these two is to be meditated upon; that is, meditation should be performed on one or the other, not both combined together. In this context, [the two are] distinct...

Because [the fruit] must be stated as the result of each recitation individually—(thus he objects)—this is not appropriate, because "mutually" means that abandonment (*hāni*) and acquisition (*upāyana*) are interdependent—that is, they possess mutual expectancy (elsewhere, giving is for the sake of acquisition, and acquisition is for the sake of accomplishing abandonment; thus there is mutual dependence). || 31 ||

Because both abandonment (*prahāṇa*) and acquisition (*upāyana*) have been stated elsewhere, the accomplishment of their connection through separate recitation occurs; that is, there is an understanding (*avagati*)—by means of scripture (*śruti*)—of the combination of each pair mentioned individually. For indeed, even a statement located in another branch (*śākhāntara*), existing in a different Vedic school, is a scriptural statement (*śrauta-vākya*); by virtue of the requirement of the injunction—the mutual expectancy for the connection between the two objects within the scope of the injunction—it becomes a supplementary part of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*). [All branches...]

Or, by way of the principle of expectancy (*pratyayanyāya*), that which attains syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) by fulfilling the expectancy inherent in the sentence becomes the producer of a cognition free from expectancy. || 30 ||

Thus, let the karma of one who knows Brahman be mixed with that of others through transmigration; this is not correct, for there is no separate recitation [of such a rule] regarding the state of contemplation (*cintā*), as it would lead to an untenable assumption. Since both [the knowledge and the fruit] are equally attainable through meditation for all who partake in liberation, it must be established in both cases that such contemplation belongs to those who know its greatness.

Thus: because the methods of abandonment (*hāna*) and attainment (*upāya*) are mutually dependent, the statement regarding attainment is subordinate to the statement regarding giving; [this refers to] the renunciation of ritual action by one who knows Brahman—the act consisting of the relinquishment of merit and demerit performed by the knower of Brahman—whereas for others... let it remain associated with friends and enemies.

"Let it be granted that [the ritual] is indeed intermingled through the entry of merit and demerit; however, regarding the contemplation (*cintā*)—specifically in the context of investigating the greatness of the *Avimukta* performed by a lay practitioner (*upāsaka*)—there must be a fixed rule: namely, that the contemplation of each [element] occurs individually and separately, because they are not recited together and because they are handed down in their respective branches (*śākhā*) in an unmixed state. (Thus he objects. This is incorrect; such an objection is unsound because it results in a difficulty regarding the construction (*klpti*), specifically with respect to the subject matter of the contemplation.

Since the conceptualization of alternatives is not logically established, for all those partaking in liberation—meaning for all sentient beings who are attaining release—the twofold result consisting of both the abandonment of good and evil deeds and their transference elsewhere is achieved through worship—that is, produced by the knowledge of Brahman—and this occurs equally, that is, without distinction; thus, by virtue of that equality, for the practitioner who knows the majesty of that knowledge, there is this reflection upon it.

Knowledge is the method of investigating the greatness of the object to be accomplished through knowledge; thus, it must be established in both cases. In this way, just as with the fruit, so too with the means, the equality between them—by virtue of both involving the objects of abandonment and attainment—must be firmly confirmed. || 31 ||
It is established in the *Karmakāṇḍa* that "the auspicious [action] is to be performed by that very agent, and the other [inauspicious action] is not";

therefore, it is incorrect to say that the ritual act of one who knows Brahman does not fall upon either an enemy or a friend. For the intended meaning of the statement is established as follows: whatever karma falls away from the wise man due to the majesty of knowledge (*vidyā-māhātmya*), the fruit of that is equal to what is to be accomplished through either hatred for the wise or devotion to them. || 32 ||

By that very agent—that is, by the person who performs both prescribed and prohibited acts—the auspicious or otherwise [inauspicious] karma, whether consisting of merit or demerit, is to be experienced; that is, it is indeed to be experienced through its results, such as pleasure and so forth, which constitute the objects of enjoyment.

In the *Karmakāṇḍa*—that is, in the earlier portion of this scripture consisting of the *Pūrvamīmāṃsā*, which determines the nature and other attributes of ritual action—it has been established—that is, determined through inquiry—that merit (*puṇya*) and so forth, which are the fruits of action, are experienced exclusively by the agent. Therefore, the view held by some—that the karma known as merit and demerit inherent in a knower of Brahman (*brahmavid*) does not "fall upon" (i.e., transfer to) a friend or an enemy—is incorrect; [they argue] that such a transition could never occur.

It does not become effective due to the greatness of knowledge—that is, by the power of the practice of worship—from the wise one, the practitioner who has attained the perfected means (*siddhopāya*). Whatever action dissolves—whether it be of the nature of merit or demerit, whatever is denoted by the term "action" (*karma*)—becomes detached; that which is to be accomplished is equal [to the cause], because the fruit produced by such action is of the same kind. This refers to the fruit of hatred toward a person who knows Brahman and of devotion to him (as related to another person).

In stating "it becomes the object to be accomplished" (*sādhyaṃ bhavati*), and thus describing it in this way, the intended meaning of the statement—"the good deeds of friends and the evil deeds of enemies [are taken up by the Lord]"—is established; for the flawless nature of that which was intended to be expressed by the sentence is thereby attained. || 32 ||
Summary of the Meaning of the Section:

In the section concerning "Deprivation" (*hāny-adhikaraṇa*), [the discussion concerns] the "deprivation" and so forth mentioned in scriptural passages such as, "Having shaken off merit and demerit," and "His friends [take] his good deeds."
Anticipating the objection that the performance [of meditations] might be optional based on reflection,
it is stated that because the means [to the goal] are not distinct, the performance must always be by way of combination alone.
The Garland of Logical Connections (Nayasaṅgatimālikā) — 0—

Just as it was previously stated in the *Hānyadhikaraṇa* that [the subsidiary nature] belongs to the ritual action (*karma*), so too, by the mark (*liṅga*) of the inherent capacity of the entities, there is mutual subsidiarity (*anyonya-śeṣatā*). Thus ends the *Hānyadhikaraṇa*.

The "reflection on merit" (*puṇyā-cintā*)—the investigation concerning the discarding and taking up of good and evil deeds—is properly to be performed at the time of death and on the path; that is, regarding the future discarding and taking up that will occur at the moment of separation from the body and subsequently while traveling on the path. This is because such a journey is logically possible only under those conditions, for it is only when this is so that the journey via the path of light (*arcir-ādi-gati*) achievable through karma becomes feasible. Therefore, it is not the case that this reflection is not to be done, nor is it improper; rather, it is to be performed at death—at the very moment of separation from the body.

One must attend to the exhaustion of all karma, because of the statement "only so long" (in the Śruti): "For him, there is delay only so long as he is not released," which declares that the limit is merely the falling away of the body. || 32 ||

If all karma were to perish here [in this life] for the wise man upon reaching the mere end of the gross body, then the scriptural statement that "his delay lasts only so long" would lose its meaningfulness; furthermore, it would be untenable to say that "having gone and attained [Brahman], there is manifestation," because the connection with subtle latent impressions (saṃskāras), which persists as the cause for remaining in a state of contraction, would still be present. || 34 ||

If, for the wise one—the conscious being who has perfected his meditation—karma, consisting of so-called merit and demerit, were to perish entirely at the mere end of the gross body—that is, upon the departure of the gross body itself—in this very place, which is the starting point for the path beginning with light (arcirādi), then the statement "for him there is that much delay" (*tasya tāvacciram*), meaning "for him there is delay only so long as he is not liberated," would be a sentence establishing the limit of the postponement until the attainment of final liberation.

For [if it were so], liberation would rest merely at the end of the gross body; indeed, it would result in establishing that the conclusion of the gross body alone is the limit [of the journey]. And in that case, the purposefulness of the journey would not exist—the scriptural teaching regarding the journey by way of light (*arcis*) and so forth would lack a meaningful object—because [liberation] would be attained even before the journey, resulting in the non-existence of the journey and its like. [Objection: Let it be accepted exactly in that way; what is the fault?

This, however, is not to be doubted. Having gone—that is, having proceeded by the path beginning with light (*arcirādi*)—and having attained—that is, having reached the supreme light—it is the manifestation [of one's true nature] that is meant; this is the meaning stated in the Śruti: "the attainment of the manifestation of form. It is incorrect to say that this is "impossible" or "inconceivable. Such a description of contradiction regarding the destruction of all karma at the very moment of separation from the body is not logical. [The notion of delay] is caused merely by the persistence of the contraction of the intellect (*dhī-saṅkoca*), which is opposed to the manifestation of the eightfold qualities (*guṇāṣṭaka*).

The cause for the persistence of the mere contraction of knowledge that has become the dharma is the connection with subtle latent impressions (*sūkṣma-saṃskāra-yoga*)—that is, the continuity of the remnants of subtle latent impressions acquired since beginningless time; it "should be followed" (*anugataḥ syāt*), meaning it ought to persist (*anuvṛtto bhavitum arhati*), because [only thus] is everything consistent even when all karma has been entirely destroyed [as previously stated]. || 34 ||
The section concerning the lack of restriction regarding each respective [cause]. 3.3.13.
A Compendium of the Collection of Aphorisms on the Body.
The inquiry regarding the path beginning with light for those devoted to that knowledge might arise from their being taught that [path];
however, this is not so because of the difference in context, whereas the statement "those who... expresses their equality.

For those established in that knowledge—meaning, for those exclusively devoted to those specific knowledges for which the path beginning with light (*arcis*) and so forth is traditionally taught—it would be appropriate that there be a reflection upon that path beginning with light as an auxiliary to the meditation on those respective knowledges, since it is mentioned at the conclusion of each specific section of knowledge; however, this would not apply to those established in other knowledges, because of the difference in context (*prakaraṇabheda*). For in all cases, the sections of knowledge are distinct from one another, and what belongs to one section cannot be connected to another section.

(Thus one might object: "Because [the path] would follow as applicable to all [who perform rites], the status of the *prakaraṇa* (context) as a means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) for grasping the subsidiary nature [of the path] would be destroyed. To this we reply: This objection is not sound. For by the statement of commonality, "But those who know thus... and those who in the forest worship with faith and austerity" (Chāndogya Up. 5.10.1), it is stated that the journey via the path of light (*arcirādi-gati*) is common to all worshippers. || 33 ||

The path beginning with light (arcirādi) may be the way for all Brahma-knowledges here, whether it be the fruit or not; if it is argued that, because it begins with the study [of the specific text], its reflection must be restricted to that particular context— no.
By the statement "all those who know thus," and by the phrase "and also those [who worship] in this way," since they follow this common path, his concern is likewise the same as theirs. || 35 ||

In this context—namely, among all the Brahma-knowledges taught in the Vedānta as means to liberation, such as those consisting of the meditations on Brahman known as the Upakośala, Akṣi, Antaryāmin, Āditya, Dahara, Pañcāgni, Vaiśvānara, and so forth—the path [of the departed] begins with the rays of light (*arcis*).

—Is the path to be traversed that of the rays of light, the day, the fortnight of the waxing moon, the six months of the northern solstice, the year, the world of the sun, the moon, lightning, Varuṇa, Indra, and Dhātṛ, and Virāj; and would its fruit be [the attainment of Brahman] or not? (In this doubt: Does it succeed as the fruit of meditation and as something to be contemplated, like the attainment of Brahman? Or does it not succeed? (Regarding this doubt: Because of the connection with the study undertaken—that is, because it is taught in the context of specific meditations known as the Upakośala and the Five-Fire (Pañcāgni) vidyās—there is the contemplation of that path beginning with the rays of light.

If it is argued that—since reflection is an ancillary part of *upāsanā* (meditative worship)—the path beginning with light (*arcirādi*), which is mentioned after introducing the knowledge (*vidyā*) restricted to a specific context, is fixed as a result only for that particular knowledge and does not follow all knowledges—this suspicion is improper. For [it is refuted] by the scriptural statement: "Those who know thus... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.1).

By the statement "Those who know thus [attain this]"—which has as its subject those devoted to the *pañcāgni-vidyā* (the knowledge of the five fires)—and subsequently, by the statement "And those who in this world [in the forest] worship with faith and austerity," which has as its subject the general class of worshippers of Brahman, [it is established that] on this path—the way beginning with light (*arcis*) and so forth—which is common to all the Brahma-knowledges taught in the Vedānta...

Since the names of all [the deities] are identical, by following them—that is, in accordance with them—the common fruit is exactly like that; likewise, even the path of thought, the contemplation itself, is indeed common. || 35 ||

The Yogi who bestows liberation upon those seeking it teaches this pair of paths consisting of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted; he sang that no one whatsoever is deluded if they understand this pair of paths. Therefore, for the sake of attaining Brahman, we—having reflected upon the words of the Teacher who makes clear what was previously unclear—have composed this entire arrangement of contemplation on the paths as prescribed. (36)

The Blessed Lord, the Teacher of the Gītā, who is skilled in bestowing liberation and the giver of freedom, instructs the seeker of liberation—one established in Brahman—regarding the two paths: that which is to be abandoned because it is tainted by return, and that which is to be accepted as it grants non-return. Out of a desire for their welfare, He makes known these two tracks: the one consisting of smoke, night, the dark fortnight, the six months of the sun’s southern course, the world of the ancestors, space, and the moon—which is accompanied by return and brings about the whirlpool of old age and death; [and the other, which leads to non-return].

The path known as the *pitṛyāṇa* (the way of the fathers) is the track of the matted-hair ascetics (*jaṭila*); and the path known as the *devayāna* (the way of the gods)—which consists of light, day, the bright fortnight, the six months of the northern solstice, the year, the sun, the moon, lightning, Varuṇa, Indra, Prajāpati, and the Virāj—is the deep path from which there is no return. Any yogi whatsoever, or any devotee established in Brahman, who knows these two paths in this manner, is not deluded, because the path is clearly discerned.

"One does not become deluded"—thus he sang; for it was sung in the Bhagavad Gītā itself: "O Pārtha, no yogi whatsoever who knows these two paths is deluded. Therefore, because it was thus sung by the Blessed One, through the contemplation of the intentional meaning of the Gītā verses—for the purpose of clarifying that meaning which remains obscure even after the study of Vedānta to those like us of limited intellect—one becomes worthy of attaining Brahman.

It has been established that those meditations (*praṇidhāna*) which, upon the attainment of the Supreme Brahman, lead to the state of an Arhat without obstruction—whether as constituent parts of that attainment or as identical with it—are prescribed by the scriptures; it should be understood that these consist in the manner of reflecting upon the path to be traversed by the knower who has departed from the body, even during the stage of practicing the means [to liberation]. (36) If it be argued: "What has been stated by the authors of the Sūtras regarding the meditation on the 'Departure' (*hāna*) and so forth, as well as on the 'Path beginning with Light' (*arcir-ādi*), for the sake of establishing their status as auxiliary to knowledge (*vidyā-aṅga*) and the like? Let that be so; then this [topic] belongs to the subsequent section. [The answer follows:]...

One should not think thus; for even when knowledge is present, this [knowledge] is distinguished from action and the rest because it is grasped as being distinct, and its mention here is intended to establish its specific position. || 37 ||

By the authors of the Sūtras—the teachers Bādarāyaṇa, the authors of the Śārīraka-sūtras—there is the consideration of the "forsaking" (*hāna*) and so forth, as well as the "path beginning with light" (*arcirādi*). What is the purpose for which this consideration—namely, the reflection upon the meaning consisting of the forsaking and taking up of the wise man's good and evil deeds, as well as the path to be traversed by the wise man, the divine route beginning with light—is stated? [It is] for the sake of establishing [the status of these matters] as limbs of knowledge (*vidyāṅga*), etc., if it is for the sake of their being helpful toward meditative worship (*upāsana*).

If it is argued that this determination of such a meaning must take place in the immediately following fourth section (the *Aṅga-pāda*, which deals with the determination of the auxiliary elements of knowledge), in order to establish that [knowledge] is to be repeated day after day just like meditation (*upāsana*), then—let it be so, let it indeed be done there—but not in this present section on the integration of qualities (*Guṇopasaṃhāra-pāda*), which is engaged solely for the purpose of determining the different varieties of knowledge. To this objection, [the author] replies: "Not so; it cannot be done in this manner, even if [the quality] is an auxiliary element of knowledge."

Even though contemplation (*cintana*) is a constituent part of meditative worship (*upāsanā*), this contemplation is also—just like worship—identical to meditation itself, because there is no difference in their nature as cognition; that is, they are non-different insofar as both consist in the form of knowledge (*jñāna*).

In order to explain that [the practice of *japa*] is distinct from *karma* and other such factors by virtue of its specific characteristics (*lakṣaṇya*), and to indicate that it is separate from the internal and external limbs of worship (*upāsanā*)—namely, the duties known as *trāta*, *rāma*, *dama*, and so forth, which are to be examined in the subsequent third quarter (*pāda*)—there is here, in this third quarter devoted to the means (*sādhana*), a systematic exposition (*sūtraṇa*) of the contemplation of those [mantras] according to the Sūtras; this is "positionally appropriate" (*sthānapāti*), meaning it occurs precisely where it is fit. || 37 ||
The Section Concerning the Imperishable (Akṣaradhyadhikaraṇa) || 3.3.14 ||
A Compendium of the Art of the Principles of the Śārīraka [Mīmāṃsā]

The specific qualities such as "not gross" and so forth, which are mentioned in particular Vidyās, belong only there; they do not apply elsewhere, because that would result in the loss of authoritative evidence, nor because of the defining nature of [qualities] such as bliss. (34) "Specifically mentioned in particular Vidyās" means that these are taken up exclusively in the two Vidyās of the Imperishable Brahman found in the *Muṇḍaka* and the *Vājasaneyaka*. "Such as 'not gross'" refers to the attributes of Brahman—non-grossness, non-subtlety, and so on—which are presented by terms such as "not gross. These are to be meditated upon only in those specific Vidyās; they are not to be meditated upon without distinction in other Vidyās, because that would lead to the subversion of the means of valid knowledge (*mānahāni*).

—(Because it is not apprehended in various instances) and because there is a lack of means of valid cognition for entering into that knowledge, as well as the consequence of the collapse of established order (thus one might object)—this is certainly not tenable, like bliss and so forth—that is, like bliss-ness, truth-ness, knowledge-ness, infinity, stainlessness, and so on; for they too are indeed the qualifiers of the very nature of Brahman. || 34 ||

"Because it is established by the method set forth in the Ānandādhikaraṇa"—that is, for the reason that [the qualities] such as "not gross" (asthūlatva) and so forth, though mentioned in a specific meditation, are established [as applicable to Brahman] according to the procedure explained in the Ānandādhikaraṇa; and because of their universal applicability—that is, because it is logical that they belong to all meditations. || 38 ||

It might be argued: "Since the realization of the true nature [of Brahman] has already been stated through the qualities such as truthfulness (*satyatva*) which recur in all meditations (*vidyā*), this present section concerning those with similar attributes would be entirely redundant. We say no. For in some cases, where the true nature is known by certain means, something else belonging to another [entity] must be negated;

the realization of the true nature does not occur there through mere exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). Thus, because the purpose of "investigation" (*prekṣaṇa*) is obstructed here [in the absence of such negation], this section is necessary. (39)

By means of its own pure attributes—namely, blissfulness (*ānandatva*), truthfulness (*satyatva*), consciousness (*jñānatva*), infinity (*anantatva*), and immutability (*amṛtatva*)—there is an understanding of the essential nature (*svarūpa-avagati*), that is, the realization of Brahman as the object of meditation. This is stated by way of demonstrating that these qualities are common to all meditations (*sarvavidyā-sādhāraṇya*) through their recurrence in all meditations; it has indeed been clearly established in the *Ānandādy-adhikaraṇa* (Brahma Sūtra 3.3.11) regarding those similar attributes which define the essential nature, such as truthfulness and the rest.

If it is argued that this section—the section concerning the Imperishable (*akṣaradhyadhikaraṇa*)—would be in vain with respect to the subject matter of qualities such as non-materiality (*asthūlatva*) and so forth (which was already undertaken in the effort to establish their connection with all branches of knowledge), and that it cannot possess a new purpose because its object has already been understood, we reply: such a doubt is not correct. For there may be certain qualities whose nature is known by some, while the essential nature [of the subject] remains unapprehended; or, regarding a particular substratum (*dharmī*), there may be something belonging to another [substratum]...

Whatever else exists within the subject (*dharmī*) that is fit for negation in the present subject—that is, something other (*anyat*), meaning different (*itarat*) [and non-existent in the subject]—is "the object of negation" (*niṣedhya*); it is that which is fit to be excluded (*vyāvartayitum arha*) by the negator. However, the nature of the subject is not apprehended merely by exclusion—that is, the cognition of the present subject does not occur simply through the demonstration of its distinction from another subject. This is the observation of the discerning person (*prekṣaṇasya*).

Thus, the thought of one with such dull intellect is refuted here by the obstruction [of the following]: because even a negative attribute, such as "non-grossness" (*asthūlatva*) and so forth, serves to define the essential nature [of Brahman] and is connected to all meditations (*vidyā*), as established in this very section (adhikaraṇa). || 39 ||

"Since that which is to be excluded is infinite, its negation would also be infinite; therefore, the contemplation of that [Brahman] would be impossible for one who knows nothing, like attempting to cross the ocean. Do not say so. For when there is an instruction that excludes all particular differences by following along with their respective general properties (*sāmānya-dharma*), such a contemplation is possible. Or rather, let it be understood as a "comprehensive inclusion" (*saṃgraha*) that is itself unsurpassed. Regarding the phrase "since that which is to be excluded is infinite": this is because the objects to be excluded—the gross and other material things—are innumerable.

The exclusion of that—namely, the differentiation from infinite counter-correlates—would also be infinite; it would indeed be incalculable. [This is the conclusion of] the inquiry into the limited knowledge [of one who is not omniscient].

Therefore, for that reason, the contemplation of that [reality]—which is to be accomplished by those who know nothing at all and can be attained only by the omniscient, and which involves the exclusion of infinite attributes—is like crossing the ocean with one's own arms; it should not be taught—it would be impossible to instruct [others in it]. (This is the objection. But this is friendly advice—let there be no such objection. In the case of teaching those respective universals—in a ground [such as] that which possesses infinite absences whose counter-correlates are white, blue, that jar, this cloth, and so forth...

When one communicates the knowledge of a difference characterized by a pervading property (vyāpakadharma) residing in all substrates (dharmin) that possess the property to be excluded (vyāpyadharma)—in the form, for example, "the state of possessing a single absence delimited by the pervading property of being a jar" and so forth—then such an inquiry is appropriate; for the nature of the substrate is established through the process of exclusion (vyāvṛtti). Alternatively, it is established either by the phrase "not non-existent" or by the teaching "the adversary of all that is to be abandoned. "Comprehension" (saṃgraha) means the inclusion of everything to be excluded; let it be grasped—that is, let it be understood as easily accessible. || 40 ||

Regarding the two questioners, although there is a difference between them insofar as they appear as two distinct individuals named Upastya and Kahola, there is nevertheless a uniformity in their inquiry—the statement of desire that establishes the answer to the question—because it is identical in both its form and its subject matter. Specifically, because the inquiry "Explain to me that which is immediate and direct... is the same in both cases, and because the two attributes related to Brahman understood from the respective answers—the sustaining of all living beings and freedom from hunger—are identical in nature, [the two questions refer to the same reality].

In the case of [the two forms beginning with] *tīvra*, there is likewise an exchange (*vyatihāra*): by means of the intellect, there is a mutual transfer (*vinimaya*) and bringing together of both forms in both places; and indeed, after having exchanged them, the meditation (*upāsana*) must be performed. The statement—consisting of two replies—is like the *Sadvidyā*: just as in the section on the *Sadvidyā* in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, where it is appropriate for instruction to be repeated again and again, as in "But let the venerable one himself tell me" and "Please inform me further. || 35 ||

Although that which is to be known as the Supreme Brahman is directly [stated] in the "In this" (*yat sākṣād ityamuṣmin*) portion of the Upaniṣad, and likewise in the "That which alone" (*yadeva*) portion, nevertheless, a difference in form arises there due to the difference in the answers. If it is argued that this is also a difference in the knowers because of the repetition of the question, we say no; for since the transcendence of defects is stated subsequently by way of restating what was already said, that [transcendence] does not produce a difference here, as it is common to both.

Even if one accepts that in the two passages from the crest of the Śruti—the Upaniṣadic statements found in the questions of Upastha, namely "That Brahman which is immediate and direct, that Self which is within all," and in the question of Kahola, namely "That Brahman which is indeed immediate and direct, that Self which is within all"—the Supreme Brahman alone is the object to be known, and that the Supreme Brahman is the sole intended object of knowledge; nevertheless—

Although the Supreme Self alone is the object of knowledge (*vedya*) without distinction in the two interrogative sentences, there is a distinct difference observed in each of the two answers given by Yājñavalkya to those two questions regarding the nature of the reply. In this context, he distinguishes the form—that is, he makes known that the form of the object of knowledge (*vedya*) is different in the two knowledges (*vidyā*). Furthermore, the difference between the questioners—namely, the distinctness of Upastha and Kahola seen in this section—also indicates a mutual difference inherent in the nature of the two knowledges.

If it is suspected that [the text] indicates this, it is not appropriate, because of the subsequent questioning after having restated [the previous point]. This is understood as making a question again after having restated, in due order, a question that was already asked previously; thus it is stated later—expounded for a second time—and furthermore, regarding the transcendence of defects (*doṣātyaya*), namely the state of being beyond defects such as hunger and so forth, this does not indicate a difference in the knowledge (*vidyā*) itself, because it is common to both, since the transcendence of defects consists in the nature of purity.
Because it is a property that defines its own nature, because it is present in all forms of knowledge (*vidyā*), and precisely because it lacks any differentiating character. || 42 ||

For just as there is a response here in accordance with the distinction between the two questions, so too, when the knowledge is one, it reveals that the supreme deity alone is without distinction therein;
therefore, Uṣasta and Kahola, having combined what was heard by each and what was heard by the other, [conclude this].
"Let them meditate on Brahman as the innermost of all"—this practice of sacred study (sabrahmacarya) there is fruitful. || 43 ||

Regarding the *Sadvidyā*—in the context of the *Sadvidyā* section found in the sixth chapter of the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*—when the unity of the knowledge (*vidyaikatve*) is established from beginning to end through a thorough study of the discourse, then, following the diversity of the questions posed by the single Śvetaketu, there is a diversity in the replies (*prativacanabhidā*) given by Uddālaka; therein, within that very *Sadvidyā*, [one finds] the supreme...

[The text] refers to the very same deity denoted by the word *sacchanda*, that is, the supreme deity itself. For it clarifies the qualificand—it clearly presents [the deity] as the object of meditation; likewise here too, it clarifies the response that the Brahman to be known through the Vidyā is of one and the same form. Because the oneness of the Vidyā is thus clearly established, Upasta—who is named after him—the meditator, even though he had heard and understood from the mouth of his teacher Kahola—that which was heard by Kahola—[attained] the excellence of the nature of the object of meditation (*upāsya-svarūpa-vaiśiṣṭya*).
