The first portion was heard by both; and that portion which Kahoḷa had also heard from Uṣasta—though grasped through hearing, it was not yet fully clear—having combined these portions and exchanged them with one another, they meditated upon Brahman as "the Innermost of All" (*sarvāntara*), that is, in its form as the inner self of all, and thus established the Supreme Brahman as the object of meditation. When their realization was thus accomplished, they remained there in celibate studentship (*brahmacarya*) regarding that same knowledge, both of them together.
The horse is the active process; it possesses fruit—that is, it becomes fruitful in the form of the attainment of clarity regarding the object of meditation. || 43 ||

It is suspected [that they are different]; however, that suspicion is not at all correct. Because of the commonality—meaning due to the non-difference in form caused by the equality—of the qualities of Brahman, such as having the heart as their abode (*hṛdayāyatana*), possessing true desires (*satyakāmatva*), and possessing true resolves (*satyasaṅkalpatva*), which constitute the very essence of knowledge and serve as the delimiters of the object of meditation; therefore, the Dahara-vidyā (the knowledge called "the small") is one and the same, even though it is established in two recensions. In some places—in the context of the Dahara-vidyā in the Vājasaneyaka—the Ākāśa...

Because the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) in the sentence "He lies in that ether," which denotes a place of reclining, refers to the heart—that is, it makes known the location called the heart—(and because that meaning is identical even in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*). (36)

"Let it be that there is a difference in 'form'—that for the Chandogas the means is celebrated here as Brahman endowed with eight qualities, while for others it is composed of [qualities] beginning with mastery (*vaśitva*). Do not say so; for even that mastery and the rest are here merely distinctions within the state of having true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpatā*)."
Thus, the identity of purpose is firmly established; moreover, the meditation on the small (dahara) is likewise twofold.

For the Chandogas—the followers of the Tāṇḍins who study the Sāma Veda—in this context of the Dahara-vidyā, [the Self] is endowed with eight qualities, namely, the eightfold attributes beginning with freedom from sin (apahatapāpmatva).

[The opponent argues: "It is endowed with qualities (*guṇaiḥ yuktam*), it is the Supreme Brahman (*brahma-param brahma*), and it is well-known as the object of meditation (*upāsyam*)—that is, its primary characteristic is the act of meditation; this is quite clear. And that [object] is indeed that same Brahman. For others—the Vājasaneyins—it is constituted by such qualities as 'mastery' (*vaśitva*); thus, being possessed of a multitude of qualities such as mastery and universal sovereignty, it is the object of meditation. Let there be a difference in form (*rūpasya bhedaḥ*)—let a difference in form indeed be admitted—and consequently, let there also be a difference in the meditative knowledge (*vidyābhedaḥ*)—so [the opponent] objects. [The author replies: Not so; reflection in such a manner is not at all [appropriate]."

Excellent! Here—in the *dahara-vidyā* of the Vājasaneyins—that collection of qualities such as mastery (*vaśitva*) and so forth, which is heard as residing in the Brahman that is the object of meditation, namely those qualities beginning with mastery, is indeed a quality of Brahman; and this mastery and the rest are merely internal subdivisions of the quality of Brahman known by the name "truthful resolve" (*satyasaṅkalpatva*).

It is not another; thus, their identity of purpose is firmly established—in this manner, the fulfillment of both *dahara* (small) meditation sections as having the same object of worship, namely a single substrate (*dharmī*), is accomplished. Furthermore, even the *dahara* meditation found in the Taittirīya, such as "the small, free from sin" (*dahaṃ vipāpmam*) and so forth—which appears as if different from this [Chāndogya version]—should be understood in the same way. Having reflected appropriately, just like the sections in the Chāndogya and other texts, it should be explained as being directed toward the same non-differentiated meditation. || 45 ||

[Objection: But was it not previously stated in the *Daharādhikaraṇa* that "space is superior to qualities and so forth"? Therefore, since there is no suspicion of any other meaning, this present section (*adhikaraṇa*) does not arise. [Reply: No;
for those who proclaim that this "small" (*dahara*) space is the material cause (*upādāna*), while that which transcends the sky is the efficient cause (*nimitta*).
Having been previously cast aside as a consequence, they are here once again rendered rootless.

Surely, sir, previously—in the section concerning the "Small" (Daharādhikaraṇa) in the third pāda of the first adhyāya—it was established that the term "ether" (ākāśa) refers to the Supreme Self by means of indicators such as its qualities and other attributes that are unique to the Supreme Self.

It has been stated that what is designated by the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) in the phrase "In this, within it, is a small ether" is the Supreme; thus it is already determined that it is indeed the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Therefore, since the purpose of this section has already been accomplished, there is no room for suspicion regarding another meaning—it is impossible for a suspicion that the word "ether" refers to something other than the Supreme Self to even arise. If it is argued that this section—the section concerning "desires" (*kāmādyadhikaraṇa*)—would not even emerge or attain its rise (because its purpose would have been fulfilled), such a suspicion is improper. The reason is that [the Supreme Self] is the cause of the universe...

Those who maintain that the reality which is the cause is "beyond the ether" (*vyomātīta*)—that is, a reality distinct from the small space (*dahara*), while this very thing, the small space itself, is merely the material cause (*upādāna*), being a dependent causal factor—such proponents (the *vyomātītavādins*) have already been refuted; they have been largely disposed of by various preceding sections (*adhikaraṇas*).

In this regard as well—in the first sūtra of this very section (adhikaraṇa), by way of a relevant digression—having relied on the occasion of refuting the doctrine of a qualityless reality (nirguṇatattva), they were once again "rendered rootless," meaning they were brought to a state of being devoid of any foundational purpose, due to the emergence of this [present] section. || 46 ||

—0— The necessity of performing [the ritual] is not intended by the Śruti, because it is purposeful—that is, because it possesses a distinct fruit in the form of non-obstruction of the fruit of the ritual action. This is because even for one who does not meditate—even for one who has abandoned the meditation on the *udgītha*—it is understood from the scriptural statement "By that, both perform [the sacrifice]" (*tenobhau kurutaḥ*) that he is a performer of the sacrifice due to the cause of having performed the ritual. || 37 ||

It has been argued that regarding the *udgītha* viewed as the vital breath (*prāṇa*), a fruit other than that produced by the ritual sacrifice was mentioned; having accepted that, the prior discussion remained established, and thus the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) here is refuted. This is not so. For those whose minds are firmly fixed on the fact that [the *udgītha*] is not an auxiliary (*anaṅga*) in this context, the suspicion of the identity of the knowledge (*vidyaikya*) must be abandoned;
and the consideration of whether it is an auxiliary or not an auxiliary—whether separately or not—would have occurred in the previous section. (48)

Regarding the meditation on the *udgītha* viewed as the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which possesses the attributes of the *udgītha* and the vital breath—namely, the meditation on the nature of being the vital breath—a result distinct from that produced by the seasons (i.e., a result different from the one associated with the *ṛtu*-meditation) has been stated; specifically, a result consisting of the destruction of the Asuras, as clearly established in the Śruti passage: "Come, let us overcome the Asuras by means of the *udgītha*. Having accepted—that is, having admitted—that [result], it was previously established in the section concerning "Difference" (*anyathātva-adhikaraṇa*) that such an inquiry stands. This refers to the inquiry.

Because it has been introduced, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) has been refuted here; that is, in this section, the prima facie view is shattered (the very occurrence of a prima facie view is not even possible). To the objection that this is not so—that the censure based on the non-arising of a prima facie view is inappropriate—it is replied: no, for one whose intellect is firmly fixed and immovable regarding the absence of subsidiarity (*anaṅgabhāva*)—that is, the lack of being a subsidiary to meditation—as established in this section, there may indeed be a doubt concerning the unity of knowledge (*vidyaikya*) in that context.

An inquiry into the difference or non-difference of the *vidyās* has been conducted; (alternatively) having set aside the relationship of being limbs (*aṅga*) or non-limbs (*anaṅga*), and having abandoned the deliberation on being subsidiary or non-subsidary—namely, whether the *vidyās* are distinct or not distinct, as in the previous section concerning "Alteration" (*anyathātva-adhikaraṇa*)—there might still be an inquiry, that is, the commencement of a further investigation. 48.
The Section on Bestowal (Pradānādhikaraṇa) || 3.3.18 ||
A Compendium of the Collection of Logical Principles Concerning the Body (Śārīraka).

Because of the reason of commonality, however, the possessor of qualities (guṇin) is not [repeated] with each [quality] during the consideration of the qualities; yet, because of the distinction of the qualified [object], the possessor of qualities must indeed be repeated for every quality. 38.

Because of the reason of commonality—since the Supreme Self is common as the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*) with respect to all qualities, and since the purpose is accomplished by contemplating the possessor of qualities just once—one might object that "in the contemplations of the qualities—which are distinct activities enjoined for the practice of contemplating the qualities—the possessor of qualities, the Supreme Self who is the substratum (*dharmin*) of the qualities being contemplated, need not be repeated; He is not an object of repeated contemplation. [To this, the author replies: "It is not so"—such an objection is not correct, because of the specific distinction (*viśeṣāt*).

Because the nature of the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*) is distinct [from the qualities] as characterized by each respective quality—for every quality, that is, in accordance with the distinctions of the qualities being contemplated—the possessor of qualities, namely the Supreme Self who is the substratum (*dharmin*) of the qualities, must indeed be repeated; that is, He alone remains the object of the repeated contemplation. || 38 ||

For this reason—because of the distinctness [of the offerings] due to the attributes such as "kingly" (rājatva) and so forth; that is, relying on the separation created by the qualifiers known as *rājatva*, *adhirājatva*, and *svarāṭtva*—the offering of the oblation (*havis*) into the single substratum (*dharmin*) designated as the sacrifice, namely Indra, becomes repeated; it has been determined in the *Pūrvakāṇḍa* that the act must indeed be performed three times. ||49||

If it is argued that when enjoyment (*bhoga*) is not realized, the worship of another [deity] composed of qualities becomes the cause of enjoyment, and liberation (*mukti*) would follow gradually—this is a false statement regarding qualities, as it is merely a figurative expression for something else. Since this scripture has not yet reached its conclusion, where has the fruit achievable through the worship of the qualityless (*nirguṇa*) been stated?
Furthermore, this chapter is renowned for its systematic arrangement of qualities, and it is not the case that the treatise lacks a formal structure. (Verse 50)

In this context—namely, regarding the meditation on the "small" (dahara), or the collection of qualities belonging to the small—whether one contemplates each quality individually or their combination, such as the group of qualities beginning with "freedom from sin" (apahatapāpmatva) belonging to the object of meditation in the form of the small ether; or whether, in the manner of "the Supreme Self is free from sin, ageless," etc., one considers the possession of those respective qualities as individual qualifiers; or whether one considers the eight qualities beginning with freedom from sin residing in the Supreme Self as a collection of various attributes within a single substratum (dharmin) as combined qualifiers or as the qualified subject itself.

Even when investigated, since the consideration of the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*)—as the substratum for the qualities—is obtained by itself through the attainment [of the qualities], why would there be a doubt here—in this section concerning the offering (*pradānādhikaraṇa*)—regarding the absence of the repetition of the consideration of the possessor of qualities? If you ask, "In what manner or by what means would it be appropriate?"—if so, such a doubt that the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of this section does not arise is certainly not tenable, because the qualities mentioned in the context of this knowledge (*vidyā*) have already ascended into the intellect.

When the nature of the possessor of qualities—the substratum (*dharmin*) which is the locus of those qualities—is to be apprehended by an intellect capable of contemplating the attributes of Brahman, and as long as that nature is necessarily required, then anything other than that—that is, a substratum characterized by qualities distinct from those attributes (such as truthfulness) that define its essential nature—is not the exclusive object of this knowledge; rather, it is the specific form known as the "small ether" (*daharākāśatva*), which belongs uniquely to the present *dahara-vidyā*.

Since there exists the specific nature of Brahman, and since [the inquiry] proceeds by veiling that [nature], it is logical for the preceding and succeeding positions (*pūrvottarapakṣa*)—which involve the contemplation of the respective qualities associated with the contemplation of the nature of such a substratum—to proceed, because the arising of the topical section (*adhikaraṇa*) thus possesses purpose. || 51 ||
The Section on the Abundance of Indicative Marks (Liṅgabhūyastvādhikaraṇa) || 3.3.19 ||
A Compendium of the Collection of Logical Principles Concerning the Embodied Self (Śārīraka).

It is not the case that, according to the principle of the preceding section, the determination [of the meaning] follows from the meditation on the "adoration of the eater" (adaha-ropāsti) because it is the subject under discussion; rather, the entire [section] is determined by the force of its own specific context. || 39 ||

[Objection: Following the method of the preceding section (*pūrvānuvāka*), since the object of meditation known as the "Small" (*dahara*) was introduced in that previous section, one might follow that same logic and argue that in the subsequent *Sahasraśīrṣā* section as well, a specific determination is made regarding the very reality that is the object of meditation in the worship of the "Small," because that alone is the subject under discussion and has been previously introduced; for it is appropriate to determine the required meaning as a supplement to that very topic. [Reply: It is not so—one should not entertain such a doubt, for this is not the case.

Excellent! By the power of its own words—that is, by the force of many statements concerning the signs of the Supreme Self found within itself—the definitive conclusion of all [teachings] is reached; it is indeed excellent that the determination of the very reality that is the object of worship for all higher knowledge (*paravidyā*) is established in this section (*anuvāka*). || 39 ||

Having made known the Supreme Person—the Supreme Being ordained as the object of worship in all Vidyās—by means of recognition in this Anuvāka, [that is,] by identifying Him with the thought "this is indeed He," and having thus recognized that Substratum in the form of the object of worship of all Vidyās, the sentence beginning with "Sahasra-śīrṣam" (Thousand-headed), which is contained within this Anuvāka, teaches His nature as the specific supreme Deity denoted by the term Nārāyaṇa, while declaring His state as Nārāyaṇa.

A collection of sentences that has attained the status of verbal testimony (vākya-pramāṇa) possesses greater force than "procedure" (prakriyā)—that is, in comparison with the means of knowledge called context (prakaraṇa); for it indeed possesses an abundance of strength in the form of having as its object its own intended meaning, without being sublated by other means of knowledge. || 52 ||

Since all the statements refer to the "all-pervading nature" (sarvārthatā), the meditation on the "small" (dahara) is also included here as a part; thus, that section, endowed with its own characteristic marks, is meaningful. Nor is it right for many [statements] to struggle against one that has already achieved its purpose. Furthermore, this context would not benefit this single [meditation]; moreover, since this reality is the life-source of everything, the intention (tātparya) here is clear—therefore, the assumption of abandoning it is futile. || 53 ||

By means of many statements—specifically the numerous passages from the *Sahasraśīrṣa* section of the *Śatarudriya* that abound in characteristics of the Supreme Self (and which possess uncontradicted authoritative status)—the universal applicability of this section is established; that is, once it is determined that this section serves to identify the specific deity to be meditated upon in all supreme vidyās, the meditation on the "small" (*dahara*)—namely, the worship of the small space—is also included within all supreme vidyās. For this reason, because it is the very object to be characterized as the single deity to be determined in the present context, its [characteristics]...

The "portion" (*bhāga*)—the specific words capable of illuminating the *dahara-vidyā* (the knowledge of the small space), such as the passage beginning with "resembling the interior of a lotus bud" (*padmakośapratīkāśa*)—is "purposeful" (*sārtha*), meaning it has attained its objective (because here too the object of meditation and the reality itself are obtained); it is "successful" (*kṛtārtha*), meaning its purpose is fulfilled; this single sentence, which possesses the indicative mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the capacity to illuminate the *dahara* (such as "in the lotus bud," etc.), must contend with many sentences—that is, with numerous sentences that have attained the status of authoritative means of knowledge and whose purport lies in various other meditations (*vidyā*).

It would not be capable—meaning it would not at all be able—to exist by way of being an obstacle; for this one [the small ether], which has entered into such a multitude of sentences and is without companion, is related to the "small" (dahara).

The context—the collection of preceding sentences related to the Dahara-vidyā—would not be of assistance; that is, it would not serve as a cooperative factor (*sahakārin*) conducive to establishing that the entire section (*anuvāka*), including this sentence, is supplementary to the Dahara-vidyā, because it is observed that a sentence such as "in the lotus-bud" obtains its status as supplementary to itself solely from the gender (*liṅga*) found within its own related sentence, and thus functions slowly. Furthermore, [the context would not help].

The investigation into contradictions found within the context of specific passages and so forth has been fully resolved. Let that discussion stand as it is; however, regarding the glorious Nārāyaṇa—who is the Supreme Reality, who is the support of each [deity] because he is the common substratum for the meditative practice (*upāsana*) of all higher knowledges (*paravidyā*) without distinction, and upon whom all depend—it is clear that the primary intention (*tātparya*) here is the desire to establish him alone as the principal subject. This is because, in this particular section (*anuvāka*), he is presented in a manner that cannot be denied and cannot be interpreted otherwise.
The attempt to abandon that [scripture]—the effort to deny the meaning of such an extremely clear Vedic revelation—is futile and fruitless. || 53 ||

The wise do not honor such unskillful assertions as that there is identity of the self, identity of the deity, equality attained by the Trika system, or that the three [deities] possess equal sovereignty and so forth.
Rather, with one voice, the Upanishads and the primary utterances of Vyasa and others in accordance with them declare:
"The glorious Narayana is our Lord; He is the soul of all bodies, the giver of liberation, and the object of enjoyment for the liberated. (54)

The identity of the Self (ātmaikya) means that the reality denoted by the term "Self" is one alone; it is not manifold. The identity of the deity (devataikya) means that the object in the form of the deity is one alone; it is not many. The equality attained through the Trika system means that the triad of deities consisting of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara possesses an exact parity, being devoid of any state of deficiency or superiority. Thus, the identity of the three is simply the non-difference of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.

"There is no difference in essential nature," meaning that sovereignty elsewhere—namely, the state of being the Lord of all—resides in that very same ontological principle which transcends the three roots (trimūrti), and so forth. Such are the [scriptural] citations. Thus begins the section.

The words of those who, due to their intensity [of passion], are incapable of investigating the meaning of the scriptures—the virtuous ones, such as Parāṅkuśanātha, Yāmunācārya, and others, who are capable of determining reality by means of valid authorities (pramāṇas)—are not respected; that is, they do not accept them because they lack the reliability of both the authorities and those who possess them. Rather, they regard it as if it were the very word of Him [the Lord], through all the Vedāntic statements (trayyantair vākyaiḥ), which are unanimous—being free from even a scent of mutual contradiction—and which clearly convey a single meaning.

This matter has been ascertained by the words of Manu, Vyāsa, and others—who are universally recognized as authoritative, whose nature conforms to the teachings of the Vedānta, who have directly realized the supreme and inferior realities, and whose speech is intent upon determining the true meaning: "Our Lord" (patiḥ)—the sovereign and master who presides over us sentient beings in our infinite individual forms—is the one whose body is the entirety of all things (akhilatanuḥ).

The glorious Nārāyaṇa—the embodied soul of all sentient and insentient beings, embraced by Lakṣmī, whose glory is imperishable, and who is the specific supreme deity known as Nārāyaṇa—is indeed the bestower of liberation (*muktida*), meaning he is the one who causes the attainment of the supreme human goal called *mokṣa*; he is the object of enjoyment for the liberated (*muktabhogya*), meaning he exists as the fruit to be enjoyed by the liberated conscious beings who have attained the nature of omnipresence. (He is thus the means to the supreme human goal, the goal itself, and the supreme human goal. [54]
The Garland of Logical Connections.

Previously, when the unity of all [texts] regarding the knowledge of the Fire-altar was accepted on the strength of the methodological principle (*prakriyā*), any doubt arising from a [conflicting] syntactical connection (*vākya*) has been dispelled in the section concerning the abundance of indicative marks (*liṅgabhūyastva*). (147)
Thus concludes the section concerning the abundance of indicative marks (liṅgabhūyastva). || 19 ||
The Adhikaraṇasārāvalī.

It might be argued that, in the case of a sacrifice previously engaged in and subsequently presented in a modified form, there could be a mental fire (agni) consisting of the intellect, such as the *manascit* and others, just as there is a "mental" [fire] during the *dvādaśāha* sacrifice; for its potency is extended [to it]. But this is not correct, because where the principal rite consists of knowledge (*vidyāmaya*), the extension (*atideśa*)—established by direct statement (*śruti*) and other means—is for the purpose of making known the equality of its assistance. 55.

The fire consisting of mind and so forth—expounded in the *Agnirahasya* as "mind-made" (*manaścit*), "speech-made" (*vākcit*), and so on—is the fire that serves as the substratum for what is being deposited; even though its nature is purely intellectual and consists solely of knowledge, in the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*) belonging to the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*), there is a mental [offering] (*mānasa*)—like a cup (*graha*) accomplished solely through the operation of the mind—which, having been previously established, is then [replaced] by the aforementioned fire consisting of action (*kiyāmaya*), known as the "brick-built" (*iṣṭakacita*) fire.

By means of the specific sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), which serves as the substratum for the fire, it may become an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the sacrifice—that is, to a particular ritual action (*kratu*) consisting of rites accomplished through bodily activity—having attained a state of being present in the intellect; that is, it ought to be helpful by taking recourse to the optional attainment [of the fire-altar] in place of the fire-altar built of bricks (*iṣṭakacita*). This is due to the extension (*atideśa*) of its potency—the capacity to serve as an instrument for the sacrifice inherent in the fire-altar built of bricks—as expressed in the scriptural statement regarding the mental fire-altars (*manaścit*): "Each one of these is as great as that former one."

(If one objects: "Because it is established on the basis of similarity," that is not correct—such an objection is not sound here. For in the very passage from the *Agnirahasya* which introduces the Mind-altar (*manaścita*) and so forth, the sacrifice (*kratu*) consisting of knowledge—which has as its nature the form of cognition accomplished solely through mental activity—is the beneficiary of the Mind-altar and the rest; this is determined by the means of proof (*pramāṇa*) that establish the relationship between the primary and the subsidiary, such as direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), namely: "By knowledge alone these [altars] become built for one who knows thus."

By means of the scriptural indications (*śruti*), marks (*liṅga*), and so forth, the *atideśa*—the extension [of properties] made by the sentence "As much... as much" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.18.1)—is clearly established; this refers to the extension of the power of the brick-built fire-altar to the fire-altars built of mind (*manaścita*) and the like. Regarding that [extension] to the fire-altars built of mind and the like—which are accomplished through the mind—the purpose is to make known the equality of the assistance rendered: namely, the demonstration that the kind of assistance which was to be produced for its own objective, the ritual consisting of action, by the brick-built fire-altar, is equal [to it] with respect to the ritual accomplished through knowledge.

It should be understood that this is for the sake of accomplishment (*siddhi*). For here, the ritual action (*kriyā*) must be postulated, as well as the season (*ṛtu*); moreover, through the power of the subsidiaries previously acquired and by means of the auxiliary elements (*anubandha*) contained within the sentence, it appears here as something brought forward. Let there be knowledge [of this]. Due to the connection with what is drawn from a distance, the connection drawn from one's own statement is stronger. 1.
For injunctionality is indeed resorted to even in that which is equivalent to a restatement regarding an object not [yet] attained; it is the same in this case as well. // 56 //

In this context—the present discussion—even a *ṛtu*, which is a specific type of sacrifice whose very nature is dependent upon bodily activity (*kriyātmā*), must indeed be postulated; for it is precisely that which falls within the scope of the knowledge of what ought to be done (*kartavyatā-jñāna*), which is governed by an injunction (*vidhi*) that is itself to be inferred. Furthermore—

Even the conceptualization of the ritual procedure (*ṛtuvidhikalpana*) occurs through the power of the previously acquired subsidiary elements—that is, by means of the capacity of the subsidiaries related to the fire-altar constructed of bricks (*iṣṭakacitāgni*) introduced earlier, which consists in their inseparable connection with their own purpose. However, the sacrifice consisting of knowledge (*vidyāmaya*), such as the "mind-made" (*manaścita*) and others—whose nature is produced by knowledge due to being accomplished solely through mental activity—is [accomplished] here by the very adjuncts (*anubandha*) present in the sentences within this context, namely those things presented by the words found in the sentences of this section that are useful for the production of the nature of the sacrifice.

Being brought near by mental acts such as hymns (*stotra*) and recitations (*śastra*), it shines—that is, it becomes mounted upon the intellect—possessing a nature conveyed by the word "nearby. Due to the connection with what is distant and drawn in—that is, because it occurs in a different section—it is not nearby; yet, through the presentation of subsidiary elements consisting of ritual action known as the "piling of bricks" (*iṣṭakacita*), it becomes the object of attraction. This is in view of its syntactic relation as a subordinate member (*aṅga*) to the ritual (*kratu*) consisting of action, which serves as the principal member (*aṅgin*). [This applies] to its own statement...

Yoga—meaning connection as a subordinate element with that sacrifice consisting of knowledge (*vidyāmaya*) which is introduced by a sentence conveying a collection of objects consisting of knowledge and is drawn forward later; being more powerful—possessing superior strength due to its rapid presentation; regarding an object whose nature is not yet known through other means of proof (*pramāṇa*), and which must necessarily be known because it is to be performed; even in the case of a specific sentence that is perceived as having a form similar to a restatement (*anuvāda*)—its status as an injunction (*vidhitva*).

The nature of being an injunction (*vidhitva*) consists in its serving as a means for performing a ritual procedure; this is indeed relied upon and accepted by the followers of the *Karma-mīmāṃsā* in the section concerning the eating of remnants (*śeṣabhakṣaṇādhikaraṇa*), specifically in the fifth chapter of the third book. Similarly, in this case regarding the "mind-altars" (*manaścit* etc.)—even though the sentences have the form of restatements (*anuvāda*)—one must consider that the completion of the sacrifice consisting of knowledge (*vidyāmaya-kratu*) occurs through the conceptualization of an injunction, just as in that [other] instance. || 56 ||
The locus of existence is within the body. (3.3.21)
A Compendium of the Collection of Logical Principles Concerning the Body (Śārīraka).
The individual soul (jīva), characterized by agency and so forth, is the object of meditation because it possesses a body;
however, the [Supreme Self] endowed with the eightfold qualities is not so, because it is that which is to be attained, according to the principle of the "agent" (kartṛnyāya). || 41 ||

The individual self (*pratyagātman*), characterized by agency and so forth—that is, distinguished by qualities such as being an agent, an enjoyer, and capable of transmigrating between this world and the next—is to be contemplated as a qualification of the Supreme Self (or rather, as its substantive), and it is to be meditated upon—that is, brought within the scope of devotional worship (*upāsana*).

(But not by virtue of possessing a nature entirely free from all adjuncts), because of the cause of having a body—since during the stage of meditation he exists in a state of embodiment (and at that time, agency and other such qualities cannot be avoided)—(thus one might object). It is not so—it is improper to object in this manner; for [the Self] would be endowed with the eightfold attributes—the individual soul (*jīva*) must be made the object of meditation precisely as being perfected by the eightfold attributes such as freedom from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*), which pertain to the state when all adjuncts have vanished (and not in the state of transmigratory existence).

By virtue of possessing qualities corresponding to the time [of practice], according to the maxim "as is the season, so is the fruit," and in accordance with the principle that "the attainment of the fruit is in proportion to the worship," because it is that which is to be attained—since it is one's own essential nature, endowed with the eight manifested qualities, that is to be attained by oneself in the state of liberation. || 41 ||

If it is argued that this is because, at that time, that form does not appear in the intellect due to its non-proximity (*asaṃnidhāna*), [we reply: no—such a doubt is not tenable. This is because there is proximity through another mode (*anyathā saṃnikarṣāt*); for proximity exists in the pure form residing within oneself (*śuddhātmagatākāre*). (Since for the seeker of liberation who is a practitioner, the pure form residing within himself, which is his own goal, is constantly present in the intellect. In this context, regarding the meditation (*upāsana*) which is intended as the means (*sādhana*), [the pure form] is the end to be accomplished (*sādhya*) as the fruit.

The intended [subject] is indeed the pure Self—the *jīva* itself when entirely free from all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), and certainly not the one possessing adjuncts (for since that state would have been attained even prior to the practice, the practice itself would become useless). The "cognition of the fruit" is the supreme intellect directed toward the goal to be accomplished; it is "inseparable," meaning it remains invariably present and unshaken in the practitioner until the attainment of the fruit; and it exists within the "functioning of the knower"—that is, to be accomplished by a person endowed with knowledge regarding both the means and the end.

"Close to the intellect"—for this very reason, when the fruit is always in proximity to the intellect, being internal; when the state of liberation (muktākāra), which is to be accomplished in view of the worldly forms that are to be ceased, has attained internality and is manifest like an object standing before one; then there is the establishment of the *tatkratu* principle—the attainment of the logic whereby the fruit corresponds to the meditation—and it is regulated by injunction, meaning that through the very injunction for meditation, the pure form of the Self is necessarily connected [to the result]. || 57 ||

It is appropriate to consider only the agent’s status as an enjoyer when there is an effort for the sake of perceived enjoyment; however, even the transition to another body for the sake of heaven and so forth is governed by one's own specific qualification (*svādhikāra*).

This is because, regarding the goal of liberation, the state of *prāya* (death) and the injunctions for *praṇidhi* (devotional focus) are taught, according to the maxim of "the action performed" (*tatkr̥ti-nyāya*).
Since the meaning has been conveyed as "the attainability of that which is to be contemplated," how can there be any suspicion of an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) or similar fallacy? || 58 ||

When an effort is made for the sake of desired enjoyments—that is, when worldly actions (*laukika-karma*) which serve as the means for experiencing fruits in this life are being undertaken—it is appropriate for the agent, the person engaged in the commencement of action, to consider only his status as an enjoyer; at the time of commencing an action, he ought to contemplate solely the fact that he will experience the fruit produced by the action he is performing. When an effort is made for the sake of heaven and so forth—that is, when sacrificial rites (*yāga*) and other such actions which serve as the means for attaining fruits in the hereafter are being undertaken—[one must consider] that which is permeated by one's own qualification (*svādhikāra*).

— [This] is accompanied by the consideration of the qualification (*adhikāra*) suitable for the performance of sacrifices, which consists of the performer’s own status as a member of the three *varṇas* and so forth; furthermore, the transition to another body—even the attainment of a body fit for experiencing a specific pleasure unmixed with suffering, distinct from the body currently serving as the means for performing sacrifices and the like—is also highly worthy of consideration by the agent. However, when meditation (*upāsana*) enjoined in the Vedānta as a means to liberation is performed for the sake of *mokṣa*, [the focus is on] the attainment...

[Nataḥ: Since it is clearly stated in the Śruti that even one’s own state, which is to be attained at the time of obtaining the fruit of worship, is itself an object of meditation, [it follows that] by conforming to that [scriptural authority], the meaning of "being attained" for that which is meditated upon is the meaning of "being experienced" for that which is worshipped; this has been brought to understanding by the statement of the *tatkratu-nyāya*—namely, by the scriptural utterance which makes known the universal rule that "the attainment of the fruit is according to the mode of worship," in the form: "As a person is in this world, so does he become after departing from here"—which has thus been made to enter the intellect regarding this subject as well.

Why is there any fear of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) and so forth?—for such a doubt, in the form of "there would be an over-extension of this principle to worldly action and to Vedic action aimed at results such as heaven," simply does not arise; (this is because this maxim is restricted specifically to the meditations prescribed in the Vedānta). || 58 ||

Since there is a disparity in the forms of the objects of knowledge across the various branches of learning (*vidyābheda*), even when the object of meditation is stated as it is, the goal to be attained is established as being complete in all respects; therefore, the prohibition here concerns the conceptualization of an attainable object.
Consequently, the thought "let there be [an attainment] for the bound soul" is not defiled, for I am not primarily concerned with the literal word.
However, from the statement of Prajāpati, its status as something to be cultivated with a stainless disposition is not established. || 59 ||

Regarding the differences among the *vidyās*—that is, among the specific forms of knowledge that are mutually distinct—the objects of knowledge (*vedyā*) are also distinct because the forms associated with the objects of meditation (*upāsya-artha*) to be contemplated at the time of worship are likewise distinct. Even though only as many forms as have been prescribed in each respective instance are established as the objects of contemplation, Brahman alone, characterized by all its attributes (the two-fold manifestations), is the goal to be attained—that which is to be experienced in the state of the fruit (liberation).

Since that is so—because Brahman, even when endowed with the specific attribute of the individual soul existing in the state of bondage (which is included within the entire range of its qualifying attributes), must necessarily be the object to be attained (as there is no part of it that is not to be attained)—how can the prohibition of meditating upon what is not to be attained be established? For in this section, what kind of reasoning could justify the prohibition (or absence) of meditating upon the form of the individual soul at the time of meditation, which is not to be attained by the practitioner at the time of liberation? Therefore—

Even the form of the bound soul (baddhajīvīyākāra), being qualified by all the aforementioned attributes, becomes a qualification of Brahman; since it is to be attained even in liberation as a qualification of the soul, let there be consideration of the bound state. One must simply accept that the meditation upon the soul’s conditioned form belonging to the time of bondage is sanctioned by the Śruti during the stage of meditative practice.

"What is the fault?"—this doubt is indeed not improper. For the *jīva*, being "defiled"—that is, possessing the impurity consisting of the conditioned form belonging to the time of bondage—is certainly not the primary referent of the word "I" (*ahaṃ*). Indeed, the word "I" occurring in the injunctive sentence for the meditation on the Great Ego (*mahāhaṃgraha*), namely "I am Brahman" (*ahaṃ brahmāsmi*), cannot possibly have that [defiled *jīva*] as its primary meaning, even when taking the full basis for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*), because the basis for the application of the word is simply the natural form [of the Self]. However, from the perspective of Prajāpati...

From the statement of Prajāpati recorded in the eighth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad—namely, "That Self which is free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true and whose resolves are true; that is what one must seek, that is what one must desire to understand"—it is established that [the Self] is to be meditated upon in its stainless state, characterized by the manifestation of the eightfold qualities and the cessation of all impurity.

Thus, by the very fact that [the state] becomes a qualification of the individual soul (jīva), it is established that the soul's being an object of meditation at the time of worship is the intended meaning of the Śruti. || 59 ||
A summary of the meaning of the section.

Regarding the locus of existence within the body— the apprehension of the individual soul (jīva) during the state of meditation in the form of agency and so forth— one might raise this doubt; however,

the apprehension must be performed precisely in the form of being "freed from sin" (apahatapāpmatva) and so on, because it is in that very form of being freed from sin and so forth that [the Self] is to be attained.
And because attainment is to be brought about through meditation, as has been stated.
