This injunction regarding the practice of devotion might apply specifically to the *udgītha* and so forth when they are sung in its own proximity; but it is not so, because here the presence of all [limbs] is established through the mouth of every sacrifice that has been commenced.

Although a general term requires a specific instance for its operation, in the absence of a restrictive rule, the word "rice" (*vrīhi*) denotes the *udgītha* alone; it does not express a distinction, for the principle of the "goat-sacrifice" (*chāga-nīti*) does not apply here. (Verse 60)

This rule regarding the vessel—namely, this injunction for the meditation on the *udgītha*, "One should meditate upon this syllable 'Om' as the *udgītha*"—would apply only to that specific *udgītha* sung in the proximity of [the particular text], that is, only to the specific subject matter consisting of the *udgītha* which is a subsidiary of the sacrifice (*ṛtu*) belonging to a particular recensional school (*śākhā*) where the injunction for meditation is explicitly stated; it would not apply to the *udgītha* in general across all recensions. (This being the prima facie view: It is not so; to accept it thus is not correct, because [it applies] to all subsidiaries...

"From the mouth"—by way of the sacrifice which has the entire *udgītha* as its auxiliary; "here"—even in this branch (*śākhā*) where the meditation on the *udgītha* is explicitly mentioned; because of the establishment of the proximity of all [meditations], that is, because the presence of all *udgīthas* (belonging even to various branches) is obtained; "the universal"—all that is spoken of as a universal; and although it must be performed by depending upon the individual, according to the maxim "there is no universal without a particular," and thus possesses the quality of being to be practiced only in dependence upon the individual which constitutes the particular—nevertheless...

When it is said, "Bring the cow," the performance of the act of bringing indeed pertains specifically to a particular cow. Nevertheless, in the absence of a restrictive rule—that is, when no means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is perceived that would result in the understanding of a specific instance alone—there occurs a culmination in the general, just as in the case of rice; for example, by the injunction "One should sacrifice with rice," any substance whatsoever that serves as the basis for the rice used in preparing the sacrificial oblation (*caru*) is included. And this word—"One should meditate upon the *udgītha*"—is likewise a word in the form of an injunctive sentence.

It speaks of the *udgītha* alone—it conveys only the universal (*sāmānya*) by way of its being based on the nature of the *udgītha*; it does not [denote] a specific *udgītha* belonging to a particular branch (*śākhā*). As for the "Chāga-logic" (the logic of the goat-sacrifice), it finds no scope here in this matter, because there is an absence of anything that would determine a specific [instance]. || 60 ||
The Garland of Logical Connections (Nayasaṅgatimālikā)

Even though there is a distinction [between the individual notes], based on the established conclusion of the preceding section, there should be a connection with the entire *udgītha* according to the principle of that which is bound to the subordinate members (*aṅgāvabaddha*). || 150 ||
Thus ends the section concerning that which is bound to the limbs (aṅgāvabaddha). || 22 ||

The Vaiśvānara Self—that is, the Supreme Self known as Vaiśvānara, who is established as the object of veneration in the Vaiśvānara-vidyā—is to be meditated upon in His distributed form (*vyasta*). Within the body consisting of the three worlds, He is to be worshipped individually and separately in the form of the head, the sun, the eyes, and so forth, because specific fruits are declared for each. Indeed, the respective fruit belongs only to one who is established in the meditation upon those specific limbs; [as it is said: "He sees abundant food that is dear."

Because meditation on each individual limb is taught with distinct results in the Śruti by such passages as, "Brahman-splendor (brahmavarcasa) accrues to his family," etc., here—in this very context of meditation—the statement of the fruit refers to the complete meditation; that is, when the act of meditating upon [the Self] endowed with all its limbs has been accomplished, [the result occurs] in all [limbs].

The statement regarding the fruit in the form of "he eats food" is merely a praise (*stuti*) consisting of a collective description of the collection of fruits that accrues when the meditations on each individual limb are completed; it does not intend to enjoin a separate, collective meditation as such. Or rather—alternatively—the Vaiśvānara Self, even in its entirety—that is, possessing all forms such as having the head and so forth—is to be meditated upon (just as in the case of the distributed meditations, by means of the combined meditation as well).

"He is to be worshipped not merely through the worship of the whole [but also the parts]"—(the meaning is that the worship of the Vaiśvānara-self must be performed both distributively and collectively)—this is not so; such an admission is certainly not correct. For there is a fault in the individual worships performed separately—a potential harm—which was described immediately after the discussion of the individual parts of the distributive worship in the passage beginning with "Your head would have fallen off," and so forth. The statement regarding those results is merely a praise.

The statement regarding the fruits of meditating on each single part, such as the head and so forth, must be understood as praise intended to demonstrate that even a single portion of the complete meditation is not to be neglected. Furthermore, in the case of the *aṣṭākapāla* and other offerings—which are parts of the *dvādaśakapāla* sacrifice—where it is established that they are not to be performed separately, we observe that the mention of the fruit of a single part, such as the *aṣṭākapāla*, takes the form of a restatement (*anuvāda*) of that specific part. Indeed, [it is seen] in the passage concerning Vaiśvānara...

Having prescribed the *jāteṣṭi* sacrifice dedicated to Vaiśvānara with the injunction, "One should offer an oblation on twelve potsherds when a son is born," the Karmakāṇḍa immediately thereafter declares, "In that it is on eight potsherds, he purifies him with the *Gāyatrī* through spiritual luster; in that it is on nine potsherds... and so forth, thus proclaiming the fruits of each individual constituent part. Consequently, since the proclamation of separate fruits is determined to be otherwise established as being intended for praise (*stuti*), [there is no such fruit] for each individual meditation (*upāsanā*).

Furthermore, by the understanding that [the individual self] is censured, and also by the separate mention at the end of the fruit of the meditation on the aggregate, it is established that the Vaiśvānara Self as a whole is to be meditated upon, being distinguished by having the three worlds as His body in their entirety.

By means of the purport of the great sentence (*mahāvākya*)—that is, by the purport of the great sentence as understood through a thorough consideration of the context, which serves as the instrument for making known the intended meaning—and when there is a connection with the whole alone—that is, when it is firmly established and determined that the meditation pertains to the entire collection of limbs belonging to the Vaiśvānara Self—then, regarding the individual parts such as the head and so forth, which constitute portions of that collection of limbs and serve as objects of meditation, the statement of the fruit follows after restating those parts one by one.

Following the method of restating [the archetypal injunction] by way of describing the individual results—beginning with "In his family, the Soma-pressing is seen as pressed, well-pressed, and thoroughly pressed"—and then praising the constituent parts according to the rule of fixed praise, there is the *jāteṣṭi* (the sacrifice on the birth of a son) as a secondary form.

In accordance with the principle found in those passages whose purpose is praise—preceded by a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the eight-potsherd, nine-potsherd, and other portions of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) used in a sacrifice accomplished by ten potsherds—one must grasp the *ānyaparya* (the shift in purport): namely, that the passage lacks the intention to convey the literal meaning expressed by the words, and instead has the sole intent of communicating the excellence of even a single part of the meditation (and not the intent to enjoin the meditation on that single part). This applies to the "Section on the Plurality" (*bhūmavākya*), which relates to the Bhūmavidyā; therein, regarding the meditations on Name and so forth, [the text mentions] Name, Speech, and...

When the meditations on the mind (*manas*) and so forth have been performed, the fruit heard as that which is to be attained—consisting of name, range, sphere, time, and conduct—is required as a limit (*avadhi*). This is because it serves to indicate the progressive excellence of the fruits produced by each successive meditation, thereby facilitating the understanding of such excellence. Thus, unlike in the *Vaiśvānara* meditation where a specific evil consequence is mentioned for each individual meditation, no such harmful result is heard here as the fruit of meditating on each part individually. Therefore, in the case of meditating on the first [part] among those that constitute a portion of the *Bhūma* meditation, no such negative fruit is heard in the scripture.

Because it has been so stated, this is an "inappropriate example" (viṣamodāhṛti): the employment of something as an example that lacks the similarity required for an example; it does not serve to establish the point—that is, it is not conducive to obtaining the intended meaning. || 62 ||
The Section Concerning the Distinction of Sound and Other Qualities (Śabdādibhedādhikaraṇa) || 3.3.24 ||
A Compendium of the Collection of Principles Concerning the Body (Śārīraka).

The knowledges such as "Being" (sad-vidyā) might be considered one because there is no difference in their injunctions regarding the fruit and so forth; yet this is not so, for they must indeed be distinct due to the differences in their names and forms.

Regarding the *sadādi-vidyās*—that is, the *sad-vidyā*, *bhūma-vidyā*, and so forth, which have the single fruit of attaining Brahman, consist of meditation upon the Supreme Self, and are taught in the Vedānta: because there is no difference in the injunction of the fruit and so forth, there would be oneness; that is, since there is no distinction between the fruit consisting of the attainment of Brahman and the injunctions concerning an uninterrupted stream of recollection in the form of "one should meditate," "one should know," "one should worship," and so on, they must indeed be non-different (this is the prima facie view). It is not so; it is not thus.

The suspicion is unfounded; for, due to the distinction between the names and forms [of the meditations]—since there is a multiplicity of designations for the meditations such as "the science of the True" (*sadvidyā*), "the science of the Earth" (*bhūmavidyā*), "the science of the small one" (*daharavidyā*), and so forth—and also because of the difference in the forms of the objects of meditation and other attributes, there must indeed be a distinction; that is, the plurality of these meditations alone is established, not their identity. || 44 ||

Because of the difference in the forms of their designations—namely, the specific names of those various sciences such as ‘Sadvidyā’ and ‘Bhūmavidyā’—and because of the difference in the form associated with the science known as the ‘aspect of the object to be known’ (*vedyākāra*), when there is an injunction regarding the realization of the object to be known as qualified by those respective particular attributes (*tadupahitavidhau*), a state of being characterized (*vaiśiṣṭya*) is established by means of each of those respective qualities which serve as qualifiers of the object to be known; thus, a distinction (*vailakṣaṇya*) or particularity is obtained within the very nature of the injunction.

In this context—among the various meditations (vidyās) proclaimed in the Vedānta—the fruits of certain meditations, such as the Madhu-vidyā and others, are distinct from one another; that is, in some meditations like the Madhu-vidyā, the fruit to be accomplished by the meditation is mixed with other fruits, while in others it is unmixed. Thus, even though there is a connection with a fruit in each case, a distinction [between the meditations] is unavoidable.

(Therefore, a distinction has been stated regarding all [texts], whether they consist of connection, form, injunction, or name. Thus—in the same way as in the case of the knowledges of Brahman which have liberation as their sole fruit, even in the case of optional knowledges such as the science of the *dṛṣṭi* which have fruits other than liberation, there is a distinction created by specificities such as connection and so forth. || 63 ||
"How did the author of the Sūtras say, 'Because of the difference in various words and so forth,' when there is identity of form?
For these [meditations] are not diverse like sacrifices, gifts, and the like, since their establishment depends on the repose of devotion.
True; this difference of word is merely figurative, intended to reinforce the difference in form."
The intention [of the author] is to refute those who assert that knowledge is an instrument (karaṇa) that cannot be enjoined. || 64 ||

When there is identity [of the object], since the words "one should meditate" (*adhyāyīta*), "one should worship" (*upāsīta*), and "one should know" (*vidyāt*)—used by the prescriber of meditation—are synonyms, their non-difference is clear; so how did the author of the Sūtras, Bādarāyaṇa, the composer of the *Śārīraka-sūtras*, say, "Because of the difference of words and so forth" (*nānā śabdādibhedāt*)? Or rather, how could he have stated a difference of words and so forth through that Sūtra? These objects denoted by the words "meditation," "worship," "knowledge," and so on, are not like sacrifices, gifts, and the like—such as "the renunciation of a substance for the sake of a deity."

Sacrifice (*yāga*) is the act of transferring ownership to another preceded by the relinquishing of one's own ownership; giving (*dāna*) is the inducing of another's ownership preceded by the relinquishing of one's own; and oblation (*homa*) is the casting of a substance into a specific location preceded by the act of relinquishment. Thus, although these entities such as sacrifice and giving possess distinct natures, they are not indeed diverse—that is, they do not possess mutually exclusive natures—because their ultimate rest is established in *bhakti*. For the objects of meditation (*dhyāna*), worship (*upāsana*), and so forth, [it is said]: "Knowledge finds its rest in meditation; meditation finds its rest in constant mindfulness (*dhruvasmṛti*)."

Since it has been stated that "that [knowledge] attains the status of a view (*dṛṣṭi*), and the view reaches the status of devotion (*bhakti*)," and because this very conclusion—that [the knowledge] culminates in devotion—is established as the final doctrine, [one might object]: "True—this objection must indeed be admitted in part; however, this difference in words mentioned in the Sūtra is merely figurative—that is, employed in a non-primary sense—for the sake of strengthening the distinction of form, in order to ensure a firm comprehension of the difference in form which brings about the difference between the two knowledges. (Thus he objects. Regarding the word...

By the word "difference" (*bheda*), which is a synonym for "another word" (*śabdāntara*) mentioned in the previous section, it is intended here that there is indeed a difference in form (*rūpabheda*). Furthermore, as for those dualists who maintain that knowledge—which cannot be enjoined (*avidheya*) because its establishment depends on sentences such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*)—is itself the instrument (*karaṇa*).

They "proclaimed" (*jaguḥ*) that it is the means to liberation (*mokṣasādhana*); the "intention" (*abhisandhiḥ*)—meaning the ultimate purport (*paramaṃ tātparyam*)—is its refutation, i.e., the demonstration that it is in no way the intended subject of the scripture's purport, because only that knowledge which is to be enjoined—known by such names as *vidyā*, *upāsanā*, and so forth—is the means to liberation. || 64 ||

Alternatively, by stating "due to the difference in words and so forth," the author of the Sūtras has correctly distinguished between ritual performance (*nyāsa*) and meditative worship (*upāsanā*), since their distinction is non-figurative, like that between the acts of sacrificing and offering oblations.
Furthermore, a difference in designation, form, and so forth is heard in scripture, and moreover, the qualification (*adhikāra*) is distinct.
And they declared that [the result] would occur through swift attainment and so forth; thus, they established the rule regarding the worship of Madhu and other such practices.

Alternatively—that is to say, this is another mode of explanation—the author of the Sūtras, Bādarāyaṇa, by employing this specific term "śabdādibhedāt" (due to the difference of words, etc. while omitting other words, indicates that [the difference] is "abhāktāt"—that is, from a difference of words in their primary sense, consisting of distinct words devoid of synonymy (as expressed by the term *śabdāntara* in the Pūrva-kāṇḍa), which exists within the Śruti and other sources.

From the difference in terminology—such as "take refuge" (*śaraṇaṃ vraja*) and "worship" (*bhajasva*), which take the form of injunctions for the practice of *nyāsa* and *upāsana*—just as sacrifice (*yāga*) and oblation (*homa*) are distinct from the verbs *yajati* and *juhoti*, so too are these two, *prapatti* and *bhakti*, both sciences (*vidye*) that have the singular fruit of attaining Brahman, yet they are clearly taught as being properly distinguished and separate. The distinction between the two lies in their names, such as *prapatti* and *bhakti*, arising from differences in verbal roots, forms, and so forth.

The difference between the two [paths] lies in their nature: one is established as a means for the sake of liberation (*mokṣa*), while the other possesses qualities such as truthfulness (*satyatva*), knowledge (*jñānatva*), and bliss (*ānandatva*). (Likewise, there are also internal differences. Furthermore, the difference in result consists in the attainment being either swift or delayed. "That which is heard" (*śruta*) refers to everything understood within the prescriptive sections (*vidhi-prakaraṇa*); "equal to the other" (*itarasama*) means that here too it is the same as in the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*), such as sacrifices, oblations, and gifts. Moreover, there is nothing further than this: [this is] the qualification (*adhikāra*).

For a conscious being engaged in devotion for the sake of liberation and one engaged in *prapatti* (surrender), the quality that renders them fit for such activity must differ—differing by way of "swift attainment" and so forth, and differing by way of intolerance versus tolerance for delay caused by the acquisition of another birth, such that it would be entirely distinct [in the case of *prapatti*]. And it is precisely in this manner that [it differs] in the *Madhu-upāsanā* and others—the meditation on the Supreme Self as having the sun and other luminaries as its body, known as the *Madhu-vidyā*.

Even for those who have such a vision of the Lord, [the commentators]—those teachers intent on describing the intention of the author of the Sūtras—have proclaimed the established order (*vyavasthā*): namely, the specific nature determined by the attainment of the state of the Vasus and others as a preliminary to the attainment of the Supreme Self, followed by the direct attainment of the Lord Himself; thus they have made clear the underlying purport of the Sūtras. || 65 ||
The Garland of Logical Connections.

In the section concerning various sounds (*nānāśabdādhikaraṇa*), by means of the sequence of the method of Vaiśvānara, the doubt regarding identity [of the Self] based on the notions of the "existent" (*sat*), the "eye," the "heart" (*hṛd*), and so forth, is dispelled. (152)

Even for one of middling capacity, various branches of knowledge (*vidyās*)—for the sake of attaining greater bliss, that is, aiming for the acquisition of superior bliss (just as there is a desire for superiority in the fruit of heaven)—should be fit for combination; they should be capable of being practiced in combination by each individual person. No single rule of worship—that is, any rule concerning the knowledge of Brahman consisting of meditation—should be restricted to only one person; it ought not to be intended for any one individual alone [since the scripture exists for the welfare of the world].

Because they have been set in motion—those various sciences (*vidyās*), though diverse, are capable of being accomplished—that is, performed, practiced, or cultivated—by relying on different specific times due to the distinction of time; therefore, such a doubt is not correct. This is because there is a mutual obstruction of the stability of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) by the sciences, that is, due to the counteraction of the mental traces (*saṃskāra*) concerning the specific objects to be contemplated associated with each individual science.

(On account of the consequence that [the practice] would become lax, leading to the attainment of what is not equal [to the goal]): here, in the Vedānta which prescribes the means to liberation, with the aim of the fruit consisting of the experience of the perfect Brahman through complete meditation on Brahman, there is an injunction regarding *samādhi* at the time of death—an injunction concerning *samādhi* in the form of uninterrupted meditation on the Supreme Brahman to be performed day after day for as long as life lasts; and this is distinct and individual for each [person] (meaning it concerns only one specific knowledge (*vidyā*) for each individual person, and thus does not involve the performance of them all in combination).
Since they are the intended objects of the treatise, the knowledges are indeed fit for optional performance.
Surely, because the specific forms of color and so forth are distinct, the worship of another [deity] is not uniform;

since the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is divided, its fruit would also be unequal, which would be consistent with logic. This would not be so, for even in all branches of knowledge, it will be stated that there is equality of enjoyment as the fruit.
And having attained oneness with those who follow many paths, this is well-known both from worldly experience and from the Veda.

And regarding the attainment of unity by people—that is, the state of having a destination accessible to only one [path]—this is well-known both from common worldly experience and from the Veda. In the world, it is seen among those traveling toward rivers, villages, gardens, and so forth; and in the Veda, too, among those who rely on various *iṣṭāpūrta* rites and others who desire specific fruits of their actions (who are the subjects)—it is understood by worldly believers that there is no contradiction regarding the unity of the fruit. || 67 ||

Furthermore, since the sentence "vidyāyai" [in the passage *vidyāṃ prakurvīta*] indicates that knowledge (*vidyā*) is the means for attaining the fruit characterized by greater efficacy (*vīryavattaratva*), there arises the inquiry: "Depending upon what does this knowledge produce greater efficacy? In response to this, it is understood from the statement "one should meditate on the *udgītha*" that it depends upon the *udgītha*, which is the object of meditation. Since this very injunction regarding the locus (*āśraya-vidhi*) possesses a connection with the fruit consisting of greater efficacy, it serves to establish the aforementioned point. || 46 ||

—Just as in that case, here too, even by relying on the indicative force (*jñāpakatva*) of the present tense (*laṭ-lakāra*) designated in the passage "Whatever one performs with knowledge" (which sets aside the injunctive form *kuryāt*), it is not possible here to follow the logic of the *parṇamayī* rule; such is the meaning. || 68 ||

The scriptural statement here does not indicate that the ritual action is for the sake of that [knowledge], since it serves merely as a basis and a support; moreover, an injunction for counteracting [the knowledge] is appropriate when there is a risk of losing that knowledge for one who seeks its fruit.
Let there be praise for the *tāra* mantra along with its meditation (*upāsana*) because of its following [the text]; however, by that much alone, it is not an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to that [knowledge].
Having set aside what was to be said previously, this statement is placed here for the purpose of introducing the topic to be established.

In this context—in the injunctive sentence prescribing the meditation on the *udgītha*, namely "One should meditate on the *udgītha*" (*udgītham upāsīta*)—the scriptural mention of the action (*karmaśruti*), which is the accusative case-ending in the word "udgītham," would not convey its status as a subordinate member (*aṅgatva*)—that is, its being for the sake of that [meditation] (which is synonymous with being an auxiliary to it)—merely because of the apprehension of the substratum; for by the accusative case, one apprehends only the substratum upon which the meditation rests, namely that which is called the *udgītha*. Furthermore, in the event of the loss of the knowledge (*vidyāhāni*), [there would be no fault] regarding that which is performed by the *udgātṛ* priest.

When a defective *udgītha*—which is essentially the absence of the knowledge consisting in the realization of the identity of the *udgītha* and the *praṇava*—occurs due to incapacity or other causes, and when the occasion arises for one who desires its fruit; that is, when the qualification for ritual action is presented for one who seeks the result of the *udgītha* meditation, namely the state of being more vigorous (*vīryavattara*) in the sacrifice—the prescriptive statement is given as a remedy: it is the teaching of a means to accomplish the desired fruit by another method through the removal of the defect caused by the defective *udgītha* (namely, through the knowledge of the identity of the *udgītha* and the *praṇava* residing in the *hotṛ*).

The demonstration of its resolution is as follows: it is indeed proper and logical, because of the following: due to the statement, "By this [syllable] this triple knowledge proceeds," and so forth, there is an assertion of its continuous application across all three Vedas in the acts of hearing, reciting, and chanting the syllable *oṃ*; and let there be praise—that is, let the excellence—be established for that *tāra* (the Savior), namely the *praṇava*, which is connected with the knowledge consisting of meditation (*sopāsana*). However, by that much—by the mere praise of the *praṇava* together with its meditation—that meditation on the *praṇava*... [is not thereby established].

Furthermore, it is not established as a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice (*ṛtu-aṅgatvena*), because there is no contradiction in the description of that [meditation], which serves the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*), resulting in praise; for the portion concerning the absence of being a subsidiary part of the sacrifice—which was to be explained earlier and is to be established in the section on the rule of determining that [meditation]—is set aside, meaning that its status as occurring in that specific place is abandoned. Here, at the end of this chapter, this statement is a description of the absence of the relationship of principal and subordinate between the meditation on the *udgītha* and the sacrifice, for the sake of establishing the correct understanding.

In the fourth quarter (the *Aṅga* quarter), the demonstration of the relationship between the constituent parts (*aṅga*) and the whole (*aṅgin*) with respect to *vidyā* is intended solely for the sake of establishing the logical connection known as "occasion" (*prasaṅga*); therefore, reflection on this point is indeed appropriate. 69.
The Garland of Logical Connections.

The doubt as to whether there is a rule regarding the meditation on the *udgītha* or a rule regarding the options [of meditations] is here dispelled by the principle of "according to the substrate" (*yathāśrayanyāya*). (154)
Thus, in this third chapter and also in its third section, the connection of twenty-six topics has been fully illustrated. (155)

The conclusion is that the person (puruṣa) meditated upon in the *Nāsadiya Sūkta* has a distinct nature [from the person in the *Śāṇḍilyavidyā*], and that [the meditation on] piercing, etc., is a subsidiary part of the study [of the Veda]. This means that mantras such as "I pierce the bright" (*śukraṃ pravidhye*) serve only to assist the study of the Vedic portions that enjoin knowledge (*vidyā*), and do not assist the meditation (*upāsanā*). || 48 || There is a mutual connection between abandonment (*hāna*) and so forth; time is for the injunction to contemplate that [Brahman];
there is commonality regarding the path (*saraṇī*), and likewise similarity with the passage beginning with "not coarse" (*asthūla*). || 49 ||

The mutual relationship between abandonment (*hāna*) and so forth: where only the abandonment of good and evil deeds is heard of, or only their acquisition (*upāyana*), in both cases there is a relationship between abandonment and acquisition consisting of mutual inseparability. The time for that meditation: the meditation on the abandonment and acquisition of good and evil deeds by the knower is delimited by the time of departure from the body. And the commonality of the path: this refers to the path beginning with light (*arcirādi-mārga*) for the knower.

There is no distinction even with respect to those established in all the sciences taught in the Vedānta; likewise, there is equality regarding the qualities such as "not gross" and so forth. This means that the qualities of Brahman—such as being non-gross and so on—which are mentioned in the knowledge of the Imperishable Supreme Brahman, are to be combined (upasaṃhāra) in all the sciences taught in the Vedānta. || 49 ||

The oneness of the vital breath with hunger and so forth, and from that, its nature as a burner; the lack of restriction regarding the meditation on the Udgītha, and the contemplation of the qualities of the object of meditation. (50)

The identity of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) with hunger and so forth: there is no difference between the two types of meditation established in the questions and answers of Upastha and Kahola, namely "he who breathes by means of the breath" and "he who [is beyond] hunger and thirst"; and likewise in the subsequent section, the identity of the small [space], meaning the non-difference between the two Dahara-vidyās taught in the Chāndogya and Vājasaneyaka; the lack of restriction regarding the meditation on the *udgītha*, meaning that the meditations on the *udgītha* and other elements based on the constituent parts of ritual action need not necessarily be employed within the sacrifices; and the contemplation of the repetition of the qualities—in all cases as well.
In the contemplations of the qualities of Brahman, there is also the contemplation of Brahman itself as the possessor of those qualities; this is the function [of the mind]. || 50 ||

The state of being the knowledge that determines all objects of worship, the meditation on the mind as the fire-altar (manaścit), the worship of the individual soul (jīva) through its attributes, and the contemplation of the Udgītha everywhere—[these are the meditations]. 51.

The definitive determination regarding the object of worship for all [meditations] is found in the section of the *Taittirīyaka* beginning with "Thousand-headed" (*sahasraśīrṣa*); this constitutes the definitive determination of that which is taught in the Vedāntas. The fact that the section of the *Taittirīyaka* determines the specific reality to be worshipped in all meditations, as well as the status of the "mind-altars" (*manaścit*) as meditations, is established by the passage beginning "the mind-altar, the speech-altar, the breath-altar," which shows that the fires mentioned in the *Agnirahasya-brāhmaṇa* enter into the nature of being composed of knowledge (*vidyāmaya*).

However, the conclusion is that there is no entry into the nature of ritual action (*kriyāmaya*); rather, there is the presence of the qualities of the individual soul (*jīva*). This means that when the meditation on the individual self (*jīvātman*) is to be performed, only those unconditioned qualities belonging to the individual soul that exist at the time of liberation are to be meditated upon, and not those existing at the time of bondage (since one must contemplate what is necessary for the attainment of the fruit of meditation)—this is the conclusion. Regarding "the contemplation of the *udgītha* everywhere": this means that the meditation resting on the *udgītha* is connected to all rituals, just like the *udgītha* itself. 51.
The totality of Vaiśvānara, the distinctness of the knowledge of Being (sadvidyā) and the rest, the collection of various knowledges, the Udgītha, and furthermore, Niyati; || 52 ||

The totality of Vaiśvānara: in the Vaiśvānara-vidyā, it is established that the worship of the self as Vaiśvānara, whose body is the three worlds, must be performed as a whole and not through partial (fragmented) worship; furthermore, regarding the distinctness of the Sad-vidyā and others, although the Brahman to be worshipped is one and the same in all the vidyās taught in the Vedānta, there is indeed a mutual difference among the vidyās such as the Sad-vidyā which constitute those respective modes of worship.

There is no lack of distinction; rather, there is no combination (*asamāhāra*) of the various forms of knowledge (*vidyā*). The determination is that those knowledges which are practiced as means to liberation are not to be performed through a collective synthesis (*samuccaya*), but rather by way of option (*vikalpa*) alone. Furthermore, regarding the non-restriction of the *udgītha*: this is a reaffirmation of the absence of a rule for the adoption of meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth—which depend upon the constituent parts of the sacrifice—in the sacrificial rites, concerning the very same matter already determined in the section on the restriction of such determinations (*tannirdhāraṇā-niyama-adhikaraṇa*). || 52 ||

The distinction and non-distinction of the sciences, as well as the grasping and non-grasping of the qualities—in this manner, by this quarter [of the verse], the matter has been most effectively deliberated upon. (53)

The distinctions and non-distinctions among knowledges—that is, the mutual difference or absence of difference in the essential nature of those knowledges established by scripture as means to liberation (or as forms of vision); and the inclusion and exclusion of qualities—that is, the combination or non-combination of the qualities of Brahman within those knowledges—in this manner, by this third quarter [of the book] called "The Combination of Qualities," that body of matter which is most essential among what must be accepted has been thoroughly investigated.
The number twenty-six has been correctly determined after being investigated within the various philosophical systems (kevalakaraṇas). || 53 ||
Thus ends the third chapter in the *Śārīrakanyāyakalāpasaṅgraha*.

The persistence of all [qualities]—the persistence of qualities defining the nature of Brahman, such as blissfulness and purity, which must be meditated upon in all meditations (vidyās) just as in the case of Brahman, the substratum of those qualities; the injunction for the contemplation of the waters used for sipping (ācamanīya) as being the abode of the principal vital breath (prāṇa); the identity of the two Śāṇḍilya-vidyās taught in two different Vedic branches; and the separate existence of the day and night [meditations].

Because the Brahman to be meditated upon has the *vyāhṛtis* as its body, its secret names—‘Ahaḥ’ and ‘Aham’—exist separately, being restricted to their respective meditations in the solar orb and in the eye. Furthermore, the collection of Brahman’s qualities, such as the gathering of power (*sambhṛti*) characterized by specific locations, boundaries, and distinct heroic energies, is connected only to those meditations on the Brahman as a qualified object in specific locations; thus, there is a restriction of place. This constitutes the distinction of the *puruṣavidyā* (the knowledge of the Person) as recorded in the Taittirīya from that recorded in the Chāndogya.

The distinctness of the mantras beginning with "śaṃ naḥ" (may there be peace for us)—namely, the mantras that bring about peace such as those addressed to Mitra and others—their fixed status as mere recitations of specific portions of the Veda, and the establishment of their lack of being auxiliary parts of knowledge (*vidyā*): these are the points to be proven in the ten topical sections (*adhikaraṇas*). || 70 ||

The mutual connection of inferiority and so forth, the appropriate time for that, the equality with the path of the gods and others, the absence of grossness and so on everywhere, the exchange [of attributes], the single nature of the meditation on the *dahara* (small) space among those heard by many disciples, the injunction regarding the fruit of qualities based on the *udgītha*, the repetition of the substratum for the sake of the qualities when they are seen, and the determination of the object of knowledge as the meditation on the entirely supreme— [these are the topics]. 71.

The mutual connection of abandonment and so forth: for the knower, prior to liberation, there is a state of universal synthesis regarding the contemplation of the casting off and the transference elsewhere of good and evil deeds; the appropriate time for this is the abandonment of merit and demerit.

The appropriate time for transition (the time of departure from the body); equality regarding the path of the gods and so forth—the uniformity of the journey by way of the path of light (*arcirādi-mārga*), which is designated as the "path of the gods," for all wise ones established in every type of knowledge; everywhere, the collection of qualities such as "not gross" (*asthūlatva*) and so on, which define the nature of Brahman and are to be meditated upon in all Vedāntic teachings; furthermore, the exchange of what was heard by various disciples; and subsequently, by two [sections], concerning Uṣasta—

The fact that [the two texts] are to be reflected upon by following the answers given in both places—namely, those understood from the Śruti as being questioned by Kahola and others (to Yājñavalkya) for the sake of instruction, such as "He who breathes with the breath" and "He who [transcends] hunger and thirst"—and that there is a single identity of the meditation on the small [space] (*dahara-upāsti*) means that the two *dahara* meditations recorded in the Chāndogya and Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣads are identical in their essential nature; and that they concern a vision based on the *udgītha* refers to the practice proceeding by taking recourse to the *udgītha*, which is a constituent part of the ritual action.

In the scriptural passage, "One should meditate upon the *udgītha*," there is an injunction regarding the connection between the quality consisting of meditation on the *udgītha* and its fruit, which is the state of being more powerful (*vīryavattara*). This is an instance of the substratum—the Brahman that is the locus of the meditation, as seen in the *dahara-vidyā*—being employed for the purpose of contemplating the qualities of Brahman.

The function of reflection (*cintanavṛtti*) consists in the determination of the Supreme Reality, which is the object of worship in all higher knowledge (*paravidyā*), by means of the *Sahasraśīrṣa* section found in the *Taittirīya*. (These matters are undertaken and must be established across nine sections, from the eleventh section up to the completion of the nineteenth. || 71 ||

The forms of knowledge, such as the *manaściti* and others, consist of the sacrifice (*kratu*) in the form of appropriate cognition; the pure field (*kṣetrin*), which is inconceivable, is the quality of the sacrifice, and the vision [of it] is present in all the parts beginning with the *udgītha*.
Thus, the worship of Vaiśvānara is performed in its entirety, and consequently, there is the establishment of many forms of knowledge.
Furthermore, for those seeking liberation, there is no fixed rule regarding the conceptualization of the *udgītha* meditation; this is what is stated here.

The forms of knowledge (*vidyārūpa*) consist of the mind, speech, and so forth—as stated in the *Agnirahasyabrāhmaṇa* with the words "the piled mind, the piled speech," etc.—which are to be piled (*cetavyā*). They are of the nature of knowledge (*jñānarūpa*), consisting of water (*ammaya*), and situated within the sacrifice that is knowledge; thus they are "fit" (*ucitāḥ*), meaning they possess the fitness to be accepted. This is the conclusion (based on the statement: "These, indeed, are piled by knowledge alone"). The "knower of the field" (*kṣetrajña*) is the individual soul (*jīva*), who is "pure" (*śuddha*), meaning he possesses his own essential nature which has become manifest and free from limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*). He is "to be meditated upon" (*anucintya*), which refers to the worship of the Lord (*bhagavad-upāsanā*).

The determination that [the Self] is the object of one's own worship as being a constituent part of the sacrifice (*kratvaṅgabhūta*)—and not as possessing attributes such as agency conditioned by the state of bondage—is established regarding all parts of the *udgītha* belonging to the sacrifice, including the *udgītha* and others mentioned in all branches (*sarvaśākhāmnāteṣu*). This refers to the connection with meditation (*upāsanā-sambandha*). The "worship of Vaiśvānara" is the meditation on the Supreme Self named Vaiśvānara as recorded in the Vaiśvānara-vidyā; this is to be performed in its entirety—that is, as a complete whole.

But it is not by way of separation; rather, after the attainment of various forms of knowledge (*vidyā*), there is indeed a plurality of meditations (*upāsanā*) for the sake of liberation, and not their unity—this is the justification of the point. Regarding the option (*vikalpa*) among those meditations for the sake of liberation—namely, the knowledges known as *sad*, *dahara*, *vaiśvānara*, and so forth—the non-combination of these within a single person means that only one may be practiced at a time. Furthermore, regarding the lack of restriction (*aniyati*) concerning the meditation on the *udgītha*, this refers precisely to what was determined in the section on the rule of determination (*tannirdhāraṇā-niyama-adhikaraṇa*).

The lack of necessity for the mandatory performance of the meditation on the *udgītha*—this point is further established once more for the sake of firmness (these sections are supported from the twentieth section through the twenty-sixth section). || 72 ||
Śrīḥ!
Salutation to the illustrious Rāmānuja. Salutation to Śrī. Salutation to Śrīdhara.
The Fourth Quarter of the Third Chapter. ||3-4||
The Section on the Goal of Human Endeavor (Puruṣārthādhikaraṇa) 11. A Compendium of the Essential Arguments of the Śārīraka [Brahmasūtra] 3.8.2.11.
Because it is an auxiliary to ritual action (*karma*), knowledge (*vidyā*) bestows fruits upon that action which determines the agent;
it does not do so by determining the Lord of the soul (*jīvādhīśa*). For you, O Lord, are the determiner of this [soul], and ritual action is merely an auxiliary to that knowledge.

Regarding the determination of the agent: [these texts] are conducive to determining the true nature of the conscious being who acts in rites enjoined by the Śruti. Because knowledge—meaning the knowledge consisting of meditation prescribed in the Vedānta—is a subordinate part of ritual action (*karmāṅgatva*), insofar as it assists the rite through the medium of the agent, that very rite—the very ritual action mentioned in the Karmakāṇḍa which has the Vedānta-prescribed knowledge as its constituent part—bestows the fruits; that is, it grants the fruits in the form of human goals (*puruṣārtha*). It is not the knowledge, as a subordinate element, that bestows them.

(Thus he objects: "Because it is logical that the capacity to bestow the fruit belongs to the principal [action] alone. (To this we reply: This is not so; it is not at all tenable both that knowledge is a subordinate factor (*aṅga*) to ritual action and that ritual action is the bestower of the fruit, because of the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*). Since the Lord—who is the Supreme Brahman, who has the individual soul as His body and who is the controller of the individual soul—is the sole decisive authority for all knowledge taught in the Vedānta, it is that very knowledge which bestows the fruits in the form of the various human goals (*puruṣārtha*). It is knowledge alone that grants these results.
It is not action; yet it is action, for it is indeed a limb of that [deity], and thus it is truly a limb of this Vidyā. || 54 ||
And that is without essence.
Those who say that the innate teleological intent (*aidamparya*) of non-human (Vedic) words regarding their meanings—

which culminates in the direct perfection of the syllables— is contradicted by the intent of the injunction for private recitation (*svādhyāya-vidhi*), [should be answered thus]: let them be satisfied by the logic of the injunction for muttering (*japa-vidhi*).
O long-lived ones, the word does not manifest its power regarding an object that cannot be apprehended by other means. || 98 ||

Regarding the words of non-human origin—that is, those devoid of "human authorship" in the sense of being uttered by an independent person—with respect to their objects, namely the rites of sacrifice, meditation, and so forth, which result in fruits such as heaven and liberation and involve specific procedural details (*itikartavyatā*): their "natural" (*naisargika*) "intentionality" (*aidamparya*), meaning their capacity for communication, is "direct" (*sākṣāt*), that is, primary; yet it "culminates in the accomplishment of the syllables," meaning it ends merely in the apprehension of the phonemes.
The intention of the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāyavidhi*)—namely, "One's own portion of the Veda is to be studied"—comes to an end, resting merely upon the apprehension of the phonemes.

Those who describe it thus—those Prābhākaras of childish intellect, long-lived ones—who say that this intention of the injunction for study "contradicts" or "obstructs" [the injunction for ritual action], do so by means of the logic of the injunction for *japa* (recitation). This follows the method of determining the meaning of the Vedic sentences enjoining the recitation of the Veda, such as "One should study the Veda three times" and "One should constantly recite the Veda alone. (For although the natural tendency of an injunction for *japa* is toward the repetition of syllables, for one who knows the connection between words and their meanings, [the understanding arises] spontaneously...)

Just as the comprehension of meaning arising from one who recites is not obstructed by the injunction for *japa* (repetition), so too, even though the injunction for Vedic study (*adhyayana-vidhi*) rests solely on the acquisition of the syllables, it does not obstruct the comprehension of meaning that arises spontaneously; reflecting thus, let there be contentment—casting aside the distress that the Vedas would otherwise fall into meaninglessness—and let it be understood that a word in the form of an injunction manifests its authority only regarding an object that cannot be obtained through other means and which has not been previously established by another source of knowledge.
"He becomes one whose activity is unrestrained"—this is the meaning accepted by those learned in logic. (98)

He who, being intent on his own ends, explains the words of the Śruti according to the intention of the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāya-vidhi*), deserves to be met with the following dilemma: must these words be accepted as having a meaningful injunction,
or are they equivalent to those [other] utterances which are meaningless?
If it were to occur in the month of Māgha, what would Fate do so suddenly elsewhere as its rival? || 99 ||

That Prābhākara who is insistent on describing the injunction "one's own Veda is to be studied" as culminating in the knowledge of its meaning—following the intention that the injunction to study ceases its operation once the mere grasping of the syllables has been accomplished—he brings about the consequence that the words of the Śruti—the Vedic utterances—would be devoid of the intent to inform regarding their own meanings; that is, he renders them non-referential toward the objects they themselves signify. He is the one who draws this undesirable conclusion.

A certain proponent of the Mīmāṃsā school deserves to offer this alternative; having formulated the alternatives according to the method to be described, he should be made the subject of the question (*kimiti?*): Is this injunction—"One's own Veda is to be studied"—meaningful?

Or rather, should it be accepted that [the Veda] is meaningless? Or should it be admitted that it has its own meaning as its purport (*svārthatātparyaka*)? Or should it be accepted that it is devoid of having its own meaning as its purport? Regarding the first case—the position that accepts the Veda as being intent upon its own meaning—it would follow that all these words, that is, all the words of the Vedas, would be equal to this [Upanishadic statement]. Just as, even in the absence of another injunction (*vidhi*) enjoining the grasping of the meaning, the injunction for study (*adhyayanavidhi*) results in the grasping of the meaning by its very nature; so too [would it be for the Vedas].

In the same way, even though there is no injunction for grasping the meaning of the entire Veda, the fact that its meaning is grasped would be established by its very nature; thus, equality with the injunction for study (*adhyayanavidhi*) is established. Otherwise—in the position that the injunction for study is accepted as being purposeless—the injunction (the injunction for study) would, "without cause" (*akasmāt*), that is, without any regulating factor, become an opponent to the knowledge of meaning that arises from the power of one's own proficiency; would it do so? Certainly not.
(In both cases, since the cognition of the object is established, there is no obstacle. || 99 ||

Regarding the listener who is a householder, occupied with the sequence of his own duties—such as fetching wood, water, and so forth at the teacher’s house—and for whom no opportunity arises; if there should be an occasion suitable for attending upon the teacher and the like, where might that space be found? To this question, some experts here provide the following resolution: || 100 ||

For a householder who has formally entered the stage of a householder (*gṛhasthāśrama*), who is engaged in hearing the inquiry into the meaning of the Vedas, and who is occupied with fetching wood, water, and other necessities at the teacher’s house—precisely because he remains in the teacher’s family (*gurukula*) intent upon serving the teacher by bringing firewood, water, and other items for the teacher’s sake—for such a person, there is no opportunity for the uninterrupted performance of those respective duties prescribed for their own caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama-dharma*), which must be carried out in their proper sequence and with strict adherence to the order of priority.

It is possible that the *samaya* (the period of study) would not be established at all; however, if there were an attainment of *samaya* through the performance of one's own duties, it would be an opportunity consistent with following the teacher and so forth—a *samaya* conducive to service for the teacher. Where would such a thing exist, and upon what kind of time could it depend? Thus, by some—certain partial Mīmāṃsakas engaged in reflecting on the consistency of performing the meaning of the injunctions—it was stated regarding the operation of the injunction for Vedic study (*adhyayanavidhi*).

The critique of those who advocate for rest [in the intellect] has been stated by means of demonstrating that [the intellect] merely grasps syllables; here—in this matter which is fraught with difficulty—the skillful, the expert philosophers, provide a resolution in the manner that will be described. || 100 ||

When one has desisted from the accumulation of Vedic syllables due to the completion of the rules for private recitation (*svādhyāya*), and when there is leisure gained through the cessation of duties toward disciples rooted in that [study],
then the opportunity for the listener and the teacher is such that the goal of the listener may be accomplished accordingly.
Out of affection and a desire for the disciple's wealth and fame, the teacher should cause him to hear [the teaching]. || 101 ||

"By which cause"—namely, because the intention of the injunction for private recitation (*svādhyāya-vidhi*), expressed as "The Veda is to be studied," has its function exhausted merely by making known that [the study] is to be accomplished through the act of studying the collection of phonemes called the Veda; therefore, for the listener—even for a householder intent on hearing the inquiry into the meaning of the Veda—that which is rooted in it...

Since the cessation of the collection of rituals to be performed by a disciple—consisting of service to the teacher as prescribed in the scriptures, which results in the attainment of the Veda—occurs immediately after the acquisition of the Veda, the various rites known as obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) duties find their opportunity; that is, their proper time has arrived. Therefore, just as for the teacher who causes one to hear the meaning of the Veda, so too for the disciple engaged in hearing, the occasion is established—the opportunity is indeed obtained. Thus it is.

— Just as during the period of formal study through the service performed by the disciple, [so too] through affection—which consists of listening to and reflecting upon the teachings—and through the disciple’s devotion, as well as with the accompaniment of a desire for wealth and fame—that is, a longing for gain and reputation—the Guru—the learned preceptor—should indeed cause the disciple to hear; he must certainly awaken the disciple to the true essence of the Vedic meaning. This is not impossible. (Thus, everything is entirely correct. || 101 ||

By the grace of the venerable teacher Vātsya Varada, this commentary on the *Padārthadharmasaṃgraha* (The Compendium of the Properties of Categories), composed by him, has been compiled by the learned Śrī Rāmabhadrācārya. May Lord Hari be pleased in heart with him—who was born into the lineage of Ṛtunātha and is the son of Śrī Vāsarāghava—in this chapter titled "Means" (*Sādhana*).
Thus ends the third chapter in the glorious *Tattvasāra*.

—But has it not been stated previously that after reflecting on action, the Supreme Brahman is what must be sought to be known?

Thus, the statement here that action is a subsidiary part of knowledge (*vidyā*) is again rendered false by the repeated injunctions regarding its abandonment. Do not say so. Action itself, when endowed with its various qualities and employed in a manner distinct from other [injunctions], is the cause for the accomplishment of different forms of knowledge; moreover, some meritorious deed may indeed be designated as "cessation" (*nivṛtti*). || 1 ||

"Prior to"—that is, before the inquiry into Brahman—having reflected upon ritual action (*karman*), the Supreme Brahman, designated as the Lord of All, is to be brought within the scope of knowledge. Indeed, this was already stated in the very aphorism that promises the commencement of the scripture: "Then, therefore, the desire to know Brahman" (*athāto brahmajijñāsā*). For, according to the principle that "between the rejectable and the acceptable, one first reflects on the rejectable and thereafter on the acceptable," ritual action is first investigated and then abandoned.

"In many ways"—that is, in various manners—because it has been stated that actions are to be abandoned; because the scriptures describe their abandonability based on defects such as their transience, lack of firmness, and capacity to bind; and "again"—having once more introduced the very same action under discussion—in this *pāda*, the fourth section of the third chapter, the statement regarding [actions] being auxiliary to knowledge (*vidyāṅga*)—the method of establishing that actions are auxiliaries to knowledge—is "vain," meaning useless, since [the question of] being auxiliary or non-auxiliary is irrelevant to a subject matter that is to be abandoned.

[This is] because such a doubt cannot be entertained by those possessed of discernment. It is not so; such a suspicion is improper. For it is precisely action—as taught in the Karmakāṇḍa, such as sacrifice, giving, and oblation—which is determined to be something to be abandoned due to defects such as its binding nature, [and this applies even when performed with] those respective qualities...

By its nature—that is, by reason of its distinctness from the performance of ritual action (viniyoga) through the concomitance of qualities such as the absence of desire for fruits—it is "different" (*bhinnam*), meaning it exists as something entirely separate from the ritual action that is the object of the realization of what is to be abandoned. It is the cause for the accomplishment of knowledge (*vidyāniṣpattihetu*); that is, by means of removing obstacles to knowledge and increasing the quality of being (*sattva*), it becomes the instrumental cause for the attainment of knowledge.
Furthermore, having considered the essential nature of ritual action, [one understands] that which is to be investigated (*jijñāsya*)—namely, that which is called the desired inquiry.

Furthermore, there exists action consisting of service to the Lord, which is of the nature of pure merit (*sukṛta*) alone—free from even a trace of contact with good or evil deeds—and which, though entirely distinct from the ritual acts prescribed in the *Karmakāṇḍa*, is designated in the scriptures of the Lord and elsewhere as "the dharma of renunciation" (*nivṛtti-dharma*) because it is characterized solely by withdrawal [from worldly activity]. (The purpose of this section is the determination that such actions are auxiliary to knowledge. || 1 ||

Thus, renunciation is taught as being threefold: in some cases, it is the abandonment of actions performed for the sake of desire by one who knows the Supreme; in other cases, it is the non-performance of prohibited actions by one whose intellect is dependent solely on the Self; and in yet other cases, it is the abandonment of even those actions intended for one's own welfare that are free from ulterior motives. In this context, however, non-violence and the like—which do not cause harm and are common to all—are [to be practiced by everyone].
They [the mantras] also serve as auxiliary limbs for the meditative worship (upāsti) of those who possess the specific determinations of caste (varṇa), stage of life (āśrama), and so forth. || 2 ||

In a particular section of the *Bhagavadgītā*, the renunciation of actions performed for desire—that is, the abandonment by nature of those rites prescribed in the Vedas and other scriptures that are undertaken with a view toward results other than the attainment of the Lord—is taught; in another specific place, the abandonment by nature of unworthy actions—prohibited deeds—is taught; and in yet another specific location, the abandonment of the notion of the individual soul's independence regarding actions is taught.

The abandonment of the notion of being one's own independent agent (*svakartṛtā-buddhi*), as well as the abandonment of the notion of self-interest unconditioned by others (*anupadhika-svārtha-buddhi*)—namely, the abandonment of the notion that actions are for the sake of one's own excellence, setting aside their status as subservient to the Supreme Self—is proclaimed by the Lord as necessary. However, in this third and fourth quarter [of the verse], there is the mention of those acts which result in the destruction of sin, which are common to all, and which are to be practiced without distinction by all castes (*varṇas*) and stages of life (*āśramas*).

The venerable Bādarāyaṇa, having deliberated, determines that non-violence and the other virtues—namely, the religious duties (*dharma*) such as the avoidance of injury, the refraining from theft, and the speaking of truth—as well as the specific ritual acts prescribed with reference to the particularities of caste (*varṇa*) and stage of life (*āśrama*), possess the status of being auxiliary members (*aṅga*) to meditative knowledge (*upāsanā*), meaning they serve as factors that assist the science consisting of meditation. || 2 ||

"The self that is the agent of actions is not Brahman, which is superior to that; therefore, in sacrifices and the like, the Upaniṣads are useful only through the notion of that [self]"—this is the meaning in the statement of the Mīmāṃsakas. [In contrast,] one whose other marks have been cast aside declares the subordinate status of ritual acts within the injunction for worship consisting of meditation upon Brahman as distinct from the individual soul, because such acts pacify impurities and increase one's own inherent nature. || 3 ||

The agent of actions—that Self which is recognized as the performer of Vedic or Smṛti rites such as the Agnihotra and so forth, the embodied being known as the individual soul (jīva)—is not something distinct from, or superior to, that [soul]; nor is there any reality denoted by the term "Brahman" that exists here in the Vedāntas as an object of knowledge. Therefore:

Precisely because there is no distinct conscious entity called Brahman apart from the individual soul (jīva), the Upanishads—the portion of the Vedas consisting of the final three books—would have their purpose fulfilled, meaning they would achieve their intended aim, solely through the understanding of that [sacrifice] in rituals such as the *makha*—that is, solely with the intent of generating a discernment of the true nature of the individual soul acting as the agent. Thus, when the discourse of the Mīmāṃsakas—who rest content with only a portion, a single part, of the totality of principles reached by investigation and determination—proceeds in this manner, it is said to be an "Ardha-mīmāṃsaka" statement.

"Having rejected other marks"—having refuted the marks (liṅgas) propounded by the half-Mīmāṃsakas because they indicate meanings contrary to his own intended view; "by means of the pacification of impurity"—preceded by the pacification of those portions consisting of passion (rājasa) and darkness (tāmasa), which have reached an excessive state and attained a state of turbidity within the quality of goodness (sattva) that is conducive to knowledge; [and] of actions that increase goodness—actions that bring about an abundance of goodness, namely those actions consisting of the Śrauta and Smārta rites, in the forms of obligatory (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and so forth.

In the section concerning the individual souls (*jīva*), the venerable Bādarāyaṇa declares and defines the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅgabhāva*)—that is, the quality of being a subordinate factor that bestows excellence—to the Supreme Self, denoted by the term *Brahman*, which is distinct from the individual conscious selves (*pratyagātman*), in the context of meditation (*upāsana*) consisting of uninterrupted contemplation, which is a mental action (*mānasa-karma*). [Commentary: Even though the Supreme Brahman has been firmly established as the object of knowledge here through these eleven chapters (*pādas*), why should this Brahma-vidyā be further disturbed by insignificant marks (*liṅgas*) that resemble "writing on the sky"?

It is true that he destroys the position declared in the heart of Jaimini—having cast it aside—for the sake of the welfare of the multitude of young students who are terrified by such petty disputes of learning and intellect. || 4 ||

In this regard—in the Śārīraka-mīmāṃsā-śāstra which has set out precisely for the purpose of investigating Brahman—it has been firmly established by these eleven chapters from beginning to end that the Supreme Brahman—the reality known as Brahman which transcends all—is the object to be known, and it must necessarily be investigated and realized through hearing and other means by those seeking liberation. (This being so,) furthermore, in this [twelfth] chapter, [the author discusses] the ether...

"By means of insignificant marks"—that is, by small indicators (the reasons adduced by the opponent's position) which are like mere lines of letters inscribed in the sky, and for that reason ineffective—to what purpose (*kim*) is the *Vidyā*—the knowledge consisting of the inquiry into Vedānta (which is called *vidyā* because it is the cause of [liberation] firmly established in the hearts of those seeking liberation)—disturbed, moved, or made to tremble by being set aside? (Thus he questions. True—it is the superiority of Brahman [that is at stake].

That which is stated—that [the Self] exists—is indeed beyond doubt; however, for the sake of the welfare of that group of immature disciples who, due to the power of the misconceptions of those of limited knowledge whose natures are characterized by such [ignorance], have fallen into apprehension, Bādarāyaṇa—having been prompted by a desire for their benefit—sets aside and refutes the position established by Jaimini:

namely, the view expressed by the sage Jaimini in the *Pūrvamīmāṃsā* with a different underlying intent, which maintains the non-existence of a Brahman distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*). He does so by raising this point in this section (*pāda*) and then demolishing it. || 4 ||

The statement "only while acting" (*kurvann eva*) is a description of the constant conduct of one who knows the Supreme; the injunction "let him endure" (*sahaset*) does not, through either the intellect or action, establish a rule of either subordination (*aṅgatā*) or primacy (*aṅgitā*). The sentence reiterating the performance of actions preceded by knowledge is connected with another purpose;
for it does not restate the knowledge of Brahman, nor is the Udgītha-knowledge a subordinate part of ritual action. || 5 ||

The statement "kurvann eva" refers to the passage from the *Īśāvāsya Upaniṣad* in the form: "Performing actions here alone, one should desire to live a hundred years. This is a declaration of regulated conduct for the "knower of the Supreme"—that is, for the knower of the supreme reality (the knower of Brahman)—as established by the Śruti and other authorities.

The statement that teaches the rule regarding the form of the inclination toward the practice of wisdom (*prajñā*)—even the mention of simultaneous undertaking through both knowledge and action (*dhī-kriyābhyām anvārambhaḥ*), which is an expression of their mutual connection (in one wise person, for the sake of bestowing their respective fruits later on)—is intended merely to express their coexistence (*sahatve*) as grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); it does not determine a relationship of either being an auxiliary (*aṅgatā*) or the principal (*aṅgitā*). It certainly does not intend to specifically teach that knowledge is an auxiliary to action, or that action is an auxiliary to knowledge.

The statement—found in the Gārgī-brāhmaṇa, beginning with "O Gārgī, he who, having known this Imperishable..."—which speaks of the performance—the execution—of prescribed rites as being preceded by knowledge (*vidyā*), establishes that such performance occurs only subsequent to the realization of the true nature of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*). This statement was not made for any other purpose; rather, it indicates the deficiency in the completion of ritual action when devoid of knowledge, according to the principle: "The action of the ignorant is destroyed."

It is engaged solely for the purpose of establishing [the independence of knowledge]; it is not for the purpose of establishing that knowledge is subordinate (*aṅga*) to ritual action. For this reason—the passage beginning with "O Gārgī, he who knows this Imperishable... or does not know it"—does not merely restate (*anuvadati*) the knowledge of Brahman—which consists of the meditation on the Supreme Self for the sake of liberation—nor does it provide such a restatement to indicate that knowledge is a subordinate part of ritual action.

And the Udgītha-vidyā—the meditation on the Udgītha enjoined in the passage, "One should meditate on this syllable 'Om' as the Udgītha"—is also not a subsidiary part of ritual action; that is, it does not possess the status of being an auxiliary to a rite, because its purpose is to bring about a specific result in the form of increased vigor (vīryavattara). || 5 ||

For study is prescribed for the sake of attaining the recitation of the Veda (svādhyāya), just like the ritual of fire-installation (ādhāna); it is not a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of the subsequent knowledge (*vidyā*), nor does the comprehension of its meaning constitute that [study], since the latter is superior in its essential nature and its fruits. Knowledge of the eternal Self alone is invariably required in the sacrifices, not any other knowledge.
How could there be a renunciation of desire-objects (*kāmyatyāga*) here along with knowledge, if that [renunciation] were also a subsidiary part of these [sacrifices]? (6)

Study (*adhyayana*)—the action denoted by the term "study"—is indeed for the sake of attaining one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*); that is, for the purpose of bringing under one's own control a specific recensional branch (*śākhā*) inherited through one's own family lineage. Thus it is stated: "One's own Veda is to be studied."

By this scriptural statement, [the knowledge of meaning] is enjoined as an independent act, not as a subsidiary part (*uttarāṅga*)—meaning it is not enjoined as a subordinate element for the performance of subsequent rites, like the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*). Just as by the sentence "one establishes the fires" (*agnīn ādadhīta*), the rite called *ādhāna* is enjoined solely with the attainment of the fires as its purpose; it is not enjoined for the sake of performing rites such as the *agnihotra* that follow thereafter (because it is more appropriate for that which is proximate to be the direct fruit), so too is the comprehension of meaning.

—Let there be an understanding whose object is the meaning of the Vedānta texts, and let it also be an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to knowledge (*vidyā*), since it serves as an aid to the Brahma-knowledge consisting of meditation (*upāsanā*); indeed, let it be an auxiliary for this reason: because that Brahma-knowledge in the form of meditation, by its very nature—through the practice of meditation performed from the beginning every day—is characterized by the attainment of excellence, the state of being a most vivid direct perception, unsurpassed dearness, and the capacity to lead to the realization of Brahman.

By its own inherent qualities and fruits—namely, the attainment of Brahman preceded by the complete cessation of beginningless ignorance, followed by a continuous succession of infinite experiences of Brahman—and by those objects which constitute its own purpose; it is "superior" (adhika), meaning it excels in every respect compared to the knowledge produced by hearing the meaning of sentences [pertaining to rituals]; and it is "required" (apekṣita) as something to be employed with necessity (niyamataḥ) in "sacrifices" (kratuṣu)—that is, in those actions prescribed by the Śruti for the sake of goals pertaining to this world or the next.

That which is to be accomplished is simply the constant knowledge of the Self—the knowledge of the existence of the eternal conscious being who does not undergo destruction like the body and who experiences the fruits of actions; it is not any other form of knowledge. Knowledge in the form of meditation upon the Supreme Self, who is superior even to the individual soul (*jīvātman*) and is the controller of all, need not be required for the sake of performing ritual acts (*karmānuṣṭhāna*). (Therefore, in every respect, the knowledge of Brahman is not a subsidiary part of ritual action. That [knowledge] also—of the Brahman who is superior to the individual soul—...

If it is accepted by the scriptures that even *vidyā* (knowledge)—if it is an auxiliary (*aṅga*), meaning a supportive factor—for all these very rituals mentioned in the *karmakāṇḍa*, then for a person endowed with *brahmavidyā* (the knowledge of Brahman) which has been established as an auxiliary to all rituals—whether obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), or optional (*kāmya*)—how and by what means can there be the "abandonment of optional [rites]" (*kāmyatyāga*) here, among these rituals that have knowledge as their auxiliary, in the form of the avoidance of those very actions performed for the sake of results?

Or how could it be logical according to the view of the treatise? (For otherwise, since there would be the undesirable consequence of the total absence of anyone who performs optional rites [kāmyānuṣṭhātṛ], the injunction for such rites itself would fall into futility. || 6 ||

Knowledge is not a constituent part of sacrifices and the like, for we do not prescribe it only for those authorized to perform them; nor can it be said that knowledge belongs to each respective rite, because there are many teachings to the contrary.
Furthermore, the rule regarding the perpetual celibate (ūrdhvaretas) is both recited by the Jābālas and restated by others. Therefore—
It is to be grasped through attainment, or otherwise by itself; here, however, the rule concerns one who is still possessed of passion, while its negation applies to one free from passion.

Knowledge—consisting of the meditation on Brahman as taught in the Vedānta—is not an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to sacrifices and other rituals; that is, it is not accepted by the Śruti as being subordinate to them. For we do not find that knowledge of Brahman enjoined for those very persons entitled to perform sacrifices and other rites—namely, householders and others who possess such entitlement (since it is intended only for such individuals)—in the Śruti. Rather, [we find it] even for those like wandering mendicants (*pārivrājaka*) who are not entitled to ritual action. Therefore, knowledge is not an auxiliary to ritual action.

It would follow that this knowledge of Brahman (*sā brahmavidyā*) would be merely an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to those various ritual acts prescribed for the respective stages of life (*āśrama*); however, even such an assumption is not appropriate. Why? Because of the teaching of manifold contradictions—that is, because in the Śrutis, contrary to the subordination of knowledge to action, it is taught that knowledge is actually the principal (*aṅgin*), while action is subordinate; and furthermore, because there are Vedic injunctions regarding those of perpetual chastity (*ūrdhvaretas*)—that is, scriptural texts enjoining the wandering mendicant stage (*pārivrājya*) and others, such as the Jābālas.

It is observed that this is recited by those studying the specific branch known as the Jābāla, in the form: "On the very day one becomes dispassionate, on that very day one should renounce," and so forth; and it is also restated by students of other branches (the Chandogas)—an echo is seen made in passages such as "There are three branches of duty. Therefore, based on this indicative mark (*jñāpaka*), the attainment [of renunciation] must be accepted; for, taking the necessity of explaining the restatement (*anuvāda*) as the cause, some prescriptive statement (*vidhivākya*) must also exist.

The consensus of the learned must be accepted; otherwise—that is, even if one does not assume another injunctive statement—here, in this very context, the statement itself, "There are three branches of dharma" (*trayo dharmaskandhāḥ*), and so forth, ought to be the injunction (*vidhi*). Its prohibition, however, results in the negation of the stage of wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājyāśrama*) through the censure of those who abandon the sacred fire, such as in the passage, "He indeed is a slayer of heroes among the gods" (*vīrahā vā eṣa devānām*). This [prohibition] should be understood as resting upon an agent who still possesses passion—that is, one who is not yet dispassionate. || 7 ||
