A Compendium of the Collection of Aphorisms on the Body.

Since it is observed that the connection with the *udgītha* and other parts of the ritual action serves merely as a praise for the essence (*rasa*) and so forth, no injunction should be inferred here on account of proximity, the excellence of what is already enjoined, or because [the praise] is not something previously unestablished. || 55 ||

Because—for that reason—the connection of the meditation on the *udgītha* and so forth, which constitute parts of the ritual action (*karmāṅga*), is seen to be merely that; it is known from the scriptural passage, "This *udgītha* is the essence of essences, the highest, the supreme, the eighth," that for that reason, the status of such statements as those proclaiming the quality of being the "essence of essences" in the *udgītha* and so forth is that of praise (*stuti*)—that is, they have as their sole purpose the demonstration of excellence by way of restating what is already established.

[The opponent] objects: "This is not right, because [the Udgītha and so forth] are not proximate to the context of the injunctions regarding the Udgītha and other [limbs]. Rather, because they are proximate, and because excellence (*utkarṣa*)—consisting in being more powerful (*vīryavattara*)—which pertains to the sacrifice enjoined by the ritual injunctions, serves as the efficient cause (*nimitta*) for the propriety of this [meditation] being enjoined, and because it has not been previously established; and for the reason that qualities such as being the 'most flavorful' (*rasatama*) are not established through any other means of knowledge regarding the Udgītha and so forth—in this sentence, 'He is the most flavorful of flavors,' there is an injunction."

—the injunction for the meditative visualization (*dṛṣṭi*) of the *udgītha* and so forth as "the most flavorful" and so on—would have to be postulated; that is, it would necessarily be something to be imagined. || 55 ||
The Adhikaraṇasārāvalī.

Let not the reasoning that [the *gaṇa*] is a praise (*stuti*)—based on the principle of the *juhū* and other [instruments]—be applied here; for it is joined with an unprecedented injunction (*apūrva-nirdeśa*) that is devoid of the context of those respective injunctions.
Here, various injunctions based on those respective [perceptions] are observed in close proximity.
Therefore, an injunction, when being postulated, is appropriate only for that which has no other purpose and which possesses a result. (8)

Just as the statement, "This [earth] is indeed the *juhū* ladle; the heavenly world is the *āhavanīya* fire,"—which, by means of establishing the nature of earth in the *juhū* and the nature of heaven in the *āhavanīya*, is intended for the praise of the *juhū* and the *āhavanīya* according to the principle of the *juhv-ādi-utkṛti* (the figurative treatment beginning with the *juhū*)—so too is the declaration of being "the most flavorful" (*rasatama*), and so forth.

—“The statement ‘This is the essence of essences’ regarding the *udgītha* as being the most essential (*rasatama*) may indeed be a praise of a subsidiary element; let it attain the status of a sentence intended for the glorification of the *udgītha*, which is a constituent part of the sacrifice—but let it not possess the character of an injunction” (thus one might object). This is not correct—it should not be suspected in this manner—because, in the absence of proximity to a context consisting of injunctions for the *udgītha* and so forth, there exists the reason that establishes its injunctive nature: namely, the fact that it states a matter not already known through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), which is joined with various [injunctions].

(The sense is that being situated within the context of a specific injunction and being a restatement of an already established fact are indicators of the status of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*); whereas proximity to an injunction and the statement of an unestablished fact are indicators of the status of an injunction. Here—in this context and in its vicinity—that is, even in the proximity of the passage establishing the quality of being the "most flavorful" (*rasatamatva*) with respect to the *udgītha*.

"Vividhaṃ" means manifold; "tattaddṛṣṭividhānaṃ" refers even to the instruction of specific meditative visions (*dṛṣṭi*) upon the *udgītha* for the sake of specific fruits. This has been clearly observed—that it is indeed manifest—and the sense is that the proximity of an injunction for meditation (*dṛṣṭividhi*) is itself a determinant of its status as an injunction for meditation. By this aforementioned collection of indicators, [it is established] that which is taught as having no other purpose (*ananyārthaśiṣṭe*), being established by scripture (*śruti*) as not serving any other function, and being fruitful (*phalavati*), producing results such as the state of being more powerful than the sacrifice (*kratuvīryavattaratva*).

Regarding the specific ritual action known as the meditation on the *udgītha*, the postulation of an injunction—that is, the very assumption of its injunctive nature—is appropriate; it is consistent with reason. It is not, however, appropriate to assume it has the status of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) by treating it as being solely for the purpose of praising [the act]. Therefore, the principle of the ladle (*juhū*) and so forth—which concerns things enjoined for another purpose and devoid of their own fruit—should not be accepted here. || 8 ||
Furthermore, because there is no attainment [of the result], there can be neither a restatement of that nor a figurative praise through superimposition;
this is the course followed when no other way is possible within a single syntactical unit with an injunction, for here there is no attachment to such a course.
If a displacement [of the mantra] is postulated, it must be done by force in a case where no other recourse exists.
This statement would be appropriate in the midst of the rules for knowledge; therefore, it must be for the purpose of [conveying] knowledge.

Furthermore—and moreover, since no other [independent] attainment exists when the investigation of reasoning has been conducted (meaning that the very point already stated is the conclusion)—because the meaning expressed by "This is the essence of essences" is not apprehended through any other sentence apart from this one, its restatement—that is, the description of being the "most essential essence" and so forth—is not a mere restatement of what has already been enjoined; and for this very reason, it is neither a figurative praise (*adhiropyastuti*), for this [text] does not proceed to describe the excellence of some portion to be meditated upon by means of superimposition upon an object that is not such.

This statement is of the nature of describing a superimposed praise; it is a "way of finding a way" (*agater gatiḥ*)—a method of interpretation to be considered for that which lacks any other way out. It is appropriate only in a sentence that forms a single syntactical unit with an injunctive sentence—that is, it possesses consistency only when it has attained the status of being part of the same sentence as an injunction, and not when it is devoid of such connection. Such a method is not appropriate here—in sentences such as "He is the best of flavors" (*sa eṣa rasānām*)—because of the absence of proximity to an injunctive sentence (*āsaktihāneḥ*).

(Since it is impossible to state that there is syntactic unity with an injunctive sentence: The idea that an injunction, which exists by its own nature in one place, is made into a single sentence with another through the superimposition of proximity—provided this is postulated—is not a sound thought, even if one were to say that [something] is superimposed (though it does not actually exist). For such a postulation of displacement (*utkarṣa*) must be accepted by force—that is, by constraint—and it is appropriate only in a case where there is no other way out, i.e., in a situation devoid of any other means of resolution.

It does not exist, however, in the present context which is fit for a conclusion by way of prescribing a philosophical view (*dṛṣṭividhi*); that is, among the injunctions for knowledge—that is, among the many passages enjoining meditation—this statement, namely the sentence "He is the essence of essences," exists; for this reason, this passage under discussion must indeed have the purpose of enjoining knowledge (*vidyāvidhāna*). || 9 ||

It is improper to say that even if [the meditation] has knowledge as its purpose, this praise is justified because it mentions what is non-existent; for if there were a transgression regarding the intended object of the vision, then the meditation would become a mere mental projection—this is the talk of a child. Furthermore, in the case of this obligatory [meditation], the Veda would result in being a non-authority if one adopts the position that it is to be set aside by reasoning;
rather, when the "how" (itthambhāva) is to be known, the word here is fruitful only for the sake of an injunction of vision.

Even if it has the purpose of knowledge—that is, even if its purport lies in an injunction for meditation—this statement of being the "most flavorful" (*rasatama*), in the form "He is the most flavorful of flavors," must be understood as praise—a description of excellence—on account of the mention of what is non-existent: namely, because of the attribution of the quality of being the most flavorful, which is impossible in the object under consideration, viz., the *udgītha*. (For praise consists precisely in the superimposition of qualities belonging to one thing onto another subject that does not possess them. Thus, this objection is improper; such a doubt is not logical. (Why?)

Regarding the mention of "view" (*dṛṣṭi*): in other cases where the injunction is directed toward another view—namely, in contexts involving the application of mantras and so forth for subduing [poisons] and the like, such as the statement "one should meditate on oneself as Garuḍa"—there is a deviation (*aticāra*). This is because the rule of pervasion (*vyāpti*)—"where there is the description of a non-existent object, there is the nature of praise (*stuti*)"—is broken due to the lack of necessity; for that [description] is not invariably pervaded by the nature of praise. Furthermore, even in the absence of certainty regarding the pervasion, there may still be a mental engagement (*viśayana*), or else there may be a doubt regarding the nature of praise produced by a doubt concerning the pervader (*vyāpakatva-saṃśaya*).

To say "it ought to exist" would be the speech of a child; such a statement would indeed be mere childish talk, for it would not be the utterance of one proficient in worldly convention. For, while this doubt persists—meaning while it continues at all times—the Veda (*nigama*) would result in being non-authoritative (*apramāṇa*), because it fails to produce certainty (since authoritativeness consists precisely in being the generator of valid knowledge). However, in the view that [the Veda] is set aside by reasoning, [this fault does not apply] to the doubt.

If, however, one accepts that [the statement] is to be set aside because it is connected with a specific vision and so forth, rather than being universally applicable, then—in this context (*itthambhāve*), namely in the reasoning that supports the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); when there is a desire to speak (*vivakṣā*) regarding what is to be known (*bubhutsye*) as something to be understood; here—that is, contained within this section—the "fruitful speech," namely the sentence "That which by knowledge alone" (*yadeva vidyayā*), which is joined with the proclamation of the fruit consisting in being more powerful; serves solely for the purpose of an injunction of vision (*dṛṣṭividhi*) regarding the *rasatama* passage in the *udgītha*.

This [passage] is precisely a determinant of an injunction for meditation in the form of viewing [the Self] as the "most flavorful" (rasatama), and it does not admit of being reduced to mere praise. 10.

Even though the two statements concerning the stages of life (āśrama) lack the status of being explanatory passages (arthavāda) regarding the state of being established in Brahman, a doubt arises that they might be explanatory passages concerning the udgītha, as is understood through the principle of praise (stuti). || 158 ||
Thus concludes the section concerning mere praise (stutimātrādhikaraṇa). || 2 ||

In the Upaniṣads, which proceed with various specific branches of knowledge, these various distinct narratives—such as those connected with Pratardana, Śvetaketu, and others—are all seen to be particular stories intended to magnify the greatness of the injunctions.

(An objection is raised: "Since they have been brought forward by the force of such injunctions as 'they recite the narratives (*ākhyāna*) during the *pāriplava*,' let them serve the purpose of the *pāriplava*—that is, let them be suitable for application in the *pāriplava-śastra* of the Aśvamedha sacrifice. (To this we reply: This cannot be so; not all specific narratives would be fit for application in the *pāriplava*, because there are narratives read within the context (*prakaraṇa*)—those recounted from the beginning of the instructional sections—which are devoted to the teaching of various forms of knowledge (*vidyā*).

Because a syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) is observed with the Vedic sentences—since in the narrative sections (*ākhyāna*) one sees a syntactic unity consisting in the fact that they convey a meaning connected to the purpose of those [Vedic] passages—it is stated therein, when the ritual procedure known as *pāriplava* is being enjoined: specifically indicated, "the mere narration of Manu and others"—that is, the narration of the specific persons to be narrated such as Manu and so forth—serves the purpose of the *pāriplava*; it is to be employed in the ritual act named *pāriplava*.

By that—namely, by the specific narratives of Manu and others mentioned specifically—the requirement [of the injunction] is satisfied; that is, when the expectancy (ākāṅkṣā) residing in the injunction for the recitation of narratives (ākhyāna-śaṃsana-vidhi)—the expectancy occupied with fulfilling its own purpose—is pacified, it is not possible to assume an extension (klpti) beyond that—that is, to assume the application of all other narratives concerning different subjects as being for the purpose of the *pāriplava* recitation. This would not be consistent. || 11 ||

"Knowledge does not exist"—this is the doubt that Brahman-knowledge is not possible at all. But this is not correct, because of the mention of the pride of belonging to various stages of life (*āśrama*). For it is stated in the Śruti, Smṛti, and other texts that even for those who have abandoned sacrificial rites and the like, and who are fit to perform the specific practices appropriate to their respective stages of life—such as the recitation of the *praṇava*, the avoidance of attachment, and so forth—there is the attainment of knowledge; and for the members of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*) engaged in any of the four stages of life, there is the union with knowledge, which is liberation.

There is a connection [of the injunction] by virtue of being a practitioner of the Brahmavidyā that has become a means of attainment (*pāyabhūta*); the injunction as well—the instruction regarding the knowledge and the manner of its practice—is equal. Indeed, it is heard without distinction from the perspective of householders and others, like the section on the sacred fires (*agnyadhikāra*), and it is known from the Vedic texts and understood from the Smṛtis. This being the case, wherever in certain Smṛtis or Purāṇas there is the mention of the "liberation stage" (*mokṣāśrama*)—that is, the designation of the renunciate stage (*saṃnyāsāśrama*) as the liberation stage—it is generally...

By means of the abundance of cities—that is, due to the excellence of the sacrificial altars for the acquisition of knowledge—it has been declared, or spoken, by the sages—the seers who are engaged in revealing the true nature of Dharma. || 12 ||

That supreme knowledge of Brahman, understood through the Śruti as the means to liberation (*apavarga*), is common to both those in the stage of renunciation (*pravrajita*)—that is, those in the order of *saṃnyāsa*—and householders (*gṛhamedhin*). Even though it lacks certain ritual limbs (*tadaṅga-hīnā*) because those ritual acts that serve as limbs of knowledge are not common [to both], its essential nature remains undifferentiated; for the status of being the knowledge that is the means to liberation is not attained merely by the distinction between the practitioners known as renunciants and householders. [Thus,] among renunciants, it attains its true form precisely in its state of lacking those limbs.

(Regarding the objection: "Furthermore, among householders, the very nature [of knowledge] is established only when accompanied by its auxiliary parts (*sāṅgā*); thus, the postulation of a distinction [between the stages of life] is untenable. (Thus he objects. (Response: This is not at all a fit objection. Why? Because of the existence of scriptural statements concerning sacrifices and so forth—namely, the presence of texts that indicate the auxiliaries of knowledge, such as: "By sacrifice, by gift, by austerity, and by fasting" (*yajñena dānena tapasā’nāśakena*). Relying on the authority (or the intended meaning) of such passages, and because one possesses the duties of one's own stage of life (*svāśrama-dharma*) in every case—that is, in all stages of life—it is established that only those duties appropriate to their respective stages constitute the auxiliaries of knowledge (since knowledge can never be produced in its essential form if devoid of its auxiliaries anywhere).
It is not so;

for they desire to produce knowledge within themselves by means of sacrifices and other such rites which serve as the instruments for accomplishing knowledge, since [knowledge] is already established [as independent]. || 13 ||

[Objection: But surely, in cases such as "he desires to go" (*jigamiṣati*) or "the word falls," there is an absence of actual motion; therefore, since the literal meaning of the word is stated [by the root], it is incorrect here to say "it is not so," because the absence of motion is equally present in both cases.

Desire would arise from a particular state of intelligence; if that [desire] does not arise, it cannot be produced by actions. Furthermore, for one who desires to attain the inquiry (*jijñāsā*), that desired knowledge does not fail to exist beforehand. (14)

Regarding the specific usages such as "he wishes to go on foot" (*padā jigamiṣati*), "he wishes to go by horse" (*aśvena jigamiṣati*), and "he wishes to strike with a sword" (*asinā jighāṃsati*): there is a loss of the sense of desire [in the case of the words *padā*, *aśvena*, and *asinā*]. This is because the meanings conveyed by the third-case endings (*tṛtīyānta*)—namely, the foot, the horse, and the sword—are [merely the instruments of] the desire to go and the desire to strike.

In the sense of the suffix *-san* (desire) having *ātman* as its object, there is an abandonment of its connection as an instrument (*karaṇa*), because there is no other way [to construe it]. Now, one might argue that when a contradiction in the form of unfitness is perceived regarding a meaning consistent with the usage [of the word], an obstacle to another means is indeed created; however, this cannot be done in the case of the means consisting of rituals such as sacrifice, which is understood from Upaniṣadic statements like "They desire to know by means of sacrifice" (*yajñena vividiṣanti*) as spoken by the Śruti—namely, the abandonment of the sense of "desiring to know. It is not possible to do so.

[The claim that] "because we must not engage in an investigation of contradiction or non-contradiction regarding the fact that wealth (*artha*) is *śrī*, [this objection is invalid]"—is incorrect; for such a suspicion is improper, since—for this reason—even here, in the present scriptural statement, there is no other way [to resolve the difficulty]: namely, that ritual action such as sacrifice leads to the accomplishment of the desire for knowledge (*jñāna*).

The absence of other means, which consists in the application of effort (*dakṣatva-yoga-rūpa*), is equal—that is, entirely non-distinct. Desire (*icchā*)—the longing directed toward an object of knowledge—may arise from a particular state of intellect (*dhī-viśeṣāt*), namely from the cognition that the desired object possesses the quality of being most pleasurable (or from the cognition of its beauty), according to the maxim: "one knows, then desires, then exerts effort. In the event of its non-arising—that is, when the cognition of the object's beauty does not occur—that longing directed toward the object of perception cannot be accomplished through ritual acts such as sacrifices. It is not capable of arising [thereby].

For a person desiring to attain the inquiry—that is, for one longing for the desire to know—that knowledge, which is the realization to be made the object of the "desire to know" (vividiṣā) accomplished by ritual action, was certainly not unloved, nor can it be said that it was not desired even prior to the performance of sacrifices and other rites for the sake of that desire to know; for it must have been indeed desired, otherwise the practice of performing those rituals for its sake would be illogical. ||14||
Surely, in this context, this prescribed action should be applied toward the pursuit of desire; what then?

It would not prevent the production of a specific cognition for the sake of desire. Furthermore, various other injunctions for action aimed at knowledge cannot be dismissed on the grounds of the principle of "contemplation" (nidhyāna); therefore, through association, it reiterates that the desired end is the object of the injunction. || 15 ||

Now, O friend! Here—in the scriptural passage beginning with "They desire to know [Brahman] through sacrifice" and so forth—this action, consisting of the performance of sacrifices and the like, is enjoined as being to be employed—that is, taught—as the cause for the continuity of the desire, namely, the uninterrupted flow of the desire to know Brahman; it must therefore be understood in that way (and not as a mere ordinary desire, which would lead to fallacies such as circular reasoning because it would already be established).

[In response to] this reflection: "What then? What benefit [accrues] from that? [The answer is: none at all. [For if it were so], the fact that action is not co-existent with knowledge—a point established by the Siddhānta—would be undermined in the case of the continuity of action for the sake of the continuity of desire. As for what was stated regarding the production of a specific state of intellect for the sake of desire—that is, the necessity of the initial arising of a specific knowledge for the sake of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*)—that would not be precluded merely by the admission that [the purpose] is the continuity of desire. It certainly would not.

[If it is argued that] it would be provided for—since desire cannot arise at all without knowledge—even another injunction for action for the sake of knowledge, as well as various other scriptural statements enjoining action directed toward knowledge as a means to liberation, consisting of diverse types such as those of Śruti and Smṛti, are observed by you.

The application of the suffix *san* in the word ‘vividiṣanti’—which consists of the suffix *san* expressing desire—is not capable of being denied as a mere negation; for, according to the logic of ‘nididhyāsitavyaḥ’, this word, like that compound term, restates what is already known for the sake of clarity and emphasis, namely, the desirability of the enjoined act—that is, it expresses that the enjoined knowledge (*vedana*) is the object of a desire. || 15 ||

It does not exist [in them], because it is contradicted by perception; therefore, for the reason stated—that is, because of the reason that they are authorized for ritual action—since we observe that those householders who possess knowledge have obtained the authority for actions known as the operations of the external and internal organs, which are devoid of the nature of cessation, their knowledge of Brahman, which is the means to liberation, cannot possibly be assisted by inner means such as tranquility (*śama*) and the like. (Thus he objects. This is not so, and this objection is not tenable, because even tranquility and the rest are constituent parts (*aṅga*) of that [knowledge], as established by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Because there exists the quality of being an aid to knowledge, both of those two—namely, the activity of the external organs and its cessation, which consist respectively of ritual action (*karman*) and tranquility (*śama*) and so forth—have distinct bases; for there is no mutual contradiction between them, as they take the form of engagement in what is prescribed and withdrawal from what is prohibited. || 59 ||

Those who have committed offenses through ignorance—(in the world, indeed, men devoted to royal service, having committed offenses either knowingly or unknowingly, become objects of the king's wrath)—recognizing their own transgression (that which was unintended by themselves and displeasing to the king) at a particular time, and when remorse has arisen, [they approach] the Lord—their own master, the king—with means that are suitable for themselves to employ, well-known in the world, and understood elsewhere in the world.

By means of activities appropriate for pleasing a master—such as begging for forgiveness, exerting personal effort, offering desired gifts, and so forth—they honor and worship him, making his inner heart gracious. Gradually pacifying their anger, they eventually find themselves with the master's wrath averted; they obtain service—that very activity which, performed previously, had pleased the master's mind and was approved by him, now consisting of the state of being a servant in his presence.

Indeed, they attain [the goal] once again in this very manner—by means of their respective offices (*svādhikāra*), which are established by the scriptures, understood through the scriptures, and distinguished as "this" and "not this"—namely, "this action is to be performed, this is not to be performed"—thereby possessing distinct forms and natures (*viviktasvarūpasvabhāva*) as individually specified; and by means of activities (*vyāpāra*) corresponding to their own caste, stage of life, time, place, and so forth, which serve as the pretext for obtaining the unconditioned and limitless grace of the Lord.

The grace—the favor—of Śrīdhara, the Lord of Lakṣmī, who is a friend without conditions—an unfeigned companion—is to be attained—that is, accomplished—for us, free from obstacles, being far removed from the fear of apprehension. || 17 ||
The Section on the Permission for All Food (Sarvānnānumati-adhikaraṇa) || 3.4.7 ||
A Compendium of the Collection of Logical Principles Concerning the Body (Śārīraka).

"The eating of all kinds of food would indeed always apply to those who know the Prāṇa because of the abandonment of specific restrictions; however, this is not tenable, for we observe that even for a knower of Brahman who possesses special powers, such eating occurs only when life is at stake. (60)

"For those who know the vital breaths" (*prāṇavidām*)—meaning for those established in the knowledge of the vital breaths (*prāṇavidyā*)—there is "the eating of all food," which is to say, the permission to consume all kinds of food (without following restrictive rules). Because there is no difference (*viśeṣahāneḥ*)—due to the equality of being established in their respective knowledges between those who know Brahman and those who know the vital breaths (since the permission granted to those who know Brahman establishes that same permission for those who know the vital breaths)—it "should always be so," meaning it ought to be valid at all times. This is the nature of this doubt; it is not [unfounded].

It becomes truly excellent by this very [rule]: for those possessing a special power—those who have an exceeding greatness compared to one who knows the vital breath (prāṇavid)—even for a knower of Brahman (brahmavid), that is, for one established in the knowledge of Brahman, it is seen precisely at the time of the loss of life, when the danger to the vital breath arises, that the permission to eat all food which was mentioned is established by the scripture. 60.

Because it is not enjoined as a subsidiary (*aṅga*)—since eating all kinds of food is not established by injunction as being helpful toward the meditation on the vital breath (*prāṇopāsana*)—the statement regarding "consent" (*anumati-vacana*) must be intended to permit the eating of all food only when there is the danger of the destruction of the vital breath; that is, for the sake of the practitioner’s intense attachment to preserving the vital breath, this [permission] ought to apply only when life is at stake—namely, the eating of all food in the event of a life-threatening emergency.

Behold the vision of knowledge in one who is established in the vital breath (*prāṇa*), whose majesty is even more exalted than that; behold it in one who is established in Brahman, a worshiper of the Supreme Brahman—namely, in Uṣasti Cākrāyaṇa. Indeed, contemplate this as understood from the *Chāndogya* Śruti. || 18 ||

How could this be?—(There would be a contradiction: if [meditation] were an auxiliary to knowledge (*vidyā*), its fruit would be eternal, since there is no dispute regarding the eternity of that fruit, which is liberation (*mokṣa*). If it were an auxiliary to the stage of life (*āśrama*), its fruit would be non-eternal, because the attainment of heaven by those belonging solely to the stages of life is established by scripture. Thus, there would be a coexistence of eternal and non-eternal fruits. It is not possible for the same nature of action (*karma-svarūpa*) to be the cause of such two kinds of fruits. Or else, the fruit of all [actions] would have to be eternally the same.)

(Or rather, "all [actions] are indeed non-eternal")—how could this be logical? How could there be a fruit that is both eternal and non-eternal, having the dual form of heaven (*svarga*) and liberation (*apavarga*)? (It is not so in any way). Thus he objects: This contingency does not arise; for there will be no contingency of the coexistence of eternal and non-eternal fruits from a single type of action being both a subsidiary to knowledge (*vidyāṅga*) and a subsidiary to the mere stage of life (*āśrama*), because of the difference in application (*viniyoga-bheda*). This is because a difference in the status of being a subsidiary—produced by differences in intention (*saṅkalpa*) and so forth—is necessarily present.

(Just as even though a single type of cotton thread serves as a constituent part for both a cloth and a sacred marriage-thread (*maṅgalasūtra*), the difference in their functions—which results from the difference in their roles as constituents—is certainly undeniable; so too it is here. || 61 ||

The performance of the daily *agnihotra* sacrifice is also accomplished; furthermore, even when the entire collection of obligatory rites (*nityavarga*) is performed by those established in the higher knowledge (*paravidyā*), [the fulfillment] of both—the ritual acts that are limbs of knowledge (*vidyāṅgakarman*) and the performance of the duties of the stage of life (*āśramadharma*)—is to be understood. This should be brought about by reflecting upon the meaning established by logic. || 19 ||
The Adhikaraṇasārāvalī.

If one who is not in an āśrama were not entitled [to perform rites] because the duties of the stages of life (āśrama-dharma) are auxiliary to knowledge (vidyā), then this objection is refuted; furthermore, those [rites] which are performed even in the interval [between āśramas] are not [excluded]. 165.
Thus ends the section concerning the one who is destitute of a body. 9.

Having returned [to the fold], even for one who has fallen—that is, one who has incurred a lapse—even in such a case of having strayed from the stage of life (*āśrama*), let there be the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*)—the knowledge consisting of the meditation on Brahman—which has received assistance through its own duties (*svadharma*) appropriate to that state; namely, those duties fit for the condition of having strayed from the *āśrama*, such as recitation (*japa*), fasting (*upavāsa*), the chanting of the Lord’s names (*bhagavannāmasaṅkīrtana*), and other physical, vocal, and mental acts. Let it be accepted as the practice prescribed by the scriptures.

[If one] objects: "Not so"—this assumption is not appropriate; for although, in reality, this state of having fallen from a high status (*ārūḍhapatitatva*) is indeed what they desire as a downfall (*upapātaka*) and regard as such, there exist many various means of purification (*śodhaka*), such as the chanting of the Lord’s names (*bhagavannāmasaṃkīrtana*) and so forth, which are worthy of all and common to all castes (*sarvavarṇasādhāraṇa*), as established by the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, and other authorities; nevertheless (*tadapi*), this— (Note: The provided text ends mid-sentence.)

The chanting of the Lord's names and so forth is not appropriate for him; a remedy capable of restoring one who has fallen from his status to the eligibility for the knowledge of Brahman cannot exist, because of such prohibitions as, "I see no atonement," which makes known the absence of any expiation that could remove the fault of falling away from one's stage of life (āśrama). || 21 ||

Sages declare that for minor and major sins, when a downfall occurs through negligence, the remedy for yogis is yoga itself. Therefore, even for one who has fallen from their practice, there is still eligibility [for yoga]; indeed, this is not to be questioned, for the scripture prescribes that "the expiation for that lasts as long as one lives"—this is the rule intended by the author of the Sūtras and others. || 22 ||

Regarding minor transgressions (*upapātaka*) and major sins (*mahāpātaka*), which are obstacles to liberation—the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) being the means for their destruction—the scriptures declare *brahmayoga*—the uninterrupted contemplation of the Supreme Self (the state of the mind being restrained within the Supreme Self)—to be the remedy for those who are intent on the practice of yoga for the sake of liberation, should a downfall occur through negligence, that is, having arisen from unintentional action.

Regarding the matter of sin: the sages—the great seers who are intent on providing beneficial instruction—prescribe yoga alone; that is, they teach the practice of yoga itself as the means of atonement (*prāyaścitta*). Therefore, from these two aforementioned indicators, even in the case of a "fall from what has been ascended"—that is, regarding the sin consisting of a lapse from one's stage of life (*āśrama*) such as that of a perpetual student (*naiṣṭhika*)—there exists eligibility (*adhikṛti*); namely, because there is the capacity for undertaking [the practice] in the form of atonement, there is also the existence of eligibility for the meditation aimed at liberation. Thus, it is not [the case that there is no eligibility].

For doubt is indeed inappropriate here, because the scripture—out of an excess of affection for sentient beings—is solely intent on making known the goals of human life that are beneficial to them; it is not to be commanded (that is, it is not subject to questioning or objection). Furthermore, the rule that "even for as long as one lives—that is, throughout one's entire lifespan—that [offense] shall be expiated" refers specifically to the rule for its atonement (meaning: the qualification for the atonement consists precisely in the contemplation of the Lord for as long as breath remains).

However, regarding the performance of knowledge (vidyā) prescribed by the Śruti as a means to liberation, neither the attainment of time nor the attainment of qualification [is required]; this is the intended meaning of the author of the Sūtras and others, namely Dvaipāyana, the author of the Śārīraka-sūtras, who stated, "I see no expiation," as well as the consensus of the authors of Smṛtis concerning the absence of expiation. || 22 ||
They declare that these— namely, one who kills a child, one who kills a woman, one who kills someone who has sought refuge, and one who is ungrateful—
are purified by penances when they associate with the virtuous;
and here, this path has been shown by the authors of the Sūtras in accordance with the Smṛtis and established conduct.
If our scripture were to be subject to instruction, then the bridge of Dharma would be submerged. (23)

The fool who kills a child—that man who deprives a child of life; he who kills a woman—that man who causes a woman to lose her life; and he who kills one who has come for refuge—furthermore, that man who, despite the other having returned to him after seeking protection for himself, mercilessly deprives him of life; or again, the ungrateful man—that man who, by failing to remember a benefit conferred by another, is designated as "ungrateful"—these [are the killers of children]: the killer of a child...

Even those sinful men known as killers of women, killers of those who have sought refuge, and ungrateful persons—who, though purified by penances consisting of those actions established in the scriptures that remove their respective sins, and thus being fit for social interaction as their transgressions have been removed—are nonetheless unfit to associate with in worldly or otherworldly dealings by the *śiṣṭas* (cultured elites) who conform to scriptural injunctions and prohibitions regarding association with the virtuous.

He said: "The learned knowers of Dharma declare this. Furthermore, even in the case of one who has fallen from the state of a lifelong celibate (*naiṣṭhika*) and so forth, this path—this method for establishing the absence of the expiatory rites (*niṣkṛti*) that would otherwise qualify one for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*)—has been shown by the authors of the Sūtras, such as the authors of the *Dharmasūtras* and the *Śārīrakasūtra*, and has been set forth in accordance with Smṛti and custom—that is, following the Smṛti texts and established practices."

The scripture (*śāstra*)—possessing unimpeded sovereignty in the instruction of what is beneficial for all—is indeed the instructor (*śāsanakartṛ*), just as it is the object of instruction (*śāsanīya*). This is so provided that [the world] is subject to our instruction; for if there were an obstruction to its sovereignty by virtue of being an object of instruction by us, then the bridge of Dharma—the scriptural reality established by beginningless tradition as the determiner of the boundaries of right and wrong (*dharma-adharma*)—would be submerged, like a dam situated within a great reservoir of water.

Since he is almost entirely submerged [in worldly existence], there is no opportunity for him to look toward the upliftment of the world. Therefore, the scripture—being endowed with an independence that renders it beyond the reach of injunctions and objections—is unfolding itself; it should merely be followed by virtuous people like us who desire their own welfare, and not subjected to further instruction. || 23 ||

Since the nature of being a portion of Brahman is common to all, yet due to the inequality of qualities, there exists purity and impurity; therefore, based on their embodied natures, there is both permission and prohibition regarding looking upon, touching, and so forth.
This was previously set forth in aphoristic form, and is now stated again here for the sake of pacifying the agitation caused by various forms of attachment.
Even though he had attained right knowledge of the self, he was awakened [to his duty] by conduct appropriate to his own body. || 24 ||

Regarding the state of being a portion (*aṃśatva*)—that is, the state of being an inseparable attribute (*apṛthaksiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*) with respect to the Supreme Brahman—when this is common (*samāne*) [to all sentient beings who constitute His body and to all insentient things], there is both the permission (*anujñā*)—the authorization derived from scripture and custom—for seeing, touching, and so forth [of the bodies of Brāhmaṇas and others], and also the prohibition (*pariharaṇam*)—the injunction to avoid seeing, touching, and so forth [of the bodies of Śūdras, Caṇḍālas, and others]. This duality arises from the inequality of qualities (*guṇaviṣamatayā*), which is the very nature of purity and impurity.

—(which has occurred when its own nature is to be accomplished), by means of the very qualities inherent in each [element] known as purity and impurity, which are acquired through the dissimilar inequality of sattva, rajas, and tamas;

"Not otherwise"—thus, such a reality of meaning was previously set forth (*sūtrita*)—explicitly demonstrated by the Sūtra itself—in the section concerning parts (*aṃśādhikaraṇīya*), specifically in the Sūtra titled "Permission and Exclusion" (*anujñāparihāra*). Nevertheless, here in this present section, once again—for the sake of pacifying the agitation caused by various "non-smearing" (*alepaka*) [doctrines]—namely, those who, by proclaiming themselves to be beyond injunctions and prohibitions, are intent on accepting the freedom of worldly activity (the term *alepaka* referring to those who act as agents within their own selves).

In order to pacify the agitation-inducing activity [of the senses], even for one who has correctly known the Self—meaning even for one who knows the true nature of the reality of the Self (and thus has accomplished all that was to be done)—the fixed conventional conduct (*samayācāra*) appropriate to his own body, which conforms to the specific duties acquired through his particular form, was brought to mind—that is, he was reminded of it as the non-transgression of established boundaries (the suffix *tasi* is used here in all case-senses). Thus, there is no fault of redundancy on the part of the author of the aphorisms. || 24 ||
(119) The Section on Ownership (Svāmyadhikaraṇa) || 3.4.11 ||
A Compendium of the Collection of Logical Principles Concerning the Body (Śārīraka)

That meditation which is connected to the constituent parts of the sacrifice belongs to the master [of the sacrifice], because he is the enjoyer of its fruit; it cannot belong to the officiating priests like those parts, precisely because of the reason that it is connected to the constituent parts of the ritual action.

Regarding the connection with the constituent parts of the sacrifice (*kratvaṅgasambandham*): that meditation which possesses a relationship characterized by the nature of the locus and the located with those things that constitute the limbs of the sacrifice—namely, the prescribed meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth (as in "one should meditate on the *udgītha")—such a meditation belongs to the master of the sacrifice (*svāminaḥ*), that is, the master of the rite (the sacrificer who is the agent).

[The opponent] objects: [Meditation is not performed by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), because the fruit thereof belongs to the sacrificer—since the enjoyment of whatever fruit results from the sacrifice and the meditations (*upāsanā*) based upon its constituent parts resides in the sacrificer alone. [The author replies: Not at all. In the case of meditations based on the constituent parts of the sacrifice, it is in no way appropriate for the sacrificer to be the agent, just as [the sacrificer is not the agent] in the case of the auxiliary parts themselves. Therefore, that meditation also must be the work of the officiating priests; it ought to be a work performed by the officiating priests precisely because of its connection with the constituent parts of the ritual action—even in the case of meditation.

Because of the existence of a connection with the constituent parts of the ritual (*kratvaṅga*), O King, by virtue of that cause; for indeed, that which is a subordinate part (*aṅga*) with respect to the principal (*pradhāna*) attains the status of a subordinate part only when joined with its own constituent parts, since the status of being a subordinate part is not impaired even for the subordinate part of a subordinate part. || 64 ||

The officiating priest (*ṛtvij*): because the meditation has as its substrate the *udgītha* chant—which is a ritual act belonging to that [priest]—other injunctions regarding qualities and fruits are like other performances of subordinate acts prescribed for the sake of a result (just as the Adhvaryu priest accepts the *godohana* vessel for the purpose of fetching water prescribed for the sake of cattle); they are to be accomplished by the priest, specifically to be performed by the priest named the *udgātṛ* alone.

It is not by the sacrificer; rather, because it possesses the nature of a means accompanied by the act of chanting (*udgāna*), this meditation (*upāsanā*) based on the *udgītha* is understood to be performed by the *udgātṛ* priest. It is restated by the Vedic sentence beginning with "Whatever one performs with knowledge" (*yad eva vidyayā karoti...*), and it is known to be established as restricted by injunction (*vidhi*) through the force of the rule for selecting the officiating priests (*ṛtvij-varaṇa-vidhi*). Indeed, "possibility" (*śakyatva*) is not a limiting condition (*upādhi*); that is, being achievable through human effort (*kṛti-sādhyatva*) is not fit to be accepted as a determining factor [for the application of the injunction]. (In this context, regarding the *udgītha*...)

In the context of the meditation performed by one who has taken refuge [in the Lord], here—in a ritual action that is to be accomplished by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) yet must be executed by the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*)—the sequence of master and servant is to be considered: the manner in which the performance of a task to be carried out by a master is entrusted to a servant through wages, as is appropriate in the case of a king and his minister, even when it concerns the sacrificer and the priest. || 25 ||

Because of the injunction "one must reflect" (*mantavya*), as seen in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* passage—"The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen, heard, reflected upon (*mantavya*), and meditated upon (*nididhyāsitavya*)"—where, just like seeing and meditation, reflection (*manana*) which serves as their auxiliary is also enjoined by the phrase "it is to be reflected upon," this serves as an indicator that "silence" (*mauna*) consists precisely of the enjoined reflection. It is restated—by the words "then [he becomes] a sage" (*atha muniḥ*)—as something already previously known as an auxiliary, being merely called to mind again.

"But it is not made known as something new"—this doubt, however, would be "unreal," that is, entirely improper; for by which reason (*hi*) the word "mauna" is well-known (*prasiddhayate*)—that is, established in its conventional usage—in the sense of "meditation" (*manana*), specifically meditation characterized by excellence (*prakṛṣṭe*), namely, consisting in the practice regarding the object of worship; by that reason (*tena*), such "mauna" must be enjoined (*vidheyam*) as something to be made known as something new, serving as an auxiliary to meditation.

Because there is a mutual distinction between reflecting upon the meaning of what has been heard through reasoning and the repeated cultivation of the object of meditation, this "mauna" (silence/contemplation)—like the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-dharma*) or like hearing and reflection—attains the status of a third [stage] by coexisting with "childhood" (*bālya*) and "scholarship" (*pāṇḍitya*). Thus, it is taught as being a previously unknown means for attaining knowledge (*vidyopayika*) in its own right. 65.

Immediately after hearing and reflection—meaning that reflection (*manana*) must indeed follow hearing and reflection as understood from the scriptural statement "It is to be heard, it is to be reflected upon"—the term "muni" (sage) refers to the state of being a sage; for while "reflection" was mentioned [previously] and "then the sage" is mentioned [later], this reflection cannot be identical [to the former]. It is well known as "mauna" (silence/sagehood); it is understood as a specific form of reflection characterized by excellence (*prakarṣa*), such that the expression "then the sage" is heard in the scripture regarding the omnipresent [Self].

The statement regarding *dhāraṇā* and so forth—meaning the instruction on *dhāraṇā* and other practices directed toward the Supreme Self which constitute limbs of yoga and are conducive to meditation (*dhyāna*)—is indeed an exposition [of that practice]. And since that [practice] consists of the repeated cultivation and exercise of the contemplation of the Lord’s form as a beautiful object of focus (*śubhāśraya*), such silence alone is here to be enjoined as the third stage, in relation to the first and second stages consisting of childhood and scholarship. || 26 ||

—0— [Objection: All such things as the practice of sensual desires and so forth are merely the practice of following one’s own whims, the eating of what one pleases, and speaking according to one’s own inclinations; they are nothing specific at all. [Reply: This is not so; this is not tenable. For by Vedic statements such as, “One who has not desisted from evil conduct, who is not tranquil, who is not composed, and whose mind is not at peace—even with wisdom, he shall not attain Him,” specific qualities conducive to knowledge are distinguished by their exclusion of evil conduct.

The commentary [explains] that because the specific forms of tranquility (*śānti*), composure (*samāhitatva*), and so forth are stated as indicators, there is a non-manifestation of one's lineage and other such things; that is, by not disclosing distinguished qualities such as one’s own family, ancestry, or scholarship, one should simply behave like a child. This "childhood" (*bālya*)—enjoined for the wise by the statement "Abide in childhood"—is included within the nature of a child; it does not consist of all the actions of a child. || 66 ||

From improper action, he restrains or wards himself off; for this reason, one who is engaged in the practice of knowledge for the sake of liberation—or a worshiper of the Siddhas—should conceal his own greatness. As ordained by the sages, he should live without manifesting those qualities that produce greatness, such as his lineage, family, or the perfection of his learning.

However, one should not look toward such things as being honored by people; for the sages have taught this beneficial truth: "One should fear people as one would a snake, and honor as one would death. Thus, the intention of the injunction regarding childhood—"one should remain in a state of childhood"—is likely the intended meaning of that prescriptive statement, and not the sense of acting according to one's own whims. || 27 ||

The fruit would be immediate—it ought to be characterized by a connection with a fruit capable of being experienced within the confines of the very body that serves as the occasion for the perfection of the performance; it is not to be experienced through the limitation of another body.

[If one] objects that [the rite] must bear fruit, [we reply: that need not necessarily be accepted; for it has been enjoined by the words "whatever one performs with knowledge, with faith, and with the Upanishad, that alone becomes more powerful," since this is exactly what is recorded in the Śruti. When there is the removal of obstacles by stronger [means]—that is, when the obstacle caused by a prior karma of greater force is absent—that may occur: the accomplishment of the fruit may come about without the intervention of the performance of sacrifices, meditations, and so forth.
But upon the arising of the obstruction, it occurs only after that [obstruction] has dissolved without remainder; thus, it is possible even in another body. || 67 ||

In the section concerning the present life (aihikādhikaraṇa), it is established that for those knowledges whose fruits are experienced in this world, their arising occurs immediately after the performance of the rituals that serve as their own means.
Anticipating this objection, it was stated that when there is an absence of an impediment, there is immediate production; and when that [impediment] exists, there is its cessation.

"Let there be an obstacle elsewhere; however, this most powerful action, characterized by sattvic renunciation and called 'withdrawal' (nivṛtti), is said to immediately bestow the knowledge of Brahman. "Do not say so. For if an offense against the Supreme Brahman is more powerful than that, its arising is for the sake of pacifying it; if that [offense] does not occur suddenly, then the attainment of the supreme practice [of devotion] occurs. (29)

Elsewhere—in the category of actions included within the *pravṛtti-dharma*—let there be an obstacle; let there indeed be a hindrance to the accomplishment of the fruit. However, this action called *nivṛtti*—that which is designated by the term *nivṛtti-dharma* and constitutes a limb of spiritual practice (*upāsanā*)—is said to be most powerful; that is, it is declared to be the strongest among all [actions] in the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, and other scriptures, being conjoined with the *sāttvika* renunciation described by the Teacher of the Gītā as: "That renunciation is considered *sāttvika*."

For this reason—that it has been reckoned as the most powerful (since there can be no obstruction of that which is strongest by weaker forces)—it would "immediately," that is, at the very moment following its practice, "bestow" or "accomplish" the "knowledge of Brahman"—the direct realization of Brahman which constitutes the means to liberation—and not have its own effect obstructed.

[If one should] suspect [this], [the author says]: "Not so—let there be no such suspicion. (If it is asked why: Because an offense against the Supreme Brahman—that is, a transgression directed toward the knower of the Supreme Brahman—is more powerful than even that ritual action which constitutes a limb of meditation known as the duty of renunciation (*nivṛtti-dharma*). If such an offense occurs—if it happens or is incurred—then, upon its pacification, that is, when such a transgression has been completely dissolved, the arising of that [knowledge]—the emergence of the science of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*)—that... [is what follows].

If there were no offense against the knower of Brahman—if such an offense did not exist at all—then the attainment of the supreme practice, which consists in the realization of the knowledge of the Supreme Brahman and the acquisition of the desired goal, would occur instantly, without any delay; indeed, it would certainly happen. || 29 ||
A summary of the meaning of the legal case.

In the *Muktiphalādhikaraṇa*, having raised the objection that— since the ritual acts which are auxiliary to the knowledge that has liberation as its fruit are powerful, no obstruction to that [knowledge] is possible, and thus those knowledges can arise immediately after the performance of their own means— it is stated that, because obstruction is indeed possible for them as well through the transgressions of the knower of Brahman (*brahmavid-apacāra*), there is no fixed rule, just as in the previous case.

The necessity of performing [the rites] by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) is established; furthermore, the injunction regarding *mauna* (silence/contemplation) as an auxiliary to knowledge—distinct from hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*) following the scriptural hearing—is found in the passage, "Then the sage" (*atha muniḥ*); and there is the state of being established in knowledge (*vidyāniṣṭha*) through the *bālya* (childlike innocence) prescribed in the passage, "One should remain in a state of childlike innocence" (*bālyena tiṣṭhāset*).

Only that which has the nature of greatness—consisting of power (*śakti*), knowledge (*vidyā*), noble lineage (*abhijana*), and so forth—is suitable for the means of knowledge (*vidyopayikatā*). (14) Regarding the actions conducive to prosperity known as heaven (*svarga*), if they are performed without interruption, they bestow heaven and the like in that very birth; if there is an interval [of obstacles], they depend upon another birth. (15) Likewise, even regarding those actions that have liberation as their fruit and constitute limbs of knowledge (*vidyāṅga*), when there is an obstruction caused by the transgressions of the knower of Brahman (*brahmavid*) and so forth, they produce knowledge only after a delay.

In this manner, by means of this chapter (pāda) consisting of fifteen topics (adhikaraṇas), the investigation concerning the multitude of matters that constitute the limbs of knowledge has been brought to completion. || 73 ||
This commentary on the third chapter of this *Sannyāyakalāpasaṅgraha*, composed by Seneśvara Ārya, has been composed by the author Śrī Rāmabhadra.

The two subjects concerning the lack of fixed rule regarding the fruit—indicating the absence of necessity for immediate succession to the performance of ritual acts—are the two sections (adhikaraṇa) concerning the fruits known as "pertaining to this life" and "liberation," which were established by the author of the treatise, Bādarāyaṇa, the composer of the Śārīraka-śāstra. || 30 ||

If it is argued: "In this context, the occurrence of obstacles is appropriate for those whose actions depend on the knowledge of others; therefore, this [discussion] has been mentioned as a means for their removal among the causes for the worship intended for enjoyment—why then is this stated here in vain? We say: No.

For in the case of optional rites (*kāmya*), the mind falls [into them] with the thought that they are free from obstacles; therefore, [this discussion is necessary] for the sake of abundant dispassion (*vairāgya*) toward them.
There arises the possibility of obstacles to that [practice], yet it shall bear fruit for one who desires the goal of knowledge. || 31 ||

1. Knowledge (*vidyā*) should have action as its constituent part—that is, Brahman-knowledge itself, which is the means to liberation, must be performed as an auxiliary to action; however, action is not something that is assisted by knowledge. 2. The perception of the Udgītha and other elements as "most flavorful" (*rasatama*) and so forth is not a restatement (*anuvāda*), because it has not been previously established—since it has not been obtained through any other injunctive sentence. It is indeed enjoined by the statement: "This Udgītha is the most flavorful of flavors, the highest, the supreme goal" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.3). 3. Knowledge... [is enjoined].

The stories (*ākhyāna*) situated near the injunctions for knowledge (*juṣām vidyāvidhāyakavākyasamīpavartinām*), as well as the specific narratives (*ākhyāyikā*) contained within the Vedānta, also have the purpose of enjoining that very [knowledge]—that is, they serve solely the purpose of the injunctions for those respective knowledges.

But it does not have the purpose of reciting the *pāriplava* [legends]. Even among those of higher life-stages (*ūrdhvaretas*), such as those in the wandering mendicant stage (*pārivājya*) and others, the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*)—along with its constituent parts (*sāṅgā*) and its specific requirements (*setikartavyatākā*) such as silent recitation (*japa*) and fasting (*upavāsa*) prescribed for each respective stage—is that very knowledge of Brahman which, existing in a householder (*gṛhavati*), i.e., in a person possessing the state of a householder (*gārhasthya*), attains its own essential nature and becomes the cause of liberation only when it depends upon sacrifice, gift, and so forth—that is, depending on sacrifice, giving, oblation, and the like. Furthermore, even a householder—one who has accepted the state of a householder and is engaged in the knowledge of Brahman—[attains this].

A person also, being worthy of tranquility and the like—that is, being truly endowed with the perfection of calmness, self-restraint, and so forth—should be one who has accomplished knowledge (sādhitavidya). Even for a learned person (viduṣaḥ)—that is, for one who has perfected their meditation (niṣpannopāsanasya)—in the absence of calamity—that is, when no calamity in the form of loss of life exists—the purity [required] is through the purity of food alone; that is, the purity of the instruments and the body conducive to knowledge is established by the cleanliness of the diet, according to the consensus of the scriptures. || 32 ||

In this quarter [of the work], it was stated that even one who is destitute of a wife is said to be "united" with knowledge for the sake of the stage of learning (*vidyāśrama*), provided he has not fallen away from it; however, there is no such requirement regarding the performance of sacrificial rites. Furthermore, the state of being a sage (*munitā*) is for the accomplishment of meditation as enjoined by scripture. Childhood is for the purpose of protecting the senses according to one's capacity from actions that strike down the powerful [faculties].
Likewise, the knowledge for the sake of liberation is not attained through other means, but rather through the merits of one’s own ancestors. Thus he spoke in this section.

"Remain thus for you, O Aditi"—[this refers to] one who knows the true nature of the state of childhood as it has been ordained. (14) Even by means of rituals—such as sacrifices performed as ancillaries to knowledge (*vidyā*)—if they are "forcibly struck down," that is, obstructed by another more powerful ritual, there is no non-attainment of other forms of knowledge; (15) just as with those [other forms of knowledge] which have fruits other than liberation, so too the knowledge intended for liberation—that is, knowledge whose sole fruit is liberation—is also obstructed by "forcible strikes," namely by the transgressions against the knowers of Brahman and so forth, which are far more powerful than itself, [acting upon] its own generative merits (*sukṛta*).

"It is not at all produced by meritorious deeds such as sacrifice and charity, which are its own constituent parts and serve to bring about [the realization of] one's own [knowledge]"—it is regarding these fifteen points that Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana spoke here in this quarter, namely the third and fourth feet of the present [chapter], having declared them after determining them through logical reasoning. || 33 ||

Whatever suffering exists, because it is momentary and fragile, it cannot be obstructed by one's own effort; nor is effort effective regarding past objects, which are already gone, nor regarding future suffering, which is unavoidable when its causes are complete.
Therefore, the injunction for the total obstruction of suffering is useless—this is half-acceptable.
Because, through supreme practice, the performance of expiatory rites removes the collection of causes for suffering. || 35 ||

That suffering which exists—namely, that which is currently present at the time under discussion, which is called suffering and is to be experienced as disagreeable—that is present suffering; because it is momentary in its duration, having the nature of perishing in a mere instant, it is not something to be warded off by effort, nor is it something to be destroyed by human action.

(That which perishes by itself even without an effort for its destruction); and regarding past objects, there is no effort—no effort need be made even for the sake of dispelling past suffering, because it has already perished (since that which is to be turned back no longer exists). As for future suffering, while the entire collection of causes remains active, it is not easily avoidable—it cannot possibly have its cessation easily accomplished (because as long as the aggregate of causes exists, the effect is inevitable).

Because suffering is unavoidable; for if it were avoidable, it would follow that there is no collection of causes [for its arising]. Therefore, since it is impossible to remove the three types of suffering—past, present, and future—the injunction regarding the means for the absolute cessation of suffering—that is, the prescription of methods in the scriptures directed toward the total destruction of sufferings—is useless and lacks purpose. Such a doubt is only half-convincing, because [it ignores] that which results from the application of words...

The meaning is that [this teaching] is not to be contemplated by the indolent, because it lacks the culmination in the realization of an uncontradicted object and because they know that knowledge produced merely by words fosters arbitrary activity. (When an inquiry is made regarding the aforementioned subject matter: "Of those performed"—meaning, by actions performed previously through ignorance while engaged in the practice of means—having attained a state of fitness for the experience of results, there is a removal of those sufferings by means of expiation (*prāyaścitta*), that is, by the performance of atonement in the form of spiritual cultivation (*upāsanā*); and furthermore—

[This is achieved] by cultivating [the means] as something yet to come; at the time immediately following the practice of the means, through non-performance—that is, by not performing those actions that possess the capacity to produce suffering—and by the removal of the causal complex of suffering, which is to say, by preventing the arising of the entire collection of causes of suffering, [and thus] because the absolute cessation of suffering is established as easily achievable. || 35 ||

Regarding "that which is disliked by the king" and so forth: you indeed avoid—out of the intention to ward off future suffering—a house, field, or other object belonging to yourself or another that is undesirable to the king, as well as snakes and the like; that is, you shun snakes, scorpions, thieves, and so on, knowing them to be causes of what is unpleasant to us. Furthermore, you carry an umbrella, such as a rain-umbrella or a sunshade, in order to distance yourself from the unpleasantness arising from future rain and heat. Thus, it concerns objects such as those disliked by the king or snakes.

Regarding the non-application of expiation (*prāyaścitta*): when there is no performance of expiation for misdeeds (*duṣkṛta*), evil (*durita*) bears fruit—that is, the misdeed becomes a bestower of results in the form of suffering. Having reflected on this, even while performing the meditative worship (*upāsanā*) which is the means to liberation, you should adopt the effort—the desire for activity—by avoiding defeat, which is the object of the suspicion that [the result] will inevitably be experienced at a later time based merely on your own presumptions. Desiring the success of your own words, [act] before the occurrence of the undesired, by that which has been employed by yourself...

You live seeking the utility of beneficial words for your wife, children, and others; and even while observing—from the young animal down to the beast—the movement of those terrified by fear, agitated by the apprehension of future suffering, you wander through this world with your own eyes. Thus, devote yourself to the method of meditating upon the Supreme Self as taught in the Vedānta, which removes all sorrow; practice it in silence, without reflecting on anything whatsoever that contradicts the traditional succession of scriptural injunctions. 36.
Thus, they speak of that which is to be accomplished or the means of accomplishment as being "unimpeded by itself," yet it remains difficult to define through erroneous paths.

In that doctrine, what is the purpose of their engagement, and why do they perform daily activities such as eating? [If you say it is] for the sake of establishing the eternality of liberation, that too is incorrect because it is unproven prior [to the attainment of liberation]. Furthermore, the Sāṅkhyas—who assert eternal liberation even while in the state of possessing the instruments [of action]—are to be questioned on this point.

Whether it be the probandum (*sādhya*) or the means of proof (*sādhana*), whether the effect (*kārya*) or even the cause (*kāraṇa*), it is difficult to define—it is unfit for definition. Thus, by employing the paths of "bad logic" (*durnīti*)—which are self-contradictory, which involve contradictions in their own conventional usage, and which have been adopted as proofs—the worldly ascetics (*laukāyatikāḥ*) merely appear to be making a presentation while speaking. Why were they engaged in that debate? For what purpose did they strive upon that ground of debate? (Because, by that [means], no objective whatsoever was established.)

Because the very relationship of cause and effect is absent: for what purpose—that is, for what designated fruit—do they perform daily, that is, every day, acts such as eating, that is, the taking of food and so forth? (This is because it is difficult to state that eating is the cause and satisfaction is the effect. Since liberation (*mokṣa*) is established as eternal—that is, by the realization that it is not produced by effort (because it is eternally established by itself)—worship, which is understood from the Vedas and other sources as the means to liberation, [is performed].

The description that "worship is fruitless" or even "useless" is also incorrect— indeed, improper— because [liberation], which is to be accomplished through the practice of the means, is not established prior to that practice; for [it is claimed] that eternal liberation exists only in the state of possessing instruments— that is, only while associated with the worldly condition consisting of the union of the body, senses, and so forth— [and this is untenable] because there is a contradiction between the worldly state and the state of liberation, which is eternally present.
Uttering—
that is, speaking— the Vyāhṛtis; here— in this context.
As for the Sāṃkhyas— only the Sāṃkhyas themselves are to be questioned— that is, they are to be challenged through interrogation. || 37 ||

Excepting liberation, which is the subject of dispute, in other cases—such as in a jar or other objects perceived in the world—"destruction" (nāśa), which is the referent of the term "destruction," consists merely in a continuity of various states; that is, its very nature is to be a continuous stream of successive states, such as the shards and so forth, which constitute the parts of the jar.

(There is no such thing as "destruction" here, as held by the Vaiśeṣikas and others. In this regard—concerning liberation, which consists in the destruction of the self’s transmigratory state—one must follow scripture (*āgama*). According to the authority of scripture, there occurs an expansion (*vikasana*) that is not like the destruction of entities such as jars (which is the counter-positive of existence); rather, it is the very capacity to grasp all objects through the attainment of unlimitedness and freedom from limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhikatva*). This is the dissolution of the contraction of the intellect (*dhī-saṅkoca-praṇāśa*), namely, the destruction of the contracted state known as the limitedness of the knowledge that constitutes an attribute of the self.

Only negation can be the referent of the term "destruction. Others, however, who are engaged in investigating the nature of liberation, maintain that for the intellect—which is the attribute of the liberated self (*muktātman*)—there is a continuity in the form of a stream, based on the principle of uninterrupted persistence through the method of a continuous flow of cognition (*dhārāvāhika-buddhi*). They recognize this as a mode of permanence. Furthermore, the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) refers to all the causes that serve as the basis for the persistence of the stream of the liberated intellect.

The "peak" (kūṭa), however, is the collection beginning with the will of the Lord—the entire assemblage of causes constituted by the resolve of the Blessed One. Thus—in the manner described—there is "non-return" (anāvṛtti): the impossibility of the liberated self falling back again into the state of transmigratory existence; this indeed occurs, as stated in such passages as "and he does not return again. || 39 ||
