Since knowledge is the means [to liberation] and that [means] ought to be performed only once, there should be a single realization; this is not so, however, because the injunction regarding knowledge prescribes its repeated practice (*upāsti*). (1)

Because knowledge—in the form of a specific cognition—is understood through scripture and other means to be a means to liberation (*mokṣopāyatvena*); and because that [knowledge], which is denoted by the term "realization" (*vedana*), ought to be performed all at once—that is, it is capable of being practiced just a single time—it follows that realization, which is the knowledge serving as the means to liberation (known as *upāsana*), should occur only once; that is, what is intended by the prescriptive scripture is that very thing performed just one time. (Thus the objection is raised. This is not so.

Performing [the practice] only once does not constitute the true meaning of the scripture; for there is an indicator—namely, the injunction that knowledge, which is the means to liberation, is of the nature of *upāsti* (meditative worship)—which establishes its character as worship, and because such [worship] necessarily must be performed repeatedly. || 1 ||

"Resorts"— that is, by means of the third chapter previously mentioned, according to the sequence of origination (*utpattikrama*)— following the sequential order existing in the accomplishment of one's own nature (*svarūpaniṣpatti*), [first, through meditation in the form of uninterrupted contemplation, there is the accomplishment of knowledge (*vidyā*), which is the means to liberation;]...

Then, [it was stated] that there is the attainment of liberation—*apavarga*, which is the fruit thereof. First, at the outset, the means to liberation—the subject matter consisting of knowledge (*vidyā*) which serves as the instrument for liberation in the form of release from the shackles of *saṃsāra*—was explained; that is, it was defined following a logical demonstration, together with its constituent parts (*aṅga*s), namely the ritual acts such as the *agnihotra*, as well as tranquility (*śama*), self-restraint (*dama*), scholarship (*pāṇḍitya*), childlike innocence (*bālya*), and silence (*mauna*), which constitute the auxiliary requirements (*itikartavyatā*) of that knowledge. Now...

Thereafter, the author of the Sūtras, Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, clarifies—that is, makes explicit—the fruit called liberation (mokṣa), which is to be accomplished by that [knowledge] and produced by it, for the "knower"—the person who has perfected their practice—by means of various stages (*parva*) consisting of success dependent on a gradual sequence. He clarifies what would be accomplished—that is, what task would be fulfilled—for this conscious being possessing the perfection of knowledge, while still abiding in the gross body—the gross body perceivable by the senses—at the time of its existence.

That aforementioned activity—such as the departure from the body through the embrace of the North-Eastern direction—which precedes liberation, is here, in the fourth chapter, first stated and established by means of logic in the first pair of verses; then, subsequently, by means of another pair of verses—the remaining two feet—he enumerates and contemplates those two matters that pertain to one who has departed, namely, the journey along the path of light (*arcirādi*) and the attainment of the Supreme Brahman. || 1 ||

If it is argued: "Since this knowledge has already been well-stated previously, why does he state it again? If there is something remaining, let him say it; for what was stated before does not coincide with the result here," we reply: No.
[The purpose is] to show that liberation cannot be achieved by other means, that this [knowledge] is inherently inseparable from it, and that its accomplishment is imminent.
And because of its continuous connection here, it manifests a flavor of steady devotion that is equal to the state of liberation. || 2 ||
Knowledge, which consists of meditation and serves as the means to liberation, has already been discussed—indeed, in the preceding chapter alone.

It has been well-determined (*sūktā*); that is, it has been thoroughly ascertained. Why—by what reason—is this very same knowledge being stated again and again, being repeatedly established? (Because the necessary purpose is accomplished by a single determination, there would be nothing further to be attained. If there remains something yet to be determined—that which is left over from the determination—if such exists! And even this collection of meanings being spoken of as remaining for now, [he says] "speak first," since they were already engaged solely for the sake of determining knowledge.

If it is argued: "Let it indeed be established in the previous chapter itself; for what purpose is there the establishment here of that which was not established there, leaving the subject to be established [there] unfinished? Indeed, because that—namely, the establishment of the remaining portions of the science—would not cohere, nor would it attain proper connection, with this chapter on results (*phalādhyāya*), whose sole fruit is the description of the reality that constitutes the result of that [previous study]."

Such a doubt is not [justified], because it is not preceded by such an investigation: [namely,] that liberation—the fruit consisting of *mokṣa*—is entirely unattainable through other means—that is, through methods other than knowledge (*vidyā*)—and that there is an invariable concomitance with the subject at hand; [that is,] the exclusion of the non-connection of the present means called "knowledge" with the fruit consisting of liberation (the necessity of its having liberation as its fruit), and its proximity to the fruit consisting of final release (*apavarga*), being near to the attainment [of the goal], equal to the state of liberation itself.

And [it is] to manifest the flavor of the steadfast vessel—which is equal to the state of liberation—and the specific joy produced by uninterrupted, continuous worship; and to make it evident as being connected with knowledge (*vidyā*), because in this chapter on the fruit (*phalādhyāya*) as well, the application of matters related to knowledge has been performed [here], thus leaving no room for [accusations of] redundancy or inconsistency. || 2 ||

When the specific details are being ascertained, it is easily understood—that is, it is fit to be comprehended with ease—that the fault of tautology, which arises from the re-ascertainment of an already ascertained object, does not at all apply here. || 3 ||
Knowledge has been declared by the Vedas to be the means to liberation, yet its number was not stated; for if it were singular, there would be ease, and thus here the injunctions would be fulfilled.

The claim that its permanence is stated because of its correctness (*samyaktva*) and not because of its persistence (*anugama*) is also insubstantial; for when there is a general statement, it is established that it rests upon the specific, according to the logic of the "animal" (*paśu-naya*). || 4 ||
Knowledge is the realization of Brahman; it is the means to liberation—that is, the instrument for achieving apavarga.

It has been declared by the Śruti through Vedāntic statements such as, "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" and "Having known God, one is liberated. Regarding the number of that knowledge which serves as the means to liberation—whether it is singular in number due to non-repetition, or manifold in number due to repetition—this point has not been made explicit in the scriptural passages conveying that realization. If it were established that it should be practiced only once (*sakṛt*), there would be ease of practice, as this would be in accordance with the Śruti.

There would be the attainment of the favor of the Mīmāṃsā principle that "the purpose of a scripture is accomplished once"; therefore, from that alone, here in this section on the instruction of the means to liberation, the injunctions—the sentences enjoining the knowledge of Brahman—would indeed achieve their purpose, meaning they would be successful. Furthermore, its status as "fixed" (dhruva)—the state of being denoted by the word "fixed" pertaining to knowledge as stated in the Chāndogya Śruti, "The memory is fixed"—is declared because of its correctness.

It has been demonstrated that [the sublation] is caused solely by being the object of a subsequent cognition, and not, on the other hand, caused by persistence—that is, by continuing uninterruptedly over a long period of time; thus, this description is also trivial. For, when there is a general statement—a word conveying an object delimited by a general property—and when there exists the apprehension of a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that brings about the understanding of something delimited by a specific property, then, following the maxim of the goat-sacrifice (*paśunaya*), in that case—

Because rest—meaning finality—is established only in an object delimited by specific attributes, since it is obtained by its very nature; therefore, the purport of all Vedānta injunctions is to establish that the means to liberation lies only in that cognition known as devotion (*bhakti*), which consists of knowledge attained through a state of similarity with repeated, uninterrupted, and continuous perception. || 4 ||
The means to liberation—that is, the instrument for attaining *apavarga*—is as follows:

furthermore, here the verb "to know" (*vidi*) occurring in a sentence intended to teach liberation functions as an injunction according to the principle of the *Āgneyī* passage. Just as the sentence, "One worships with the *Āgneyī* [verse]" found within the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, enjoins that very verse addressed to the deity Agni—which is already heard within the context of the primary sacrifice—to serve as a subsidiary element for the worship of the sacrificial shed called the *Āgnīdhra*, which is connected to that sacrifice; so too does this [injunction] function.

However, it does not refer to any particular ṛc verse belonging to the ten maṇḍalas of the Ṛgveda that has Agni as its deity; rather, it expresses the very meaning of the word "meditation" (dhyāna), for the passage beginning with "Om, thus meditate upon the Self" (oṃ ity evaṃ dhyāyathātmānam) establishes precisely the meaning conveyed by the term "meditation" within that context.

However, it is not any random speaking [of meditation]—for between what is relevant to the context and what is irrelevant, it is only the relevant that is rightly grasped—and there is the use of the term "upāsana" (worship/meditation) for that very meditation; furthermore, in subsequent passages such as "those desires who worship the Puruṣa," the employment of the word *upāsana* serves to indicate that its essence is service, by way of conveying that it consists in worshipping an object superior to oneself through supreme devotion.

He explains that [the root *vid*] culminates in the meaning of devotion (*bhakti*), which is synonymous with service (*sevā*); therefore, the words *vedana*, *dhyāna*, *upāsana*, *sevā*, and *bhakti* converge upon a single meaning. In this very way, the two roots—the root *vid* and the root *ās* preceded by the prefix *upa*—are heard used interchangeably through mutual transference to convey a single meaning: beginning with "he worships" (*upāsīta*) and ending with "he knows" (*veda*), and beginning with "he knows" (*veda*) and ending with "he worships" (*upāsīta*).

A scriptural application (*śruta-prayoga*) is observed that brings about the realization of the same goal and final consummation; this occurs in relation to the effects of devotion—such as chanting (*kīrtana*) and worship (*arcana*) which are accomplished through devotion—as well as the causes of devotion—the means for achieving devotion, such as hearing (*śravaṇa*), remembering (*smaraṇa*), and serving the feet (*pādasevana*). In some instances, there is a discourse on the varieties of devotion—a conventional usage in the *Smṛtis* and *Purāṇas* regarding the specific forms of devotion—which is metaphorical (*upacarita*), being prompted by a figurative identification (*anusandhāna*) of cause and effect (whereas it is primary [mukhya] only in the context of meditative worship).
The Supreme Self is attainable by one who is intent on yoga and whose object of choice is that [Self];

and because it is dear, it becomes an object of perception. Indeed, that [dearness] arises from its qualities; thus it has been heard in scripture. That [cognition] consists of love, and when it reaches a state of excellence, it may even transcend memory. Therefore, this is called "constant mindfulness" (*dhruvānusmṛti*) because it flows continuously like a stream of oil.

Among those engaged in yoga—those who have set out to practice the means prescribed by such scriptural passages as "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon"—he who becomes the object of the Supreme Lord’s choice—that is, the kind of qualified seeker who comes within the range of the Supreme Lord’s acceptance—it is by that very specific qualified seeker alone that the Supreme Lord is to be attained; for the Supreme Lord, established by scripture as the ultimate reality dependent on others, is to be reached through the performance of the prescribed means.

He would become worthy of attainment; and the state of being graspable—namely, the status of being the object of the Supreme Self’s choosing—also belongs to the individual soul because of his dearness, for that [dearness] arises precisely from the soul’s being the object of the Lord’s love. Furthermore, even the status of being the primary locus of the Lord resides in the soul, since it is established solely through the quality inherent in the soul, which consists in its being the unsurpassedly dear Supreme Self. Thus, with regard to the teaching of such a meaning, [the text says]: "Whomever He chooses... by that...

When reflecting on the manner of the purport of the scriptural statement, "He is obtainable," it is established by scripture that devotion alone—devotion residing in the individual soul directed toward the Lord—is the instrumental cause for the Lord’s choosing [the soul] based on His own affection for the soul as its object. And that devotion is a specific form of knowledge characterized by a particular state denoted by the word "affection" (prīti), consisting of love directed toward a certain object that is exceedingly superior—that is, far more excellent than oneself. Therefore:

Since the meaning of the Śruti concludes in this way, there is also no sublation by Smṛti. Furthermore, the sublation caused by the Smṛti passages such as "But by unswerving devotion He can be known" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.21), which teach that devotion is the means to liberation, is also avoided—because this [devotion] is indeed the intellect itself having taken the form of devotion. It is called "constant remembrance" (*dhruvānusmṛti*) because it flows continuously like a stream of oil; for the reason that it proceeds in a continuous succession like a stream of oil, it is also designated by the term "constant remembrance" (*dhruvā smṛtiḥ*) in the passage, "In the purification of the self, there is constant remembrance" (Bhagavad Gītā 18.52). || 6 ||
Activity begins with passion and so forth; among hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*), meditation (*dhyāna*) alone is to be enjoined.

In that context, the word "to be seen" (*draṣṭavya*) expresses its distinctiveness through its extreme clarity. As for those who claim that the vision arising from the word has an object [other than Brahman], the elaboration of contradictions and other faults in their position must be investigated here by the discerning with subtlety, due to the contradiction with the statement regarding "knowing" (*vedana*). || 7 ||

Of that person who possesses an immediate intuitive realization concerning the subject matter of Vedānta, arising from the study of the Vedas together with their auxiliary sciences and the Upaniṣads, [the thought arises]: "The Self, indeed..."

Among those [means] heard in the scripture, such as "Hear ye," "Reflect ye," and so forth—namely, *śravaṇa* (hearing), which is the hearing of the true meaning of Vedānta from the mouth of the Guru, and *manana* (reflection), which is the contemplation through reasoning (*nyāyataḥ*) for the sake of establishing the meaning of what has been heard—the engagement, that is, the effort, occurs at the very outset, even prior to the operation of an injunction, solely out of *rāga* (inclination) or desire. However, *dhyānam ekam*—meditation alone, specifically *nididhyāsana*—is *vidheyam*: it is not obtained from any other source and must be made known by the operation of an injunction itself, as indicated by the word "to be meditated upon" (*nididhyāsitavyaḥ*). The term "to be seen" (*draṣṭavya*)—H.
In the case of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), the application of the term "vision" (*dṛṣṭi*) occurs merely by way of metaphorical usage due to its clarity;

that is equally true in your own system as well, for the word "vision" refers to visual perception even when one desires [to see] through the mind. The word "clear" (*spaṣṭā*) would not apply in its primary sense to that which is devoid of a sense organ;
however, our own position—which possesses the merit of many logical perspectives—is to be accepted, whereas yours must indeed be rejected.

The application of the word "vision" (*dṛṣṭi*) to *dhyāna* occurs when the referent—the nature of *dhyāna*—is included within the scope of mindfulness (*smṛti*). It is the usage of a word composed of the verbal root *dṛś* (to see), which possesses the inherent nature of denoting visual knowledge (*cākṣuṣajñāna*), [as observed in scripture, etc.]. This is a figurative usage (*upacaraṇavatī*), occurring in the absence of the primary grounds for application, based on proximity to the primary meaning. It arises solely from clarity—that is, by taking as its ground merely the extreme lucidity found in visual knowledge. (This is according to the Viśiṣṭādvaita school).

The abandonment of the primary meaning and the acceptance of a metaphorical meaning—that acceptance of a metaphorical meaning is equal indeed, that is, exactly the same, both in your own view and in the view of the Advaitins who consider our position to be faulty; for this reason, the word "vision" (*dṛṣṭi*), which is the employment of a term derived from the verbal root *dṛś*, intends a specific cognition produced by the eye (*cākṣuṣī dhīḥ*), [yet it is applied] to that which is devoid of instruments—that is, to that which lacks the sense organs (since the sense organs are the instruments of knowledge).

When applied to Brahman, the word "ghātā" (the smeller) would refer to the olfactory organ; the word "spraṣṭṛ" (the toucher), which denotes one possessing knowledge dependent on the sense of smell, or the word "spraṣṭṛ" itself, which denotes one possessing knowledge dependent on the sense of touch, could not have their primary (mukhya) function—namely, that they must not be used [in this way] because they are employed with a full set of grounds for application (pravṛttinimitta). For that reason, it possesses many methodological excellences (*bahunayaguṇavān*), being accompanied by many methods such as the principles of the general and the particular (*sāmānyaviśeṣanyāya*), and so forth, in accordance with the Śruti, Smṛti, and other authorities.

Furthermore, our own position, which follows Viśiṣṭādvaita, is indeed to be accepted; it is to be adopted by the discerning. On the other hand, your position, resorted to by the Advaitins, is strictly to be rejected and is certainly not to be adopted. || 8 ||
For indeed:

the arrangement of the door and the door-keeper is somehow possible; if there is a rest in a particular, it cannot be made light by particulars that are heavy, nor can it be conceived when there is identity of the agent. When there is identity of meaning, memory is figuratively applied through the expression "seeing" for the sake of establishing clarity.
That the metaphorical designation of "seeing" [the truth] is based on mindfulness—as stated by Smṛti—is an entirely different matter from our [actual] result. // 9 //

If a resting upon a specific meaning is appropriate—(since "vedanā" is a word denoting knowledge in general)—then a connection is possible through the function of *paryavasāna* (final determination) upon a specific type of knowledge consisting of meditation (*dhyāna*), worship (*upāsanā*), and devotion (*bhakti*). (In that case), there is the establishment of a relationship between the means and the end (*dvāra-dvārikā-kalpanā*)—(namely, that "feeling" (*vedana*) produces "meditation," meditation produces "steady remembrance" (*dhruvā smṛtiḥ*), steady remembrance produces "vision" (*darśana*), and vision produces "devotion")—on the basis of the fact that feeling generates devotion through the intermediaries of meditation and so forth.

The conceptualization of a relationship between the door and the door-keeper, consisting of the employment of such terminology, does not in any way cohere—it is not consistent in any manner (due to the complexity of such a conceptualization)—with the object which is of the nature of a universal, namely, knowledge in the form of pure sensation, together with its particulars, such as meditation (*dhyāna*) and steadfast mindfulness (*dhruvasmṛti*), which possess subordinate attributes of the nature of knowledge.

There is no option (*vikalpa*): it cannot be prescribed as an alternative means because [the means] are conceptualized [only when they are distinct]. When the identity of the agent—the person who practices the means—is established, a means that is "light," i.e., accomplished with little effort, is not to be treated as an option alongside "heavy" means, i.e., those accomplished with great exertion; it is not fit to be prescribed as an alternative (because an option is possible only between two things that are equal). This is because there is an identity of purpose (*arthaikye*), namely, the non-difference of the knowledge that constitutes the means to liberation.

When there is mindfulness—meaning the auspicious mindfulness of the form of the Lord, who is the object of refuge and the means to liberation—for the sake of attaining clarity of realization—that is, for the attainment of the state of being most vivid—it is appropriate, that is, consistent, to employ figuratively a word denoting direct perception (*darśana*) in a metaphorical sense; for it would be improper, not correct, to figuratively describe such direct perception—which is knowledge in the form of immediate intuition—by using a word denoting recollection (*smṛti*).

"Superior service is joined with the inferior; however, inferior service is not joined with the superior. For this reason, it is established that *smṛti* alone—attained through direct perception (*pratyakṣatāpannā*) and consisting of continuous meditation—is the means to liberation. This "knowing" (*vedana*) is distinct from—that is, separate from—the "seeing" (*darśana*) which constitutes the fruit; for "seeing" is enjoined as the object of worship (since the fruit itself cannot be something to be enjoined, and because the injunctive suffix in the phrase "it is to be seen" [*draṣṭavyaḥ*] is clearly heard in the scripture). || 9 ||

One who is incapable of performing arduous penances (kṛcchra) but possesses firm remorse should perform the recollection of Keśava for the sake of all goals; this alternative is appropriate according to one's capacity. Because it is common to all defects, this practice is beneficial; the Sage maintains that such a form of meditation is the very root of all occasional rites and even of liberation.

Regarding *kṛcchra* and other such [penances]: in the case of rites established by the scriptures—such as the *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, *sāntapana*, and *parāka*—which serve as expiations for specific misdeeds, a person who is "lacking in capacity" is one who is remote from the physical, mental, and other qualifications necessary for performing them according to the prescribed rules.

One who possesses firm austerity (*dṛḍhaparitapana*) and brings about remorse (*paścāttāpa*), and who, through the perfection of meditative yoga (*sampannadhyānayoga*), has the capacity to effect complete purification (*kṛtsnatāpādana*) by first restraining the mind and other senses in the mental activity known as the remembrance of the Blessed One (*bhagavatsmaraṇa*); [such a person] is worthy of the remembrance of Keśava (*keśavānusmṛti*)—which serves as the expiation for all kinds of misdeeds, as it is taught that "remembrance of Kṛṣṇa is the supreme expiation for all sins"—and which consists of the meditation upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa.

One should maintain uninterrupted mindfulness—that is, one should practice—for this reason, "as appropriate" (*yathārham*), meaning in accordance with the expiation for misdeeds (in the place of expiation, as a form of performance). An "option" (*vikalpa*)—the operation of performing [a rite] on an alternative basis—is applicable and proper; for, in general, when all those faults exist, even among all those occasional expiations performed on account of them, this [following procedure] is to be performed at the end.

The remembrance of Kṛṣṇa assists [the practice]—by bringing about the fulfillment of the expiation (prāyaścitta), it produces an excellence; furthermore, it is a continuous stream of remembrance of the Blessed One, characterized by a specific form consisting of unsurpassed love and having attained the state of most vivid direct perception, which is the remembrance of Keśava.

The Sage—Bādarāyaṇa—here, in this Śārīraka-śāstra, considers even liberation to be a means [to the ultimate goal]; that is, he regards even knowledge accumulated since beginningless time as a form of expiation that brings about the cessation of the bondage of saṃsāra (in this Ākṛty-adhikaraṇa, by the phrase "and because of the indicative mark," he cites the Smṛti of Parāśara as authoritative). || 10 ||
Indeed, it is asserted that those who have sought refuge in Mukunda, even if they are devoid of the yoga of meditation,
transcend death and go to the supreme abode like those who practice self-restraint.
True, they too [attain this] by virtue of the word "api" (even), despite their lack of proficiency in the practice of yoga which has its objects strictly regulated.
The treatise on meditation has been attained by yogis who know yoga, together with their aspirants, during the stage of the vow. || 11 ||

Indeed, O sir, if it is thus determined that the contemplative yoga (*dhyānayoga*)—consisting of the uninterrupted remembrance of Kṛṣṇa—is itself the universal atonement, liberation, and the means for all [spiritual] capacities; then what of those sentient beings who have approached Mukunda as their refuge—having accepted the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the giver of liberation, as their protector and having surrendered the entire burden of their self—and yet are devoid of the practice of contemplative yoga, which is established in the Vedānta as the means to liberation through various forms of knowledge?

There are those who are devoid of meditations that have become like pillars; yet even such conscious beings, having transcended death and crossed over saṃsāra, go to the supreme abode—just as ascetics who have attained the yoga of renunciation reach the highest realm—meaning they attain Viṣṇu’s supreme station; thus the scriptures declare and establish: "Those who have taken refuge in You, though devoid of the yoga of meditation... (Śrīmad Bhāgavatam 10.2.32).

"Even they, having transcended death, go to that state of Viṣṇu. Given this being established, one might ask: "How could what was stated previously be consistent? To this doubt, the answer is: True—everything stated must indeed be accepted, because there is no dispute regarding the fact that taking refuge (*śaraṇavaraṇa*) is also a means to liberation. This is because of the word "even they" (*te'pi*); for in the phrase "even they, having transcended death," those who have taken refuge are mentioned alongside practitioners of meditation and yoga (*dhyānayogin*). Thus, whether in terms of weightiness or lightness, both [paths] are capable of directing the mind toward their respective fixed objects.

Between these two means, which have their respective scopes established according to the rule that the practice of yoga is "heavy" while the practice of prostration is "light" for one who is incapable of the former due to possessing qualities such as absolute poverty and having no other recourse—the treatise on meditation (*dhyānaśāstra*), which prescribes meditation as a means to liberation, [is intended] for yogis in the stage accompanied by *praṇidhi* (dedication), who possess the full set of limbs (*aṣṭāṅgayoga*) and whose instruments are fit for the dedication of the mind.

By the great masters of yoga—who possess specific bodily states characterized by the perfection of the physical frame, who are endowed with the knowledge of the true nature of the methods for practicing yoga (that is, who are perfected in the practice of wisdom), and who have attained their goal—the [teaching] becomes effective through its scope and practical application.
Dharma is worthy of being practiced by those of the various castes and stages of life because it pacifies defilement and benefits the increase of the sattva quality;

likewise, surrender (*prapatti*) removes obstacles during times when there is no other recourse. Indeed, when a capable and compassionate protector is available, everything that is to be accomplished becomes easily achieved through taking refuge.
And it is heard in a certain mantra: "I, desiring liberation, take refuge, saying 'I seek shelter'."

Dharma appropriate for the respective castes and stages of life—consisting of the study of the Vedas, sacrifice, charity, austerity, and so forth, as ordained by injunction—is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to devotion, being a means for the production of the essential nature of that devotion known as *upāsanā*, which is the instrument for liberation; it serves as an aid to devotion by purifying the impurities—that is, by removing the sins that act as obstacles—and by increasing the quality of *sattva* through the necessary means. Just like that—

Just like the duties pertaining to caste, stage of life (*varṇāśrama*), and so forth, *prapatti*—which is even a petition for the Lord as the sole means to achieve one's desired goal when that goal cannot be accomplished by any other means—is the remover of obstacles during times of helplessness; that is, on occasions when one has no other refuge, it wards off the hindrances of the devotee. (By standing in the place of ritual action (*karma*) which is an auxiliary to devotion, it removes the impediments to devotion and becomes a cooperative factor in the accomplishment of devotion. [This is] the fruit of capacity.

Indeed, for a person who is capable of giving, compassionate—that is, possessing the desire to eliminate the suffering of others—every goal whatsoever, which is established as something to be accomplished by various means in both worldly and scriptural traditions, becomes easily attainable, capable of being achieved without effort, through the act of taking refuge—the prayer for protection—from such a person. As stated in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad mantra: "He who first created Brahmā..."

In the mantra, it is heard: "I, desiring liberation—endowed with the longing for liberation—take refuge," meaning, "I approach [Him] with the prior acceptance of His role as protector. Furthermore, it is seen that this is also recorded in the final portion of the mantra: "I, indeed desiring liberation, take refuge [in Him]. || 12 ||
The Garland of Logical Connections (Nayasaṅgatimālikā)
Now, these are considered the primary themes of the fourth chapter:
the departure through the crown of the head (*utkrānti*), the path (*mārga*), and the attainment of the Supreme Brahman (*parabrahmopasaṃpad*). || 173 ||
The first two sections constitute one casket which purifies knowledge;
the other consists of six principles, while the [final] one of five principles awakens to the fruit.

But if the meaning of the treatise were established all at once, what would be the point of considering its completion? It is to refute such an objection that the possibility of the principle of repetition (āvṛtti) is introduced. (175)
Thus ends the section concerning repetition (āvṛttyadhikaraṇa). || 1 ||
The Adhikaraṇasārāvali.

That [Lord] is declared to be entirely distinct from the individual soul (jīva) by means of defining characteristics and other proofs. In this meditation for the sake of liberation, once darkness has been dispelled, there is no application of the "vision of Brahman" (brahmadṛṣṭi) and so forth. Such worship as "I am He" is not possible here for one who knows reality and is free from passion;
for even the word "I" does not function in its primary sense here with respect to the Inner Self, which is one's own self. || 13 ||

By means of the characteristics [described] in the sections on the means of attainment—that is, by the three chapters ending with the *Sādhanādhyāya*—that All-pervading Lord (*vibhu*), the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) who possesses the qualities of being the cause of the universe and the object of worship, is declared to be absolutely distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*); He is defined as being entirely different from the individual self. In this meditation, which has liberation as its purpose and whose primary subject matter was established in the *Sādhanādhyāya*, there is freedom from contact with delusions and errors caused by darkness within the "thickest darkness" (*mupitatamasi*).

There is no logical justification for the "view of Brahman" and so forth; for it is impossible that there could be consistency in viewing what is not Brahman as Brahman, or viewing Brahman as what is not Brahman. This is because knowledge in the form of a "view" is inevitably an error, consisting as it does of perceiving one thing as another (*atasmiṃstadbuddhi*). Furthermore, with respect to liberation, only knowledge that is true and has the ultimate reality as its object can possibly serve as a means; therefore, the view of one thing as another—which is essentially false knowledge—cannot logically function as a means. This is the intended meaning.

"Therefore"—for that reason—“in one who knows reality,” that is, in one possessing knowledge of the actual state of things (and thus devoid of erroneous cognition), “in one who is free from passion,” that is, in one who is unattached to the fruits of desire, “here”—in the worshiper engaged in the pursuit of liberation—the worship consisting of the thought ‘I am He’—the possibility of such a form of worship as ‘I am indeed the Supreme Self,’ ‘I am Brahman’—is not tenable; it does not occur at all, because it would be sublated due to the consequence of being a mere superimposition (this is the objection). To that, [the reply is]: “That is not so”—that objection is not valid.

This is logical, because even with respect to the individual soul (*jīva*), the Supreme Self—which is its inner self (*antarātman*) by virtue of being its very nature—is the object of worship; and thus, even the expression "I"—that is, even the supreme speech which delineates "I-ness" and asserts non-difference from one's own self—functions primarily and not figuratively, as it operates in its primary sense by its very nature (since there is no room for superimposition or the like in this meditation). (13) (445) In the meditation on Vasu, Indra, and others, the previously mentioned contemplation of their own selves as qualified by *prakṛti* was taught.

In some instances here, the pure Self is to be meditated upon as the all-pervading Lord endowed with such attributes; nevertheless, when there is a distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa), the meditation must be performed using words in different grammatical cases (*vyadhikaraṇapada*). Even so, the expression "I-grasping" (*ahaṅgraha*) is employed for the sake of achieving firmness in the realization of one's own nature as being dependent on Brahman. [This applies] in the *Madhuvidyā*, which consists of the worship of Vasu, Indra, and others—in other words, the worship of Indra consisting of the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas.

In the *Indra-prāṇa-vidyā*, there is meditation upon the Supreme Self as qualified by the individual soul (*jīva*) who is the embodied being within a specific body denoted by the word "Vasu" and so forth—this meditation being characterized by the term "prakṛti" (nature/material cause) along with its own attributes—and meditation upon the Supreme Self as qualified by the individual soul who is the embodied being within a body possessing a specific configuration denoted by the word "Indra. This was established previously in the first and second quarters [of the first chapter] of the *Śārīraka* [Brahma-sūtras], namely, in the *Madhu-adhikaraṇa* and the *Indra-prāṇa-adhikaraṇa*.

The "stated" (*ukta*) is that which has been determined as dependent on *nyāya* (logical principle); the "pure" (*śuddha*) is that which is devoid of the impurity dependent upon contact with non-conscious matter (*acit*); and the "Self" (*svātmā*) is the conscious being (*cetana*) who has become the worshipper. In certain cases—namely, in specific forms of worship such as the Pañcāgni-vidyā, which consists of the worship of the individual soul (*jīva*)—He is "to be meditated upon" (*cintya*), meaning He is sanctioned by the Śruti as the object of worship. However, in this context—referring to all forms of higher knowledge (*paravidyā*) consisting of the worship of Brahman, which is the means to liberation—the "all-pervading Lord" (*vibhu*) is joined with such a Self, that is, with the individual soul characterized by purity in the form of being free from contact with *prakṛti*.

The "Distinguished One" (*viśiṣṭa*) is the Supreme Self alone, who is the intended object of the Vedāntas by virtue of being the object of contemplation. Regarding the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), there is this form of meditation (*upāsanā*) consisting of the difference between the individual soul and the Supreme Self. When beginning the contemplation using words in different grammatical cases (*vyadhikaraṇa-pada*), one abandons the use of words denoting the object of worship and the worshiper—the Supreme and the individual soul—in the same case-ending (such as "Thou art indeed I; I am indeed Thou"), and instead begins the meditation with words of dissimilar case-endings, such as: "Thou art my Master; I am Thy own."

[The opponent objects: "While [the meditation] is being performed, it might indeed become accomplished—that is, it would be realized—but not by means of co-referential words (*samānādhikaraṇa-pada*) whose nature is to indicate non-difference in the forms previously mentioned. Therefore, such expressions as 'I am Brahman,' 'Brahman alone am I,' and 'Thou art I' are unsuitable for the forms of meditative worship (*upāsanākāra*). [To this we reply: Even if there is some degree of validity in the stated point, [it remains that] dependence on Brahman...

For the sake of perfection—namely, to attain the state of being absolutely unshakable through the knowledge of the true nature of the individual soul (jīva) as being entirely dependent upon the Supreme Self (paramātman)—the use of the term "I" (ahaṅgraha) is entirely appropriate in the Śruti. This is because it demonstrates that meditation preceded by the grasping of the word "I," which involves a realization of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) rather than mere difference of substratum (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), results in a meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) that culminates in the non-difference between Brahman and the referent of "I. || 14 ||
Nevertheless—

having abandoned the meditation on unity, how could the notions "I am you" and "you are I" exist regarding the attributeless [Brahman]? The expression of difference and non-difference is not primary, according to the analogy of the hand, the jewel, and the space within them.
For those who say, "You are equal to me" or "I am equal to you," even a figurative expression is not appropriate;
therefore, the notion "this is I" regarding the Inner Self of all is established by the logic of the nature of the Wise One (Ākṛti). 15.

In the case of the *nirviśeṣa* (Brahman as the object of meditation), when it is intended as being devoid of all distinctions, within the meditation on unity—namely, the form of meditation characterized by the assumption of identity such as "Thou art indeed I"—there is contained the thought: "I am Thou; Thou art I. This [thought] consists in the realization of non-difference between that which possesses selfhood characterized by being the utterer of the word "I" and that which possesses selfhood characterized by being the person addressed; and likewise, [the realization of non-difference] between that which possesses selfhood characterized by being the person addressed and that which possesses selfhood characterized by being the utterer of the word "I."

And how could there be a cognition that apprehends non-difference [between the individual self and Brahman], as in the case of the self characterized by being the agent of utterance? Or in what manner would such a cognition be logical? (For if one considers specific attributes such as being the agent of utterance or being the object of address, they would result in a lack of ultimate reality; yet if one does not consider them, the practice of meditation cannot be accomplished. It is like the principle of the water-jar (*karaka*) and the pitcher (*maṇika*)—(the *karaka* and *maṇika* are specific types of earthen vessels for holding water)—wherein there is a difference between the two earthen vessels based on their own essential nature.

The position of Bhāskara—that the expression of both difference and non-difference is ultimate in the sense that there is non-difference in the nature of the space contained therein (*tadgata-ākāśa-svarūpe*) while difference is merely imagined, and that the practice of meditation in the form "Thou art I" and "I am Thou" proceeds by relying upon this imagined difference—is also improper. This is because it is not primary; for the contemplation of two contradictory things—difference and its absence—in a single locus cannot be sustained unless one of them is secondary. Thus, for those who say "Thou art equal to me" and "I am the same as you," the meaning of the statement regarding the meditation on unity is as follows: [the meaning is that the self-nature is identical, while the distinction is secondary].

"O you who have become the very object of worship! The claim of those who maintain that the words *tvam* (you) and *aham* (I) refer respectively to 'one similar to you' and 'one similar to me'—that is, their view that these terms possess a figurative application (*upacāra*) even in common usage—is untenable; it does not conform to reason, as it lacks a primary sense. Therefore, because every other conception is tainted by defects, [the truth lies] in the Inner Self of all, which, having entered within all individual souls (*jīvas*), governs them, and for that very reason is the All..."

In the Supreme Self—which is both the substrate (*prakārin*) and the manifested form (*prakāra*), and which is the ultimate qualificand (*paramaviśeṣya*) with respect to all worldly transactions—the cognition "this is I" (*ayam aham*) consists of the realization of non-difference between oneself and the Supreme Self and between the Supreme Self and oneself, in the form of the identity of the substratum (*prakāryaikya*). This cognition—expressed as "He who is that, I am He; I who am this, He is this," and "Thou art I, I am Thou"—is evoked by the Śrutis and established by the principle of the *ākṛti* (form). It is determined, according to the logic established in the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa* of the Pūrva-mīmāṃsā, to possess a primary sense that is non-figurative (*anupacarita*). || 15 ||
Non-duality cannot be easily asserted when duality has been abandoned, because it is its very opposite;
yet duality here contains non-duality within it, for these two are indeed non-different from their own essential nature.
And such a state of both duality and non-duality is established precisely by not abandoning the regulation of both.
Everything would remain in its proper place for those who are governed by valid cognition, but not at all for others.
Upon the abandonment of duality—that is, when the relinquishment of the object denoted by the term "duality" is effected through non-acceptance—there is non-duality (advaita).

Even the nature of the reality denoted by the term "non-duality" (*advaita*), which is the opposite of duality, is not easily expressible—it is not fit for clear exposition—because it is the counter-correlate of duality (since the establishment of a negation presupposes the establishment of its counter-correlative). And duality—that which is expressed by the word "duality"—is also permeated by non-duality; that is, its very nature is constituted by the object denoted by the term "non-duality. For, within this very meaning of the word "duality," there is that which is non-different from its own essential nature.

Each [entity] is a non-substratum of difference relative to its own nature; thus, a pair—consisting precisely of two parts, each of which is a single entity—is fit to be the object of the linguistic usage "duality" (for the words *bheda* and *dvaita* are synonyms). This is because, since each individual element within a composite of two lacks difference from itself, non-duality (*advaita*) is unavoidable; consequently, the application of the term "duality" can only occur with respect to a collection that possesses two distinct entities, just as the term "non-dual" applies to such a collection.

"Such"—meaning both similar to duality and similar to non-duality in the form of its absence; and "both duality and non-duality"—the reality denoted by the terms "duality" and "non-duality"—would indeed be established only by not abandoning the respective rules: namely, the rule for the establishment of the referent of the term "duality," which consists in the non-exclusion of being constituted by non-duality; and the rule for the establishment of the referent of the term "non-duality," which consists in the non-exclusion of its own counter-correlative, duality. It would be established—that is, it would attain its own nature—only by leaving aside those rules. (Therefore, this [reality] is merely ignorance.)

All three [systems] are not favorable to those who are dogmatically attached to their respective views; on the contrary, they are indeed opposed to them. However, for those who are devoted to valid cognition (*pramiti*) and dependent upon the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), everything—that is, all that has been stated—is "in its proper place" (*sthāne*) regarding the appropriate object; it would be "situated," meaning endowed with the nature of abiding. But for others—those who do not follow the means of knowledge, who follow their own whims, and who take refuge solely in their own opinions—not even a single point of the reality of things (*arthatattva*) would ever be established. || 16 ||
[Objection: Surely, in non-duality (advaita), difference must be established through delusion as something to be negated, like a flower in the sky.

[Reply: Not so, if it is non-different from Reality; for in that case, its establishment through delusion is certainly not established. And if its difference from that [Reality] is false, know that the answer has already been given. But if it is real, then you have accepted real difference—thus your running far away is in vain. (17)

O you who are engaged in analytical investigation! Let it be granted that in non-duality (advaita), duality—the difference denoted by the term "dvaita" and constituting the counter-positive of the negation understood from the negative particle (*nañ*) within the meaning of the word "advaita"—is like a sky-flower; that is, let it be established merely through delusion, having a nature that is the object of error alone, and not a nature that is the object of valid cognition (*pramā*), just as a sky-flower is the counter-positive in the negation "there is no sky-flower."

(For by this, even that [non-existence] would have to be accepted as real; for a sky-flower, when being negated, does not acquire reality merely by virtue of being the counter-positive of that negation.)

Similarly, regarding the term "non-duality" (*advaita*), one might object: "Even the duality that is being negated by the phrase 'there is no duality' is established as an object of perception for those of false vision, the ignorant whose minds are shrouded by ignorance; therefore, the ultimate reality of duality cannot be denied merely because it serves as the counter-correlate of a negation. To this, [the author] replies: "It is not right to suspect this. If the difference in the form of duality, which is the object of negation in the term 'non-duality,' were non-distinct from Reality—that is, if it were not separate from Brahman, the Ultimate Reality—[then your objection would hold]."

In that case, the proof of its being established by illusion is certainly not [established]—because even difference, which does not exceed the ultimate Brahman, must necessarily be ultimately real just like Brahman itself, and because being remote from error is precisely what constitutes ultimate reality—with respect to the aforementioned difference.

Establishment through delusion is not at all possible through logical reasoning; therefore, if this difference—which is the very thing to be negated—and its distinctness from Brahman, as well as its separateness from Brahman, were false—that is, if it were indeed illusory—then know that the answer has already been given: understand that this has already been answered previously (since, by accepting even difference as non-different from the ultimately non-dual Brahman, it would follow that it too is [non-dual] according to the logic of "that which is non-different from what is non-different from X").

Because difference must necessarily be ultimate—if it is true that difference from Brahman is real, and if this is accepted as being ultimately real, then there follows the acceptance of a real difference; and since this would entail the acceptance of something else, distinct from Brahman, namely "the difference from Brahman" as a reality, the doctrine that Brahman alone is real would fall into the error of having no subject matter. For this reason, your running far away—from your attempt to establish the meaning established by the non-dualist school—is futile.
The undertaking of great effort is in vain—that is, entirely useless; it does not accomplish what is desired. ||17||
Summary of the Topic:

In the section concerning the meditation on the Self (*ātmatva-upāsanādhikaraṇa*), having raised the objection that because the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman are distinct, Brahman should be meditated upon as something other than the soul; [the author proceeds to refute this].

It has been stated that there is meditation [on Brahman] as the Self, because in passages such as "I am indeed Thou," we observe that previous worshippers engaged in the contemplation "I am Brahman"; and because even though that [Brahman] is a distinct entity, its contemplation as "I" is not contradictory when it exists as the inner controller (antaryāmin) of the Self.
—0— *Adhikaraṇasārāvali*:

If it is argued that even when one perceives the Name and so forth as Brahman, the cognition "I am That" would still arise as before, due to the commonality of being meditation on Brahman; [the answer is] no, for these are certainly not symbols (*pratīka*) of the Inner Self.

The view of anything other than Brahman is in no way possible, because He is the supreme over all; therefore, when viewing another as Brahman, that [other] must here be understood through its specific, fixed characteristics. || 18 ||

Even in the case of the meditation on symbols (*pratīkopāsana*)— such as the meditations enjoined by scriptures like "One should meditate on Name as Brahman" and "One should meditate on Mind as Brahman," which consist of a cognition characterized by the nature of Brahman with respect to the qualifiers such as Name and Mind— the realization "I am That" would indeed occur; that is, a specific state of consciousness denoted by the term "meditation on Selfhood," in the form "The object of meditation is non-different from me," would arise, just as in the case of the higher knowledge (*paravidyā*).

One does not slacken one's secluded state, nor is one able to cast it off; for the superimpositional thought of identity with Garuḍa—performed for the sake of a specific result in the form "I am Garuḍa"—is not capable of destroying the existing, natural distinction between the thinker and Garuḍa.

In the same way, even the contemplation "I am Brahman," when performed in accordance with the intention of the Śruti, would not be able to remove the real distinction between the object of meditation and the meditator; this is the meaning. From such mere delusion—from the ignorance consisting merely in observing that the vision of non-difference between two distinct things can yield results—one who establishes "this is I" strives to firmly fix in the mind the thought: "I myself am that Brahman which possesses the nature of being the cause of the universe and so forth."

One should swiftly attain—that is, reach immediately—the state of the great serpent Nahuṣa, who was cast down from his position as Indra; namely, the condition resulting in the acquisition of a python's body for that king named Nahuṣa, who, having lost his discrimination by relying on the pride produced by the temporary attribution of Indrahood to himself, became engaged in the great enjoyment of union with Indrāṇī (which was unworthy of him). There is no doubt in this matter. || 19 ||
The section concerning the person [meditating] on [the Self] as having the Āditya and others as its limiting adjuncts. 4.1.4.
