The view of the *udgītha* applied to the sun is indeed superior to that applied to the low [fire], for action alone is the bestower of fruit;
yet even that [action] does not bestow fruit independently, but rather through the worship of Him (the Lord), and not otherwise. || 4 ||

Regarding the meditation on the *udgītha*—namely, the meditative worship enjoined in the passage, "One should meditate upon him who shines there as the *udgītha"—it is argued that while such a meditation might be appropriate for a subordinate deity whose primary status is defined by its role in a sacrifice, it is more fitting for the Sun (*āditya*) himself, because he is the bestower of fruits; that is, since he is capable of granting the fruits desired by persons, ritual action alone—such as sacrifice—is superior and ought to be considered preeminent. To this, [the author replies]: that objection is not at all sound.

It occurs; for even that [action], because it is a form of worship, has the nature of being a cause for producing the satisfaction of the deity. Therefore, its "bestowal of fruit"—that is, its accomplishment of the result understood through the injunction—would not otherwise exist if it did not produce the satisfaction of the deity; thus, there would be no conferring of fruit at all. (Since the excellence of the purpose resides in the deity, between the primacy of the purpose and the primacy of the verbal expression, the primacy of the purpose alone is superior. Thus, the perception of deities such as Āditya and others in the *udgītha* and other parts of the ritual is indeed the intended meaning. || 4 ||

Indeed, it is the deity alone who bestows the fruit; for this reason—that she grants the desired object, such as heaven, which is established by injunctions as being achievable through ritual action—she is the primary factor in terms of actual fact. It is the deity alone who possesses excellence dependent upon the nature of the object [to be attained]; it is not the ritual action [for, between the formal and the real primacy, that which is real and effective must be accepted]. || 20 ||
In this context, the view that there is the perception of one thing as another is reduced to a mere verbal quibble under the theory of *anyathākhyāti* (misapprehension).
Furthermore, if it is held that all cognition possesses correspondence with reality (*yāthārthya*), then the perception of one thing as another is untenable.
Therefore, since the first [theory] would not exist, the doctrine of error (*bhrānti*) as intended by the opponent is not accepted here. As for the second [theory], it is not so.
This is because there is an injunction for establishing a pair of cognitions whose intellects are afflicted by the non-apprehension of such a distinction. || 21 ||

In this context—such as in passages like "One should meditate on the mind as Brahman" and "One should meditate on name as Brahman"—there is an injunction regarding the perception of one thing in another; that is to say, the scriptural prescription for the contemplation of the non-difference of the mind, name, and so forth from Brahman, with respect to objects such as the mind and name which are distinct from Brahman.

In the theory of *anyathākhyāti*—that is, in the view of those who maintain that error consists in the cognition of something as otherwise (the Naiyāyikas, who hold that a specific type of cognition, namely one whose qualifier does not reside in its qualificandum, is itself the nature of error)—let it be granted that there is "accordance with reality" (*yāthārthya*). For in their view, the absence of having a property as a qualifier that does not reside in the qualificandum (*viśeṣyāvṛttidharmāprakārakatva*) is what is common to all cognitions, being shared by the general class of cognitions consisting of both valid knowledge (*pramā*) and invalid knowledge (*apramā*).

In the view of the Prābhākaras who accept this [theory], and for those who maintain the doctrine of identity-in-difference (*viśiṣṭaikya*), the contemplation of the identity of Brahman with the mind and other [internal organs]—which is understood through scripture as being the perception of one thing in another—is not at all consistent; [thus he objects]. That is not so—that objection is indeed not tenable. Here, between these two positions (or, regarding the subject of perceiving one thing in another), in the first case—the position of *anyathākhyāti* (misapprehension)—there would certainly be no disagreement; that is, such a contradiction would surely not exist.

(Resolution through non-disagreement: it is established) in the latter, subsequent position of *yathārthakhyāti* (the theory that all cognition is true), the method for resolving the case of error—such as the delusion of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell—is the method of resolution [as follows].

"Abhimatā" means as accepted by the proponents of *yathārthakhyāti* (the theory that cognition is always of a real object), [namely]: "The meditation (*dṛṣṭi-upāsanā*) consists precisely in the two cognitions of both the mind (*manas*) and Brahman, accompanied by the non-apprehension of their difference. This is because of the injunction to establish the pair of cognitions situated in such a state of non-apprehension of difference—that is, the stabilization of the two cognitions consisting of the knowledge of the mind and the knowledge of Brahman, which grasp their respective objects while being accompanied by the absence of the apprehension of difference between them, similar to the non-apprehension of difference found in the locus of the illusion of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.

Because the injunction regarding the vision has a specific intended meaning. (In either case, there is no contradiction with the scriptural injunction regarding the vision. Some [teachers] maintain that the vision of the Self as the object to be seen is prescribed for one who is deluded by the notion of non-duality;

thus, such a vision would not be a superior offense. Therefore, they hold that there is no fault in such a vision, according to the principle of the "Garuda-vision" (*tārkṣyadṛṣṭi*) and other such methods.
Is it not the case that elsewhere there is a twofold perception of difference—both in terms of individual manifestation and in terms of genus? (22)

*Dṛṣṭi*—in injunctions of contemplative vision (*dṛṣṭividhi*) such as "The mind is Brahman" or "Name is Brahman," *dṛṣṭi* refers to that which is enjoined as something to be performed; it is spoken of in the Śruti as something to be accomplished by following a person who is under delusion (in accordance with his delusion), based on the principle of "seeing what is to be seen."

The explanation that the contemplation of the one Brahman alone occurs by means of the denial of objects such as the mind—which are the objective domain of perception (that is, by not taking their existence as an object of cognition)—is a delusion of non-duality (*advaitamoha*). This is like the expression "the thief is a post," where, just as in the case of a thief being perceived as a post, non-duality is established through the denial of the thief and the remaining only of the post.

Likewise, since the establishment of non-duality (*advaita*) occurs through the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), wherein only Brahman remains after the negation of the mind and other [factors] during the prescription of a meditative vision (*dṛṣṭividhi*), this is the root of the inquiry into non-duality (*advaitā-mīmāṃsā*). Therefore, for the reason stated above, the "vision of suchness" (*tādṛśatva-dṛṣṭi*)—that is, the contemplation of identity with Brahman (or similarity to Brahman)—enjoined here in the scriptural passages prescribing such visions (whether directed toward the mind or other objects), though it is "excellent" (*utkṛṣṭā*) insofar as it consists of a vision that excels the inferior, would nonetheless constitute a "transgression" (*aparādha*) when applied to an unreal object.

Because it would result in the realization of identity with Brahman (*brahmatādātmyānusandhānarūpatva*), it could not lead to [the perception of] existence as a mere portion; rather, by resulting in an offense, it would lead only to fault—or indeed, it would become a supreme offense, reaching the ultimate limit of transgression. This occurs when, through the method of the "Garuda-vision" (*tārkṣyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth—such as the injunction "one should know oneself as Garuḍa"—there is an ascertainment of non-difference from Brahman based on similarity to Brahman, just as in the contemplation of one's own non-difference from Garuḍa [which neutralizes the affliction of poison]. (The affliction of poison...)

[This is] useful for prevention; therefore—some maintain that even from the contemplation of non-difference [of the self] with Brahmā in the mind and so forth, there is no fault, meaning "no transgression will occur"—others hold that "the vision of one thing in another" consists of the superimposition of the identity of one substrate upon another substrate, and that this occurs in two ways: by individuality and by genus, namely, by immersing oneself in the thought "I am indeed Garuḍa" through non-difference from the individual Garuḍa, and "I belong to the class of Garuḍas" through non-difference from that class.

In two ways: is it not already attained—meaning, is it not something already known in the world (or elsewhere)? [For if it were previously known, there would be no novelty whatsoever in the prescription of the vision taught in the Śruti. || 22 ||
Some say: "How can those with attentive minds have the vision of Brahman as 'one' if Brahman is indeed primarily one? For no contradiction is to be suspected when there is a powerful injunction.
Others say: "The conceptualization of difference here is due to one's own whim, like the delusion of two moons."
And just as in the Vedas, the ignorant wander about [in confusion], thinking that Brahman appears in many diverse ways. || 23 ||

The primary [reality]—Brahman, the reality known as Brahman, which constitutes the ground of all worldly transactions—is indeed one alone and does not exist as manifold; for those whose minds are attentive—that is, whose consciousness is unerring (those of certain intellect)—there arises the vision of Brahman.

—How could there be the determination of identity with Brahman (*brahmatādātmyādhyavasiti*) regarding the mind and so forth? Or in what manner would it be possible? It would have to be through oneness—that is, through the oneness of the substratum itself. This is because [the superimposition of one substratum upon another, which is a specific mode of perception,] is incompatible with the simultaneous ascertainment of the non-existence of that other substratum; for even in the empirical usage of the mind, Brahman alone is indeed the substratum. Not...

"For mind and Brahman are distinct entities" (so say some). If there are certain opponents who thus raise objections against those who maintain the identity of the qualified Brahman (*viśiṣṭabrahmaikya*) by means of the inconsistency of the injunctions regarding meditative vision (*dṛṣṭividhi*), then this is the resolution: In the scriptural statement intended for the injunction of viewing the mind and so forth as Brahman—while that authoritative text remains potent by virtue of its strength, which consists in its capacity to remove all logical contradictions—the "contradiction"—that is, the contradiction consisting in a logical conflict arising from the intellect—is [overcome].

Indeed, that which is subject to doubt should not be established by means of doubt; for those who possess firm conviction in the authority of the injunctions, it is impossible for their minds to waver due to perceived merits or defects. In this context of the injunction regarding the contemplative vision (*dṛṣṭi-vidhi*), although the object of superimposition (*āropya*)—such as the mind—and the locus of superimposition (*āropaṇīya*)—Brahman—are in reality non-different, [the practice] proceeds by way of a mental operation preceded by one's own will, like the delusion of two moons produced by pressing the eyeball with a finger.

Others say—others, certain Advaitins who are engaged in establishing unity (who, without relying on the doctrine of the Brahman-reality based on the unity of the substratum, are primarily engaged in supporting the doctrine of a single reality)—say and describe: "It is like [the cognition] 'mine' which, having as its object a single moon, apprehends the qualifier called duality; this is the fabrication of difference—the production of the attribution of bifurcation. (This is an illustration of that: "The ignorant..."

Those who are unskilled in reflecting upon the meaning of the Vedas—which is consistent with the natural sense of the literal, non-metaphorical scriptures—wander excessively, becoming utterly deluded, thinking: "The Supreme Brahman, which is essentially other than [the world] and indeed non-dual, appears as a manifold Brahman within the Vedic words; it shines forth through various modes such as the duality consisting of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, or the triad consisting of the conscious (*cit*), the unconscious (*acit*), and the Lord (*īśvara*), and likewise through other such ways, being propounded as a plurality. Thus they wander and become exceedingly confused.

"In the same way"—thus [it is said]. (This entire description is produced by a lack of skill in reflecting upon the meaning of the Śruti; for, having suspected a logical contradiction between the scriptural meaning and one's own imagined meaning, one proceeds to reinterpret it. In reality, however, the injunction to view the Brahman in its symbol (*pratīka*)—which consists of a determination of non-difference based on similarity to Brahman and so forth, resembling a superimposition (*adhyāropa*) that conforms to worldly and Vedic usage involving error—is easily sustainable as a teaching intended for a specific result. || 23 ||
A summary of the meaning of the legal case.

In the section concerning [meditations] such as "having the Āditya as the first" (Ādityādimaty-adhikaraṇa): having raised the objection that because the *udgītha* and other elements are superior by virtue of being means to the attainment of results, one should practice the contemplation (*dṛṣṭi*) of the *udgītha* and so forth upon the Āditya and others—the section concerning "one who is seated" (Āsīna-adhikaraṇa) follows. (4.1.5)
A Compendium of the Collection of Logical Principles Concerning the Body (Śārīraka)
If it were argued that [meditation] must be prescribed even in all activities because the specific qualification "seated" is omitted, it would not be so;
for there is no such specific qualification of one-pointedness [in those cases], and because meditation is enjoined only for one who is seated in the Upanishads.

She—the contemplation of the Blessed One, which is the means to liberation—is to be practiced (*vidheyā*)—that is, intended as something to be performed by the Śruti and other authorities—even during all activities such as sitting, standing, walking, and lying down, and even in all states whatsoever. [An objection is raised: "This cannot be so; for there is no authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the state of sitting alone as a requirement, such as the specific restriction 'one should perform it only while seated'. [The response is: Such an objection would not be appropriate, because of the presence of a specific one-pointedness of mind (*aikāgrya*).

Because there must necessarily be a specific object for the focus [of meditation], and because of the scriptural injunction for meditative reflection—namely, the Vedic text "It is to be deeply reflected upon" (*nididhyāsitavyaḥ*), which indicates that the contemplation of Brahman is of the nature of *dhyāna*—therefore, that contemplation of Brahman prescribed as the means to liberation is taught as a duty to be performed by one who is seated (*upaniṣeduṣaḥ*), that is, by one who is actually sitting; (and not by one who is standing, lying down, or otherwise, since one-pointed concentration would not be achieved). || 5 ||

Having reached the state of sitting on one side—having sat down when the option of the means (karaṇapakṣa) has been reached as something to be performed—he comes to rest precisely in the state of sitting upon a seat such as a cloth or a deerskin.

(But this is not the case when meditation is to be performed merely by sitting down as a general rule. Therefore, for the reason stated above, this meditation—performed for the sake of liberation and other goals—is possible, that is, fit to be practiced, even during the states of standing, walking, and lying down—that is, during the bodily conditions of rising, moving about, walking, and sleeping—for a person whose senses are unshakable and who has removed all restlessness. (If one objects thus: "This is not established by any means of valid knowledge."

It cannot be attained; for one whose stream of consciousness is uninterrupted, whose continuous reflection is incapable of being severed, how—by what manner or method—could it possibly occur in a person who, while engaged in such states as remaining seated or the like, is accompanied by effort, or who is occupied with sleeping or lying down in a manner consistent with those efforts? (It is not at all possible; therefore, meditation is appropriate only for one who is actually seated. || 24 ||

For the sake of attaining one-pointedness of mind, they establish fixed rules regarding place, time, and posture; yet they also constantly reflect that it is permissible at other times provided there is no lapse, and they remain mindful of this. Because their intellects are firmly established through the abundance of prior mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), all the actions of the yogi at the proper time are performed with a mind focused on the Supreme, characterized by detachment and accompanied by the realization of the Self, as if they were mere curds and other such objects. 25.

For the sake of attaining one-pointedness of mind—that is, for the perfect accomplishment of a state of mind directed solely toward the object of meditation—the Śrutis and the sages who remember them prescribe the necessity of observing the rules (*niyama*) regarding place, time, posture, and so forth; that is, they teach that for the purpose of meditation one must resort to a secluded place, a specific time such as the junctions of the day (*saṃdhyā*), and a seat such as cloth or antelope skin. Furthermore, at other times—that is, during periods of ordinary worldly activity other than meditation—even if there is an interruption (*sacchidram api*)...

Even when intermingled with other heterogeneous cognitions, they constantly recollect [the object]; that is, the sages teach that during the time of meditation, one must practice the constant recollection of the meditative support (*ālambana*) which serves as a perpetual basis for the auspicious. Through the abundance of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), by means of this gradually perfected inward-turning activity and the power of the excellence of beneficial impressions, the yogis have their intellects fixed upon the Supreme (*para*); that is, their minds are established in the Brahman.

For the practitioner, the entire range of activities—including all ritual acts such as obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites that constitute limbs of worship (*upāsanā*), as well as worldly, domestic, and other duties necessary for physical life—becomes filled and permeated by the realization of *tādātmya* and other such states; that is, it is saturated with the certainty that these actions are prompted by the activity directed toward the Supreme Self and culminate in His delight. At the proper time—the prescribed or opportune moment—it proceeds according to the principle of focused engagement, being particularly intent upon that specific task at hand.

Just as even for an ordinary person whose mind is bound [to worldly objects], there occurs an engagement in unavoidable actions necessary for maintaining the body, as well as an engagement in worldly dealings with sons, friends, wives, and so forth—so too it happens, for it indeed functions; thus, there is no contingency of failure in action for those devoted to meditation. || 25 ||

That which was declared here in the first [quarter] as being subordinate to ritual action and meditation, and that which was stated by the venerable teachers to be the supreme duty—namely, the vision of Brahman through yoga—is established as primary by that [fact]. Everything else should be understood as being subordinate to it; and thus, for the most part, the application of time has been fashioned with a lightness of touch upon the yoga already introduced. (26)

Action—consisting of a collection of rites such as sacrifice, charity, and austerity—is that which is to be performed as a constituent part of meditation by a person engaged in meditation; "here" means in this Śārīraka-śāstra (the Vedānta system), and "for those intent upon that" refers to the determination of the constituents of meditation.

In the primary section, the first quarter—the third and fourth quarters concerning the limbs [of yoga]—that which was declared, having been investigated and determined by authoritative persons (*āpta*) who possess both the vision of things as they truly are and the quality of speaking truthfully, namely Yājñavalkya and others: that the "vision of Brahman through yoga"—the direct realization of the Supreme Brahman by relying on the yoga of meditation—is the "supreme duty," meaning the most excellent among all duties established in the scriptures as being to be practiced; and this is what has been stated.

By this and other passages which clearly establish—through both reasoning and authoritative testimony—the preeminence [of the practice], namely, the certainty that the meditation on Brahman possesses preeminence in the form of being necessarily to be performed (*avaśyānuṣṭheya*) and in the form of being the principal element (*aṅgitva*), [it follows that] the entire collection of other ritual acts, such as the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites, is subordinate to it.

This [instruction] is to be practiced in such a way that it accords with and does not contradict the primary practice of meditation (*upāsana*). Furthermore, since it is firmly established that the fruits of ritual actions (*karman*) serve solely to assist meditation, for a person who has commenced yoga—specifically the yoga called *yuñjāna*, whose mind is eager to begin yoga—the following is intended for the sake of attaining a superior degree of proficiency, due to the cause of a slight deficiency in skill caused by the sluggishness of the recitation.

Temporal yoga (*kālayoga*) is the rule that meditation must be practiced at the appropriate time; it is "prescribed" (*kalpita*), meaning it is ordained in the scriptures. [Objection: Since the limbs of knowledge (*vidyāṅga*) were explained previously, why is there this further consideration here of the limbs beginning with mental impression (*āsanā*)? [Response: It is not for the sake of mere proliferation, but rather to expand upon the portion concerning perceptible results by dividing them. True, the state of the flowing stream called meditation (*dhyāna*) must be cultivated daily, even before the discussion of the limbs such as tranquility (*śama*).
This must be explained: that [the goal] would be achieved through one-pointedness of mind even in the absence of all effort. 27.

Regarding the "limb of knowledge" (*vidyāṅga*): everything previously mentioned that assists the primary knowledge has already been determined in the third and fourth [pādas]. Here—in this first pāda of the fourth [adhyāya]—this investigation into the limbs such as posture (*āsana*) is being undertaken; why, then, is it performed again? [This is the question: because it would result in redundancy. [The answer is: having distinguished the portion of visible purpose among those limbs that provide visible or invisible assistance toward the primary [knowledge], [the author] [discusses] the limb that provides visible assistance.

Having separated [the topics], even to expand upon or demonstrate them—here, the determination of the limbs of *āsana*—it is certainly not possible to discern [them separately] because they were already [discussed] previously (in the third and fourth chapters) through the discussion of the limbs such as tranquility (*śama*); for since tranquility, self-restraint (*dama*), and so forth, which are directly beneficial to *yoga*, have already been described, it would result in an inconsistency [to discuss them again here]. [Objection: True, this question is indeed appropriate.

Day after day, it must be accomplished with one-pointedness of mind—until death, for as long as life lasts—a stream called "meditation" (dhyāna) that acquires excellence through daily practice by means of a mind solely inclined toward the object of meditation. The state of "carrying the intellect," however, refers to the continuum of cognition denoted by the term "meditation."

The ultimate state of remaining with the stream [of consciousness] uninterrupted can only be achieved—meaning accomplished—by the cessation of all effort, that is, by the removal of every effort directed toward objects other than meditation; this alone is what is most essential to be revealed—that is, it is what the venerable author of the Sūtras intended to make clear to practitioners. || 27 ||

The requirement that [the practice] be performed on a single day alone does not hold; for it is established by scripture (*śāstra*) that it must be performed "as long as life lasts" (*yāvadāyuḥ*), based on the very words of the Śruti passage—"He, indeed, living thus as long as life lasts"—which contains the term *yāvadāyuḥ* and whose meaning is beyond doubt. Furthermore, this is because its performance until death as a daily duty is clearly enjoined by the injunction itself. (The fulfillment of the scriptural mandate is not achieved by performing it only once; rather, it is achieved only by performing it every day until death. 6.0-
The Adhikaraṇasārāvalī.

If devotion in the form of supreme meditation (*paradhyāna*) occurs within that very same state of concentration, then the ritual injunction (*vidhi*) finds its rest therein; however, it is illogical to claim that the contemplation of Brahman (*brahmacintā*) would be fruitless thereafter.
For in the *Chāndogya*, the practice of good conduct (*sucarita*) throughout one's entire life is prescribed for the sake of attaining the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*).
For that [meditation] leads to the increase of dhyāna, and it is also prescribed in some cases as lasting until death.

On a single day alone—that is, on one and the same day—if devotion in the form of supreme meditation (*paradhyāna*)—devotion which is the means to liberation because it is designated by the term "meditation upon the Supreme Self"—should come to be, that is, if its true nature should be attained, then the injunction—the injunction for the knowledge of Brahman as the means to liberation—[is fulfilled].

[The injunction] found in the Śruti and other sources would find its rest there—it would terminate solely in making known that it is to be performed for only a single day; however, thereafter—that is, after the performance of the rites whose purpose is established at the conclusion of the scripture, during the remainder of one's life (āyuḥśeṣe)—there is "contemplation of Brahman" (brahmacintā), which is the worship of Brahman (brahmopāsanā).

It is incorrect to say that [the injunction] is devoid of purpose or deficient; such a suspicion is inappropriate. For in the *Chāndogya*—in the *Chāndogya Śruti*—it is stated (*uditam*) that "good conduct" (*sucarita*), which is denoted by the term "well-performed deeds," must be practiced throughout one's life (*yāvadāyuḥ*), until death, as the means for attaining the world of Brahman—that is, as the cause for the fruit consisting of the attainment of Brahman. As it is said: "Living thus throughout his life, he reaches the world of Brahman. Therefore, [this practice] is prescribed every day until the end of life.

The performance of good deeds is indeed for the increase of meditation—that is, for the attainment of extreme clarity in meditation—and that very meditation is prescribed even until the end of life, until the departure from the body; for in a specific scriptural passage it is clearly enjoined as something to be practiced: "One should meditate upon the syllable Om until the end of one's life. || 28 ||
The Garland of Logical Connections (Nayasaṃgatimālikā)

Even one who has returned [to worldly life] may resume [the practice] at will; such is the doubt that is set aside in the *Āprayāṇādhikaraṇa* on account of the observation of scriptural authority. (180)
Thus ends the section concerning [the persistence of the soul] until the departure from the body (āprayāṇādhikaraṇa). 6.

This has been clarified by the statement of the Purāṇas; therefore, on the basis of that indicative evidence, even the scriptural texts concerning the non-clinging (*aśleṣa*) and destruction (*praṇāśa*) of sin—such as the Vedic declarations: "In one who knows thus, evil action does not cling," and "Thus all his evils are consumed"—which teach the absence of clinging and the destruction of sins like those called "subsequent" and "prior" for a person who knows Brahman, must be understood as a description of the glory of the knower of the Supreme (*paravidvat*), meaning they function with the sole intent of making known the extraordinary greatness of the most eminent knower of Brahman.

"But it should not be taken as having a meaning strictly literal" (thus one might object). Not so—it is not at all correct to raise such an objection. Even the Smṛti statement beginning with "What has not been eaten... and "What has not been experienced does not perish," which speaks of the action known as good or evil deeds, declares—and thereby clarifies—the certainty of its own production of fruit through the absence of any obstacle in the generation of that fruit. Here, in the Vedic word, "devotion to the Supreme" means the worship of the Supreme Self for the sake of the cessation of karma.

In order to ensure that all actions which obstruct liberation (*apavarga*) do not produce their fruits, expiations (*prāyaścitta*) have been prescribed—just as they are for various sins—in accordance with various other scriptures through the process of atonement; this is to be understood as having been ordained. (29) The nature of this [atonement] as a purification (*niṣkṛti*) is established for the purpose of uprooting the aforementioned evils. Herein, there is no rule regarding heaven and the like; rather, upon the removal of obstacles, the expansion of the intellect occurs spontaneously. The "stain of sin" is merely the endurance of what arises from negligence; thus it is established for the sake of following the authoritative injunctions.
If it were not so, there would be no progress, nor would there be the state of non-cessation; for such is the teaching of the Yogins and because of their engagement [in practice]. || 30 ||

For this meditation on the Supreme Self—which uproots previously arisen evils, meaning it effects the eradication of all sins—it is appropriate (upapanna), that is, logically consistent (by that very reason), that its nature is expiation (niṣkṛtyātmatva), meaning it takes the form of a rite of atonement; for (hi), when the obstruction is removed—that is, when impediments have been dispelled—the expansion of the intellect (dhīvikāsa) is obtained by itself, dependent solely upon the nature of consciousness, which is the state of uncontracted knowledge-as-an-attribute (asaṅkucita-dharmabhūta-jñānatva) conducive to the experience of Brahman.

Therefore, in this context of the practice of meditation upon the Supreme Self for the sake of liberation (*apavarga*), the principle of heaven and so forth does not apply; that is, the principle by which rites such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma*—which are performed with desire—serve as causes for specific pleasures called "heaven," does not exist here as a cause for liberation. Furthermore, regarding the "non-staining by sin"—the scriptural teaching that there is an absence of taint for one whose nature is devotion to the practice following the completion of meditation—and regarding "obedience to the command"—the continued observance of the injunctions by the practitioner for the rest of their life even after the perfection of meditation.

To demonstrate the continuity of service (*kaiṅkarya*) for the sake of attaining perfection, it must be established that there is "endurance of what arises from negligence. This means that the Supreme Self’s forbearance is exercised precisely toward those sins incurred involuntarily through negligence; thus, it must be maintained that there is no room for intentional misconduct. Otherwise, if one were to disregard the phrase "incurred through negligence" and, without restriction, consider the intent to be the non-clinging to all sins—a view supposedly sanctioned by scripture—then it would contradict the words of the scripture: "Not one who has not ceased from evil conduct, nor one who is not tranquil, nor one who is not composed... (*Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* 3.2.30).

Otherwise, there would be no way to account for the scriptural statement, "Neither can one whose mind is not tranquil attain Him through wisdom," nor for the activity of yogis—such as Janaka, Kekaya, and other great yogis—which consists of engaging in prescribed duties and avoiding prohibited ones, as established by the Śruti, Purāṇas, and other authorities; thus, there would be no appropriate resolution of these facts.

(If the doctrine of the Śruti were such that those who worship perfected beings (siddhas) must transgress both injunctions and prohibitions, then why would Janaka, Kekaya, and others—who are heard of in the scriptures as followers of scriptural boundaries—be mentioned in the scriptures? || 30 ||
The non-arising of the power of action (*karma-śakti*) is its suppression (*bhaśleṣa*); its arising is its cessation, which is destruction.

That power belongs to the author [of the act] and consists of the infliction of punishment or the granting of favor, resulting in a fruit appropriate to that [act]. As for the question, "How can there be expiation (*prāyaścitta*) when [the power] has not arisen?"—this is not at all to be questioned.
"One must indeed grasp the heart [of the matter], thinking: 'That shall not be unrighteousness for him,' regarding words that lack connection [to reality]. (31)

Non-adherence (*aśleṣa*): As stated in the passage, "In one who knows thus, evil action does not adhere," this refers to the non-adherence of evils in the knower; it is the non-arising of the power of action, meaning that even when actions of a sinful nature have been performed, the power opposed to knowledge simply does not arise therein. Destruction (*vināśa*): As stated in the passage, "Thus all his evils are consumed," this refers to the destruction of all evils for the knower; it is the cessation of that [evil] upon its arising—that is, when the power opposed to knowledge has arisen regarding actions, there is the destruction of that very power.

It is an obstruction, and that power—the power residing in karma which is opposed to the state of uncontracted knowledge—is the producer of appropriate fruits for each respective conscious agent of those various actions. It consists solely of the will of the Supreme Lord, the universal controller, to punish or favor specific individual souls; it is not something else denoted by terms such as *apūrva*. By the term "expiation" (*prāyaścitta*), [it refers to this very power].

"How does the action prescribed by the scripture acquire its essential nature when the occasion [for it] has not arisen—that is, while the occasion that necessitates an expiation has not yet occurred?"—this question is not at all to be raised here, because [the subsequent remorse and the performance of specific rites prompted by it] were not previously applicable. Thus, there is a double entendre (*śleṣa*) regarding the phrase "of the subsequent sin" (*uttarasyāghasya*): in the context of the impossibility of expiation for that which has not been committed, one must not object to the statement of the non-adherence (*aśleṣa*) of the subsequent sin. This is the meaning of the expression "non-adherence of the subsequent sin."

The "heart" means the intended meaning; that indeed must be understood as not being unrighteousness—namely, that an accidental performance of sin does not constitute a sinful act for the practitioner; this is precisely how it should be grasped by one who reflects upon the meaning of the scripture. || 31 ||
One who knows the higher truth always acts with prior wisdom and remains ever vigilant;
he either immediately dispels what has arisen through appropriate remedial measures or consumes it.
This was observed in the case of Vṛtra and others, through the power of destiny, resulting in the attainment of the eight supernatural powers (aṇimā, etc.).
Whether in a state of meditative union or at other times, the sage here considers liberation for one who is established in Brahman.

A person who is devoted to the uninterrupted meditation on the Supreme Self (*paravit*), acting with deliberate intent (*dhīpūrvam*)—that is, with conscious awareness—does not produce subsequent evil (*uttarādham*), namely the sin that arises after the practice of meditation; for he does not seek to bring it about through the performance of prohibited acts and the like, because he is ever vigilant—from the commencement of his engagement in meditation until the end of his life—never abandoning it even for a moment, remaining truly heedful.

He who lives [heedlessly]—that is, he who is devoid of attentiveness—[commits] a sin born of negligence; he quickly dispels—that is, he swiftly destroys within the very time remaining until the fall of the body—such a sin by means of appropriate expiatory rites prescribed for specific occasions according to the nature and form of each respective transgression, or by means of seeking forgiveness, taking refuge, and so forth, as commanded by the assembly; or else, he may experience that [sin] quickly in this very life, in a manner such that it does not persist into future births.

Or one may indeed exhaust [the sins] through experience; this is the removal, according to the method described, of possible sins for a conscious being whose sole essence is contemplation of the Supreme Self—a phenomenon observed in the case of Vṛtra and others. It is known from the narratives of the Purāṇas and other texts that even though a specific conscious being had attained birth in the form of Vṛtra and was a knower of Brahman, he first underwent the state of being slain by the son of Devaka (Arjuna) and immediately thereafter attained liberation, due to the power of destiny—that is, by the force of the greatness of Fate—and thus achieved the perfection of the King of Cedi and others.

It is heard that for a particular conscious being who is a devotee of the Lord, even when he has assumed a form such as Śiśupāla, his attainment of the Lord preceded by enmity is logical and indeed proper; thus the sage Bādarāyaṇa, the author of the Sūtras, in this *Śārīraka*, maintains that for one established in Brahman—the seeker of liberation who contemplates Brahman—liberation is inevitable, whether today or at another time, in this birth or in another birth, and he reveals this as his own intended view in accordance with the scriptures. || 32 ||

Attachment and destruction, however, do not at all apply to beneficial actions for the sake of attaining happiness; yet they clearly do apply to one seeking liberation, because they are equally obstacles to liberation. (8)

Regarding beneficial actions—which are of the nature of well-performed deeds and are essentially wholesome (i.e., meritorious actions)—their non-adherence (*aśleṣa*) and destruction (*nāśa*), like those of sins, are not at all applicable; that is, they are in no way possible. One might object: "Because of the attainment of happiness—that is, due to the cause of obtaining desired forms of pleasure through meritorious actions (since even a seeker of liberation who is a lay practitioner must rely on them for the sake of producing desired fruits)," but such an objection is not valid.

Since that [bondage] is indeed not appropriate—because it is equal in its nature as an obstacle to liberation, as the capacity to obstruct liberation is common to meritorious deeds (*puṇya*) just as it is to sinful ones (*pāpa*)—it follows that for a person desiring liberation (*mumukṣu*), one who wishes to release his own self from the shackles of *saṃsāra*, both the non-clinging (*aśleṣa*) and the destruction (*nāśa*) of even meritorious actions must necessarily be expected and are indeed possible when they clearly arise without doubt. || 8 ||

Because of the attainment of the characteristic of "tallakṣma"—namely, because of the connection with the fact that the characteristic of sin consists in obtaining undesirable things such as the minor pleasures of heaven and the like, which are other than the attainment of the most desired Lord; and because this merit also possesses the nature of sin—that is, the state of being sinful—it is not "well-done" (sukṛta). This is clearly stated even in the Śruti itself: "Neither good nor evil; all sins turn back from there. || 33 ||

If merit is conducive to knowledge, it bears fruit here because it bestows that knowledge; however, even that which is not useful for it must be avoided, as it acts as a bond like sin. When a servant of a sovereign is confined in prison by a pair of shackles, both the golden and the iron ones must be broken together at the time of his release. (34)

Here—among those meritorious acts designated as "bases of merit" (*puṇyapada*), that merit which is conducive to knowledge—that is, the merit known as *nitya* (obligatory) and *naimittika* (occasional) which serves as a means for the attainment of knowledge that is the instrument for liberation—for such merit enjoined by scriptural injunction, its fruitfulness here consists in the bestowal of knowledge; because it brings about knowledge, which consists of uninterrupted meditation on the Lord, by way of producing the purification of the internal organ (*sattva*). Thus, there is the practice of knowledge here.

It is not established that utility (i.e., the capacity to produce an effect) exists solely by way of delimitation through a useful body; for even that kind of merit which remains in this knowledge consisting of the worship of the Lord, devoid of any utility in the form of assistance, such merit—even as an action—must be warded off (i.e., abandoned and removed) because it is a cause for the increase of saṃsāra, being equal to sin (just like *durita*, or evil).

When a certain man, a servant of the sovereign—the emperor—was confined in prison, bound by a pair of shackles made of gold and iron respectively, having been imprisoned in a jail—a house for binding thieves and other offenders (being restricted to the prison due to his offense)—at the time of favor, that is, at the moment when the king was inclined to grant him release upon the completion of the period of his punishment, [the king saw] the golden and the iron... the golden...

Both types of binding objects, even those made of iron, must be broken together—that is, their release must indeed occur simultaneously; for the mere fact that a golden shackle is golden does not grant it acceptability [as a means of release]. (In the same way, at the time of liberation, the simultaneous shaking off of both merit and demerit, which are the causes of bondage to worldly existence, is indispensable. || 34 ||
It is not employed— that is,
as a cause of bondage— if one who is dispassionate does not desire what is prompted by longing; for if he should indeed perform it, it would bear fruit through the connection with passion.

One should not perform any optional rite (*kāmya*) preceded by Vedic study, nor should one who is ignorant of Dharma direct another to do so. If it is asked, "Why then is he tainted by the pursuit of knowledge?", [the answer is: let there be no taint from other things that are accompanied by obstacles, born of delusion, or followed by remorse; but let there be taint from those arising from kinsmen. (35)

The dispassionate person—one who desires liberation and has no longing for the fruits of worldly existence—should not desire that which is called "kāmya," meaning meritorious deeds performed as a cause for results in this life; he should not even strive to perform them (if he does not even strive, he will certainly not do them).

If even the mere arising of desire does not occur, what need is there to speak of its fulfillment? This is because of the connection with passion—which is dependent on latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—and the association with spontaneous desire (that is, a specific desire that arises unexpectedly). For if one were indeed to act—if one were ever to perform even a meritorious deed born of desire!—then that would bear fruit; such a well-performed action, having given its intended result during the very lifetime, would cease to exist; it would not remain until the time of death.

For one for whom non-attachment (*alepa*) must be practiced so as not to obstruct liberation—whether it be performed intentionally (*adhīpūrva*) or even unintentionally (*abuddhipūrvaka*), and whether it be a meritorious act denoted by the term "desirable" (*kāmya*)—nothing whatsoever would be possible [to hinder him]. This is because "desirability" consists in being the object of a desire preceded by knowledge; therefore, the state of being intentional (*adhīpūrvakatā*) is inapplicable there. Thus, a specific merit existing therein, remaining entirely unknown (*ajñātadharma*) to the seeker of liberation who is a practitioner, shall not bring about bondage.

One should not present *saṃsāra*—the state opposed to liberation—to him [the seeker of liberation] (meaning: one should not, by giving this seeker of liberation worldly fruits that are contrary to liberation, render him incapable of attaining liberation); furthermore, he is indeed tainted (*lipyate*) by meritorious deeds (*sukṛta*) performed for the sake of knowledge—that is, as auxiliary parts of knowledge (for if they were not so, those deeds would not even be conducive to bestowing knowledge).

Alas, what could be more harmful than this? If it is asked, "What else [could there be]?"—[the answer is: once it is established that the statement regarding non-attachment (*alepa*) is inapplicable to all the aforementioned types of meritorious deeds (*sukṛta*), what other kind of merit remains to be described as not partaking in attachment (*asaṃśleṣabhāj*) so as to obstruct his liberation? None whatsoever.

One might object that a statement of non-connection is indeed useless; however, this objection is improper. For there exist "excessive" factors—those beyond what is required for the accomplishment of knowledge—which, though performed for the sake of knowledge, remain as they are because they are obstructed by impediments and thus fail to assist in the attainment of knowledge. Furthermore, there are "factors for other purposes" born of delusion (*moha*), which, although by their very nature they produce results other than knowledge, are mistakenly conceived by those seeking knowledge as being for the sake of knowledge due to delusion (*bhrānti*). Thus...

And by means of the *bandhujas* (relatives born of the same womb)—that is, through one's own merits that have been shaken off at the time of departing from the body, or through those merits that have returned to one's own self as dear kinsmen—the one who feels remorse for whatever kind of merit there may be that obstructs liberation; for such a seeker of liberation who has attained repentance, let there be *alepa*—the absence of any possible taint—as determined by the author of the Sūtras.
(Thus, the intention is that the impropriety of the statement regarding "being unstained"—which arises from the absence of merit produced by the act of writing—is thereby avoided. || 35 ||
