In the subsequent section, although there is infinity of merit, as in the previous case, these two—destruction and non-attachment—pertain respectively to faulty action (*duṣkarma*) arising from negligence and to virtuous action (*satkarma*). (182)
Thus ends the section concerning the other [the individual soul]. || 8 ||
Section on those whose effects have not yet begun (Anārabdhakāryādhikaraṇa) || 4.1.9 || A Compendium of the Essential Logic of the Śārīraka [Brahma-sūtras] ||

Indeed, for everyone, the specific term [of the scripture] implies both the non-clinging to and the destruction of karma; however, this does not apply to one whose fruit has already begun to manifest, because the specific term "until I am liberated" is used [only in that context]. || 9 ||

Regarding all that is denoted by the terms "good and evil deeds"—namely, the objects pertaining to the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*) and the practitioner (*upāsaka*), comprising both those whose effects have already begun and those whose effects have not yet begun—there indeed occur non-clinging (*aśleṣa*) and destruction (*nāśa*); for this means that there is no clinging of what is subsequent and the exhaustion of what is prior. This is because of the absence of specific terminology (*vaiśeṣikaśabda-hāniḥ*), that is, the absence of words capable of conveying the distinct meaning of good and evil deeds whose effects have not yet begun. (Thus he objects. No, this objection is not tenable, because—for which reason:

The specific term "until I am released" (yāvanna mokṣye)—that is, "until I am liberated, then I shall attain [Brahman]"—is clearly heard in the Śruti as conveying the specific condition of having the liberation from the body as its limit. Therefore, there is no destruction whatsoever of the karma known as *sukṛta* and *duṣkṛta* that has begun its effects and is engaged in yielding its fruit; otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence that in the remaining time there would be no cause for the maintenance of the body. || 9 ||

If it is argued that the word [denoting] the specific [destruction] called "karma" is neither studied nor recited in the Śruti—since even the phrase "all evils" (*sarve pāpmānaḥ*) has been mentioned [as referring to sins], and on the contrary, the very sentence containing the word "all," namely "all evils," which teaches the cessation of both commenced and uncommenced karma, is indeed recited in the Śruti—this suspicion is incorrect, because it is sublated by perception and other means of knowledge; for there is a contradiction with direct perception and so forth regarding the meaning of the word's power [if taken literally]. Indeed, even a person who has perfected their meditation...

Subsequently, for as long as life lasts, one maintains the body and obtains engagement in what is desired and withdrawal from what is disliked. Thus, due to contradiction with both direct perception and inference, the destruction of all karma is by no means a certainty.

"For the body is indeed commenced by karma; how could it be sustained once all karma has departed? Thus, the *Sadvidyā-prakaraṇa* (the section on the Knowledge of Being, consisting of the sixth chapter of the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*) states: "For him, there is delay only so long as he is not released," and this scriptural fragment (*śrutikhaṇḍa*) clearly and explicitly declares, by its very words, the postponement of time until the fall of the body. Furthermore, those who know the tradition (*āgamajña*), who perceive specific recensions (*śākhā*) that have been lost to transmission, and who are the preservers of the sacred texts (*smartāraḥ*)...

The sages, moreover, made clear through their own memories and other means that the persistence of good and evil karma continues until the fall of the body; even the term "liberation while living" (*jīvanmukti*)—as well as scriptural expressions such as "he becomes immortal here" and "he attains Brahman here"—which convey the attainment of liberation while still maintaining the body, are merely figurative, based either on the assumption that all future karma will be destroyed or on the basis of the most vivid direct realization (*aparokṣya*) of Brahman.

It is figurative; (for it does not refer to the complete establishment of the meaning of the word "liberation" even in a person possessing a body begun by past karma, because there is a contradiction in the simultaneity of being a living soul and being liberated—states consisting respectively of the connection with karma and the total destruction of karma). Therefore, by means of the scriptural declarations and the like which treat [the state] as if it were already established here and now through the designation of metaphorical immortality and so forth, those who are dull-witted—or unskilled (or "deluded")—become deluded, and being possessed of confusion, they [cling to] the doctrine of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*).
There are methods for pacifying the onset of diseases and other afflictions, such as giving gifts and performing worship;
even the Lord himself, through his own incarnations and so forth, taught that the one who has realized this attains the state of no further rebirth.

Therefore, the statement regarding the necessity of results for actions whose effects have not yet begun appears difficult to maintain; do not say so, for is it not the intention of the author of the Sūtras and others that there is indeed a necessity of results for those who have not performed expiation? 37.

Regarding the methods for the pacification of those past sins that initiate diseases and so forth—namely, those sins which bring about the experience of sufferings such as illness and poverty—there certainly exist means of prevention enjoined by the Smṛtis and other authorities, well-known through the traditional practice of the elders. What are they? They are acts such as giving and worship: the giving of wealth in the form of cows, gold, grain, clothing, and so on, to those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*); likewise, the special worship and other rites of the Lord which serve to ward off disease and the like; the consumption of medicine; and specific fire-offerings (*homa*) with sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, parched grains, and so forth. (These are the specific ritual acts.)

The Lord—the Teacher of the Gītā—declared that even for one who contemplates His own divine activities, such as His incarnations, there are means recognized for the destruction of even *prārabdha* karma; He sang of the attainment of freedom from rebirth (*apunarjanmatā*) even for a person devoted to reflecting upon the divine life of the Supreme Person, the Blessed One Himself.

By this statement, "My birth and action are divine... he does not undergo rebirth," for that reason—from the aforementioned cause—it appears difficult to reconcile that the scriptural teaching regarding the necessity of experiencing the fruit in an action undertaken when its effects have already begun (*ārabdhakārya*) is inconsistent; it is understood as being unconnected. (Thus one might object: "Do not think so; do not entertain such a doubt. For those who are not freed by expiation—that is, those who have not performed expiation (by means of *prāyaścitta*s)—"

Regarding "the necessity of the fruits" (*phalaniyati*) of those [karmas] that have already begun (*prārabdha*), namely their being avoidable only through experience—surely this is accepted by the author of the Sūtras and others; indeed, it has been admitted by the author of the *Śārīraka-sūtras* and others. ||37||

Such a doubt is certainly not correct; rather, this must indeed be done—namely, that these rites such as the *agnihotra* must be performed. This is because of the word "sacrifice" (*yajña*) in the passage, "They desire to know by means of sacrifice," whereby sacrifice and the like are prescribed by the text itself as a means for knowledge. Furthermore, it is because the rites of the stages of life (*āśrama-karma*), such as the *agnihotra*, possess the power to produce knowledge, either by removing obstacles or by bringing about the perfection of the very nature of knowledge. || 10 ||

"—0— Regarding *sarvāpekṣā*: In the section [of the Brahma-sūtras] beginning with *sarvāpekṣā ca yajñādiśruteraśvavat*, the author of the Sūtras stated that with respect to the worship of the Supreme (*parabhajane*), i.e., the meditation upon the Supreme Self (*paramātmopāsana*), rites such as the Agnihotra possess the status of being auxiliary members (*aṅgabhāvam*), meaning they have the character of being subordinate (*śeṣatvam*) by virtue of being helpful to that meditation. Now, [one might object]: Did the author of the Sūtras not indeed state in the Śārīraka [Sūtras], while this was the case, that "the Agnihotra and so forth are for the sake of that very [meditation] alone, because of the scriptural vision thereof" (*agnihotrādi tu tatkāryāyaiva taddarśanāt*)?"*

Thus, even in this present section (*prakṛtādhikaraṇa*), the author of the Sūtras declares that those works constitute a state of being auxiliary members (*aṅgabhāva*) with respect to supreme devotion; for this reason, [the objection] here—that "one" [section], namely either the *sarvāpekṣā* or the *agnihotrādi* section, is "in vain" (*mudhā*)—meaning useless (since the desired goal is accomplished by one alone)—is not correct. Such a suspicion is not sound, because in the preceding *sarvāpekṣā* section, the doubt was raised regarding the independence of knowledge (*vidyā*) from works, which would result in its lack of auxiliary support (*tadaparikaratā*) in the case of knowledge consisting of meditation (*upāsanā*).

The contingency that [meditation] would lack the status of being an auxiliary to ritual action—due to its inherent nature of effecting liberation as its own goal independently of anything else—is rejected; this is because [the inherent nature of meditation] has been established as not requiring dependence on ritual action. However, in the present context of the section concerning the Agnihotra and other rites, the very absence of such dependence is addressed: for one who has begun meditation and is possessed of knowledge, even while meritorious actions are being performed, their lack of auxiliary status—which depends on the inherent nature of those actions—is refuted.

Due to the reason of suspicion arising from apparent inconsistency, that inconsistency in the method [of exposition] is established—since the mutual distinctness of the two principles accomplished by the respective sections (adhikaraṇas), one of which is intent on refuting the absence of ritual subsidiaries for knowledge and the other on establishing it, is proven; thus, there is no suspicion of futility caused by redundancy. || 39 ||
The Section on the Destruction of Other [Defilements] || 11 ||
A Compendium of the Collection of Logical Principles Concerning the Body (Śārīraka)

Because of the presence of a different intended meaning—namely, that the phrase "from this body" refers specifically to the ordinary, worldly body—and because of the memory of multiple bodies, since it is established by the *itihāsas*, *purāṇas*, and traditional law (*smṛti*) that even for those engaged in the practice of yoga, the connection with various bodies serves as a means for experiencing the fruits of *prārabdha* karma; therefore, in the final body—that is, in the last body which constitutes the limit where the *prārabdha* karmas reach their complete exhaustion—for one whose samādhi is firmly arisen, [the state] is unshakable.

For that one wise person who possesses the perfect samādhi consisting of the experience of Brahman that has become manifest, liberation—the release from the shackles of saṃsāra—is accomplished. || 40 ||

Being impartial (*samāna*), they are free from partiality; and even karma—which is manifold (*vividham*), meaning of various distinct kinds, and beginningless (*anādi*)—referring to the karma associated with individual souls known as merit and demerit—is "equal" (*tulyam*), meaning it functions with equality, both here among the class of living beings and even toward the Supreme Person, Mukunda, who is disposed to bestow liberation. Thus, defects such as partiality toward certain souls, cruelty, and the like, do not exist—indeed, they do not exist at all—in Him.

Otherwise, if faults were admitted in the Blessed One, there would be a collapse of the scriptures—meaning that the scriptures which proclaim the Blessed One to be one from whom all defects have been eliminated would have their subject matter contradicted. Therefore, for this reason, regarding the granting of liberation to living beings, the pursuit of partiality—by resorting to some delay in time, such as a long interval, and [granting it] quickly to others—is not tenable; such is the objection.

Such an objectionable question is of little substance— extremely weak— because, when it is certain that the stream of karma— the web of actions stretching from beginningless time— is variegated, consisting of various distinct forms and natures, the inevitability of a difference in the timing of results— the distinction in the time for the production of fruits corresponding to the ripening of each respective action— is accepted (*āśritā*) by all systems (*sarvatantraiḥ*), that is, by all philosophical schools. || 42 || — 0— *Śārīrakanyāyakalāpasaṃgrahaḥ* ||
The Adhikaraṇasārāvalī.

The science of Brahman, when practiced repeatedly, results in the realization "I am [Brahman]," which may or may not manifest immediately in the symbol (*pratīka*). There should also be daily meditation (*praṇidhi*) upon the sun and other objects as being the Lord. Regarding sin and merit, there is their destruction and so forth; however, their state of being experienced persists as long as the *prārabdha* karma remains.
It is stated here that liberation occurs upon the cessation of that *prārabdha* through the practice of one's own chosen path.

*Brahmavidyā*—the knowledge pertaining to the Upaniṣads, consisting of the meditation upon Brahman—attains the status of being enjoined by the Śruti as a means to liberation only when it is repeated—that is, only when it has been performed many times; not when performed but once. This is because the knowledge in the form of meditation on Brahman must consist of the grasping of "I-ness" (*ahantva*) with respect to the object of meditation, Brahman (i.e., it must be "I am Brahman"); it cannot exist as something other than the meditator [for the Śruti says], "He does not know, for he is incomplete."

Because it is stated that [this] is not of the nature of *upāsanā* (meditative worship), it would not be appropriate to meditate upon a symbol (*pratīka*)—such as the mind or the name—which is understood as an object of worship for the sake of attaining a specific fruit, by identifying with it through the thought "I am the mind" or "I am the name. For instance, in the case of the subsidiary parts of a ritual (*karmāṅga*), one must apply the vision of the exalted (such as the Sun) to the inferior object which is the constituent part of the rite (such as the *udgītha*), but one does not apply the vision of the *udgītha* and so forth to the Sun and other such objects.

Because that would be improper, even *praṇidhi*—the means to liberation consisting of meditation—must be "with a seat" (*sāsana*), meaning it must possess a physical posture such as the lotus-posture (*padmāsana*) which is an auxiliary of yoga; (it should not, however, exist in states such as walking, running, or lying down). Furthermore, *praṇidhi* must be daily; the means called meditation must be practiced every day throughout one's entire life.

However, on a single day alone, there is no destruction and so forth—namely, both "destruction" (*praṇāśa*) and "non-clinging" (*aśleṣa*)—regarding the sin and merit, the evil deed and the good deed, associated with the living soul. Rather, in the immediately preceding section, it was stated that for both of those—merit and sin—in the case of a person whose work has begun (i.e., one possessing karma ready to yield its fruit), there is "state of being experienced," meaning they must be exhausted solely through experience.

"But for a person whose [past] effects have not yet begun, there is non-clinging and destruction" (IV.1.13). Regarding the duty of one's own conduct: it is the necessity of performing, as a rule, the Agnihotra and other rites by a person who is a practitioner (*upāsaka*), in accordance with his own caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*). And when there is the cessation of what has been begun—that is, upon the exhaustion of all *prārabdha* karmas—liberation occurs; liberation, consisting of the experience of the perfect Brahman preceded by release from all bonds, is established here, as was determined in the first quarter of the fourth chapter.
The Garland of Logical Connections.
Thus, in the first quarter of the fourth chapter, a summary of the connections of the eleven principles is presented in their proper order. (186)
Thus ends the first quarter of the fourth chapter. || 1 ||
Salutation to the illustrious Rāmānuja. Salutation to Śrī. Salutation to Śrīdhara.
The second quarter. || 2 ||

In the *Adhikaraṇasārāvali*, the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*) was skillfully expounded in the second chapter through its eternality, omniscience, and other attributes; then, in the third chapter beginning with "Awakening" (*jāgari*), the exhaustion of the great traveler through the forest of the world was described. Furthermore, that which is to be meditated upon by the supreme contemplator from the commencement until the conclusion of knowledge was stated;
finally, it describes the commencement of the departure for one who casts off the body at the end of their *prārabdha* karma.

In the second—namely, in the second chapter titled "Non-contradiction" (*avirodha*)—the nature of the sentient being (*jīvatattva*), which is included within the triad of reality consisting of the sentient, the insentient, and the Lord (*cid-acid-īśvara*), has been thoroughly (*nipuṇam*)—that is, correctly (*samyak*)—described (*abhihita*) and defined (*nirūpita*) by means of attributes unique to the individual soul (*jīva*), such as eternality, consciousness, and the necessity of possessing the quality of knowledge, along with its freedom from origination and destruction. Now, in the third chapter, [the nature] of the Great Soul of the universe...

For this individual self (*jīvātman*), who has set out upon a great journey on foot through the vast wilderness known as *saṃsāra*—being intent on wandering through the forest of existence without cessation—the mass of suffering (or the exhaustion) arising as it wanders through the states called waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and fainting, is also described [in the following verses].

— Having been described (for the sake of strengthening the engagement in the practice of the means), further—thereafter, in this fourth chapter, in its first section, for the meditator—the person engaged in meditation upon the Supreme Self which serves as the means to liberation—whatever else there may be that occurs in the interval between the commencement and the conclusion of knowledge—that is, taking the commencement of knowledge as the prior limit and the completion of knowledge as the subsequent limit, whatever arises as occurring in the middle, all that is required for knowledge.

Whatever exists for the sake of accomplishment has all been stated and determined here—in this fourth chapter, the second pada titled "Departure" (utkrānti)—at the conclusion of what has begun, when the exhaustion of those karmas set in motion to yield fruit has occurred without remainder, [the author] speaks of the commencement of the departure of the conscious being who abandons the body—that is, who relinquishes the final physical frame; he describes the process of departing from the body and setting out for the supreme state. || 1 ||

Although such agitation of the subtle body and the collection of organs has been described in the section on dispassion (*vairāgyapāda*), this connection is nevertheless made here for the purpose of making it known that death occurs even for one who knows Brahman at the appointed time. It is appropriate to state the general rule here in order to explain the specific details regarding his departure (*utkrānti*);
by mentioning death in the midst of the fruits of knowledge, he speaks of that which is dear to him. || 2 ||

Such a disturbance of the body and the collection of instruments—the agitation occurring in the physical frame and the aggregate of the senses, which is designated as "death"—is a specific state of unwell-being; although it is appropriate to describe it, it is to be treated in the first section of the third chapter of the *Vairāgyapāda*, which serves as a means for generating detachment.

(However, this is not the case in the *Phalādhyāya*, which is devoted to the attainment of the supreme goal of man. Nevertheless—despite the fact that such a description is necessary there according to the aforementioned perspective—the "connection" (*anubandha*) here refers to the detailed exposition of that description in the *Phalādhyāya*. Even for a person who knows Brahman—a knower of Brahman—death, in the form of separation from the body, occurs at a specific time; it is indeed unavoidable and inevitably arrives.

However, there is no immortality of the body whatsoever for one who knows Brahman. In order to produce this realization—that is, to generate such knowledge—it is stated here in this section that a distinction—the difference from the general case of embodied beings (consisting of exiting through the *nāḍī* at the crown of the head)—must be explained regarding the departure, the exit from the body, of that person who knows Brahman. Thus, there is a general statement concerning death, which occurs in a common manner for both those who know Brahman and those who do not.

Among the specific states described as the fruits of knowledge—specifically among those extraordinary results of the realization of Brahman, such as the non-clinging and destruction of good and evil deeds—the author of the Sūtras, while mentioning even death, describes that particular state called death and speaks of it as something dear: "Death also should be contemplated with affection by the knower of Brahman" (II.3.16). This is because death is instrumental for attaining the unconditioned essential nature, which leads to the attainment of the supreme state. Thus he says that death too is to be contemplated with love by the knower of Brahman. || 2 ||

Whether [the body] consists of the elements (*bhūta*) or consists merely of their conjunction (*saṃyoga*), and so forth—the investigation of such matters in the *Phalādhyāya* (Fourth Chapter) of the *Śārīraka* [Brahma-sūtra] serves as an aid toward some purpose, such as the establishment of the true nature of knowledge (*vidyā*). On this basis—that it functions as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) by being a means of accomplishment—all these points, which possess the sequence stated in the Śruti, are established and supported according to their fitness through the necessary application of reasoning.

Having stated that the individual soul (jīva) is eternally liberated, or alternatively that liberation occurs while still living— in order to pacify the agitation caused by various disputations and sophistries regarding the Vedas— he will describe the departure [of the soul] for the attainment of Brahman as being equal up until death, effective for the wise man through the exhaustion of prārabdha-karma, and further elaborating on the piercing of the channels (nāḍī-bheda), entry [into the heart], and so forth.

Those Advaitins or Sāṅkhyas who have declared the *jīva*—the individual soul—to be eternally liberated (*nityamukta*), describing it as possessing a natural and perpetual state of release; and likewise those who speak of liberation while still living (*jīvanmukti*), asserting that liberation consists in being freed from the bondage of *prakṛti* even while remaining in the body, or that it is based upon the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*)—all such talk is for the sake of peace, yet these discourses of the Advaitins and those called Kapilas are merely distractions that cause one to fall away from the path of truth.

By these [functions], the collection of Vedic words—which has been rendered to have non-established meanings—is brought to a state where the agitation in the form of an apparent contradiction residing therein is removed; thus, for both the wise and the ignorant individual soul (*jīva*), the "commenced action" (*prārabdha-karma*)—that is, the merit and demerit known as *prārabdha* which has begun to yield its fruit—becomes fruitful, meaning it continues to bestow the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth.

It is not fruitless. Having stated and established that "until the end of life"— meaning everything up to the departure from the body— is "equal," being the same for both the knower of Brahman and the other, [the text] begins with the entry into the specific channels and so forth,
starting from the entry into the one called the *mūrdhan* (the crown of the head) which bears the name of Brahman,
for the sake of the "attainment of Brahman"— that is, what is additionally required for reaching Brahman.
The knower of Brahman is distinct from and superior to others; this the author will state—that is, will describe—in this chapter. || 4 ||
Having perceived here his own life-limit through many desired [signs], whatever this yogi should do for himself and for his sons and others— since that cannot be inferred here, it is not mentioned;
even that which was reckoned in the Gītā and other texts regarding the final moment is according to the method of yoga previously described.
Having attained each respective [result] in accordance with its nature, it is determined; thus, one should here understand that the intellect remains as it was before.

That yogi— a person devoted to yoga in the form of the worship of Brahman— having observed through many diverse signs, such as omens, astrology, and other indicators that portend the undesirable, and having discerned the limit of his own lifespan (that is, death), whatever he should do— that which ought to be performed by him at the end of his life according to scripture or tradition— and whatever he should say regarding his son and others— his wife, friends, and so forth.

Whatever might be conceivable regarding what is to be performed and so forth, pertaining to this world and the next—that too, here, in the body, is not to be reasoned about, meaning it is not to be reflected upon; for that reason, there is no mention of those various specific matters, that is, no detailed exposition of them here, [as they are found] in the Gītā and other such works, beginning with the Bhagavadgītā.

Regarding that which was reckoned at the final moment—that is, what was declared as the task to be performed at the end of one's life—even such a category of matters was determined as something to be attained by one engaged in the practice of yoga in accordance with previous [preparations]. For this reason, having ascertained that "this is thus" according to the specific mode of yoga practiced previously, and in conformity with that, it was taught based on the ancient tradition, in a text dedicated to the instruction for the performance of yoga that has come down through the lineage, or in the established traditional practice. Thus, because it was taught as being fixed, it is certain.

In this regard, just as there was previously [the principle of] "prior cognition"—namely, that investigation itself, which precedes deliberation, must be performed in this section of the *Śārīraka* (Vedānta) as well—this is the established conclusion; it is to be accomplished through the contemplation of what is yet to be. 5.
Thus ends the introductory prelude to the commencement of the chapter.
The Adhikaraṇasārāvalī.

The group consisting of action, knowledge, and the senses does not undergo dissolution into the mind, because it does not originate from that [mind]; rather, since their functioning depends upon it, the word "sampatti" (merging/attainment) here refers to their cessation. This [interpretation] is not tenable, because if both were to dissolve, there would be an equal lack of resolution regarding the objection;
therefore, "sampatti" is merely a conjunction intended to establish the primary status of the words referring to the instruments and their objects.

The group of organs of action and organs of knowledge—the aggregate of the *karmendriyas* and *jñānendriyas*—does not undergo dissolution into the mind; that is to say, it cannot attain the state of dissolution within the organ that is the mind.

Because it cannot arise from that—since the group consisting of the organs of action and the organs of knowledge lacks the mind as its material cause (for dissolution in the form of merging occurs only in the material cause)—and because their function, which consists of the activity of speech and the other organs, is dependent upon it, that is, subordinate to the mind; therefore, "its cessation" means the stopping (withdrawal) of the activity of speech and the rest, as stated here in the context of departure: "Of this person who is departing, speech merges into the mind."

In the Śruti passage concerning the attainment of the collection of speech-instruments (*lik-karaṇa-grāma-sampatti*), the word "attainment" (*sampatti*)—as in the verb "he attains" (*sampadyate*)—is intended to mean "becoming manifest," that is, it says "it makes manifest" (and not that there is an actual merging of the nature of speech and so forth into the mind). Such an objection—that [the merging] is untenable because the mind cannot be the material cause (*prakṛti*) of speech and the rest, and thus merging is impossible even when describing the dissolution of speech and its functions—is neither appropriate nor consistent. This is because [in this context], the description of dissolution refers to the dissolution of speech and so forth, or their functions, [into the mind].

Thus, because the objection (*ākṣepa*) depends upon the mind, it is connected with that [mind]; and because the resolution (*nistāra*) and the refutation (*parihāra*) share the same logical status (*samānayogakṣema*)—since both the formulation of the objection and the formulation of the refutation are equal in both cases—for the sake of establishing the object of the instrument (*karaṇaviṣaya*)... in order to obtain the capacity of the word "speech" (*vāk*) found in the scripture to convey its primary meaning without resorting to metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—for indeed, the word "speech" cannot denote the function of speech by means of primary denotative power (*śakti*).

Therefore, if figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) were accepted, the primary sense would be lost; [the term] "attainment" (sampatti)—as in the phrase "he attains" (sampadyate)—refers to the attainment that constitutes the meaning of the verbal root, which is merely a conjunction, that is, a relationship in the form of contact, and not dissolution (laya). || 5 ||
The Garland of Logical Connections.

In this [chapter], there shall be two "boxes" (peṭikā) consisting of seven and four principles respectively, which have as their scope, in order, the general course and the specific course [of transmigration]. The reflection on the principles of speech and so forth is intended to refute the objection that there is a delay in the fruition [of karma] even at the end of what has been commenced, due to the uncertainty of the departure [from the body]. (187–188)
Thus ends the section concerning speech (vāg-adhikaraṇa). || 1 ||

It has been stated that the mind is a modification of food, as in the passage: "For the mind, my dear, consists of food" (*annamayaṃ hi somya manaḥ*), where the word *anna* combined with the suffix *maya*, which signifies a modification, declares that the mind is a modification of food. Furthermore, in the scriptural statement regarding the merging of the vital breaths, "the mind [merges] into the breath" (*manaḥ prāṇe*), which explains how the mind merges into the breath at the time of the soul's departure, the merging described therein is possible because the breath has water as its material cause (*prakṛti*).

Because a transformation is impossible—since the statement "prāṇa consists of water" establishes that prāṇa has water as its material cause (*upādāna*), and this relationship between material cause and effect remains uncontradicted—and because the sequence [of dissolution] is maintained by the rule "earth dissolves into water"—let there be a dissolution of that [earth] into prāṇa, which is of the nature of water and constitutes its own material cause (*svaprakṛti*). Thus, let it be a dissolution into its own source.

[The opponent] objects: "But [the mind] is not, as before, merely of the nature of conjunction. [The author] replies: "Not so"—such an objection is not appropriate. Regarding the scriptural statements concerning its being composed of those [elements]: the scriptural statement that the mind is composed of food (*annamaya*), the statement that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is composed of water (*apmaya*), and the statement that speech (*vāk*) is composed of fire (*tejomaya*)—these refer to their nourishment by earth, water, and fire respectively; that is, the nourishment of the mind, the vital breath, and speech (which is the manifestation of the capacity consisting in the fitness to perform their respective functions). [The text says] *abhimanute*: he intends.

It indicates the intended meaning [of the text], but not a relationship of material cause and effect (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*). Therefore—for that reason—here, in the case of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), as before—in the same manner as with speech and the mind—the thinkers of logic (*nyāya-cintaka*) describe the scriptural view, stating "the mind in the vital breath" (*manaḥ prāṇe*), as merely a conjunction, indeed a mere state of being joined. || 7 ||
The Section on Direct Perception. 4.2.3.
A Compendium of the Collection of Aphorisms on the Embodied Self.
The vital breath (prāṇa) would partake in the fire (tejas), and likewise [the soul] would hear sound;
however, this is not so because of the scriptural statement regarding the soul's departure, whereas the hearing of the breath by the fire occurs only later.

"Prāṇa"—meaning the air called *prāṇa*—should become a participant in fire; that is, it ought to become closely joined with fire. Not elsewhere, because of the hearing of the word in exactly that way: "prāṇaḥ tejasi. Since the hearing of the scriptural word is so clearly stated, this [objection] should not be raised—such a doubt cannot possibly arise—because of the words concerning the departure of the *prāṇa* along with the individual soul (*jīva*), which establish the departure of the *prāṇa* from the soul: "At the time of death, all the *prāṇas* [depart] from this self..."

They merge [into it], because of the existence of the scriptural word "they" (*iti*); as for the mention of heat (*tejas*), however, the statement "the breath [merges] into heat" (*prāṇas tejasīti*) is intended to show the attainment of the breath by heat, and it serves to establish the subsequent conjunction of the breath with heat immediately following its approach to the individual soul (*jīva*). || 3 ||

It may be so—it is possible—just as the Yamunā reaches the ocean by way of falling into the Gaṅgā: having fallen into the river Gaṅgā and thus becoming conjoined with it, when the Gaṅgā reaches the ocean, the Yamunā’s union with the ocean occurs through that conjunction; thus, like an indirect attainment, it depends upon an indirect acquisition, not upon a direct acquisition. || 8 ||

It resorts [to all three], because of the scriptural statement regarding their being made tripartite: "Of these, I shall make each one threefold" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.3); and because of the Smṛti: "Being then separate and without combination, they were unable to create beings" (Mahābhārata), due to incapacity—since the elements, when uncombined, are individually incapable of producing effects, and since it is impossible for the individual soul (jīva) together with its vital breath (prāṇa), which moves about as consisting of all the elements, to merge into light alone. [Note: Here, in place of "tattejasi," the reading "syāttejasī" appears more appropriate. This is a summary of the meaning of the section.

In the section concerning the elements (*bhūtādhikaraṇa*), having raised the objection that— based on the scriptural statement "the vital breath [merges] into heat" (*prāṇas tejasī*)— the vital breath, conjoined with the individual soul (*jīva*), merges into heat alone, it is stated that the merging occurs into heat conjoined with the other elements; for there is a scriptural declaration that the transmigrating soul consists of all the elements, as seen in passages such as "consisting of earth, consisting of water," and so forth.
The Adhikaraṇasārāvali.
Verses 10–14:

Here itself one finds Brahman; being immortal, he becomes Brahman in this very life through the scripture. For him who is established in Brahman, there is no departure [of the soul], for his departure and other such things are denied by the Upaniṣads. This is not for the sake of reaching another place, as there is no increase or decrease anywhere even in that which is superior to the qualified [Brahman].
Therefore, by virtue of the statements beginning with "immortality" (amṛtatva) here, such a state of that [condition] is described. || 10 ||

The one established in Brahman—the wise person who has directly realized the supreme reality—finds Brahman right here, in this very body; he attains Brahman and becomes immortal in this world—he attains liberation while still in this physical frame. This is because of the scriptural authority of such Vedic texts as, "Right here he enjoys Brahman," and "The wise man becomes immortal here. Therefore, for such a knower, the notion that there is an "exit"—meaning a departure from the body—is not tenable and lacks authoritative basis; thus, such an objection is incorrect.

For this reason—the movement and so forth of even one who knows Brahman: the movement of such a person, as well as their departure for that purpose, their arrival at the Virajā river, and so on—are taught by the Upaniṣads in such Vedāntic passages as, "Going upwards by that, he attains immortality," and "He comes to the river Virajā. These scriptural statements regarding movement, departure, and the like do not aim at the attainment of something else; rather, these Upaniṣadic declarations concerning movement and departure have as their sole purport the attainment of the Saguna Brahman, which is secondary to the primary [Brahman].

However, it is not correct to say that [this text] does not have as its purport the attainment of the qualityless Brahman (*nirguṇa-brahma*); for, regarding any object to be attained that is superior to the qualified (*saguṇa*), distinct from the qualified, or even more excellent than that—since no means of valid cognition (*māna*) whatsoever is observed [to establish such a thing] (for to accept any arbitrary matter even without a means of valid cognition leads to license and is equivalent to the ravings of a madman). Therefore, for the reason stated here—from the statements concerning immortality and so forth, such as "he becomes immortal here"—[it follows that the goal is indeed the qualified Brahman].

By such statements as "here one attains Brahman," that state—meaning the state of liberation which is similar to that [state of Brahman], namely the state of the knower of Brahman occurring immediately after the completion of meditation—is described, that is, made clear. || 10 ||
If the karma of one who knows the Supreme (paravid) were to dissolve entirely while still in the state of enjoyment, then the departure at death for the sake of reaching the goal,

as well as the persistence of the subtle body due to its atomic nature, would be rendered fruitless. Furthermore, regarding the objection that there must be a "meeting" on the path with a body appropriate to that [state], let it be so.
It must be stated that the complete cessation of ignorance depends upon reaching the supreme state, and so forth. || 11 ||

For those who have known the Supreme and realized Brahman, at the time of departure—that is, at the end of the body when the karma known as "evil" has dissolved entirely and perished without remainder—then, immediately after the fall of the body, for the sake of the journey—that is, for the accomplishment of the path beginning with light—the following would be fruitless: the persistence of the subtle body for that which is established as atomic—that is, for that which is proven to possess the dimension of an atom through its subtlety. [Otherwise] the pursuit of the subtle body would be useless; for while motion in the form of reaching another place from one place is unimpeded for an object of atomic form, it is indeed obstructed in the case of an all-pervading entity.
Thus, regarding the dialogue:

the act of conversing with the Moon during the journey is indeed seen in the Śruti; however, let that conversation take place by means of a temporary body produced on the path—specifically the *arcirādi* path—that is appropriate for such a form and conducive to the dialogue. When such an inquiry was raised, [the answer given] was that there occurs the cessation of all ignorance—the complete and total removal of every trace of *avidyā*—which is required for reaching the Supreme State (*parapada*).

"Dependent upon the attainment of the state of Brahman"—meaning "desiring the time culminating in the attainment of the Blessed One," and so forth—such statements must be spoken as the resolution to the question that has been raised. || 11 ||

At the beginning of the aeon, a body arises from subtle elements and the like, which is destroyed at the end of the aeon; it follows each distinct living being, being both determinate and indeterminate, and persists through gross bodies.
Known as the *liṅga*, it remains within the bellows-like [body] like a curved hook—thus is it proclaimed by the Sāṅkhyas.
The subtle portion of the original form is considered here to be the seed of the subsequent body.

At the beginning of the aeon—at the time of creation—it arises from the subtle elements and so forth; it is produced by the subtle portions of the five elements, the organs of action and knowledge, and the vital breath, mind, and intellect. It is perishable at the end of the aeon—vanishing at the conclusion of creation—and is fixed for each individual among the various classes of living beings, having a distinct nature established in every single person. It follows the unstable gross body, assuming various forms that are not fixed as one passes through different births according to the diversity of lives.

That which persists as a unity even through many gross bodies, abiding like a thread within a bellows, possessing a nature of hidden existence similar to a puppet inserted into a wooden frame—this is the body called the *liṅga*, the subtle body designated by the term *liṅga*, as proclaimed and described by the Sāṅkhyas (the followers of Kapila). In this regard, according to the Vedāntins, that subtle body is the subtle portion of the previous form belonging to the past.

A very minute portion of the most essential part of the previous body is accepted—that is, admitted in accordance with valid means of knowledge—as the seed, meaning the causal basis, of the subsequent body—the future body. || 12 ||

It is said that bondage dissolves through the knowledge of reality; yet, if this were not by way of transcendence (*utkramaṇa*), it would be as essence-less as saying "the mother is barren"—for such a claim regarding liberation while living contradicts one's own words.
If he is liberated here in this embodied state through the awakening to reality, then he is not a sufferer of suffering.

If that suffering is then considered false, tell me when you accept its reality. Through the knowledge of truth—the realization of the non-superimposed unity of Brahman and the Self—the bondage of saṃsāra, it is said, dissolves immediately upon the arising of that knowledge; it does not cease through the process of departing from the body. Thus, this view—that liberation occurs while one is still living—is devoid of substance and cannot withstand scrutiny, for [it contradicts] the doctrine of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti-vāda*).

In this conventional usage—"liberation for one who still possesses a body"—there is a contradiction of one's own statement (svavacanavihati), that is, a contradiction of one's own assertion, similar to the conventional usage "the mother is barren," which means "the mother is devoid of the capacity to give birth to offspring. [The term] *tanubhṛt* refers to the embodied conscious being (*cetana*).

If one is liberated here—meaning, if one has become detached from bondage even during the period of life—due to the realization of that [truth], that is, through the knowledge of reality acting as the cause, then, such a position being correct, this conscious being liberated by mere knowledge would not suffer—that is, would certainly not encounter suffering—in "that subsequent state," namely, during the period of life following the knowledge of reality.

(The suffering arising from hunger, thirst, and so forth, which is being experienced, cannot be denied. Then—at the time of living immediately following [the realization of] knowledge—if suffering were false—that is, if the suffering being experienced were unreal—when did you accept its reality? That is, when did you accept the actual existence of that suffering? Tell me! Speak clearly on this point: for you, who maintain that everything other than Brahman is false, [when is the reality of suffering accepted]?
Since [the world] is always false, what distinction is there in liberation while living (jīvanmukti)? — thus [it is asked]. || 13 ||
If it is argued that because embodied beings depart from this body while recollecting various states and thus go to those very states,
therefore the equality of the departure [of the soul] is not established— that is not so, because of the equality regarding the subtle elements (*tanmātra*).
For indeed, inequality occurs in the final cognition (*antima-pratyaya*) according to the principle of the distinction between types of knowledge (*vidyā-bheda*) and so forth.
In a doctrine based on mere partial similarity, a complete establishment of identity is not necessarily established.

(14) Embodied beings, possessors of bodies and consciousness, whatever state they remember—being those whose internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) have been permeated by the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of such and such objects—they leave this body, they abandon the body they have assumed (they die); they go to that very [state], they attain in the hereafter a specific body corresponding exactly to that. (Thus: "Whatever state of being one remembers when leaving the body at the end...")

"O son of Kuntī, being constantly permeated by that [thought], one goes to that very thing. This is established by the statement of the Bhagavad Gītā. Therefore, if it is argued that "equality regarding departure" is not tenable—that is, the lack of distinction stated concerning the departure from the body for both the knower and the ignorant is inconsistent—then that is not correct; such an objection is improper because the equality is established only insofar as it concerns the mere act of "departure from the body."

(Since the internal distinction between the departure [of the soul] and its movement is not denied), with respect to the final cognition and so forth—that is, the specific meditations on objects occurring at the very last moment of the body's end—there exists a disparity (as well as a similarity) by way of the differentiation of the types of knowledge (*vidyābhedanyāya*); for even while the internal distinctions such as being the "Knowledge of Being" (*sadvidyā*) or the "Knowledge of the Small One" (*daharavidyā*) are not set aside, there is indeed a mutual difference in their dissimilarity, despite their commonality in the form of being "knowledge of Brahman. (The general nature of departing remains.)

Indeed, in the discussion of some commonality (*sādharmya-vāda*)—that is, in a context where there is a description of similarity in some particular respect—the establishment of total identity is the attainment of complete equality in every respect (by way of statement); yet it is neither restricted nor fixed, (nor is it non-deviant). || 14 ||

In the section concerning the commencement of the journey (*āsṛtyupakrama*), having raised the doubt that "there is no departure for the knower" because of the statement "here indeed he attains immortality" (*atra brahma samaśnute*) in such passages as "then the mortal becomes immortal," [the author proceeds].

Since the departure of the knower is also seen in the passage, "Going upwards by that, he attains immortality," and because the scriptural statement beginning with "then he is mortal" is intended to establish that immortality—which consists in the non-clinging and destruction of subsequent and prior karmas—for a living being whose bodily connection has not yet been burnt away, it is stated that even for the knower there is departure, and that [departure] is the same up until the entry into the vein.

Since it is clearly stated in the sacred tradition that "the wise one attains Brahman here," the investigation into the logic of the river [of the subtle body] is for the purpose of resolving the doubt regarding the departure [of the soul]. (192)
Thus ends the section concerning the sequence up to death. 5.

It should not be suspected that [the organs] merge into those [elements] because they would be useless due to the absence of enjoyment and so forth, for it is taught that "they go to the light of the Supreme" (tejaḥ parasyām). Thus, this [objection regarding uselessness] does not apply. || 6 ||

Those subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*), being conjoined with the individual soul (*jīva*), are purposeless due to the absence of experience such as pleasure, because no specific purpose—such as the engagement in or withdrawal from activity—which is to be accomplished by means of a body, can possibly exist hereafter; therefore, their continued existence in association with the soul would serve no purpose.

Because of their existence, according to their respective fitness (*yathāyatham*); they may go anywhere whatsoever, but it should not be suspected that they do not merge into the Supreme Deity—that is, they do not become fully absorbed in the Supreme Deity, the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). This must not be so suspected; for it has been stated: "The light [merges] into light."

Because it is enjoined that "all subtle elements characterized by their respective locations merge into the Supreme"—that is, into the Supreme Deity, which is the Supreme Brahman, the highest of all deities—and because this is taught by the scripture in the form of the statement, "Light [merges] into the Supreme Deity," [this merging is distinct from the merging at the time of deep sleep and cosmic dissolution, as it serves the purpose of rest]. || 6 ||

The statement regarding the departure of the living soul (jīva) is applicable at the time [of death] for the wise one; however, the refutation of that [departure] is established later, following the departure of the elements (bhūta), as it would somehow find its connection upon their subsequent arrival.
Therefore, although it is common to all, that heart-yoga is established above;
even though this [yoga] is equal, the channels (nāḍīs) are unequal due to their different openings and the difference in the goals to be attained. || 15 ||

Regarding the section on the departure of the soul (*jīvotkrānti*): at the very time of considering the departure of the soul in general from the body, there is a refutation of that [departure] in the case of the knower (*vidvān*). That is to say, the denial of the departure from the body in the case of the knower of Brahman—who is a specific type of soul—is set aside; this is consistent and appropriate. This consistency arises after the consideration of the departure of the elements—that is, following the discussion of the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*) departing from the body—and occurs when the refutation of the soul’s departure in the case of the knower is being resolved.

In some way, there might be a connection for introducing the inquiry, though it would involve a strained interpretation; therefore—on account of the reason already stated—this "union with the heart" (*hārdayoga*), which is about to be explained as the union with the Self through the heart, even though it is common—that is, indistinguishable for both the learned and the ignorant—is established thereafter; that is, after supporting the departure of the soul from the body even for the learned, it is introduced and supported in this context of union with the Supreme Self by way of being the primary path.

Because they serve as the gateways to various paths, even though they are equal—meaning common to all—and despite the difference in the goal to be reached, which corresponds to the specific destination intended, the channels—that is, the vessels designated by the term "nāḍī"—are unequal; they possess distinct forms for the wise and the ignorant respectively (for the identity of the paths cannot be established merely on the basis of their being the single gateway to various routes). || 15 ||

When an embodied being strives to attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation, what is gained by attaining a subtle body for oneself, when that which is sought is found in the Deity who dwells within the heart’s core?

Therefore, let the established tradition remain as it is: "One's own light is [identical] with the Supreme. Even though this has been long established, let it be a restatement of what is already proven.
Let it not be so; for the sake of quelling fatigue, there is a transition to the Supreme, wherein the fruit arises from following [the path of] pride. 16.

When the embodied soul (*tanubhṛt*)—the living being (*jīva*) possessing the gross body—is about to depart, having emerged from the body, desiring to attain either worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*) such as heaven or liberation (*apavarga*) consisting of the realization of the Supreme Brahman; and when he has acquired his own subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*), which consists of the essential portion of the previous body that serves as the cause for the construction of another body; and when the Supreme [Consciousness] is residing, having taken refuge in the "good heart" (*supau*) known as the heart, which is the most subtle location— [The verse continues: "O Goddess, who art established in the supreme state, grant me that supreme state. This means: O Goddess, who art established in the supreme state—that is, in the nature of the Supreme Self (*paramātmasvarūpa*)—grant me that supreme state, which is the very nature of the Supreme Self. By this, it is indicated that the attainment of the Supreme Self is the ultimate goal. Alternatively, [it may be interpreted as follows]: "O Goddess, who art established in the supreme state," refers to the Supreme Goddess herself, who is established in the supreme state of the nature of the Supreme Self. Grant me that supreme state, which is the very nature of the Supreme Self. By this, it is indicated that the attainment of the Supreme Self is the ultimate goal. Or again: "O Goddess, who art established in the supreme state"—that is, in the nature of the Supreme Self—grant me that supreme state, which is the very nature of the Supreme Self. By this, it is indicated that the attainment of the Supreme Self is the ultimate goal. Or yet again: "O Goddess, who art established in the supreme state"—that is, in the nature of the Supreme Self—grant me that supreme state, which is the very nature of the Supreme Self. By this, it is indicated that the attainment of the Supreme Self is the ultimate goal. Or furthermore: "O Goddess, who art established in the supreme state"—that is, in the nature of the Supreme Self—grant me that supreme state, which is the very nature of the Supreme Self. By this, it is indicated that the attainment of the Supreme Self is the ultimate goal. Or finally: "O Goddess, who art established in the supreme state"—that is, in the nature of the Supreme Self—grant me that supreme state, which is the very nature of the Supreme Self. By this, it is indicated that the attainment of the Supreme Self is the ultimate goal.

Regarding the deity—that is, the Supreme Self, who is synonymous with the Supreme Deity—what is obtained through "attainment," meaning through the union denoted by the term *sampatti*? Is some previously unobtained new fruit attained? Nothing at all; therefore, let this "attainment" not be accepted. Thus...

Therefore, for the reason stated, let there be a restatement of what is already established regarding this very Supreme Self, which is eternally united even though it has been joined for a long time—let it be in the form of a restatement of a pre-established union—as in the scriptural fragment: "The light in the highest deity" (*tejaḥ parasyāṃ devatāyām*).

(But [the opponent] objects: "It does not mean that there will be a special attainment at the time of departure. [The author replies: Not so; such a doubt would not be correct. According to the authority of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), one must consider that there will certainly be some result or purpose, following the evidence that conveys such a meaning—this is what must be reflected upon by one who has faith in the scriptures. (One should not conclude its non-existence merely on the basis of one's own non-perception, for by doing so, one would ultimately resort to the path of nihilism. Thus, [it is said] "but rather... (*param*).

The transition into the Supreme Self is a form of union attained at that moment, a specific kind of meeting for the sake of quelling exhaustion—the fruit consisting of the removal of the particular fatigue born of the departure from the body. || 16 ||

—0— May there be attainment in the deity; let there be absorption (laya) therein, for she is the source of all. Furthermore, [the view that the soul is] "born from the non-existent" is untenable due to the defect of the incongruity of the expressed meaning (*vācyavairūpyadoṣa*). Nor is separation from the subtle elements possible here; moreover, the arrangement of creation is said to be complex, and even the journey through the path of smoke and so forth is described as being for those bound by existence (*bhavin*) who are aided by collyrium (*añjana*). || 17 ||

This is the merging into the Supreme Deity—stated at the end as "into the Supreme Deity [the individual soul attains] its radiance. Let this be accepted as the merging of the living being along with the subtle elements into the Supreme Deity, a dissolution (pralaya) consisting of the attainment of the cause; for that Supreme Deity is the source (yoni)—meaning the material cause—of the entire world consisting of effects, and is thus denoted by the term *bhūtayoni* (the source of beings), and is capable of creating again for the sake of a future course of existence.

It is incorrect to argue that [the Self] is capable even of producing a body—[on the grounds that] "indeed, the dissolution of everything into its own cause is natural and unimpeded"—for such a suspicion is improper. This is because of the defect of inconsistency in the expressed meaning (*vācyavairūpya*) with the term "attains" (*sampadyate*), which is understood from the preceding context; for in one case, the expressed meaning is "conjunction" (*saṃśleṣa*).

Since stating that "elsewhere dissolution is the expressed meaning" would result in the defect of breaking the structural continuity (*prakramabhaṅga*) by describing a discrepancy in the expressed meanings, the separation from the subtle elements—the division consisting of becoming distant from the subtle elements such as fire and the rest—is not appropriate here; it is not consistent with this context.

Because there would be the consequence of contradicting the future activity of going and so forth; furthermore, the postulation of creation is cumbersome—describing the creation of a body again for the sake of going and so forth by the Supreme Deity, who possesses all powers, would be vitiated by the fault of conceptual complexity. Moreover, even the movement of the transmigrating soul (*jīva*) who has not yet transcended the path of saṃsāra along the path of smoke and so forth—the procedure of traveling on the "Path of the Fathers" (*pitṛyāṇa*) described as "smoke, night, and likewise the dark fortnight," etc.—is stated to be by means of being enveloped by those [subtle elements], that is, through the embrace of the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*).

"Simultaneously"—this has been established in the section concerning the transition into another body (Antarapratipattyadhikaraṇa); likewise, on the path of the gods as well, the movement occurs precisely through being embraced by that [subtle body], and thus everything is well-established. || 17 ||

"There will surely be dejection regarding the excellence of others"—to refute such a doubt, there is the determination of the method of non-differentiation. (194)
Thus ends the section on non-differentiation (Avibhāgādhikaraṇa). || 7 ||

In the extremely subtle—that which is exceedingly difficult to discern—within the network of channels (*nāḍījāla*), that is, amidst the multitude of channels through which one must travel, the channel of liberation (*muktināḍī*)—the cranial channel that serves as the path for exiting for the sake of liberation—is not easily possible to distinguish, meaning it cannot be easily known through analytical discernment. It is by no means easy to accomplish.

It may be so; therefore, for that reason, the passage through the channel at the crown (*mūrdhanya-nāḍī-gati*)—that is, the entry into the Brahma-channel called *suṣumnā* located at the head—is certain for the person being liberated, who is attaining release. As for the scriptural statement, "A hundred and one... and so forth, let it proclaim immortality for one who goes upward by that [channel], since such an upward journey via the path of that channel is possible; thus, the potentiality of liberation is restated as a descriptive reference (*anuvāda*).

"It might indeed be so" (thus the opponent objects); "it is not so"—this is not appropriate. For one who desires to reach the supreme state, there is the easy attainment of entry through the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*), which occurs by means of the light of the grace of the Supreme Self—the grace of the Heart (*hārda*) whose heart is pleased with the devotee through the knowledge consisting of the meditation on Brahman—and by means of the illumination of the departure from the heart resulting from the entry into one's own channels. || 18 ||
It is indeed indeterminate and unsettled; the one known as the "Heart" is not self-dependent, for it is alone together with its own unimpaired perfection.
Abiding within the center of the heart-lotus, concealing his own body while dwelling as the householder of the seven worlds,

he— having measured out Suṣumnā, the sustainer of all, which extends from the navel to the crown of the head through the network of channels, and having projected it like an arrow shot through the central aperture— leads the seeker of liberation.

The Lord of the seven worlds—the Supreme Person who exists as the protector and master of the seven worlds beginning with Bhūr and ending with Satya; being independent—indeed not subject to karma—and alone—the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) who is preeminent within this aggregate of self, body, and senses; impelled by His own will alone; together with unimpaired prosperity—that is, with a wealth that is non-deficient, unrestricted, or free from limiting adjuncts, and which is eternal and irreproachable—He remains veiled.

His own body—his divine form, which is unknowable by those with physical eyes—abides within the heart-lotus of embodied beings, specifically in the pericarp of the lotus of the heart; thus, by his appropriate name "Hārda" (the Heart-abiding), he remains there through attributes such as being the protector and the controller (abiding with impartiality and neutrality, according to the teaching: "I am the same toward all beings"). Toward the seeker of liberation—one who desires release from the shackles of saṃsāra—he [is] natural, unsurpassed, and unconditional...

Or rather, desiring the bliss of union with his own sister, he—like a conscious archer—having raised the arrow, that is, having drawn the bow upward, desires to lead [her] to his own state; in the wheel of channels (*nāḍīcakra*)—within the immeasurable multitude of channels—he [seeks] the most preeminent one, which provides all support, which, by virtue of sustaining the entire universe, resides in the middle of the body between the navel and the head—that is, extending from the location of the navel within the body up to the head, she is the source of subsistence for all channels, [surpassing] the other channels.

And having pierced the *suṣumnā*—the channel of Brahman known as *suṣumnā*—which stands for the sake of others, and which, though its door is closed so that non-practitioners (*ayatīn*) may not enter, has had its door opened by His own resolve to grace His devotees; and having caused [the soul] to enter the cavity in the middle of that [channel]—having made it pass through the interior of the hollow within the *suṣumnā*—He becomes the leader, the one who leads [the soul] along the path beginning with light (*arcis*). || 19 ||
A summary of the meaning of the legal case.

Having raised the objection that the departure through the cranial channel (*mūrdhanya-nāḍī*) is uncertain— because the location of that abode is difficult to distinguish from other channels due to their proximity to one another, as in the statement "going upwards from there, one attains immortality"—
it is stated that the departure through the cranial channel is indeed certain, because the gateway has been illuminated by the grace of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).

—0— *Nayasaṅgatimālikā* Even though the destination is the same, when the channel (nāḍī) becomes difficult to discern, the doubt raised regarding its lack of necessity is removed by the principle of "that abode" (*tadoka*). Thus ends the section on "that abode" (8).

In the scriptural statement, "Now, when he departs from this body, then by these very rays he ascends upwards" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.5), that upward journey—the ascent to the destination which has been declared and clarified—which belongs to the yogin, the person who has perfected his meditation, by means of taking hold of the sun's rays—that is to say, by relying upon the solar rays—occurs even at night.

If it is argued that [death] by means of the improper method is impossible at night because rays [of light] are absent due to the lack of the sun, and that death during the day occurs only as a certainty when death itself is certain—and not for death in general—this is not so; such a doubt is not tenable, for indeed, even during the day, in the shade—that is, in places devoid of water—and likewise even at night (in times and places where the sun is not directly visible), [death is known] by signs, such as the perception of perspiration, heat, and so forth.

It is certain that the solar rays existing in sunlight are of a smaller magnitude compared to those [atmospheric] rays, as they can indeed be inferred by their presence; for if there were no heat—meaning if the perception of warmth, perspiration, and so forth were absent during the night of the rainy season (the monsoon)—then this absence of the perception of heat would be like a winter day, because even in the sunlight of the winter season, the non-perception of heat is caused by the predominance of water particles that overpower the rays.
This should be reflected upon and resolved. (Therefore, even during the night of death, the yogin indeed continues to follow the path of the sun. || 20 ||

A Compendium of the Collection of Logical Principles Concerning the Body (Śārīraka)

It perishes; in this—namely, in the attainment of Brahman by the wise man—there is no delay, that is, an absence of protracted time. This is what was stated in the Śruti: "Just for so long," meaning "only for so long is there delay as I am not yet liberated. Therefore—for this reason—that conscious knower, through knowledge in the form of meditation on Brahman beginning with the feet and consisting of devotion to the Supreme Self, attains the Supreme both by day and by night; he becomes one who has approached the Supreme Brahman.
One does not become subject to rebirth merely by dying at night. ||22||

Where the liberation of a single individual is reckoned by those who know the *jātaka* according to fixed rules, that must indeed be the final body; for from that [finality], there follows the exclusion of any other [subsequent] connection. Indeed, even at the time of death, there is no such distinction between day and night, nor between different locations, and so forth.

And in this regard, one should reflect upon such passages as, "They perform the funeral rites for him," and "Whether it be this way or that," and so forth. By astrologers who know the *jātaka* (birth-horoscopes)—that is, by those astronomers who, relying on the time of birth of an embodied being, contemplate its subsequent results—it is determined through calculation that for a certain person, in whichever body he has come to reside, liberation (*apavarga*) is reckoned as being necessarily and inevitably attained; such a body is like a *jātaka* that serves as the object of that certainty.

Indeed, that body is the final one, meaning it is certainly the last among the bodies used for its enjoyments; even from this—the certainty derived from the calculation of the birth horoscope—there occurs the exclusion of other connections, and the firm conviction arises that there will be no further connection with another body. In this regard, even concerning such a conscious embodied being, the distinction between day and night—that is, the disparity caused by the excellence or lack thereof in dying during the day or at night—is certainly not possible.

According to the reasoning stated above, distinctions such as the difference of place—such as "death in a superior field" versus "death in an inferior field," which would imply a distinction in the excellence of death based on location—are not possible at all. Likewise, even scriptural statements, like the reasoning, support this; for instance, the statement from the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, "Whatever they do for him here, whether it be much or little" (*yadu ca yadu ca na*), and specifically, "Whatever they do for him here, whether it be much or little" (*yadu caivā'smin śavyaṃ kurvanti yadu ca na*), establishes that there is no doubt regarding liberation even in the absence of the subsequent funeral rites related to the corpse.

This [verse], which is intent upon establishing [the point], should be contemplated: one must especially consider that which indicates the attainment of the Supreme Brahman by the yogi, even without taking into account the irregularities of time, place, and other factors, once the prārabdha-karmas have been exhausted without remainder. 22.

But it indeed exists; for this being the case, for this wise person who has cast off the body during the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana), there is union with the Moon (*indau sāyujyam*)—that is, the state of being conjoined with the moon as established by scripture. He strives for serenity; his waiting for the time of the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*)—that is, the waiting for the time of the northern solstice performed by the grandfather of the Kuru clan, the teacher Bhīṣma, for the sake of casting off the body—is indeed for the benefit of the world. Furthermore—there is something else that must be understood after careful discernment. He developed a unique and independent will, conforming to such a state and taking such a form; and he—Bhīṣma—became a Vasu. Just as he had previously been among the eight Vasus, so exactly did he arise again; this Bhīṣma was directly [born] from a body named Bhīṣma.

Having traveled by means of the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi-yāna*), one would surely attain the perfection of the Supreme Brahman; there is no doubt in this matter. The praise and censure regarding death during the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*) and its opposite refer respectively to the case of the knower and the case of others—namely, those who, desiring something other than liberation, perform sacrifices and works of public utility (*iṣṭāpūrta*).

Regarding the attainment of one's own path by one whose nature is the practice of dharma—which proceeds with total dedication toward the presentation of favorable and unfavorable times—the two paths indicated by the word "time" (*kāla*) in the *Gītā* passage, "At what time yogis attain non-return or return," are indeed the path of light (*arcir-ādi*) and the path of smoke (*dhūma-ādi*). They are not, however, of the nature of time itself; thus, everything is entirely beyond reproach. || 24 ||

Speech, however, merges into the mind—at the time of departure, the organ of speech, joined with the other organs, becomes merged in the mind (which is called *cetas*). Immediately after merging into the soul, it becomes merged into the light (*tejas*) along with the soul; and as for the light, its union with the others [occurs].

For the *tejas* (heat/light) that becomes united with the living *jīva*, there is not merely the state of being *tejas* alone; rather, it is the form of *tejas* conjoined with the other elements (the nature of having the subtle essences of all elements as its essence). 5) Equality up to that point—the departure [of the soul] remains undifferentiated for both the wise (*vidvas*) and the ignorant (*avidvas*) *jīva* up to this extent. Their going to the Supreme—the merging of the senses and so forth, ending with the subtle elements together with the *jīva*, into the Supreme Self—is the state of union denoted by the term "becoming one" (*sampatti*).

Furthermore, the meaning [of the word *sambandha*] consists solely in the nature of a mere relation suitable for expression by a term denoting conjunction; it does not, however, consist in the nature of being a cause or an effect. Regarding the rule of the cranial channel (*mūrdhanya-nāḍī-niyama*): the determination is that for the knower, the departure occurs only through the *suṣumnā* channel—which extends to the end of the head and is therefore designated by the term "cranial" (*mūrdhanya*). Regarding the rule of the rays (*raśmi-niyama*): the departure occurs precisely by following the rays of the sun.

The essential point is that "it is not otherwise. Furthermore, regarding "even at night, there is liberation for the virtuous": even upon death during the nights, for the virtuous—that is, for the wise—liberation is indeed certain; there is no absence of liberation even for conscious beings who die during the southern transit (*dakṣiṇāyana*). This is because liberation depends solely on the exhaustion of all *prārabdha* karma, and since that [exhaustion] is equal regardless of whether it occurs by night or during the southern transit—all this meaning has been contemplated by the author of this verse through this single quarter.

The other sense-faculties merge into the mind; that [mind], joined with them, merges into the vital breath (prāṇa);

that [breath], together with them, merges into the presiding self (adhyakṣa); and he, accompanied by them, merges into the subtle group of elements. The departure (utkrānti) is the same [in all cases], and the union with the Supreme is merely a state of contact.
Then, by means of the *brahmanāḍī*, one should emerge through the rays [of the sun]; thus, one is liberated from both the kingdom of night and the kingdom of the gods.

The other sense organ—meaning the ten organs of action and knowledge distinct from the mind—merges into the mind; that is, at the time of departure from the body, it attains merger into the internal organ in the form of the mind. That organ, which has taken the form of the mind, being conjoined with the organs of action and knowledge that have merged into itself, merges into the vital air known as *prāṇa* (the support of the life-force). That vital air known as *prāṇa*, accompanied by those [organs] along with the mind and the senses, [merges into the self].

Being thus endowed, it merges into the *adhyakṣa*—the individual soul (*jīva*), who is the lord of the instruments (*karaṇa*). And that [soul], being likewise possessed of all those [instruments]—the soul itself being joined with the senses, mind, and vital breaths—merges into the subtle group of elements, that is, into the aggregate of the five elements beginning with ether which exist in their subtle state. Departure (*utkrānti*) is the same: the departure described here, starting from speech and the other organs up to the mind, is of an identical form for both wise and ignorant souls; and furthermore, subsequently, there is union with the Supreme (*para*) for the soul.
The merging of the aggregate of the five elements into the supreme Brahman is merely a state of union; and that which is called "merging" is simply a relationship denoted by the term "union."

But dissolution is not in the form of merging into the cause; rather, the liberated soul—the one possessing liberation—should depart through the *brahmanāḍī*. That is, having exited by means of the *suṣumṇā*, which is designated by the term "Brahma-artery" and serves as the gateway, he goes upward along with the rays of the sun. Furthermore, even if he dies at night—that is, during the "night of the gods," the nocturnal period of the gods—he becomes a liberated soul, a wise person worthy of liberation.
