The third section (Gati-pāda) of the fourth chapter. Section 4.3.1: On the Path Beginning with Light (Arcirādy-adhikaraṇa). A Compendium of the Collection of Śārīraka Reasonings.
Because the scriptures contain many accounts of the path and because the texts regarding the route are diverse, there is no fixed rule concerning the path of light (arciḥ) and so forth;
therefore, there can be no such restriction, since signs such as the sun and others are possible everywhere.

This one—by whom this liberated Self is joined, and by whichever path He goes—is being honored with offerings presented by hosts of gods stationed along the way who pay homage with sounds of praise; such a One, leading us—who desire the attainment of the Supreme—to the further City on the shore beyond the ocean-like, difficult-to-cross expanse of ignorance called the realm of *prakṛti* (beyond darkness), [is] that which is called Ayodhyā, the Unconquered.

Singing the words, "The city of Brahman (Ayodhyā) stands beyond the firmament (nāka)," Muktighaṇṭāpatha—the royal road leading to liberation belonging to Mukunda—establishes and confirms through five distinct logical methods (nyāya-bheda), that is, five specific topical sections (adhikaraṇa), this city of Brahman in the third quarter of the fourth chapter. || 1 ||
It is taught in the various Vedic branches that the destiny [of the soul] differs according to the specific Upaniṣads studied;

thus, by the logic of the disparity in knowledge, the destiny (or path) itself is also diverse, and there is no fixed rule regarding the sequence beginning with *arciḥ*. This is not so; for when the recognition "this is that very same thing" is established here through various means everywhere, all matters such as deficiency or excess are proven to be non-contradictory in this context.

In the various branches of the Vedas (*śākhābheda*), such as the *Chāndogya*, *Vājasaneyaka*, and *Kauṣītaki*—which are portions of the "head" of the Śruti included within specific Vedic branches—it is taught (*adhīyate*) that there are different paths (*bhinnāṃ gatiṃ*), meaning distinct and mutually differing routes for the journey to the supreme state, for that person who desires liberation (*mumukṣoḥ*) and has attained knowledge of the Supreme Brahman through the desire for liberation. Therefore, the path of the one desiring liberation—the conscious being seeking release—is also [various].

Even the path for attaining the supreme state (*paramapada*) is indeed diverse (*viṣama*), having attained a distinct character (*vailakṣaṇya*) in accordance with the logic of the differences among the various forms of knowledge (*vidyā*) to be practiced for the sake of liberation. For this reason, there is no insistence that the sequence beginning with light (*arcirādi*) must be the very same path for everyone; such is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). However, such a doubt cannot possibly be correct, because [the path] is the same everywhere—in every specific branch of the Veda (*śākhā*).

When, through those various signs such as fire and wind that serve as the unique markers of the path, there is the establishment of recognition in this regard—that is, concerning the path to be traversed for the sake of liberation—such that the cognition in the form of recognition, which conveys oneness in the form "this very same path is that one," is attained (and when the certainty has been produced that "the path heard of everywhere is indeed one and the same"), then all [defects] such as deficiency or excess—herein [are resolved].

Regarding this matter, all instances of deficiency, excess, and so forth encountered here and there should be understood as not contradicting the established doctrine; rather, one should investigate and reach a conclusion in such a way that it remains consistent with the reality established through recognition (pratyabhijñā). || 2 ||

For Caidya and others, for Puṇḍarīka and others born as both mobile and immobile beings, for Bhīṣma and others whose worldly stations consist of the manifestations of the vyuhas arising from the sequence of their worship,
and for the creators and their sons upon the cessation of their office— may they all attain Brahman.
The departure of others should be considered as appropriate by those of sharp and expansive intellect. || 3 ||

Of the Caidyas and others—Śiśupāla and his ilk (who, having met their death at the hands of the Blessed One, became famous in the Itihāsas for being absorbed right there into the Blessed One); of the inhabitants of Ayodhyā, both mobile and immobile—those residing in the city of Sāketa (who, at the time of Śrī Rāmacandra’s ascent to the supreme abode, departed with him to reach the world of those who perform ancestral rites); of the sentient beings possessing bodies that are both stationary and moving; and of Puṇḍarīka and the others (who were led away by the Blessed One himself).

Of those distinguished devotees known from the Purāṇas, such as Puṇḍarīkākṣa and others—namely Bhīṣma and his peers, who were renowned in the Mahābhārata as the grandfather of the Kurus and the foremost among the knowers of Brahman—who, by virtue of being portions of the Vasus, attained the abode of the Lord through the acquisition of the status of a Vasu; and who, through the manifestation of their power arising from the sequence of their worship, abide in the worlds of the Lord’s manifestations such as Śrī Rāma and Śrī Kṛṣṇa, which serve as the successive bases for their existence in accordance with their mode of devotion, [and] Vāsudeva...

[This applies] to those who occupy the worlds of the manifestations of the Lord, such as Saṅkarṣaṇa and others; to the sustainers (*dhātṛ*), namely the infinite Supreme Lords (*parameṣṭhin*) authorized to maintain various cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*), who at the end [of their term] proceed from their own worlds to the supreme state (*paramapada*); to their sons—the Prajāpatis such as Marīci and Kaśyapa known from the Purāṇas as the sons of Brahmā, as well as Sanaka, Nārada, and others—who, upon the cessation of their office, attain the Brahman when their respective authority has reached its conclusion.

That same state—the manner of departure for liberation (*mokṣaprayāṇarīti*)—is understood through various Purāṇas, Itihāsas, and other sources, even for others besides those already mentioned, namely for those sentient beings seeking liberation; it is [described] by those of sharp and expansive intellects, whose minds are habituated to penetrating subtle objects like the tip of a blade of *kuśa* grass, and by wise ones possessed of vast knowledge that delves into the expansion of various distinct and ultimate truths, each according to their fitness—that is, in accordance with the actual reality residing in the subject matter.
"Cintanīyā" means that which is to be extracted and reflected upon; it does not mean that it is to be determined according to one's own arbitrary will. || 3 ||

It has been described; therefore, from that aforementioned propriety of meaning, this is demonstrated here: *nirvikalpam*—free from the opportunity for the defects of conceptual construction; *tadaikyam*—the very non-difference between the entity of Vāyu and the world-realm; and *ucitam*—that which is logical and appropriate. || 4 ||

Those mentioned in the Kauṣītaki-āgama—namely, "He [goes] to the world of Varuṇa, he to the world of Indra, he to the world of Prajāpati"—as established by the Kauṣītaki Śruti: Varuṇa, Śatakratu (Indra), and that Prajāpati who is heard of in scripture—even by straining the scripture, even by setting aside the sequence established by the Śruti which is understood elsewhere, they must necessarily be placed somewhere; otherwise, their...

Therefore, for the reason stated, it is improper to raise such an objection: "Since Varuṇa, Indra, and Prajāpati are mentioned immediately after the world of Vāyu—insofar as they follow the world of Vāyu in the sequential reading—they should remain there; that is, they should be placed immediately after Vāyu. This is incorrect, because of the connection [with lightning]. From the lightning...

From the connection consisting of proximity to the cloud, immediately after the lightning—on account of Varuṇa being "to be settled"—the subsequent Indra and Prajāpati, following the order of the text, follow immediately after Varuṇa. || 5 ||

As for the scriptural statement regarding this "Mānava" (the person of Manu) that he brings others to the goal here, that remains uncontradicted even if it refers to a good door; furthermore, there is an abundance of fitness for that scriptural statement in the case of [the lightning] being assisted by him.

And as for the one called "Mānasa" who is said to be the cause of reaching the world of Brahman after the lightning—that is not the leader, but another; therefore, one knows that the carrying across is accomplished by the person of lightning alone.

The state of being a guide to the Supreme—that is, the quality of leading one to the Supreme Brahman—belongs to the non-human (amānava) being known as the "luminous" (vaidyuta), who is characterized by non-humanity and is of a transportive nature (ātivāhika). This is what is heard here—in this context concerning the transport of liberated persons, from the scriptural statement: "That person is non-human; he leads them to Brahman. This means that the non-human person is the leader to Brahman; and even though there is the mediation of Varuṇa, Indra, and Prajāpati in the process of leading one to Brahman, this [status of being the leader] remains uncontradicted.

Even though it is not actually sublated—(for even if the primacy of the non-human person is established, there is no loss of the quality of being a "conductor")—nevertheless, when the state of being a conductor to Brahman has a non-human as its agent, and the status of Varuṇa and others as mere assistants is established, then in that scriptural passage (*tacchruti*), there is an exceeding consistency (*cityabhūmā*) with the meaning understood from the context (*prakaraṇa*). (This is because the agency of the non-human is natural. However, beyond that—that is, immediately after the luminous person (*vaidyuta-puruṣa*)—is mentioned the one called Mānasa, who is the cause for attaining the world of Brahman.

Because he is the cause for attaining Brahman, there is a specific person named Mānasa, who is established by the Śruti text: "The Mānasa person, coming from the lightning, leads them to the worlds of Brahman. From such a person known as Mānasa—that leader recognized as the one who causes [them] to go—the non-human (amānava) person is none other than him; he is not someone different or separate (he is indeed non-different).

[The soul] is indeed superhuman, yet it is mental. For that reason—from the aforementioned cause—the "carrying across" (ativahana)—that is, the action consisting of the form of the liberated person's vital breath which proceeds further and further by transcending each preceding boundary—is said to be by the lightning-person alone; those who contemplate the meaning of the Śruti describe this firmly as being by the lightning-person alone. || 6 ||

The meanings read as "flame," "day," "the waxing fortnight," and so forth, are indeed the marks for the journey; that is, they serve as the indicators for the path to be traversed for the sake of attaining the supreme state, because such is the nature of the instruction provided by the teachers.

(Thus he objects: "This is not so; this is not tenable, because from the word 'causing to go'—in the passage 'He leads them to Brahman'—we hear a clear statement indicating that the person of lightning is the one who brings the knower to Brahman. Furthermore, all those [deities] such as Light and the rest, who are heard of after the person of lightning—that is, other than the person of lightning—are indeed *ativāhika*s (conveyors)."
Those who are appointed by the Supreme Person for the purpose of leading the liberated souls (to the attainment of the state of Brahman) must necessarily be persons themselves. || 4 ||

"—it exists merely by way of the shadow of a common proverb: 'Having crossed this river and having taken recourse to this adjacent region of the mountain pass, this field is obtainable by you. It stands precisely because of its similarity to such sentences intended to instruct on specific paths established through worldly convention; yet, that it is likewise seen in the Śruti is not a ground for suspicion, nor is it logical [to claim otherwise], because in the case of words denoting time—such as 'day,' 'the first fortnight,' and so forth—which are capable of expressing time, the designation of a path-marker is impossible."

Alternatively, because the denotation of the word *bhūman* as "earth" is sublated; and in certain cases—namely, in the one called Vaidyuta (the Lightning) and in the one named Mānasa (the Mental), which are non-human—the two qualities of being a leader (*netṛtva*) and masculinity (*puṃstva*)—that is, both the state of leading to Brahman and the state of being a person—are clearly and without doubt understood from the scriptural passage: "He leads them to Brahman."

In the same way—as by the person of lightning and by others such as the day and so forth—the "carrying across" (ativahana)—that is, the bringing near [to the Supreme Self] in accordance with the command of the Supreme Self—is indeed what must be done (*kāryam*). In a case that is doubtful—that is, a subject matter which is a locus of uncertainty due to being stated unclearly—the "resolution" (*gati*)—the definitive interpretation—is derived from the remainder of the passage (*vākyaśeṣāt*), namely from another proximate sentence that has attained syntactic unity with it and functions as an auxiliary to the principal statement.

"They denote [the presiding deities]," so say those who know the principles—thus the Mīmāṃsakas have declared in the sūtra "But in case of doubt, [the meaning is determined] from the remainder of the passage" (*sandigdhe tu vākyaśeṣāt*). For words such as "Agni" and others, which are recited in the Śruti and other texts, denote—that is, they signify—the possessors of those names, namely the specific deities who are the respective presiding beings (*abhimantṛ*). || 7 ||

Having heard which [teaching], the flood of darkness belonging to those of the three-fold path—who fall away from or deviate from the Dharma—whirls violently upon the wheel of the mechanism of the ancestral stream; whereas for those non-returners who have heard of the Path of Radiance and so forth, that [Dharma] is shared there, and thus the words "day," "fortnight," "month," and so on, speak of it as being exceedingly difficult to overcome, unlike the other [dark] side.

Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma and the delighter of Dharma, upon merely hearing—that is, as soon as he received it through his ears—the description of that path to hell frequented solely by evildoers, fell down, having reached a state of fainting due to the pain.

He fell to the ground; that mass of darkness—that multitude of people of a great tamasic nature, fit for the blinding darkness—would rush toward, or pursue headlong, that most terrible path of hellish rebirth, driven by the whirlwind of his own karma, even though he belongs to the class of the three higher castes.

The supreme [state] for those sentient beings who, desiring various enjoyments known as worldly and otherworldly, along with the sovereignty corresponding to them and the appropriate stations and so forth, engage in the practice of dharma (being solely attached to rites for specific desires), is the realm called Pitṛvāna. Therein, like a water-lifting wheel (*ghaṭīyantra*) on a water-wheel, they revolve incessantly through repeated cycles of returning and turning back; thus it "whirls," being always characterized by an activity that is not under their own control.

This path beginning with light—famed as the route described by the Upanishadic texts in such passages as "They reach the light, from the light to the day"—is further delineated by the Śrutis, that is, the words of the Vedānta, specifically for those beings who have attained the means consisting of devotion (*bhakti*) and surrender (*prapatti*), which are capable of ensuring they do not return to the wheel of birth and so forth; it is thus described exclusively for such individuals. In that regard—such being the case—

The word *ahaḥ* (day), which denotes a fortnight, a month, and so forth—meaning the words for a day, the bright fortnight (*pūrvapakṣa*), the northern solstice (*udagayana*), the six months, and so on—just like other such terms, such as those for the Vaidyuta and Mānava [fires], expresses by its own function only those specific presiding deities (*abhimānidevatā*) who lead one to the state of the Supreme Brahman. || 8 ||

In the case of those who have performed meritorious deeds on the path beginning with smoke (dhūmādimārga), the attainment of the Moon was previously described; that other [attainment] mentioned in the section on the science of Nyāsa is union (sāyujya); and another view is stated regarding the lunar [attainment]. Here, another [attainment] occurs through the leading by the attendants of the Radiant Path (arcirmukha) to the Moon in the eighth [world];
thus is the well-established order for those whose hearts are attentive, and other subtle points are likewise understood.

Previously—in the section devoted to describing the path of those who perform sacrifices and other rites—regarding the virtuous, that is, with respect to the conscious souls intent on performing meritorious deeds such as *iṣṭāpūrta* and *datta*, the attainment of the moon—their reaching the moon, which is described by the passage beginning with "They attain the smoke" and continuing with "from space to the moon"—was explained as being of a different nature (distinct from the other path), because [that path] consists of the state of King Soma, who is the object of enjoyment for the gods; this was stated in the section on the *nyāsa-vidyā*.

"Therefore, they say that among all these [paths], none is superior to austerity"—in this context thus introduced, the *cāndra* union (*sāyujya*)—the attainment of being conjoined with the Moon—is taught as being of a different kind, distinct from the previously mentioned attainment of the Moon. It is established [in the text]: "Now, he who dies in the southern path, having gone to the greatness of the ancestors, attains union with the Moon. And that [union] [occurs when the knower], having rested for a short time on the path of Brahman...

Regarding the means of transport (*yānopayika*): here, within the passage of the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad* beginning with "They pass into the flame" (*te 'rciṣam abhisambhavanti*), there is the attainment of the moon—the perception of the moon mentioned in the phrase "from the sun to the moon. This consists in the attainment of the moon as the eighth member of the group of conducting deities (*ativāhika*) who lead those departing by way of the flame; it is distinct—that is, dissimilar—to others. It is in this manner, by this method, [that it occurs].

A firm and well-established state—meaning a stable and secluded abiding related to the attainment of the Moon—in this very manner; furthermore, whatever range of subjects is taught in various places by the Śruti in an unambiguous way yet might give rise to doubts regarding confusion, that must be properly inferred and ascertained by those with attentive hearts—that is, by those whose minds are focused and vigilant. || 9 ||
Some beings consider these few [beings] to be preceded by the lords of the earthly realm; for when there is identity of sound here, the formulation of other mantras for them becomes weighty.
And others [view them] through the perspective of Manu’s leadership as the Supreme Brahman who has attained his own station.
In that same way, they declared all these eternal servants of Vaikuṇṭha to be likewise eternal.

Certain wise ones, engaged in reflecting upon the meaning of the Śruti, consider these—the *arcis* (flame) and others—to be *ativāhikas* (conveyors); some living beings, however, believe them to be none other than Agni and the rest, the lords of the three worlds consisting of earth, atmosphere, and heaven, namely Vāyu and Āditya, who remain within the sphere of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāramaṇḍala*). In this view, since the identity of the word—meaning the non-difference resulting from the same sequential order of phonemes in the expressive term—is clear, here...

Regarding the objects such as fire and so forth, the postulation of other presiding deities for them—both for those within the cycle of transmigration and for others—is merely a conceptual construction; it becomes excessively heavy—that is, it is burdened by weight (this is beyond dispute). Furthermore, others—namely, those intent on contemplating the true meaning of the Śruti—view [the matter] from the perspective of the non-human being known as the *amānava*, who is the super-mundane person acting as the leader to the Supreme Brahman situated in its own state.

Since the Śruti reveals that [the path] leads to the Supreme Self situated in the highest ether, its eternity must necessarily be accepted—specifically, the state of being an eternal celestial being (*nityasūri*) conjoined with non-transmigration (*asaṃsāritva*). Just like those non-human beings (*amānavapuruṣa*), they described all these—the entire sequence beginning with the Rays (*arcis*) and so forth—as the eternal servants of Vaikuṇṭha; that is, they extracted and delineated them as being by nature non-transmigratory, the eternal attendants of the Supreme Person named Vaikuṇṭha who resides in that immutable, unsurpassed, and supremely radiant station called Vaikuṇṭha. || 10 ||
The section on the effect. 4-3-5.
This is the compendium of the branches of the Śārīraka-nyāya.
This is the destination for one who worships the Four-faced [Brahmā]; however, the attainment of the Supreme is achieved through the fullness of the Transcendent, which is attained eternally.
That [attainment] does not belong to one who worships the Supreme [in a limited sense], for according to the Śruti, that [limited state] is also unreal.
But even after that [attainment], there is subsistence, because both types of scriptural evidence are observed. || 5 ||

This is the path—the path beginning with light (arcirādi)—which is sanctioned by the Śruti for one who worships the Four-faced One, that is, for one who meditates upon Hiraṇyagarbha as the *kāryabrahman*. For it is he, Hiraṇyagarbha, who is indeed Brahman himself; having previously been unattained, he is worthy of attainment. Because he exists within a limited space, he is distinct from the Supreme—the eternal Brahman in the form of the *parabrahman*—on account of his being fully pervasive everywhere (*paripūrṇataḥ*) at all times (*satatam eva*).

And because [the goal] is attained everywhere—since attainment is established by itself and, being already present, cannot be reached through a prior movement—it is not correct to say that "this going by way of the path beginning with light belongs only to one who meditates on the Supreme," meaning only to one meditating on the Supreme Brahman; for both of those [assertions] are incorrect. This is known from scripture alone, by the very force of the Śruti: [it applies] to one meditating on the Supreme Brahman, and also to one who follows Him, who is of the nature of the Supreme Self.

It is well established that the group of conducting deities leads even one who meditates upon his own Self as liberated from primordial nature (prakṛti) by way of the path beginning with light; for this is seen from the scriptural evidence on both sides—having mentioned both types of persons in the passages "those who know thus" and "and those who in the forest worship with faith and austerity," the scripture shows the path of light and so forth in the words "they attain the light. || 5 ||

The reality of Brahman, which is the object of worship—here, in its own supporting locus—is certainly not unobtainable; indeed, it is by no means inaccessible (since an all-pervading reality is eternally attained by all). Because he dwells in the lotus (*sarasijavasatiḥ*), the four-faced one with the lotus-seat (*kamalāsana*), and because of his extreme proximity to Brahman due to being the first-born, he is designated as "Brahman" in the passage: "He leads them to Brahman."

The view that liberation—defined as the non-return consisting in the cessation of all ignorance for those who meditate upon the effected Brahman (*kāryabrahma*)—is "joined with him," namely with Hiraṇyagarbha, both as the one he meditated upon and as the one he has attained, because this is supported by authoritative scripture such as "All those [attain] together with Brahman," and so forth—such is the opinion of Bādari; however, it does not possess correctness, because of various scriptural passages...

Because of the contradiction [otherwise]: for it would be impossible to contradict the scriptural authority established by many Vedic texts regarding the abode of Brahman called the "Supreme State" and the departure to that state. || 11 ||

Jaimini has rightly determined that this path beginning with light (arcir-ādi) leads to the supreme abode because of the connection with the act of going and because the scriptural statement regarding Brahman is used in its primary sense;

however, something must be said here: it leads those who know the Supreme and are established in the Brahman associated with themselves, as well as those established in their own selves within their bodies, according to the distinction of their respective entrances, for these are all fully established in their goals.

The path beginning with light—namely, the path to Brahman consisting of light and so forth, accompanied by the conducting deities (*ativāhika*)—is established because of its connection with movement and other such factors; for the destination, which is the attainment of Brahman, is not sublated. Furthermore, because of the primary sense of the mention of "Brahman"—that is, since the designation by the word "Brahman" (in the phrase "he leads them to Brahman") is understood to be non-figurative—it leads them, that is, causes them to attain, the supreme abode, which is the very station of the Supreme Brahman. Thus indeed did Jaimini, the one named Jaimini, determine.

The Teacher has determined that this is correct—what was established by Jaimini is indeed logical—but something must be said here. There is something to be mentioned in this context: [if one asks] what it is—it leads both types of knowers of the Supreme (*paravidas*): those devoted to the Supreme Brahman (*parabrahmopāsakas*), who are established in Brahman as their own self (*svānvitabrahmaniṣṭhas*), meaning those who worship the Supreme Self as having their own individual self as its body; and also those established in their own self as the body of that [Supreme Self] (*taddehasvātmaniṣṭhān*), meaning those who worship their own inner self (*pratyagātman*) as being the body of the Supreme Self. He leads them to the Supreme...

The *ativāhika* group leads them to their destination; and these aforementioned two types of worshippers are distinguished by the difference in their orientation—namely, whether the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is the primary object of focus or one's own self (*svātman*) is the primary object of focus. They are indeed "complete worshippers" (*sampūrṇa-niṣṭhāḥ*), meaning they worship the whole [of Brahman] (since their status as worshippers of the Self remains intact), and not "incomplete worshippers" (*akṛtsnopāsakāḥ*) as described in the passage, "For this [Self] is incomplete. || 12 ||
This is the subject at hand:

those who would meditate upon individual souls—whether as conjoined with primordial nature (*prakṛti*) or in their isolated state—as they please; or even upon a multitude of insentient things through the vision of Brahman, or by means of some other perspective.
For all of them, having set their minds against [rebirth], will before long become fit for the higher path;
and this sinless journey, which is a sign of the meditation on Brahman, has already been indicated previously.

And those who, moreover, as worshippers (*upāsakāḥ*), should meditate upon—or worship—as they desire—that is, in accordance with their own inclinations—the sentient beings (*jīvān*) who are of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpān arthān*), whether they have deviated from *prakṛti* or not, whether they are mixed with it or alone, and whether they are pure or impure; and those who should meditate upon or worship those very same sentient beings through the vision of Brahman (*brahmadṛṣṭyā*), that is, by superimposing the state of Brahman (*adhyasta-brahmabhāvena*) upon them—whether they have deviated from *prakṛti* or are indeed merely [sentient]—and likewise those who should meditate upon even the mass of the insentient (*jaḍanivaham api*), the category of the non-conscious, by means of themselves...

Whether they worship by way of the [deity's] own nature, or through another perspective, or by superimposing it upon another substratum— all such worshippers, as previously described, being those whose minds are fixed on a mere symbol (pratīka), with their hearts attached to an object that has become their very body, do not possess the path to Brahman consisting of the escorting deities beginning with Light; for even these worshippers are "sinless" only insofar as the sixfold sin is absent.

Therefore, this path—the journey by way of the *arciḥ* (light) and so forth—is not for those who are remote from [the connection with] evil, but is suitable for those on the path beginning with *arciḥ*. It is the mark (*liṅga*)—that is, the infallible indicator—of the very practice of the meditation on Brahman (*brahmopāsana*) performed without interruption; this is made clear by the Sūtra: "And because of the mention of the path for one who has heard the Upaniṣads" (*śrutopaniṣatkagatyabhidhānācca*). || 13 ||

It was already summarized previously: first, the manner of reversion; then the culmination of the application of karma and so forth, which possesses specific determinations; the section on the divisions of knowledge; liberation through the power of supreme devotion; the pacification of obstacles; the determination of the final state; the attainment of rest in the separate paths of transmigration; and finally, liberation either directly or gradually—all this is to be understood as that which removes the inability [to understand], and which is not to be refuted by others. (14)

And by others—those who rely on other philosophical systems (even those established in the Advaita view)—there is an engagement in the means to liberation through desire in a particular state that is naturally established and free from ignorance; there is an unshakable inclination toward practice, characterized by specific regularity, conforming to the system of castes, stages of life, and so forth, and endowed with the various sets of duties pertaining to Karma-yoga or Jñāna-yoga; and for one who knows the distinction between types of knowledge, regarding the matter of death, [the distinction between] day and night...

The absence of specific distinctions such as the southern and northern solstices (*dakṣiṇāyana* and *uttarāyaṇa*); the attainment of rest upon reaching either solstice—whether at the northern solstice or its opposite, the southern solstice (*gatau*) occurring in death; the attainment of intermediate rest within both the sun and the moon; or liberation as it is divided according to whether it is "direct" or "gradual"—that is, direct liberation for those who worship the Supreme Brahman without mediation and are established in specific knowledges such as the *sadvidyā*, and [liberation through the specific knowledge] of those established in the particular form of the *madhuvidyā*.

Whether it be the attainment of the status of Vasu and other gods, or gradual liberation—this entire range of objects, being "unavoidable" by those who have no other way out (*agatikaiḥ*)—that is, by those for whom there is no other means of sustenance—is "not to be rejected" (*apraṇodyam*).

This means that, taking as its basis the fact that the soul's [return] is understood through the Veda, it must somehow be necessarily accepted as not subject to refutation. However, regarding that very object established by the scripture, the distinctions such as "empirical reality" (*vyāvahārikatva*) and "ultimate reality" (*pāramārthikatva*), which are merely imagined by themselves, appear to them as if they were the cause of difference. || 14 ||

Having reached this path traveled by the gods upon the final fall of the body, he transcends your hymns and crosses the celestial river there. Having obtained a divine body and the like, free from birth and dwelling, he goes to that abode of Viṣṇu;
blessed by his dialogue with Brahmā, he enjoys great honor until his ascent onto the couch.

At the end of the body—meaning at the final dissolution of the body—he who possesses consciousness, having reached and attained this very path of the gods—the path to Brahman established by the Śruti under the name "Devayāna"—having reached the worlds ending in darkness, that is, the individual manifestations beginning from earth and ending in darkness according to the manner stated in the passage starting with "Earth dissolves into water" and concluding with "The Imperishable dissolves into darkness; darkness becomes one with the Supreme Deity."

He transcends—meaning he oversteps and ascends beyond—all the collections of collective principles (*samaṣṭitattva*) that have been functioning as his own bonds since beginningless time; there, at the seat of the supreme state, he crosses—the divine river, the celestial stream called Virajā—and having crossed it (being thereby liberated from all attachment to *prakṛti*), he passes beyond it; having attained a divine body and so forth—having obtained the physical form, organs, and so on, which are unique to the supreme state—he becomes free from birth and dissolution.

Untouched by arising or destruction—that which consists of the sixfold attributes such as knowledge and so forth, which are beyond the range of speech and mind; the supreme word, the abode of Viṣṇu—the station of Mahāviṣṇu, the Primeval Person of the universe—he goes to, he attains. He partakes of, he obtains, the highly esteemed fulfillment of being honored by Brahmā, ending with the act of ascending the Lord’s couch. Fortunate through his dialogue with the Supreme Brahman, he becomes one designated by the term "fortunate" (dhanya) because of having obtained this [state] at the end, which was not previously obtained, through an immortal conversation with the Blessed One who has become the Supreme Brahman. || 15 ||

In the Saṅghāta hell there is no permanence whatsoever, nor is there any state such as earth and so forth; likewise, for the Blessed One of infinite and perfect power, nothing remains to be accomplished through postures such as the paryaṅka.
Even upward movement for the sake of attaining pervasiveness would be futile—such are the arguments of the logicians.
The Veda, independent and possessing marvelous meaning, shall silence those who prattle like intoxicated children.

In the case of a *saṅghāta*—a divine collection of elements (*bhūtasaṅghāta*) consisting of a multitude of parts (*avayavastoma*) that must necessarily be accepted by those who assert [the existence of] eternal *Vaikuṇṭha*—eternality, that is, an indestructible nature, can never be admitted anywhere whatsoever. This is because a conjunction of parts, being produced by action, is necessarily subject to destruction; for "being an effect" (*janyabhāvatva*) is the causal factor (*prayojaka*) for that which is delimited by perishability (*nāśatvāvacchinna*). If, on the other hand, eternality were admitted in such a collection, then it could not be the state of earth and the other elements.

Otherwise, earthness (*pṛthivītva*) and other such properties—which are invariably concomitant with origination and destruction—would not be tenable at all. Likewise, for the Supreme Brahman, the Blessed Lord, who is full and limitless in power, omnipresent, and endowed with infinite potency, there is nothing whatsoever to be accomplished by means of specific requisites such as couches, beds, and seats—(which, according to the Viśiṣṭādvaitins, possess the inherent nature of providing enjoyment for those who are incomplete and of limited power). Nothing at all remains to be achieved.

The fruit [of such action] is simply not possible; for the sake of attaining that which pervades all—namely, the attainment of Him who is all-pervasive—even the upward journey, the ascent by way of the path beginning with light (*arcis*), is fruitless, being entirely devoid of purpose. Thus, one should disregard the trivial and feeble chatter of the rationalists (*haituka*), who proceed according to their own whims, whose discourse is like the incoherent ravings of a madman arising from nowhere, and who are independent of the marvelous truth.

The Veda—that is, the word of the Vedas—which possesses its own intrinsic authority (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) independent of anything else in establishing a previously unknown object, would "extinguish" it—meaning it would leave nothing remaining. (For when one considers the authority of the Veda, which is entirely independent, no one at all could ever bring about a sublation of its meaning by means of mere reasoning, since such reasoning would only result in the appearance of contradictions. || 16 ||

Where existence and non-existence are both present without qualification, there is no contradiction; even when there is a contradiction regarding the pervasion of what is to be known, the establishment of one's own object occurs through valid cognition by virtue of its own superior strength. This is seen and desired by all; for if it were not so, there would be no other means of knowledge than direct perception, and sublation would occur either within perception itself or between two perceptions—just as the wondrous [event] of sleeping on a banyan leaf must be understood in this same way. || 17 ||

"It is indeed not to be denied" means that eternal glory (*nityavibhūti*) and so forth do not become objects for refutation. "Seen" (*dṛṣṭam*) means experienced even in the world regarding a particular object; "desired by all" (*sarveṣṭam*) means accepted by everyone in various contexts as follows: that which is made manifest within the scope of a particular object by a specific means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), which itself is a general means of knowledge—this [fact] would not be [possible] if it were not accepted by the *prāṇa* (the Veda) in the form of scripture concerning the subject of eternal glory and so forth; if that were so, then [it would be known] through perception (*adhyakṣataḥ*) rather than otherwise.

— Whatever else there may be besides perception, such as the words of a reliable person (*āptavākya*) and so forth, would not be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); it would simply not be a valid authority. There would be sublation (*bādha*) regarding perception: if the words of a reliable person and other such means, which are other than perception, were invalid, then sublation of the very perception that serves as their basis would become unavoidable. Or, there would be mutual sublation (*mitho bādha*): both inference based on universal concomitance (*vyāpti*) and the words of a reliable person would mutually sublate one another. [This is illustrated by the example of] "lying upon a banyan leaf"—having swallowed within his own belly infinite, endless world-systems (*brahmāṇḍa*).

Having established the form of the Lord’s reclining and so forth upon the banyan leaf, as well as His wondrous deeds—His marvelous activities well-known from the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and other sources—one should likewise infer in this manner: having considered the possibility that perception, inference, and other means of knowledge might contradict the subject matter known through scripture, one should reach a sound conclusion. || 17 ||
A Summary of the Meaning of the Sections contained in the Third Pāda of the Fourth Adhyāya:
A Compendium of the Collection of Śārīraka Reasonings.

The restriction [of the path] to the flame, the oneness of Vāyu and Svarga, the attainment of Varuṇa from lightning, and thereafter the state of being a charioteer (Śaṅkha); this fruit of the meditation on the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme (Brahman)—namely, this journey via the path of the Arcis and so forth—is all considered by means of this very quarter [of the verse]. (6–7)

1) However, there is a restriction regarding the "Agni" [arcis] and so forth: for the wise who are fit for the attainment of Brahman, at the conclusion of their final body, immediately after the departure of the soul from the body, the path consisting of the group of conducting deities beginning with light (arcis) alone constitutes the way to Brahman.

1) The restriction that [the path] belongs to no other; 2) the identity of Vāyu and Svarga—there is no difference in meaning between what is expressed by the word "Vāyu" in some scriptural passages and by the word "Devaloka" (Svarga) in others; 3) the attainment of Varuṇa from lightning—the station of Varuṇa occurs immediately after lightning; 4) the state of being a conductor thereafter—the nature of the light, day, and so forth, which are mentioned along the way, is precisely that of being a "conductor" (*ativodhṛ*) who leads the knower to the state of Brahman.

However, it is neither the signpost of the path nor the place of enjoyment; rather, this journey beginning with light (*arcirādi-gati*) is the fruit of both the meditation on the individual soul (*jīva-upāsti*) and the meditation on the Supreme Self (*para-upāsti*). This aforementioned path of light is obtained as the result specifically of the pure meditation on the Supreme Self—viewing [the soul] as the body of the Supreme Self—and not of meditations on effects or symbols (*kārya-pratīka-upāsti*). Thus, all these five points of meaning have been examined and determined with supporting evidence by this very section—the third quarter of the fourth chapter—which has been explained in this manner. || 6, 7 ||

The mention of the world of the gods (*devaloka*) would refer to the wind—provided that the word "world of the gods" found in the scripture is used as a designation for the very entity in the form of wind recited in the sequence beginning with light (*arcirādi*). Furthermore, the connection with Varuṇa and the others—the placement of Varuṇa, Indra, and Prajāpati—occurs only above the entity in the form of lightning situated on that path. All [stages] from light onwards, ending with the non-human being—all those mentioned along the way—are the leaders in the journey to the Supreme State (*parapada*).

They are the guides for the wise on their journey toward the abode of Brahman— the excellent bearers; this is that very path, the way beginning with light (arcis) as previously described, which is the "path of Brahman" (brahmapatha) to be traversed by those who know it— that is, by the worshippers of the Supreme Self— and not by those who worship through the perception of symbols (pratīka) and so forth,
as stated in the Śruti in this manner.

In the third section (pāda) of the fourth chapter—that is, in the third quarter contained within the fourth chapter—the path is described through five topical sections (adhikaraṇas); thus, the journey of the wise to Brahman has been deliberated upon. [18] By means of these topical sections—
The Fourth Chapter on Fruition (Liberation), Section 4-4. The Topic of Manifestation upon Attainment (Sampadyāvirbhāvādhikaraṇa). A Compendium of the Essential Principles of the Śārīraka [Mīmāṃsā].

It would be incorrect to say that there is a connection with liberation for one who possesses happiness in any form whatsoever, because [liberation] is characterized by constant perception and the absence of suffering; furthermore, this is evident from the word "by oneself" (svena). || 1 ||

Because it is eternally perceived—since one's own self is always apprehended by oneself—and because it is not [identical with] pleasure: for at the time of one's own self-experience, its nature as bliss is not an object of cognition; therefore, for the liberated soul (*jīva*) who has attained release from the shackles of saṃsāra, there must be a connection (*anvaya*) during the state of liberation with some particular form distinct from itself—a form that is the sole locus of happiness and the exclusive abode of bliss.

But that [attainment] does not consist in the acquisition of its own essential nature (*svarūpa*); for such a doubt would be unfounded—it would be incorrect—because [the self] is not concealed. This is because the word "by itself" (*svena*) refers to a state of non-concealment that is the opposite of the concealment occurring during the state of bondage; and because the specific qualification "by itself" is employed in reference to the self's essential nature even when the eight qualities and the contraction of knowledge-in-being (*dharma-bhūta-jñāna*) are present, since scripture does not intend for the self to be associated with any form other than its own. Thus: "He manifests in his own form. (*svena rūpeṇābhiniṣpadyate*)

From such a clear statement found in the *Chāndogya* Śruti, which serves as an indicator, [it is understood that] because [the nature] is not concealed during the state of transmigratory existence—since the meaning of the Śruti is merely the cessation of concealment of that essential nature which consists solely of bliss, which was previously concealed during the time of saṃsāra [before liberation]—[the liberated soul is identical with Brahman]. || 1 ||

The author of the Sūtras explains—demonstrates—by means of this final, fourth section on the fruit (*phala-pāda*), namely liberation (*mokṣa*), the "unconditioned great bliss" (*nirupadhika-mahānanda*) of the conscious self whose mass of adjuncts has been shaken off—that is, the entire collection of adjuncts such as karma and the like has ceased—for the liberated soul which is yet to come. In this section as well, he establishes this through three *adhikaraṇas* by means of three principles (*nyāya*) consisting of the *sampadyāvirbhāva*, the *avibhāgena dṛṣṭatva*, and the *brāhma* *adhikaraṇas*.

Self-manifestation (*svāvirbhāva*) has been described as "attaining perfection in one's own form"; this is the manifestation of one's true nature through liberation from concealment in the state of *mukti*. This is to be reflected upon (*cintya*)—that is, determined through inquiry—by means of the three subsequent sections (*adhikaraṇa*) known as "Absence of Volition" (*asaṅkalpa*), "Exclusion of Worldly Activity" (*jagadvyāpāravarja*), and "Freedom of Will" (*chanda-vṛtti*). Regarding freedom of will, it is stated: "He becomes self-ruling; he moves at will in all worlds. This refers to the independent movement during the time of liberation (which is nonetheless dependent on the will of the Lord).

[The text] "acting in accordance with one's own will" is to be reflected upon; thus there are two sections (*peṭikā*). These two sections exist as two forms of the three previously mentioned topics (*adhikaraṇa*). [The first is] "by itself," which is connected to the essential nature of the Self (*ātmasvarūpa*). This pair—namely, the manifestation of the essential nature and the unimpeded movement in accordance with one's own resolve—is not due to any limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), nor is it dependent on a condition (*upādhinibandhana*); rather, it is entirely dependent on the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), the refuge, whose resolve is true. || 1 ||

In the opponent's statement, it would be fruitless—that is, it would be useless—because the meaning is established even by the word "form" (*rūpa*) alone, without the word "own" (*sva*), since the object consisting of a specific physical form is obtained. || 2 ||

The wise declare that this abiding in the nature of one's own eternal Self is the "attainment" (abhiniṣpatti); they do not understand that this alone would be the fruit of knowledge, for [knowledge] is eternally established and not something to be produced. While an already established thing becomes a "fruit" through its penetration by what is to be accomplished—such as the destruction of ignorance and the like—or rather, it is the awareness of that which is already established; thus, the Sūtra beginning with "the liberated one" (mukta) and so forth is not contradicted here. || 3 ||

This is the manifestation—namely, the manifestation of one's own true nature at the time of liberation, as stated in the passage, "Having reached the supreme light, he manifests in his own form," which is eternal...

"Stability" (*sthiti*) means abiding in that very form which is the beginninglessly established essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the individual soul (*jīvātman*). Those who have said this—the Advaitins who offer salutations—[hold that] "that alone"—merely abiding in the beginninglessly established essential nature—would not be the fruit of knowledge (*vidyā*); that is, it ought not to be the fruit of practicing the means to liberation (*mokṣa*) prescribed by the Vedānta. They do not know, or rather, they do not understand at all, [the fact that] "but what is eternally established"—meaning that which is beginninglessly established—is supreme and "unattainable" (*asādhya*), [in the sense of] not being something to be accomplished along with an object that is yet to be achieved.

It is capable of attaining identity [with the goal], because there is no possibility of non-difference between the already established and that which is to be established, as they are mutually contradictory. Even though it is "established"—that is, even though the entity was previously established—it becomes the "fruit," having attained the state of being a purpose (having attained the state of being that which is to be accomplished), due to its permeation by the "to-be-accomplished" (due to the entry of the factor of the "to-be-accomplished" into it, because of the difference in its qualified form). That very "actualization," having attained the nature of the "to-be-accomplished," is the destruction of ignorance and so forth—the destruction of ignorance, which consists of the latent impressions of karma and primordial nature (*prakṛti*).

The complete destruction of the connection—of the connection belonging even to *prakṛti*, which is twofold in its nature as gross and subtle—is itself a qualification of the eternal Self; or else, "the realization of what is already established" means that the manifestation (*abhiniṣpatti*) is simply the cognition of the eternally established nature of the Self, which possesses such qualities as being free from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*). For that reason (*tat*), in this context (*iha*), the sūtra beginning with "the liberated [Self], because of the promise" (*muktaḥ pratijñānāt*) and so forth, is not contradicted.

[The objection] has been rendered fruitless. [This is because] since the portion pertaining to liberation—which serves as a qualifier of the individual soul—is connected with the status of being a goal due to its being something previously unestablished, there is no contradiction in the self, though beginningless, possessing the status of being a goal by virtue of its specific state as qualified by liberation. || 3 ||
At that time, the individual soul (jīva) shines forth with a greater degree of bliss than its own form which previously appeared as eternal;

even when there is merely the manifestation of its perfected state (siddha), the term "perfection" (abhiniṣpatti) is employed. This perfection of the intellect, described as the absolute removal of contraction, is said to be adventitious;
yet, even though it is an external adjunct to the unimpeded essential nature, the word "by itself" (svena) is used to denote it.

The *jīva*—the conscious inner self—at that time, namely at the moment of liberation (*mokṣa*), [is] superior to its own form which is eternally manifest—that is, to the form established as its own essential nature consisting of inwardness, favorability, and so forth, which is always appearing; (in comparison to that form,) superior—

By way of bliss—that is, by way of being exceedingly favorable (in the form of pure bliss)—it shines, meaning it manifests for itself. Even in the case of the manifestation of an object that was previously established yet unmanifested (upon the removal of its concealment), speakers employ—the usage of—the word "accomplishment" (*abhiniṣpatti*); they authorize its use (as in such expressions as "by this means, this object is accomplished"). This [is the point].

*Abhiniṣpattiḥ* (manifestation): Manifestation as understood from the scriptural statement, "He manifests in his own form" (*svena rūpeṇābhiniṣpadyate*), is the absolute cessation of the contraction of the intellect (*dhiyaḥ saṅkocātyantahāni*). It consists in the complete disappearance of that contraction which the knowledge—which is the attribute of the individual self (*jīvātman*)—has undergone during the state of transmigratory existence; it is the state of non-contracted knowledge. It is said to be adventitious (*āgantukā*), meaning it was non-existent during the time of wandering in *saṃsāra* and is attained for the first time only at the time of liberation (and therefore, it is of the nature of something to be accomplished). At that time—

At the time of liberation, even that manifestation of knowledge—which is free from obstacles and dependent upon the nature of the pure individual self (*jīvātman*), being devoid of intervening veils such as ignorance—is also [attained]. This refers to the apprehension of one's own essential nature through its own attribute of knowledge, characterized by the fullness of the forms of knowledge, bliss, and so forth. The word "by itself" (*svena*)—as found in the scriptural passage, "He manifests in his own form" (*svena rūpeṇābhiniṣpadyate*)—expresses this clearly. || 4 ||

Generally, whatever is seen within oneself, in one’s own embodied self who is a treasure-house of faultless virtues, or in the two-fold manifestation of His glory, becomes like a mere water-drop in the experience of liberation when attained through meditative absorption (*samādhi*). That entire [experience] becomes as sweet as the ocean of nectar overflowing from a multitude of jars;
therefore, he who says that there is no fruit in the illumination of one's own Self is a pitiful "well-tortoise" (a narrow-minded person).

In one's own [Self]—in the pure essential nature free from all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); in the repository of faultless qualities—in the storehouse of all auspicious attributes eternally devoid of even a trace of defect; in the embodied Self—the Supreme Soul who is one's own self without limitation—or in His two-fold manifestation known as the eternal manifestation (*nitya-vibhūti*) and the playful manifestation (*līlā-vibhūti*), that is, in either of the two types of manifestations of the Supreme Soul; for the most part—that is, predominantly—in *samādhi*, which is accomplished through long-term, uninterrupted meditation.

Whatever may be seen—that is, whatever is experienced—in that particular state called samādhi, all that which was experienced in samādhi becomes, within the ocean of experience belonging to the liberated one (muktānubhūti)—that is, within the experience of the liberated self—like a water droplet; it exists like a single drop of water.

All of that—everything combined, which constitutes the entire range of experience during the state of liberation (including both the nature of the individual soul and the Supreme Self, along with the multitude of their attributes and the two-fold manifestation)—manifests as something exceedingly sweet to taste, like an ocean of nectar mixed with a mass of sugar-candy; it expands as a form whose very essence is the relish of supreme bliss. Therefore, for the reason stated above, one who says that there is no further fruit in the self-manifestation of one's own Self at the time of liberation— [The sentence continues: ...[is refuted]. At the time of liberation, [the Self] manifests as the very form of the bliss of the Self, which is the object of the experience of the state of liberation. This is because, in the state of liberation, the Self shines forth as the supreme bliss, and since this is the ultimate goal, there is nothing else to be attained beyond it. Thus, the claim that there is no fruit in the self-manifestation of the Self at the time of liberation is untenable. This is because the Self, being of the nature of infinite bliss, is itself the fruit, and its manifestation is the final end. Therefore, the experience of the liberated state is indeed the fruit of all spiritual practice. Consequently, the statement that there is no fruit in the self-manifestation of the Self at the time of liberation is contradicted by the very nature of liberation itself. Hence, it is established that the manifestation of the Self at the time of liberation is the ultimate fruit. Thus, the objection is refuted. This concludes the discussion. A person who, out of ignorance, prattles that there is no purpose whatsoever once one's own true nature has been manifested, is like a "well-tortoise"—a tortoise existing within an extremely confined reservoir of water—and for that reason, he is merely a fit object for compassion (*ghṛṇā*), not worthy of investigation or the like. || 5 ||

Just as the Mallikā jasmine produces a pure flower at the proper time, free from the conditions that cause its coloring, so too does the Lord’s compassion produce a fruit equal to that of a perfected master (sūri), wherein all obstructions have been stilled. Therefore, because there is no conceptualization even toward that which is adventitious, this process of the internal self attaining its own inherent nature is described here for one who has achieved realization.

The *mallī*—the creeper known as *mallikā*—at the time when it is free from coloring adjuncts—that is, at the time of being released from adjuncts such as the *kiṃśuka* flower which imparts redness—produces, that is, brings forth, a pure blossom, meaning a flower of exclusively white color.

Just as the production of white-colored flowers by the *mallī* creeper—though established by its very nature—is interrupted in the interim due to the influence of external conditions (*upādhi*), yet upon the removal of those conditions, it proceeds naturally once again; in that same way, the compassion (*anukampā*) of the Lord—the refuge of all worlds—having extinguished the obstruction (*avagraha*)—that is, having eradicated all impediments (*pratyūha*) and brought about freedom from hindrance—produces a fruit equal to that of a *sūri*, namely the eternal [attainment] of Ananta, Garuḍa, and the other [Lords].

At the time when it is freed from the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) that causes coloring—namely, at the time when the limiting adjuncts such as ignorance (*avidyā*), desire (*kāma*), and action (*karman*), which produce attachment to the fruits of saṃsāra for the individual soul (*jīva*), have vanished—it brings about, or manifests, [the fruit]. Therefore, for this stated reason, even though there is an adventitious expansion of the consciousness-attribute (*dharmabhūtajñāna*) during liberation—a state characterized by the non-contraction of the intellect—and even though it has acquired its own nature at a specific later time (having previously been non-existent), because there is an absence of obstruction—that is, because no cause of destruction is applicable—in such a state...

—While [the Self] is innate and eternally imperishable, the "order of its own bestowal" (*pratyāpannasvadāyakrama*) is explained. That which is the son’s acquisition of paternal wealth and so forth, which is interrupted in the interim but obtained by right (*nyāya*) through its very nature—that is the "right" (*nyāya*). Here—in the context of liberation, regarding the manifestation of one's innate true nature—it is spoken of as having been determined through inquiry, concerning the *pratyak* (the inward-turned) who has attained perfection, that is, the inner self (*pratyagātman*) for whom the means to liberation have been accomplished. || 6 ||
Some, disregarding the distinction of liberation pertaining to the lower path (arvāñca), maintain that there is only the experience of one's own self;

in that case, it must be considered whether the realization of Brahman therein occurs through a limiting adjunct (upādhi) or by itself. Since defects exist in both cases, the term "liberation" (mukti) is appropriately used here only figuratively.
This same principle should be discerned by the attentive even regarding the various grades of liberation, such as Sālokya and the rest.

A few [others]—a certain number who subsequently engaged in the contemplation of the meaning of Vedānta—did not count the experience of one's own self alone—that is, the experience of one's own self as being solely the inner witness—as a particular kind of liberation (*muktibheda*); they determined it to be so. Regarding that matter, there is something to be considered: in that [state of] liberation consisting of mere personal experience, there is an obstruction to the experience of Brahman—an absence of the experience of Brahman—due to [the presence of] limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

It must be considered whether [the absence of the experience of Brahman] occurs "by itself" (*svataḥ*)—that is, is it caused by a particular limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), or is it inherent (*svābhāvika*)? This is the inquiry to be undertaken. For in both cases—whether the absence of the experience of Brahman is held to be adventitious due to a limiting adjunct or inherent—there are defects: in the case of the adventitious view, there is the impossibility of a limiting adjunct such as karma existing; and in the case of the inherent view, there is the impossibility of the specific self alone being inherently devoid of the experience of Brahman.

Thus, faults arise in both cases; therefore, for that reason, here—in the experience of one's own pure Self—the application of the term "liberation" (*mukti*), that is, the use of the word "liberation," is appropriate by way of metaphorical usage—that is, it is appropriate as being based on a secondary sense. This same method—this rule regarding the metaphorical nature of the word "liberation"—is to be discerned and determined by those who are attentive and skilled in reflecting upon the meaning of the scriptures, even with respect to the specific states known as *sālokya*, *sāmīpya*, and *sārūpya*.

Since liberation (*mokṣa*) is defined as the experience of the fullness of Brahman through the release from all obstacles, it is necessarily figurative (*aupacārika*) to apply that term to one who merely possesses proximity to it. || 7 ||

*Parānubhūti*: In the state of liberation (*mokṣa*), there is the experience of the Supreme Brahman. However, this must occur as a distinct existence separate from oneself; it does not occur through non-differentiation between Brahman and one's own self. This is because of the term "extreme similarity" (*atisāmya*)—as in the Śruti text, "The stainless one attains supreme similarity"—which establishes that for the liberated soul, there is only supreme similarity characterized by difference from the Supreme Self. Furthermore, this is indicated by the term "similarity of attributes" (*sādharmya*) in the *Bhagavad Gītā*: "They have attained similarity with me."

(Thus one might object: "At the time of liberation, because of the attainment of equality with the Dharma, it has been clearly stated that this—namely, the experience of Brahman as distinct from oneself—would not exist; for [the individual] is indeed of the nature of Brahman (due to the existence of the body-soul relationship)."

It must be so, because it is of that nature—this Śruti from the Muṇḍaka, "He attains supreme equality" (*paramaṃ sāmyam upaiti*), refers to the liberated self; it functions on the basis of the equality of its own qualities with the qualities of Brahman, due to the attainment of equality with those qualities. (Therefore, at the state of liberation, the experience of the individual soul regarding Brahman is "I am Brahman" precisely as non-different from itself, and not as something separate. || 8 ||

The aspect of manifestation is accepted as having separateness as its object; however, when the state of the body being the self—namely, the relationship between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme—is established and determined, then at this time, which is characterized by the non-constriction of attribute-become knowledge (*dharmabhūtajñāna*), the perception of that [Supreme] as residing in itself—the cognition of the Supreme Self as a distinct and independent reality—is not indeed joined with the nature of a pot. || 8 ||

If, as stated in the mantra, there were co-existence in the state of being the enjoyer, then Brahman would not be the Pradhāna; therefore, let it be so in the state of being the object of enjoyment, for that is appropriate given the Brāhmaṇa’s exposition. Even in both ways, since the reality of Brahman is one, anything else here would be distinct from it—this argument is trivial; for once difference is established, the avoidance of its remaining fixed in itself is what must be proven by the Sūtra.

The mantra states: "He enjoys all desires together with the wise Brahman. If this co-existence established by the section of the Vedic verse were intended to mean that the individual soul (jīva) possesses the status of an enjoyer together with Brahman—that is, if their companionship as enjoyers were accepted;

In that case, Brahman would not be the primary subject—just as in the expression "the father has gone with his son," the father is the primary subject while the son is not, so too here Brahman would not be the primary subject [and no Vedic scholar would ever concede primacy to the Supreme Brahman, the controller and owner of all]. Therefore, for the reason stated, let that association exist in the capacity of being enjoyed—that is, let the qualities of Brahman and Brahman himself be objects of enjoyment for the liberated self who is the enjoyer; thus, Brahman exists as an object of enjoyment.

Let there be concomitance in literature; however, this does not apply to the state of being the enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*). This has already been stated: "Concomitance is appropriate in the state of being the object of enjoyment (*bhogya*)," which is indeed logical. Furthermore, this is appropriate because it takes the form of an explanation of the Brāhmaṇa passage, "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" (*brahmavidāpnoti param*). [In that context,] the explanation of the meaning of the word *brahman* is "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite" (*satyaṃ jñānamanantaṃ brahma*); and the explanation of the portion "the knower attains the Supreme" (*vid... āpnoti param*) is "he who knows... (*yo veda...*).

"He enjoys all desires together with the omniscient Brahman"—since the consistency of this textual context is established only in the view that there is a coexistence of objects of enjoyment, then in both cases—namely, "being an enjoyer together with the individual soul" and "being an object of enjoyment together with its own attributes"—in this passage "he enjoys," the *itara* (the other) would be the individual soul (*jīva*), and it would be distinct from—that is, separate from—Brahman, which is the supreme reality known as Brahman.

The thought that "it is not non-distinct"—that is, this very reflection—is merely conventional (*vārtam*), resting on mere convention; it is not real. For when the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman has been established and determined through means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), reasoning (*tarka*), and so forth, the abandonment of one's own independent status—namely, the removal of the notion that the soul exists as something separate from Brahman—is indeed what is to be propounded here in this section, in accordance with the sūtra: "Because [the soul] is seen as non-different" (*avibhāgena dṛṣṭatvāt*). || 9 ||

Furthermore, that supremacy which is heard in the scriptures regarding equality is certainly not absolute; this has also been studied [in the texts], just as the statement that a stone and gold are identical when held on a balance scale is merely figurative.
Thus, while he remains in the state of possessing such a body, by virtue of the abundance of various uncontradicted scriptural authorities...
The statement beginning with "brahmavit" proclaims such equality, for it is likewise studied [in the scriptures]. || 10 ||

In this context, regarding the inner self that has attained the state of liberation, its equality (*sāmya*)—that is, its identity—with the Supreme Brahman constitutes its supremacy (*pāramya*), meaning it has reached the highest limit. Furthermore, as for that which is heard in the Śruti—"The stainless one attains the supreme equality"—and that which is likewise recited in the Śruti, namely the equality of the individual soul (*jīva*) with Brahman, even in every respect—that is, even in all the various modes inherent in Brahman—that too is certainly not un-studied; indeed, it is not unrecorded by name in the Śruti, [just as there is no difference] between a stone and gold.

Regarding the weighing of a piece of stone and a piece of gold—when they are placed in two pans of a single balance and their weight is being held, there is that statement: "These two, the rock and the gold, are equal. This is a statement of equality; it would be such that it perceives only the extent of the measure as it is without contradiction—that is, it concerns only the equality made by the mere quantity of measurement.

But it is not by means of abandoning the state of being a stone and taking on the state of being gold; for if that were so, there could be no statement regarding the attainment of equality between gold and its substrate, or between the stone and its substrate. In the same manner, here—despite the supreme equality of the individual soul with Brahman—the statement must have as its intended meaning the attainment of equality in all respects except those attributes that are not sublated.

(But it cannot possibly have as its purport the attainment of Brahmanhood by the individual soul through the abandonment of its status as an individual soul. Thus—according to the manner established by the means of valid knowledge such as Śruti and Smṛti; while the state of being the body of the Supreme Self—that is, the soul's being a body for the Paramātman—is firmly established by the force of numerous scriptural statements found in many places, which are free from contradiction by various other forms of evidence; and while this remains unshakable and firm, the statement "He is indeed Brahman," etc., [is to be understood].

Scriptural passages such as "He becomes Brahman itself," which appear to establish the attainment of Brahmanhood by one who knows Brahman, proclaim equality—they establish only similarity; they do not establish non-difference, because the word "tādṛk" (such-like) is also studied [in the texts]: for there is a scriptural reading of the word "tādṛk," which establishes similarity, in the passage: "Just as pure water poured into pure water becomes exactly like that, so does the self of the silent sage who knows become. || 10 ||
The Garland of Logical Connections.

Regarding the state of being pure consciousness (*jñānatve*)—that is, when the liberated self remains as nothing but the nature of pure consciousness—what fruit would there be? What fruit, consisting of a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), could possibly be accomplished in the state of liberation? For the reason that there would be none at all, such [a view] is what is stated in the Śruti: "He becomes just like that. The equality with Brahman (*brahmasāmyam*)—the equality of the individual soul (*jīva*) with Brahman—may be joined with the eight qualities, such as freedom from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) and so forth; let it be that which defines the nature of the individual soul. (This is the opinion of Jaimini.)

"By those [attributes] not entered into the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*), what fruit would be produced? Therefore, let the liberated soul consist of the manifestation of the form of pure consciousness—that is, let it have the nature of a manifestation whose sole essence is knowledge (this is the view of Auḍulomi). In this manner, both intended positions—the two views accepted by his own disciples Jaimini and Auḍulomi—have been explained one by one."

Because there is no contradiction between the two types of scriptural passages—the Chāndogya scripture in the form of Prajāpati’s discourse [teaching] freedom from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) and so forth, and the Bṛhadāraṇyaka scripture [teaching] the state of being a mass of consciousness (*vijñānaghana*)—having taken this lack of contradiction regarding these two attributes in the Self, and having "shaken off" or set aside [objections], and then, subsequently, having accepted on the basis of established reality the connection with freedom from sin and so forth as proven by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), as well as the nature of that [Self] as consisting of knowledge and its substrate, there occurs a twofold manifestation, accompanied by both forms.
Or, having manifested [the meaning], the author of the Sūtras joined it—without contradiction—to the liberated self. || 11 ||
The two terms *mukti* and *kaivalya* are recited consecutively in the lists of synonyms;

and since *kaivalya* is defined as the abandonment of association with anything else, how can there be a relationship between this [state] and its attributes (*dharma*)? Do not say so, for here there is indeed nothing whatsoever that exists independently of the nature of Brahman.

A substance cannot be devoid of qualities; thus, this pair of loci is free from flaw. Regarding the recitation of names—among the names being recited in the *Nāmaliṅgānuśāsana* (the grammatical treatise on gender)—the two words "mukti" and "kaivalya," which denote liberation (*mokṣa*), are synonyms. They are listed consecutively as a pair of words that produce a cognition having a single referent: "muktiḥ, kaivalyam, nirvāṇam, śreyaḥ, niḥśreyasam, amṛtam. And as for *kaivalya*—

Kaivalya, which is synonymous with liberation, consists in the abandonment of association with others—that is, it is precisely the release from connection with any other substratum (*dharmin*) or attribute (*dharma*). For this reason, one might ask: "How can there be a conjunction of attributes and substrata for this individual soul (*jīva*) that has reached the state of liberation? How is the association of Brahman as the substratum and of qualities such as knowledge as the attributes logically tenable? (Thus the objection is raised. It is not so—one should not raise such a doubt—because [the liberated soul] is not something other than the nature of Brahman, the Supreme Self.

"Distinct from its own nature"—here, within the two manifestations of the Supreme Self—there exists nothing whatsoever that is established in itself, that is, any object whatsoever capable of being perceived as existing separately from Brahman; indeed, there is nothing at all that exists apart from Brahman (as established in the previous section). Furthermore, "substance"—anything denoted by the term 'substance'—"would not be devoid of qualities"—it could never exist without attributes (as established in this section). Therefore, for this reason, this...

The pair of sections—the two consecutive sections concerning "being seen as non-different" (avibhāgena dṛṣṭatva) and "that which is called Brahman" (brāhma), which are under discussion—remains awake, being free from affliction and thus beyond the scope of any suspicion regarding the defect of determining a sublated meaning. || 12 ||

The summary of the meaning of the section (*adhikaraṇārthasaṃgraha*) regarding the Brahma-section: In the passage "he manifests in his own form," there arises the doubt whether that which is said to be manifested is (1) only the state of being free from sin and so forth, (2) knowledge alone, or (3) both. Having restated the opinion of Jaimini—that the liberated soul manifests in that very form because qualities such as freedom from sin are mentioned with reference to the liberated one—[the author proceeds].

Having presented the view of Auḍulomi—that because of the understanding from passages such as "a mass of consciousness alone" (*vijñānaghana eva*) that his essential nature is mere knowledge, and because words such as "freed from sin" (*apahatapāpmā*) refer to the absence of grief and so forth, he manifests in the form of mere knowledge—the author refutes both positions on the grounds that either would contradict scripture. He does so by asserting his own view: that he manifests in both forms. This is because the restriction in the phrase "a mass of consciousness alone" is intended merely to exclude the suspicion of partial insentience, and not to deny other qualities. Thus, both views are rejected.

In this regard, [the objection] would arise from the absence of the power of true resolve—because of the lack of true resolve; however, that [objection] does not apply to liberated souls who possess true resolve. || 4 ||

Just as the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of this entire universe proceed according to the will of the Universal Creator, so too here do the eternally liberated souls possess a variety of continuous successions of actions. Through their uninterrupted activity, these [actions] are distinct at every moment and flow in such a stream;
yet, the direct perception of that [divine] intellect remains constant and indivisible, like the cognition of Brahman.

Just as the uncontradicted construction of the birth, maintenance, dissolution, creation, existence, and destruction of this entire universe—the fashioning of the world by the Creator, the Supreme Self—coheres according to its proper manner, so too do those actions of the eternally liberated beings such as Ananta and others, of the eternal goddesses, and of souls released from bondage through the practice of spiritual means, which are established in the Śruti, cohere according to that same manner, due to the diversity in the continuity of their wills.

From a particular desire (*icchā-viśeṣa*) that persists without interruption, there arises *niyati*—an unbroken order. Here, regarding the subject matter described in the context of the state of liberation, such as "eating, playing, and rejoicing" or "if he is desirous of the world of the fathers," one must reflect upon this: by the very fact that the continuity of that stream of desire persists without interruption—that is, without being severed—it becomes, at every moment, of a distinct and different nature; and these [moments] belong to the eternal ones.

And the activities of the liberated ones are also such streams—that they must be understood as being real precisely because their nature is continuously extended without interruption.
