Regarding that cognition—the intellect which is the very attribute (*dharma-bhūta-dhī*) of the eternal and the liberated ones—its "immediacy" consists in its possessing the quality of grasping objects without obstruction; it is not, however, the state of being a cognition dependent on the senses. Being incessant—uninterrupted—and moreover indestructible—existing without ever being lost—it truly exists just like the knowledge of Brahman, the Supreme Self.
The days of obstacles belong to the virtuous, beginning with the lords of creatures (*prajeśa*), because their wills are true;

for we observe that in the case of human undertakings and desires, there is the creation of various other living beings and so forth. Therefore, the success or failure of these successions of desires belongs to these [beings] through merit and demerit.
As for the Lord who is liberated, His desire to act has an unimpeded object; thus, the gradation [of results] is not a fault. || 15 ||

Regarding the lords of creatures (*prajeśa*)—that is, those specific conscious beings headed by Prajāpati who have attained their respective offices through particular merit—the quality consisting of the state of having unimpeded resolve (*satyasaṅkalpabhāva*) becomes subject to obstruction (*pratyūhārha*). This is because, even when there is a desire for the creation of mortals or a desire to create human beings, there is the observation of other [factors]; for it is heard in the Upaniṣads and elsewhere that there is the possibility of creating various kinds of beings other than humans. Therefore, for these [lords of creatures], by the reason thus stated...

The fruitlessness—the presence or absence of results—of the successions of desires belonging to those persons authorized as Prajāpati and others, which consist in the persistence of their expressed inclinations toward specific tasks, occurs solely through the merits and demerits—known as good and evil deeds—of these very individuals. As for the "desire to act" (cikīrṣā) mentioned in the case of the liberated one, it is taught in the Śrutis with reference to the liberated self.

The supreme will known as *saṅkalpa* remains truly vigilant even when directed toward harmful objects, being entirely free from obstruction in its fulfillment of its own objective. There is a gradation—a mutual distinction among actions and the objects produced by them—yet this is not a defect; for it does not indicate the failure of the will, since that [will] is impelled by the diverse and distinct *saṅkalpas* of the Lord. || 15 ||

In the Sūtra, even one who is liberated is declared to have no other lord; therefore, by that very scripture which states "He is self-ruling" (svarāṭ), what other superior could there be for Him? Thus, the refutation of those [objections] established previously is [as follows]: Do not say so; for here, the status of being a subordinate is rejected only with respect to others than the Lord.
He who is recited as the Self, the Lord, and the Master of the universe—His status as Master is indeed unassailable. || 16 ||

In the *Śārīraka-sūtra*, in the aphorism "And for this very reason, he has no other lord" (*ata eva cānanyādhipatiḥ*), even one who is liberated—one who has attained release from saṃsāra—and even though he is a conscious being (*cetana*), is declared to have "no other lord"; that is, it is established that he is devoid of any other person who might govern him. Therefore, by this indicator—the state of having no other lord as established in the sūtra—who could be his subordinate? Or who could be the master of the liberated soul? There is none at all; he is self-sovereign (*svarāj*).

Furthermore, it has been stated by the Śruti itself that He is self-effulgent—He is taught in the Upaniṣad as "He becomes His own sovereign" (sa svarāḍ bhavati). Therefore, for this reason, there is the release (*vihati*)—that is, liberation—at the time of emancipation, of those attributes of consciousness previously established and supported by the Śruti and other means of valid knowledge, such as being subordinate to the Lord and dependent upon Him.

(Regarding the doubt that there is no continuity: It is not so—such a doubt is not correct. Here, in the Sūtra "ananyādhipatiḥ" and in the Śruti "sa svarāṭ," that which is prescribed as being based on evil karma—the state of being subordinate to others, meaning the lack of independence for the sake of others toward other living beings and so forth, excluding those who are the refuge of all—is cast off or removed at the time of liberation. Furthermore, he who is described as the Lord of the Self and the Master of the universe is read as: "the husband... (partim).

The Supreme Person is declared by the scripture, "He is the Self and Lord of all," as the ruler of all selves and the one to whom everything is subordinate (*śeṣin*). Furthermore, His status as their Master—which consists in being the determiner of that subordination—is never sublated; it does not cease even in liberation, because His essential nature, which depends on His own being, never undergoes any decline. (16)
The Garland of Logical Connections.
Thus, when the sovereignty of the liberated one consists of all enjoyments, this objection—that this is merely cyclic existence occurring in succession—is thereby refuted. || 210 ||
Thus concludes the section concerning the mental resolve (saṅkalpa). 4.
The Section on Non-existence (Abhāvādhikaraṇa) || 4.4.5 ||
A Compendium of the Collection of Principles of the Śārīraka [Upaniṣads].

The liberated one is bodiless because of the word "bodiless," yet he possesses a body at will because of the scriptural statement "in many ways. This is not a fixed rule; rather, due to the word "in many ways" and the hearing of [the possibility of] manifold enjoyment, this [possession of a body] must be voluntary. The liberated one—the conscious being who has attained liberation from saṃsāra—is indeed bodiless, devoid of a body, because of the word "bodiless"—namely, because of the scriptural testimony making known the bodilessness of the liberated one: "Verily, neither pleasure nor pain touches one who is bodiless" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.1). (This is the first position. Alternatively, the liberated self possesses a body at will—he is one who assumes a body dependent solely upon his own volition.

[The opponent says: "He does not possess a body dependent on karma, nor is he bodiless; for there is the scriptural word 'in many ways' (*bahudhā*), which indicates a plurality of bodies—as evidenced by such Vedic passages as 'he becomes one-fold, he becomes three-fold,' and so forth. This is the settled conclusion: neither of the two alternatives—namely, being strictly bodiless or possessing a body not dependent on karma—is individually established, because of the word 'in many ways,' which indicates a connection with multiple bodies, in the form of the statement 'he becomes three-fold.'"

And because of the scriptural statement regarding experience: "Beholding these desires with the mind, he rejoices"—since scripture teaches that the attainment of enjoyment occurs through the mind alone even without a body, this assumption of a body would be voluntary; it would be merely a product of his will, not something fixed. || 5 ||

"He becomes one" refers to the possibility of becoming manifold—the state of existing as distinguished by various bodies—which has been studied and handed down in scripture (*āmnāta*). This includes singing *sāman* hymns, playing, and so forth; even activities such as wandering about (*vihāra*) have been mentioned. As taught in scriptural passages such as "Singing the *sāman*, laughing, and playing," there are two traditional views (*ārṣa matadvandva*) consistent with those [two] types of scriptures. Rejecting—that is, setting aside by removing the restriction—the two positions held by the sages named Bādari and Jaimini, [the author speaks of] the independent one...

For the liberated self, who is no longer subject to karma, both states—both bodilessness and embodiedness—are possible; that is, they are indeed conceivable. This is his own view—the intention of Bādarāyaṇa, the author of the *Śārīraka-sūtras*—which the author of the Sūtras, Bādarāyaṇa, makes explicit with the sūtra: "It is of both kinds, like the twelve-day sacrifice. All of this—that is, everything stated concerning the liberated self—[is thus established].
—Just like the Supreme Brahman, even for the liberated self which is equal to that [Supreme Brahman], its existence would arise from karma—it would indeed be dependent upon karma. || 17 ||

Since merit and the like are absent in liberation, the state of being devoid of a body conditioned by them is not a defect; nor is the position that there is a beautiful body in that state—where suffering has ceased and the body is abandoned—contradicted. If this were so, one might ask: "What kind of state of the liberated is described here by the Sage? Do not say so; for there is an underlying intention here in establishing the rule regarding the voluntary assumption of a body. || 18 ||

In liberation—that is, in the state of liberation—due to the absence of merit and so forth (meaning the non-existence of the two types of karma consisting of merit and demerit), there is the state of being devoid of a body conditioned by those [karmas]—that is, the liberated one’s freedom from connection with a body bound by karma (the view of Bādari). This is not to be refuted; it is not subject to rejection. Furthermore, when that liberated self is free from a body that is the locus of suffering—that is, when it has abandoned the connection with a body that causes the experience of suffering—even the position that it possesses an auspicious body is [not to be refuted].

Even the position that the liberated soul possesses a body composed of auspicious elements (as accepted by Jaimini) is not subject to sublation—it is not open to refutation. This being the case—since both positions are irreproachable regarding the matter of the liberated soul’s body and its absence—in this section, what kind of state of the liberated soul would have been formulated by the Sage Bādarāyaṇa, or in what form would it have been determined by the Sūtra? (In this regard, there is no room for any definitive conclusion whatsoever.)

[If one objects: "It could not be so; therefore, the commencement of this section (*adhikaraṇa*) is indeed purposeless"—to this doubt, we reply: "That is not correct. Such an objection is improper because the intention of the author of the Sūtras here lies precisely in establishing [the Lord's] independence—namely, in supporting the position that there is no fixed necessity regarding either having a body or being bodiless for one who possesses the aspect of assuming a body based solely on His own will (since the section would otherwise be rendered meaningless). || 18 ||

If there were multiple bodies simultaneously for a person who has attained equality with Brahman, then it would follow that their pervasive nature is inherent in them, which would entail the loss of their prior atomicity. This is not so; for since pervasion is established by the fact that the world is permeated [by the soul], and since this is the cause [of such pervasion] as seen in the case of Saubhari and others, one is not able to reject this equality with Brahman on the grounds of [the soul's] movement. (19)

For a person who has attained equality with Brahman—that liberated soul who has reached supreme identity with Brahman—if there were multiple bodies simultaneously, that is, if indeed many bodies were to exist at one and the same time, then it is appropriate that there be a connection with their pervading essential nature; that is, the bodily activity would consist of a connection precisely with the nature of the individual soul (jīva), which is capable of simultaneous pervasion by all those bodies.

(An objection is raised: "Because one becomes fit [for liberation] by being a sustainer (*nirvāhaka*), the abandonment of the prior atomicity follows; that is, the destruction of the atomic dimension—which was established as the soul's dimension at the time of bondage—must be admitted at the time of liberation. Therefore, it is only logical to accept the omnipresence (*vibhutva*) of the soul in liberation. (Response: This is not so. It is not at all logical to admit the relinquishment of the soul's natural dimension in liberation, because its pervasiveness through cognition is established—that is, the individual self's pervasion by means of its attribute, which is knowledge (*dharmabhūtajñāna*).

Since the all-pervasiveness [of the soul] is established by the scriptural text, "And he is fit for infinity," the expression regarding the entry into the world—namely, "He attains everything in every way"—which describes the soul's entrance into the entire universe, becomes meaningful as being based on that very cause of non-pervasion; it is thus intentional. Furthermore, there is the equality with Brahman—the equality of the liberated self with the Supreme Brahman known from the scripture, "He attains the highest equality"—and the state attained by Saubhari and others.

It would not be capable—that is, it would not at all be able—to refute or invalidate the manner of simultaneous pervasion across multiple bodies, which has been established as the specific nature of the Self in the case of Saubhari and others. || 19 ||

In former times (during the state of *saṃsāra*), due to the instrumental cause of the power of yoga acting as the motive for assuming many bodies—in the act of taking on various bodies by Saubhari and others—the bondage of karma (the connection with merit and other karmas conducive to that end) must also be taken into account; that is, it must be required as the motive for the assumption of multiple bodies. (For such assumption of multiple bodies is well-known in the Purāṇas and Itihāsas not for all yogins or even for all sages, but only for certain specific individuals such as Saubhari and others. || 20 ||
By such power of yoga— that is, by the power bestowed by the omnipotent Lord—
the power of volition residing [in that power] is designated as the "knower of the field" (kṣetrajña) by the sages; it is enveloped by its own karmas.

Even though the intellect (*buddhi*) of the person (*pums*) is partless, it is indeed admitted to undergo manifold transformations; let that be so. However, according to the statement "for the sake of the child" (*bālāya*) and so forth, this [intellect], though atomic, would also be infinite; yet it could not be liberated, because its transformations have been discarded by the Jains and others, and its uniformity remains unimpaired. (21)

The power known as the *kṣetrajña*—the power in the form of the individual soul (*jīvātman*)—is said by the sages, such as the seer Parāśara and others, to be "enveloped," meaning covered, by its own actions (*svaiḥ karmabhiḥ*), that is, by those actions designated as merit and demerit (*puṇya-pāpa*) which are termed "ignorance" (*avidyā*) and serve as the means [of bondage]. This is established in the statement: "By which the power of the *kṣetrajña* is enveloped. It belongs to the person (*puṃsaḥ*).

The intellect, which is designated as the attribute-knowledge (*dharmabhūtajñāna*) of the person (*puruṣa*, i.e., the *jīva*), although partless—that is, devoid of constituent parts—is accepted by you as possessing manifold transformations; that is, it is admitted to be subject to contraction and expansion through various formal modifications, being at the time of bondage characterized by contraction dependent upon karma.

[It is said that] at the time of liberation, [the intellect] possesses natural expansion; and that which serves as the substratum for such an intellect is the *jīva* itself. Let it be so—let it indeed be accepted that, although inherently partless (*niravayava*), it is the locus of various modifications consisting of contraction, expansion, and so forth. What is the harm? Even though the *jīva* under discussion is atomic—that is, possesses the nature of an atomic dimension—it becomes liberated upon attaining the state of liberation, according to the scriptural passage beginning with "A hundredth part of the tip of a hair... and continuing: "And that part divided a hundredfold again... [and so on].

"Jīva is to be known as a part, and it is capable of infinity"—from this authoritative Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad text, one might suspect that the jīva could be infinite—that is, it should be accepted as having an all-pervasive dimension (*vibhu-parimāṇa*). [To this we reply: It cannot; the jīva is atomic and cannot be all-pervasive. This is established in the *Asambhavādhikaraṇa* (the section on impossibility), which refutes non-Vedic schools such as the Jainas who maintain that the nature of the self undergoes modification; for the jīva remains fixed in its state of being changeless, having set aside all transformation.
Because of the non-departure from uniformity—since one must not admit the departure from the state of being changeless and uniform (i.e., the occasional occurrence of change). || 21 ||
For when the individual soul departs one by one, withering occurs in the branches of the tree; therefore, in this case where the veil has been removed, the primary infinity would be unconditioned.
Let it not be so; for in the branches, abandonment consists in the destruction of the limiting adjuncts that determine the locus of experience.

By the logic of the field and so forth, because of the absence of conceptual construction (abhimati), this [cognition] would be "learned" (adhīta) and possess the capacity for movement (jaṅghāti). || 22 ||
The intellect explains:

for the *jīva*—the Self abiding as the presiding deity of the tree—it is indeed by relinquishing each part one by one—that is, precisely through the abandonment of each individual portion that constitutes the tree—that wilting, meaning the occurrence of dryness (or saplessness), arises in the branches—that is, in each of the individual branches belonging to the tree—as it is said: "When it sheds a single branch..."

This has been stated by the scriptural passage beginning with "Then she withers," and so forth. Therefore, because of the indicative evidence that [the soul] remains in another part after abandoning a portion of its own body, there is "infinity"—the state of having unlimited dimensions as declared by the scripture, "And he is fit for infinity"—which exists directly without resorting to a medium, namely, the medium consisting of the attribute of knowledge (*dharma-bhūta-jñāna*); this primary infinity resides in the very nature of the Self when the soul has its covering removed—that is, when the concealment caused by karma has ceased and its true form has become manifest.

"It is fitting that [the soul] should indeed be non-limited" (this is the objection); "it is not so"—from the perspective of the soul's own essential dimension, it is entirely improper to suspect that the Self undergoes modification; for what is called the "abandonment" in the branches—that is, in the parts of the tree—is indeed the relinquishing of connection with the individual soul, namely the destruction of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) which determines the locus of experience and the constraints thereof; it is simply the liberation from the association with the limiting adjuncts known as merit and demerit, which establish the conditions for the soul's own experience of pleasure and pain.

(But for the individual soul [jīva], there is no pervasion of its own nature over the entire tree, because of the absence of pervasion over one part and its remaining in another part, etc. This "leaving" refers to the verbal root *hā* heard in the expression "he leaves the branch. According to the logic of fields and so forth—just as there is the common usage of a person such as Devadatta "leaving" gardens, fields, and the like—it occurs due to the absence of identification (*abhimati*), that is, due to the relinquishing of the conceit of ownership regarding that object (whether caused by one's own effort or by the will of the Lord), which serves as the causal agent.
It would have been studied—that is, recited from the Śruti—but not by means of pervading its own form or excluding it. || 22 ||

Those who wander like the fool Kakṣīvat, claiming that the Self is "one yet not one," "distinct from the Supreme yet not distinct," "liberated by its own nature," and "the enjoyer of all its desired objects by itself"— let them examine the contradiction of their own words, the subversion of hundreds of Śrutis, and the fact that their various assertions have other intended meanings;
then, even if they harbor the pride of supporting the Jaina view, let those who wish to abandon strife take refuge in the True Path.

The liberated one—the conscious being who has attained release from the bondage of *saṃsāra* (the soul in the state of liberation)—by its own nature, that is, directly through its own essential form without the mediation of its attribute of knowledge (*dharmabhūtajñāna*), is both one and not one: it is of an undivided form due to the absence of various distinctions, yet it is also of a divided form by virtue of possessing those [distinctions]; it is both separate and not separate from the Supreme—possessing distinctness from the Supreme Self and yet devoid of it—solely by virtue of its own will, which is independent of the will of the Supreme Self.

By determining the nature of the liberated soul according to the method described—that it is the enjoyer of its own desired remnants and possesses the state of being the enjoyer of all activities regarding the objects it has craved—it is shown that those who wander like a "pṛthuka" (unripe grain) or a "kṣība" (intoxicated person)—meaning those who are like children or the intoxicated—or those certain self-styled philosophers who possess either non-comprehension or erroneous comprehension, such philosophers face a contradiction within their own words (svoktibādha), that is, an internal inconsistency within their own statements.

[He has] effected a crushing blow and a refutation of hundreds of scriptural passages—namely, the clear contradiction of his own doctrine arising from many scriptures proclaiming the plurality among individual souls (*jīvas*), the distinction between the individual soul and Brahman based on the relationship of ruler and ruled, and the non-identity between the world and Brahman based on the relationship of created and creator; [and he has achieved this] by demonstrating that those [scriptures] have other intended meanings (*anyaparya*)—specifically, that the scriptures concerning the non-difference among souls intend to convey the lack of difference in essential nature (*svarūpa*) caused by their being of the form of knowledge (*jñānākāratva*), and [the same regarding] the individual soul and Brahman...

Setting aside the stubborn adherence to alternative interpretations that you yourself do not accept—such as the view that the Śrutis concerning difference intend to convey the conventional usage of non-difference based on the similarity of knowledge, bliss, and so forth, or the relationship between body and self, or their non-separation from Brahman; and the view that the Śrutis concerning the non-difference of the world and Brahman intend to convey a specific qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*) based on a fixed relationship of qualifier and qualified—you should examine this with proper discernment. Even if one relies on the Jaina perspective, the dispute arising from such views is mutually contradictory.

By taking recourse to the ideal of the Jains—who serve as the primary exemplars in the acceptance of the Dharma—they have removed the mutual friction among various teachers whose minds fail to penetrate the true reality; let them take refuge in the path of truth and, having resorted solely to the way conducive to the realization of the Existent Reality as propagated by the venerable Rāmānuja, may they become peaceful. 23.

It is traditionally taught that one obtains everything through mere volition (*saṅkalpa*), and it is stated in the aphorisms (*sūtra*) that there is no restriction regarding the assumption of bodies according to one's own will; therefore, [your objection] is merely grinding what is already ground. That is not so, for the course of the scriptures is mutually restrictive; there is no assumption of multiple bodies at will.
This refers to the intention of the author of the Sūtras in stating that the process of acceptance and so forth is not subject to fixed necessity. || 24 ||

"Everything"—meaning all that is desired, such as the world of the ancestors and so forth—"obtains from mere volition," that is, he attains it from volition alone, independent of effort and other means; thus it is declared in the scripture: "If he...".

This is recited in the scripture beginning with "The ancestors of this [liberated soul] are his volitions" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.2.1), and it has been aphorized in the Sūtra: "From volition alone, because of that scriptural statement" (Brahma-sūtra 4.4.8). Although this has already been investigated and determined along with its reasons, there is here a statement regarding the lack of necessity in the union with a body or its absence according to one's own will; for in this section concerning non-existence (abhāvādhikaraṇa), there is no fixed rule that either the connection with a body or its absence must necessarily follow from the liberated soul's own volition.

"Establishing [what is already established] is like grinding what has already been ground"—that is, it is merely a repetition of an activity of making that was already performed previously; it is not something new or a meaning not yet understood. (Thus one might object. That is not so; what was stated by way of this objection is not correct, because... mutual... [text fragment].

*Niyati*—the determination of the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of scriptural passages that appear to be mutually contradictory (regarding such matters as having a body or being bodiless); the manner of assuming various bodies through multiple incarnations, whether by His own will or by the will of the Lord; and the description of the absence of necessity (*aniyati*) in these and similar respects—that is, the lack of absolute certainty regarding any one side—is due to the supreme intention (*paramatātparya*) of the author of the Sūtras, Dvaipāyana Vyāsa, the author of the *Śārīraka-sūtra*. || 24 ||
A summary of the meaning of the legal case.

In the section concerning non-existence (*abhāvādhikaraṇa*): Having first restated the view of Bādari—that there is no body for the liberated one because the body is a cause of suffering—and having refuted it by means of Jaimini’s view that "he is indeed with a body"—on the grounds that the liberated one is heard of as becoming manifold in such passages as "He becomes onefold," and because becoming manifold is impossible for one who is indivisible and partless without a body, and because only a body produced by karma is a cause of suffering—it was then set forth as his own view that, due to the power of his true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpatva*), he is sometimes with a body and sometimes without a body, according to his will.
The Adhikaraṇasārāvalī.

Although it was previously stated that the liberated one is of the nature of the Supreme (paratanu) and non-different from It—thus [the Lord's] aspect of activity [is attributed to Him]—nevertheless, here [it is argued that] supreme equality is unshakeable;
for even the arising of everything proceeds from His mere will. Thus he offers this counter-argument.
While others cut short their office, he establishes equality of enjoyment for the other two who possess merit. || 25 ||

Although, in reality, the liberated conscious being—one who has attained liberation from saṃsāra—is "paratanu," meaning non-distinctly established (*apṛthaksiddha*) as the body of the Supreme Self, such that he possesses that non-distinct establishment by virtue of being a body; and although this was previously stated and established after deliberation in the preceding section of this same chapter, namely the *Avibhāgena Dṛṣṭatvādhikaraṇa*, nevertheless, even though that point is already proven, it is heard here in the Upaniṣad within the context of the liberated one: "The stainless one [attains] the supreme..."

"attains equality"—that is, supreme equality (*paramasāmyam*), which is the complete identity of the liberated soul with the Supreme Self; this is followed even in the aspect of activity—that is, even in the aspect consisting of the Lord's activities such as the creation and governance of the world—and it becomes truly unavoidable (*akṣobhaṇīyam*), meaning it is indeed inescapable (for supreme equality cannot be established by abandoning any part whatsoever).

Otherwise, the qualification "supreme" would be meaningless; therefore, for the reason stated—that the activity of the world also exists in the liberated self—even the fulfillment of all objects within the range of one's desires, such as one's father and so forth, would come about through mere volition (*saṅkalpa*). Indeed, just as it is for the Blessed Lord, this [fulfillment] would be accomplished by His mere will alone. Having thus raised this objection—the doubt of the opponent in this form—in the final section, which constitutes the conclusion of the *Śārīraka-śāstra*:

In the section concerning the exclusion of the world-activity [from the individual soul], while establishing the equality of enjoyment between the Lord—who possesses the activity of the universe—and the individual soul (jīva), who lacks it; and while reconciling the unsurpassed equality declared in the Śruti—which is based on non-difference regarding the aspect of enjoyment consisting in the uninterrupted experience of the nature and attributes of the Supreme Self—he cuts away—that is, he utterly eradicates [the notion of inequality]. || 25 ||
The wise have calculated that *sāyujya* (union) is the equality of enjoyment (*bhoga-sāmya*), because it is not contradicted by the power of the words and so forth;

yet that [equality] is not possible if there is no equality of activity, since that would entail the loss of the relish for one's own actions. Therefore, let it not be said that the liberated soul’s engagement with the world—beginning from creation—is equal to that of Brahman. For how could that definition apply both to him and to another? (26)

*Sāyujyam*—the meaning of the word *sāyujya*, established by not subverting the etymological derivation of its constituent parts through the power of the words themselves (*śabdaśakti*), etc.: taking as the basis for its establishment the non-subversion [of that derivation], [it is explained as follows]: *yuk* is that which is joined; it is an object of enjoyment (*bhogyabhūta*) connected with the person (*puruṣa*) for the sake of experience. *Samāna* means "without distinction" (*availakṣaṇya*). Those whose *yuk*—the object of enjoyment—is the same are *sayujaḥ*. [The state of being such is *sāyujyam*].

Their state is *sāyujya*—this is the etymological meaning derived from the word itself. By those who are skillful and proficient in the analysis of words and their meanings, it has been determined that *bhogasāmya* (equality of enjoyment) consists precisely in the absence of distinction regarding all aspects of enjoyment; however, it does not consist in the identity of essential nature (*svarūpābheda*). And that *sāyujya*, termed "equality of enjoyment," [is] activity—

But in the absence of equality—when the entirety of the functional activity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is non-existent—it is not possible; it does not at all stand to reason, because of the loss of the relish of one's own activity. Since the experience of bliss resulting from reflecting upon one's own activity is included within the category of enjoyment (*bhoga*), and since that very activity is absent in the liberated self, the bliss preceded by such reflection is also absent; thus, the equality of enjoyment is not established. Therefore, because the equality of enjoyment must be maintained, the liberated one attains *brahmasāyujya* (union with Brahman).

[The opponent] objects: "For a conscious being who has attained [this state], even his engagement with the world—from creation onwards, consisting of the regulation of creation and so forth, as well as the accomplishment of activities related to the world—must necessarily be admitted to be equal to Brahman, bringing about similarity with the Supreme Self. [The author] replies: "It is not so; even by connecting him with worldly engagement, the establishment of equality with Brahman is certainly not tenable. That worldly engagement which constitutes His defining characteristic—that is, the worldly engagement which is the very definition of the Supreme Self—is [the mark] of Him and of no other."

How could it be possible—that is, how could it be logically tenable—for the definition [of Brahman] beginning with "from which indeed these... to apply by way of commonality (*anugama*) to both the Supreme Self, who is characterized by such marks (*lakṣaṇa*), and the individual soul (*jīva*), the liberated self who is other than that which is characterized (*lakṣya*)? (For if the definition were common to both the individual soul and Brahman, its status as a definition of Brahman would be lost; this is because a definition must be unique (*asādhāraṇa*). Furthermore, even if it were a definition of Brahman, its application to the individual soul would result in over-extension [*ativyāpti*], which constitutes a logical inconsistency. || 26 ||
In certain passages concerning creation, liberated souls (*muktas*) are nowhere mentioned as being the cause of the world;

let it be that they possess unrestrained freedom (*kāmacāra*), yet from that it would not follow that they are the originators of the universe. Because their cognitions regarding the Lord—who is the object of enjoyment in every form—are equal, equality of enjoyment is logical;
thus, in the *Ānandavallī*, equality was reckoned by the All-pervading Lord only with respect to bliss itself.

In any scriptural passage whatsoever—any statement within the Vedānta that declares the cause of the creation of the universe—liberated souls (*muktas*), whose transmigratory existence has ceased, are not described as the cause of the world, nor are they presented as the agents who bring about the creation of the universe. As for the "free movement" (*kāmacāra*)—the independent and unrestricted wandering through the worlds of liberated selves—it is well-known from such scriptural texts as: "Moving at will among these worlds, assuming forms at will. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.1)

Granted that this may be clearly stated in the tradition; however, the mere fact of its being mentioned in the Śruti regarding the movement at will does not establish that [the liberated soul] is the originator of the world—the causality of the liberated souls toward the world would certainly not be proven. (For the independent movement within the world does not constitute the cause for the creation of the world, because there is an absence of such positive and negative concomitance [anvaya-vyatireka] in one who merely moves about. [The soul is] of all forms...

*Dhiyaḥ*—of the intellect (*buddhi*) which has as its object the Supreme Self whose nature is bliss to be experienced both by its own essential form and by all its inherent qualities; *sāmyataḥ*—due to equality, that is, because there is no distinction between the Supreme Self and the liberated self; *bhogasāmyam*—the equality of enjoyment, meaning the non-distinction in the enjoyment of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Highest (*para*); *yujyeta*—is established or accomplished; *ānandavallyām*—in the portion of the Taittirīya Upaniṣad known as the Ānandavallī; *vibhunā*—with the all-pervading Supreme Self; *ānandamātre samatvam*—equality in the matter of pure bliss alone.

"The bliss of a Brahmin who has mastered the Vedas and is free from desire" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.8)—in this way, non-distinction is described only with respect to the aspect of bliss; not even with respect to other aspects. || 27 ||

Desiring to describe the joys that increase a hundredfold at each successive stage up to Viriñca—each greater than the human bliss equal to that of a desireless Śrotriya—how could this inferior, painful state, though desired by you, be acceptable? For liberation consists in eternal bliss like that of Mukunda’s beloveds; indeed, this [human joy] is merely a partial description of it. || 28 ||

Starting from a human being up to Prajāpati—that is, progressively, from one to the next—the Taittirīya Ānandavallī, desiring to declare and establish the increasingly superior joys (*ānanda*)—specific instances of happiness—that result from multiplying each preceding joy by a hundredfold, speaks of the bliss of a *śrotriya* free from desire, even of a *śrotriya* unassailed by desire (one who is far removed from all hope for conditioned, worldly pleasure and whose mind is fixed on the unconditioned Great Bliss).

Even for the liberated self (*muktātman*), there is a pleasure equal to human bliss—meaning an enjoyment similar to that of humans. This is indicated by the use of words denoting similarity; it does not describe the actual nature of that bliss directly. Compared to the hundredfold human bliss and so forth, this collection of pleasures designated by terms such as "human bliss" is considered inferior—that is, it is regarded as lesser—and because of this inferiority, it is "painful," being of the nature of suffering, even for the liberated one.

O You who possess unconditioned supreme bliss, how could that which is desired by you—namely, your doctrine asserting a gradation of bliss in liberation—be acceptable or even logical? For it is impossible for there to be inferior bliss in liberation. Indeed, all such things as inequality and gradation are possible only for one who is still connected with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Since the liberated one is devoid of all adjuncts that cause inequality, inequality and the like cannot possibly apply to him; if they did apply, his state of liberation would be untenable.

Therefore, the purpose of this extended application (*atideśa*) must be described as follows: [The scriptural statement] is a partial restatement (*ekadeśānuvāda*)—according to the maxim of "fifty in a hundred"—of the bliss that constitutes a single part within the collective whole, like a drop of water in the ocean. This restatement is consistent with the Śruti because it refers to the liberated self (*muktātman*), who possesses indestructible bliss (*avināśyānanda-bhāgin*) and is equal to the eternal sages (*nityasūrī*), the Lord’s eternal beloveds, in their similarity to the beloved of Mukunda through the absence of limitation by time and space. Thus, [the text] is properly reconciled. || 28 ||

The Śruti declares here that bliss increases a hundredfold until it becomes infinite in the passage beginning with "from whence words turn back," and this has been stated by the eminent Yāmunācārya: "Its rest occurs simply from exhaustion; even by a hundred injunctions, its bliss cannot be measured, just as the sky cannot be measured by a staff."
And it has been said: "What difference is there between sinking in the ocean and sinking in the lap of a mountain? (29)

Indeed—for this reason—in this context, which is intended for the enumeration of the bliss of Brahman, there is the Śruti beginning with "from whence words return," namely the Taittirīya Śruti: "From whence words return along with the mind, having failed to reach it, he who knows the bliss of Brahman. This [Śruti] declares the infinity of bliss; that is, the Bhāgavata states that the bliss [of the Lord] is unlimited by time, space, or by words and mind through any limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). The "resting place" (*viśrānti*) of this [description] occurs when it is engaged in the glorification of the Lord's qualities.

"The cessation of Vedic speech is due to mere exhaustion— that is, solely because of being fatigued by the labor of description, and not because of the completion of the description"— thus it was stated and specifically set forth by the eminent Ācārya Yāmunamuni, the supreme teacher Bhagavān Rāmānuja, also known by the name ‘Āḷavandār’, even in his *Vidhiśata-vacana* (The Hundred Verses on the Injunction), after pointing out the hundred Prajāpatis and [showing] their possession of bliss increased a hundredfold.

Even when Brahman is described, its bliss—the supreme excellence of the bliss of this present Brahman—cannot indeed be measured; it certainly cannot be demonstrated by way of dimension or limitation. It is just as if one were to make an effort to measure the sky with a staff! Even if such measurements of the staff were extended by the millions upon millions, just as the limit of the sky would never be stated, so too it is with the Supreme Self. And that...

It has been said that an illustration regarding this matter has also been made clear: between the Lord of the Ocean and the Lord of Mountains—between the ocean, which is a great flood of water, and the mountain, which is a minute atom—when both are subject to sinking, that is, when their own forms are concealed by submerging within it, what distinction is there? What kind of relative degree of difference exists? None at all. What difference is there between the two who are sinking—the Kulaparvata and the atom? (Stotraratna, Verse 8). ||29||

The body of the liberated one is certainly not a material cause [of the world], for it is not perceived as being non-different from Him; therefore, it is improper to speak of it [as such], since that would entail the loss of His omnipotence. Nor is it the Self, for He would not desire to create what is impossible; His will is unimpeded regarding all other objects, and even when His activity differs, an absence of partiality is observed in the world. || 30 ||

The universe—the world—is not indeed the body of the liberated sentient being who has attained liberation; that is, it has not attained the state of being a body by way of being supported (*ādheyatva*), being subject to control (*vidheyatva*), or being subordinate (*śeṣatva*). This is because one observes in the universe precisely the absence of that inseparability (*tadapṛthaksiddhi*)—defined as the state of existing and being perceived only in concomitance with another, while being incapable of existing or being perceived separately—which determines the status of being that [other's] body. For the universe consists of both sentient and non-sentient entities, and [thus does not belong to] the Supreme Self.

Because it is certain that [the world] is established as separate [from the liberated soul], and because it has the Supreme Self as its material cause; therefore, since the liberated one lacks the state of being the creator of the universe while being non-separately established from Himself, this liberated soul is not fit to be called the material cause—he is not worthy of being described as the material cause of the world, because the liberated soul would lose His omnipotence, as omnipotence is necessarily concomitant with being a material cause. This being the case, the liberated conscious self would not desire to act—that which cannot be accomplished by Himself, He would certainly not wish to create.

If one should desire to perform an action regarding something other than that—regarding an object that is either impossible or otherwise—the desire associated with liberation is such that it is unimpeded, meaning it cannot be obstructed by the Supreme Self or by anyone else. Even when activities differ—whether in household duties such as the act of cooking, or in other activities such as guarding the fields—even while various other activities exist for the people residing in the house, there is an absence of unevenness in flavor regarding objects such as the eating of cooked food.

Uniformity (*aikarasyam*)—the absence of gradation in aesthetic flavor (*rasa*)—is seen nowhere in the world. Among worldly beings, the favor of a sovereign, brought about by the steady transformation resulting from various specific services, produces equality for a servant, with the sole exception of that which is personally undesired by the master. In this same way, that which cannot be obtained elsewhere is attained by those who have approached the compassionate Lord as their refuge.
With the suspicion of recurrence shaken off, possessing the flavor of the unconditioned, it is both with and without formal constraints.

Of the servant—of one engaged in service who has obtained [favor] through the faultless performance of various specific tasks in the form of service received from the command of the Great King—the favor of the Emperor (*sārvabhaumaprasāda*), which is a distinguished and extraordinary royal grace; "excluding what is not desired"—setting aside those imperial insignia such as the parasol, fly-whisk, and so forth, which are undesirable to the King and to himself, who is his servant—the equality.

Regarding objects such as dwellings, seats, and food, he enjoys them equally with the king; and in that which has become his own, he accomplishes it spontaneously, even without the prompting of distinguished persons. Thus, for sentient beings who have approached—having taken refuge as their protector and as their goal—the Compassionate Lord, the Master of Śrī, the Supreme Self whose sole essence is mercy, [the attainment] is unobtainable by others and difficult to reach, with all doubts regarding the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) shaken off. [This applies to those entering] the desert wilderness of worldly existence...

It is far removed from even a scent of the possibility of returning [to worldly existence]; it is the unconditioned essence—having the singular nature of bliss liberated from all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); it is the state that does not transgress its own boundaries; it is the distinguished condition dependent upon its own essential nature; it is attained by itself, as it is spontaneously realized. || 31 ||
Regarding this, some say that the final Sūtra constitutes a separate section because it attains its own direct meaning;

for the word "this" (*imam*) arises as a doubt concerning the prohibition of repetition (*āvarta*). This [view] is not seen in the Bhāṣya and other works, and its status as a supplement to the preceding section is easily understood;
moreover, since the creation of the entire world involves repetition, there might arise a doubt regarding [the Lord's] equality [with the individual soul]. (32)

Some teachers—certain masters engaged in reflecting on the meaning of the *Śārīraka* (Brahma-sūtras)—state that in this section, the final sūtra is the concluding sūtra on non-return (*anāvṛtti*). Having considered the attainment of consistency in the application of the sūtra—that is, the attainment of the propriety of its operation—they describe it as a separate section, the seventh section, because the word "this" (*imam*) is present in the sense of the subject of the prohibition—the cycle of rebirth (*āvarta*)—which is to be understood as the state of returning for the liberated soul; [as in the phrase]: "this human cycle" (*imaṃ mānavam āvartaṃ*).

Since the word "this" (*imām*) is found in the Śruti in the context of the phrase "they do not return," which refers to some specific kind of return, a doubt arises; for that reason, they state the reason for the necessity of another topical section (*adhikaraṇa*), namely that a doubt has arisen regarding the possibility of returning again during the cycle of a *manvantara*. However, that [separation into] another topical section is not seen in the Bhāṣya and so forth, nor is it even introduced in the Śrībhāṣya or its commentaries.

The determination of the meaning of the sūtra concerning non-return (anāvṛtti) constitutes its status as a subordinate element (śeṣatva) characterized by the nature of being a means of attainment; and this becomes easy to understand—that is, it remains well-known—even from the context of "return," because of the contingency that a liberated one might return, which has already been addressed.

A doubt regarding equality in the creation of the entire universe might arise—namely, that for one who has attained liberation upon reaching the realm of *prakṛti*, there might occur the suspicion of attaining equality with the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*) in the task of creating the entire universe through His power of true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpa*). (In order to dispel this, the possibility of returning [to *saṃsāra*] is utterly eradicated by this sūtra, which explains the meaning of the preceding sūtra. || 32 ||

The Lord, having gradually released the individual soul (jīva) appointed to the rod of punishment—which is accompanied by the aesthetic delight of the sport of creation and so forth—enjoys that state which is blessed with union. Furthermore, because it is traditionally taught that "due to the absolute cessation of karma, he does not return here again," any doubt arising from the description of inexhaustible fruits rooted in karma is pacified. || 33 ||

In this world-ocean, which is devoid of a beginning of creation— wherein the soul (*jīva*) is repeatedly cast into the whirlpool of *saṃsāra*, a process resembling the sport of playing with a staff, consisting of the cycles of creation, maintenance, and dissolution, and accompanied by the specific pleasure born from activities performed for its own delight without being prompted by another— the Lord (*deva*), the Sovereign (*īśvara*) who bears the burden of the world’s play, has appointed [the soul].

Having gradually, in the appropriate manner and according to the fixed method, liberated [the soul] by freeing it from the whirling of the whirlpool, and having rendered it blessed through the state of union (*sayugbhāva*)—that is, having brought it to fulfillment through the *sāyujya* (union) bestowed upon it—he "enjoys" it, meaning he himself protects that liberated soul who has attained union. Because of the absolute cessation of karma—that is, because all karmas which are the causes for entering into *saṃsāra* have been uprooted without remainder—[he does not return] again to this realm of *prakṛti*.

Furthermore, because of the scriptural reading and the indicative mark [found] in the Śruti: "The Blessed One does not return again; he does not make a resort for rebirth"—thus it is stated in the tradition.

"Peace has karma as its root"—by such Vedic statements as "The merit of one who performs the Cāturmāsya sacrifices is indeed imperishable," which aim to establish the imperishability of the fruits produced by rites such as the Cāturmāsya, and which, though using figurative language, intend merely to convey a state of long duration; and even in passages such as "He does not return again," there arises the suspicion that they intend only a return after a very long period of time—[this is countered] by the fact that [the texts] possess a non-figurative, primary, and real sense.
The refutation is not made by this Sūtra through the demonstration of non-return; thus, there is no contingency of it being a separate topic (adhikaraṇa). || 33 ||
Summary of the Topic:

Regarding the section on the activity of the world—having raised the objection that since scripture declares the liberated soul attains supreme equality with the Lord, the power of governing the world and so forth must also belong to the liberated soul—it is stated that "except for the activity of the world. This is because, in those passages intended to demonstrate the governance of the world, the Supreme Self is the subject under discussion, whereas the liberated soul is not present there; furthermore, there is evidence indicating that the equality of the liberated soul pertains only to enjoyment.

In the section concerning non-return (Anāvṛttyadhikaraṇa), having raised the objection that the return of the liberated soul is possible due to the sovereign independence of the Lord, it is concluded that there is no return for the liberated one; for their non-return is heard in the scripture stating, "They do not return to this human whirlpool," and because it is impossible for the Lord—who is dependent upon those who have sought refuge—to revoke His resolve to bring about that [liberation].
"Through one's own will, there is the enjoyment of all things and the arising of the fruit of liberation"—such is the collection of meanings intended by this quarter-verse. (8)

In liberation, for the conscious self, the meaning of the term "manifestation" (*abhiniṣpatti*) as stated in the phrase "he manifests in his own form" (*svena rūpeṇābhiniṣpadyate*) is simply the appearance of its very own nature, characterized by the eightfold qualities, which was previously concealed by beginningless karma; it is not the assumption of some other form non-existent within itself, nor is it the experience of the Supreme Self by the liberated soul as an external object, but rather [the realization] of one's own self as the Self, in a state of non-differentiation from itself.

The nature of the liberated self is not something separate; rather, it is indeed characterized by qualities such as freedom from sin and by innate knowledge. It does not consist of each [quality] individually. Regarding the liberated self’s capacity for eating, playing, and so forth, as well as its possession of parents and other relations as described in the Śruti, the sole operative cause is the very state of being true (satyatva), which depends on the grace of the Lord and requires no further effort. Every kind of enjoyment of the liberated self as taught in the Śruti conforms to the will of the Lord.

The perfection of the body dependent upon the aggregate [of the subtle body], as well as the experience of Brahman through the state of bodilessness (*aśarīratā*)—both of these are the fruit for the liberated one who is released from all bonds. This includes the attainment of those sovereign powers of the liberated that are distinct from the Lord’s unique activities over the world, and its conjunction with the state of non-return (*apunarāvṛtti*). These six topics have been thoroughly investigated and determined by means of the fourth quarter on the fruit, which belongs to the Fourth of the Fourth (*turyaturya*). || 7, 8 ||

Thus ends the *Śārīrakanyāyakalāpasaṅgraha* composed by the venerable Seneśvarācārya, together with the commentary (*vivaraṇa*) composed for Rāmabhadra. This commentary on this *Śārīrakasannyāyasaṅgraha* composed by Seneśvara has reached its conclusion, having been composed by the scholar Śrī Rāmabhadra.
May this auspicious commentary, composed for the satisfaction of students of knowledge, lead to the pleasure of Śrī Hari; may there always be well-being for all.

"Subservience (*śeṣatva*) means being the servant of another; indeed, suffering is seen everywhere in the world as being nothing other than that which is contrary [to one's will]. Therefore, since the state of being subservient is certainly experienced as something contrary, it is not appropriate for liberated sentient beings—those who possess liberation characterized by being entirely freed from all suffering—to have subservience to the Blessed One. (Thus he objects. "Do not say so. For in the state of liberation, subservience to the Blessed One does not take the form of suffering, nor does it lead to it."

The claim that the liberated soul does not accept being subordinate to Him—both [these positions] are incorrect. That which is known from the Upaniṣads (*aupaniṣada*)—the state of being subordinate (*śeṣatva*) to the Lord of Śrī (*mādhavadāsya*)—awakens with ever-increasing love; it expands as the ultimate object of affection. Therefore, for this reason, the inferential construction of hostility toward the service of the Blessed One—which is the means to the state of suffering—is refuted by the very authority that apprehends the subject (*dharmin*), namely, the apprehension of the goal consisting of liberation characterized by the absence of suffering.

By Janaka, [the claim that servitude is not undesirable] was refuted by the authority of scripture (*śruti*) stating, "Neither disease nor suffering [is found there]. Alternatively, if it were to be established through inference (*anumāna*)—that is, if it were postulated that servitude distinct from Him, namely subservience to anyone other than the Lord, results in unhappiness—that is, has the nature of suffering, then that nature of servitude to anyone other than the Lord would indeed be something already established and well-known in the world! (In a matter already known in the world, inference does not operate;
for one cannot establish through inference that water is hot, as it would result in the fallacy of proving what is already established.)

That non-inert reality denoted by such terms as "Being," "Brahman," and "Self"—according to the analogy of a goat or a sacrificial animal—is the supreme, peerless, and unique object of worship for the seeker of liberation, known as Nārāyaṇa. For, from the beginning of the great Upaniṣad with the words "Ekoha vai... up to the end with "...yataḥ jāyate," there is the understanding within the Nārāyaṇa Upaniṣad that [the world] was created by Nārāyaṇa according to scriptural injunctions. || 104 ||

By means of words such as *Sat*, *Brahman*, and *Ātman*—as in "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.2.1) where it is expressed by the word *Sat*; in "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite" (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 2.1.1) where it is expressed by the word *Brahman*; and in "Verily, in the beginning, this was the Self alone" (*Aitareya Upaniṣad* 1.1.1) where it is expressed by the word *Ātman* (and likewise by words such as *Akṣara*, *Paratattva*, and *Paramātman*)—according to the logic of the goat and the sacrificial animal.

It has been stated: Just as the Mīmāṃsakas have determined that the animal intended for the immolation dedicated to Agni and Soma is specifically the one called a "goat"—on the grounds that the object understood by the word "animal" (paśu) through its general form in the injunction "one should immolate an animal dedicated to Agni and Soma" is the very same object denoted by the word "goat" (chāga) in the mantra-text "of the goat's omentum for the sacrifice"—so too [is this case].

In the same manner, having spoken in general terms, [the scripture] finds its finality in the particular: the unsurpassed, incomparable, and peerless reality called Nārāyaṇa—non-inert, singular, denoted by the word "Nārāyaṇa," and consisting of self-luminous form;
the one supreme principle that is Pradhāna, the means for achieving the desired liberation for the seeker of release (mumukṣu), who desires to free his own self from the shackles of saṃsāra.

In the *Mahopaniṣad*— beginning with "There was indeed one [object of service in the form of *bhakti* and *prapatti*], there was indeed one," and starting from "Nārāyaṇa alone existed" up to the passage ending with "the Person is born"— as well as in the *Nārāyaṇopaniṣad*, in the inquiry beginning with "In the boundless waters," there is the understanding that all sentient beings, beginning with Brahmā, were created according to the injunctions.

Thus, the determination that [the Lord] is born from Nārāyaṇa itself is established. Furthermore, it is established that only the Reality which is the cause of all things is the object of meditation for the sake of liberation, according to the scriptural statement: "But the Cause is to be meditated upon" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.3). || 104 ||
A summary of the meaning of the section.

The manifestation of one's own nature in liberation is restricted to the unconditioned; it is the perception of the limit of one’s own effects, which belongs to the very nature of consciousness. Likewise, there is the vision [of the Self] together with its own modes as crowned by the Śruti. Accomplishment occurs through mere volition, and in the bodies, there is freedom from the constraints [of karma]. Upon attaining equality with Brahman, there is the abandonment of those portions characterized by that [limited state]; such is the essence of the fourth quarter of the final chapter. 34.

Regarding *apavarga*—in the state of liberation—there is the manifestation (*svāvirbhāva*) of one's own essential nature (*svasvarūpa*), which was previously concealed, through the removal of that concealment; it is not the manifestation of any other form. There is the "vision free from limiting adjuncts" (*nirupadhi-dṛṣṭi*)—the experience at the time of liberation of one's own self-nature as far as the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*), who is the fixed and natural illuminator (*prakārin*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) in its unconditioned state; that is, the vision of one's own nature as distinct from the Supreme Self, [and likewise] of the Supreme Self as the fixed illuminator of oneself.

The vision of one's own self, which is of the nature of consciousness and of the nature of knowledge itself, occurs together with its own modes as defined by the crest-jewels of the Vedas—that is, together with its own modes consisting of qualities such as freedom from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) which constitute the objects of knowledge in the Vedānta, and with knowledge and its own attributes. Furthermore, there is the accomplishment through mere volition (*saṅkalpa*): the attainment of enjoyments mentioned in the Śruti, such as eating, playing, and so forth, as well as the summoning of fathers and others, occurring through volition alone without dependence on any other auxiliary cause; and [this applies] to the bodies as well.

Freedom from restriction (*niyamonmuktatā*) means that even when the liberated soul assumes various bodies, there is an absence of the constraints [associated with them] (whether embodied or disembodied as appropriate). The abandonment of specific characteristics upon attaining equality with Brahman (*brahmasāmyaprāpti*) means that when the liberated soul achieves supreme equality with the Supreme Self, it discards the unique attributes of the Supreme Brahman; in the unconditioned experience of the Supreme Brahman and its qualities, there is perfect equality in every respect other than those [unique attributes]. This is the final essence.
Thus, this compendium of the essence of the meaning of the final section (the section on liberation) of the Śārīraka [Brahma-sūtra], consisting of six topics, should be reflected upon. || 34 ||

From this body-self—which is like a prison-house because it is experienced as the obscuration of the light of one's own self and the Supreme Self—one departs through the *suṣumṇā* for the sake of liberation; one also proceeds by the "good path" (*supatha*) in the form of the "path of light" (*arcirādi*) and other such righteous ways toward the station of Brahman. Furthermore, the goal to be accomplished is the manifestation of one's own self-luminous nature—which had been concealed—as a liberated being, as well as the creation of one's own desired worlds according to one's will.

How could one who stands by the doctrine of Māyā—that is, one who has faith in the Advaita system—possibly reconcile, or even coherently contemplate, the following points which are established in the final chapter (the *Phalādhyāya*) of the *Śārīraka* [Brahma-sūtras]: namely, that for the liberated soul there is the attainment of all desired objects through mere self-will; and that there is a supreme equality with the Supreme Brahman through the mere experience of enjoyment—this "supreme equality" consisting solely in the liberated soul’s experience of Brahman and its attributes along with the Supreme Self attained by the liberated;
in what manner, indeed, could such matters be made consistent? In no way whatsoever. (35)

In the first part concerning ritual action (*karmabhāga*), there is no room for even a scent of falsehood anywhere in this three-part *Mīmāṃsā*, because it analyzes the distinctions between honor and dishonor and so forth; in the middle part concerning the deities (*devatāṃśa*), because it subsequently explains "various deities" and the like; and in this [final] part, because it sets forth the nature of difference and other attributes, while also refuting the Buddhists and others. (36)

In the first [part]—in the initial portion consisting of the *karmakāṇḍa* and *brahmakāṇḍa*, specifically in the *karmabhāga* or *karmamīmāṃsābhāga*—because of the "division of means and non-means" (*mānāmāna-vibhajanāt*), that is, because of the making of a distinction between the objects of valid cognition and their opposites; in the middle—situated between the two sections—regarding the *devatā* in the *devatākāṇḍa*, because of the reading "or variously" (*nānā vā*), meaning that by such statements as "or variously, because the deities are distinct," the difference among the deities is clearly established; and in this [final] section—consisting of the four chapters of the *Śārīrakasūtra*.

And because of the exposition of the nature of difference and other attributes in the *Brahmabhāga*—through the definition of specific meanings such as the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), and the unique attributes of the Supreme Self—and because of the refutation of the Buddhists and others, that is, the clear rejection of the Buddhists who propound conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), [this is established] within the *Trikāṇḍī Mīmāṃsā*—that is, in the *Karmamīmāṃsā* consisting of three sections, in the *Devatāmīmāṃsā*, and even in the *Brahmamīmāṃsā*—in some part, that is, in any portion whatsoever.
There is no room for the scent of false speech; even the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of untruthful discourse does not apply here. || 36 ||

This Smṛti, which is like a shore for the ocean of the three Vedas, has been proclaimed by the Teachers (deśikas) who act as its helmsmen; it clearly leads one to the further shore of the knowledge that results in liberation.
However, regarding other matters pertaining to liberation, the authors of the Kalpasūtras have stated certain differences arising from doubts concerning what ought to be done.
Even in such cases, though there may be some discrepancy, the understanding of those portions useful to oneself is not false. (37)

By the helmsmen—those equal to navigators—and by the guides—the preeminent teachers intent on showing the path—this [path], which consists of the meaning propounded by the Śārīraka-mīmāṃsā, [is reached] by those who have reached the end of the three Vedas...

The *sṛti*—the path leading into the great ocean of Vedānta, which serves as the route for the final departure—is thus revealed (*uditā*) and made manifest. It leads (*gamayati*) those seeking liberation to the ultimate limit (*pāram*) of the knowledge of reality that is conducive to liberation. Furthermore, whatever other subject matter remains to be stated becomes clearly visible (*viśadamīkṣyam*)—to be seen with perfect clarity—within the supreme ether (*parame vyomni*) alone during the state of liberation; for every aspect [of truth] is found right here.

Complete and exhaustive knowledge is difficult to attain; indeed, the mere absence of such total knowledge regarding every single aspect does not constitute an obstacle to the practice of the means of liberation, the attainment of divine grace, and so forth. Even by the authors of the *Kalpasūtras*—such as Baudhāyana, Āpastamba, and others—who were engaged in extracting the procedures for the performance of Vedic rites, there are, in certain instances concerning matters to be performed, distinctions of doubt regarding what ought to be done, arising from a lack of definitive determination as to whether "it should be done thus" or "it should be done otherwise."

Specific doubts indeed have been stated—they are seen expressed in the *Kalpasūtras*—even regarding the reality (*tattva*), that is, even concerning the subject matter of the reality known through the Vedānta; in certain instances—that is, in specific places—such may be the case, meaning that a particular doubt might indeed arise. Nevertheless, the understanding of the portions useful for oneself—the distinct comprehension of those parts necessary for knowing the means and their subsequent practice, which is free from contradiction and the like—is not false; it cannot possibly be fruitless (for a person of discrimination ought to be satisfied with whatever has been attained). || 37 ||
In upholding the weight of the sequence of reasoning that is exclusively devoted to the Upaniṣads, the host of [non-Vedic] mountains is like cotton;

the mass of darkness consisting of other systems is but a mere semblance before the light of the sun that is the realization of the Brahman established therein. In the sole sovereignty of the means to liberation, all other injunctions serve as its attendants;
and the other human goals (puruṣārthas) vie with but a single drop of curd in the ocean of the nectar of the bliss of liberation. (38)

When one maintains in the mind that specific methodological approach established in the *Śārīraka* (Vedānta)—the logic whose sole fruit is the definitive determination of the meaning of the Upaniṣads—then the collection of arguments belonging to other systems of philosophy, which, like a mass of stones, consists primarily of mere harshness and fails to culminate in the means for attaining the supreme human goal, is seen to be as devoid of essence as cotton-wool, because it is established [only] by those [other systems].

*Ruci*—when the light (*kānti*) of the sun, which consists of the knowledge of Brahman derived from the Upaniṣads and produced by the power of reasoning based on such a Śārīraka [text], is active within the external and internal senses (the word *ruka* takes the locative case *ruci*), then in its presence, *anyajalpaḥ*—the flow of speech of others who lack devotion to the subject matter of the Śārīraka (various positions or mere ostentation)—is *tamaḥstomakalpaḥ*, that is, exactly like a mass of blinding darkness.

(Since even the operation of the internal and external organs of their own nature is rendered impure by those doctrines and their proponents' words,) while the sole sovereignty of the means to liberation—the empire of the practice of the means to *apavarga*, which is the supreme human goal—is prevailing, all other injunctions—those injunctions for sacrifice, charity, and so forth, distinct from the injunctions for the means to liberation—assume the status of servants.

Being auxiliaries to the means such as devotion (bhakti) which constitute the path to liberation, the other human goals—namely all [other] aims of man (puruṣārtha), beginning with liberation (apavarga)—depend upon being subordinate to the injunctions for the means to liberation; they do not attain an independent status. All these human goals, including liberation, are rivals to the bliss of liberation; they consist of a specific kind of bliss experienced by liberated beings, yet they are merely like a single spray belonging to a portion of the ocean of nectar. In no way whatsoever are they equal to the bliss of liberation. || 38 ||

Having first distinguished between the higher and the lower through unerring scriptures regarding the category of reality, he feels intense fear toward cyclic existence and possesses exceedingly intense passion for the supreme attainment. Having mastered a particular branch of knowledge along with its auxiliaries, and having become one whose internal obstacles are stilled, he realizes Brahman and enjoys it without limitation; thus is the meaning of what has been heard, namely that there is no return.

One who has heard the meaning—meaning a person endowed with correct knowledge regarding the reality, the welfare, and the human goals, acquired through listening under the guidance of a teacher according to prescribed rules—having first, in the beginning, distinguished and firmly retained the higher and lower states (that is, the excellence and deficiency) within the group of realities known as the triad of consciousness, unconscious matter, and the Lord, by discerning them through their respective natures and characteristics via the unerring scriptures (*āgamas*) such as the *Śruti* and other means of valid cognition; [the Lord...]

Having determined that the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa is the supreme reality (paraṃ tattva), while the sentient and insentient are subordinate realities (avaratattve), [the seeker] feels intense fear regarding worldly existence—being filled with unavoidable dread in this wheel of birth, old age, and death that is incessantly revolving—and possesses an exceedingly perfected passion for the realization of the Supreme, having an irrepressible longing for the attainment of the Supreme Self. (His fear arises because worldly existence consists in association with subordinate realities).

Because the attainment of the Supreme Self consists in union with the Supreme Reality, there is an intense longing for it; [one should practice] a particular form of knowledge—any one of the distinguished knowledges such as the Sadvidyā or Daharavidyā (other than the Dṛṣṭividya)—together with its accessories, that is, along with its constituent parts (*aṅga*).

Together with the subtle body (*pena*), having taken hold of it as the means for liberation (*mokṣasādhanatayā*) and having resorted to it, he becomes one whose internal obstacles are stilled—having cast off the entire collection of hindrances known as merit and demerit (*sukṛta-duṣkṛta*). Having attained Brahman—that is, having reached the Supreme Brahman—he is free from return (*anāvṛtti*), meaning he is devoid of the recurrence that consists of re-entering the wheel of *saṃsāra*. He enjoys Brahman—the unconditioned Supreme Brahman endowed with unsurpassed splendor—shining forth with a mind of bliss, experiencing it continuously and free from all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). || 39 ||

O you who are peaceful—possessing goodness through devotion to the Supreme Self—and O virtuous ones! That [work] is this very one, known by the name Bhagavad-anugṛhīta-vedāntācārya, in accordance with the promise of its meaningful title.

This work, *Brahmasūtrāvali*, has thus been completed in its true form; it is a series of verses in the *sragdharā* meter that provides a summary of the essence of the five hundred and forty-five *sūtras* of the *Śārīrakabhāṣya*, the one hundred and fifty-six (*156*) topical sections (*adhikaraṇas*) contained therein, and the sixteen chapters (*caraṇas*) of the four books (*adhyāyas*). It is intent upon attributing faults to the virtues of the opponent's system.

That which is the root-principle (*mūlanīti*)—capable of completely exhausting the views of those other philosophers who are averse to the path of the Upanishads; which, being free from figurative interpretation and capable of establishing the full meaning of all Vedic texts, serves as a flight of stairs for the ascent of the intellect toward the fundamental logical principles; and which is the revealer or the means of attaining the Lord—who is endowed with the three pairs of qualities such as knowledge and power (and is complete in the sixfold sovereign attributes)—is the *Triyuga-sūtra*.

The path beginning with light (*arcirādi*) consists of the act of mounting the chariot, which is the performance of the means for attaining that [path]. A discerning person indeed mounts the chariot itself, which is joined with a charioteer; he should certainly produce a specific kind of enthusiasm characterized by unimpeded activity. Likewise, through the realization of reality (*tattvabodha*), which possesses the power to uproot the afflictions of the intellect that arise from time to time during the study of the *Śārīraka* (Vedānta) scriptures—a realization that is skillful in pacifying the distress of the body—one must surely generate such enthusiasm.

—By means of the correct understanding (*yathāvadavabodha*) of the reality that constitutes the subject matter of the treatise (*śāstraprameyabhūtārtha*), which has arisen within [you], may it produce for you—a longing for liberation (*mumukṣūṇām*) and therefore seekers of truth (*tattvabubhutsūnām*)—a lasting (*santam*, meaning enduring rather than merely momentary) satisfaction (*santoṣam*, a mental exultation). || 40 ||
In this section on the division of boundaries within the *Adhikaraṇagaṇa*, we have clearly stated one hundred and fifty-six [verses].

May a few fortunate ones follow what we have said; what is the use of others who are merely prone to criticism? Seeing this entire universe as subject to the heart enslaved by the machinery of the three qualities (*guṇas*), we do not here engage in idle jesting toward our Lord, who stands as our witness. (41)

"One hundred and fifty-six"—meaning one hundred in number, followed by fifty-six; thus, by means of groups of topics (*adhikaraṇa-gaṇaiḥ*)—that is, by the collections of the *Śārīraka* topics dedicated to establishing the principles (*nyāya*)—in this section (*kāṇḍa*) which has been described, namely the *Brahma-kāṇḍa* known as the *Śārīraka*, which possesses a clearly established division and limit (*vyakta-sīmā-vibhāga*), those few who are intent on reflecting upon the meaning of the *Śārīraka* [should understand] the range of subjects (*viṣaya-jāta*) set forth by us in the manner we have demonstrated.

Certain wise men "understand"—that is, they know by following and indeed without contradicting [the truth], because their primary aim is the ascertainment of things as they truly exist. What business have we with others who consider themselves blessed merely by the insults uttered by another—"by others who think themselves fortunate simply through the mere abuse directed at them"? We, observing this entire universe—the world—to be subservient to minds constrained by the "weighing" (*guṇanikā*) of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), that is, by the weighing of the qualities consisting of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—[we observe] the excellence and so forth of all things [at specific times].

And regarding a particular individual: by means of a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that manifests states of depression or exaltation through the process of emergence and suppression, there is a grasping of their respective natures and so forth—both how it occurs and how it does not. Thus, the minds of perceivers are constrained; and since beauty and other qualities depend upon those [minds], we—who possess the nature of ascertaining the essence of the three *guṇas* (being unprepared to specifically conceive of sin or offense in any particular individual)—are, in such a most praiseworthy state, [not affected].

While the Lord of Śrīraṅgam—the Lord who is our direct witness, manifest before our very eyes, and who stands as the witness for us as we proceed in the task of clarifying the meaning of reality (having placed the command of the Blessed One at our forefront)—is awake, we do not, even for a moment, engage in idle jesting—that is, the playful employment of humorous speech—regarding those persons who either praise or revile us here; indeed, we do not set ourselves to perform such a futile action. (For such a futile act would never arise within us...)
