Because it is devoted to the Blessed One and because it removes obstacles, one must by all means abandon any action that causes aversion toward meditation on Śauri. (41) The universe has been clearly explained in the *Tattvamuktākalāpa* through its divisions of substance and so forth;

here, however, the form of the *Śārīraka* [Brahma-sūtra] is firmly constructed from head to foot. Therefore, like nectar vomited forth from the ocean of our own tradition, both of these works should be held by those possessed of teachers who, with unwearied devotion, lend each other their hands. (42)

Thus, these *sragdharā* verses, having arrived upon the path described by Śārīra, are honored by wise men of pure disposition who face him with faith; like divine *apsarases*, they adorn and celebrate him for his fitness as the Arhat, having embellished him with many ornaments of Brahman that are the very craftsmanship of the essential meaning of the Upaniṣadic sūtras. (43)

In this manner—by the method described above, on the path set forth by this treatise known as the *Śārīraka*—the *sragdharās*: verses composed in the *sragdharā* meter, which have come together—that is, which have been fully realized through the grace of the Lord as a means for elucidating its meaning—are [here presented].

(The agents are) those who are full of faith—possessing unshakable confidence in the teachings of the scriptures and the guru, and for that very reason, who are "facing toward" [the disciple] with eyes full of grace, intent on being oriented toward the true disciple; by the wise ones (*sūribhiḥ*) whose hearts consist of unconditional affection for the disciple—by the teachers (*ācāryaiḥ*) who strive solely to lead the disciple to the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) through the awakening to the true meaning, [acting] as a means (*sādhana*) by virtue of their own internal fitness to deliver the disciple.

Sent across the ocean of *māyā*—dispatched toward the further shore of the realm of *prakṛti*, which has an inaccessible limit and which conceals the true nature of the Blessed One; [describing] one whose inner being was first filled with intense longing for liberation and who subsequently attained a liberated self; [composed] with ornaments of Brahman—resembling the ornaments bestowed upon liberated souls after they have crossed over the passionless state (*viraja*); and with the craftsmanship of the essential meaning of the *Upaniṣad-sūtras*—the *Upaniṣads* which have the Supreme Brahman as their direct object.

Likewise, indicating that meaning: by means of artistic works in the form of a perfect application to the Supreme Consciousness—the ultimate goal of the Sūtras of Vyāsa which are intent upon churning that [reality]—having refined it so that the tendency toward the modifications of primordial nature (*prakṛti*) does not arise again, and having made the inner self pure, they have arrived upon the path beginning with the *arcis* stage; brought forth by the command of the Supreme Person, they have come of their own accord as *sragdharās*—bearing garlands in their hands—like divine *apsarases*.

Just like divine women residing in the sphere of the supreme, non-material sky, they honor [the Lord]—that is, they treat him with respect—having brought him into a state endowed with perfect disposition for the sake of his divinity as an Arhat, which is to say, for the purpose of establishing his fitness for the enjoyment of the Supreme Person. || 43 ||

May I— who am radiant with the world and purified by service to the wise, which is like the fragrance of jasmine flowers bound in the braided hair of wisdom— be graced by these verses, which are pleasing to the heart and endowed with the fortune of being refined by the assembly of the Vedas, following the sequence of the Pāñcajanya conch, whose greatness is equal to that of the Praṇava.
"Ranganatha himself has been well-recited," he said aloud, and rejoiced. || 44 ||

Raṅganātha—the presiding deity of the Śrīraṅga temple—O Blessed One! [May I attain] that which has obtained illumination through the manifestation of the true meaning of reality, which is unshakable and spontaneously accomplished by means of serving through prostration, inquiry, and attendance those who are wise—that is, whose nature is wisdom, whose form is the knowledge of the true essence of reality, and who are permeated by the fragrance of the jasmine flowers worn upon their braided hair; therefore, they are truly wise.

(But not by resorting to lords or the wealthy)—me, who am named Vedāntācārya; me, who have attained the extraordinary good fortune of entering the series of the *apauruṣeya* (authorless) Vedic speech and adorning it by clarifying its meaning; [me] having filled [this work] myself with these collections of verses (*ślokastoma*)—which have taken form up to this point, which are worthy of being established in my own heart, and which are my own compositions.

In the manner of the greatness of the *praṇava* (the syllable Om), like his own conch named Pāñcajanya—which possesses a majesty equal to the *oṃkāra* both internally and externally—he himself, directly, made it resound—having caused it to sound according to the method described—and rejoiced himself; he attained supreme joy himself (*harṣam avāpa*).
(The intention of the venerable teachers is that [the Lord] caused this to be done by His own power for His own pleasure. || 44 ||
This work has emerged solely from a distinguished effort; the intention is that no conceited claim of personal ownership exists here on my part. || 45 ||
Śrīḥ.
Salutations to the illustrious Rāmānuja. Salutations to Śrī. Salutations to Śrīdhara.
Krama number Pra-saṃ III: "agnir jyotiḥ" (Agni is light).

The light called "fire"—which is a synonym for "rays" (arcis) and refers to the deity presiding over it—the deity known as "day" who presides over the day, the deity presiding over the bright fortnight, the deity presiding over the six months known as the northern course (uttarāyaṇa), and so forth; these are the escorting deities (ātivāhika) who exist upon that path. Upon such a path beginning with "light" (arcir-ādi), the yogins who have attained upward progression—the foremost among the knowers of Brahman—attain their own object of worship, the Supreme Brahman itself, known as Nārāyaṇa.
"He comes to the world of Agni" (as stated in *Praśna Upaniṣad* at "sa etam");
"Agni indeed shall accept the office of the Hotṛ."
(Tāṇḍya Brāhmaṇa 21.10.11) O Agni! You have known the office of the Hotṛ. For the sake of our protection, turn toward me that Vaiśvānara, who is my protector and the benefactor of all men.

"Ungraspable, for it cannot be grasped; indestructible, for it cannot be destroyed; unattached, for it is not attached; unfettered, undistressed, it is not shaken and suffers no harm. This Supreme Self is thus described: because it is beyond the senses, it is not made an object by them; because it lacks connection with parts capable of disintegration, it does not undergo destruction; because its nature is untainted like space, it is not clung to by sin or its fruits. For this very reason—by virtue of its nature being unattached to actions—it does not partake in grief, delusion, and the like, nor is it within the scope of violence."
I have indeed impelled Father Vaiśvānara for protection;
everything other than this is afflicted— everything other than this is afflicted.
"Therefore, indeed, it is truly more difficult to escape from this.
[The number of transitions.]

For a soul who has performed sacrifices and works of public utility (*iṣṭāpūrta*) and remains in the realms of enjoyment such as heaven for as long as there is residual karma that produces pleasure, and having experienced those fruits, descends to the mortal realm at the exhaustion of its karma—after attaining the state of stationary beings such as rice plants, its emergence from that state will be exceedingly delayed;
(for the rejoining with a human body and the like is most difficult to obtain) [the reading *durniṣprapataram* is equivalent to *durniṣprapatataram*, the elision of one *t* being Vedic].

"O dear one, he who meditates upon this Vaiśvānara Self in this manner sees the food of the last [stage] and there arises in his family the splendor of sacred knowledge (brahmavarcasa). However, this is merely the head of the Self."

The worshiper of the Vaiśvānara Self, through the excellence attained by that worship, experiences even worldly objects of enjoyment; having obtained a circle of kinsmen such as sons and grandsons who bring joy to the mind, he experiences the happiness born from seeing them. In the lineage of that person who has worshiped the aforementioned Vaiśvānara Self in the manner described, an increase in Brahmanic luster (*brahmatejas*) is established that persists for a long time.

"O Aupamanyava! This celestial world (*dyuloka*), which is being meditated upon by you with the thought that it is Vaiśvānara, is merely the limb called the head of the object of meditation, Vaiśvānara; it is not the complete Vaiśvānara. If this meditation were only this much, it would indeed be incomplete.
(Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.16)

The sequential number [of the chapters] is as follows: "Now, the higher [knowledge], by which that Imperishable is attained—that which is unseen, ungraspable, without lineage, without color, without eyes or ears, and without hands or feet.

Immediately after the exposition of the lower knowledge—consisting of the knowledge born from hearing the recitation of the Veda along with its limbs (*aṅga*), its appendices (*śiras*), and its supplements (*upabṛṃhaṇa*), and which is of a mediate nature—the higher knowledge is now set forth. And by means of that knowledge consisting of immediate intuition—which is accomplished through the sevenfold means beginning with discrimination and which has reached the state of meditation identical in form to direct perception—[the goal of] knowledge [is realized].

The true nature of the objects of the organs of action is directly realized as being far removed from the inequalities of caste, lineage, and so forth—which are based on the distinctions of qualities, actions, and the like—and as itself not being the locus of either the organs of knowledge or the organs of action, yet having entered into the interior of all things due to its extreme subtlety.
Then the sage [realized] the supreme reality, which transcends all limitations dependent on time, space, and so forth, and which is designated by the term "the Imperishable" (*akṣara*).
II. Now, the Sage:
"Now, that which is the Self is the bridge, the support.

That Supreme Self who exists, being immortal, fearless, and of the nature of Brahman, and who is designated by the term "the True," is like a bridge because He is the sustainer through the preservation of the boundaries of all worlds and by ensuring their non-confusion. (He is called a *setu* because He binds [the collection of sentient and insentient entities] within Himself so that they remain unmixed.)
15. "Now, those in this world who worship with the thought, 'Sacrifices and meritorious works have been given,' proceed toward smoke."

Now, as for those in the village who worship [the idea] that "sacrificial rites and works of public utility are what is given"—persons distinct from the aforementioned worshippers who, although devoted to the performance of Vedic and Smṛti rituals, perform sacrifices and other rites with heaven and the like as their fruit, or the construction of tanks, wells, and ponds with the benefit of the world as their fruit, or the giving of grain, clothing, houses, fields, gardens, and so forth which are useful for the daily livelihood of people, yet live solely depending on houses and such things belonging to the village—[they are described here].

Furthermore, because they are *ativāhika*—conveyors who lead them to their respective destinations such as the world of the Moon—they first reach the deity presiding over smoke. For them, the path is indeed as stated: "Smoke, night," and so forth; it is not the path beginning with light (*arcis*), etc.
II.

Now, those who depart from here without having discovered the Self and these true desires—for them there is no freedom of movement in any of the worlds (as stated in the Upaniṣatkośa: "Those here who, without having discovered the Self..."). Furthermore, those persons who, having spent their lives without having meditated upon the Supreme Self—who is characterized by qualities such as being free from sin and who takes the form of the small ether (daharākāśa)—and likewise without having meditated upon the eternally auspicious and excellent qualities inherent in Him, depart from this body and go to the other world;

Since even upon the attainment of any such world, dependence is unavoidable due to the inevitability of being subject to karma, liberation in the form of supreme equality with the Supreme Self is certainly not obtained.
"Now, when he departs from this body, he ascends upwards by means of these very rays.

When this individual soul (jīva) undergoes departure from this body, which is dependent upon karma, then, by means of the previously mentioned rays of the sun (which serve as the vehicle and support), it ascends to and reaches its destination.
Furthermore, when one is thus asleep—when, being fully composed and serene, one does not perceive any dream—one has then entered these channels (*nāḍīs*).

These channels, numbering seventy-two thousand, are called "beneficial" (*hitā*) and reside within the body. When the general rule "he chooses the *ārṣeya* [lineage]," "he chooses the *hotṛ* [priest]" is applicable, there arises the consideration of a prohibition of that part obtained from the archetype (*prakṛti*) by means of a specific statement within the context of the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices, namely: "He does not choose the *ārṣeya*, he does not choose the *hotṛ*. Likewise, there is no such consideration of a prohibition regarding the performance of the *ye yajāmahe* formula—which is generally applicable to all sacrifices by the rule "at sacrifices, one performs the *ye yajāmahe*"—within the specific sacrifice called the *anūyāja*, as in the rule: "At the *anūyājas*, one does not perform the *ye yajāmahe*."

That being the case, since both the injunction and the prohibition—namely, "He chooses the *ārṣeya* lineage" and "He does not choose the *ārṣeya* lineage," as well as "He performs the *ye yajāmahe*" and "He does not perform it"—are present, there arises a contingency of option (*vikalpa*) consisting in the acceptance of either one of the two (the choice of lineage or its absolute absence; or the performance of the *ye yajāmahe* or its absolute absence). This option, which takes the form of an indefinite, partial acceptance, is improper—that is, contrary to what is right—because it is tainted by the eight defects and must therefore be avoided.

Rather—on the contrary—the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣaḥ*) would be so; that is, both parts of the passage appearing as prohibitions, namely "he does not choose an *ārṣeya* priest" and "he does not perform the *ye yajāmahe*," would constitute a remainder of the sentence by having their own meaning integrated into the sense of the extended application (*atideśa*) rule: "the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) is to be performed like the archetype (*prakṛti*)."

And that being the case, even these two sentences—which appear to be prohibitions—would merely have the sense of an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), namely: "In a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) that possesses the *ārṣeya-varaṇa* and other archetypal desires, one should perform [the rite]; in the subsequent sacrifices (*anuyāja*) other than those [specified], one should employ the *ye yajāmahe* formula. A portion that is observed as being accompanied by a negation that induces conceptual construction (vikalpa) of such a kind must consist of the very sentence-part that functions as a positive injunction; it cannot, however, consist of a subverting statement (bādhakavākya) that is separate from the injunctive sentence and independent.

"For I am indeed the enjoyer and the Lord of all sacrifices; since I alone am Vāsudeva, who is to be propitiated by all rites and the giver of the fruits of all actions, therefore those seeking the three goals of life and those seeking liberation should worship Me alone—the indweller of all those respective deities—rather than perceiving Indra and others, who are subject to decay, as the sole objects of worship through rituals or as the givers of ritual fruits."

Just as space, though existing in conjunction with various objects such as jars or houses that occupy distinct locations, remains untouched by the defects inherent in those jars and so forth, and thus persists in its own unaltered nature; and just as the single sun, though reflected individually in various reservoirs of water such as ponds, wells, and lakes, does not possess a divided form;

even so, the Supreme Self, although present within all things—both sentient and insentient—is untouched by the defects belonging to those respective objects and remains in its own unaltered, singular nature.
"Verily, Space (Ākāśa) is the bringer-forth of name and form; that which is within them is Brahman.

Being of the nature of self-luminosity, the Supreme Self alone has as its sole essential character the illumination of both itself and others; it is the producer of the name and form of the universe—that is, of the words denoting each respective object and of their corresponding shapes. And that reality which is designated by the word "Space" and remains untouched by the aforementioned name and form residing in the world possesses the nature of Brahman, characterized by uncontracted knowledge.

"The Vedas do not purify one devoid of conduct":

even though the Vedas have been studied for the purpose of recitation (*japa*) and systematic study (*pārāyaṇa*), they do not cause a person who is devoid of the performance of rituals such as the *saṃdhyā* prescribed in the scriptures to become free from sin. Therefore, one who desires the destruction of sin through the Veda must certainly perform conduct such as the *saṃdhyā*.

"Having studied the Veda in the house of a teacher according to the prescribed rules, and having performed the duties for the teacher with the remainder of his time, and having returned home, [he should dwell] in a pure place within the household."

Having reached the family—meaning the house or hermitage—of his teacher for the purpose of studying the Veda (*svādhyāya*), the young student (*māṇavaka*) remains there; having spent the time required for service to the teacher at that *gurukula*, he takes up the Veda from the presence of the teacher during the remaining time according to the rules for receiving the Veda. After completing the study of the Veda along with its auxiliary sciences (*sāṅga-vedādhyayana*), he returns from the *gurukula* and, having entered the householder stage (*gṛhasthāśrama*) according to the ritual prescribed by his own *Gṛhya-sūtra*, [remains] in his own station, such as the householder stage, endowed with purity.

Devoted to the repeated recitation and study (*pārāyaṇa*) of his own specific Vedic branch as received from his teacher, and likewise intent upon the performance of duties appropriate for the householder stage, he should engage his sons, disciples, and other worthy qualified persons in righteous actions established by the world and the scriptures; restraining the unrestrained activity of the senses and avoiding injury to living beings and the like, he remains unshakable in his worship of the Lord until the completion of his full lifespan through the exhaustion of his own karma.
One's own nature, while exhausting the lifespan, attains the Supreme Brahman which is realized through the means of meditative form; and indeed, one does not return again to saṃsāra.

"This [earth] indeed is the *juhū* offering-ladle; the heavenly world is the *āhavanīya* fire."

By these two statements, praise is offered through the non-difference [of the sacrificial ladle] from the earth—which serves as the support for all herbs and trees—acting as the means for taking up what is to be offered; and praise is offered through the non-difference of the *āhavanīya* fire (the receptacle of the oblation) from the world called heaven which the sacrificer desires to attain.

Since this [ladle] joins the mortal sacrificer on earth with immortality at the time of performing the *gāyatrī* and other rites, it results ultimately in the praise of the ritual action being performed.

Even deities such as Agni, Vāyu, Sūrya, and Candra exist solely as bodies of the Supreme Self (paramātman), who is the object of worship in all ritual acts; they appear as if they were the ones to be propitiated by those respective rites. Just as when the life-force (jīva) presiding over the body is present, the body appears to be the receiver of the food being consumed, whereas in reality it is the jīva alone who receives it through the medium of the body, so too the Supreme Self is the receiver of all ritual acts through the medium of the other deities, such as Agni and the rest.

112. "All this is enveloped by the Lord" (the remainder of the mantra being: "Whatever moves in this world, by renouncing that [attachment], you should enjoy; do not covet the wealth of anyone"). All the world, consisting of both sentient and insentient beings, which is established through means of valid cognition such as direct perception, exists as something already pervaded—being pervaded by the Supreme Self, the Supreme Person, who is distinct from it and the universal regulator.

Precisely because He exists as all-pervading everywhere, His recognition as the "Pervader" (Vyāpaka) is established in the scriptures as "Vāsudeva. In such a world as this, our cognition of Him as an object of enjoyment, as well as our cognition of Him as our master, and our own cognition of self-interest and independence—while we are in fact characterized by constant subservience and dependence upon Him—all of this is merely the manifestation of delusion.

Therefore, through the knowledge of this reality, you should mentally renounce these objects of enjoyment with the thought, "All this belongs only to You; we have no independence here," and consume them only as necessary for the maintenance of the body which serves as a means for the worship of the Lord. Do not consume them by transgressing the boundaries of the scriptures out of the mere delusion that they belong to you. Do not harbor a greed to claim as your own what belongs to another relative or anyone else, thereby causing them harm.
One should also reflect on this meaning: "Whose wealth is it? It is the wealth of the Supreme Self; do not entertain the thieving thought that it is your own property."
"Ut-tham, ut-tham," indeed do creatures say. This very thing is the *uktha*; this very earth is it.

A certain *śastra* (recitation) that has become a constituent part of the ritual is what Vedic creatures designate by the name *uktha*. Because it is employed for the purpose of rising up through the favor of the deities, the word *uktha* is used in the context of the *śastra* (the hymn of praise consisting of *ṛc* verses). A *śastra* is defined as the declaration of qualities residing in a subject, accomplished by means of non-chanted (*apragīta*) mantras. And when that *śastra* is prescribed as a constituent of the ritual, one should perceive the earth within it; such is the sequence and number.

Furthermore, even the earth cannot be designated by the term *uktha*, because it is not the cause of the arising of all things— such as medicinal herbs and forest trees— which depend upon consciousness.

The four types of devotees—the distressed (*ārta*), the seekers of knowledge (*jijñāsu*), the seekers of wealth (*arthārthin*), and the seekers of knowledge (*jñānin*)—have me alone as their object of worship.

In this life, they obtain all desired human goals from me alone. Because they do not depend on anyone other than me for any purpose whatsoever, they reveal my own magnanimity; therefore, they too are noble. Among them, the last—the man of knowledge (*jñānin*)—is supreme, for he is my very self, being one who sustains me as well; such is my intention.

For that wise one, being called "yuktātmā" (one whose self is disciplined) because he constantly aspires to union with the Supreme Self and possesses a disciplined mind, exists having attained Me alone—who am both the supreme goal of human life and the means to attain it—and having taken refuge in Me with exclusive devotion and as his ultimate support.

"He gives the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the officiating priests" (Kalpasūtra 1).

Regarding the statements "there are four officiating priests," "sixteen officiating priests," or "seventeen officiating priests," and so forth, the officiating priests—namely the Brahman, Hotṛ, Adhvaryu, Udgātṛ, and others—are chosen by the sacrificer according to each specific sacrifice for the purpose of successfully completing that particular rite. While they perform the sacrifice, the sacrificer gives them cows, land, clothing, gold, and other such items as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), in accordance with what is appropriate and according to the injunctions; he does not give them to others. It is called *dakṣiṇā* because it serves to provide capability (*dakṣatā*) [for the performance of the rite].

For the single Self of all beings is established in every being;
although the Supreme Self, who exists as the inner controller (antaryāmī) of all beings, is one alone by its very nature, it is present in each and every being.

While remaining entirely distinct from one another due to their extreme difference in form and nature, [the Self] persists within the innumerable aggregates of sentient and insentient beings, never abandoning its own form and nature. Just as the single moon alone shines in the expanse of the sky, yet that same moon is indeed seen in many ways within various reservoirs of water and upon the waves therein; so it is here.

One who desires to determine that "it is exactly thus" must contemplate this supreme Brahman—which has become the Self of all beings—as being immovable and as a unity immediately following the stages of hearing and reflection; not as a plurality. Because there is no distinction between the connection of the fruit with the action as understood from injunctions and so forth, the substance and deity which constitute the form of the action, the essential nature of the injunction for the action, and the name of the action, one must conclude that an action recited in another location or in another recensional branch (śākhā) is indeed one and the same.

Purāṇa Saṃhitā, Krama Number: Prior to creation, the Lord Nārāyaṇa alone existed. Neither the gods such as Brahmā and Rudra, nor heaven and earth, nor the stars existed. Then, for him whose mind was one-pointedly absorbed in meditation in the form of the volition regarding creation, there arose a state of mind characterized by changelessness suitable for the designation "daughter," as well as the ten organs of knowledge and action.

138. These very things are the worlds: namely, days and nights; half-months (*ardhamāsa*); months (*māsa*); seasons (*ṛtu*); and years (*saṃvatsara*). Days and nights are of the nature of day and night. Half-months are those consisting of fifteen days and nights, synonymous with "fortnights" (*pakṣa*). Months are those consisting of thirty days and nights, designated as two fortnights. Seasons consist of two such months. Years, synonymous with "the rainy season" (*varṣa*), consist of six such seasons and are measured by twelve months. Thus, there are these objects well-known in the world as components of time.

These very same [worlds] are designated by the term "worlds" (*loka*) in the Śrutis; they are the planes of enjoyment. Having entered this path of the gods (*devayāna*), one performs that very act of "not-mind-ing" and "not-reflecting" (*ananamanana*).

Remaining in their respective places, restrained by their boundaries, and acting as the sustainers of the world, they exist for a long time with their existence firmly established. "But this very Self, O Maghavan, I shall explain further to you"—I shall once again clearly elucidate for you, who desire to know the truth, that very Self previously taught to you, in such a way that it is free from the defects mentioned by you and not in contradiction with the meaning stated before; listen.

"O Gārgī, this indeed is that Imperishable (akṣara) which the Brāhmaṇas declare: it is neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long; it is without blood, without fat, without shadow, without darkness, without air, and without ether; it is unattached, without smell, without eye, without ear, without speech, without mind, without radiance, without breath, without happiness, and without measure; it is without interior and without exterior; nothing whatsoever eats it."

O Gārgī! Having brought face-to-face this very Brahman called the Imperishable (akṣara), which is to be known through all the Vedāntas, those who know Brahman describe it clearly and without contradiction: that Brahman does not possess a limited dimension defined by grossness or subtlety, nor even a measurable extent known as shortness or length—[this is] the sequential enumeration [of its attributes].

No; it does not possess the specific forms of various substances such as redness and the like, nor does it possess specific qualities such as viscidity and the like (because it is partless); it is far removed from shadow and darkness, devoid of connection with the vital breaths and so forth produced by karma, devoid of space created by porosity and the like, free from contact with binding agents, devoid of materiality dependent upon connection with taste, smell, and so forth, endowed with innate knowledge that is not subordinate to the organs of action, and possessing its own existence through its own mastery, independent of heat, the vital breaths, and the like.
Therefore, the cognition of the eye, ear, speech, and so forth is incapable of being known through specific determination; it is pervaded by cognition that is not dependent on the mind,
and it is not the locus of pleasure accompanied by suffering.

(Or rather, its nature and essence transcend the limits of the senses), like that which lacks any region not pervaded by itself. This Supreme Brahman, known as the Imperishable (*akṣara*), because it has attained all desires, is devoid of hunger, thirst, and so forth—unlike the individual soul (*jīva*)—and thus possesses no satisfaction derived from the enjoyment of sense objects.

"This is indeed the further explanation of this very syllable" (the words "iti khalu" mark the beginning of this sentence). For those like us who possess the beloved Supreme Brahman as our very life, this mortal world—which is itself mortal and whose nature consists solely in being an object of enjoyment for progeny—is of no avail.

When it is observed that a mantra intended for application to specific rites and the rite itself, which possesses the application of that mantra, are prescribed in different places by general scriptural injunctions, and when there arises the simultaneous occurrence of various mutually contradictory accents—such as loudness (*uccais*) and whispering (*upāṃśu*)—belonging respectively to the Vedic text prescribing the mantra and the Vedic text prescribing the rite, such that a conflict between the accent of the subordinate (*aṅga*) and the principal (*pradhāna*) results, [the rule of *guṇamukhyavyatikrame* applies].

Since an auxiliary (*aṅga*) has as its sole inherent nature being subordinate to the primary (*pradhāna*), the connection of the accent with the Veda occurs only through the primary, and not through anything other than the primary. The latter half of that verse is: "The distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the man of wisdom, O bull among the Bharatas. O best of the Bharatas, Arjuna! All four types of conscious beings—the distressed (*ārta*), the seeker of knowledge (*jijñāsu*), the seeker of wealth (*arthārthin*), and the man of wisdom (*jñānī*)—are performers of meritorious deeds (*puṇyakarmāṇaḥ*). For the sake of attaining their respective desired goals, they all approach Me alone as their refuge and worship Me. This fourfold division among those of meritorious deeds depends upon the relative degree of their merit. (The *ārta* is a person who has fallen from his established position and desires to regain it.)

One who possesses the eightfold sovereignty (*aṣṭaiśvarya*) is one who desires sovereignty; this is the meaning. One who seeks knowledge (*jijñāsu*) is one who desires to attain the true nature of his own self, which is distinct from primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and consists solely of the form of knowledge. One who seeks wealth (*arthārthī*) is a person who, having already attained the eightfold sovereignty, still desires further sovereignty. The knower (*jñānī*) is one who knows the essential nature of the inner self as having the sole essence of being a subordinate to the Blessed Lord (*bhagavat*); such a person considers the Blessed Lord alone to be the goal to be attained and the supreme human end (*parama-puruṣārtha*).

Following the attainment of a body, there is also acquired the excellence of intelligence characterized by the capacity to eliminate opposing factors, as well as proficiency in grasping and retaining specific meanings and speech; furthermore, there is the attainment of distinguished enjoyments consisting of wealth, gold, and other such objects serving as instruments, along with the fullness of vehicles, houses, gardens, fields, and so forth, together with the perfection in the practice of the true Dharma as proclaimed in the scriptures.

That which is denoted by the word *puruṣa* is indeed Brahman, spoken of as such because it is free from transformations such as the body and its states (like old age) which are dependent on karma; for this very reason, since it is superior to everything else, those who worship this Brahman denoted by the word *puruṣa* uninterruptedly and realize it directly, they become partakers of the state of immortality, which is another term for liberation.

And those who are not such as these—lacking devotion to the worship of the Blessed One—enter again and again into that very wheel of saṃsāra, which is called "birth" because it abounds in suffering and is full of the miseries known as old age and death; they do not emerge from sorrow.
"A superhuman *tatpuruṣa* leads them to Brahman. This is the sequence and number.

In the Purāṇa-Saṃhitā, it is stated: "The Reality is Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme. In such scriptural passages and other authoritative treatises, the very object known by the term "Nārāyaṇa" is superior to all else, having reached the ultimate limit of infinite excellence. He alone, whose nature and other attributes are never subject to subversion by any limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as time, space, and so forth, and who transcends all such adjuncts, is denoted by the word "Tattva" (Reality).
203. "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*):

Brahman, whose body is the individual soul (*jīva*) as qualified by non-consciousness, is non-different from the Supreme Brahman, which is omniscient, possesses true volition, and is the cause of the universe. (This is stated generally; specifically: O Śvetaketu! The Supreme Self who has your body is non-different from the Supreme Self characterized by omniscience and other such attributes.
"204. He shakes off his good deeds and evil deeds; his dear kinsmen obtain his good deeds, and those who are not dear obtain his evil deeds. (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad)
1–37) II. He shakes off his good and evil deeds.
III.

For a person who is being liberated and about to depart by way of the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi*), his merits and demerits are taken up by his kinsmen, such as his sons, in the form of inheritance. Among them, well-wishing relatives take over his merit, while ill-wishing relatives take over his demerit. Consequently, that conscious self becomes one from whom merit and sin have been cast off, and whose impurities have been shaken away.

"Likewise, through the destruction of the qualities to be abandoned, the qualities such as awakening (*avabodha*) are manifested; they are not produced, for they are indeed eternal to the Self. (Ratna-prabhā). By contemplating the similarity between the jewel and its light, and between the reservoir of water and the space situated within it, with respect to the individual soul (*jīvātman*) and its qualities, it is established that the qualities of knowledge and so forth are inherent in the very nature of the individual soul. They are brought to manifestation by the removal of the qualities to be abandoned which obstruct the expression of knowledge; they are not newly produced. Since those qualities are eternally established for him, it is proven that they are not adventitious.
The sequential number (Prasam 2.1.14):
"Its non-identity [with the cause] is established on account of the word 'originating' and so forth."

It is determined that the non-existence of any difference between the world—the effect of the Supreme Self—and the Supreme Brahman, which is its own cause, is more convincingly established by the scriptural passages such as "the modification is a mere verbal handle, a name" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.4), beginning with the word *ārambhaṇa*, which support that conclusion.
Then, the wise one, having shaken off both merit and demerit, becomes stainless and attains supreme equality.

When indeed the conscious one, through uninterrupted practice of meditation—which serves as the means to liberation—directly perceives the Supreme Self who has become manifest as the golden-hued one; then, by virtue of having perfected his meditation, he becomes one to be addressed by the term "the Knower" (*vidvān*). Having shaken off from himself the two types of karma known as merit and demerit—which were attached to him and were capable of obstructing liberation—and being thus free from the taint of karma, [he realizes] the identity of his own self and the Supreme Self, which, though attained by its very nature, has now become manifest.

Endowed with the collection of qualities common [to all liberated souls], such as the removal of sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) and so forth, he attains a supreme equality with Brahman (*brahmaparamasāmya*) brought about by the perfection of such qualities. As it is said: "That very same thing becomes a source of pleasure and then again gives rise to suffering; it arises for anger and also for serenity. Therefore, nothing exists that is essentially of the nature of suffering, nor is anything essentially of the nature of pleasure."

For this reason, a single entity, depending on differences of time, place, individual, and so forth, becomes the cause of both pleasure and pain; likewise, it becomes the basis for both anger and favor without distinction. Therefore, no object whatsoever can be defined as having an invariable nature such that one could say, "This is of the nature of happiness," or "This is of the nature of suffering. "That alone is the pure, that is Brahman, that alone is called the immortal. In it all worlds are supported; no one transcends it. (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1)

The sequence-number (krama-saṃkhyā), primary number (pra-saṃ.), is the very Supreme Brahman itself; by virtue of its independence from anything else, it is the self-luminous illuminator of both itself and others, and it is eternally endowed with the states of being Brahman and immortality (amṛtatva) due to its being free from all limiting adjuncts (nirupādhika). Within that very Supreme Brahman, all worlds abide, supported [by it] like the spokes on the hub of a chariot-wheel. No one whatsoever is able to exist beyond it.
Regarding the sequence and number:

that very [Self] which is my own self is indeed the self of Manu and the others, as well as of the Sun and other conscious beings. Thus, realizing the oneness of the Self everywhere, he contemplated the non-difference of Manu, the Sun, and so forth within himself, thinking, "I alone am Manu; I alone am the Sun."
214. Those who know this thus, and those who in the forest worship with faith and austerity, they pass into the light.

And those who know the nature of the individual self (*jīvātman*) as it has been introduced, according to the method described in the Pañcāgni-vidyā; and those who, having abandoned the desires for sons, wealth, and worlds, become dwellers of the forest and, relying on faith, engage in the worship of the Supreme Brahman—which is denoted by the term "austerity"—both these groups are indeed worshippers (*upāsakāḥ*).

Those who meditate on their own self as having the Supreme Self as its body, and those who meditate on the Supreme Self as having their own self as His body, both rely—when reaching the path of the Blessed Lord—exclusively upon that specific deity designated by the term "light" (*arciḥ*), which is the first *ativāhika* (conductor), as the means for attaining their respective goals; thus, the path beginning with light is exactly the same for both groups.

"Those here whose conduct has been pleasant will, it is likely, attain a pleasant womb—either the womb of a Brāhmaṇa, the womb of a Kṣatriya, or the womb of a Vaiśya. But those here whose conduct has been foul will, it is likely, attain a foul womb—either the womb of a dog, the womb of a pig, or the womb of an outcaste."

Among living beings, those who have completed the enjoyment of the fruits of their karma in the other world return from that world to this one; (*abhyāśa*—meaning *abhi*, *ā*, and *aś*). Indeed, when those souls possess the remainder of matured well-performed deeds (*sukṛta*) after they have been enjoyed, then, in accordance with their own merit, they obtain the attainment of a body belonging to any one of the three social classes (*varṇas*) known as Brahmin, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya, which is suitable for the performance of meritorious actions (*puṇyakarma*) called *sukṛta*.

However, those living beings who have performed despicable deeds remaining after their enjoyment—such souls obtain a physical endowment connected to the wombs of dogs, pigs, outcastes, and so forth, which corresponds to their own inferior karma and leads them again and again to the performance of base actions.

there is freedom of movement in all worlds.

III. Therefore, those living beings who have obtained bodies in this world, having properly worshipped according to the prescribed rules the Supreme Brahman—which is the Self of all—as well as its auspicious qualities such as freedom from sin, and having left this world and gone to the higher world, for such beings there is established the experience of enjoyments existing in all worlds that constitute the manifestation of Brahman, as well as an independent state not subject to karma. This is seen in the Upanishad beginning with the words, "Now, those here who [meditate] on the Self," and so forth.
"That which is true is this: he who is that person in the solar orb, and he who is this person in the right eye.

That person known as Āditya, who is understood from the Śruti as "this golden person within the solar orb" when the sun's disc is shining in the sky, and the person residing in the eye, who is described as "this person seen within the eye"—both of these are denoted by the term *satya* (the Real) because they are devoid of change (*nirvikāratvāt*).
"Just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, even so evil action does not adhere to one who knows thus.

Just as drops of water fallen upon a lotus petal do not become stained at all, even so, in a person who is a devotee of the Blessed One, every action—whether called good or evil—is not stained at all because it is designated by the term "evil" due to its opposition to liberation. It does not become an obstacle to the attainment of the Self. "In that state where he is deep asleep..."

"At that specific time when this person has fallen into deep sleep, having withdrawn the entire collection of his own organs and being free from the impurity produced by contact with external objects, yet devoid of the experience of his own self—this alone is to be contemplated as the Self; and this alone is the substratum of immortality, fearlessness, and Brahmanhood. Thus did Prajāpati instruct Indra and Virocana.

"Just as a great highway, being stretched out, goes to both villages—this one and that one; even so these rays of the sun go to both worlds—this one and that one. They extend from yonder sun and have entered into these channels (nāḍīs). From these channels they extend forth."

They have entered into that very sun. Therefore, just as a long road connects two villages—one near and one distant—so as to traverse both locations, even so these rays of the sun under discussion connect this mortal world inhabited by us with the supreme world called Āditya which is sought but not yet reached, and thus they exist spanning both worlds.

They become pervaded by both. Having attained their expansion everywhere from the distant solar world, those rays of the sun are connected to the channels (nāḍīs) associated with the heart; likewise, having emerged and spread out from those channels, they are of a nature connected even to the distant sun. "Just as a tuft of reed-wool thrown into a fire would be completely consumed, even so all his evils are consumed."

Therefore, just as the tuft of cotton from a reed touched by fire is said to be burnt by the mere touch itself, leaving nothing but its name and no longer remaining in its own form; even so, all the sins of the knower who knows Brahman are completely burnt away without remainder by the fire of knowledge. "That which I am, that is He; that which He is, that am I."

I, the disciple who am the inner self (*pratyagātman*), am indeed non-different from the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) whom I worship. Likewise, the Supreme Self who is my object of worship is indeed non-different from me, the disciple who am the inner self. Although there is a difference in the essential nature (*svarūpa*) between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Being (*para*)—who stand as the worshipper and the worshipped—their non-difference, established by the relationship of body and self (*śarīrātma-bhāva*), remains unimpaired. Thus, just as in the expression "I am Devadatta," a non-difference is conventionally treated between the body denoted by the term "Devadatta" and the self which is the referent of "I."

"And when there is a condition consisting of that [object], a single continuity arises, free from longing for anything else; thus is that meditation accomplished by means of the first six factors. (pṛ.saṃ. A continuous stream of mindfulness—characterized as a flow uninterrupted by heterogeneous intervening conditions and directed toward the Lord’s divine and auspicious form, which serves as a beautiful substratum—is what is expressed by the term "meditation" (*dhyāna*).

Regarding the sequence and number: that meditation (dhyāna) attains its true nature through the six auxiliaries of yoga known as restraint (yama), observance (niyama), posture (āsana), breath control (prāṇāyāma), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), and concentration (dhāraṇā). With these limbs, the principal practice (aṅgin) of meditation is accomplished; that itself is the seventh [stage]. The eighth, however, is samādhi, which is the culminating stage of meditation.

"Because of the observation of a restrictive rule regarding that [act], the fruit is indeed a distinct connection [to the result]. Those learned Śrotriyas, when about to eat, sip water; having eaten, they sip water. They consider this very act to be making [the mouth] non-naked. Therefore, one who knows this should sip water when about to eat, and should sip water after eating; he thereby makes this very [mouth] non-naked."

In the manner described, because the wise (*śiṣṭas*)—who are devoted to reflecting upon the meaning of the Vedas and performing their injunctions—contemplate the waters as possessing the quality of being a covering by virtue of their status as the clothing of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), they perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) both before and after eating. By doing so, they conceive of it as a covering for the vital breath and recognize: "We are making this vital breath free from nakedness.
Therefore, any person in the world who knows this truth must necessarily perform the *ācamana* both before and after eating, in order to ensure that the vital breath remains unclothed.

"Having sought the Self through austerity (*tapas*), celibacy (*brahmacarya*), faith (*śraddhā*), and knowledge (*vidyā*)"—the first part of this sentence is "then by the northern path," and the final part is "they conquer the Sun. Having meditated upon the Supreme Self, who has become the self of all, and for that very reason, having departed by the path known as the northern course consisting of light and so forth, they reach the station called Āditya, which serves as the gateway to the attainment of Brahman.
"He spoke to her on the earth" (referring to the passage:

"Prajāpati desired to place Agni; he spoke to her on the earth"). This means that a specific deity named Prajāpati desired to establish Agni upon the earth as his substratum; at that time, the deity presiding over the earth spoke with reference to him.

"When asked by Candramas, 'Who are you?', that conscious being who has reached the Moon and answers in the manner about to be described—that conscious being Candramas permits to go to the world of the Blessed One."

We worship Him, the Supreme Maheśvara among the lords, and the Supreme Deity among the deities—that is, He who is the most eminent among those possessing lordship and is therefore designated by the title "Maheśvara," and likewise, because He is the object of worship, He is the most exalted deity among those understood by the term "devatā" (the Supreme Self).
"As he departs, the vital breath (prāṇa) departs after him; as the vital breath departs, all the vital functions (prāṇas) depart after it.
"As he departs, the vital breath departs after him."

From the blazing at the tip of the heart located in its own place, preceded by the movement through the specific channels to be traversed, the chief vital breath (*prāṇa*) also departs from the body, following the individual soul (*jīva*), the lord of the organs, as it exits. And following that chief vital breath, all the other vital breaths—speech and the rest (the organs of action and knowledge)—also depart from the body.
"231. This very Self the Brahmins seek to know through the study of the Vedas, by sacrifice, by charity, by austerity, and by fasting."
III–IV.

Those belonging to the three higher castes who desire to know the Supreme Self under discussion—Him who is filled with attributes such as being the Lord of all and who is conducive to attainment and other goals—should, for the sake of the means required for that desired knowledge, perform the following: the repeated recitation of the *svādhyāya* (one's own Vedic study) according to the prescribed rules; sacrificial acts such as *yāga* which please the gods; and the dedication of one’s own wealth to worthy recipients with a mind free from possessiveness—all these to be performed in the manner that pleases the Lord.

They perform the prescribed duties, such as austerity (*tapas*)— which includes the practice of eating food according to restrictions regarding time and place, along with rules such as fasting— and other such enjoined dharmas, following their sequential order and number.

"Only by knowing Him does one transcend death"— only by directly perceiving the Supreme Person, the cause of all, through worship in the form of uninterrupted meditation, does the seeker of liberation, having transcended the path of saṃsāra which is as difficult to cross as death and abounds in negligence,
proceed to the supreme state.
233. "In whatever way one worships it, that very thing one becomes. II.iii.11.

People seeking liberation constantly worship this aforementioned Supreme Self through the various modes of His perceptible attributes; and having attained Him, they indeed experience Him as possessing those very same modes.
"Going upwards by these two, one attains immortality; the others lead to departing in various directions. (Praśna Upaniṣad 3.7)

Step number [1] (*udānaśabda*): Since the capacity to impel the upward movement of that which is to be expressed resides only in *tejomātra*, the living being (*jīva*), characterized by the departure of bodily heat and desiring death, approaches the vital breath (*prāṇa*)—which is conjoined with the organs of action and the organs of knowledge such as speech, having attained a specific union with them through the mind in accordance with the desire for rebirth prior to death (in order to depart together with all of them).
"Therefore, one who knows this, having become calm, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, and concentrated, should see the Self in the very Self"—
this is the sequence (Krama-saṃkhyā), page [number].

"Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa does not drink liquor, thinking, 'Lest I be released by evil' (Kaṭha Saṃhitā). Because engaging in prohibited conduct except in times of distress causes sin, any person born of the first caste, reflecting "May I not be tainted by evil," must never perform the prohibited act known as drinking liquor.

Therefore, those about to eat surround this [the mouth] with water both before and after, for the very reason that water is the garment of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Even today, cultured people (*śiṣṭas*) are observed performing the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) with water both when they are about to eat and when they have finished eating; by doing so, they clothe the vital breath with water.
From that very Self, indeed, space was produced.

From the Supreme Brahman, which is endowed with attributes that define its nature as truth and so forth, ether was produced;
this is the sequence of enumeration.
"In that which is within it, one should meditate" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.23).
Having dwelt there until the time of their falling away, they then return again by this very same path.

The delay in attaining Brahman lasts only until the time when liberation from the body that was commenced occurs; immediately upon the release from the body, the attainment of Brahman takes place exactly as understood through the scriptures. (Regarding the first human goal, the Vedic supreme person:
"His sons inherit his property; his friends his good deeds, and his enemies his evil deeds."

For the knower of Brahman, who is conscious and about to be liberated from the cycle of transmigration— at the very moment of departing from the body— his collection of meritorious deeds (*sukṛta*), as well as his sons who are the recipients of his affection, [are considered] in the form of an inheritance;
[this is the] sequence and enumeration according to the *Prasaṃkhyā*.
They take it; his sons, sharing in that displeasure, accept as their inheritance that collection of his actions known as evil deeds.

Of that [personality-sheath] designated as "consisting of food" (annamaya), which extends up to the gross body, the very object denoted by the word "prāṇa"—namely, the vital breath—is its head; for it is the sustainer of that which is indicated as the self (ātman) in the form of the person consisting of prāṇa (prāṇamaya), and thus, being the primary element, it occupies the position of the head.

"Pleasure is indeed its head": for that Supreme Self, designated as *ānandamaya* and possessing a human form—who is in reality the very self of everything from the *annamaya* up to the *vijñānamaya* by virtue of being the unconditional sustainer—pleasure, which is denoted by the word "dear" (*priya*), occupies the position of the head.
"He has freedom of movement in all worlds. The form of that person is like a garment dyed with saffron;
it is the radiant [form] of the Supreme Brahman, whose body consists of both the manifest and the unmanifest, the conscious and the unconscious.
He possesses a divine and auspicious form; clad in garments resembling those dyed with turmeric, he is lovely and exists as the very embodiment of meditative auspiciousness.
"At its end is a subtle cavity": within the center or the inner portion of the heart-lotus situated in the middle of the body, which is connected by channels, there is a single, most subtle aperture.
"In the center of that crest (śikhā), the Supreme Self (paramātman) is established.

He is Brahmā, he is Śiva, he is Indra; he is the Imperishable, the Supreme, the Sovereign. In the center of that slender flame of fire—described as being subtler than an atom, rising upwards, situated within the heart, and resembling a dark cloud with lightning—the Supreme Self resides. By virtue of having Brahmā, Rudra, and Indra as His body, He is designated as non-different from them. For the conscious being established in the science of Nyāsa, there is a sacrifice consisting of the five limbs, which takes the form of living and is composed of the science of Nyāsa. The fuel (idhma) to be cast into the fire to be worshipped by the sacrificer at the time of sacrifice is, in fact, the body itself, which serves as the substratum for the senses and the self; the sacrificial altar, which is the locus of the sacrificer and the implements of the fire to be worshipped in the sacrifice, is likewise the chest region, which consists of the seat of the heart; and the bundle of darbha grass serving as a sacrificial implement is simply the hairs of the body.

"When that [karma] of theirs comes to an end"—meaning, when the karma that serves as the means for experiencing pleasure and pain comes to exhaustion for those conscious beings whose true nature is veiled by action and who are habituated to repeated wandering on the path of *saṃsāra*, which consists of merit and demerit; then, due to the casting off of the burden of karma intent upon producing experience, those conscious beings, becoming light like the sky, become oriented toward descending. "Of these very beings, there are indeed three seeds: the egg-born, the viviparous, and the soil-born. This is the sequential enumeration.

The primordial substances (*prakṛtidravya*) related to the elements previously mentioned—namely fire, water, and earth—which serve as the causes for individual creation (*vyaṣṭisṛṣṭi*), are triadic in nature; they are the causes for the creation of birds, serpents, and so forth, the causes for the creation of humans, cattle, and so forth, and the causes for the creation of stationary beings such as trees and shrubs.

In various places, those very things which are designated by the term "seed" (*bīja*) and which arise therefrom are known in the world and in the scriptures as "egg-born," "womb-born," and "sprout-born. (An *aṇḍa* is a shell that serves as the cause for the production of birds and the like; a *jarāyu* is the womb; an *udbhid* is the most subtle primary matter in the form of a seed that serves as the cause for production after breaking through the earth. Whatever collection of rites exists in the performance of a sacrifice, whether primary or subsidiary, all that was made entirely mental (*manomaya*), being accomplished by the mind alone within the "mind-piled" and other such [fires].

"Or rather, you are I, O Blessed One, O Devatā; indeed, I am you, O Blessed One, O Devatā."

O Blessed One, O Supreme Deity (in the form of Brahman), who are the object of my worship! I am the worshipper, and because you are the object of worship, I am non-different from you; and you too, as the object of worship, are non-different from me, the worshipper—since the object of worship is one’s own Self and the worshipper is its body, and there is non-difference between the body and the embodied.

Furthermore, in this very context, both the presentation and the question relate exclusively to three things—the object of meditation, the meditator, and the act of meditation—which correspond to the three categories of the goal, the attainer, and the means; from beginning to end, both the answer and the inquiry are seen to concern these three objects of knowledge alone, and there is no possibility whatsoever, anywhere, of the Pradhāna being taught as an object of knowledge.

"The small [space] is indeed the threefold seed; because of the subsequent [texts].

The entire sin of the Blessed One is removed by that place known as the heart-lotus, which is His supreme abode; even in that subtle place, there exists the even more subtle Brahman, which transcends sorrow and is situated with an unbounded dimension like space; and within that Brahman, the collection of auspicious qualities—both of these must be meditated upon by one seeking liberation.
289. "The daytime, the bright fortnight, and the northern course of the sun—these are recommended for one who is about to die; the opposite is censured. 353. "The daytime and the bright fortnight..."

For embodied beings whose death is imminent, among the divisions of day and night, the time known as "day" is superior; among the bright and dark fortnights, the time known as the "bright fortnight" is superior; and among the southern and northern solstices, the time known as the "northern solstice" is superior. These are worthy of praise because they lead to the attainment of the desired celestial state. Conversely, the other times—known as night, the dark fortnight, and the southern solstice—are inferior, as they obscure the path to the gods (*devayāna*).

Those objects—such as chariots, their yoking, efforts, their movements, and chariot-paths—which are experienced by the *jīva* while situated in the state of dream, do not at all become fit for experience upon waking from that dream-state into the waking state.

The Blessed Lord, bestowing fruits in accordance with each person's respective karma, creates all these objects so that they rest solely upon the particular individual and the particular time.

"Indeed, for him there is no food that has been eaten which is unfit to be eaten, nor is there anything unfit to be accepted that has been accepted.

For a person who maintains the contemplation (*dṛṣṭi*) that all things to be consumed by living beings—such as food and so forth—are the food of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), the fault arising from eating what should not be eaten or accepting what should not be accepted does not at all accrue to him.

"Indeed, for one who knows this, nothing whatsoever becomes non-food. That is to say, regarding any object that is to be eaten by the entire class of living beings—such as food and the like—no fault whatsoever arises from eating what is not fit to be eaten, because the practitioner is a person who views [all things] through the perspective of their being the food of the vital breath (prāṇa).
"For one who possesses a body, there is indeed no removal of the pleasant and the unpleasant. But for one who is truly bodiless, neither the pleasant nor the unpleasant touches him."

As long as the connection with a body produced by karma persists, it is not possible for the living being (*jīva*) to avoid the pleasure and pain that depend upon that bodily connection. Only when there is the complete destruction, without remainder, of the contact with a body caused by karma, does the state of being free from pleasure and pain become established. [This is seen in the injunctions] "One should not harm any beings" and "Not harming any beings," which mean that one should never perform an action conducive to the separation of life in regard to any living being whatsoever.

"322. For there is nothing else higher than this 'not this, not this. Now, its name is 'the Truth of truth. The vital breaths (prāṇas) are indeed truth; of them, this [Brahman] is the truth. The Supreme Self is immutable even by its own nature and essence, and being uncontracted, it is the reality; thus, He is "the Truth of truth. The individual soul (jīva), however, is not such, because it possesses occasional contraction of knowledge.

karma performed by a living being, known as good and evil deeds, does not reach its own destruction through infinite time without that being having personally experienced the pleasure and pain that constitute its fruit.
327. "This Self is not to be attained by instruction, nor by intellect, nor by much hearing. Only by whomsoever this [Self] chooses him is he attained; to him this Self reveals its own form."

This Self is not attained by recitation... nor by hearing; this Self is not attainable by mere instruction, [but only by him whom this Self chooses]. It is his own body that he chooses. This Self is not attainable by mere instruction.

This Supreme Self has been described; yet, even through the practices of hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*) performed with absolute regularity, His glory cannot be attained by one who is devoid of exclusive devotion to the worship of the Lord. Rather, this Supreme Self Himself desires to bestow His own self upon whichever conscious being is engaged in His worship, out of boundless love for that person, and He causes Himself to be experienced along with His essential nature, attributes, form, and manifestations.
Therefore, the Supreme Person is attainable solely through meditation that has taken the form of love.
"Neither one who has not desisted from evil conduct, nor one who is not tranquil, nor one who is not concentrated, nor even one whose mind is not at peace, can attain this through wisdom. (3.2.28)

329. This does not age with his aging; this is not slain by his being slain. This is the true City of Brahman. Within it, all desires are contained. "This does not age with his aging."

This city called Brahman is changeless and designated by the term "Reality" (*satya*); for even when the body—which serves as its substratum and locus—becomes decayed by old age, or is even struck down by the act of killing, this city of Brahman, which is the object of that substratum, never undergoes decay, nor does it become subject to being slain. And within this city called Brahman, the auspicious qualities desired by those seeking liberation are perfectly established.
"Indeed, he does not at this time know himself thus: 'I am this,' nor these beings. He has gone to utter destruction; I see no prospect of enjoyment here."

This individual soul (*jīva*) is in the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*); in that state, unlike in the waking and dreaming states, it is not able to perceive its own self along with its attributes—such as form, name, lineage, and country—as "I am such-and-such," nor can it perceive its own objects of enjoyment. It is, as it were, almost extinguished. Alas! In this [state] which is proclaimed to be the very nature of the Self, the capacity for enjoyment by those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*)... [end of fragment].

That which is undivided by time and space, because of its extreme subtlety, which exists as the Self by entering into the interior of all things—that Supreme Brahman the best of yogis clearly recognize as the material cause of all beings.

"That which is designated by the word 'Akṣara' (the Imperishable), which is changeless, and which is eternal among the eternal and conscious among the conscious" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 5.13). And that which...

For the Supreme Self, though He Himself is eternally one and pure consciousness, effortlessly bestows upon the countless eternal individual selves the objects they require in the form of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). By realizing that Supreme Self dwelling within oneself through direct perception (*aparokṣajñāna*), the conscious being attains supreme peace.
"He is to be meditated upon.
"The stainless one attains the supreme equality— partless, actionless, tranquil, faultless, and stainless."

The Supreme Brahman is, by its very nature, partless; it is devoid of action because it has accomplished all that was to be done and because of its omnipresence; it is untouched by the six waves such as hunger and thirst; it is faultless (carrying its dependents without blemish due to its extraordinary affection for those who have taken refuge in it); and it is, like space, of an unattached essence.
337. It is not the other, because it is untenable.

The individual soul (*jīva*), being other than the Supreme Brahman, is not denoted by the term "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) found in the *Ānandavallī* of the Taittirīya Upaniṣad; for in that [soul], there is an impossibility of possessing unlimited bliss reaching its ultimate limit, which is what is being repeatedly meditated upon as culminating in a state of unsurpassed excellence.

[he is] the Lord of all, the inner ruler."
Depending solely upon Nārāyaṇa—who is the protector of the entire world without conditions, whose nature is the governance of all selves, and who is the Supreme Self—the entire universe exists.

The heart, resembling the interior of a lotus bud and facing downwards—shaped like the closed bud of a white lotus (*puṇḍarīka*)—is the locus for both the individual self (*jīvātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*). This place called the heart, situated below the attachment of the neck, faces downward; it is the locus for those seeking liberation to practice the worship of the Supreme Person.

"Having reached the highest light, he emerges in his own true form. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.2–3)

"That which is higher than the high, greater than the great"— that from which no other thing more excellent can possibly exist, and from which no other thing more vast can possibly exist, is that supreme Brahman, which is without equal and without superior.

"He attains the divine Person who is higher than the high"; "But by meditating on the higher [nature], that which was concealed becomes manifest"; "His supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold, as are His innate knowledge, strength, and action."
"Having become disillusioned with scholarship," "Of his feet are all beings"— beings.
All things, consisting of the moving and the non-moving, and containing within them both the conscious and the unconscious, are merely portions of this aforementioned Puruṣa.
This is King Soma;
from the world of the fathers he goes to space, and from space to the moon.
That is the food of the gods; the gods eat it. Having dwelt there for as long as the [merit] has been exhausted, they then return again by this same path.

Those who do not abide in Brahman, but perform only sacrifices (*iṣṭa*) and works of public utility (*pūrta*), reach the deities presiding over smoke, the night, the dark fortnight, the southern solstice, and the six months—acting as *ativāhika* guides—and through them reach the world of the fathers (*pitṛloka*). After reaching the world of the fathers, they there attain space and the moon; having reached the state of being King Soma, they obtain a divine body to experience the celestial worlds. The gods born of the womb (*ājānajā devāḥ*) residing there [approach] these living beings endowed with such a divine body.

They utilize [the body] as an instrument for their own enjoyment. Having remained there until the completion of the visible results, they then cease from the path of saṃsāra, which consists of coming and going, and turn back.

"He performs meritorious action; he performs sinful action" (this is worldly usage). He practices action that is a means to prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), as well as action contrary to that. "The person (*puruṣa*), having approached the mental [self], leads [the soul] to the worlds of Brahman"—this is the sequence and number according to the *Pūrva Saṃhitā*.

356. "The sacrifice, indeed, is man. Those twenty-four years which constitute his life—while he lives, man himself is to be contemplated as the essence of the sacrifice. Within that span of life, those first twenty-four years are to be contemplated as the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) belonging to the sacrifice. Furthermore, there are three divisions of life, and three pressings of the sacrifice, known as the morning, midday, and third (evening) pressings. Because the man is non-different from the sacrifice, there is a correspondence between the three sacrificial pressings and the periods of his life."

"Having realized the Self and the Impeller as distinct"—that is, having understood one's own conscious self and the Supreme Self who has entered within as its controller, and having discerned them as separate through their mutually distinct natures by way of the relationship between the controlled and the controller, and the relationship between the body and the embodied; and having likewise meditated upon them, one becomes an object of the love of the Supreme Self who impels one, and thereby attains immortality—liberation.

"Consisting of earth, consisting of water... consisting of fire" (referring to the previously introduced individual soul, whose nature is knowledge and whose attribute is knowledge, even though it is endowed with the qualities of Brahman): [it means that] this soul has the elements such as earth and water as its instruments, as well as fire as its instrument.

359. "But the other is not like this, as in the case of light and so forth. The individual self (*jīvabhūta*), which is the inner self (*pratyagātman*), is like the radiance of gems, the sun, and so on; it possesses a status as a partial aspect (*ekadeśatva*) resulting from its being a qualification (*viśeṣaṇatva*) of the Supreme Brahman, which is characterized by both the conscious and the unconscious. However, the Supreme Self is not similar to the individual self. Therefore, the defects residing in the individual self would not belong to Brahman. "And [Brahman is] the material cause (*prakṛti*), because there is no contradiction with the initial proposition and the illustrative examples."

The Supreme Brahman is not only the efficient cause (nimittakāraṇa) with respect to the world, but also its material cause (upādānakāraṇa); for this is the only way to avoid contradiction with the scriptural declaration that "by the knowledge of one, all is known," as well as with the analogy of the lump of clay and clay products found in the Śruti.

"Prajāpati is indeed the year; this Mahāvrata is his very self. Time, consisting of the year, is the referent denoted by the word Prajāpati. This Mahāvrata is that which constitutes the self of that Prajāpati.

"I enter the assembly hall, the abode of Prajāpati. I seek refuge in that station of Brahman which is the assembly hall by virtue of being the locus of Him who is designated by the term "Prajāpati"—the Supreme Self who, as the protector of the multitude of sentient and insentient beings created by Himself, has become the progeny (prajā). I enter that abode of Brahman which takes the form of an assembly hall.
"Pratardana, the son of Divodāsa, indeed approached the beloved abode of Indra.
This means that Pratardana by name, the offspring of the Kṣatriya Divodāsa, attained the dear station of Indra, the king of the gods.

The first, second, and third are the three types of paths for the accomplishment of Dharma. Among these, the first is the stage of the householder (*gṛhasthāśrama*), characterized by sacrifices and other such duties; the second is the two stages of the forest-dweller (*vaikhānasa*) and the wandering mendicant (*pāritrajya*), characterized primarily by austerity (*tapas*); and the third is the stage of the student (*brahmacaryāśrama*), characterized by residing in the teacher’s household (*gurukula*) under discipline, consisting of service to the teacher and study. (This is a grouping of the four stages of life into three categories). Among these, one who is established in Brahman becomes a partaker of liberation.
All others as well, who are devoted to their respective stages of life (āśrama), shall attain the worlds of merit.
"The Lord of Pradhāna and Kṣetrajña, the Master of the Guṇas"—
the Blessed One, the creator of all, being the controller and the sovereign remainder of both Prakṛti and Puruṣa, is the Lord of the six qualities beginning with knowledge,
or of the three [qualities]: sattva, rajas, and tamas.
The controller.
"He lives for one hundred and sixteen years.
This "Puruṣavidyā" which has been stated— whosoever knows it with faith, that person lives for one hundred years plus sixteen years (that is, a full human lifespan) without deficiency.

367. Prācīnaśāla Aupamanyava—the son of Upamanyu, named Prācīnaśāla—and others, five in number who were perfected in the study of the Vedas, conducted an inquiry with the desire to know the nature of Vaiśvānara, asking: "Who is our Self? What is Brahman?"

"Prājāpatya belongs to the Brāhmaṇas" means that for those Brāhmaṇas desiring that [state], who are devoted solely to the stage of life (āśrama) associated with the Brāhmaṇa caste, the place to be attained as its fruit is the world of the Prajāpatis—a realm of enjoyment; it is not, however, the station of the Supreme Brahman.
369. "Embraced by the conscious Self (prājña ātmā), he knows nothing that is external, nor anything that is internal.

Being conscious, in the state of deep sleep, having attained a specific kind of close contact called "embracing" that pervades all his limbs through the Supreme Self known as the Prājña, he does not experience the collection of objects consisting of the internal and the external.
"He who, having fallen into a life-threatening danger, eats food from whatever source it may come,
is not tainted by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
This means that when there is a risk to one's life, one may disregard the rules regarding food and eat from any source whatsoever.
A person who, having taken food, preserves his life, is not smeared by evil, just as a lotus leaf touched by water is not stained by it.

"Having reached the end of that karma, whatever he does here, from that world he returns again to this world for the sake of karma"—thus [it is] for one who desires. "Having reached the end... he does here; from that... for the sake of karma"—thus [it is] for one who desires.

This mortal being, possessed of consciousness, having performed in this world whatever action—whether small or great—driven by the attachment to agency and its fruits, experiences the fruit of that entire collection of actions in the next world; thereafter, in order to perform action once more, he returns to this very world. Thus described is the conscious being who is attached to the desire for results.
"For I am exceedingly dear to the knower, and he is dear to Me. All these [others] are indeed noble, but the knower is My very Self; this is My conviction."
