"For he, with a disciplined mind, is established in me alone as his unsurpassed goal. (4.23) Since I am exceedingly dear to the man of knowledge, whose sole goal is to attain Me, for that very reason that man of knowledge cannot endure separation from Me even for half a moment. Because He is so exceedingly dear to him, I too cannot endure separation from Him even for a moment. All the aforementioned types of devotees—the distressed and the rest—worship Me alone; they do not expect anything from any other deity. Therefore, because they manifest My generosity, they are indeed truly munificent.

Among these, the one who is exceedingly dear to Me, who cannot endure separation from Me, and who possesses knowledge—because he is My sustainer—he exists to Me even as My very Self; this is the meaning intended by Me. For that man of knowledge, perceiving Me, Vāsudeva, as the supreme goal to be attained, takes refuge in Me alone and remains ever established in Me.
"The fruit [of knowledge arises] from this, because it is logical:
'At the end of many births, the man of wisdom resorts to Me, realizing that Vāsudeva is everything; such a great soul is very rare.'"

Indeed, at the conclusion of many births of meritorious birth, having attained some most meritorious birth, one realizes the true nature of my own essential form and nature—which are the supreme Self—and becoming a man of knowledge (*jñānī*), takes refuge in me alone as the Supreme Self.
He alone is the Great-Souled One (*mahātmā*). Thinking of me alone as the supreme goal and the highest human end (*puruṣārtha*), such a person is exceedingly difficult to find.

"Having become disillusioned with both childhood and scholarship, one then becomes a sage" (Praśna Upaniṣad 3.1), and "Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa... (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.5.1); in this context, [it is said] "He should abide in childhood.
(Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.8.1) Oke.

[Pravrajyā-vidhi] (In the passage beginning with "Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa..."): "Having completed the student life (*brahmacarya*), one should become a householder; having become a forest-dweller from the household, one should renounce. Or else, otherwise, one may renounce directly from the student life, or from the household, or from the forest. On whatever day one becomes dispassionate, on that very day one should renounce."

Having completed the study of the Vedas at the teacher's house and having fulfilled the fruit of that study by completing the stage of studentship (*brahmacarya*), one should enter the householder’s stage of life (*gārhasthya*). From there, having adopted the forest-dweller’s stage (*vānaprastha*), one should take up renunciation (*sannyāsa*), which has the abandonment of all attachments as its fruit. Some, however, say that one may enter the stage of liberation directly from the stage of studentship, even without passing through the householder’s stage.
In reality, however, at the very moment that an exceedingly intense dispassion arises, one should proceed from whatever stage of life one is in to the stage of liberation (mokṣāśrama).

"The third is the student (brahmacārin) who dwells in the teacher's household, exhausting himself completely in the teacher's household. Among the three types of stages of life (āśramas), which serve as the means for accomplishing dharma, the stage characterized by dwelling in the teacher's household is the third type. Abiding therein, the student, within the teacher's family alone, should bring his own body to its end through total devotion to the service of the teacher.

"Virtues have been gathered with Brahman as the eldest; in the beginning, Brahman extended the supreme heaven. He was indeed born as the first among those who have become Brahman; who, therefore, is able to rival Brahman? (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 2.4.7.26).

By the Supreme Brahman, the Lord of All, the most excellent virtues such as splendor and strength are held by His very nature. Therefore, this Brahman transcends all; it is the foremost in the world by virtue of being the Lord of the universe. Its sequence and number are established accordingly.

He pervaded and remained within even the well-known abodes of Indra and the other gods, such as heaven; for he had manifested himself spontaneously even prior to the manifestation of all the Prajāpatis. Who indeed would strive to rival such a Brahmā, possessed of such exceedingly wonderful and great majesty?
"When the time for reabsorption has arrived, all those perfected souls, together with Brahmā,
at the end of the highest [cycle], enter the supreme state."

Furthermore, those who worship Hiraṇyagarbha, who has entered the category of the effected (kārya), all of them—having fulfilled their purpose through the attainment of the knowledge that serves as the means to liberation—at the conclusion of the lifespan of the four-faced one known as Parā, when the great dissolution (mahāpralaya) has set in, attain together with their own worshipped Hiraṇyagarbha the state of Viṣṇu called Vaikuṇṭha, the station from which there is no return.

Having formed the resolve: "For the sake of Brahman, for You who are the Great One, with the syllable *om*, I shall unite the Self," one should offer one's own self to that Brahman by means of the instrument which is the form of *oṃ*— that is, one should join the Self to That.
He attains the greatness of Brahman—
the person who, having entrusted the burden of himself and his possessions to the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign of All, is established in the knowledge of *nyāsa* (renunciation).
By that very means, having been liberated from all the bonds of saṃsāra, he attains the majesty of Brahman, which consists in the manifestation of the qualities of Brahman within himself.
"For I am the foundation of Brahman, of the immortal and the imperishable,

of the eternal dharma, and of absolute bliss. Since I, Vāsudeva alone, am the primary cause for the manifestation of the imperishable nature of the individual soul as Brahman— which constitutes the supreme human goal— and since I am the principal means for the attainment of sovereignty that transcends all and for the uninterrupted experience of the Lord, I alone am to be served for the sake of attaining the state of Brahman.
Kamakhyā Pṛ.saṃ.:

In the beginning, this universe was indeed Brahman alone; being one, it did not flourish. It created from itself that which is superior in form: the *kṣatra*—those who are the *kṣatra*s among the gods: Indra, Varuṇa, Soma, Rudra, Parjanya, Yama, Mṛtyu, and Īśāna.

This entire universe, prior to its manifestation, existed as Brahman with name and form undifferentiated; it was a single reality, designated solely by the term "Brahman. Because it was in a state of oneness, it was devoid of the glory produced by diversity, manifoldness, and so forth. That Brahman, being of such a nature, created from its own body the preeminent form called *kṣatra*, which is the most excellent of all. These are the forms of the *kṣatra* included among the gods, known as Indra, Varuṇa, Soma, Rudra, Parjanya, Yama, Mṛtyu, and Īśāna.
"He who knows Brahman attains the Supreme. (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1)

A conscious worshiper of Brahman attains only the Supreme Brahman, which is the most excellent object of his own worship;
thus, the injunction "one who desires the attainment of the Supreme [should do so] through the knowledge of Brahman" reaches its final conclusion.
388. "Established in Brahman, one attains immortality. II.iii.12.
"Brahman alone is all this.
All this universe comes to be as the body of Brahman, through its connection with Brahman, and by virtue of its identity with Brahman.
"The state of Brahman is ordained for renunciants:
for those who have entered the fourth stage of life (caturthāśrama), whose vital energy is drawn upward (ūrdhvaretas), only the station of Brahman—that is, the station of Viṣṇu—is to be attained."
"Having risen above the desire for sons, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worlds, the Brāhmaṇas then lead the life of mendicancy.

Having meditated uninterruptedly upon the Supreme Self—the innermost of all, transcending hunger and other such states, and whose very nature is untouched by suffering—those Brāhmaṇas who are qualified for renunciation (prātaḥ-saṃnyāsa), having abandoned the longing for sons, the longing for wealth, and the longing for the worlds attainable through sons and so forth, remain far removed from attachment and perform only the wandering for alms in order to sustain their physical bodies alone.
"Let the Blessed One indeed tell that to me.
"My father, you yourself are my teacher; please instruct me in the object that must be known, the ruler of all. Do not, however, send me back to the house of the guru.
He who knows this becomes one whose enemy, the evil rival, is defeated by himself."

He who meditates upon the Udgātṛ as the vital breath (prāṇa) becomes one whose mind is well-refined and preeminent among all. Any person who hates such a man—whether that person be called "evil" or an "enemy"—meets with defeat.
"He who knows thus shines and glows with fame, glory, and the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*).

He who meditates in the manner described becomes radiant through renown born of liberality and through celebrity born of valor; likewise, he becomes brilliant through excellence in conduct and Vedic study, and he becomes zealous in his own duties.
"The knot of the heart is severed, all doubts are cut asunder,
and his karmas are exhausted when that which is both high and low is seen."
"From fear of Him the wind blows; from fear the sun rises."

VI. "From fear of Him the wind blows"—out of fear of the Supreme Self, all five—wind, sun, fire, Indra, and death—set themselves in motion with swift speed to perform their respective functions, such as blowing, shining, protecting the world, and withdrawing it.
"May the Blessed One explain this to us once more; you, who are endowed with the knowledge of reality, should explain this matter again clearly to me, who am desirous of knowing the truth."
Furthermore, because of the designation of difference,

the subject matter propounded in the *Ānandamaya* section is not the individual soul (*jīva*). This is because the scripture, in the passage "The inner Self consisting of bliss is other than the one consisting of cognition," clearly establishes the distinction of the *Ānandamaya* from the individual soul— which is designated as "consisting of cognition" and exists in both bound and liberated states.
"Mind piled upon breath" (401), "mind-piled," "speech-piled," "breath-piled," "eye-piled," "ear-piled," "action-piled," and "fire-piled.

This has been explained: the mind itself—specifically, the multitude of mental fluctuations arising from each single day within the human lifespan consisting of thirty-six thousand days—is the fire called "mind-piled" when it is meditated upon through the perception of being fire. [He saw those fires as belonging to himself, worthy of worship, and produced by the mind.]

This has been described as speech itself; the aggregates of the functions of speech arising from each of the aforementioned days, which are the operations of the organ of speech, are the fires named "Speech-built" (*vākcita*) when meditated upon through the vision of them as fire. (He saw those [fires] as connected to himself, as objects of worship to be accomplished by means of speech). (In this same way, the "Breath-built" (*prāṇacit*) and others are also to be understood). By the term "fire-builders" (*agnicitaḥ*), the operation of the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*) is intended.
"He draws away the senses, with the mind as the sixth, which abide in their own nature.

As the individual soul (jīva) departs from the body, it draws along the external senses—such as sight and the rest—which are fixed in their respective natural functions of speaking, grasping, moving, and so forth; it also draws along the internal organ, the mind, for the sake of utility in a future body. Having drawn them along, it proceeds, leading them under its own control; indeed, it does not go without them.
And:
"It is to be perceived by the mind alone; there is not the slightest diversity here. He who perceives diversity here goes from death to death."

It has been stated that Brahman, which is to be made an object of realization through the memory established by profound meditation (*nididhyāsana*), must be apprehended by the mind alone, purified by hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*). In such a Brahman, who is the substratum of all, no diversity caused by the multiplicity of its own superstrates is even conceivable; for everything is non-different from the perspective of its nature as Brahman-Atman. In this regard, he who fails to perceive the non-difference produced by the identity with the Self-as-Brahman, and instead contemplates even the slightest difference, shall repeatedly enter the cycle of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) and shall not become a partaker of liberation.
404. ‘Manu Vaivasvata the King’—Manu, the son of Vivasvat, named Vaivasvata, was the first king. ‘The cups were drawn with the mind; they praised with the mind; they recited with the mind.’

In these fires, such as the mind-made fire (manaścit) and others—which are produced by the mind alone—the sacrificial vessels denoted by the word "graha" were also grasped by the mind alone; those engaged in the *udgītha* chant performed the acts of chanting (*stotra*) by the mind alone, and those engaged in recitation (*śastra*) likewise accomplished the ritual recitation (*śastra*) by the mind alone.
406. Having sat down in a place that is agreeable to the mind and conducive to increasing the object of meditation, one should perform the practice of meditation.
"One should meditate upon the mind as Brahman":
one should perform meditation by superimposing the nature of Brahman upon the sense organ that is the mind. (Praśna Upaniṣad Saṃhitā)
The sequential enumeration:

"This person consists of mind, he is light, he is truth. Within his heart, as a grain of rice or a grain of barley, he is the ruler of all, the lord of all, the sovereign of all; he governs all this, whatever exists."

This Person, consisting of light, is perceivable by the purified mind; He is called "Real" because His essential nature remains unmodified even upon the destruction of the body and other things that serve as His locus. Due to being the presiding controller over a small locus, He appears as if having a small dimension, like a grain of rice or barley. He is the one who holds all categories of sentient and insentient beings under His own control; He is the Ruler of all, the Remainder of all, and He sustains everything—past, present, and future—by means of His own creative governance.

409. "Under my supervision, Nature brings forth the moving and the unmoving; by this cause, O son of Kuntī, the world revolves. "Under my supervision... the moving and the unmoving; by this cause... it revolves."

Gazed upon by me—the Supreme Self, the presiding lord of all beings, the foremost of all, whose will is ever true—my own Prakṛti brings forth the universe known as the moving and the non-moving. By my glance, acting as the instrumental cause in accordance with the karma of all fields (kṣetras), this universe perpetually unfolds, subject to transformations that are not governed by any other.
"And he who serves Me with unswerving yoga of devotion,
having transcended these qualities, becomes fit for the state of Brahman.
(Krama Saṃkhyā)

These conscious beings, whose minds are intensely attached to Me and who are exceedingly dear to Me, do not at all attain rebirth in the worldly cycle, which is by nature utterly unstable in its form and essence. Having attained perfection through uninterrupted worship of Me, they have reached Me alone, who am the supreme goal of human endeavor. [As it is said: "From the months to the world of the gods; from the world of the gods to the sun";
and "From the months to the year; from the year to the sun."
In the passage beginning with "atha yadu caiva" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.6.7), [the principle is stated]:
"When a primary sense is possible, a metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā) is not logical."

When an object endowed with the fullness of the grounds for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of any given word is perceived as suitable, it is not logical to resort to the verbal function called *lakṣaṇā*—which depends on the primary meaning, which obstructs the connection of the primary meaning with the action at hand, and which establishes a connection with a meaning related to the primary meaning—unless there is no other way; for [the function of *lakṣaṇā*] is resorted to only when there is no other recourse. When a reservoir is constructed by some person, the space occupied by the reservoir or the water situated therein is not created by him; rather, that which was already existing previously merely becomes manifest. 389. *Punarāvartanam* (returning): the re-entry into the world of mortals after the exhaustion of karma following the enjoyment of its fruits in the other world. 390. *Punarbhavaḥ* (rebirth): the attainment of birth once again. 391. *Purītat*: a specific mass of flesh situated within the heart; it is also the Brahman situated within. 392. *Puruṣaḥ*: the body; *puruṣavacasaḥ*: those who are designated by the word "person" (*puruṣa*).

394. *Puruṣavidhatvam*—the state of being similar to a person. 395. *Puruṣārthāḥ*—objects consisting of pleasure and its means, which are independent of conscious beings. *Puṣkariṇyaḥ*—lotus ponds (reservoirs of water serving as the support for lotuses).

397. *Pūrvakāṇḍam*: The first section [of the Mīmāṃsā], the scripture in the form of the Jaiminīya and Sāṅkarṣaṇa [Kāṇḍas], which is devoted to the investigation of ritual action (*karman*) and the deities (*devatā*). 398. *Pūrvapakṣabījāni*: The seeds of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*); those elements that give rise to the prima facie argument. 399. *Pūrvabhāvaḥ*: The prior existence; the presence of previously mentioned qualities. 400. *Prakaraṇam*: Context; the mutual expectancy residing in two things that are related to one another.

401 *Prakaraṇāntaram* — A section concerning matters other than those under discussion, such as ritual actions (*karma*) and so forth. 402 *Prakāratvam* — The state of being a qualifier (*prakāra*), which is a type of objecthood (*viṣayatā*) standing in a correlative relation to the state of being a qualificandum (*viśeṣyatā*). 403 *Prakupyeyuḥ* — They would become frustrated; they would find themselves without any scope for application.
404 *Prakṛti*: A verbal root (*dhātu*) or similar element established by grammatical instruction (*anuśāsana*) as the basis for the arising of an affix (*pratyaya*).
405 *Prakriyābheda*: A different method of analysis; a distinct section (*prakaraṇa*).
406 They insert, cast out, or establish.
407 *Pracyutiḥ*: falling away, decline, or stumbling.
403 *Prajāpativākyam*: the statement concerning the nature of the Self spoken by the Four-faced Lord (Brahmā) to Indra and Virocana in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*.
409 *Prajñāntaram*: another form of knowledge; a different type of wisdom.
410 *pratāyante* — they become continuous;
412 *pratikṣepaḥ* — the demonstration of irrationality;
413 *pratipattiḥ* — attainment, going.
414 *pratipattibhedaḥ* — the distinction (difference) residing in those who study the various branches of the Veda (*vedaśākhā*).
415 *pratipadyante* — they attain or reach. 416 *pratibruvan* — giving a reply, about to respond.

417 *Pratisañcāra*: dissolution (*pralaya*). 418 *Pratiṣedharūpa*: having the nature of negation (*abhāvātmaka*; those whose essential form is expressed by the negative particle *nañ*). 419 *Pratiṣṭhā*: establishment.
Pratiṣṭhā: A firm connection (the continuity of mindfulness).
420 One who relies on a symbol (*pratīka*)—that is, one who meditates upon an effect such as Hiraṇyagarbha, or meditates upon names and so forth by perceiving them as Brahman.
421 Pratīkopāsana: The contemplation of what is not Brahman by means of the perception of it as Brahman.
422 *Pratyakṣa* and *anumāna*—the *śruti* (Veda) and *smṛti* (tradition).
423 *Pratyanīkaḥ*—an adversary, an opponent, or something contradictory. 424 *Pratyabhijñāyate*—it is recognized as "this is that very same thing"; it is identified through synthesis.
425. *Pratyabhisandhiḥ*—reconnection (*anusandhāna*).
426. *Pratyayaḥ*—cognition (*pratīti*), specifically the cognition of identity as "this is that very same thing.
427. *Pratyayāvṛttiḥ*—meditation (*dhyāna*), synonymous with worship (*upāsanā*), which is the repeated practice (*paunaḥpunya*) of contemplating the auspicious object of focus (*śubhāśraya*).
428 *pratyavasṛpya*—having returned;
429 *pratyavarūḍhāḥ*—those who have descended from that world to reach the mortal world;
*pratyavāyaḥ*—the Lord’s punishment arising from the transgression of his command (the cause of downward rebirth).
Pratyāharaṇam – withdrawal; pratyekam – individually, for each turn;
prathitiḥ – renown, recognition (bhā).
434 *pradughe*—he milked forth, that is, he produced in an eminent manner;
435 *pradyotaḥ*—illumination;
436 *prabodhaḥ*—the attainment of the state of waking.
437. *Prabhuḥ*—capable of bestowing the fruit [of actions such as ritual acts and meditation]. 438. *Pramāṇam*—that which determines an object.
439. *Prayut*—the joy arising from the application [of something] by one who has recognized it as their own;
it is an activity distinct from volition (*saṅkalpa*).
*Prayogavidhiḥ*: A rule that instructs on the swiftness of execution during the performance (*prayoga*) or practice (*anuṣṭhāna*) of rituals.

442 *Pravargya*: A collection of rites to be performed during the twelve days that constitute a subsidiary part of the *Jyotiṣṭoma*. 443 *Pravrājinaḥ*: Renunciants who have abandoned all attachments; those who have taken up the life of a *saṃnyāsī*.
The vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*): the primary breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*) and the organs of knowledge and action.
Living selves (*jīvātman*).
A state of life-threatening danger (*prāṇātyayāpatti*): a physical condition in which the departure of the vital breaths is imminent.
*Prāṇitā*—a living being (*dehin*) by virtue of breathing or living (447).
*Prāptiḥ*—the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consisting of scriptural injunction (*śruti*), which is the comprehension established by a mandatory rule (*vidhi*). *Upakramaḥ*—the introduction.

448 *prāmāṇikāḥ* – those who have ascertained an object obtained through a means of valid cognition that is not sublated. 449 *prāmādikam* – that which has occurred through lack of attention. 450 *prāyaścittam* – an action understood from the scriptures as a means for removing a fault that has arisen; [it serves] for that which has been destroyed.
451. *Karma-sandhāna*: that by which the connection of action is made; such action. 452. *Prārabdha-karma*: action consisting of merit and demerit that has begun and is engaged in yielding its fruit.
453. *Phala-śruti*: a scriptural statement that bestows the fruit of ritual action, meditation, and so forth. *Pretya*: having departed from this world and gone to that other world.
454. *Phalābhisandhiḥ*: the expectation of a fruit for an action performed other than the pleasure of the Blessed One.
455. *Phalī*: the performer of the sacrifice (*yajamāna*), who is the master of the fruit of the ritual action such as a sacrifice.
456. *Bandhaḥ*: transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) which conceals one's true nature.

457. *Balīyastvam* (in the context of a means of knowledge): The capacity to produce the ascertainment of invalidity (*aprāmāṇya-niścaya*) regarding a cognition produced by that which is contradictory to itself.

458. An alternative (*vikalpa*) containing sublation (*bādhagarbha*) consists of: the sublation of the understanding of the means to the result (*phalasādhanatva*), the sublation of the performance (*anuṣṭhāna*), the sublation of the production of the *apūrva*, and the sublation of the result (*phala*). Each individual head [of this category] possesses four defects; thus, there are eight defects in total.

459. *Vikalpa*: mental construction; 460. *Bādha*: a cognition that penetrates negation; 461. *Bālya*: adopting a nature resembling that of a child, characterized by not manifesting one's own excellence; 462. *Buddhy-artha*: for the purpose of meditation.

462. *Brahmacarya*—the collection of duties prescribed with reference to a celibate student (*brahmacārin*). 463. *Brahmaloka*—Brahman itself as the world; Brahman being directly realized. 464. *Brahmavid-apacāra*—an action that causes displeasure to those who possess knowledge of Brahman. 465. *Brahmavidyā*—the knowledge of the Veda.

466. *Brahmavidyāprāptiḥ* — The attainment of the knowledge of Brahman; the realization of the experience of Brahman established in the state of direct intuition (*sākṣātkāra*). 467. *Brahmaikaniṣṭhatvam* — Being centered exclusively in Brahman; the state of finding ultimate rest in Brahman alone. 468. *Bhakṣyatvam* (of individual souls by the gods) — The attainment of being an instrument for the enjoyment of the gods.

469. *Bhaktatvam* — The state of being a devotee; speaking with an intended meaning directed toward the indicated sense (*lakṣyārtha*) while abandoning the literal sense (*śakyārtha*), i.e., figurative usage (*aupacārikatva*).

The word *bhāva*—a term such as "one should meditate" (*upāsīta*) or "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), which conveys an object that has entered the state of being something to be accomplished (the *sādhya*).
*Bhīṣā*—accompanied by fear.
*Bhūtagrāmavān*—the individual soul (*jīva*) possessing a body composed of the five elements.

473. *Bhūtasūkṣmāṇi*—the subtle elements (*tanmātras*), which are the five elements (*pañcabhūta*) serving as the basis for the body that brings about experience (*bhoga*). 474. *Bhūmā*—vast, all-encompassing. 475. *Bhūyastvam*—abundance, excess.

476. *Bhedaśrutayaḥ*—scriptural passages intended to convey the existence of two entities in the form of quality (*guṇa*) and the possessor of quality (*guṇin*). 477. *Bhogaḥ*—the experience of pleasure and so forth, which constitutes the fruit of meritorious and non-meritorious actions, both in this world and the next. 478. *Bhraṣṭāḥ*—those who have fallen away from the duties of their stage of life (*āśrama-dharma*).
479. *Bhrātṛvyaḥ*—an enemy; one who seeks to destroy.
480. *Maṭacī*—a shower of stones; 481. *Maṇḍalāni*—the worlds; 482.
*Maraṇam*—the cessation of the connection between all vital breaths and the body.
483. *Mantrasāmarthya* (the efficacy of mantras) refers to the efficacy of the object understood through the mantra. 484.
*Mahāpātakāni* (great sins) consist of killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, stealing gold, violating the teacher’s bed, and associating with those who commit these acts.
485. *Mahāvratam*—a specific ritual act that is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the *sattra* sacrifice;
*mānasagrahaḥ*—a specific sacrificial vessel (*yajñapātra*) to be accomplished solely through mental concentration (*manana*);
*māyāmātram*—having a wondrous form.
488 *māhārājanam* — a garment dyed with safflower (*kausumbha*), or a garment made of turmeric (*haridra*).

489 *mukhyatvam* (in the case of a word) — the communication of meaning through the fullness of the ground for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*). *mugdhaḥ* — one who has fallen into a state of fainting.
*mud*—affection characterized by the sense of ownership toward an object; 492 *muniḥ*—one whose nature is preeminent reflection;
493 *mumūrṣavaḥ*—those whose death is imminent.
494 *mūrtiḥ*—the body;
495 *mūrcchā*—the state of remaining in connection with the subtle vital body (*prāṇadeha*);
496 *meghaḥ*—a cloud, a water-carrier characterized by the state of being ready to rain (*miha* means "to sprinkle").

497. Knowledge as the means to liberation (*mokṣasādhana-jñāna*): knowledge in the form of a most vivid recollection (*smṛti*) that has attained the state of direct perception (*pratyakṣatāpanna*) regarding the auspicious substratum (*śubhāśraya*). 498. Silence (*mauna*): the repeated cultivation (*saṃśīlana*) consisting of the meditation upon the nature of the auspicious substratum, which is the object of concentration (*dhyānālambana*). 499. Yakṣa: one worthy of worship (*pūjya*) [from the root *yaja*, meaning "to worship"]. 500. As it came (*yathetam*): according to the manner of arrival; following the very sequence of the journey [from the root *i*, meaning "to go";
*itam*]. Until the exhaustion of the momentum (*yāvat-sampātam*): until the end of the persistence of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) which brings about the enjoyment of the fruit.

506. The performance of the *ye yajāmahe* formula: "The utterance of the seventeen-syllable mantra—*āśrāvaya*, *astu śrauṣaṭ*, *yaja*, *ye yajāmahe*, *vaṣaṭ*—is performed at sacrifices with the injunction: 'One performs the *ye yajāmahe* at sacrifices.'"
Thus it is ordained:
507. *Rathayogāḥ*—horses, oxen, and so forth, being yoked to chariots; 508. *Ramaṇīyacaraṇāḥ*—those whose nature is the performance of meritorious deeds.
509 *Rasatama*: Most essential; most substantial.
510 *Raṃhati* means it moves or goes;
*rāga* means desire (the longing for a result).
512. *Rāgaprāpta*: That which is the object of an activity dependent on desire (*icchā*).

513. *Rātrisatra-nyāya*: Even when no result is explicitly heard in an injunctive sentence (*vidhi-vākya*), one must adopt as the result that which is mentioned in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), in accordance with the requirement for a result inherent in the injunctive sentence.

514 *rūpam* (in the context of sacrifice and meditation) – the substance and the deity; the form of that which is to be meditated upon. 515 *rūpaṇam* – the conceptualization of even an attribute (*dharma*) that does not exist in the substrate (*dharmī*) [for the purpose of making it ascend to the intellect].
516 *lakṣyate* – is inferred.
517. *Lambhuka*: worthy of being obtained.
518. *Lākṣaṇikatva*: the state of indicating a meaning by means of a portion of the ground for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*) or through a possible connection (*sambandha*).
519. *Liṅga*: an indicator, that which causes inference.
The means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that establishes subsidiary status (*aṅgatva*) by means of *śruti*— which consists of *sāmarthya* (capacity)—

is the statement in the present tense (*vartamānāpadeśa*). This occurs when there is no indicative suffix (*liṅ*) or the like that makes known the nature of an injunction (*vidhitva*), such as the expression "he is" (*bhavati*) or "he does" (*karoti*).
526. *Vasti*: water produced in the bladder (or the bladder itself).

527. *Vākya*: a syntactical unit consisting of the co-occurrence of words expressing the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*upādeya*), serving as an authoritative means of application (*viniyojaka-pramāṇa*).
528. *Vākyabheda*: the failure of a section (*praghaṭṭa*) to culminate in a single meaning (or a single action).
529 *vākyaśeṣaḥ* – another sentence within the same context that assists the injunctive statement.
530 *vāgvṛttiḥ* – the function of the vocal organ; the operation of the speech faculty.
531 *vācoyuktiḥ* – the nature or form of speech.
532. *Vājasaneyins*: followers of the White Yajurveda branch.
533. *Vikalpa*: the adoption of one of two contradictory positions in turn;
a manifold arrangement (*vividhaḥ kalpaḥ*), i.e., variety.

534. [From the perspective of conceptual construction, there are eight faults: the abandonment of accepted validity, the acceptance of invalidity, the abandonment of accepted invalidity, and the acceptance of abandoned validity (alternating between the two positions). ELE
535. *Vikāraloka*: worlds that are effects; (*vikāra* = effect). 536. *Vikāsa*: the attainment of a state capable of performing its own function.
537. *Vijihīte*: it expands its own parts, making them porous.
538 *vitataḥ* — specifically pervaded (*vitatiḥ* — extension).
539 *vittaiṣaṇā* — the desire for the acquisition of wealth and the wish to perform sacrifices, giving, and so forth.

540 *vidyā* — a specific kind of knowledge consisting of meditative worship (*upāsanā*), [which involves] auspicious meditation until the end of one's life (*yāvadāyuṣam*). 541 *vidyādhikāraḥ* — the introduction to or the section concerning knowledge (*vidyā*).
542. *Vidyānugrahaḥ* – the state of being a cooperative cause for the accomplishment of knowledge.
543. *Vidyārthavādaḥ* – a statement intended for the praise of knowledge.

544. *Vidyāsāmarthyam*—the fullness of knowledge (*vidyā-pauṣkalya*), or [alternatively] the firmness of knowledge in its capacity as a means toward its own goal. 545. *Vidhi*—a word synonymous with *codanā* (impulsion), which makes known what was previously unknown. 546.
*Vidhi-niṣedha-śāstrāṇi*—the scriptures such as the *Śruti*, etc., which are intent upon engaging one in what is beneficial and withdrawing one from what is harmful. 547.
*Vidhi-pratyaya*—the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, residing in words such as "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) or "one should meditate" (*upāsīta*).
548 *vidhura*: one whose wife has died; separated. 549 *vidheyabheda*: the distinction between the subordinate and the principal [acts]; the distinction between the auxiliary and the primary.
550 *vidhyādi*: the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama*) such as sacrifice, etc., and [the virtues] such as tranquility (*śama*) and self-restraint (*dama*).
551 Destruction (vināśa) — non-perception.

552 Destruction of evils (pāpmanām vināśaḥ) — the disruption of the capacity of the arisen karma to produce its own effects. It is the cessation of the Lord’s desire to bestow the fruits of karma from a previous time, upon the arising of knowledge (vidyā).
553. *Viniyoga*: the apprehension of subsidiarity (*aṅgatva*).
554. *Viniyoga-pṛthaktva*: the establishment of separate subsidiary status for a single performed action by means of conferring two distinct types of assistance.
555 *Viparīta*: those who have abandoned their own duties;
556 *Viparyaya*: (of bondage)—a specific state opposed to bondage (the state of liberation); 557 *Vibhāga*: separation, the state of being distinct, the nature of being isolated.
558 Contradiction (virodha) – impossibility (anupapannatā).
559 Distinctiveness (viśiṣṭatā) – excellence (atiśaya), pre-eminence (utkarṣa).
560 A distinguished place (viśiṣṭo deśaḥ) – a non-material place (aprākṛto deśaḥ) distinct from all other locations belonging to anything else.

561. *Viśeṣa* (particularity): that which possesses a pervaded property (*vyāpyadharman*; i.e., being encompassed by a universal). 562. *Viśeṣaṇa* (qualifier): a property that distinguishes its own substratum, the subject (*dharmin*). 563. *Viśeṣita* (qualified): made known as possessing a particularity.
564 *Viṣvaśvaḥ*—those who partake in various inferior wombs.
565 *Vīryavattaratvam* (in actions)—the capacity to yield one's own fruit without delay due to the absence of obstacles. 565 *Vṛddhiḥ*—increase, accumulation.
567 *Vedanam*—meditation (*upāsanā*), the uninterrupted contemplation of the object of meditation.
568. *Veśāntāḥ*—ponds (small lakes); *vaikhānasaḥ*—a forest-dweller, a forest-recluse (*vānaprasthaḥ*). 570. *Vaitṛṣṇyam*—dispassion (the avoidance of craving for trivial objects).
571 *vyatikaraḥ*: mutual displacement of positions. 572 *vyatihāraḥ*: the taking of what belongs to another preceded by the offering of one's own.

573 *vyatihārānusandhānam*: a form of contemplation (*anusandhāna*) consisting of the cultivation of mutual identity. 574 *vyavacchidyate*: it is understood as being distinguished from others through exclusion.
575. *vyavatiṣṭheran* — they would become established; 576.
*vyastopāsanam* — meditation upon individual parts contained within the whole;
577. *vyāvartanam* — a distinguishing characteristic.

578. The *vyāhṛtis*—the seven beginning with *bhūḥ* and ending with *satya*, or the three: *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svaḥ*. 579. *Śakti*: the substantive; an attribute not established separately [from it] (*pṛthaksiddha*); residing in action—the desire to bestow desired or undesired fruits. Its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is the quality (*dharma*) consisting of the pleasure or displeasure of the Supreme Person.

580. Distinction of words—the distinction within prescriptive words; a non-synonymous verbal root (*dhātu*, e.g., *yajati* and *juhoti*). 581. Inference from words—*śruti* and *smṛti*; faith and water; a particular modification of the mental faculty (*manovṛtti*) related to the individual soul (*jīva*);
a particular state of the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*); the intellect of conviction (*āstikyabuddhi*).
592. *Śruti*: A means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consisting of an independent verbal expression that apprehends subsidiarity (indicated by the second case ending, etc.);
a word that directly conveys a necessary meaning.
593. *Śrotriyas*: Those whose minds are inclined toward the performance of what is prescribed by *śruti* and the avoidance of its opposite, based on non-contradiction.

594. *Śrautakrama*: The sequence of performance among the rites to be executed, established by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) regarding case endings and so forth. 595. *Ṣoḍaśī*: A specific sacrificial vessel bearing this name. 596. *Sakṛtkṛtam*: That which has been performed once. 597. *Saṅkoca*: The state of remaining capable of performing its own function (in the case of knowledge, etc.), or non-expansion. 598. *Saṅkhyā*: Number, such as duality or plurality (as in "one offers three oblations," etc.), which serves as a means of proof for the distinction between ritual acts. 599. *Saṃjñapanam*: The immolation of the animal body used for sacrifice.
600 *Satya*—free from any alteration of its essential nature (*svarūpa*), it is endowed with an unconditioned existence (*nirupādhika-sattā*).
601 *Satyakāmatva*—the possession of a multitude of auspicious qualities (*kalyāṇaguṇa-gaṇavatva*) and being the leader of the eternal manifestation (*nityavibhūti*).
602 *Satyasaṅkalpatva*—the state of having an unimpeded resolve (*apratihata-pratijñatva*).
603 *sandehaḥ* – doubt – the middle body;
604 *sandhyam* – the state of dreaming.

605. *Samanvārambhaṇa*—conjunction, association (*samavāya*) [of the means of knowledge such as scripture]; it is the coexistence (*samāveśa*) that occurs simultaneously with the contradiction regarding their own respective objects of cognition.
607. *Samaṣṭi-puruṣa*—the four-faced one, Hiraṇyagarbha.
608 *Samastopāsana*: meditation endowed with all constituent parts.
609 *Samākhyā*: a word that indicates subsidiarity (*aṅgatva*) through the power of its individual components.
*Samāhāra*: the rectification of a defect that has arisen.

611 *Samāhāra-dvandva*: A *dvandva* compound in which the collective whole composed of the meanings of both members is predominant. 612 *Samuccaya*: The acceptance of everything that has been presented without contradiction. 613 *Sampatti*: Death (*bhā*). 614 *Sampadyate*: Joins together; becomes united. 615 *Sampariṣvaktaḥ*:
Enveloped; closely joined; accompanied.
616 *Sampātaḥ*—karma that brings about enjoyment (*"by means of this one falls [into] heaven"*).
617 *Samprati*—at present (*now*).
*Samprasannaḥ*—free from the turbidity produced by contact with external objects.
Samprasāda—the state of being embraced by the Prājña Ātman; deep sleep (and the individual soul [jīva] possessing that state).
620 Saṃyamana—the command of Yama;
they fought in the battle for self-restraint.

622. *Saṃyoga*: the connection of a prescribed action with its fruit. 623. *Saṃyogacodanā*: an injunction regarding the connection with the fruit; that is, a rule prescribing the connection with the fruit.
624. *Saṃrādhana*: the thorough propitiation of a deity; meditation characterized by the form of devotion.

*Savāḥ* refers to the various specific oblations (*homaviśeṣa*) related to the single fire (*ekāgni*) of the *Atharvaṇikas*, beginning with the seven suns and ending with the hundred-pot rice offering (*śataudana*).
(626) *Saṃpāraḥ* is the worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) consisting of identifying oneself with non-sentient things; it is the connection with the body.
(1627) *Saṃskāraḥ* is an action that assists by direct contact (*saṃnipatyopakāraka-karma*).

The principle of the uniformity of all Vedāntas: Even though a particular meditation (vidyā), such as that on the "small ether" (dahara) or Vaiśvānara, occurs in various different Upaniṣads, there is identity alone due to the existence of a means of recognition; there is no multiplicity.

(629) The principle of the uniformity of all recensional branches (sarva-śākhā-pratyaya): When it is established that sacrificial rites (kratu) known in different recensional branches are non-different, it is logical that their constituent parts (aṅga), which are understood in one place, should be combined (upasaṃhāra) elsewhere as well.
630. *Sarvānnīnatvam*—(In times of distress) the fitness for consuming all kinds of food and the non-participation in the faults incurred thereby. 632. *Sākṣāt*—without mediation.
633. *Sāṅkarṣaḥ kāṇḍaḥ*—the section named Saṅkarṣa, concerning the deities (composed by Kāśakṛtsna).
634. Attainment of similarity (*sādṛśyāpatti*): the liberation from the forms that cause differentiation.
635. Perfection of qualities (*sādguṇya*): the necessary completeness of qualities [in a sacrifice or similar rite].
636. Those with residual karma (*sānuśaya*): those who rely on the remnants of karma already experienced.
*sāmparāyaḥ* – the time of departure from the body;

638 *sāmpādikatvam* – the state of being conceptual, established through superimposition; 639 *sisādhayiṣitam* – that which has become the object of a desire characterized by the mode of being something to be accomplished (*sādhya*); 640 *sukṛtam* – action prescribed by the scriptures that causes the gratification of the Lord, or merit (*puṇya*) achievable through action; 641 *sucaritāni* – actions established by the Vedic texts inferred from the conduct of the virtuous (*śiṣṭa*); 642 *supiram* – a hole or cavity.

643 *Suṣuptiḥ*—the state of deep sleep (*nidrāvasthā*), [which is] the state of being closely embraced by the *prājña-ātman*. 644 *Sūcakaḥ*—an indicator, that which makes known an object even though it is not in close proximity in terms of space or time. 645 *Sṛtiḥ*—a path or way. 646 *Mṛtyupakramaḥ*—the commencement of departure; the commencement of the journey, [specifically] the entry into the channels (*nāḍī*). 647 *Sṛptaḥ*—entered; those who have attained a connection through gliding—that is, through movement. 648 *Setuḥ*—a bridge (over a river, etc.), that which serves as the means for reaching the opposite bank.
—The Supreme Self (paramātman) is so called because He binds (sinoti) within Himself the entire collection of distinct conscious and unconscious entities (cid-acid-vastu-jāta).

*Stotra*—the recitation of qualities residing in a virtuous object, accomplished through chanted mantras. 652. *Sthāna*—(the means of proof that establishes [the relationship of] being a subsidiary part)—having the form of proximity (*saṃnidhāna*).
The state of being stationary (*sthāvarabhāva*)—the state of herbs, trees, and so forth (that which has no movement).
654. Stability (*sthemā*)—firmness, steadfastness.
655. Memory (*smṛti*)—the word of the sages (*ārṣa-vacana*) which originates from the Vedas (*śruti*) and serves as an inference for the Vedas.

The flowing rivers or the torrents are *svapna*— the state of experiencing sensory objects through the mind alone, while the activity of the external senses has ceased (verse 658). Those who know the *Svapnādhyāya* are those who understand the portions of the Veda dedicated to the knowledge of things indicated by dreams.
659. *Svara*: Pertaining to the utterance of sound, such as loudness, softness, and so forth.
660. *Svarāṭ*: One who is not subject to karma;
[the term refers to] qualities of essential nature (*svarūpa-guṇa*), which are qualities dependent upon the very nature of a thing and which exist as long as that substratum exists.
662 *Svādhyāya*: deep sleep (*suṣupti*).
(Bhā. 663 *Svābhāvikam*: established by its own nature (*svarūpasiddha*).
*Svāmī*: the agent of sacrifice and other rites; the enjoyer of the fruit produced by karma.
Unique to itself—its own occurrence is that which does not occur in anything other than itself. Sweat-born—those originating from the heat and moisture of the body, such as worms and the like.
Beneficial channels—the bodily veins that serve as means for the welfare of the living being.

668 *Hetvābhāsāḥ* (fallacious reasons) – those which are devoid of both pervasion (*vyāpti*) and presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), and which are the objects of an error characterized by the notion of being a valid reason (*hetutva*).
