(Śrībhāṣyam):
The analogy of the serpent and its coils; the authoritative self-study of the sacred texts.
The Deceiver [taught] the Divākīrtya,
which describes the revolution of the wheel of saṃsāra.
In the forest there is that which is to be recited; it is truth, the city of Brahman,
both king and servant.
Fire and wind are the higher knowledge; they are kinsmen.
The head-vow concerns the means of abandonment and acquisition; one who has attained the Brahman [is so called].
Completely liberated from all bonds,
O being, [perform] sacrifices, gifts, and austerities for the increase of goodness.
The lifelong student and the forest-dweller [attain] the hearing of the fame of one whose life is free from evil.
The wandering mendicant:
the state of wandering is the small ether.
Celibacy is the lotus of the heart;
it is the expiation.
Brahmā, Nārāyaṇa, and Śiva are merely ascetics who destroy themselves.
The ritual season consists of action; those established in Brahman [transcend] even the great sins.
A sacrifice consisting of knowledge,
the recitation of the *diṣṭa* [mantras], and the *āgnīdhra* office— these constitute a minor offense (*upapātaka*).
There is a difference in tone for each Veda,
just as firewood assists the fire.
The collective meditation is for those who have gone outside;
[there is] fasting unto death.
The learned and wise ones [advocate] the worship of the individual [aspects].
The New and Full Moon sacrifices,
as well as self-restraint, tranquility, and so forth,
are injunctions regarding ritual action.
The first section concerns the concentration of the mind;
[it is taught for] a learned brahmin who is unaffected by desire.
The permission for all food [is granted] to Him who is the sole cause of the entire universe, from whom the scent of every defect has been dispelled,
and who is an ocean of boundless and sublime virtues— [to Him] in His entirety...
The Vedāntas establish that the supreme Brahman, which is distinct from those [three], is to be meditated upon by those seeking liberation.

And Gaya, who was worthy of being honored at the commencement of his spiritual practice, attained a dispassion toward worldly objects that transcends material things, as well as the thirst for what is truly attainable.
It is understood that the individual soul (jīva), when migrating to another body, goes there enveloped by the subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣma) which serve as the cause for the new body.
For the commencement of the body and so forth is indeed [described] by the statement: "Of those, He made each one threefold"—this is the process of triplication (*trivṛtkaraṇa*).

When the individual soul departs, it is heard in scripture that the vital breaths follow after it; and since movement is not possible for those that are without a support, one must also admit the movement of the subtle elements which constitute its substratum.
The scriptural statement regarding the dissolution of the eyes and other organs at the time of living death is intended to refer to the departure of the presiding deities.
It is thus established that the individual soul departs enveloped by waters mixed with other elements.

It is understood that it has been stated: "The individual soul (jīva), characterized by the body in the state of faith, becomes characterized by a body in the form of Soma. Since the word denoting the body functions as a qualifier of the individual soul, its referent ultimately culminates in the qualified entity itself—the individual soul.

Because those who perform sacrifices do not know the Self, they exist here and in the hereafter as instruments for the enjoyment of the gods. Having reached this world granted by the gods, who are pleased by their worship, such a person performs that worship here through sacrifices and other rites;
there, possessing enjoyments equal to theirs, he becomes an instrument for them (a means for their satisfaction).

Having gone to that world—those who performed only meritorious deeds and no forbidden acts—they return again by way of ascent through smoke, night, the waning half of the month, the southern solstice, the year, the world of the fathers, space, and the moon; and by another manner, from the station of the moon, through space, wind, mist, smoke, cloud, and rain. (3.1.9)

For pleasure and pain are indeed the fruits of karma in the form of merit and demerit. Therefore, the scriptural mention of "conduct" (*caraṇa*) in the passages "those of pleasant conduct" and "those of foul conduct" is for the purpose of indicating karma; the teacher Kārṣṇājini maintains that by the word "conduct," karma in the form of merit and demerit is denoted, because it is impossible to obtain pleasure and pain from mere behavior alone.
"Only one who possesses proper conduct (ācāra) has the qualification for meritorious deeds;
one who neglects the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā) is perpetually impure and unfit for all rites.
The Vedas do not purify one who is devoid of conduct. From such statements as these.

Good and evil deeds alone are denoted by the word "caraṇa" (conduct), because the verb *carati* is used in the sense of action in such expressions as "he performs a meritorious deed. The teacher Bādari maintains that the result [of conduct] is the conferring of eligibility for other ritual acts, such as the twilight worship (*saṃdhyāvandana*) and so forth, which are enjoined by Vedic texts inferred from established custom (*ācāra*). (3.1.17) Just as it is not possible for those who perform undesirable acts and the like to travel by the path of the gods due to their lack of knowledge (*vidyā*), in the same way, it is not possible for them to go to the moon by the path of the fathers due to their lack of performed sacrifices (*iṣṭa*), public works (*pūrta*), and gifts (*datta*). [This is] because of the absence of ascending to and descending from the heavenly world.

Regarding the third stage, because it is stated that [the self] is completed solely through sinful actions and volitions, this third stage does not require a fifth oblation for the commencement of a new body.

In this world, it is recorded in tradition that even for some who have performed meritorious deeds, the commencement of a body occurs without depending on the fifth oblation, as in the case of Draupadī, Dhundhumāra, and others.

The deep sleep (*suṣupti*) of the living being (*jīva*) occurs in the channels (*nāḍī*), in the pericardium (*purītat*), and in the Self (*ātman*). Among these, the channels and the pericardium stand in the place of a palace and a couch, while Brahman stands in the place of the bedstead. Therefore, Brahman alone is the direct locus of deep sleep.

While in deep sleep, though still transmigrating, with all the organs exhausted and incapable of cognition or enjoyment, one reaches the Supreme Self—the place of rest—and having become refreshed, rises again for the sake of experience. (Because) the merit and demerit in the form of karma performed previously by the one who was asleep must be experienced by that very same person; furthermore, there is the recognition, "I who was asleep am now awake," and scripture also shows that it is he alone who is awakened from sleep. Therefore, it is the very same person in deep sleep who rises at the time of awakening, and not another.
For immersion in pus, blood, and the like—even if performed according to one's own will—is indeed not a human goal (apuruṣārtha).

Since the Supreme Brahman is described in the Śrutis and Smṛtis as possessing both sets of characteristics—namely, being endowed with the quality of being free from all defects and being the source of all auspicious qualities—therefore, even by virtue of its abiding in locations such as the earth or the self, not even a trace of that which is contrary to the supreme human goal can possibly exist in the Supreme Brahman. This is because of the statement regarding the immortality of the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmin), "That is your Self, the Inner Ruler, the Immortal," which precludes any undesirable consequence resulting from His connection with those respective locations, as He exercises His governance according to His own will. (3.2.12, 13)

For those subject to karma, by virtue of the will of the Supreme Person (paramapuruṣa) in accordance with the nature of their respective karmas, even a single object becomes a source of pleasure or pain at different times and for different persons. If, however, the specific nature of an object were determined solely by its own intrinsic essence (*vastusvarūpa*), then everything would always be either exclusively pleasant or exclusively painful for everyone; yet this is not observed to be the case. Therefore, if the individual soul (*jīva*) were subject to karma, that which is not the ultimate human goal (*apuruṣārtha*) would follow from the pursuit of various such karmas.
But for the Supreme Brahman, who is independent, that very relationship exists solely for the sake of the rasa of his divine play (*līlā*), which consists in various wonderful acts of governance.

Certain followers of the Śākha also [cite]: "Of these two, one eats the sweet pippala fruit, while the other looks on without eating" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.1), which shows that within the very same connection with a body, there is the lack of the human goal for the individual soul (jīva), whereas for the Supreme there is its absence, as well as the possession of a radiance dependent upon His sovereignty in the form of governance.
Furthermore, the collection of Vedānta texts reveals that He is a mine of auspicious qualities and is entirely free from all defects.
Therefore, because Brahman, although present everywhere, possesses both characteristics (liṅga), defects caused by its particular locations do not touch the Supreme Brahman.

For this reason, although the Supreme Brahman resides in various locations, it does not partake in the defects caused by those locations; therefore, the scriptures employ the analogy that "the Supreme Self, though situated here and there like the sun reflected in water, mirrors, and so forth, remains free from defect."

Just as space, though joining with individual objects such as jars or water-pots that undergo increase and decrease, is not touched by defects such as increase or decrease; and just as the sun, though seen in various receptacles of water, is not touched by the increase or decrease occurring therein;

so too the Supreme Self, abiding within the diverse forms of insentient things such as the earth and others, remains untouched by the defects of increase, decrease, and so forth found in them. Although existing everywhere, He is one alone, untainted even by the scent of defect, and a mine of auspicious qualities.
Thus.

As for the claim that Brahman’s possession of specific attributes previously mentioned is what is negated by the words "not this, not this" (neti neti), this is not tenable; for if that were so, it would be nothing more than the prattle of a deluded person. Indeed, no sane person, having first taught everything unknown through other means of knowledge as an attribute of Brahman, would then go on to negate that very same thing.

Furthermore, because [the scripture] speaks of the multitude of qualities belonging to Brahman immediately after the negation, it follows that the negation refers merely to Brahman’s connection with those specific attributes previously mentioned. (3.2.21)

The individual souls (*jīvas*) are indeed real, for they lack any modification consisting of a change in their essential nature, unlike ether and the other elements. This Supreme Person is even more real than those individual souls; for while the individual souls undergo contraction and expansion of knowledge in accordance with their karma, such [changes] do not exist in the Supreme Person, who is free from all evil. Therefore, He alone is more real than them as well.

Worship, which has taken the form of devotion (*bhakti*), is the perfect propitiation of that Supreme Brahman. It is understood from both Śruti and Smṛti that the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Him occurs only in such profound meditation (*nididhyāsana*) and not elsewhere. For, in the case of Vāmadeva and others who have directly realized the nature of the Supreme Brahman, we perceive—in their vision—that just as [Brahman] possesses the nature of knowledge, bliss, and so forth, the state of being qualified by the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) of both the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*) is likewise a quality of Brahman without distinction. Furthermore, [the scriptural text] "Not this, not this" (*neti neti*) negates only the extent of what has been previously mentioned, and does not negate the state of being qualified by the formed and the formless.

The insentient substance (acidvastu), like the individual soul (jīva), possesses the status of being a part (aṃśatva) of Brahman by virtue of being an inseparably established (apṛthaksiddha) attribute. The designation of non-difference arises because it constitutes a single portion of the qualified entity (viśiṣṭavastu), while the designation of difference is primary due to the distinction between the essential nature (svarūpa) and the specific character (svabhāva) of the attribute and the substantive.

Thus, just as light is a part of a gem, a universal (jāti) of an individual (vyakti), qualities (guṇas) of a possessor of qualities (guṇin), and the body of the self (ātman)—all by way of being attributes defined by inseparable establishment—so too here do the individual soul and the insentient substance constitute parts of Brahman.

The relationship of part and whole exists precisely through the distinction of qualifier and qualified. [Thus,] Brahman is qualified by gross sentient and insentient entities as the effect-Brahman; through the knowledge of the causal Brahman, there is the knownness of the effect—everything such as this is thus established. Therefore, the non-difference of the effect from the cause consists in the cause-Brahman being qualified by subtle sentient and insentient entities; and the faultlessness of the causal Brahman is thereby preserved.
Therefore, because of recognition through these [three criteria: connection, form, and injunction], the identity of the knowledge is established even across different recensions.

For where there is both a repeated mention (*punaḥśruti*) and a different context (*prakaraṇāntara*) regarding a single subject of comprehension (*pratipatti*), there is a difference in the knowledge (*vidyābheda*) due to the difference in what is enjoined (*vidheyabheda*), because it cannot otherwise be accounted for. But when there is no difference in the subject of comprehension, since the repeated mention and so forth are justified as being for the sake of that very comprehension, there is no possibility of another thing being enjoined therein.

Thus, since the meditation is the same in all Vedāntas, the qualities mentioned in one Vedānta must be combined with those mentioned in another Vedānta. Just as a specific quality—such as the Vaiśvānara or Dahara meditation—heard in one Vedānta is practiced because it is connected to that particular meditation for the sake of achieving its purpose, which consists in its assistance; so too, a quality declared in another Vedānta must be combined, because it is likewise connected to that meditation and its assistance is no different.

Since Brahman, the possessor of attributes, is non-different in all meditations, and since the attributes are not separate from the possessor of attributes, qualities such as bliss and others must be combined everywhere.

Those attributes which, by their very nature of defining the essential form of the object, are invariably concomitant with the cognition of that object—such as reality (*satya*), knowledge (*jñāna*), bliss (*ānanda*), purity (*amalatva*), and infinity (*anantatva*)—follow the object everywhere, just like the object’s own nature; they follow it everywhere for the sake of comprehending the essential form of the object of meditation. However, those qualities such as compassion (*kāruṇya*) and the like, which are understood as belonging to Brahman whose essential form has already been defined, do not have the status of being invariably concomitant with its cognition despite their non-separation from the possessor of the qualities (*guṇin*); therefore, they are to be combined [only] where they are specifically mentioned in a scriptural passage.

The small ether (daharākāśa) is one alone, being the substratum of qualities such as freedom from sin. Since that [ether] was first meditated upon merely in its essential nature, and since the form qualified by those qualities is distinct from it—and because it is prescribed as an object of meditation specifically as qualified by those qualities—a repetition must be performed for the purpose of contemplating what was previously grasped in its essential nature as being qualified by freedom from sin and the other attributes.

Many indicative marks (*liṅga*) are presented here to establish that this section (*anuvāka* beginning with "sahasraśīrṣam") is devoted to determining that which is to be meditated upon through all higher knowledge (*paravidyā*). The object of meditation in higher knowledge—designated by such terms as the Imperishable (*akṣara*), Śiva, Śambhu, the Supreme Brahman (*parabrahman*), the Supreme Light (*parajyotis*), the Supreme Reality (*paratattva*), and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)—is referred to here by those very same terms, and its identity as Nārāyaṇa is then enjoined.

By restating what has been heard in numerous scriptures regarding the injunction that Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme, there arises an abundance of evidence for the conclusion that Nārāyaṇa alone is the object of worship in all sciences—that supreme Brahman characterized by qualities such as bliss, specified by attributes like "not gross" (asthūla) and so forth.

Since it is stated that whatever sacrificial ritual action consisting of performance (*kriyāmaya*) is performed in the fires built of bricks, that very same thing is performed here as consisting of mind (*manomaya*) in the fires such as *manas* and others which have the mind as their source, it follows that even the sacrifice (*kratu*) is understood here as consisting of knowledge (*vidyāmaya*). Thus, for one who possesses such knowledge—that is, for one who has the sacrifice consisting of knowledge—all beings always build up [his fires].

Since the inner self (pratyagātman) is also included within the category of the object of worship by virtue of being the body of the Supreme Brahman who is the object of worship, the Self must be meditated upon during the time of worship in exactly that form which it possesses in the state of liberation. For it is heard in scripture: "In whatever way a person intends in this world, so does he become after departing from here"; thus, attainment is indeed in accordance with one's meditation. Therefore, through such passages as those concerning Prajāpati, the result of meditating on the Supreme Self—whose qualities include freedom from sin and so forth—and who has the inner self as His body, is the attainment of that very same form.
Thus, the inner self (pratyagātman) must be investigated precisely as it appears in its attained form.

The words "one should know," "one should meditate upon," and so forth—which, occurring in their respective contexts, bring about the realization through the repetition of the cognition whose object is Brahman characterized by attributes such as being the sole cause of the world and being free from sin—distinguish these meditations (*vidyā*) consisting of the repetition of cognition. Furthermore, it is determined that the syntactically complete sentences in each context, which designate specific meditations connected to the fruit consisting of the attainment of Brahman, designate distinct meditations.

For Brahman, when experienced by oneself as one's own, is an unsurpassed and limitless bliss; and if such an experience of Brahman is attained through a single means of knowledge (*vidyā*), what need is there for another? Thus, the possibility of their combination (*samuccaya*) does not exist. For in the case of heaven and the like, since they are limited in terms of space, time, and essential nature, a greater degree of them is possible depending on factors such as location; therefore, for one who desires those [limited results], a combination is possible.

All forms of knowledge (vidyā) result in the attainment of Brahman by way of dispelling beginningless karma and ignorance that are contrary to the experience of Brahman; thus, because their fruit is non-distinct, there is indeed an option (vikalpa) among them all.

However, in the case of ritual actions (karman), since the individual soul (jīva)—the agent—is taught as being distinct from the supreme Brahman, who possesses infinite, unsurpassed, and excellent auspicious qualities that are the opposite of all that is to be abandoned, Bādarāyaṇa’s opinion is that the fruit arises solely from knowledge (vidyā).

From the statement, "They desire to know [Brahman] through sacrifice and so forth," meaning they wish to attain knowledge by means of sacrifice and the like, it is understood that sacrifices and such acts are instruments for attaining knowledge—just as one speaks of "desiring to kill with a sword. Furthermore, this knowledge is distinct from the mere intellectual comprehension of the meaning of scriptural sentences; it is denoted by terms such as *dhyāna* (meditation) and *upāsana* (worship); it takes the form of a most vivid memory characterized by direct perception; it is supremely dear; it acquires excellence through daily practice; and it persists until death as the means to liberation.

Through such meditations (*dhyāna*) performed day after day by means of obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites—which consist in the propitiation of the Supreme Person—knowledge arises through the grace of the Supreme Person. This is established by the scriptural text: "They desire to know [Brahman] through sacrifice and so forth" (*yajñādinā vividiṣanti*). Therefore, for householders who possess ritual duties, knowledge depends upon all rites, both obligatory and occasional, such as sacrifice.

Since knowledge arises from the state of mental concentration (*cittasamādhāna*), tranquility (*śama*) and the other [disciplines] serve as its visible prerequisites; furthermore, because tranquility and the rest must necessarily be practiced for the attainment of knowledge, they too must be practiced. Nor is there any mutual contradiction between ritual actions (*karman*) and tranquility, self-restraint (*dama*), and so forth, on the grounds that the former consist of the activity of the organs while the latter consist of their cessation; for the activity of the organs applies to what is enjoined, whereas its cessation applies to what is not enjoined and to those things devoid of purpose, thus having distinct spheres of application.
Therefore, tranquility and the other virtues must also be practiced by the householder.

Therefore, for the wise person established in any of the stages of life (āśrama), silence—along with sacrifices and other duties of his own stage—is prescribed as another auxiliary to knowledge, in the words: "Then he becomes a sage."

The wise man should live performing those actions of a child that consist in the non-manifestation of his own nature; for the specific stage of life known as childhood is not something to be adopted [as a practice], and because other [characteristics of childhood], such as acting according to whim and so forth, are heard in scripture to be contrary to knowledge.

Even for meditation (*upāsana*) which has liberation as its fruit, there is likewise no fixed rule regarding the time of its arising when it is produced by means of its own specific instruments—namely, superior ritual actions (*karma*); for, as in the previous case, its state is understood to consist in the absence of obstacles and the completion of obstacles. Even in that case, since the possibility of obstacles exists due to the potential occurrence of powerful transgressions against those who know Brahman committed in the past, there is indeed the possibility of obstruction.

Having meditated upon Brahman as the Self of the meditator—that is, as that which is to be meditated upon as one's own Self—the meditator, who is the inner self (*pratyagātman*), is like the Self of his own body; likewise, the Supreme Brahman is the Self even of one's own self. Thus, one should meditate upon the Brahman to be meditated upon as "the Self. For this [Supreme Self] is the Self of all conscious and unconscious entities, because "all this, indeed, is Brahman, for it is born from That, dissolves into That, and breathes in That" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 3.14.1); and because He is their source, their support, their end, their controller, and their body, He is the Self of everything.

Just as there is the identification "I am a god," "I am a human," because the inner self (pratyagātman) is the Self with respect to one's own body, so too, since the Supreme Self is also the Self of the inner self, it is logical that there should be the identification "I" with respect to Him as well.

Thus, accepting that all cognitions have Brahman as their ultimate ground (brahmakaniṣṭhatva) as established by the scriptures, they likewise accepted that all words have Brahman as their ultimate ground; and so they spoke with mutual identification: "I am indeed you, O Blessed Deity! You are indeed me, O Blessed Deity!"

Thus, the injunction "one should meditate [on the Self] as 'I am the Self'" and the prescription of meditating on distinctness in the passages "meditate on the Self as non-different" and "having known the Self and the Impeller as distinct" are not contradictory. Because one meditates on it as one's own self through the thought "I am," the prohibition against meditating on it as something else—namely, "But he who worships another deity... he does not know"—is preserved.

Just as one contemplates the superiority of one's own body over oneself, so too, by contemplating the superiority of the Supreme Self over one's own self, the injunction for the contemplation of distinctness is preserved.

Since the Supreme Brahman is the Self of the inner self (pratyagātman), and that [inner self] is the body of Brahman, it was stated in the prohibitive passage, "For this is incomplete. Therefore, it is established that Brahman is to be meditated upon as the Self of the meditator.

In meditations on symbols (pratīkopāsana) such as "One should meditate on the mind as Brahman" and "Vaiśvānara Upastha meditated on Name as Brahman," one must not contemplate the symbol as being the Self. For the symbol is certainly not the Self of the meditator. In meditations on symbols, the object of meditation is the symbol itself; it is not Brahman. Brahman, however, is merely a qualifying attribute for the vision [superimposed] thereon. Indeed, a meditation on a symbol consists in contemplating something that is not Brahman as being Brahman.
Since the symbol, which is the object of meditation, lacks the nature of being the Self of the meditator, it should not be contemplated in that manner [as the Self].

Since it is logical that Āditya and the others alone possess superiority with respect to the *udgītha* and so forth, one should indeed cultivate the meditative vision (*dṛṣṭi*) of Āditya and the rest upon the *udgītha* and other auxiliary elements of the sacrifice; [but not the meditative vision of the *udgītha* and so forth upon Āditya and the rest]. For it is by means of propitiating deities such as Āditya that even ritual actions become instruments for attaining their results.

One should practice, while seated, that knowledge—which is enjoined by the Vedānta scriptures as the means to liberation, denoted by such terms as *dhyāna* (meditation) and *upāsana* (worship), and consisting of a continuous stream of memory that is repeatedly renewed. For it is only for one who is seated that one-pointedness of mind is possible; this is because both standing and walking require physical effort, and because sleep may occur while lying down. To ensure the cessation of the effort required to support the lower half of the body, one should sit with a backrest (*sāpāśraya*).

Since meditation (*dhyāna*) constitutes the very nature of worship (*upāsana*), one-pointedness of mind is necessarily required. For meditation is the contemplation of a single object uninterrupted by heterogeneous cognitions. Through this one-pointedness of mind, steadiness (like that of the earth or mountains) can only belong to the worshipper while remaining seated. And they [the authorities] remember that meditation belongs only to one who is seated: "In a clean place... having made the mind one-pointed... sitting on a seat, one should practice yoga for the purification of the self."

Since no specific place or time other than one-pointedness is heard of [in the scriptures], that very place and time which are conducive to one-pointedness are the [fitting] place and time for meditation (*upāsana*), because of the supplementary statement [in the scripture]: "in a place favorable to the mind."

Power (*śakti*) as well is simply the displeasure of the Supreme Person. Thus, knowledge (*vidyā*), being itself supremely dear because the object of knowledge is dear to the knower, and having the nature of propitiating the Supreme Person who is the object of knowledge, destroys the displeasure of the Supreme Person produced by the accumulation of previously committed sins. That same knowledge also obstructs the arising of the displeasure of the Supreme Person caused by future sins that would otherwise occur after its own production.

By the same reasoning already stated, merit (*puṇya*) also undergoes non-clinging (*aśleṣa*) and destruction (*vināśa*) through knowledge (*vidyā*), because it shares the common characteristic of being opposed to the fruit of knowledge. This is evident from the scriptural statement, "All evils (*pāpmānaḥ*) turn back from here," since even merit is designated by the term "evil" (*pāpma*). For one desiring liberation (*mumukṣu*), even merit results in an undesirable fruit; therefore, merit is designated by the word "evil. However, after the fall of the body, those merits that yield visible fruits conducive to knowledge perish.

Prior to the arising of knowledge (*vidyā*), both good and evil deeds whose fruits have not yet begun to operate are destroyed by that knowledge without distinction. This is because of the scriptural statement regarding the limit of delay until the fall of the body: "For him there is delay only so long as he is not released; then he shall be merged [in Brahman]" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.14.2). Furthermore, there is no evidence for the existence of residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) serving as the cause for the continued existence of the body other than the Lord's satisfaction produced by meritorious and non-meritorious karma.

The duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-dharma*), such as the *agnihotra* sacrifice and others, must indeed be performed because there is no possibility of their fruits adhering [to the knower]. For the wise person, the performance of the *agnihotra* and other rites is solely for the sake of the effect known as knowledge (*vidyā*); since those rites have that [knowledge] as their purpose, there is no possibility of the adherence of their [own] fruits. Indeed, the status of the *agnihotra* and other rites as means to knowledge is observed in such passages as: "Him [one seeks to know] by the recitation of the Vedas... and so forth.

Since knowledge—which is capable of receiving further excellence through practice—must be produced day after day until death, the duties of the stages of life (āśramakarma) must also be performed daily for the sake of its production. Otherwise, if the duties of the stages of life are neglected, the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) would become defiled, and the arising of knowledge itself would not occur.

Thus, in this manner, the infinite karma—consisting of merit and demerit—that has been accumulated since beginningless time, which was performed prior to the knowledge of Brahman, whose fruits have not yet been experienced, and whose results have not yet begun, is destroyed by the majesty of that knowledge. Furthermore, that which is performed after the commencement of knowledge does not adhere to the knower. In this regard, all merit is taken up by the friends of the knower, while his enemies take up his demerit; thus, [the doctrine] is faultless.

Regarding the scriptural statement, "In a person who is self-restrained, speech merges into the mind," this teaching of the merging of speech into the mind is appropriate only if it is the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of speech that merges into the mind, not merely its function (*vṛtti*). Speech is conjoined with the mind; it does not dissolve therein, because the mind is not the material cause (*prakṛti*) of speech.

(Thus: The mind, together with all the sense organs, is merged into the vital breath (prāṇa); it is not merely the function of the mind. This is because of the scriptural statement: "The mind [is merged] in the vital breath."

And that vital breath (prāṇa) merges into the individual soul (jīva), who is the lord of the organs. The merging of the vital breath, conjoined with the soul, occurs into heat (tejas); for as the soul migrates, it is understood to consist of all the elements (sarvabhūtamaya).

This departure [of the soul] prior to entering the channels is common to both the knower and the ignorant. However, regarding the state of having entered those channels, a distinction is heard in scripture: departure through the crown of the head pertains to the knower; and the statement "here he attains Brahman" refers to that experience of Brahman which occurs at the time of meditation.

The knower departs solely through the hundred-and-first channel that leads to the crown of the head. For the knower, by virtue of the power of the knowledge of the threefold sacrifice—which constitutes the supreme worship of the Supreme Person—and through the application of recollecting the extremely dear goal of the Self as a residual effect of that knowledge, becomes graced by the gracious Supreme Person with His heart. Consequently, the heart—the abode of that individual soul—becomes illuminated at the top.
Thus, the knower, having his path revealed by the grace of the Supreme Person, recognizes that channel; in this way, the departure of the knower is logically established.

For even during the summer season, the presence of the sun’s rays is observed at night; therefore, for the wise who die at night as well, the attainment of Brahman indeed occurs by means of the path of light alone. Because actions whose effects have not yet begun—which serve as causes for downward rebirth—are destroyed through their connection with knowledge, and because future actions do not adhere [to the soul], and because the effect that has already begun lasts until the final body, the attainment of Brahman is established even for the wise person who dies at night.

For the very same reason that was stated as the cause for the attainment of Brahman even for one who dies at night, the attainment of Brahman is established for one who dies during the southern solstice as well.

Since all these scriptural passages establish the single path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi*) everywhere—though with variations of omission and addition—the knower proceeds by that very path of light and so forth.

The venerable Bādarāyaṇa maintains that the group of conducting deities, beginning with the Radiance (arcis), leads both those who worship the Supreme Brahman and those who worship the Self—which is distinct from primordial matter (prakṛti) and identical with Brahman—as being of these two kinds.

This very Self, whose nature is one of having its [defects] such as sin destroyed, has its true form obscured during the state of transmigratory existence by ignorance known as *karma*. Upon attaining the Supreme Light, it becomes one whose true form is fully manifested. Therefore, qualities such as freedom from sin belong to the individual self (*pratyagātman*) through its union with the Supreme Brahman; for when the concealment by ignorance has ceased, the conscious being perceives its own Self in its true reality. Thus, the liberated one, as the Self of the Supreme Self and as His body—thereby being a mode of Him—experiences its own Self as non-different from the Supreme Brahman, realizing: "I am Brahman."

For the liberated one, from whom all concealment has been cast away, there is the sovereignty consisting of the unimpeded experience of Brahman—excluding the activity of governing the world—which consists in the regulation of the nature, maintenance, and specific functions of all sentient and insentient beings.

Just as it is understood from scripture that "there exists the Supreme Person, designated as the Supreme Brahman, who is the ocean of affection for those who take refuge in Him, supremely compassionate, whose will is ever true, omniscient, distinct from all other entities, the cause of the birth and so forth of the world, a continuous stream of auspiciousness opposed to everything that is to be abandoned, and free from any possibility of being equalled or surpassed."

Thus, from the very words [of the scripture], it is understood that: "He, being pleased by the propitiation—which consists of the worship supported by the duties of the castes and stages of life performed day after day—having turned back the ignorance consisting of the accumulation of beginningless and infinite karma for those who worship Him, and having caused them to attain His own nature, which is the experience of boundless and unsurpassed bliss, does not cause them to return."
May Mādhava be pleased by that learned Rāmabhadra, who has appropriately compiled the words of the Siddhānta in this Śrībhāṣya.
